authors.name: Berni Francesco
authors.biography: Francesco Berni (Ferrara, 1610–13 October 1673), not to be confused with the celebrated sixteenth-century Tuscan poet of the same name, was a Ferrarese jurist, civic official, professor of eloquence, academician, dramatist, librettist, and author of occasional and historical works. His career belongs to the cultural world of papal Ferrara after the devolution of the duchy in 1598, when municipal institutions, aristocratic households, academies, religious confraternities, and visiting princely courts jointly sustained an active culture of ceremonial oratory and theatrical spectacle. Berni served as secretary to the civic magistracy and was employed as its orator before Pope Innocent X and two of his successors. He also taught eloquence at the University of Ferrara. His position combined legal and rhetorical training with the practical duties of public representation: addresses, commemorations, festival descriptions, academic discourses, and dramatic texts were complementary aspects of a single professional identity.Academies provided one of the principal structures of Berni’s intellectual and social activity. He belonged to the Accademia dei Confusi, before which he delivered L’omicidio amoroso di Radamisto, an academic discourse drawn from the twelfth book of Tacitus’s Annals and printed by the ducal and camerale printer Francesco Suzzi in 1640. He was also prince of the Accademia degli Intrepidi and a founder of the Accademia dei Fileni, in which he bore the name L’Aggirato. These affiliations were not merely titular. His surviving publications show sustained participation in collective exercises that united rhetoric, historical exemplarity, poetry, music, and ceremonial display. L’Accademia raunatasi nel Castello di Ferrara il dì 16 giugno 1645, addressed to Marchese Ercole Trotti, records one such occasion, while the two-volume Dell’Accademia, printed at Ferrara in 1657–1658 by the episcopal printers Alfonso and Giovanni Battista Maresti, assembled a broader body of academic material. The edition was embellished with an engraved frontispiece by Silvestro Maria Curletti, an indication of the visual and bibliographical care accorded to Berni’s learned persona.Berni’s earliest securely documented activity already places him within the culture of the courtly festival. In 1631 he described a foot tournament and its allegorical invention, together with the piscatory fable Alcina maga, represented in the Sala dei Giganti at Ferrara during Carnival. His subsequent writings repeatedly served occasions involving distinguished visitors, marriages, funerals, and civic or dynastic commemoration. Le pretensioni del Tebro e del Po (1642), for which the poetic composition was supplied by Ascanio Pio di Savoia and the description by Berni, commemorated the arrival in Ferrara of Prince Taddeo Barberini. L’esequie trionfali del marchese Guido Villa (1656) documented the elaborate obsequies celebrated in the Ferrarese church of San Francesco. Such publications belong to the bibliographical category of the festival book: they preserved otherwise transient performances by recording their allegorical programmes, scenic actions, ceremonial structures, and political meanings.His historical interests are most conspicuous in De gli eroi della Serenissima Casa d’Este ch’ebbero il dominio in Ferrara, printed by Francesco Suzzi in 1640 and dedicated to Francesco I d’Este, Duke of Modena. Conceived as a sequence of lives commemorating the former rulers of Ferrara, the project remained incomplete: of the twenty-four biographies apparently planned, only five were published, treating Almerico, Tedaldo I, Bonifacio III, Matilda, and Azzo VIII. The volume contained an engraved title and five portrait plates. Contemporary prefatory evidence associated its engravings with Catarino Doino, although the attribution and relationship between these plates and other contemporary series of Este portraits remain bibliographically problematic. Berni’s work participated in a competitive antiquarian and iconographic enterprise through which seventeenth-century authors and engravers reconstructed Este genealogy after the dynasty’s removal from Ferrara. Its combination of historical narrative and portraiture also exemplifies the close collaboration among author, engraver, and printer characteristic of local commemorative publishing.Berni’s most sustained contribution was to musical theatre. In Ferrara he worked within a relatively stable collaborative group comprising the composer Andrea Mattioli, the theatrical engineer Carlo Pasetti, and the patron and organizer Cornelio Bentivoglio. Mattioli set Berni’s La palma d’amore, performed at the theatre of San Lorenzo during Carnival 1650 for the marriage of Francesco Maria Estense Mosti and Caterina Pio di Savoia, and Il ratto di Cefalo, staged on 26 June 1650 in the theatre of the Sala Grande with machinery devised by Pasetti.Il ratto di Cefalo was revived during the following Carnival, when Berni’s L’esiglio d’Amore, composed by Mattioli in collaboration with Filiberto Laurenzi, was likewise performed; the latter was repeated in May 1651 with a new prologue honouring the papal legate Benedetto Odescalchi. The same Ferrarese circle produced Gli sforzi del desiderio, described as a dramatic-musical recreation and mounted in Palazzo Miroglio in 1652 for the passage of the archdukes of Tyrol, and L’Antiopa, performed in the Sala Grande on 23 and 24 February 1653. These works disclose a dramaturgy conceived in conjunction with music, transformations, stage machinery, and the architecture of temporary performance rather than as an autonomous literary text.Berni’s reputation extended beyond Ferrara. He was favourably received by members of the Austrian archducal house and by the ducal courts of Parma and Mantua; in 1658 the Duke of Mantua conferred upon him the title of count. His connection with the Farnese court culminated in the festivities for the marriage of Ranuccio II, Duke of Parma, and Margherita Violante of Savoy in 1660. For the Teatro Farnese he wrote La Filo, overo Giunone rappacificata con Ercole, a musical drama associated with Francesco Manelli, and I sei gigli, a tournament intended for performance on a subsequent evening. Other compositions connected with the same nuptial celebrations included La gara degli elementi and Le ali d’Amore. In these works spoken and sung drama, dance, tournament, allegory, and dynastic compliment formed parts of a coordinated ceremonial programme. The geographical movement of Berni’s texts between Ferrara and Parma demonstrates the mobility of librettists, musicians, engineers, and printed festival descriptions within the courts and aristocratic networks of northern Italy.In 1666 Berni consolidated his dramatic reputation through I drami del signor conte Francesco Berni, da varie impressioni qui raccolti e ristampati, issued at Ferrara by Giulio Bolzoni Giglio and Giuseppe Formentini and dedicated to Ranuccio II. The collection detached a substantial portion of his theatrical writing from the ephemeral circumstances of individual performances and presented it as a coherent authorial corpus. This act of collection is important in the history of the libretto: like several other seventeenth-century dramatists, Berni sought to preserve texts originally printed as occasional performance books by gathering them into an edition intended for continued literary circulation. He nevertheless remained an occasional writer to the end of his life; an ode celebrating the marriage of Hebe and Hercules in honour of Cardinal Sigismondo Chigi, legate of Ferrara, appeared in 1673.Berni died at Ferrara on 13 October 1673, aged sixty-three. His historical significance rests less upon any single work than upon the unusually complete intersection represented by his career: university eloquence, municipal service, academy culture, historical commemoration, dynastic patronage, festival publishing, and opera. His writings document the mechanisms by which seventeenth-century spectacle was conceived, financed, performed, described, and transmitted in print. They also illuminate the professional transformation of the librettist from an occasional supplier of verse into a recognizable author capable of collecting, revising, and presenting his dramatic works under his own name.

Worm track to the lower outer corner of the first ten leaves, which then becomes just a small hole, never affecting the text, other work track to the outer margin of the final leaves with no loss of text, two small holes on l. Extremely rare first and only edition of the account by Francesco Berni (1610-1673, disguised under the academic name of “Aggirato”) of the first festival held in Ferrara after the War of the Mantua Succession (1628-1631), to celebrate the wedding of Giovanni Francesco Sacchetti (1595-1656) and Beatrice Estense Tassoni (1611-1633), in the presence of the Duke of Mantua, Charles de Nevers -to whom the volume is dedicated- and Cardinal Giulio Sacchetti. The book describes a tournament organised by Borso Bonacossi at Carnival time and accompanied by recited texts (one of which is signed by Ottavio Magnanini), as well as poems, stage designs, and machinery (pp. 6-86). It also contains the Alcina maga, a “favola pescatoria” by Sebastiano Martini (pp. 87-96), a wedding ode by Francesco Berni recited that same evening (Il Tebro, overo la Pittura loquace del pittor muto, pp. 99-107), two sonnets, by Alfonso Fiornovelli and Ippolito Visdomini, and a Latin poem by I. Visdomini. The plates depict the allegorical and historical re-enactments that were performed, including two scenes from the Alcina maga.

authors.name: Bosse Abraham
authors.biography: Introduction & Humanist/Historical Signification. Abraham Bosse, born in 1602 in Tours, France, stands as a pivotal figure in the realm of 17th-century engraving, a period marked by the flourishing of baroque art and the burgeoning influence of scientific inquiry on artistic practices. His works, numbering over 1500 engravings, are not merely artistic expressions but serve as invaluable historical documents that capture the zeitgeist of Louis XIII's France, offering insights into the social customs, fashion, and furniture of the time.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education. Bosse was born into a family likely engaged in crafts or trade, a common background for many artists of the period, which provided him an early exposure to the intricacies of design and craftsmanship. His formative years in Tours, a city known for its vibrant cultural life and as a hub of artistic production, would have nurtured his artistic inclinations. Bosse's education in perspective under the tutelage of Girard Desargues, a prominent mathematician and engineer, was instrumental in shaping his technical precision and innovative approach to engraving. Desargues was a key figure in the development of projective geometry, and his influence on Bosse is evident in the latter's meticulous attention to spatial composition and depth in his works.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks. Bosse's oeuvre is characterized by a keen observational acuity and a delicate sensibility, which he applied to a wide array of subjects. His series such as 'Le Jardin de la Noblesse Française' (1629) and 'La Noblesse Française en Église' (1630) offer a vivid portrayal of the French aristocracy, while 'Le Mariage à la Ville' and 'Le Mariage à la Campagne' (1633) provide contrasting views of urban and rural nuptial customs. His depiction of everyday scenes, such as 'Les Cris de Paris', echoes the genre scenes popularized by Dutch artists, yet with a distinctly French elegance. Bosse's religious and allegorical works, including 'Les Vierges Sages et les Vierges Folles' and 'Les Quatre Saisons', reflect the period's fascination with moral and philosophical themes, rendered with a baroque theatricality. His intellectual network included associations with the Academy of Painting, where he initially taught before his expulsion in 1661 due to ideological clashes with Charles Le Brun, the Academy's autocratic director. This conflict highlights the tension between individual artistic expression and institutional control during this era.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation. The publication of Bosse's 'Traité des manières de graver en taille-douce' in 1645 marks a significant contribution to the technical literature on engraving, providing a comprehensive guide to the art of copperplate engraving, a method that would dominate printmaking for centuries. This treatise, reprinted multiple times, underscores the enduring relevance of his technical insights. The typographical context of 17th-century Paris, a city at the forefront of printing and book production, facilitated the wide circulation of Bosse's works, contributing to his reputation across Europe. Parisian printers and publishers, benefiting from the city's status as a cultural and intellectual capital, played a crucial role in disseminating his engravings, which were valued not only for their aesthetic qualities but also as educational tools and collectibles.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy. Bosse's work was met with critical acclaim during his lifetime, though his career was not without controversy, particularly his exclusion from the Academy of Painting, which reflects broader debates about artistic autonomy and institutional authority. Despite these challenges, his engravings have been celebrated for their technical mastery and nuanced portrayal of contemporary life. His influence extends beyond his immediate period, impacting subsequent generations of artists and engravers. The enduring legacy of Abraham Bosse is evident in the continued scholarly interest in his work, as evidenced by the numerous studies and catalogues dedicated to his oeuvre. His engravings remain a vital resource for historians and art historians alike, offering a window into the social fabric and artistic milieu of 17th-century France.

publishers.name: Jombert Charles-Antoine
publishers.biography: Charles-Antoine Jombert was one of the most important Parisian booksellers and publishers of the middle decades of the eighteenth century. His career unfolded at the intersection of several fields that were becoming increasingly interconnected during the Enlightenment: military science and engineering, architecture, drawing and the graphic arts, the history of artists, and the systematic organization and dissemination of printed knowledge. A member of a Parisian family of booksellers, Jombert inherited a well-established commercial tradition but developed it into a publishing enterprise distinguished by its particular concentration on technical, military, architectural, and artistic literature. He was not simply a retailer of books. Over the course of four decades, he acted successively and simultaneously as bookseller, royal bookseller, printer, publisher, author, editor, bibliographer, and compiler of catalogues of artists' works.Jombert's importance lies above all in the breadth and coherence of this activity. His shop, identified by the sign À l'Image Notre-Dame, became closely associated with books concerning artillery, engineering, architecture, drawing, and the graphic arts. His commercial and editorial activity connected institutions, artists, engineers, architects, engravers, collectors, and readers who otherwise belonged to different professional and intellectual milieus. His publications consequently provide an important case study in the circulation of practical and theoretical knowledge in eighteenth-century France. They also demonstrate the extent to which the Parisian book trade could function as an intellectual infrastructure: a place where technical expertise, artistic practice, bibliographical information, and the history of art were brought together in printed form.Jombert was born in Paris on 14 March 1712 into a family already established in the Parisian book trade. His father, Claude Jombert, was a bookseller active in Paris, and Charles-Antoine became his successor following his father's death in May 1735. Jombert entered professional life at a moment when the Parisian corporation of booksellers and printers remained tightly regulated and when mastery of the trade required both commercial experience and formal admission to the guild. He was received as a maître libraire on 27 July 1736. His subsequent career, however, extended considerably beyond the ordinary functions of a bookseller. He developed a highly specialized publishing profile, cultivated relationships with authors and artists, and eventually obtained the additional status of printer. On 30 January 1754, he was received as an imprimeur, acquiring the printing establishment of Joseph Bullot. He later transferred his printing establishment to his son-in-law Louis Cellot in 1760, while continuing his activities as bookseller and publisher.The chronology of Jombert's addresses is itself revealing of the development of his business. From 1735 to 1742, the firm operated on the Rue Saint-Jacques, opposite the Mathurins, under the sign À l'Image Notre-Dame. In 1742 the establishment moved to the Quai des Augustins, at the corner of the Rue Gît-le-Cœur, where it remained until May 1750. From June 1750 until Jombert's retirement in 1775, the business was located on the Rue Dauphine, near the Pont-Neuf, continuing to use the sign À l'Image Notre-Dame. Contemporary imprints consequently allow the development of Jombert's business to be traced with unusual precision. His addresses were not merely commercial details: they also reveal the geographical mobility of a publishing enterprise operating within the highly concentrated ecosystem of the Parisian book trade.Jombert's official relationship with the French military establishment formed one of the defining characteristics of his career. He became associated with the title Libraire du Roi pour l'Artillerie et le Génie, or, in some imprints, libraire du Roi pour l'artillerie & le génie. His shop consequently acquired a distinctive position within the market for military and engineering literature. Rather than concentrating exclusively on belles-lettres or the conventional repertory of the Parisian bookseller, Jombert specialized in publications concerned with fortification, artillery, engineering, surveying, hydraulics, architecture, drawing, and related mathematical disciplines. His catalogue therefore reflected the close relationship between theoretical knowledge and practical expertise that characterized the French Enlightenment.This specialization is particularly evident in his publication of works by Bernard Forest de Bélidor, whose writings were fundamental to the development and transmission of eighteenth-century military and engineering knowledge. Jombert published editions of Bélidor's Architecture hydraulique, as well as other technical works intended for engineers and artillery officers. The title pages of such publications explicitly identify Jombert as the royal bookseller for artillery and the engineering corps, demonstrating the institutional identity under which his firm operated.His publishing programme extended beyond military engineering, however, and it was precisely the relationship between technical and artistic knowledge that distinguished Jombert's intellectual profile. Drawing occupied a particularly important place within his interests. In 1740 he published the Nouvelle méthode pour apprendre à dessiner sans maître, a substantial instructional work accompanied by 120 plates. The complete title describes the book as an exposition of the elementary principles and general rules of drawing, together with methods for studying the art, examples, academic figures drawn from nature, and proportions of the human body derived from antique models. The work includes explicit sections on geometry, the study and practice of drawing, human proportions, and related principles.The Nouvelle méthode is especially significant because it demonstrates that Jombert's interest in art was not limited to the commercial distribution of luxury books. He was actively engaged in the formulation and dissemination of practical knowledge. Drawing was presented not simply as an accomplishment of artistic taste but as a disciplined practice founded upon geometry, proportion, observation, and method. The organization of the work therefore corresponds closely to the broader Enlightenment tendency to make specialized knowledge teachable through systematic exposition, ordered demonstrations, and carefully designed illustrations. The surviving digital copy shows, for example, dedicated sections on the geometrical principles necessary for drawing and on the proportions of the human body.The book also illustrates the importance of collaboration in Jombert's publishing practice. Bibliographical records associate the Nouvelle méthode with Charles-Nicolas Cochin, whose participation connects the project to the Parisian world of academic drawing and engraving. Rather than treating Jombert as an isolated author, therefore, it is more accurate to understand him as an editor and mediator operating within a network of artists, engravers, authors, and technical specialists.Architecture represented another major component of Jombert's publishing activity. His relationship with the architect Jacques-François Blondel was particularly consequential. Before the appearance of the great Architecture françoise, Jombert had already published Blondel's De la distribution des maisons de plaisance, et de la décoration des édifices en général in 1737–1738. This collaboration established a durable connection between the bookseller and one of the principal French architectural theorists of the eighteenth century. Jombert subsequently became the publisher of Blondel's most ambitious historical and descriptive survey of French architecture.Published in Paris between 1752 and 1756, Blondel's Architecture françoise, ou Recueil des plans, élévations, coupes et profils des églises, maisons royales, palais, hôtels & édifices les plus considérables de Paris, ainsi que des châteaux & maisons de plaisance situés aux environs de cette ville, ou en d'autres endroits de la France appeared under Jombert's imprint in four large folio volumes. The BnF records the publication as Paris, chez Charles-Antoine Jombert, 1752–1756, in four volumes with plates.The Architecture françoise was an exceptionally ambitious undertaking. Its purpose was not merely to provide illustrations of buildings but to combine architectural representation, historical description, measurement, and theoretical discussion. The surviving bibliographical evidence indicates that Jombert had acquired a substantial group of copperplates associated with Jean Mariette's earlier architectural publishing projects around 1750. He intended to reorganize and expand this material and commissioned Blondel to supply a new and more extensive text. The resulting publication was planned on an even larger scale than the four volumes ultimately issued: the original project envisaged eight volumes and approximately 1,200 plates, but publication ceased after the fourth volume in 1756.The significance of the Architecture françoise consequently resides partly in the way it demonstrates Jombert's editorial conception of architectural knowledge. Earlier architectural books could function as pattern books, collections of models, or repositories of exemplary buildings. Jombert's project, by contrast, brought together extensive visual documentation, architectural description, historical information, and theoretical commentary. The publication thus belongs to the broader eighteenth-century movement toward the systematic documentation and classification of artistic and architectural knowledge. Its plates, many of them large or folding, made the physical and spatial characteristics of buildings available to readers who could not directly inspect them. The book became an important documentary source for the architecture of Paris and its surroundings.Jombert's interests in architectural history also extended to the organization of material relating to earlier artists and designers. His Répertoire des artistes, published in 1765 in two volumes, is particularly important in this respect. Its full title describes it as a collection of ancient and modern architectural and ornamental compositions, accompanied by a concise historical account of the life and works of the artists represented, and conceived as a continuation of the architectural works of Jean Le Pautre. The work incorporated designs associated with a broad range of artists, including Jean Marot, Jacques Androuet du Cerceau, Jean Le Pautre, Cottart, Pierretz, Cotelle, Le Roux, and Bérain.The Répertoire is especially revealing because it combines two functions that would increasingly become central to the modern history of art: the reproduction of visual works and the construction of biographical knowledge about their makers. Jombert did not merely reproduce ornamental and architectural designs. He accompanied them with abbreviated historical accounts of the artists responsible for them. The result was a hybrid publication situated between the pattern book, the illustrated repertory, and the biographical history of art. Its organization illustrates Jombert's sustained interest in transforming dispersed graphic material into an ordered and usable body of knowledge.His activities as a compiler of artists' catalogues reached another important stage with the publication in 1770 of the Catalogue de l'œuvre de Ch. Nic. Cochin fils. This catalogue concerned Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Younger, the prominent draughtsman, engraver, and administrator associated with the French Royal Academy. The BnF records the work under Jombert's authorship and gives the publication as Paris, Imprimerie de Prault, 1770, in 144 pages.Jombert's catalogue-making should be understood within the wider eighteenth-century development of systematic documentation of artistic production. The catalogue raisonné was not yet a fully standardized genre in the modern sense, but the attempt to establish a comprehensive and ordered record of an artist's works represented an important development in the history of art collecting and connoisseurship. Jombert contributed substantially to this process through his attention to the identification, ordering, and description of graphic œuvres.His Essai d'un catalogue de l'œuvre d'Etienne de la Belle, published in 1772, provides another example. The work is explicitly organized according to the historical sequence in which the individual prints were engraved and includes a life of the Florentine painter and engraver, translated from Italian and supplemented with notes. The existence of this publication demonstrates that Jombert's catalogue-making was not restricted to French artists and that his interests extended to the wider European history of printmaking.The culmination of this aspect of his career was the publication in 1774 of his two-volume Catalogue raisonné de l'œuvre de Sébastien Le Clerc, chevalier romain, dessinateur et graveur du Cabinet du Roi. The title itself announces the methodological principle on which the work was organized: the prints were arranged in historical order according to the year in which each piece was engraved, from 1650 to 1714, and the catalogue was accompanied by a biography of Le Clerc.The Le Clerc catalogue is one of Jombert's most significant contributions to the history of print scholarship. Rather than presenting an undifferentiated inventory, Jombert sought to impose chronological and biographical structure upon a large engraved œuvre. The first volume contains, among other preliminary materials, an account of certain print collections, a discussion of the works of Le Clerc known to Jombert, a historical biography of the artist, and the principal portion of the catalogue; the second volume continues the catalogue and includes a supplement and alphabetical index.This work deserves particular attention because it illustrates the emergence of a more critical approach to the documentation of prints. Jombert's method was fundamentally bibliographical and historical. He attempted to reconstruct an artist's production through dated works, documentary evidence, collections, and comparison of surviving impressions. It would be anachronistic to describe this methodology as identical to the modern catalogue raisonné, and it would be equally misleading to claim that Jombert single-handedly transformed print collecting into an exact science. Nevertheless, his catalogues belong to an important early phase in the development of systematic documentation of artists' graphic œuvres. The BnF itself places Jombert's catalogues of Cochin and Sébastien Le Clerc among the significant ancien régime examples of the catalogue raisonné.Jombert's engagement with prints was reinforced by his position within the Parisian collecting culture of the period. In 1750, he acquired part of the stock and collection associated with the celebrated print dealer and connoisseur Pierre-Jean Mariette. This transaction was important not only commercially but intellectually, because Mariette's activities represented one of the most sophisticated forms of eighteenth-century engagement with prints, artists' œuvres, and the history of collecting. Jombert's subsequent work on catalogues and artistic repertories should therefore be viewed against the background of a Parisian culture in which the collection, identification, classification, and historical interpretation of prints were increasingly interconnected.The relationship between Jombert's bookselling business and the culture of connoisseurship was also evident in the character of the publications he issued. His catalogue included works that addressed artistic technique, architectural design, engraving, military engineering, and the history of artists. He thereby operated across professional boundaries that might appear distinct from a modern disciplinary perspective but were closely related in eighteenth-century practice. The engineer required drawing; the architect required geometry and perspective; the military engineer worked with plans, elevations, and fortification; the engraver translated visual information into reproducible form; and the publisher provided the material and commercial infrastructure through which all these forms of knowledge circulated.Jombert's publishing activity in engraving is particularly revealing. In 1758 he issued an important edition of Abraham Bosse's De la manière de graver à l'eau-forte et au burin, et de la gravure en manière noire, a work concerning the techniques of etching, engraving, mezzotint, and the construction and operation of presses for intaglio printing. The publication involved a network of contributors and practitioners, including Pierre Soubeyran, Étienne Fessard, Franz Ertinger, Charles-Nicolas Cochin, and Louis Marin Bonnet. Such a publication illustrates Jombert's role in preserving, transmitting, and updating technical knowledge about graphic production. The same intellectual orientation can be observed in his publication of technical dictionaries and manuals. Jombert issued works intended for engineers and artillery officers, including Bélidor's Dictionnaire portatif de l'ingénieur and related editions. These publications reveal that his enterprise was not simply an adjunct to the fine arts. Technical literature constituted one of the central pillars of his business. His identity as libraire du Roi pour l'artillerie et le génie was therefore not an ornamental title but a reflection of a genuine specialization within the Parisian publishing market.Architecture, military engineering, drawing, and printmaking were consequently not separate compartments in Jombert's publishing programme. They formed a coherent field of practical knowledge organized around representation, measurement, geometry, proportion, and the reproducibility of visual information. The same engraved plate could function simultaneously as an artistic image, a technical diagram, an architectural record, or an instructional model. Jombert's publishing activity exploited precisely this overlap.His commercial enterprise was also European in its scope. Paris was the centre of his operations, but the books he published belonged to an international market for scientific, military, architectural, and artistic literature. The very nature of his catalogue—particularly its concentration on engineering and architecture—made it relevant to professional readers beyond France. Jombert's publications participated in the circulation of French technical and artistic knowledge throughout the European Republic of Letters. It is therefore appropriate to regard his firm as an important node in the transnational movement of books and technical expertise, while avoiding the stronger and less demonstrable claim that he personally controlled or “dominated” European distribution.The material form of his books was equally important. Large-format architectural publications such as Blondel's Architecture françoise depended upon substantial investments in copperplate engraving, paper, typography, and the physical production of large folio volumes. The Architecture françoise, for example, was issued in four imposing folio volumes containing hundreds of engraved plates, many of them folding or double-page. Its production required the coordination of authorial, editorial, engraving, printing, and commercial resources on a considerable scale.Jombert's significance therefore cannot be reduced to the conventional image of the eighteenth-century bookseller as a commercial intermediary. His career demonstrates the active role that publishers could play in determining which forms of knowledge were made available, how they were organized, and in what visual and textual forms they reached readers. He selected projects, collaborated with authors and artists, assembled existing graphic resources, commissioned or reused plates, arranged editions, and developed publications for specialized professional audiences. In doing so, he participated directly in the intellectual construction of the books he brought to market.This editorial role is especially evident in his treatment of architectural and graphic material inherited from earlier generations. The Répertoire des artistes and the Architecture françoise both involve the recovery, rearrangement, and republication of material that had circulated in earlier forms. Jombert's work was therefore partly archival. He preserved older graphic material while placing it within new editorial frameworks designed for eighteenth-century readers. The resulting publications could function simultaneously as repositories of historical memory and as practical resources for contemporary artists, architects, engineers, and collectors.His conception of artistic history was likewise closely connected to the physical survival and organization of prints. A print was not merely an illustration. It was an object capable of being collected, classified, dated, compared, attributed, and studied. Jombert's catalogues participated in the gradual development of this attitude toward graphic works. His 1774 catalogue of Sébastien Le Clerc, in particular, attempted to reconstruct the artist's production chronologically and to provide a biographical framework through which individual prints could be understood.Jombert's work thus occupies an interesting position in the history of eighteenth-century art historiography. He was not a theorist of art on the scale of major philosophical writers of the Enlightenment, nor should he be portrayed as a direct counterpart to the principal academic historians of art. His importance was of a different kind. He created and edited the bibliographical and visual instruments through which artists' works could be recorded and consulted. His contribution lay in the organization of evidence: titles, dates, artists, prints, architectural designs, biographies, and technical descriptions were assembled into coherent publications that made artistic production more accessible to systematic study.This distinction is important because it avoids attributing to Jombert a modern conception of art history that did not yet exist in fully developed form. His catalogues were products of eighteenth-century collecting, connoisseurship, bibliography, and publishing. Their methods were shaped by the categories and expectations of their own period. Yet precisely for this reason they are historically valuable: they reveal how the classification of artistic production was being constructed before the nineteenth-century institutionalization of art history and before the modern catalogue raisonné acquired its later standardized form.Jombert's professional network extended into the artistic and intellectual circles of Paris. His association with Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Younger was especially significant, given Cochin's position as draughtsman, engraver, writer, and administrator within the French artistic establishment. Their collaboration on the Nouvelle méthode and Jombert's later catalogue of Cochin's work demonstrate a relationship that extended from practical artistic instruction to retrospective documentation of an artist's œuvre.Jombert's intellectual interests should also be understood in relation to the wider culture of the Enlightenment, although he should not be transformed into an encyclopedist in the strict sense. His publications participated in the same general movement toward classification, systematization, and the practical dissemination of knowledge that characterized eighteenth-century French intellectual life. His books attempted to make specialized information usable: drawing was broken down into principles and exercises; architectural monuments were measured, represented, and described; artists' works were arranged chronologically; technical disciplines were codified in manuals and dictionaries.The breadth of his catalogue is consequently one of the strongest arguments for his historical importance. His publications ranged from drawing manuals to architectural surveys, from engineering treatises to works on engraving, from technical dictionaries to catalogues of artists. This variety was not accidental. It reflected a conception of the book as a vehicle capable of translating specialized knowledge into reproducible textual and visual form.His association with the French military establishment further demonstrates the permeability of disciplinary boundaries in the eighteenth century. The libraire du Roi pour l'artillerie et le génie operated at a point where the interests of the state, the professions, the book trade, and scientific culture converged. Military engineering demanded sophisticated forms of mathematical and visual knowledge, and the publication of manuals, dictionaries, plans, and technical illustrations became an essential component in the transmission of such expertise. Jombert's catalogue positioned his firm at precisely this intersection.By the 1770s, however, the circumstances of Jombert's career were changing. His health deteriorated, and he became increasingly impaired in his sight. He ceased substantial publishing activity after 1775 and retired from the book trade that year. In September 1775, he sold the greater part of his bookselling stock to his son Louis-Alexandre Jombert and his son-in-law Louis Cellot. The same year he withdrew to Saint-Germain-en-Laye. He subsequently disposed of much of his private collection in April 1776.His retirement did not represent a complete rupture with the world he had inhabited. By then, his family remained active in the Parisian book trade. His sons and other relatives continued aspects of the business, and the Jombert name remained associated with bookselling and publishing. The family therefore provides an illuminating example of the hereditary character of the Parisian book trade, in which professional expertise, commercial capital, publishing privileges, addresses, and networks could pass across generations.Charles-Antoine Jombert died at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on 30 July 1784, at the age of seventy-two. His death brought to an end a career spanning almost half a century of the Parisian book trade.The historical importance of Jombert rests ultimately on the unusual combination of functions that he performed. He was at once a bookseller and publisher, a specialist in military and engineering literature, an author and editor of works on drawing and architecture, a compiler of artists' catalogues, and an intermediary between the worlds of technical knowledge, artistic practice, and collecting. His career demonstrates that the eighteenth-century publishing industry was not merely a mechanism for reproducing texts already conceived elsewhere. Publishers could actively shape intellectual production by determining which works were assembled, illustrated, revised, catalogued, and circulated.His contribution to the history of the graphic arts is particularly noteworthy. Through the Nouvelle méthode pour apprendre à dessiner sans maître, he participated in the pedagogical codification of drawing; through the Répertoire des artistes, he assembled architectural and ornamental designs with biographical information; through the Catalogue de l'œuvre de Ch. Nic. Cochin fils and the Essai d'un catalogue de l'œuvre d'Etienne de la Belle, he contributed to the systematic documentation of individual artists; and through the monumental Catalogue raisonné de l'œuvre de Sébastien Le Clerc, he produced one of the most substantial eighteenth-century attempts to reconstruct an engraved œuvre according to chronological and biographical principles.The Catalogue raisonné of Le Clerc is particularly revealing in this regard. Its chronological arrangement, preliminary discussion of collections and surviving works, biographical account, main catalogue, supplement, and index demonstrate an ambition to transform a dispersed body of prints into an ordered historical corpus. Jombert did not possess the methodological apparatus of modern print scholarship, and his work should not be judged by standards developed much later. Nevertheless, his enterprise represents an important moment in the emergence of systematic graphic documentation. It is precisely this intermediate position—between the collector's inventory, the connoisseur's notes, the artist's biography, and the modern catalogue raisonné—that makes his work so significant.Jombert's legacy should therefore be understood less as that of a solitary “genius” of publishing than as that of an exceptionally productive mediator of knowledge. His career illuminates the mechanisms through which eighteenth-century France converted practical expertise, artistic production, historical memory, and collected objects into organized bodies of printed information. His books made architectural monuments measurable and reproducible, drawing teachable through systematic principles, technical knowledge portable across professional communities, and the œuvres of individual printmakers available for chronological and bibliographical study.In this respect, Charles-Antoine Jombert occupies a distinctive place in the history of the eighteenth-century book. He stood at the convergence of the Parisian book trade, the royal military establishment, architectural publishing, artistic pedagogy, engraving, collecting, and the emerging historical consciousness surrounding works of art. His publishing house at the sign of À l'Image Notre-Dame, moving from the Rue Saint-Jacques to the Quai des Augustins and ultimately to the Rue Dauphine, became the material setting for an enterprise in which books were conceived not simply as literary commodities but as instruments for organizing and transmitting specialized knowledge.The lasting importance of Jombert consequently lies in the intersection of publication, documentation, and mediation. He did not single-handedly invent the catalogue raisonné, modern art history, or systematic bibliographical criticism. Such claims would obscure the collective and gradual nature of these developments. What he did accomplish, however, was substantial: he helped to establish a durable model of publishing in which artistic and technical knowledge could be collected, ordered, illustrated, contextualized, and distributed to specialized readers. His career offers an unusually clear example of the role played by the eighteenth-century publisher in the transformation of practical and visual knowledge into historical and bibliographical knowledge.For that reason, Jombert deserves to be considered not merely as a successful Parisian bookseller but as a significant editorial and bibliographical figure of the French Enlightenment. His publications occupy an important place in the history of architecture, military and engineering literature, drawing pedagogy, engraving, collecting, and the early formation of systematic catalogues of artists' œuvres. His career demonstrates how closely the material history of the book was intertwined with the intellectual history of art and science in eighteenth-century France. Through the books he authored, edited, published, and catalogued, Jombert helped give durable printed form to a wide range of knowledge at a moment when European intellectual culture was increasingly committed to its classification, reproduction, and transmission.

related_names.biography: Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Younger was one of the most prominent French engravers, designers, and writers on art of the eighteenth century. Born and deceased in Paris, he belonged to a distinguished family of artists and engravers and played an important role in the artistic culture of the reign of Louis XV and the early decades of the reign of Louis XVI. His career extended across courtly representation, book illustration, printmaking, artistic criticism, and the documentation of contemporary artistic and architectural culture. He was also closely connected with the intellectual and artistic circles associated with the Enlightenment, including Denis Diderot and other figures involved in the production and circulation of illustrated books.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationCochin was the son of Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Elder (1688–1754), himself a distinguished engraver, and of Madeleine Horthemels, who also belonged to the Parisian printmaking milieu. His father produced numerous reproductive engravings after works by artists including Antoine Watteau and Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin and was active in major royal and publishing enterprises. Cochin the Younger therefore grew up within an established artistic and professional environment.His technical training developed principally through his family environment and through his studies with established artists. The Louvre identifies his father, Jean Restout, and Laurent Cars/Le Bas among the figures associated with his formation, while later accounts particularly emphasize the role of Jacques-Philippe Le Bas in his training as an etcher. Rather than treating his education as the result of a single institutional apprenticeship, it is more accurate to understand it as part of the interconnected Parisian network of painters, engravers, designers, and publishers in which he developed his practice.Court Career, Major Works, and Intellectual NetworksCochin's rise to prominence was closely connected with the representation of royal ceremonies and spectacles. From the late 1730s he produced engravings commemorating important events at the French court, and in 1739 he became formally associated with the Menus-Plaisirs du Roi as a designer and engraver. His collaboration with the brothers Slodtz was particularly important in documenting the elaborate theatrical and decorative settings devised for royal festivities. Among his best-known works are engravings recording the celebrations surrounding the marriage of the Dauphin in 1745, as well as representations of courtly spectacles such as the Jeu du Roi and the funeral ceremonies of members of the royal family.Cochin was received into the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture in 1741, consolidating his position within the institutional structure of the French art world. His activities subsequently extended beyond engraving: he worked as a designer, writer on art, and artistic adviser, while maintaining close relationships with figures involved in court culture and the emerging Enlightenment.A decisive episode in his intellectual and artistic development was his journey to Italy in 1749–1751. At the initiative of Madame de Pompadour, Cochin accompanied her brother Abel Poisson, later Marquis de Marigny, together with the architect Jacques-Germain Soufflot and other members of the travelling group. The journey enabled him to study first-hand the painting, sculpture, architecture, and antiquities of the principal Italian cities. His subsequent writings reveal the importance of this experience for his understanding of classical art and for the development of the classicizing tendencies that would become increasingly influential in French art.Cochin later published an account of his Italian observations in the Voyage d'Italie, published in 1758. His interest in antiquity also led to his collaboration with the architect Jérôme-Charles Bellicard on the Observations sur les antiquités de la ville d'Herculanum, first published in Paris in 1754 by Charles-Antoine Jombert. The work combined observations on the newly excavated antiquities of Herculaneum with reflections on ancient painting and sculpture and thus belongs to the broader eighteenth-century effort to document and interpret the archaeological discoveries of southern Italy.Printing History, Book Illustration, and the Circulation of ImagesCochin's importance extended beyond individual prints to the wider history of illustrated books and the circulation of artistic knowledge. He contributed designs to a number of important publishing projects and occupied a particularly significant position within the visual culture surrounding the Encyclopédie of Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert.The famous frontispiece of the Encyclopédie, however, requires precise attribution. Cochin did not engrave the final plate himself. He produced the original design in 1764, which was exhibited at the Salon of 1765 and discussed by Diderot. The final engraving was executed by Benoît-Louis Prévost in 1772, after Cochin's design. The image subsequently circulated among subscribers and became one of the most recognizable visual statements associated with the Encyclopédie.This distinction is historically significant because it illustrates the collaborative nature of eighteenth-century print production: the conception of an image, its drawing, its translation into an engraved plate, and its subsequent dissemination through a large publishing enterprise could involve several different specialists. Cochin's role was therefore not simply that of an engraver but also that of a designer and intellectual contributor to the visual culture of Enlightenment publishing.Critical Reception and Historical LegacyCochin occupied a distinctive position between the institutions of the ancien régime and the changing artistic and intellectual culture of the Enlightenment. His work for the court preserved an extensive visual record of royal ceremonies and spectacles, while his activities as an engraver, designer, and writer connected him with the broader circulation of artistic knowledge through prints and books. His Italian journey and his writings on ancient art further demonstrate his engagement with the historical and theoretical dimensions of artistic practice.His historical importance consequently lies not only in the considerable number of prints and drawings he produced, but also in the range of functions he performed within eighteenth-century French visual culture. He participated in courtly representation, academic institutions, the production of illustrated books, the documentation of antiquities, and contemporary debates concerning artistic taste. His work thus provides an important point of intersection between the traditional institutions of the French monarchy and the expanding culture of artistic and historical inquiry characteristic of the Enlightenment.

academic_description: 8vo (192x124 mm). Engraved frontispiece, XXXII, 186, [6] pp. and 19 engraved folding plates. Large engraved headpiece before the dedication and 4 smaller headpieces at the beginning of each book, illustrating scenes in printmaking studios, engraved by Fessard and Soubeyran after Cochin and Bosse. Contemporary mottled calf, gilt spine in compartments with red morocco lettering piece, marbled endleaves, red edges (worn and rubbed, joints partly cracked). Marginal staining and foxing, overall a good, genuine copy. Third edition of Bosse’s fundamental manual on engraving, originally published in 1645. The text of this edition was expanded and edited by Charles-Nicolas Cochin. Abraham Bosse, born in 1602 in Tours, France, stands as a pivotal figure in the realm of 17th-century engraving, a period marked by the flourishing of baroque art and the burgeoning influence of scientific inquiry on artistic practices. His works, numbering over 1500 engravings, are not merely artistic expressions but serve as invaluable historical documents that capture the zeitgeist of Louis XIII's France, offering insights into the social customs, fashion, and furniture of the time. Bosse was born into a family likely engaged in crafts or trade, a common background for many artists of the period, which provided him an early exposure to the intricacies of design and craftsmanship. His formative years in Tours, a city known for its vibrant cultural life and as a hub of artistic production, would have nurtured his artistic inclinations. Bosse's education in perspective under the tutelage of Girard Desargues, a prominent mathematician and engineer, was instrumental in shaping his technical precision and innovative approach to engraving. Desargues was a key figure in the development of projective geometry, and his influence on Bosse is evident in the latter's meticulous attention to spatial composition and depth in his works.Bosse's oeuvre is characterized by a keen observational acuity and a delicate sensibility, which he applied to a wide array of subjects. His series such as 'Le Jardin de la Noblesse Française' (1629) and 'La Noblesse Française en Église' (1630) offer a vivid portrayal of the French aristocracy, while 'Le Mariage à la Ville' and 'Le Mariage à la Campagne' (1633) provide contrasting views of urban and rural nuptial customs. His depiction of everyday scenes, such as 'Les Cris de Paris', echoes the genre scenes popularized by Dutch artists, yet with a distinctly French elegance. Bosse's religious and allegorical works, including 'Les Vierges Sages et les Vierges Folles' and 'Les Quatre Saisons', reflect the period's fascination with moral and philosophical themes, rendered with a baroque theatricality. His intellectual network included associations with the Academy of Painting, where he initially taught before his expulsion in 1661 due to ideological clashes with Charles Le Brun, the Academy's autocratic director. This conflict highlights the tension between individual artistic expression and institutional control during this era.The publication of Bosse's 'Traité des manières de graver en taille-douce' in 1645 marks a significant contribution to the technical literature on engraving, providing a comprehensive guide to the art of copperplate engraving, a method that would dominate printmaking for centuries. This treatise, reprinted multiple times, underscores the enduring relevance of his technical insights. The typographical context of 17th-century Paris, a city at the forefront of printing and book production, facilitated the wide circulation of Bosse's works, contributing to his reputation across Europe. Parisian printers and publishers, benefiting from the city's status as a cultural and intellectual capital, played a crucial role in disseminating his engravings, which were valued not only for their aesthetic qualities but also as educational tools and collectibles.Bosse's work was met with critical acclaim during his lifetime, though his career was not without controversy, particularly his exclusion from the Academy of Painting, which reflects broader debates about artistic autonomy and institutional authority. Despite these challenges, his engravings have been celebrated for their technical mastery and nuanced portrayal of contemporary life. His influence extends beyond his immediate period, impacting subsequent generations of artists and engravers. The enduring legacy of Abraham Bosse is evident in the continued scholarly interest in his work, as evidenced by the numerous studies and catalogues dedicated to his oeuvre. His engravings remain a vital resource for historians and art historians alike, offering a window into the social fabric and artistic milieu of 17th-century France.

authors.name: Cirino Andrea
authors.biography: Andrea Cirino (Messina, 1618–Palermo, 6 September 1664) was a Theatine cleric, preacher, antiquarian, and compiler of works encompassing sacred exegesis, classical philology, natural history, and Roman antiquities. Early Theatine biographers describe him as belonging to a noble Messinese family. He entered the Congregation of the Clerics Regular while still an adolescent and made his solemn profession at Messina on 5 July 1634. His intellectual formation joined the scholastic and scriptural disciplines required by his order to an unusually extensive reading of pagan antiquity. Contemporary and near-contemporary accounts repeatedly emphasize his capacious memory, facility in retrieving passages from the Fathers and classical authors, and ability to employ this accumulated learning in preaching. Such testimony is conventionally encomiastic, but it corresponds closely to the conspicuously compilatory structure of his surviving publications.Cirino’s religious career was associated particularly with Messina and with the Theatine house of San Giuseppe in Palermo. He acquired a reputation as a preacher and was remembered for addressing the Palermitan populace during a period of civic disorder, urging the restoration of tranquillity. His earliest identified publication is the funeral oration delivered for Cardinal Giannettino Doria, archbishop of Palermo, printed there by Decio Cirillo in 1643. A devotional discourse for the Messinese feast of the Madonna della Lettera followed at Monteleone in 1649. These works place him firmly within the public culture of the seventeenth-century religious orator, in which sermons and ceremonial addresses served simultaneously as instruments of pastoral instruction, civic representation, and learned display.His most distinctive contribution, however, lay in the immense antiquarian compilations devoted to hunting and animals. The Variarum lectionum, sive De venatione heroum libri duo, printed at Messina by the heirs of Pietro Brea in 1650, examined the origins, practices, and cultural meanings of hunting through an accumulation of testimonia drawn from classical, Christian, historical, and mythographical literature. This enterprise was enlarged in the De venatione et natura animalium libri quinque, issued at Palermo by Giuseppe Bisagni in 1653. The publication is bibliographically complex, comprising separately titled sections, among them the extensive De natura et solertia canum and a book on fishes. Its title advertises the consultation of approximately thirty thousand passages from earlier authors, an assertion characteristic of Cirino’s conception of scholarship as the ordered recovery of an encyclopaedic textual inheritance. The work treats animals not solely as physical creatures but also as scriptural signs, medical substances, political and moral exempla, objects of legal or ritual practice, and witnesses to the customs and migrations of ancient peoples. Its woodcut illustrations and multipart organization also give it a notable place among the scientific and antiquarian books produced by the Palermitan press in the middle decades of the seventeenth century. Although sometimes classified as natural history, its governing method is more accurately described as sacred and classical erudition than as experimental zoology.Cirino’s interests extended beyond animal lore. His Historia delle cause et effetti della peste, published at Genoa in 1656, addressed the epidemic through the medical, historical, providential, and moral categories available to a learned cleric of his age. In 1657 he published at Naples a life of the Theatine Francesco Olimpio. He is also associated with the account of the festivities held in Naples for the birth of Philip Prospero, Prince of Asturias, an example of the richly illustrated festival literature generated within the dominions of the Spanish Habsburgs. His work thus moved between several characteristic forms of Baroque print culture: the occasional oration, devotional biography, civic and dynastic celebration, epidemic history, and large-scale Latin compilation. Modern scholarship has also drawn attention to his connection with the mathematician and natural philosopher Giovanni Alfonso Borelli, describing Cirino as a friend and supporter within the intellectual environment of seventeenth-century Messina and Rome.At his death Cirino left a substantial body of unpublished material. Theatine bibliographers record commentaries on the Apocalypse and other books of Scripture, together with writings on duties, Epictetus and constancy, Platonic philosophy, medicine, prodigies, and apparitions of the Cross. The present whereabouts or survival of all these manuscripts cannot be securely established. His principal posthumous publication was the Variarum lectionum de urbe Roma eiusque conditore Romulo liber singularis, printed at Palermo by Agostino Bossio in 1665 under the supervision of his confrère Francesco Maria Maggio. Devoted to Rome and its founder, it applied Cirino’s characteristic method of cumulative textual comparison to chronology, foundation legends, institutions, religion, and the antiquarian problems surrounding Romulus. The work subsequently entered wider European antiquarian circulation when Albert-Henri de Sallengre included it in the second volume of his Novus thesaurus antiquitatum Romanarum, published at The Hague in 1718.Cirino died in the Theatine house at Palermo after prolonged illness, attributed by early biographers to incessant preaching and study. The best early evidence places his death on 6 September 1664, although some later accounts give 7 September. His posthumous reputation rested less upon an original system of natural or historical explanation than upon the amplitude and organization of his learning. He belongs to the learned ecclesiastical culture of Spanish Sicily in which biblical interpretation, patristics, classical antiquities, civic history, medicine, and natural lore remained mutually permeable fields. His books are consequently important not only for their particular subjects—especially hunting, dogs, fishes, and Roman origins—but also as material witnesses to the compilation, illustration, and printing of encyclopaedic scholarship in seventeenth-century Messina and Palermo.

authors.name: Graziani Girolamo
authors.biography: Girolamo Graziani (1 October 1604–11 September 1674) was an Italian poet, diplomat, and statesman whose career unfolded at the intersection of the literary culture and political life of the seventeenth-century Este court. Born in Pergola in the Duchy of Urbino, he spent much of his adult life in the service of the Este dynasty in Modena, combining administrative and diplomatic responsibilities with an extensive literary production that included epic poetry, panegyric verse, political and historical writings, and tragedy. His principal works, particularly Il conquisto di Granata (1650) and Il Cromuele (1671), place him among the significant representatives of seventeenth-century Italian literary culture.Graziani was born in Pergola on 1 October 1604 to Antonio Graziani and Lavinia. His father served first as a uditore di rota in Ferrara and subsequently held important judicial offices in Modena. In 1619 the family moved to Modena, where Graziani continued his education. He studied at Parma and Bologna and obtained degrees in both jurisprudence and the humanities. His early formation consequently combined literary studies with the legal and administrative culture that would later prove essential to his career at the Este court.Graziani began publishing at a remarkably young age. In 1621, when he was seventeen, he published his first collection of verse, Rime di Girolamo Graziani della Pergola, in Parma. The volume contained love poetry as well as panegyric compositions addressed to members of the Este and Della Rovere families.His political career developed gradually. After the death of Duke Cesare d'Este in 1628 and the abdication of Alfonso III, Graziani was appointed secretary to the ducal princes. In 1632 he entered the personal service of Prince Obizzo d'Este, brother of Duke Francesco I, and during the following years he began to undertake diplomatic missions on behalf of the Este state. His early career was interrupted in 1641 by a political conflict surrounding Obizzo's unsuccessful attempt to obtain the cardinalate, after which Graziani was forced to leave Modena and returned to Pergola.Graziani's early literary production included La Cleopatra, an epic poem first published at Modena in 1631 and subsequently expanded and reissued. The poem established his reputation among contemporary men of letters and already displayed his characteristic interest in combining historical subjects, emotional and pathetic episodes, and dynastic themes.His major achievement in epic poetry was Il conquisto di Granata, first published at Modena by Bartolomeo Soliani in 1650. The poem consists of twenty-six cantos in ottava rima and recounts the final phase of the Christian conquest of Granada in 1492. Its narrative combines warfare, love, disguise, supernatural intervention, religious themes, and historical material, while drawing upon the traditions of Italian chivalric and heroic poetry.Contrary to some later characterizations of the poem as a straightforward continuation of Marino's poetic style, its language and structure are more complex. The poem is relatively restrained in its use of concettismo and combines epic, romance, magical, historical, and pathetic elements. Its final cantos also contain significant political and religious allusions, including prophecies concerning Christian expansion and the appearance of Christopher Columbus, whose role connects the conquest of Granada with the subsequent expansion of Christianity beyond Europe. The first edition was dedicated not to Louis XIV or Cardinal Mazarin, but to Francesco I d'Este, Duke of Modena. The dedication was rewarded by the duke with an annual pension of 200 scudi, in addition to Graziani's existing salary.Graziani's return to Modena in 1647 marked the beginning of the most important phase of his political career. He succeeded Fulvio Testi as secretary to Alfonso d'Este, son of Francesco I, and in December 1648 was sent to Paris on a diplomatic mission to seek French assistance for Modena in its war against Spain. His mission coincided with the Fronde, and his negotiations were facilitated in part by his relationship with Cardinal Mazarin.In July 1652 Graziani was formally appointed Segretario di Stato. In this capacity he accompanied Cardinal Rinaldo d'Este to Rome and was present during the conclave of 1655 that elected Pope Alexander VII. In 1658, in recognition of his services, he received the fief of Sarzano in the Duchy of Reggio together with the title of count. Under Duke Alfonso IV, who succeeded Francesco I in 1658, Graziani retained an important position at court and was appointed Consigliere di Stato.His diplomatic activity continued during the regency of Laura Martinozzi. One of his most significant diplomatic achievements came in 1673, when he helped negotiate the marriage of Maria Beatrice d'Este, daughter of Alfonso IV and Laura Martinozzi, to James, Duke of York, the future James II of England.Graziani participated in the literary academies and intellectual networks characteristic of seventeenth-century Italy. His membership in the Accademia dei Gelati of Bologna is documented by contemporary sources, including Ottavio Zani's Memorie, imprese e ritratti dei sigg. Accademici Gelati (1672).His literary activity was also closely connected with the ceremonial and political culture of the Este court. Works such as La gara delle stagioni (1652), Il trionfo della virtù (1660), and the panegyrics devoted to Cardinal Mazarin and Louis XIV demonstrate how his literary production functioned within the culture of dynastic celebration and political representation.The collection Varie poesie e prose, published at Modena by Soliani in 1662, brought together a substantial portion of his literary production and is particularly significant for understanding the relationship between his poetry, prose writings, courtly activities, and political thought. The collection also contains early evidence concerning the composition of Il Cromuele.Graziani's most distinctive contribution to political drama was Il Cromuele, a five-act tragedy dealing with the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, and the rise of Oliver Cromwell. The work was conceived during the 1660s and was first printed in Bologna by the Manolessi press in 1671; a parallel Modenese edition was issued by Viviano Soliani in the same year. The Bologna edition is particularly notable for its material presentation. It contains an engraved frontispiece and five engraved folding plates illustrating scenes from the tragedy. The surviving copies therefore demonstrate the close relationship between literary drama, visual representation, and the culture of the illustrated book in seventeenth-century Italy.The tragedy transforms the recent history of England into a drama of tyranny, regicide, and political legitimacy. Cromwell is represented as an isolated and increasingly tyrannical figure, while Charles I is presented as a noble and just sovereign whose execution acquires the symbolic character of a political and familial crime. The historical events are thus adapted to a courtly and monarchical political framework appropriate to a work dedicated to Louis XIV. Rather than treating Il Cromuele simply as a precursor of later Enlightenment historical drama, it is more accurate to regard it as a significant example of seventeenth-century Italian political tragedy and of the ways in which recent European history could be transformed into courtly dramatic discourse.The publishing history of Graziani's works reflects the close relationship between literary production and courtly patronage. Il conquisto di Granata was first printed at Modena by Bartolomeo Soliani in 1650, while Il Cromuele appeared in Bologna from the Manolessi press and in Modena from the ducal press of Viviano Soliani in 1671. Both works subsequently circulated in additional editions, demonstrating the continuing interest in Graziani's poetry and drama. The illustrated Bologna edition of Il Cromuele is particularly important in this regard. Its engraved frontispiece and theatrical plates demonstrate how the printed book could function not merely as a textual vehicle but also as a visual extension of courtly and dramatic culture.Reception and Historical LegacyGraziani enjoyed considerable recognition during his lifetime, although his later reputation proved less stable. His Conquisto di Granata was repeatedly reprinted during the seventeenth century and was regarded by later critics as one of the most accomplished Italian epic poems produced after Tasso. Modern scholarship has emphasized the poem's ability to combine epic, romance, historical, magical, and pathetic elements rather than reducing it to a simple imitation of either Tasso or Marino.His political and diplomatic career also distinguishes him from the figure of the court poet in a narrowly literary sense. Graziani occupied several important offices in the Este administration, undertook diplomatic missions to Paris and Rome, received a comital title and territorial fief, and played a significant role in the diplomatic negotiations surrounding the marriage of Maria Beatrice d'Este and James, Duke of York.Graziani died at Pergola on 11 September 1674, after leaving Modena earlier that year. His career therefore represents an unusually close conjunction of literary production, courtly patronage, diplomatic service, and political communication in seventeenth-century Italy. His works, particularly Il conquisto di Granata and Il Cromuele, provide valuable evidence for the interaction between literary culture and political thought in the European Baroque.

academic_description: 4to (190x138 mm). Engraved frontispiece, [14], 160, [2: errata] pp. and [5] engraved folding plates. Collation: [+]4(-+2) ++4 A-V4 χ². Lacking the final (blank?) leaf. Woodcut arms of the dedicatee, King Louis XIV, on the title page. Woodcut initials, head- and tail-pieces. Later boards, red sprinkled edges (joints repaired, slightly rubbed and soiled). Upper outer corner of the half title repaired, lower margin of the title page trimmed with loss of a line of text, some foxing, marginal tears to some of the plates skilfully repaired, tiny portion of a plate missing, all in all a good copy. Rare first illustrated edition, also printed in the same here without illustrations in Modena by Soliani and reprinted in Bologna by Manolessi in 1673, of this five-act tragedy by Count Girolamo Graziani, a man of letters from Modena who served as secretary and advisor to the Duke of Modena. The play, conceived in the 1660s during Laura Martinozzi’s regency in Modena, depicts the dramatic events of the English Civil War, pitting the tyrant Oliver Cromwell against the martyr Charles I. Inspired by the typically seventeenth-century tendency to rewrite recent historical events for political purposes, the play paints a hagiographic portrait of the English monarch, whose blood comes to take on a strong symbolic and almost Christ-like significance following his death sentence (cf. P. Di Nepi, Girolamo Graziani e la politica come arte: “Cromuele”, in: “F.M. Annali dell’Istituto di Filologia Moderna dell’Università di Roma”, 2-1979, Rome, 1981, pagg. 113-24).From the very beginning, the tragedy presents itself as a Baroque device in the service of defending the monarchy, through a pseudo-historical - yet theatrical - reconstruction of the events of 1649. It is true that the tragedy makes use of specific historical references, but - as is usually the case in seventeenth-century theater - these are condensed into a single night, that of January 30, 1649 (cf. S. Miglierina, Il sangue di Carlo: apologia e licenza teatrale nel Cromvele di Girolamo Graziani, in: “Krypton”, vol. 1, 2013, p. 47).The first mention of the tragedy’s composition appears in the preface to Girolamo Graziani’s Varie Poesie e Prose (1662). Beginning in 1666, the composition of the Cromuele was accompanied by an extensive correspondence with Jean Chapelain, with whom Graziani - who was on the payroll of Colbert on behalf of the Sun King - corresponded regularly (cf. R. Galli Pellegrini, La Tragédie Italienne à l’école du classicisme Français: le rôle de Chapelain dans la genèse du “Cromuele” de Graziani, in: “Quaderni del Dipartimento di Lingue e Letterature Straniere Moderne, Università di Genova”, 2-1987, pp. 35-57).There is no mention of a performance of Il Cromuele in the preface to the second edition of 1673, nor is there any trace of it in the extensive documentation on theatrical performances in the Este States preserved in the State Archives of Modena. The likely reason for the play’s failure to be staged was the dynastic marriage that took place in 1673 (just two years after the 1671 publication) between Maria Beatrice d’Este and Giacomo Stuart, who had been widowed in the very year of Il Cromuele’s publication by Anna Hyde - the woman with whom he appears to be in love in the tragedy. This was an inconvenient presence for Graziani, who, as secretary of state, had looked after the Este family’s interests in that marriage (cf. M. Fasce, Introduzione e note alle edizioni de Il Cromuele, in: “Storie Inglesi, l’Inghilterra vista dall’Italia tra storia e romanzo XVIII sec.”, C. Carminati-S. Villani, Pisa, 2011, pp. 297-330).Girolamo Graziani, who earned a degree in law and humanities in Bologna, served as an advisor and secretary to the princes, that is, to the sons of Alfonso III of Modena. After several legal disputes, he traveled in 1648 on a diplomatic mission to Paris, where he witnessed the Fronde, before returning to Modena in 1649, where he continued his diplomatic and literary career. Graziani was in Paris, at the French court, at the time of the execution of the King of England, and this suggests that he was a direct witness of the scandal that the event could have caused at the court of the nephew of the murdered king. Graziani decided to recount those events in a dramatized version twenty-two years after Charles’s death, thirteen after Cromwell’s, and eleven after the restoration of the monarchy in England (cf. F. Tarzia, Graziani, Girolamo, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 58, Rome, 2002, s.v.).
