publishers.name: Vögelin Ernst
publishers.biography: Ernst Vögelin (1529–1589), Latinized in scholarly imprints as Ernestus Voegelinus or Voegelius, stands as one of the most intellectually ambitious, typographically refined, and politically controversial master printers and publishers of the Holy Roman Empire during the second half of the sixteenth century. Operating primarily from the vibrant mercantile and academic hub of Leipzig, and later from Frankfurt am Main and Constance, Vögelin transformed a modest printing enterprise into the celebrated Officina Voegeliniana, a cultural engine that propelled the intellectual dissemination of Northern Protestant Humanism, late Renaissance philology, legal jurisprudence, and neo-Aristotelian philosophy throughout Europe. Situated historically at the precarious intersection of humanistic erudition and intense confessionalization (Konfessionalisierung), Vögelin’s publishing career exemplifies the pivotal role played by printer-scholars in defining the doctrinal, literary, and academic contours of the post-Reformation era. His output not only shaped the curriculum of Protestant universities such as Leipzig and Wittenberg, but also situated him at the center of the explosive theological controversies surrounding Philippism and Crypto-Calvinism that rocked Electoral Saxony in the 1570s.Born on August 10, 1529, in the imperial city of Constance (Konstanz), Vögelin belonged to an established civic family deeply integrated into the urban patriciate and the intellectual currents of Southwestern Germany. His early formative education was steeped in the classical humanities, combining rigorous training in Latin and Ancient Greek with exposure to the emerging evangelical theology of the Swiss and Upper Rhenish Reformation. Seeking advanced scholarly opportunities in Northern Germany, Vögelin migrated to Saxony and matriculated at the University of Leipzig during the late 1540s. It was in Leipzig that Vögelin made the decisive transition from academic student to print entrepreneur. He gained intimate entry into the elite publishing apparatus of the city by forming a close professional alliance with Valentin Bapst the Elder (also rendered Papst), one of Leipzig’s leading civic printers. Following Bapst’s death, Vögelin cemented his social and commercial position by marrying Bapst’s daughter (and heiress), thereby acquiring ownership of the established printing house, its presses, typographical fonts, and active publishing privileges around 1559. Through this strategic inheritance and his own formidable capital investments, Vögelin rapidly expanded the shop into a premier printing house, securing imperial printing privileges (privilegia impressoria) from Imperial authorities as well as territorial protections from Elector Augustus of Saxony.The scholarly orientation of the Officina Voegeliniana was defined by Vögelin’s intimate integration into the elite intellectual networks of Melanchthonian Humanism—frequently designated as Philippism after the influential Wittenberg reformer Philipp Melanchthon. Vögelin maintained extraordinarily close intellectual and personal ties with Melanchthon’s primary disciples and intellectual heirs, most notably Joachim Camerarius the Elder, the celebrated classicist and rector at Leipzig; Caspar Peucer, Melanchthon’s son-in-law and physician-philosopher at Wittenberg; Esrom Rüdinger; Viktorin Strigel; and David Chytraeus. Under their editorial guidance, Vögelin issued monumental editions of classical Greek and Latin literature, advanced philological treatises, legal commentaries, and academic textbooks that became standard across European faculties of arts and law. His press printed authoritative editions of Demosthenes, Cicero, Aristotle, Homer, and Hesiod, frequently embellished with parallel Latin translations and detailed scholarly commentary by Camerarius. Furthermore, Vögelin became the principal printer for major legal compilations and municipal codes, establishing Leipzig’s primacy in European legal publishing. His theological production focused on irenic, humanistically oriented Lutheran scholarship, avoiding the vitriolic polemicism of the rigid Gnesio-Lutheran party and emphasizing dialectical rigor, pedagogical clarity, and civic morality.From a technical and typographical perspective, Vögelin raised the standards of Saxon printing to levels that rivaled the supreme continental workshops of Johannes Oporinus in Basel, Plantin in Antwerp, and the Estienne family in Paris. The material production of the Officina Voegeliniana was characterized by exceptional presswork, pristine paper Sourced from top Rhenish and Bohemian mills, and meticulous proofreading executed by university-trained correctors. Vögelin acquired and commissioned extensive sets of high-grade Antiqua and Italic types cut after Italian and French punches, alongside exquisite Greek fonts and specialized Hebrew characters designed to handle complex polyglot apparatuses. His books were frequently adorned with elaborate Renaissance woodcut title borders, elegant architectural frames, historiated initial letters, and striking printers' devices. Vögelin’s primary printer's emblem was a vivid visual pun on his surname (derived from Vögelin, meaning 'little bird'): it typically depicted a bird soaring toward the sun or perched resiliently beside a palm tree, accompanied by moralizing Latin or Greek mottos emphasizing perseverance, divine favor, and scholarly devotion. To ensure the rapid distribution of his massive print runs, Vögelin operated a sophisticated commercial distribution network anchored in the bi-annual Leipziger Buchmesse and the Frankfurter Buchmesse, where he maintained dedicated sales vaults and traded sheets with book merchants from Venice, Lyon, London, and Basel.The trajectory of Vögelin’s life took a tragic and dramatic turn in the mid-1570s, as the latent doctrinal rift between radical Gnesio-Lutherans and moderate Philippists erupted into open political warfare within Electoral Saxony. Elector Augustus, initially supportive of the Philippist faculty, became convinced that his court physicians and theologians—including Caspar Peucer and printer networks associated with Leipzig and Wittenberg—were secretly undermining Lutheran orthodoxy by orchestrating a clandestine movement toward Reformed Calvinism, a crisis known as the Crypto-Calvinist Controversy (Kryptocalvinismus). In 1574, the publication and covert distribution of controversial Calvinistic Eucharistic treatises, such as the anonymous Exegesis perspicua controversiae de Coena Domini, ignited an electoral purge. Vögelin, who had printed, financed, and distributed numerous works by Peucer, Rüdinger, and other suspected Philippist theologians without obtaining strict territorial censorial clearance, was identified as a primary instrument of the alleged conspiracy. In 1576, electoral inquisitors suppressed Vögelin’s Leipzig workshop; his presses were impounded, his books confiscated, and he was subjected to intense legal interrogation and temporary imprisonment.Stripped of his Saxon privileges and forced into exile, Vögelin displayed remarkable resilience by relocating his family and remaining capital to the Free Imperial City of Frankfurt am Main, the undisputed capital of the international book trade. Re-establishing his printing operations in Frankfurt and maintaining close operational links with his native Constance, Vögelin resumed publishing under his own name and through cooperative ventures with Rhenish and Palatine pressmen. Free from Saxon censorship, he continued to issue critical scholarly editions, humanistic compendia, and Protestant literature until his death around 1589. His monumental legacy was actively maintained and extended into the seventeenth century by his sons—most notably Gotthard Vögelin and Ernst Vögelin the Younger—who established celebrated printing firms in Frankfurt, Heidelberg, and Neustadt an der Haardt, remaining central suppliers to the Palatine Calvinist and pan-European humanist republic of letters. Today, Ernst Vögelin is remembered by historians of the book and scholars of the Reformation as a quintessential Renaissance printer-publisher whose commitment to humanistic learning and intellectual freedom withstood the fierce storms of confessional intolerance.

publishers.name: Kündig Jakob
publishers.biography: Jakob Kündig (frequently Latinized in imprints as Jacobus Cyndicus or Jacobus Cundisius; active c. 1542–1560) stands as an influential, if frequently understated, figure within the vibrant typographical landscape of mid-sixteenth-century Basel. Operating during the critical transitional era following the initial wave of the Protestant Reformation and the death of Desiderius Erasmus, Kündig contributed significantly to the dissemination of humanist learning, Reformed theology, and scientific treatises across Transalpine Europe. Basel, situated at the geopolitical and commercial crossroads of the Swiss Confederation, the Holy Roman Empire, and France, had established itself as one of the premier printing capitals of the Western world through the pioneer efforts of Johann Amerbach, Johann Froben, and Henricus Petri. Within this competitive and intellectually charged milieu, Kündig established an independent printing workshop (*officina*) that bridged the rigorous standards of Erasmian humanism with the urgent polemical and pastoral demands of second-generation Protestantism.Little is preserved regarding Kündig's early youth and formal lineage prior to his matriculation and establishment within the civic and guild structures of Basel. Archival records from the Basel guild books (*Zunftakten*), specifically those of the *Zunft zu Hausgenossen* and the *Zunft zum Safran*, indicate that Kündig emerged from the regional artisan class of the Upper Rhine, acquiring his foundational training in letterpress printing, typefounding, and shop administration under the tutelage of established Basel masters during the late 1530s. By the early 1540s, Kündig had secured the necessary capital and civic standing to register his own press. His establishment coincided with a dynamic reorientation of the Basel book trade, as printers increasingly diversified their output to cater not only to Latin-educated scholars but also to a burgeoning vernacular readership seeking German translations of biblical commentaries, practical medical manuals, and educational textbooks.The intellectual network surrounding Kündig's press was defined by intimate collaborations with leading Swiss Reformers and international scholars. Most notably, Kündig played a vital role in providing employment and publishing outlets for English Marian exiles who sought refuge in Basel during the Catholic restoration under Queen Mary I Tudor (1553–1558). Among these exiles, the martyrologist John Foxe worked intimately within the printing shops of Basel, serving as a corrector, editor, and author. Kündig, alongside his frequent printing partner Johann Oporinus (Johannes Oporinus), facilitated the composition and production of early Latin drafts of Foxe's monumental historical project, which would eventually culminate in the Actes and Monuments. Beyond English exiles, Kündig's press issued key works by prominent Continental theologians, including Heinrich Bullinger, Theodor Bibliander, and Wolfgang Musculus, alongside classical school texts and grammatical manuals designed for the Reformed academies of Switzerland and the southern German principalities.From a typographical and bibliographical perspective, the imprints produced by Jakob Kündig exhibit the high structural and aesthetic standards characteristic of sixteenth-century Basel typography. Kündig maintained a versatile inventory of metal types, encompassing crisp Roman (*antiqua*) founts modelled on Venetian and Baslean precedents, dynamic Italics for marginalia and liminary verse, scholarly Greek types, and robust German Fraktur for vernacular works. His workshop relied upon the established paper mills along the St. Alban-Teich in Basel, ensuring high-quality rag paper bearing recognizable watermarks. To distinguish his production in the international book market, Kündig adopted distinct printer's marks (*insignia typographica*), often incorporating allegorical motifs of justice, truth, or biblical emblems accompanied by Latin or Greek mottoes. He routinely exhibited and distributed his catalogue at the biannual Frankfurt Book Fair (*Frankfurter Buchmesse*), leveraging regional trade routes along the Rhine to circulate his editions to booksellers in Strasbourg, Zurich, Nuremberg, and Geneva.The critical reception of Kündig's output highlights his essential position within the second generation of Basel printer-publishers. While earlier scholars of print culture sometimes overshadowed figures like Kündig in favor of grander press patriarchs like Froben or Oporinus, modern analytical bibliography recognizes Kündig as an indispensable operator whose pragmatic partnerships and high technical standards sustained Basel's typographical hegemony. His willingness to undertake joint printing ventures with figures such as Nicolaus Brylinger and Michael Isengrin demonstrates the collaborative economics of early modern publishing houses, where shared capital and presswork mitigated the severe financial risks of large-format printing. Today, surviving imprints bearing the mark of Jacobus Cyndicus are preserved in major research institutions worldwide, serving as enduring monuments to the intellectual vibrancy and technical precision of the Northern Renaissance.

academic_description: The miscellany contains six works, five from the 16th century (but one is just a fragment) and one from the beginning of the 17th century: BASILIUS CAESARIENSIS Sanctus (330-379) et al. D. Basilij Magni De instituenda studiorum ratione ad nepotes suos oratio paraenetica Graece & Latine, ut cum annotationibus Iustini Gobleri conferri possit. Item Ioannis Pici Mirandulę De homine opusculum omnino diuinum. Eiusdem De Christi regno, & vanitate huius mundi. Loci christianam uitam breuiter complectens. Et Commentaria in Psal. 15. Præterea Rodolphus Agricola De Formando studio, & Erasmi Roterodami ac Philippi Melanchtonis studiorum rationes, atque locorum communium index. Basel, Heinrich Petri, (1537). [16], 229 [of 262] pp. Also lacking the final leaf with the printer’s device. Collation: a8 A-Q8 R4. Over 30 pages (half quire P to R) at the end, containing the Ratio colligendi exempla, the famous method theorized by Erasmus of Rotterdam in his rhetorical-pedagogical treatise De duplici copia verborum ac rerum (1512), have been expunged. Other signs of censorship such as this are also visible on the title page and on l. P3r, where Erasmus’ name has been erased. Additionally, on leaf P4v, the beginning of Erasmus’s aforementioned treatise is covered by a blank leaf and some scribbles. Leaf N8v is also covered by blank paper strips to censor a brief text by Melanchthon and Erasmus. Some old manuscript annotations, partly trimmed by the bookbinder. Woodcut decorative initials. Roman and Greek types. Curiously, and in apparent contradiction with the aformentioned censorships, the owner of the present Sammelband bound between the title page and leaf a2 a dedication that Melanchthon addressed to his friend and fellow scholar Simon Grynaeus taken from Peuerbach’s Theoricae novae planetarum in the Wittenberg 1551 edition printed by Hans Lufft with a preface by Melanchthon (cf. VD16, P-2061).Saint Basil the Great’s famous homily, De instituenda studiorum ratione ad nepotes suos oratio paraenetica, printed here also in its original Greek text, was a cornerstone of Christian humanism, as Saint Basil argues that young Christians should actively study pagan classical texts (like Homer and Plato) for their moral virtues, using them as a preparatory stepping stone before diving into Holy Scripture. This specific edition is accompanied by the annotations of the German jurist and humanist Justin Gobler, providing contemporary readers with philological and practical insights into Basil’s rhetoric.The edition also includes two works by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his celebrated Oration on the Dignity of Man and a lesser-known text De Christi regno, & vanitate huius mundi, a sort of commentary on Psalm 15, as well as Rudolph Agricola’s De Formando studio. As said, the final texts by Erasmus and Melanchthon were expurgated by the owner of the volume.VD16, B-650. OLYMPIODORUS (fl. 6th cent.). Olympiodori Doctissima in Ecclesiast. scholia, nova & latinis auribus insueta tralatione inserta, Aquilae videlicet, Theodotionis, & 70. Zenobio Acciaiolo Florentino interprete. Divi Gregorij Neocaesariensis In eundem metaphrasis, uel ut Suidæ placet, […] Ioanne Oecolampadio interprete. Aristeae De 72. legis Hebraicæ interpretatione libellus, […] Matthia Palmerio Vicentino interprete. Basel, Johann Bebel, 1536. 8vo. [8], 248 pp. Collation: α4 a-p8 q4. Printer’s device on l. o8v.These are the commentaries (scholia) attributed to Olympiodorus the Deacon (not to be confused with the Neoplatonic philosopher of the same name), which contain some of the the most ancient lost Greek translations (“unusual to Latin ears”): those of Aquila of Sinope, of Theodotion, and the Septuagint. The translator from Greek to Latin is the Florentine humanist Zenobio Acciaioli (1461-1519), a Dominican friar and prefect of the Vatican Apostolic Library, who rediscovered and translated this commentaries precisely to make fragments of the first Greek biblical translations available to scholars. The second part contains the paraphrase (metaphrasis) of Ecclesiastes written by Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus (or of Neocaesarea), a third-century Church Father. The title cites the Byzantine encyclopedia Suidas for the attribution of the text. The Latin translation here is by Johannes Oecolampadius (1482-1531), a renowned German humanist, Hebraist, and leader of the Protestant Reformation in Basel. The final section is the celebrated Letter of Aristeas to Philocrates, a seminal Hellenistic text that recounts the legendary story of the birth of the Septuagint Bible. The Latin translation is by the humanist Matteo Palmieri (1423-1483).VD16, O-727. ATHENAGORAS ATHENIENSIS (ca. 2nd cent.)-AENEAS GAZAEUS (430-486). Athenagoras De mortuorum resurrectione, Petro Nannio interprete [followed by:] Aeneas Gazaeus De immortalitate animarum, et corporum resurrectione, Ioanne Vuolphio interprete. A fragment from Philo Alexandrinus’ (25-40) Lucubrationes quotquot […] Latinae factae per Sigismundum Gelenium (Basel, Nikolaus Episcopius d.J., 1558). 8vo. 1401-1526, [2 blank] pp. Collation: RR-Aaa8.Athenagoras was one of the most refined Christian philosophers and apologists of the second century. His treatise on the resurrection of the dead is a fusion of Christian theology and Platonic and Aristotelian logic. Rather than relying solely on Scripture, Athenagoras uses pure philosophical argument to demonstrate that the resurrection of the body is logical and morally necessary for the final judgment of humanity. The Latin version is the work of the Flemish humanist Pieter Nanninck (Petrus Nannius, 1500-1557), a highly esteemed professor of Latin at the prestigious Collegium Trilingue in Louvain.Aeneas of Gaza was a Neoplatonic philosopher who converted to Christianity and lived between the fifth and sixth centuries. His work is structured like a Platonic dialogue: in it, Aeneas refutes traditional Neoplatonic doctrines that viewed the body as a prison of the soul to be destroyed, philosophically arguing for the immortality of the soul and the glorification and final resurrection of the material body. The translation from Greek and the philological restoration of the text are due to Johann Wolf (Ioannes Vuolphius, 1521-1571), a theologian and professor in Zurich.VD16, ZV-12449. PLUTARCHUS (45-120)-CAMERARIUS, Joachim, ed. (1500-1574). De natura et effectionibus daemonum libelli duo Plutarchi Cheronensis, cum explicationibus, & proemio Ioachimi Camer. Quibus & eruditae, & rarae & iucundae & non inutiles cognitu rerum mirabilium & singularium expositiones continentur. Leipzig, Ernst Vögelin, [1565]. 8vo. [54], 151 [i.e. 152], [2: errata] pp. Collation: A-N8. Woodcut historiated initials and woodcut geometric figures in the text. Inked marginalia and underlinings in later hand (partly trimmed).Extremely rare first edition (reprinted by Vögelin in 1576). The book combines the text of Plutarch, translated in Latin by Adrien Turnèbe (1512-1565), with the commentary of the German humanist Joachim Camerarius (1500-1574). Plutarch, who was a priest at the Oracle of Delphi, explores in these pages the nature of the “daimones”, understood in Greek culture as intermediary entities between gods and men, responsible for prophetic inspiration. Plutarch’s two works on oracles and prophecy cover a wide range of topics, including spirits, demons, witchcraft, astronomy, and geometry.Camerarius’s lenghty preface, followed at the end by another long text, which features geometrical figures, called Annotatio, is significant because it not only comments on Plutarch’s text on oracles and prophecy (De Defuctu Oraculorum and De Figura ei, consecrata Delphis), but extends the discussion to contemporary concerns about witches.“Joachim Camerarius the Elder is routinely praised for his critical acumen in editing classical texts. In this paper I would like to blame him for his role in fostering the witch craze that swept southern Germany a decade after his death. The fifty years between 1581 and 1631 saw the arrest, trial, and execution of some 2,500 witches in Trier, Bamberg, and Würzburg. Although Camerarius is not associated with those trials, I would like to suggest he be held responsible for helping create the intellectual climate that made them possible.We all go crazy sometimes. Late at night, a sudden noise can set your mind whirring or make you freak out. When that happens, it isn’t always easy to get a grip on yourself and realize that your thoughts are running wild. That happened to Joachim Camerarius one night and it changed his life. He tells us so in the preface to a book he published in Leipzig in or around 1568. The book is a Latin translation of two mystical essays by Plutarch, On the Failure of Oracles and On the E at Delphi, but the surprising thing about it is the title Camerarius gave it: De natura et effectionibus daemonum, ‘On the Nature and Activities of Demons’.The preface takes the form of a letter from Camerarius to a friend, named Adrianus Albinus, who had stopped twice to visit him in Leipzig while on his way to and from Speyer: It is 51 pages long. In it Camerarius says the conversations they had had led him to stay up late one night reading a book, a book that made him rethink everything he thought he knew. In the pages that follow he proceeds to lay out his revised thoughts about the reality of demons, of witches, and of witchcraft. At length he states his new view to Albinus (p. 28):Neque est res ista nova, sed priscis quoque temporibus nota atque usurpata. Nomina tantum et voces mutantur, caetera sunt cadem.That thing you mentioned? It’s nothing new. People knew about it and did it in anti-quity. It’s all the same; only the names have changed.As becomes clear, the meaning of ista res, ‘that thing you mentioned’, is sexual intercourse. Camerarius and Albinus had talked about sex, but not of the typical kind. Rather, the great scholar and his friend had heatedly debated the reality of sexual intercourse between human beings and demons. From the letter it is obvious that Camerarius was already a true believer in ghosts, mediums, and conjuring the dead, but that is nothing unusual for a man of his times. What is unusual, and bizarre, is his newfound conviction that women literally have sex with demons […]An incidental clue allows us to fix the date of the letter. On p. 52 Camerarius remarks that 48 years have passed since he last studied with Richard Croke (1489-1558), a teacher with whom he first read bits of Plutarch. That was in 1517, so Camerarius wrote the letter to Albinus in 1565. As we will see, this is precisely the date to which external indications also point.The letter begins with a convoluted and cryptic sentence (p. 4 = A2r):Cum nuper hac ex Nemetum urbe revertens transires, et me, perpetua consuetudine tua, humanissime salutasses, recordari te puto, Adriane Albine, factae mentionis inter alios sermones nostros, cuiusdam a me, de mirabilibus cogitationibus meis, quibus causam dedissent narrationes tuae superiorum dierum, quando proficiscens ad Rhe-num huc veneras.I bet you remember, Adrianus Albinus, that when you passed through here not long ago on your way back from Speyer and (as kindly as ever) you came to see me, I mentioned, among other things, some strange thoughts I'd been having. They were prompted by what you told me about some recent events (narrationes superiorum dierum) when you stopped here on your way to the Rhine.These ideas certainly could have been stated more clearly. Working backward in time, the sentence says that on a recent trip, Albinus had stopped in Leipzig to see Camerarius, not once but twice. The first time was on his way to Speyer and the second was on his way back. On his first stop, Albinus had told Camerarius about some recent events that set his mind thinking. Camerarius was still brooding on them when Albinus stopped again on his way home, so they discussed them a second time. And after Albinus left again, Camerarius still couldn’t stop thinking about them […] Camerarius goes on (p. 5 = A2v):Extatque liber cuiusdam titulo Mallei maleficarum, et Francisci Pici alter de Strigibus, in quibus huius generis exempla et plurima numero et factis teterrima leguntur. Atque ego me aliquando paulo antequam cubitum irem librum Pici percurrentem, memini noctem illam habuisse valde gravem ac difficilem, obversantibus animo terroribus variis de is quae ibi referuntur.There’s a book out there called Malleus Maleficarum (‘A Mallet for Malefactresses’), and another one by Francisco Pico about witches (strigibus). We see case after case like that - really shocking stuff! - in them. I remember leafing through Pico's book that night just before going to bed and having an awful, simply horrible, night. My mind was haunted by all kinds of frightening thoughts about the stuff in that book.He adds (ibid.):Mihi vero post tuum discessum de istis ita multae et variae cogitationes obstrepere non destiterunt, ut non possem facere quin de tota re anquirere et considerare accu-ratius et diligentius instituerem.After you left, I was obsessed by all kinds of thoughts about what you said, and I couldn’t help it: I just had to investigate the whole thing, had to take a really good, hard look at it.‘The whole thing’ (tota re) turns out to mean not only sex with demons, but demonology as a whole. In the 50 pages that follow Camerarius ransacks classical pagan literature for evidence of the existence and harmful activity of demons, ghosts, nightmares, madness, visions, magic cures, and witches. He conflates fact and fiction; he cites hearsay evidence and stories of evildoing to which no names or dates are attached. Remarkably, he chooses not to invoke his Christian faith for his belief in witches, preferring instead the evidence of classical authors. Fifty pages later, he has concluded that witches are real and that this was a fact known to all ancient authorities. He also concludes that witches celebrate orgies and do have sexual intercourse with demons. Although that was an old rumor in Catholic countries, it was something new in Germany, especially Protestant Germany; I will come back to this point. Camerarius goes on at such length not out of prurience or misogyny but because he is plainly trying to prove to himself that demons (or rather, daimones - meaning both good spirits, like angels, and evil spirits) are corporeal […]When he published it, Camerarius was hailed as the leading light in Europe and the successor of Erasmus. On the last page of the letter, he addresses Albinus once more and makes two important points. First, he reveals why he wrote the letter (p. 51):Tuae, Albine Adriane, narrationes illas cogitationes, quas exposui, commoverunt, casque ut scripto completerer, ne quasi evanescerent, cum alia me impulerunt, tum quod eas ipsas abs te legendo cognosci cuperem.All these thoughts of mine were prompted by what you told me, Adrianus Albinus, and that induced me to write them down, not just to ensure they wouldn’t vanish (so to speak when I became preoccupied with other matters, but also because I wanted you to read and learn from them).He then offers a prediction about the fate of these efforts (p. 53 = p. D2v):Quod autem ad rem ipsam attinet, habes, Adriane Albine, meam sententiam de iis, quae et tractata sunt sermonibus nostris te praesente, et his Plutarchi libellis dis-putantur, habes operam quoque interpretationis. [..] alios, si qui illa forte legerint eruditi et docti, confido studium diligentiae meae non esse improbaturos.And there you have it, Adrianus Albinus - my thoughts on what you and I talked about when you were here, matters that these essays of Plutarch’s also discuss. You’ve also got my best shot at making sense of them. [...] If any other sophisticated readers come across them, I’m positive they won't criticize the careful attention I gave them.It isn’t clear in that last sentence whether Camerarius is referring to his thoughts on demonology or to the annotations he adds to the translations of Plutarch; but at any rate, Camerarius’ Plutarch book was reprinted in Leipzig in 1576, two years after his death. Five years later, in 1581, and closer to Würzburg, the preface was reprinted in Frankfurt am Main. It appeared as a supplement to the Flagellum haereticorum fascinariorum (‘A Scourge for Heretical Witches’), an inquisitor’s treatise that asserted the equivalence of heretics and witches. Two years after that, the flames of a thousand bonfires began to light up the heavens in Trier. The Great Witch Craze had come to southern Germany.Camerarius’ addressee is not a famous man. Who was Adrianus Albinus, and what did he tell his friend to shock him so? Born in Lauban, Silesia (today Lubań, in southwest Poland), Adriarius Albinus (1513-1590) studied law in Poland, Germany, France, and Italy. In 1541, at the age of 28, he briefly taught law in Leipzig. There he probably met Camerarius, who arrived the same year as Professor of Latin and Greek. In 1544 Albinus became Professor of Roman Law at the University of Frankfurt-Oder, in Brandenburg, and the year after that, in 1545, the 32-year old Albinus was named the Chancellor of Neumark (cancellarius Neomarchiae) and legal advisor (consiliarius, Rat) to John, Margrave of Brandenburg-Küstrin" (1513-1571). Thirty-five years later, in 1590, Albinus died and was buried in Küstrin. A contemporary obituary says he had been a devout Christian and lifelong devotee of Plutarch’s Parallel Lives.!? The Plutarch connection could explain why Camerarius dedicated the book to him, but probably not. That brings me to the topic of their conversation, and in particular the narrationes superiorum dierum, as Camerarius called them (pp. 4-5 = A2t-A2v):Commemoravisti enim tunc, quid apud vos compertum prolatumque fuisset, de mulie-rum quarundam veneficarum horribilibus facinoribus, deque superstitionis incredibili efficacitate, et eiusmodi operibus, de quibus non modo sollertiae humanae consideratio quaerens conturbari, sed religiosae quoque pietatis attentio vacillare quoddamodo posset. [..] Atque me ea repetentem animo quae audiveram ex te, percusserunt similia quaedam de aliis cognita. Nam quod tu de consuetudine spirituum quadam occulta ceteris, ipsis illis infelicibus mulieribus manifesta, exposuisti, perquam multa altis temporibus atque locis pariter depraehensa, et atrocibus suppliciis vindicata esse constat.You see, when we spoke you mentioned what an inquiry back home (apud vos) had discovered (compertum) and brought to light about the awful crimes of some poisoner-women (veneficae) and the incredible power of superstition and workings of that sort. As you put it, looking into those things doesn’t just befuddle a clever man’s reason; it can even shake firm religious faith. […] And while I kept brooding on what you told me, I was struck by some legal discoveries about other women (de altis cognita) that resemble the ones you were talking about. You see, what you said - about a certain ‘sexual intercourse with spirits’ that those terrible women themselves can see but nobody else can - well, it’s a fact that lots and lots of cases were detected and punished by dire penalties at other times and places.Camerarius next mentions the awful night he stayed up reading Pico’s book. Since he blames that incident for converting his worldview from skepticism to belief, whatever Albinus told him must have been grave indeed. After some sleuthing, I think I have figured out what it was. The facts are as follows.Mark Brandenburg, where Albinus was from, was one of the earliest regions in central Europe to prosecute and execute witches. Witch trials elsewhere in Germany only began in earnest around 1570, but in Brandenburg the trials peaked before 1580. In its northwest there is a district called Prignitz. Its capital is a small city called Perleberg, whose population before the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) was about 3,000. That is where, in 1565, all hell broke loose - literally. In two waves, small groups of women were tried, convicted, and speedily executed for the crime of sorcery. Though he says nothing of the details, Gerhard Schormann considers the second of these trials a watershed: ‘1565 marks the first time’, he observes, ‘that five women were convicted at one trial and with it, the first appearance of witch lore, including Walpurgis Night on the Blocksberg’.It all happened so fast. Four days after Walpurgis Night in 1565 (the night between April 30 and May 1), three women of Perleberg were arrested, interrogated, convicted, and executed for sorcery. A week later five more witches were caught and tried and, like the first, met their fiery fate on the Weinberg hillside in Perleberg. The witches had been accused of poisoning, but […] the Perleberg women [also] admitted to celebrating a witches’ sabbat, just days before their arrest, on the Blocksberg. This was an unprecedented admission in Christian Germany […] The fate of these latter four women is not clear, but in just one week's time, at least eight and perhaps twelve witches were caught, tried and burned in one small city.Those confessions, certified by execution, must have sparked fears that an evil conspiracy was afoot. This was the moral panic Albinus told Camerarius of […] The Perleberg trials took place in Altmark, in West Brandenburg. Although Adrianus Albinus lived in Neumark, in East Brandenburg, he certainly knew about them. As chancellor of Neumark he would not have been a member of the Appeals Panel, but he was well aware of its activities […] [All this brings to the probable conclusion] that it was this spate of witch trials in Perleberg in 1565 that Albinus told Camerarius about during his two stops in Leipzig […] It is clear from the letter that Camerarius had already believed in demons and, presumably, witchcraft or harmful magic (maleficium) - poisoning, uttering oaths, casting spells, and other physical interventions - long before Albinus arrived. His revelation, therefore, was the sudden realization that the witches’ sabbat, replete with lurid demon sex, was real and was being celebrated right there in Germany. The Perleberg confessions, and executions, had just proven it […]By 1580, six years after Camerarius’ death, belief that a witches’ sabbat was celebrated on the Blocksberg had spread throughout Germany. For example, it is the subject of an anonymous treatise printed in Rostock that year titled Concerning the Witches' sabbat in Brocken Mountain, which is also called Blocksberg Camerarius did not mention the sabbat explicitly in his Plutarch book, but he did discuss sex with demons. So did his book - and its reprints - help promote belief in it? […] He took an existing idea and amplified it, and not only as a radio tower amplifies sound. He also amplified it in stature, adding dignity and authority to a rabble-rousing mistake. His authority authenticated and relayed the idea throughout Germany, where it went viral […] What Camerarius did was worse than authenticating a forgery, like spurious fossils or a Vermeer painting. Camerarius - the university reformer, the ‘eye of Germany,’ the heir of Erasmus - authenticated a mistake. Should we condemn him, and Albinus, for their credulity? […]Like many of his contemporaries, Camerarius made the fatal leap of faith from physical harm (poisoning: cf. veneficae) and threats of it (invoking the devil) to supernatural crime - the witches’ sabbat. But that is less a giant leap than a small step on the journey […] Well-entrenched ideologies - such as messianic Christianity had been […] - are, of course, not easily refuted. Once the basic premises of an ideology are accepted, new observations are perceived in its imagery and articulated in its vocabulary. The result is that while no fresh observation can undermine the belief system, new ‘facts generated by the ideology constantly lend further support to it. This was true in the past for the belief in witchcraft and the corresponding prevalence of witches […] Camerarius did this. He relied on his well-entrenched ideology to generate new ‘facts’ about witches and the corresponding prevalence of witches, and lent his support to it […] So I would not be too quick to condemn Albinus and Camerarius for their credulity. His decision to get involved - to speak out publicly - is a different matter. If public intellectuals are responsible for their public statements, we must condemn Camerarius for his. He abused classical literature - taking the fictions of Plautus, Ovid, Apuleius, and others as evidence of reality, and, to judge from the reprints of his letter to Albinus, he persuaded others he was right […]Did Camerarius recant his belief in witchcraft on his deathbed? In Lea [Materials Toward a History of Witchcraft, Philadelphia] 1939, vol. 1, 248 we read:[…] Camerarius was consulted in 1571 by William IV of Hesse Cassel (son of Philip the Magnanimous) [1532-1592] about some women arrested for jugglers’ [i.e. swindlers’] tricks on a boy. Camerarius opposed the use of torture in such cases and also the water ordeal which Wilhelm was disposed to employ, as he was sure that they would sink, and warned him against the cruelty of witch-burning and the prosecutions by which the innocent were obliged to confess.This suggests Camerarius, who died in 1574, repented late in life for the views he expressed in his letter to Albinus a decade earlier. Sadly, it is apocryphal. Lea has mistaken Camerarius the Elder for his son, Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534-1598), a distinguished physician and naturalist of Nuremberg and a known associate of William’s over many years” (M. Fontaine, Joachim Camerarius on Witches, Witchcraft, and Criminal Responsibility, or, How to Philologize with a Witches’ Hammer, in: “Camerarius Polyhistor”, Th. Baier, ed., Tubingen, 2017, pp. 335-356).While the second 1576 edition occasionally appears on the market, to find another copy of this first edition on the market, one has to go back to the Sotheby’s New York auction sale of 20 April 1931, when a copy was purchased by McLeish.VD16, P-3696. ACRONIUS, Johannes (1520-1564). Miraculorum quorundam et eorundem effectuum descriptio, per Iohannem Acronium Frisium Mathematicum Basiliensem. Basel, Jakob Kündig, 1561. 8vo. [14 of 16], 46, [2] pp. Collation: *8 A-C8. Without the title page, removed probably for security concerns. Woodcut initials and ornaments. Printer’s device on last leaf recto.Rare first edition. Born in Friesland (in Akkrum, hence the name Frisius) around 1520, Johannes Acronius moved to Basel, where he first obtained a chair in mathematics (1547), then in logic (1549), and finally, in the last year of his life (1564), graduated in medicine before tragically dying of the plague. His Miraculorum quorundam et eorundem effectuum descriptio (‘Description of certain miracles and their effects’) was published in 1561, a period of enormous ferment in pre-Galilean astronomy. As a mathematician and expert in astrolabes, Acronius analyzed the phenomena of the upper atmosphere and outer space, attempting to calculate their physical, mathematical, and meteorological effects on Earth. As was almost always the case in the 16th century, the scientific description of comets and meteors was not entirely unrelated to astrology and historical accounts. The text examines the “effects” of these celestial bodies, which the contemporary mindset still considered indicators or physical messengers of major political changes, famines, or climate changes.“Die Schrift […] behandelt Meteore, Kometen und andere Himmelserscheinungen und ihre Einflusse auf das irdische Geschehen. Dabei werden sowohl Ereignisse aus friiheren Epochen als auch Beobachtungen von Acronius und seinen Zeitgenossen erwahnt. Acronius vertritt den Standpunkt, daB die Himmelserscheinungen von Gott geschickt wurden, um seine GroBe zu demonstrieren, dem Menschen Zeichen zu geben und gegebenenfalls kunftiges Unheil anzukundigen. Seine Erklarungen iiber Struktur und Aufbau des Himmels und der uberirdischen Korper steht noch in der Tradition des Aristoteles” (‘The text discusses meteors, comets and other celestial phenomena, as well as their impact on events on Earth. It references events from earlier eras, as well as observations made by Acronius and his contemporaries. Acronius believed that celestial phenomena were sent by God to demonstrate His greatness, provide signs to humanity, and foreshadow future calamities when necessary. His explanations of the structure and composition of the heavens and celestial bodies follow the Aristotelian tradition’) (M. Folkerts, Eine Verwechslung mit Folgen: Die Humanisten Acronius und Atrocianus, in: “Sudhoffs Archiv”, vol. 85.1, 2001, p. 59).VD16, A-135. COGAMANDOLUS, Theonestus. Secreta Secretorum. Calvino-Turcica Secreta, Eorundemque Apocalypsis. XCIV. Considerationibus Exposita, & futuro Principum Conventui exhibenda. In qua praecipue demonstratur, Calvinistas, Catholicis, Lutheranis, Suis Confoederatis Exitium Molitos. Auctore, Theonesto Cogmandolo […] Acta, & revisa in secretissima Cancellaria Anhaltina omnia, cum originalibus collata, & hac tertia editione aucta. Notulas addidit Nicolaus Herris Ab Isecera, Iprensis, Auctoris discipulus. N.pl., n.pr., 1621. 8vo. 94 [i. e. 88] pp. Collation: A-E8 F4.One of three editions printed in the same year. Theonestus Cogmandolus, or Cogamandolus, is a pseudonym that has been erroneously identified with Étienne Moquot (1570-1625). The identity Nicolaus Herris ab Isecera, or Herisbarisecera, is also a pseudonym that cannot be identified.This pamphlet is a Counter-Reformation and anti-Calvinist propaganda pamphlet, most likely published in Germany. The text fits into the tense climate preceding the Thirty Years’ War, aiming to demonize the Calvinist faction in the eyes of European rulers. A text with a similar title and subject matter had already been published in Antwerp in 1597, Calvino-turcismus, id est, calvinisticae perfidae, by the English theologian William Reynolds.The author accuses the Calvinist Church of having entered into a secret political and ideological alliance with the Ottoman Empire (the Turks), then considered the archenemy of Christianity. The work often circulated anonymously or, as in this case, under the pseudonym Theonesto Cogmandolo.VD17, 12:108122C. Six works in one volume (154x95 mm). 18th-century full marbled leather (worn at edges and rubbed), gilt spine with morocco lettering piece (“miscellanea”), red edges. Large restoration to the title page of the first work with loss of text, some leaves of the Basilius detached, worm track to the final four leaves slightly affecting the text, browned at places, some occasional staining.

Baier, ed., Tubingen, 2017, pp. 335-356; M. Folkerts, Eine Verwechslung mit Folgen: Die Humanisten Acronius und Atrocianus, in: “Sudhoffs Archiv”, vol. 85.1, 2001, p. 59.

title: Las Heroidas de Ovidio traducidas por un Mexicano

authors.name: Ovidius Publius Naso
authors.biography: Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC–AD 17/18), universally known as Ovid, was one of the three great canonical poets of the Augustan age, alongside Vergil and Horace, and arguably the most formally experimental and culturally pervasive of the three. Born in 43 BC, the final year of the Roman Republic, and dying in exile at Tomis on the Black Sea under the early Roman Empire, Ovid belonged to the generation that inherited the political settlement of Augustus rather than the republican crisis itself. His poetry nevertheless transformed the literary possibilities of the Augustan age. Where Vergil developed epic as a vehicle for Roman origins, destiny, and imperial ideology, and Horace cultivated lyric, satire, and philosophical reflection within the complex cultural world of Augustan patronage, Ovid made poetic art itself the principal field of experimentation. His characteristic instruments were metamorphosis, irony, erotic play, rhetorical virtuosity, narrative instability, shifting perspectives, and an extraordinary sensitivity to the psychology of desire.Ovid mastered virtually every major form of Latin poetry available to him: elegiac couplets in the Amores, Heroides, Ars Amatoria, Remedia Amoris, Medicamina Faciei Femineae, Fasti, Tristia, and Epistulae ex Ponto; epic hexameter in the Metamorphoses; and invective in the Ibis. His influence subsequently extended far beyond classical antiquity. Medieval Latin poetry and mythography, French vernacular literature, Renaissance humanism, European painting and sculpture, opera, drama, and modern literature all repeatedly returned to Ovidian narratives and techniques. His Metamorphoses in particular became one of the foundational mythological books of European culture.Early Life, Family, and EducationOvid was born on 20 March 43 BC at Sulmo (modern Sulmona), in the territory of the Paeligni in central Italy. He came from a prosperous equestrian family and was therefore socially well positioned to receive the elite education customary for young Romans destined for public careers. His father intended him for the law, but Ovid's literary vocation became evident at an early age. He had an elder brother who died at the age of twenty, an episode that Ovid later remembered with particular poignancy.The brothers were educated at Rome, where Ovid studied rhetoric under two of the most distinguished teachers of the period, Arellius Fuscus and Porcius Latro. The influence of the rhetorical schools is unmistakable in his poetry: Ovid's verse is extraordinarily sensitive to declamatory structure, antithesis, suasive argument, paradox, sententiae, and the dramatization of conflicting emotional positions. The elder Seneca, who knew the rhetorical milieu of Ovid's youth, preserved an important characterization of the young poet as one whose natural gift was for poetry rather than forensic oratory. Ovid himself later recalled that whenever he attempted to write prose, verse spontaneously imposed itself upon him.After completing his rhetorical education, Ovid undertook the travels expected of a cultivated Roman of his social standing. He visited Athens, travelled through parts of the Greek East and Asia Minor, and spent time in Sicily. These journeys enlarged the Greek literary and cultural horizon that would become fundamental to his poetry. Among his literary acquaintances was the poet Aemilius Macer, while in Rome he subsequently entered the wider networks of contemporary elegiac and Augustan literary culture.Ovid briefly undertook the minor magistracies associated with the vigintivirate, including service as a tresvir and subsequently as one of the decemviri stlitibus iudicandis. These offices constituted the beginning of the conventional public career of a Roman aristocrat. He nevertheless abandoned the path toward the quaestorship and a senatorial career, choosing poetry instead. The decision was not merely a personal rejection of politics: it also illustrates the transformation of elite Roman culture under Augustus, in which literary distinction could become an alternative form of prestige to the traditional cursus honorum.The Amores and the Reinvention of Roman ElegyOvid's first major success was the Amores, a collection of elegiac poems first issued in five books and subsequently revised into three. The surviving three-book form belongs to the final version of the collection. At its centre stands Corinna, whose precise historical identity is unknown and who should be regarded primarily as a literary construction rather than automatically identified with a particular historical woman.The Amores inherit the conventions of Roman love elegy established by Gallus, Propertius, Tibullus, and their predecessors, but Ovid transforms them through theatricality and irony. The elegiac lover becomes less a helpless victim of amor than an intelligent performer conscious of literary convention. Love is repeatedly presented as a game involving deception, competition, rhetoric, sexual negotiation, and poetic self-fashioning. Ovid's achievement was not simply to make elegy more polished: he exposed the mechanisms through which elegy itself creates its characters and emotions.The same experimental tendency appears in the Heroides, a collection of poetic letters attributed to mythological and legendary women. Penelope, Dido, Ariadne, Medea, and other heroines are given first-person voices through which familiar stories are radically reframed. The Heroides exploit the dramatic possibilities of absence, separation, memory, and unrequited desire, transforming epic and mythological women into psychologically complex speakers. The work also established one of Ovid's most characteristic techniques: rewriting canonical narratives by shifting the point of view.Erotic Didactic Poetry: Ars Amatoria, Remedia Amoris, and MedicaminaOvid's next phase extended his experimentation into didactic poetry. The Ars Amatoria (The Art of Love), in three books, adopts the authoritative voice and formal conventions of didactic literature while applying them to erotic behaviour in contemporary Roman society. The first two books primarily address male lovers; the third turns to women. The poem is deliberately artificial, witty, self-conscious, and often paradoxical: Ovid presents seduction as an art governed by rules, strategies, rhetoric, timing, and performance.The Remedia Amoris (Cures for Love) reverses the Ars by offering techniques for escaping erotic attachment, while the fragmentary Medicamina Faciei Femineae (Cosmetics for the Female Face) applies didactic form to female beauty and cosmetic preparation. Together these poems demonstrate Ovid's extraordinary ability to transform apparently minor subjects into sophisticated literary exercises.The Ars Amatoria subsequently acquired a political significance that it may not originally have possessed. Augustus had instituted a broad programme of moral legislation concerning marriage, adultery, and elite sexual behaviour, including the lex Iulia de adulteriis coercendis. Ovid's playful treatment of erotic conduct could consequently appear dangerously out of step with the moral climate promoted by the imperial regime. Modern scholarship, however, is cautious about presenting the Ars alone as the straightforward cause of his later relegation: Ovid himself explicitly names both a carmen and an error.Metamorphoses: Ovid's Epic RevolutionOvid's supreme achievement is the Metamorphoses, a fifteen-book epic in approximately 12,000 hexameter verses, probably composed principally between the late 1st century BC and AD 8, with the decisive phase of composition falling in the years immediately preceding his exile. The poem describes itself as a carmen perpetuum, an uninterrupted song extending from the creation of the cosmos to the contemporary world of Augustus. Rather than constructing a conventional epic around a single hero, Ovid creates an enormous interconnected sequence of myths whose unifying principle is transformation. Gods become animals, humans become plants and stones, bodies change sex or species, identities dissolve, and stories continually generate new stories.The Metamorphoses contains approximately 250 individual transformation narratives, although the boundaries between individual myths are deliberately porous. Ovid draws upon an enormous range of Greek and Latin sources, including Hesiod, Homer, the Hellenistic poets, Callimachus, Nicander, and earlier Roman poetry. He does not merely reproduce this inherited material. He recomposes it into a narrative universe in which causation, perspective, genre, and identity are continually unstable.The poem's relation to Augustan ideology is correspondingly complex. It contains unmistakable gestures toward the imperial present, including the apotheosis of Julius Caesar and praise of Augustus, yet it also constructs a world in which permanence is impossible and even gods are subject to transformation. The Pythagorean discourse of change near the conclusion of the poem provides a philosophical framework for this extraordinary vision: nothing remains permanently what it was, while forms of life and matter continually pass into new configurations.Ovid's epic therefore differs radically from the Aeneid. It does not offer a linear teleology culminating in Rome. Its governing principle is metamorphosis itself. The result is simultaneously a mythological encyclopedia, an epic, a sequence of tragic and comic narratives, a meditation on artistic representation, and a sustained experiment in narrative continuity.The FastiAt approximately the same time, Ovid worked on the Fasti, an elegiac poem organized according to the Roman calendar. Each book was originally intended to correspond to one month of the year. The surviving poem contains six books, January through June, and consequently represents only half of the projected twelve-book work. The Fasti combines mythology, Roman religion, festivals, antiquarian traditions, astronomy, etymology, and historical memory. It is consequently one of the most important literary sources for the Roman religious calendar. The work also reveals Ovid's sustained interest in the relationship between poetry and official Roman memory. His explanations of festivals and rituals repeatedly transform antiquarian material into dramatic narrative.The poem was interrupted by Ovid's relegation in AD 8 and subsequently revised in exile. The surviving text contains evidence of this later situation, including changes in the poem's imperial address and its relationship to the new political order.Literary Networks and the Augustan Cultural WorldOvid belonged to the broad network of Roman literary circles associated with the late Republic and Augustan age. He had connections with Messalla Corvinus and the literary milieu surrounding him, although the precise nature and extent of Ovid's relationship with individual members of these circles must not be exaggerated. He knew or encountered many of the leading poets of his generation and frequently represents contemporary literary figures within his own poetry.He was, however, not simply a poet of imperial propaganda. His literary career developed largely through his own social and literary networks rather than through the kind of direct patronage associated with Maecenas and Vergil. This relative independence contributed to his distinctive position within Augustan literary culture.Ovid's poetry constantly tests the boundaries between literary convention and political reality. Yet it would be misleading to describe him simply as an anti-Augustan or dissident poet. His relationship with imperial ideology is more complicated: he could celebrate Augustus, exploit Augustan mythology, and simultaneously create forms of poetic play that destabilized the very certainties on which imperial ideology depended.Exile: Tristia, Epistulae ex Ponto, and IbisIn AD 8, at the height of his literary career, Ovid was ordered by Augustus to leave Rome and settle at Tomis, on the western coast of the Black Sea, in the province of Moesia. The punishment was technically relegatio, rather than the more severe deportatio or exilium: Ovid retained his Roman citizenship and property but was permanently confined to Tomis.The poet famously summarized the causes of his downfall as:perdiderint cum me duo crimina, carmen et error—“two charges brought about my ruin: a poem and a mistake.”The carmen is generally understood to be the Ars Amatoria. The error, however, remains unknown. Ovid repeatedly refuses to explain it, and the subject has generated an enormous secondary literature. Theories have included an affair involving the imperial family, knowledge of an adulterous scandal, religious misconduct, political involvement, or some connection with the succession crisis of the final years of Augustus. The frequently repeated theory that Ovid was directly implicated in the affair of Julia the Younger should therefore be presented as a hypothesis, not as established fact. Modern scholarship continues to debate whether the error was primarily sexual, political, religious, or connected with the imperial succession.The exile transformed Ovid's poetry. The five books of the Tristia and four books of the Epistulae ex Ponto constitute a sustained literary representation of displacement, loneliness, geographical marginality, physical suffering, memory, and political dependence. The Ibis, a poem of elaborate imprecation against an unnamed enemy, represents a darker continuation of his earlier mastery of invective.The exile poetry is not merely autobiographical lamentation. Ovid constructs an elaborate poetic persona of the condemned writer who seeks survival through literary communication. Rome becomes simultaneously a geographical absence, an imagined audience, and the political centre upon which the poet's fate depends. Poetry itself becomes the only means by which the exiled Ovid can continue to participate in Roman cultural life. Ovid died at Tomis, probably in AD 17 or 18, without having obtained permission to return to Rome.Manuscript Transmission and Medieval SurvivalThe transmission of Ovid's works from antiquity into the Middle Ages was complex and uneven. His poetry survived through the continuous production of manuscripts, particularly in the intellectual and monastic centres of the Carolingian and post-Carolingian periods. Contrary to an older simplified picture in which Ovid supposedly disappeared after antiquity and was rediscovered only in the twelfth century, recent manuscript scholarship demonstrates that substantial interest in Ovid was already present by the ninth century. The traditional term aetas Ovidiana, associated especially with the twelfth-century revival of Ovidian poetry, therefore describes a major phase of medieval expansion rather than an absolute beginning.Among the important early witnesses to the elegiac corpus are the ninth- and early tenth-century manuscripts Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, lat. 8242 (Puteaneus) and Paris, lat. 7311 (Regius). The Puteaneus preserves part of the Amores and material from the Heroides, and its relationship with the Regius remains an important issue in the textual criticism of Ovid.The Metamorphoses also enjoyed a rich medieval manuscript tradition. Medieval copies frequently incorporated glosses, commentaries, moralizations, and visual programmes. Ovid's myths thus became not only literary texts but also repositories of allegorical, ethical, historical, and Christian meaning.One of the most influential medieval transformations of Ovid was the French ** Ovide moralisé**, a large-scale vernacular adaptation and Christian moralization of the Metamorphoses. By transforming pagan myths into Christian allegories, medieval interpreters made Ovid compatible with theological and pedagogical frameworks that would otherwise have viewed his erotic and pagan subject matter with suspicion.Ovid and the Invention of the Printed Classical AuthorThe invention of printing radically changed the circulation of Ovid. His works were among the major classical texts transmitted through the European incunabular book trade, and the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries transformed him from a predominantly manuscript authority into one of the most widely reproduced classical poets in print.The first printed complete edition of Ovid's works is generally dated to 1471, associated with the Bologna press of Baldassarre Azzoguidi and the textual revision of the humanist Francesco dal Pozzo (Franciscus Puteolanus). This edition belongs to the earliest generation of classical texts produced in Italy after the invention of movable type and marks an important stage in the transition of Ovid from manuscript auctor to printed classical authority.The Venetian printing industry soon became equally important. Ovid's works were repeatedly reprinted in Italy, France, Germany, and the Low Countries, often accompanied by commentaries, textual notes, glosses, translations, and increasingly elaborate illustrations. The printed Ovid became not merely a book to be read but a pedagogical, antiquarian, literary, and visual instrument.The Aldine Ovid, 1502–1503A decisive milestone was the Aldine edition of 1502–1503, printed in Venice by Aldus Manutius. It was issued in three octavo volumes, an exceptionally portable format for a classical author. The first volume contained the Metamorphoses and related material; the second contained the Heroides and erotic works; the third contained the Fasti, Tristia, and Epistulae ex Ponto. The three-volume configuration is documented by surviving bibliographical records, with the Metamorphoses issued in October 1502, the erotic works and Heroides in December 1502, and the Fasti, Tristia, and Ex Ponto in 1503.The Aldine edition was especially important for the history of the classical book because it combined small octavo format, Roman and italic type, efficient page design, and portability. It belonged to Aldus's broader programme of making Greek and Latin classical texts available in compact scholarly editions. The association of Ovid with Andrea Navagero is also significant for the humanist editorial culture surrounding the edition.The Aldine Ovid helped establish a model for subsequent classical printing: a portable, relatively economical text that could circulate among scholars, students, poets, and educated readers rather than remaining primarily a monumental library object.The Illustrated MetamorphosesThe Metamorphoses became one of the most influential illustrated classical books in European printing history. The combination of hundreds of myths with a succession of visually spectacular transformations made the poem exceptionally attractive to printers, illustrators, publishers, painters, engravers, and collectors. A landmark example is the Frankfurt edition of 1563, associated with Virgil Solis, whose woodcuts supplied a visual cycle for the fifteen books of the Metamorphoses. The surviving copies contain a large sequence of illustrations—one museum record documents 178 woodcuts—and demonstrate how Ovid's mythology became a practical visual repertory for artists.The tradition continued into the seventeenth century. Antonio Tempesta designed a celebrated series of illustrations for the Metamorphoses, engraved and published at Antwerp in 1606 by Pieter de Jode I. The resulting series of approximately 150 plates became one of the most influential graphic interpretations of Ovidian mythology. These illustrated editions had consequences far beyond the history of the book. Ovid's myths became an iconographic repertory for Renaissance and Baroque art, influencing representations of Apollo and Daphne, Pyramus and Thisbe, Venus and Adonis, Perseus and Andromeda, Europa, Narcissus, Orpheus and Eurydice, Phaethon, and innumerable other subjects.Humanist Scholarship and the Establishment of the Ovidian TextThe sixteenth and seventeenth centuries also witnessed increasingly sophisticated attempts to establish the text of Ovid through the comparison of manuscripts, earlier printed editions, conjectural criticism, and philological annotation.The culmination of this phase was the work of the Dutch classical scholar Nicolaas Heinsius (1620–1681). His Operum P. Ovidii Nasonis editio nova, issued by the Elzevir press at Amsterdam, represented a major advance in Ovidian textual criticism. The edition appeared in a three-volume form, with the 1661 general title-page and individual volumes dated 1658, 1659, and 1661; its third volume included the Fasti, Tristia, Epistulae ex Ponto, and Ibis.Heinsius's work was decisive because he treated Ovid not simply as a canonical author whose text could be reproduced from the vulgate tradition, but as a classical text requiring systematic comparison of manuscript witnesses and careful evaluation of variant readings. His recension subsequently became one of the principal foundations of modern Ovidian textual scholarship.The significance of the Heinsian tradition is reflected in the subsequent history of Ovidian editions. Even later editors who rejected individual readings or revised Heinsius's conclusions worked within the textual-critical framework that he had helped establish.Reception in the Renaissance and Early Modern EuropeThe Renaissance reception of Ovid was exceptionally broad. His poetry supplied both literary models and mythological material to authors including Giovanni Boccaccio, Francesco Petrarca, Ludovico Ariosto, Edmund Spenser, and William Shakespeare.Ovid's influence on Shakespeare is particularly extensive. Venus and Adonis develops an explicitly Ovidian narrative of erotic pursuit and transformation; A Midsummer Night's Dream incorporates multiple forms of Ovidian metamorphosis and myth; and The Tempest, although much more complex in its classical sources, participates in a theatrical culture deeply shaped by Ovidian ideas of transformation, magic, and unstable identity.The influence extended beyond literature. Renaissance artists repeatedly drew upon Ovid as a principal source of mythological subject matter, while printers and publishers exploited the Metamorphoses as a text ideally suited to the interaction of word and image. Ovid thus became one of the central conduits through which ancient mythology entered the visual and literary culture of early modern Europe.Ovid's Status in European Literary CultureBy the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, Ovid had become more than a classical poet: he had become a cultural language. His myths functioned as a common repertoire shared by poets, dramatists, painters, sculptors, emblem-book authors, composers, schoolmasters, and antiquarians.His extraordinary adaptability derived partly from the structure of his poetry. The Metamorphoses does not prescribe a single ideological interpretation of its myths. Instead, it provides narratives that can be moralized, eroticized, allegorized, dramatized, illustrated, philosophized, or transformed into new literary works. The same story could therefore serve radically different cultural purposes in medieval Christianity, Renaissance humanism, Baroque art, and modern literature.This adaptability explains why Ovid survived repeated changes in literary taste. He could be read as an erotic poet, a mythographer, a moral allegorist, a rhetorician, a philosopher of change, a political poet, a master of narrative technique, or a precursor of modern psychological literature.Modern Critical ReassessmentModern scholarship has increasingly moved away from the older characterization of Ovid as merely an elegant, witty, and superficial poet. His extraordinary formal control is now understood as inseparable from an equally sophisticated engagement with questions of identity, authorship, memory, gender, power, temporality, and representation.The Metamorphoses in particular has become a major object of modern literary theory because its characters repeatedly cross the boundaries between human and non-human, male and female, body and landscape, victim and narrator, original and copy. Transformation becomes not simply a mythological event but a structural principle governing the poem itself.Similarly, Ovid's exile poetry has been reassessed as a complex literary construction rather than a transparent diary of suffering. The Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto deliberately negotiate between autobiography, rhetoric, political petition, self-presentation, and literary performance. The exiled poet creates an identity through poetry precisely because political power has deprived him of physical presence in Rome.The circumstances of the exile remain particularly important to modern scholarship. The Ars Amatoria is almost universally accepted as the carmen referred to by Ovid, but the error remains unresolved. Contemporary research continues to test competing explanations rather than treating any single reconstruction as definitive.LegacyOvid's historical importance ultimately rests on the extraordinary combination of formal invention, mythological range, psychological insight, rhetorical sophistication, and adaptability that characterizes his poetry. The Amores transformed Roman love elegy by making the poet simultaneously lover, actor, critic, and literary artificer. The Heroides reinvented myth from the perspective of absent and abandoned figures. The Ars Amatoria converted erotic behaviour into didactic literature and tested the boundaries of Augustan moral culture. The Metamorphoses created one of the most ambitious mythological narratives in world literature, while the Fasti fused poetry with Roman antiquarianism and religious memory. Finally, the Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto transformed personal displacement into a major literary mode.Through medieval manuscripts, moralized adaptations, Renaissance editions, Aldine printing, illustrated books, humanist commentaries, and the textual criticism of scholars such as Nicolaas Heinsius, Ovid became one of the most continuously transmitted and repeatedly reinvented authors of classical antiquity.His influence on European culture is consequently not reducible to the survival of particular myths. Ovid supplied Europe with a poetics of transformation: the idea that inherited stories can be endlessly rewritten, that identities are mutable, that literary genres can absorb one another, and that the ancient past remains alive precisely because every generation changes it.Few classical authors have therefore possessed a more continuous editorial, artistic, and literary afterlife. From the ninth-century manuscript witnesses to the Aldine press, from Virgil Solis and Antonio Tempesta to Renaissance and Baroque painting, from Heinsius's textual criticism to modern classical scholarship, Ovid's history is also the history of the changing European book. His poetry survived not because it remained fixed, but because successive cultures continually transformed Ovid—in precisely the spirit of the Metamorphoses itself.

related_names.name: Ochoa y Acuña Anastasio María de
related_names.biography: Anastasio María de Ochoa y Acuña (1783–1833) stands as one of the most intellectually versatile, stylistically refined, and historically interesting figures in Mexican literary history during the momentous transition from the late Viceregal period of New Spain to the consolidation of the First Mexican Republic. Operating at the intersection of Enlightenment Neoclassicism, classical humanism, and nascent national costumbrismo, Ochoa y Acuña distinguished himself as a poet, playwright, translator of classical Latin and early modern French drama, and secular priest. His voluminous production—published across newspapers, ephemeral broadsides, theatrical stages, and posthumous anthologies—reflects the complex ideological and aesthetic shifts that defined late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Spanish American intellectual life. Scholars of Hispanic letters recognize him not merely as a master of festive and satirical verse, but as a critical agent in the vernacularization of classical Latin texts and European dramatic models for an emerging Mexican reading public.Born in the town of Huichapan (in the contemporary state of Hidalgo, Mexico) in 1783, Ochoa y Acuña belonged to a Creole family of modest distinction. Recognizing his early intellectual talent, his family sent him to Mexico City to pursue his education at the prestigious Royal and Pontifical Colegio de San Ildefonso, an institution renowned as the crucible of the Creole Enlightenment. At San Ildefonso, Ochoa received a rigorous education grounded in scholastic philosophy, canon and civil law, rhetoric, and classical Latinity. His years at the college profoundly shaped his world: he acquired an exceptional mastery of Latin prosody, ancient Roman literature, and patristic theology, while simultaneously immersing himself in European Enlightenment thought. Following his academic formation, Ochoa took holy orders and was ordained a secular priest, eventually serving as a parish priest (párroco) in Huichapan, Tula, and other regional centers, before settling into the literary and ecclesiastical life of the capital. Throughout his clerical career, Ochoa maintained a harmonious synthesis between his pastoral duties and his devotion to the republic of letters, treating literature as both an instrument of moral instruction and an outlet for civil society.Ochoa y Acuña’s formal entry into the public sphere coincided with the rise of periodical print culture in late viceregal Mexico, most notably marked by the founding of El Diario de México in 1805 by Jacobo de Villaurrutia and Carlos María de Bustamante. As the first daily newspaper in New Spain, El Diario de México served as the primary organ for the Academia de los Alegres and the broader Arcadian literary movement in Mexico City. Ochoa became one of its most prolific and celebrated contributors, adopting various Arcadian and satirical pseudonyms, most famously "Damasio de Joseph de Yanguas", "Anfiso", and "Un Colegial de San Ildefonso". Masked behind these personas, Ochoa published hundreds of epigrams, fables, festive sonnets, and verse epistles that captured the idiosyncrasies, social hierarchies, and hypocrisies of viceregal society. His verse exhibited a linguistic agility reminiscent of Spanish Golden Age and Neoclassical masters such as Francisco de Quevedo, Leandro Fernández de Moratín, and Tomás de Iriarte. Yet, Ochoa injected these European forms with a distinctly Mexican sensibility, utilizing local vernacular expressions, satirical sketches of urban types (such as pedantic scholars, corrupt officials, and vanity-driven elites), and subtle social critiques that prefigured nineteenth-century Mexican costumbrismo.Beyond his original poetry, Ochoa y Acuña achieved historical renown as one of early nineteenth-century Latin America's premier translators of classical literature and European drama. Deeply grounded in Roman antiquity, he undertook ambitious translations of Virgil's Bucolics (Eclogues) and Georgics, as well as Ovid's Heroides (published in Spanish as Cartas de las Heroínas). His translations were praised for their formal elegance, metric precision, and fidelity to the spirit of the Latin originals, avoiding the rigid literalism of contemporary pedants while avoiding excessive domesticating license. In addition to his Latinist endeavors, Ochoa turned his attention to French and Italian theatrical masterpieces, adapting Jean Racine's tragedy Phèdre (as Fedra), Molière's comedy L'Avare (as El Avaro), and several operatic libretti by Pietro Metastasio into Spanish verse. These translations were not merely academic exercises; they were actively produced for the professional stage of Mexico City, enriching the repertoire of the Coliseo de México and elevating the aesthetic standards of colonial and early republican drama.Ochoa’s contributions to original dramaturgy were equally significant. In 1811, amid the turbulence of the Miguel Hidalgo revolt and the outbreak of the Mexican War of Independence, Ochoa composed his celebrated tragedy Don Alfonso. Written in hendecasyllabic blank verse and assonated romance meter, Don Alfonso drew upon Iberian medieval history to explore themes of political legitimacy, tyrannical rule, filial duty, and tragic destiny. Performed at the Coliseo de México, the play served as one of the very few indigenous Mexican neoclassic tragedies of the era, showcasing Ochoa's ability to engage with complex political philosophy through the medium of high drama. While maintaining a politically cautious stance during the War of Independence—balancing his status as a Catholic priest under viceregal authority with his patriotic Creole sentiments—Ochoa ultimately embraced the independence of Mexico in 1821, writing celebratory odes and civic verse that hailed the sovereign nation.The material circulation of Ochoa y Acuña’s works illuminates the evolving print landscape of late colonial and early national Mexico. Initially disseminated through ephemeral broadsides and the pages of El Diario de México printed by early typographers such as Juan Bautista de Arizpe and Mariano de Zúñiga y Ontiveros, his writings achieved widespread popularity across Hispanic America. Following the political consolidation of the Mexican Republic, the demand for a collected edition of his works led to major publishing efforts. In 1828 and subsequently in a landmark posthumous edition in 1840, his legacy was solidified through the press of the master printer Ignacio Cumplido in Mexico City, as well as foreign printing houses such as that of Robert Rafael in New York. The 1840 Cumplido edition, titled Poesías de Don Anastasio María de Ochoa y Acuña, was meticulously edited and presented in elegant typography, serving as a monument to Mexican Enlightenment literature and securing his place in the continental literary canon.Ochoa y Acuña’s life came to a tragic end in 1833, when Mexico City was devastated by the catastrophic cholera pandemic (la gran peste de cólera morbo) that swept through North America and Europe. Serving his parish and ministering to the sick and dying until his final days, the venerable priest succumbed to the disease in August 1833. His death was mourned across the capital by scholars, clergy, and the literary public alike. In subsequent decades, his literary legacy was critically examined by major nineteenth- and twentieth-century literary historians. While conservative critic Francisco Pimentel praised his metric mastery and moral purity, Spanish scholar Marcelino Menéndez y Pelayo lauded Ochoa as one of the finest Neoclassical translators in the Western Hemisphere. Modern scholarship continues to reassess Ochoa y Acuña not as a mere imitator of European models, but as a crucial bridge figure whose mastery of classical humanities and acute observational satire helped lay the intellectual and aesthetic foundations for a distinct Mexican national literature.
