academic_description: Two works in one volume, folio (395x250 mm). Smith: [12], L, [2], 159, [25] pp. Engraved portrait of Sir Robert Cotton by R. White after C. Johnson, title vignette of the Sheldonian Theater and 2 engraved headpieces by M. Burghers. Text printed in two columns. Bernard: two parts: [32], 374 [i.e. 376], [44], 88, [10], 89-274 [i. e. 174], [8] pp.; 403 [i.e. 308], [24], 65, [9] pp. Engraved frontispiece portrait of Sir Thomas Bodley, with inset portraits of the Earl of Pembroke, Archbishop Laud, Sir Kenelm Digby and John Selden, engraved vignette on title-page of the Bodleian Library. Epistola dated September 1698. Contemporary sprinkled calf, spine gilt (rubbed, upper joint split, spine ends a little worn). Some foxing and browning due to the quality of the paper, overall a good, genuine copy from the Macclesfield Library (with its engraved bookplate and embossed stamp). I. First edition “of the only complete record of the celebrated manuscript library of Sir Robert Bruce Cotton which to the present day is one of the best-known components of the British Library; presented by his grandson, Sir John Cotton, to whom the volume is dedicated, to the nation in 1701, it fell victim to a disastrous fire in 1731, when 212 of 958 manuscripts were destroyed or badly damaged. Thomas Smith, a non-juring divine and scholar, at times of Magdalen College, Oxford, had a rather checkered career, but finally settled down in the household of Sir John Cotton and his grandson, another Sir John, and a fine collector himself, was for twelve years in charge of the Cottonian manuscripts” (Bibliotheca Bibliographica Breslaueriana, Christie’s, New York, 2005, part II, no. 161).One of the three collections acquired by the British government to form the British Museum Library, the library of Sir Robert Bruce Cotton (1571-1631) is “arguably the most important collection of manuscripts ever assembled in Britain by a private individual” (C.J. Wright, Sir Robert Cotton As Collector: Essays on an Early Stuart Courtier and His Legacy, London, 1997). The library, which was transferred to the British museum in 1757 and contains spectacular treasures like the Lindisfarne Gospels, two of the contemporary copies of the Magna Charta, and the only surviving manuscript of Beowulf, was the result of Cotton’s forty-year research and effort to preserve manuscript materials, principally relating to England’s history and governmental affairs. Located in Cotton House in the Palace of Westminster, the library was housed in a narrow room and had an unusual arrangement. A bronze bust of a historical personage, including Augustus Caesar, Cleopatra, Julius Caesar, Nero, Otho, and Vespasian, was placed at the head of each bookcase. In total, there were fourteen busts, and the shelf marks were thus formed by bust name, shelf letter and volume number. The catalogue, compiled by Thomas Smith, includes a life of Cotton and a history of the library (cf. C.G. Tite, ed., Catalogue of the manuscripts in the Cottonian library, 1696, Cambridge, 1984).II. “First edition of Bernard’s great catalogue of manuscripts in British libraries. This is ‘one of the most notable achievements of early English bibliographers […] When G. Haenel, in 1830, printed his ‘Catalogi librorum manuscriptorum’, he thought so much of Bernard’s work that he endeavoured to supplement him rather than to duplicate his lists’ (De Ricci, p. 9). Part I [Bibliotheca Bodleiana] contains a life of Bodley, a description of the Bodleian, lists of various collections of manuscripts contained in it, such as those of Pembroke, Cromwell, Digby, Laud, Junius, Hyde and Ashmole. Part II [Bibliothecae collegiorum oxiniensium] lists the manuscripts in Oxford Colleges; Part III [Academia Cantabrigiensis] those in Cambridge Colleges. Part I of vol. 2 [Publicae quam privatae Angliae bibliothecae] contains the manuscripts in public, cathedral, and school libraries and in some fifty private collections, including those of Evelyn Hobbes, Brotherton, Sloane, Lord Derby, Leneve, and Isaac Vossius. All parts have general indices” (Bibliotheca Bibliographica Breslaueriana, Christie’s, New York, 2005, part III, no. 1180). Part II of vol. 2 [Bibliothecae Hiberniae] is dedicated to the manuscripts in Irish libraries.

authors.name: Désaugiers Marc-Antoine Madeleine
authors.biography: Marc-Antoine Madeleine Désaugiers (1772–1827) stands as one of the pivotal intellectual, dramatic, and musical figures in the history of early nineteenth-century French popular theatre, comic opera, and convivial sociability. Operating at the tumultuous crossroads where the aristocratic salon culture of the Ancien Régime collided with the commercialized print and theatrical markets of Post-Revolutionary, Napoleonic, and Restoration Paris, Désaugiers radically elevated the vaudeville and the chanson à boire into sophisticated instruments of cultural cohesion. Over the course of a prolific career cut short by surgical complications, he composed or co-authored upwards of one hundred and fifty theatrical works, authored hundreds of widely anthologized songs, and served as the guiding impulse behind both the iconic Société du Caveau Moderne and the prestigious Théâtre du Vaudeville. His career illustrates the resilience of light comedy and musical satire in navigating the shifting political regimes of modern France, mediating between royalist nostalgia, bourgeois pleasure, and popular theatrical craft.Born on November 17, 1772, in the Provençal city of Fréjus, Désaugiers inherited a profound artistic lineage. His father, Marc-Antoine Désaugiers (1742–1793), was an accomplished classical composer of musical comedies and sacred works who had established a firm reputation in the capital with operas such as Le Petit Figaro (1782) and his musical settings for the Académie Royale de Musique. Sent to Paris during his early youth, the younger Désaugiers was educated at the famous Collège des Quatre-Nations (Collège Mazarin), where he received a rigorous classical training in Latin humanities, rhetoric, and prosody. Displaying an precocious talent for improvisation, versification, and keyboard performance, his early educational trajectory was abruptly derailed by the political tremors of the French Revolution. In 1793, following the death of his father and amid rising revolutionary violence, the young Désaugiers embarked on a harrowing transatlantic voyage to the French Caribbean colony of Saint-Domingue (modern-day Haiti) to oversee family affairs and seek financial fortune.Désaugiers’s Caribbean venture coincided with the peak of the Haitian Revolution, precipitating an extraordinary chapter of captivity, exile, and survival. Caught in the catastrophic uprising in the island's northern province, Désaugiers was captured by insurgent forces. According to nineteenth-century biographical tradition, he narrowly escaped execution on multiple occasions solely through his musical virtuosity, entertaining his captors by performing popular airs on the piano and harp. Fleeing the devastated colony, he boarded a vessel bound for the United States, arriving destitute in Philadelphia in late 1793 or early 1794. During his American exile, Désaugiers integrated himself into the vibrant community of French émigrés, earning his livelihood as a pianist, music master, and harp teacher, while concurrently serving as a répétiteur and orchestral musician for the newly established French Theatre of Philadelphia. This American interlude deeply shaped his theatrical sensibilities, imbuing his work with a pragmatic understanding of stagecraft, musical pacing, and cosmopolitan broadsheet culture.Upon returning to Paris in 1797 under the Directory, Désaugiers found a capital undergoing a theatrical renaissance following the abolition of royal dramatic monopolies. He immediately threw himself into the boulevard theatre circuit, supplying comedies, light operas, and parodies to venues such as the Théâtre des Variétés, the Théâtre des Troubadours, and the Théâtre de la Gaîté. His breakthrough came through his unmatched skill in crafting lighthearted, rhythmic verses adapted to popular melodies (*timbres*). In 1806, alongside notable men of letters such as Pierre-Antoine-Augustin de Piis, Armand Gouffé, and Charles-François-Jean-Baptiste Moreau de Commagny, Désaugiers co-founded the Caveau Moderne, reviving the legendary eighteenth-century goliardic dining society. Meeting monthly at the famed restaurant *Rocher de Cancale*, the Caveau served as an influential literary academy of song, where poets, dramatists, and musicians gathered to perform satirical and bacchanalian compositions. Elected perpetual president and master of ceremonies of the society, Désaugiers transformed the *chanson* into a quintessential expression of French bonhomie. His creative dynamic with his contemporary, Pierre-Jean de Béranger, established a double pole in French song: while Béranger weaponized the genre into radical political opposition against the Restoration monarchy, Désaugiers cultivated a poetry of epicurean contentment, harmless social satire, and royalist fidelity.In 1815, following the fall of Napoleon and the Restoration of the Bourbon monarchy, Désaugiers was appointed director of the prestigious Théâtre du Vaudeville, located on the Rue de Chartres. Under his artistic direction, which lasted with brief interruptions until his death, the venue enjoyed an golden age. Désaugiers possessed a genius for collaborative composition, frequently partnering with leading dramatists of the day, including Nicholas Brazier, Gentil de Chavagnac, Xavier Saintine, and Michel-Joseph Gentil de Chavagnac. Among his vast theatrical production, works such as La Petite Cendrillon (1810), Le Diner de Madelon (1813), Monsieur Sans-Gêne (1816), Le Chaperon rouge (1818), and Jeanne d'Arc ou le Lévrier de Trianon (1821) achieved unprecedented long-running successes across France. His plays were characterized by sparkling dialogue, rapid structural pacing, ingenious rhyming, and an affectionate, non-malicious parody of bourgeois manners and romantic tropes.The print history and publishing circulation of Désaugiers’s works reflect the rapid expansion of early nineteenth-century print capitalism. His libretti and songbooks were published extensively in duodecimo and octavo formats by major Parisian theatrical publishers, most notably J.N. Barba at the Palais-Royal, François-Louis Huet, Chez Mme Masson, and Chez Veuve Dabo. Sheet music incorporating his lyrics accompanied by guitar or pianoforte arrangements circulated widely throughout the European continent and the Americas. Bound anthologies of his works, such as the multi-volume Chansons et Poésies diverses de M. Désaugiers, went through numerous expanded editions during his lifetime (notably in 1808, 1816, and 1827), proving to be lucrative commercial properties for Parisian booksellers and establishing broadside distribution (*feuilles volantes*) as a mainstay of provincial culture.The final years of Désaugiers’s life were darkened by severe health issues. Suffering from agonising urinary calculous disease (bladder stones), he underwent a surgical lithotomy in the summer of 1827, performed by the leading surgical authorities of Paris. Tragically, surgical complications and severe postoperative infection ensued, leading to his death in Paris on August 9, 1827, at the age of fifty-four. His funeral drew thousands of admirers, fellow dramatists, and actors, marking a period of national mourning for the popular stage. Désaugiers was buried at the Père Lachaise Cemetery. His enduring legacy lies in his structural reform of early French popular comedy: by blending musical numbers seamlessly with spoken dramatic narrative, Désaugiers created the immediate historical prototype for the nineteenth-century boulevard farce, directly influencing the dramatic mechanics of subsequent comedic masters such as Eugène Scribe, Eugène Labiche, and eventually Georges Feydeau.

publishers.name: Janet Pierre-Étienne
publishers.biography: Pierre-Étienne Janet (1746–1830) stands as one of the most versatile and commercially astute figures in the history of late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Parisian publishing. Operating across four turbulent decades of French history—from the twilight of the Ancien Régime through the revolutionary cataclysms, the Napoleonic Empire, and the Bourbon Restoration—Janet transformed the landscape of commercial print culture. As a libraire-éditeur, print vendor, and music publisher, he played a pivotal role in refining small-format luxury printing, perfecting the aesthetic of illustrated gift books (livres d'étrennes), and establishing enduring distribution channels for both engraved sheet music and literature. His press on the historic Rue Saint-Jacques served as a nexus where artistic craftsmanship, commercial agility, and literary dissemination converged, defining the visual and tactile sensibility of bourgeois and aristocratic readership during a period of profound socio-political metamorphosis.Born in Paris in 1746, Janet was reared within the vibrant urban culture of the French capital during the height of the Enlightenment. Seeking entry into the prestigious corporate hierarchy of the Communauté des libraires et imprimeurs de Paris, he underwent a rigorous apprenticeship designed to master every facet of the book trade, from paper selection and typography to binding, bookkeeping, and trade privileges. Janet’s institutional and social standing was significantly bolstered by his marriage to Marguerite-Thérèse Savoye, the daughter of Étienne-François Savoye, a highly respected Parisian bookseller. This union allied Janet with an established dynasty of the book trade, providing him with immediate access to established capital, commercial credit, and intra-guild networks. Received officially into the Parisian booksellers' guild in the early 1770s, Janet established his shop on the Rue Saint-Jacques, the historic artery of Parisian academic and literary publishing since the Renaissance. Operating under the sign of the Hôtel de Rohan and later at specific street numbers such as n° 59, Janet positioned his firm at the physical and economic heart of the French print marketplace.Janet's publishing program was characterized by an extraordinary visual and material refinement. He recognized early in his career that the expanding reading public—particularly literate women, affluent bourgeois families, and aristocratic patrons—craved portable, aesthetically pleasing volumes that served simultaneously as functional instruments and decorative tokens of status. Consequently, Janet specialized in small-format publications, notably in-18, in-24, and in-32 volumes. Among his most celebrated achievements were his miniature almanacs and gift publications, such as the Almanach des Dames, the Étrennes mignottes, and various editions of the Petit Paroissien. These works were adorned with exquisite copperplate engravings (gravures en taille-douce) executed by premier artists and engravers of the period, including Jean-Michel Moreau le Jeune, Clément-Pierre Marillier, Joseph de Longueil, and Augustin de Saint-Aubin. By combining delicate typography, fine rag paper, elegant engravings, and elaborate publisher bindings, Janet transformed the annual almanac from an ephemeral calendar into a coveted collector's item.Beyond literary and devotional works, Janet established himself as a major force in French music publishing. Recognizing the growing domestic market for amateur vocal and instrumental music, he expanded his business to publish and distribute engraved musical scores (musique gravée). His catalog included compositions by leading contemporary figures such as Ignaz Pleyel, François-Adrien Boieldieu, Luigi Cherubini, and Giovanni Paisiello, alongside popular romances, operatic arrangements, and instructional tutors for keyboard, harp, and violin. The intricate technical requirements of music engraving—which relied on punched copperplates rather than movable type—demanded specialized craftsmen, and Janet's shop became renowned for the clarity, elegance, and accuracy of its musical impression.The outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789 drastically reconfigured the operational environment of the French book trade. The abolition of corporate guild monopolies by the Allarde and Le Chapelier laws of 1791, combined with the collapse of royal privileges and severe economic instability, forced Parisian publishers to adapt rapidly to an unregulated marketplace. Janet navigated these tumultuous decades with remarkable resilience. While many traditional booksellers succumbed to bankruptcy or political repression, Janet sustained his enterprise by diversifying his output, balancing revolutionary political pamphlets with politically neutral instructional works, sheet music, and secular almanacs. Following the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte and the subsequent re-imposition of state regulation under the Imperial decree of 5 February 1810, Janet formally registered his business and obtained his official brevet de libraire from the Imperial administration, securing his firm's legal standing in the newly ordered trade landscape.In the final decades of his career, Janet engaged in strategic commercial partnerships to consolidate his market dominance. Most notable was his association with Alexandre Cotelle, forming the famous firm Janet et Cotelle around the end of the Napoleonic era. This partnership expanded the firm's reach into large-scale music distribution, international trade, and the publication of comprehensive library editions of French classical authors. The firm maintained extensive commercial networks spanning major European capitals, exporting French luxury volumes and sheet music to London, Vienna, Amsterdam, Saint Petersburg, and Madrid. Janet's operational model relied on innovative sales strategies, including subscription prospectuses (souscriptions) and pre-bound editions encased in elaborate gilt-tooled morocco leather or decorated cardboard slipcases (cartonnages d'éditeur), setting a precedent for nineteenth-century publisher bindings.Pierre-Étienne Janet died in Paris on 25 February 1830, leaving behind a monumental legacy that profoundly shaped nineteenth-century print culture and bibliophilia. His descendants and extended family continued to influence French intellectual life; notably, his lineage connects to the distinguished nineteenth-century philosopher Paul Janet and the pioneering psychologist Pierre Janet. In the annals of bibliography and print history, Janet is remembered not merely as a merchant of paper and ink, but as a master curator of the book as a physical artifact. XIXth- and XXth-century bibliophiles and historians—ranging from Henri Cohen and John Grand-Carteret to modern print historians—have consistently hailed Janet’s publications as supreme exemplars of French graphic art, typographic precision, and commercial craftsmanship.

academic_description: 64mo (28x18 mm). 64 pp. Engraved throughout, with 8 full-page illustrations. Pamphlet-stitched in contemporary (editor’s?) red straight-grained morocco, borders rolltooled in gilt with gilt centre-piece of a dog, spine gilt, edges gilt. Stain at head of title-page, some creasing to corners, a few light marks, textblock loose, very slight wear to extremities. Rare miniature almanac for 1810 on a gastronomic theme, published during the Empire by Pierre-Étienne Janet. The volume begins with Marc-Antoine Madeleine Désaugiers’s (1772-1827) gastronomic song ‘Il faut boire et manger’, each page of lyrics with a facing engraving, the scenes depicted including people eating at a table and the harvesting of grapes. This is followed by collections of mottos for girls and then boys, with references to gluttony, Bacchus, and wine, and the volume ends with a calendar for the year (St Napoleon’s Day is celebrated on 16 August). Pierre-Étienne Janet (1746-1830) began his career as a binder before branching out into bookselling, specialising in almanacks and music.

authors.name: Böckler Georg Andreas
authors.biography: Georg Andreas Böckler (c. 1617 – 21 February 1687) stands as one of the most prolific, influential, and visually stunning exponents of early modern German architecture, hydraulic engineering, and mechanical theory. Active during the traumatic aftermath of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) and throughout the energetic period of Baroque reconstruction in the Holy Roman Empire, Böckler occupied a vital nexus between practical craftsmanship, humanistic learning, and the burgeoning print culture of Central Europe. Serving as a municipal architect (Stadtbaumeister) in Nuremberg and later as court architect (Hofbaumeister) to Margrave Johann Friedrich of Brandenburg-Ansbach, Böckler translated complex classical architectural theories, Renaissance engineering marvels, and advanced mathematical concepts into accessible, richly illustrated compendia in both German and Latin. His monumental treatises—most notably the Theatrum Machinarum Novum (1661) and the Architectura Curiosa Nova (1664)—became ubiquitous reference works across early modern Europe, consulted by prince-bishops, urban magistrates, military engineers, fountain designers, and cabinet-of-curiosity collectors. Through his fruitful collaborations with the prominent publishing houses of Nuremberg and Frankfurt, Böckler helped establish the German-speaking lands as a premier center for technical publishing and copperplate illustration in the late seventeenth century.Born around 1617 in Cronheim near Gunzenhausen in the Franconian region of Germany, Böckler was raised in a Lutheran family deeply steeped in intellectual and clerical traditions; his father, Nikolaus Böckler, served as a Protestant pastor. The devastation wrought across Franconia by the Thirty Years' War profoundly shaped Böckler's early youth and professional disposition. While precise details regarding his formal university education remain sparse, historical evidence indicates that Böckler received a rigorous education in practical mathematics, surveying, Euclidean geometry, draftsmanship, and classical Latin. Unlike many of his contemporary Italian or French architectural peers who benefited from formal grand tours through Rome and Florence, Böckler's technical education was grounded in Northern European guild traditions, practical military engineering, and the systematic study of foundational texts by Vitruvius, Sebastiano Serlio, Andrea Palladio, Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, Agostino Ramelli, and Jacques Besson. By the late 1640s, Böckler had established himself in the Imperial Free City of Nuremberg, a major hub of early modern science, instrument-making, and copperplate engraving. There, he married and began offering private tuition in geometry, perspective, architectural drawing, and fortification, establishing networks among the city's patrician elite and artisan guilds.Böckler’s literary and professional career reached its zenith in the 1660s during his residence in Nuremberg, followed by his appointment in 1679 as formal court architect to the Margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach. His intellectual contribution was twofold: he systematized architectural theory for a German-speaking audience and popularized the genre of the machine book (Maschinenbuch or Theatrum Machinarum). In 1661, working with the famed Nuremberg print publisher Paul Fürst, Böckler issued his masterpiece of mechanical engineering, the Theatrum Machinarum Novum, Das ist: Neu-vermehrter Schauplatz der Mechanischen Künsten. Containing over one hundred meticulously executed folio copperplate engravings, the treatise surveyed every conceivable variety of mill (grinding mills, sawmills, gunpowder mills, paper mills, and oil presses), water-raising devices, Archimedean screws, pumps, and complex gear arrangements driven by water, wind, livestock, or human power. Böckler did not merely present theoretical designs; he provided rigorous analyses of mechanical advantage, friction, force transmission, and practical construction techniques. Recognizing the international demand for his work, a parallel Latin translation, Theatrum Machinarum Novum, exhibens opera molaria et aquatica, was issued almost simultaneously, ensuring its rapid dissemination into intellectual circles across Britain, France, Italy, and the Dutch Republic.Equally groundbreaking was Böckler's 1664 publication, the Architectura Curiosa Nova, a monumental four-part folio treatise dedicated to hydraulic architecture, fountain design, waterworks, and grotto arrangement. Divided into distinct sections covering civil hydrostatics, artificial fountains, cascade designs, water jets, labyrinthine garden layouts, and palatial garden pavilions, the Architectura Curiosa Nova synthesizes functional engineering with Baroque aesthetic spectacle. In this work, water is treated not simply as an essential urban utility or agricultural resource, but as a dynamic medium for dynastic display and sensory delight. Böckler illustrated elaborate water organ mechanisms, automaton systems, hidden splash jets (Vexierwasser), and intricate stone basins that influenced garden design across European courts for generations, directly informing projects at Salzburg, Hellbrunn, Nymphenburg, and Wilhelmshöhe. Beyond hydraulics and mechanics, Böckler authored comprehensive instructional manuals on arithmetic and practical geometry (Arithmetica Nova, 1661), civil architecture (Compendium Architecturae Civilis, 1648), domestic and rural estate management (Nützliche Haus- und Feldschule, 1678), and heraldic art (Neu-vermehrter Helm-Schatz, published posthumously in 1688).The physical production and printing history of Böckler's treatises illustrate the sophisticated commercial machinery of the seventeenth-century German book trade. Collaborating closely with Nuremberg’s elite engravers—such as Balthasar Schwan, Abraham Aubry, Johann Georg Switser, and the printing house of Christoff Gerhard—Böckler oversaw the production of hundreds of high-density copperplate etchings. These plates combined clear isometric projections with decorative Baroque cartouches, figures in contemporary costume, and picturesque landscapes. The publisher Paul Fürst, and subsequently his widow and son-in-law Johann Andreas Endter, invested heavily in Böckler's projects, recognizing their immense commercial value across Europe. The plates were subjected to repeated printings and re-engravings well into the eighteenth century, with major revised editions appearing in Frankfurt, Nuremberg, and Amsterdam. Böckler's ability to seamlessly bridge the Latinate academic sphere and the German vernacular vernacular craft sphere allowed his books to serve simultaneously as theoretical manuals for university scholars, practical pattern books for master builders, and luxury prestige items for aristocratic libraries.The critical reception and historical legacy of Georg Andreas Böckler reflect the transition of early modern Europe from Late Renaissance natural magic and empirical craftsmanship toward Enlightenment mechanical philosophy and industrial engineering. While nineteenth- and early twentieth-century historians of technology occasionally criticized Böckler for incorporating speculative or unworkable perpetual-motion schemes alongside valid engineering designs, modern historiography recognizes his crucial role as a systematizer and visual codifier of technological knowledge. Scholars such as Marcus Popplow, Alexander Keller, and Wolfgang Lefèvre have demonstrated that Böckler's machine books functioned as indispensable intellectual instruments that conceptualized machines as modular, interchangeable assemblies of fundamental mechanical powers. His architectural writings demystified classical proportional systems for Northern European builders adapting to post-war reconstruction needs. When Böckler died in Ansbach on February 21, 1687, he left behind an intellectual legacy that fundamentally altered the visual language of European engineering and shaped the development of Baroque garden and hydraulic architecture across Central Europe.

academic_description: Folio (330x220 mm). Engraved title-page (Noribergae, sumptibus Pauli Furstii, technipragmatici, 1662), [10], 55, [1 blank] pp. and 154 full-page plates engraved by Eberhard Kieser and Balthasar Schwan after drawings by Böckler himself. Collation: ¶4-¶¶1 A-G4. Contemporary stiff vellum, spine with five raised bands and ink title. On the front pastedown engraved bookplate “Otiis comitis Fontanellati &c” of Alessandro Sanvitale di Fontanellato (1731-1804), founder of the Accademia degli Erranti in Fontanellato. Some occasional light browning and staining, small loss of paper to the outer blank corner of pl. 39 and 49. A very good, unpressed and genuine copy. First Latin edition, in the translation by Heinrich Schmitz, of one of the most accomplished and successful 17th-century machine books. It first appeared in German at Nuremberg in 1661. The Latin edition was reprinted in 1686, the German edition in 1673, 1703 and 1705.“It was in Germany that two of the most eminent engineering visionaries lived. The first of these was Georg Andreas Böckler who published a truly remarkable book […] called Theatrum Machinarum Novum, written and illustrated as a record of the progress of the art of engineering […] As one might gather, not just from the title page but from a knowledge of the general conditions pertaining in Germany after the Thirty Years’ War, Böckler’s acquaintance with machinery was restricted almost entirely to mills of one sort or another. In most of these, regardless of the motive power, he depicts the precursor of the geared transmission familiar to this day. The seventeenth-century engineers had neither the theoretical knowledge nor the technical equipment to design and shape gear-wheels which would mesh with minimum friction. In fact, friction as such, although made use of in such applications as the sack-lift in a mill, was little understood. The construction of pinions to mesh with larger gear-wheels had yet to assume the form common today. However, the problem of shifting the direction of rotation of a drive through 90° was solved by the invention of the wallower driven either by a contrite wheel (a wooden wheel with tooth pegs protruding around the circumference parallel to the axis) or by a cogwheel having teeth projecting radially around the circumference at right-angles to the axis […] The wallower comprised two discs of wood, each drilled with a matching set of concentric holes near the perimeter. The discs, usually with square centre bores to aid fixing and to transmit rotary motion, were mounted on a shaft separate by a gap of as much as the mechanism dictated, and threaded through the holes, from one disc to the next, were wooden rods. The result looked not unlike a birdcage or lantern, hence its more common name. When it was meshed with a large wheel having suitably spaced wooden pegs around either its diameter (the contrite) or its periphery (the cog), depending on whether parallel or perpendicular motion was desired, a serviceable gear train was the result. Friction, though cut efficiency drastically. All this is depicted in Böckler’s Theatre of New Machines, but what is a far more striking feature of the illustrations is the constant recurrence of the germ of perpetual motion” (Arthur W.J.G. Ord-Hume, Perpetual Motion. The History of an Obsession, Kempton IL, 2005, pp. 47-48).The strongly inked plates show hydraulic and mechanical machines powered by intricate systems of wheels that employ water, wind, weights, animal or human power, or some combination of these. These machines include many curious inventions applicable to all trades and human activities, such as paper and grain mills, drilling machines, roasting machines, water pumps, wood saws, blowing machines, fire engines, roasting spits, and so on.In particular, plate 5 pictures a hand mill for making ink for copperplate printing; plates 34, 36, 37, 41, 46, 47, and 59 depict mills used for grinding flour and sharpening stones, tools and knives; plate 72 shows a ‘fulling mill’ for pounding cloths to clean them; plates 73 and 74, considered as “the clearest delineation of the art to this date” (D. Hunter, The literature of papermaking 1390-1800, New York, 1971, p. 18), illustrate in detail paper-making by showing the linen rags being pulped with water-powered hammers, while the vatman stands ready with a mould, the coucher presses the post, and the drying sheets hang on ropes above, ready to be sized, calendared, gathered into reams, and packaged; the last plate (154) is remarkable for its depiction of a fire engine water pump made by the Nuremberg inventor Hans Hautsch in 1658, which is considered as the basis of the modern fire engine.A comparison of Böckler’s work with earlier machine books illustrates how “the focal point within the illustrations has shifted from the human to the mechanical […] Böckler shows a more developed awareness of how machines alter the status of workers was well as owners in his seventeenth-century illustrations. In one, a curtain has been drawn aside to reveal a couple at leisure eating dinner while the mill, tended by workers, operates on the floor beneath them (plate 53). Here the machine begins to determine the roles played by humans. The various illustrations portraying humans attentively watching a machine’s operation indicate even further the centrality of the apparatus in the drama being portrayed” (K.J. Knoespel, Gazing on Technology: Theatrum Mechanorum and the Assimilation of Renaissance Machinery, in: “Literature and Technology”, M.L. Greenberg & L. Schachterle, eds., London-Toronto, 1992, p. 110).Born in Cronheim, Böckler was mostly active as an architect in Nuremberg. In addition to the present work he is the author of the Architectura curiosa nova (Nuremberg, 1664), which dealt with hydrodynamics applied to water-jets, fountains and wells. Böckler died in Ansbach in 1667.

authors.name: Petit-Radel Louis-Charles François
authors.biography: Louis-Charles-François Petit-Radel (1756–1836) stands as one of the pivotal intellectual figures spanning the tumultuous transition between the late Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and the institutional consolidation of nineteenth-century European antiquarian science. A polymath whose erudition embraced classical philology, ecclesiastical history, bibliography, and comparative archaeology, Petit-Radel redefined the study of Mediterranean antiquity through his seminal hypotheses on megalithic and polygonal architecture. As a long-standing member of the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres and chief administrator of the Bibliothèque Mazarine in Paris, he occupied a central junction in the Republic of Letters, bridging the Benedictine traditions of erudite text-criticism with the emerging empirical methodologies of classical field archaeology and post-Revolutionary institutional historiography.Born in Paris on July 17, 1756, Petit-Radel belonged to an extraordinarily distinguished Parisian bourgeois lineage characterized by deep intellectual and artistic ambition. His brothers achieved equal renown in their respective domains: Philippe Petit-Radel (1749–1815) became a prominent professor of surgery, anatomist, and Latin poet, while Louis-François Petit-Radel (1740–1818) distinguished himself as a Neoclassical architect trained under the influence of Jean-François Chalgrin. Formed in an environment saturated with Enlightenment rationalism, classical humanities, and artistic rigor, Louis-Charles-François pursued an ecclesiastical vocation, studying at the prestigious seminaries of Paris and obtaining his doctorate in sacred theology at the Sorbonne. His intellectual acumen earned him early ecclesiastical advancement, resulting in his appointment as Vicar General of the Diocese of Saint-Pol-de-Léon and subsequently of Couserans. During these pre-Revolutionary years, his mind was forged in the meticulous traditions of Gallican scholarship and patristic textual analysis, laying the analytical groundwork for his future philological and bibliographical endeavors.The outbreak of the French Revolution in 1789 and the subsequent radicalization of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy shattered Petit-Radel’s ecclesiastical trajectory, forcing him into exile in Italy. Far from being a period of passive refuge, his Italian sojourn (1788–1797) transformed him into a pioneering field archaeologist. Traveling extensively across Latium, Umbria, Etruria, Campania, and the regions of Magna Graecia, Petit-Radel turned his attention away from classical textual sources to the physical, unwritten monuments of the Mediterranean past. He was captivated by the massive, unmortared, polygonal stone wallings found at ancient sites such as Alatri, Ferentino, Cora (Cori), Segni, Arpino, and Norba. Synthesizing his field observations with classical references in Hesiod, Homer, Herodotus, and Pausanias, Petit-Radel formulated his celebrated and controversial theory of "Pelasgic or Cyclopean Monuments" (Monuments cyclopéens). He postulated that these colossal polygonal fortifications were not the chaotic works of mythical giants or late Roman military engineers, but rather the remnants of an archaic, uniform, pre-Hellenic and pre-Etruscan pan-Mediterranean civilization—the Pelasgians—who had disseminated a standardized architectural technique across Greece, Asia Minor, and the Italian peninsula long before the rise of classical antiquity.Upon his return to France under the Consulate, Petit-Radel entered the newly reorganized national cultural apparatus. In 1801, he was appointed to the administration of the Bibliothèque Mazarine, a position he would hold for over three decades, eventually becoming its head librarian (conservateur-administrateur). Under his stewardship, the Mazarine was transformed into an exemplar of post-Revolutionary library science, organizing vast collections confiscated from religious orders and émigré estates. In 1810, his monumental contributions to classical learning led to his election to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres, where he succeeded Pierre-Charles Levesque. Within the Académie, Petit-Radel became a principal contributor to the monumental continuation of the Histoire littéraire de la France, a massive historiographical enterprise originally initiated by the Benedictines of Saint-Maur. Across Volumes XIV through XVII, Petit-Radel authored dozens of exhaustive bio-bibliographical essays on medieval scholastic theologians, twelfth-century Latin poets, canonical canonists, and troubadour literature, establishing critical frameworks for the study of medieval intellectual history that influenced generations of French medievalists.Simultaneously, Petit-Radel remained deeply engaged with classical literature and philosophical critique. In 1801, he published his monumental Examen analytique du poème de Lucrèce De Rerum Natura, a deeply nuanced work of philosophical commentary that analyzed Epicurean atomism and Lucretian physics through both a historical and a critical theological lens. Rather than simply dismissing Lucretius on dogmatic grounds, Petit-Radel dismantled the materialist metaphysics of De Rerum Natura with subtle philological precision, contextualizing ancient philosophical materialism within the broader development of classical natural philosophy. His architectural and antiquarian thesis culminated in numerous memoirs presented before the Institut de France and was eventually synthesized in his magnum opus, Recherches sur les monuments cyclopéens ou pelasgiques, published posthumously in 1841. This work established a systematic taxonomy of ancient masonry styles (distinguishing between primitive polygonal, irregular jointed, and regular squared opus quadratum), laying the foundation for modern comparative stratigraphic architectural typology.Petit-Radel died in Paris on November 7, 1836, leaving behind an extraordinary legacy that bridged eighteenth-century erudition and nineteenth-century academic discipline. While later nineteenth- and twentieth-century archaeology—led by figures such as Heinrich Schliemann, Arthur Evans, and modern architectural historians—revised his over-broad attribution of all polygonal masonry to a single 'Pelasgic' ethnic group, his empirical methodology of recording, surveying, and comparing non-literary physical ruins marked a decisive evolutionary step in archaeological science. His vast printed legacy, preserved in the proceedings of the Institut de France, the annals of the Mazarine Library, and the volumes of the Histoire littéraire de la France, remains a monument to the endurance of classical humanist scholarship during one of the most volatile epochs in European history.

With an extensive index. Contemporary light brown calf, by Antoine Chaumont, Paris (with his ticket), gold-tooled outer border with eagles, Pan’s head, vase containing flowers and other ornaments, inner border in blind of laurel leaves in arches, flat spine with seven false bands and black morocco title label, gilt edges, blue endpapers, inner dentelles (joints starting). A fine and beautifully bound copy. First edition of this valuable history of libraries, which offers an overview of the public libraries, especially in France, including those in provincial cities, from the 6th century onwards. A long section is devoted to the foundation and holdings of Bibliothèque Mazarine (Notice historique sur la Bibliothèque Mazarine, pp. [249]-337). The two folding plates depicts the floor plans of that institution. Petit-Radel (1756-1836) was librarian at the Mazarine from 1814 to 1836.

authors.name: Fregoso Antonio
authors.biography: Antonio Fregoso, known variably as Campofregoso, Fulgoso, and later adopting the appellation Fileremo, emerges as a significant yet complex figure within the tapestry of Italian humanism during the transition from the 15th to the 16th century. Born around 1460 in Carrara, he was a scion of the noble Genoese Fregoso family, albeit through an illegitimate line. His life and works provide a window into the intricate interplay of politics, literature, and philosophy during the Italian Renaissance, a period marked by profound cultural and intellectual ferment.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education.Antonio Fregoso's birth into the Fregoso family, a lineage steeped in Genoese nobility, was complicated by his illegitimacy. His mother, Giovanna, remains an elusive figure in historical records, while his father, Spinetta Fregoso, played a pivotal role in his early life. Spinetta's political alliances, particularly with Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, positioned young Antonio within a sphere of influence that would shape his future. The irregular legitimization of Antonio by Emperor Frederick III underscores the era's intricate web of political and familial negotiations. Following Spinetta's death in 1467, Antonio came under the tutelage of Cicco Simonetta, a testamentary guardian appointed by his father, which facilitated his integration into Milanese society. The grant of Milanese citizenship by Galeazzo Maria Sforza in 1472 further cemented his status, although subsequent political upheavals, including Simonetta's execution, would challenge his position.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks.Antonio Fregoso's literary output reflects the intellectual currents of his time, blending classical influences with contemporary philosophical discourse. His notable works, 'Riso di Democrito' and 'Pianto di Heraclito,' written in 1505 and 1507, respectively, employ a dantesque structure to explore themes of laughter and sorrow, drawing upon the philosophical dichotomy of Democritus and Heraclitus. These works, alongside the 'Dialogo de Fortuna,' reveal Fregoso's engagement with notions of human fortune and virtue, resonating with the ideas of Erasmus and echoing the allegorical style of Ludovico Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso.' Fregoso's intellectual milieu included figures such as Lancino Curti, Bartolomeo Simonetta, and Gaspare Visconti, with whom he shared literary exchanges that enriched the cultural landscape of Lombardy.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation.The publication and dissemination of Fregoso's works were facilitated by the vibrant printing culture of Renaissance Italy. The typographical landscape of Milan and Genoa, characterized by the proliferation of humanist texts and the influence of the Aldine Press, provided a fertile ground for Fregoso's ideas. His works were not only circulated within Italy but also translated into French and Spanish, as evidenced by the translations by Michele d'Amboise and Alonso Lobera, respectively. This international reach underscores the broader impact of his writings and their alignment with the humanist ideals that transcended national boundaries.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy.Antonio Fregoso's legacy is marked by both recognition and obscurity. His mention in Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' attests to his contemporaneous relevance, while later literary historians, such as Crescimbeni, acknowledged his philosophical inclinations. The allegorical richness of his works, situated between medieval and Renaissance sensibilities, reflects the transitional nature of his era. Despite the political vicissitudes that marred his life, Fregoso's contributions to Italian literature and philosophy endure, offering insights into the complexities of human fortune and the pursuit of wisdom.

publishers.name: Zoppino Niccolò
publishers.biography: Niccolò d’Aristotele de’ Rossi, known as Zoppino, was a Ferrarese bookseller, publisher, printer, and bookseller-editor whose activity, documented from the end of the fifteenth century until 1544, places him among the most important figures in the development of the Italian vernacular book market in the first half of the sixteenth century. He was born in Ferrara no later than 1478. His father, Aristotele de’ Rossi, was a notary and probably died in that year; his mother is unknown. The sobriquet Zoppino, apparently connected with a physical disability, became his principal professional designation and frequently appears in imprints, archival documents, and contemporary references. Although Venice became the principal centre of his activity, Zoppino maintained close connections with Ferrara and developed a commercial network that extended across northern and central Italy.The earliest documentary evidence of his career dates from Bologna. In 1495 a “Zopino de Ferara libraro” was recorded as owing money to the printer Bazaliero Bazalieri. By 1503 he was associated with Bazalieri's press in the production of Il libro del maestro et del discipulo by Honorius of Autun, to which he subscribed as “Nicolo di Aristotile dicto il Zoppino da Ferrara”. An undated edition of the works of Serafino Aquilano, also produced by Bazalieri during the Bentivoglio period, describes Zoppino as “impressore & venditore da libri”. These documents are important because they reveal from the beginning the composite nature of his profession: he could act simultaneously as bookseller, publisher, financial intermediary, and printer or commissioner of printing.Around 1505 Zoppino moved the centre of his activity to Venice, then the principal Italian centre of the book trade. During the first phase of his Venetian career he did not necessarily print all the books that appeared under his name: he commissioned or arranged editions through different printing workshops in Venice and elsewhere, including Milan, Pesaro, and Ancona. This distinction between publisher-bookseller and printer is essential to understanding his enterprise. Zoppino was not simply the proprietor of a single workshop; he developed a flexible production and distribution system in which printing was entrusted to different presses according to the nature, format, and intended market of individual books.From 1513 to 1524 Zoppino was in partnership with Vincenzo di Polo, a bookseller and itinerant performer who is described in his 1524 testament as a cantor circumforaneus. Their partnership produced 139 small books and operated through a network of printing firms extending beyond Venice to Perugia, Ancona, and Pesaro. The association is particularly significant for understanding the relationship between commercial print and oral or performative culture. It is therefore possible to situate part of Zoppino's early commercial strategy within the world of itinerant bookselling and popular literary performance, although the precise extent of his own participation in public performance remains uncertain.The partnership also became involved in a politically sensitive episode. Zoppino and Vincenzo di Polo were arrested in Venice in 1513 in connection with the printing and dissemination at Ferrara of an anti-Venetian barzelletta composed in the aftermath of the battle of Agnadello. They were imprisoned for approximately three months before being released following an appeal by the influential Venetian patrician Marino Morosini. The episode is particularly valuable because it demonstrates that Zoppino's activities could extend beyond the production of books in the conventional sense into the circulation of topical, ephemeral, and politically charged vernacular print. The Ferrara barzelletta is the only edition currently known to have been produced there under his name.The episode also provides a plausible context for the recurrent association between Zoppino and the culture of the piazza. Pietro Aretino's literary representations of a Zoppino who “canta in banco” cannot be treated as straightforward biographical testimony, but they acquire a suggestive background from Zoppino's long association with Vincenzo di Polo. A further contemporary trace of his connection with popular and satirical culture is provided by a 1542 Roman engraving of the torso of Pasquino by Antonio Salamanca, whose accompanying verse explicitly names Zoppino. Such evidence does not justify identifying every literary Zoppino with the historical printer, but it confirms that his name circulated within the culture of vernacular performance, satire, and popular print.Zoppino was also the first printer-publisher of Pietro Aretino. Aretino's Opera nova del fecundissimo giovene Pietro pictore Arretino was printed in Venice by Zoppino in 1512 and constitutes the writer's first published work. The relationship between the two men continued thereafter, and Zoppino remained an important publisher of vernacular literature associated with Aretino's generation. After the dissolution of the partnership with Vincenzo di Polo, Zoppino increasingly consolidated his own printing enterprise in Venice. From 1525 until the end of his documented activity in 1544, he operated a press while continuing to collaborate with printers and commercial partners elsewhere. His network included Perugia, Florence, Bologna, Rome, Savona, Ravenna, Faenza, and other centres. In 1536 he is documented as a member of the Florentine Arte dei medici e speziali, the guild to which booksellers belonged. During the final phase of his career he was active as a bookseller in Ravenna and Faenza, where his son Sebastiano also participated in the family business.The scale of the enterprise is remarkable. Lorenzo Baldacchini's analytical catalogue records 438 editions associated with Zoppino between 1503 and 1544, while recognizing that the census cannot necessarily be considered absolutely complete. The corpus demonstrates an overwhelming preference for Italian vernacular texts, with Latin occupying a comparatively minor position and Greek virtually absent. The production was particularly oriented towards relatively inexpensive and portable formats, above all the octavo, although Zoppino also issued quartos and folios when the subject or intended readership required them. His catalogue therefore cannot be reduced to “popular” literature in a narrow sense: it encompasses literary, devotional, technical, scientific, educational, geographical, and practical works, often combining commercial accessibility with substantial typographical and illustrative ambition.Zoppino's publications developed a recognizable visual and typographical identity. Many of his books employ woodcut title-page borders or illustrations, recurring ornamental material, prominent colophons, and several variants of his printer's or publisher's device. The best-known device represents Saint Nicholas, sometimes with the kneeling maiden to whom he gives the three golden balls, accompanied by the initials N and Z. The recurrent use of such elements contributed to the creation of what Baldacchini has described as a recognizable “house style”, anticipating in certain respects the more systematic publishing series developed later by Gabriele Giolito de' Ferrari.Illustration was one of the defining characteristics of the enterprise. More than one hundred Zoppino editions are illustrated, often with woodcuts adapted to the specific genre and readership of the book. The relationship between Zoppino and woodcutters was not limited to the reuse of generic decorative material: his workshop and its collaborators developed sustained programmes in which image and text were deliberately coordinated. Giovanni Andrea Vavassore is among the artists associated with the broader Venetian milieu of illustrated vernacular printing in which Zoppino operated, although individual blocks and their authorship must be established case by case rather than attributed systematically to a single artist.The literary core of Zoppino's early catalogue was formed by vernacular poetry and narrative, particularly courtly and lyric literature. His books included works by Serafino Aquilano, Antonio Tebaldeo, Vincenzo Calmeta, Antonio Fileremo Fregoso, Matteo Maria Boiardo, and other writers active in the transition between late Quattrocento literary culture and the more strongly codified linguistic norms associated with Pietro Bembo. Zoppino's catalogue is particularly valuable because it preserves a wide range of vernacular practices at precisely the moment when the literary prestige of the Petrarchan and Bembist models was becoming increasingly dominant. His editorial policy should not, however, be interpreted as a deliberate anti-Bembist programme. It is better understood as a commercially and culturally eclectic strategy that responded to established readerships and to the continuing popularity of literary forms associated with oral performance and courtly entertainment.Chivalric literature constituted one of the most sustained areas of his production. Zoppino published several editions of Matteo Maria Boiardo's Orlando innamorato, as well as continuations commissioned from Niccolò degli Agostini. These projects combined serial publication, textual intervention, illustration, and the cultivation of a readership familiar with oral and performative traditions. The culmination of this interest came with Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando furioso of 1530. Zoppino's November 1530 edition was the first illustrated edition of the Furioso to employ a systematic programme of woodcuts specifically conceived for the poem: a series of images was placed at the opening of the cantos, visually summarizing the narrative that followed. The surviving programme comprises forty woodcuts for the forty cantos then constituting the poem. The model proved exceptionally influential and was reused and adapted in later Zoppino editions.Zoppino's production nevertheless extended well beyond literary entertainment. It included devotional works, collections of recipes, arithmetic and abacus books, manuals of handwriting, prognostications, theatrical and narrative texts, practical guides, and pattern books for embroidery and other forms of ornamental work. Such books are particularly important for the history of material culture because they reveal how printed images could function as practical models rather than merely as illustrations. The combination of inexpensive formats, woodcut imagery, and vernacular instruction allowed Zoppino's books to circulate among readers well beyond the traditional humanist and aristocratic clientele of large-format Latin books.At the same time, Zoppino did not confine himself to small popular books. One of the most ambitious projects associated with his press was Benedetto Bordone's Libro nel qual si ragiona de tutte l'isole del mondo, first published in Venice in 1528. The work is a richly illustrated geographical and cartographical compilation containing numerous maps and plans, including representations of the Americas and a celebrated plan of Mexico-Tenochtitlan. A substantially revised or reissued form appeared in 1534 under the title Isolario. These editions demonstrate that Zoppino could undertake technically and financially demanding illustrated productions alongside his much larger output of inexpensive octavos.Another important example is the 1535 edition of Vitruvius's De architectura, edited by Francesco Lucio Durantino and printed by Zoppino in Venice. The book is an illustrated vernacular edition and belongs to the important sequence of sixteenth-century Italian adaptations of Vitruvius that followed Cesare Cesariano's 1521 translation. Its 136 woodcut illustrations demonstrate the technical and graphic capabilities of Zoppino's workshop and its ability to produce books for readers interested in architecture, engineering, and antiquarian learning.Zoppino also intervened directly in the editorial presentation of the texts he published. His addresses to readers repeatedly claim correction, linguistic clarification, and the restoration of works allegedly corrupted by previous printers. In the 1524 edition of Iacopo Caviceo's Libro del peregrino, for example, he emphasized orthographic correction and the explanation in Italian of obscure Latin words. In the Vita Sanctae Mariae of Antonio Cornazano, published in 1525, he similarly presented himself as having corrected errors and made the text more useful to readers. Such declarations were partly conventional elements of early modern publishing rhetoric, but their recurrence indicates that Zoppino understood the publisher as an active mediator between inherited texts and their contemporary readership.An especially distinctive feature of his editorial practice was the use of printed marginalia. Between approximately 1519 and 1523, a number of Zoppino editions incorporated extensive vernacular marginal annotations. Examples include the Italian Apulegio of Boiardo (1519), the vernacular Trionfi of Petrarch (1519), Fregoso's Cerva bianca (1521), and Poliziano's Stanze (1521). In the case of Boiardo, the printed marginalia have been described as exceptional within the history of the poem, while their recurrence in several Zoppino publications indicates a broader editorial practice. These annotations provided interpretative guidance and helped to construct a more intensive reading experience for vernacular texts.Zoppino's catalogue also intersected significantly with religious reform. In 1525 he printed Uno libretto volgare con la dechiaratione de li dieci comandamenti, del Credo, del Pater noster, a collection of writings associated with Martin Luther and representing the first Italian translation of Luther's writings to be printed. The following year he reissued the work under the protective attribution of Erasmus. He subsequently published Erasmus in Latin and works by Bernardino Ochino and other figures associated with evangelical or reforming currents. This activity demonstrates Zoppino's willingness to exploit controversial and rapidly circulating religious material, but it should not be transformed into evidence of a consistent personal Protestant commitment. He continued to publish orthodox devotional works and retained papal privileges; his religious catalogue is therefore better interpreted as evidence of a commercially and intellectually receptive publishing policy operating within the unstable confessional environment of 1520s–1540s Italy.The final phase of Zoppino's activity was characterized by a marked contraction in production. His output ceases after 1544, conventionally taken as the probable year of his death, although neither the precise date nor the place of death is known. His son Sebastiano is securely documented as a bookseller and collaborator in the family business at Ravenna and at the fairs of central Italy. Other individuals bearing the Zoppino name appear in the Venetian printing trade later in the century, but their precise relationship to Niccolò cannot be established with certainty.Zoppino's historical importance therefore lies less in the individual originality of the texts he published than in the exceptional coherence and breadth of his role as a mediator of vernacular culture. He combined printing, publishing, bookselling, commissioning, distribution, editorial intervention, illustration, and—through his early association with itinerant performers—the circulation of books within the wider culture of the piazza. His catalogue brought together canonical and non-canonical literature, chivalric poetry, religious texts, technical manuals, geographical works, recipes, educational books, and practical pattern books. In doing so, Zoppino contributed decisively to the expansion of the Italian vernacular book beyond the restricted world of courtly and humanist readers and helped establish the commercial, visual, and editorial forms through which the Italian printed book reached a much broader public in the first half of the sixteenth century.

publisher_data: Colophon: Stampata in Vinegia per Nicolo Zoppino di Aristotile di Ferrara ne l’anno di nostra salute MDXXVIII (Venice, Niccolò Zoppino, 1528)
academic_description: 8vo (149x99 mm). 82, [2 blank] leaves. Collation: A-K8 L4. Title page within an elaborate woodcut border. Leaves L3 and L4 are blank. Colophon and register at l. L2v. Roman and italic types. Variant A before the correction of “guanci” in “guancie” in the final line of text at l. A6r. On title-page verso note to the reader by Enrico Boscano. Later stiff vellum, inked title on spine, marbled edges. Lacking a small portion of paper from the upper margin of ll. F6 and F7 with minimal loss of text, marginal staining, some occasional foxing. From the collection of the bookseller Giuseppe Martini (his pencil notes on the front flyleaves, cf. E. Barbieri, ed., Da Lucca a New York a Lugano: Giuseppe Martini libraio tra Otto e Novecento, Florence, 2017). Rare second edition. In 1521 Fregoso vulgarised Lancino Curti’s Silvae and in 1525 in Milan at Giovanni Giacomo Da Legnano and Bartolomeo da Crema’s press he published his own ‘silvae’, also known as Opera nova, which includes Lamento d’Amore mendicante, Dialogo de musica, Pergoletta de le laudi de Amore, Discorsi cottidiani non vulgari, De lo istinto naturale, De la probità and, finally, De i tre peregrini.In this work, all of Fregoso’s favourite themes return. Fortune, in contrast to Love, returns victorious thanks to her alliance with the blind Pluto who has wreaked havoc everywhere (Lamento d’Amore mendicante), while Platonic and Neo-Platonic concepts are repeated several times, in dialogue with Antonio Telesio and Simonetta: the correspondence between the harmony of the heavens, the harmony of nature and the harmony of the inner world (Dialogo de musica); the distinction between human and divine Love (Pergoletta de le laudi de Amore); the theory of demons that influence the actions of men according to their nature (Discorsi cottidiani non vulgari); the act of faith in the Reason innate in man, which allows even the child abandoned on the desert island to achieve his own form of education (De lo istinto naturale); the celebration of Probity, which comforts the embittered poet to flee the vanity of studies (De la Probità); and finally the fantastic journey of I tre peregrini, in which Eutimia accompanies Apuano, Filarete and Fregoso to a fair, which is the emporium of Fortune, and prevents them from buying what Fortune and Lust offer them through Epicurus, to follow instead the path of intellectual exercise and literature nourished by philosophy.Antonio Fregoso (or Campofregoso or Fulgoso) Fileremo (or Filareno, i.e. lover of solitude) was probably born in Carrara, around 1460, the illegitimate son of Spinetta of the noble Genoese Fregoso family and lord of the city. Lacking male heirs, his father legitimised Antonio by an act later ratified by Emperor Frederick III. Spinetta, linked to the Duke of Milan Francesco Sforza, appointed in his will Cicco Simonetta as administrator of his estate and guardian of his son. After Spinetta’s death in 1467, Fregoso lived with the latter in Milan. In 1472 Galeazzo Maria Sforza officially granted Milanese citizenship to Fregoso, but the following year Simonetta, as ducal minister, deprived him of Carrara and Lunigiana, which had passed to Federico Malaspina, rewarding him in exchange with the fief of Sannazzaro in Lomellina. In 1478, on the occasion of Gian Galeazzo Sforza’s ducal appointment, Fregoso was made a knight. After a brief absence, he returned to Milan, where he married Fiorbellina Visconti di Lodrisio. In 1499 he swore allegiance to Louis XII when the latter conquered the Duchy of Milan, thus keeping his knighthood but losing the feud of Sannazzaro.Fregoso then decided to retire to the villa in Colturano, on the road to Lodi, from where he sent his first works to Iafredo Carlo, president of the Milanese Senate. His retreat outside Milan did not, however, prevent him from frequenting the circles of Cecilia Gallerani and Ippolita Sforza Bentivoglio (as can be seen in the novelle I, 21 and III, 9 by M. Bandello). It is not clear what changes in Fregoso’s life the succession in Milan of the Sforzas, French and Spanish after 1512 brought. He probably died around 1530. The fact that he is mentioned among the poets in the 1532 edition of L. Ariosto’s Orlando furioso (XLVI, 16, v. 3 ff) does not serve to shift the terminus post quem since many of those mentioned in the poem were already dead at that date (V. De Matteis, Fregoso, Antonio Fileremo, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 50, Rome, 1998, s.v.).Respectively in 1506 and 1507 Fregoso published two poems, the Riso di Democrito (“Democritus’ Laughter”) and the Pianto di Heraclito (“Heraclitus’ Weeping), each in fifteen chapters of tercets. The translations into French by Michael d’Amboise (1547) and into Spanish by Alonso Lobera (1554) testify to the international fame of the two poems (often published together as I doi filosofi- ‘The Two Philosophers’).The issue of fortune is presented in the form of a dialogue between the author, Lancino Curti and Bartolomeo Simonetta in the Dialogo de Fortuna (Milan, Pietro Martire Mantegazza, 1507). No longer in tercets but in octaves is the poem Contentione di Pluto & Iro (‘The Contention of Pluto and Irus’), first printed in Milan by Mantegazza in 1507. Also in octaves is Fregoso’s most famous work, the Cerva bianca (“The White Doe”, Milan, Mantegazza, 1510) (cf. A. Dobelli, L’opera letteraria di Antonio Fregoso Fileremo, Modena, 1898).“In definitiva prodotti come quelli del Fregoso stavano a testimoniare, nel primo ventennio del ‘500, la vitalità di una ‘letteratura mista e multiforme, drammatica, narrativa, allegorica, pronta a ogni sorta di esperimenti e però sufficientemente sciolta dall’impaccio delle regole... letteratura tutta moderna, se anche variamente assistita da antichi modelli classici e volgari’. E ne rende fede quel mannello di presenze raccolte intorno al Fileremo, vuoi interlocutori dei suoi dialoghi, vuoi pubblici laudatores delle sue imprese poetiche: editori, poeti nell’una e nell’altra lingua, letterati, oratori, quegli stessi che si ritrovano se si ha la pazienza di seguire certi fili che porge il sistema delle dedicatorie bandelliane: gli esponenti insomma di una cultura legata in fondo ancora alle sue origini cortigiane e destinata nel terzo decennio del ‘500 a frantumarsi per ‘un naturale e mirabile accordo della storia letteraria con quella politica’ ” (G. Dilemmi, Un capitolo della cultura settentrionale all’inizio del ‘500, in: A. Fregoso, “Opere”, Bologna, 1976, pp. XXIX-XXX).

title: Gli Ordini della divota Compagnia delle dimesse; che vivono sotto il nome, et la protettione della purissima Madre di Dio Maria Vergine

authors.name: Pagani Antonio
authors.biography: Antonio Pagani (born Marco Pagani; Venice, 1526 – Vicenza, January 4, 1589) stands as one of the most intellectually compelling and institutionalized figures of the Franciscan Observance and Catholic Reform within the sixteenth-century Republic of Venice. Operating at the crucial historical intersection between the final sessions of the Council of Trent (1545–1563) and the rigorous execution of Tridentine decrees under prominent prelates such as Saint Charles Borromeo and Bishop Agostino Valier, Pagani embodied a rare synthesis of rigorous jurisprudence, Franciscan affective mysticism, and pastoral innovation. His life's work reshaped early modern Italian spirituality by articulating a sophisticated theology of lay holiness, creating novel institutional frameworks for uncloistered consecrated women (the Compagnia delle Dimesse), and producing a vast corpus of ascetical and mystical literature that circulated widely throughout Western Europe.Born into a respectable Venetian family in 1526, Marco Pagani received an elite education rooted in Renaissance humanism before matriculating at the prestigious University of Padua. Padua was then the premier center for legal and Aristotelian scholarship in Northern Italy, attracting minds from across the continent. There, Pagani pursued rigorous studies in both civil and canon law, culminating in the conferral of the doctorate (doctor utriusque iuris). This formidable legal foundation imbued him with an acute analytical methodology, a precise Latinity, and an enduring interest in institutional organization—traits that would uniquely distinguish his subsequent theological writings and monastic reforms from those of his contemporaries. Despite the prospect of a lucrative judicial or diplomatic career in the service of the Venetian Republic, Pagani underwent a profound spiritual crisis during his early post-academic years. Drawn to the ideal of evangelical poverty and interior recollection, he renounced his worldly honors in 1545 and entered the Order of Friars Minor Observant (Ordo Fratrum Minorum Regularis Observantiae) at the friary of San Biagio in Vicenza, adopting the religious name Antonio.Upon completing his novitiate and receiving holy orders, Friar Antonio Pagani quickly emerged as a dynamic preacher, spiritual director, and theological polemicist. His deep erudition in Patristic theology, scholasticism, and canon law elevated him to key positions within the Venetian province of the Observants. During the mid-sixteenth century, as Northern Italy grappled with the infiltration of Protestant ideas across the Alpine borders, Pagani was mobilized as a defender of orthodox Catholic ecclesiology. He traveled extensively throughout Venice, Vicenza, Padua, Verona, and Udine, delivering powerful Lenten sermon series that combined fiery rhetoric with rigorous moral theology. His theological expertise caught the attention of eminent Counter-Reformation leaders; he maintained close intellectual ties with Cardinal Agostino Valier, Bishop of Verona, and Nicolò Ormaneto, Bishop of Padua and former vicar to Cardinal Reginald Pole. Through these networks, Pagani actively participated in the local implementation of Tridentine reforms, emphasizing clerical discipline, frequent reception of the sacraments, and the systematic catechesis of the laity.Pagani's written output is vast and multifaceted, spanning ascetical manuals, mystical guides, and institutional constitutions. Among his most celebrated works is L'Huomo Apostolico (first published in Venice, 1575), an exhaustive treatise outlining the spiritual, moral, and practical duties of Catholic priests and missionaries engaged in pastoral care. In this text, Pagani harmonized Bonaventurian Franciscan affectivity with the structured discipline required by post-Tridentine pastoral theology. Another major work, Le Divine Solitudini and its companion Specchio della perfettione Christiana (1577), explored the interior life, providing lay readers with systematic methods of mental prayer and meditation drawn from the Devotio Moderna and Franciscan mystical traditions. Pagani's mystical synthesis reached its apex in his Somma della Teologia Mistica, wherein he adapted pseudo-Dionysian apophatic theology and Saint Bonaventure's Itinerarium Mentis in Deum for a broader, vernacular audience, arguing that supreme contemplation was not the exclusive domain of cloistered monastics, but was accessible to all Christians striving for charity and evangelical perfection.The publishing history of Antonio Pagani's works provides a vivid window into the vibrant print culture of late sixteenth-century Venice. Venice was the undisputed capital of European typography, housing prestigious printing establishments that specialized in religious and liturgical texts designed to fulfill the vast demand created by the Catholic Reformation. Pagani worked in close collaboration with renowned Venetian printer-publishers, most notably the houses of Domenico & Giovanni Battista Guerra, Francesco de' Franceschi, Giorgio Angelieri, and Andrea Muschio. These publishers issued Pagani's texts primarily in octavo and duodecimo formats—portable, durable volumes intended for daily personal devotion, spiritual direction, and pastoral travel. Printed with clean Roman and Italic types, decorated with elegant woodcut initials, and frequently featuring allegorical frontispieces or woodcuts of Saint Francis receiving the stigmata, Pagani's books were immediate commercial and devotional successes. They underwent numerous printings and editions, receiving the necessary ecclesiastical imprimatur from Venetian inquisitorial censors and the Senate, and circulating heavily throughout Italy, Spain, France, and the Southern Netherlands.Central to Pagani's historical and spiritual legacy was his revolutionary contribution to the status of religious women in early modern society. Recognizing the social constraints of his era—where women were frequently forced into institutional cloisters against their will (monacazione forzata) or left without social protection—Pagani envisioned a novel form of consecrated secular life. In 1579, alongside the noblewoman Maria Alberghetti, Pagani founded the Compagnia delle Dimesse (Sisters of the Annunciation) in Vicenza. The Dimesse were pious women who took private vows of chastity, poverty, and obedience, but remained in their family homes or small uncloistered communities, active in teaching, charitable work, and the education of young girls. This institutional model offered women spiritual autonomy and an active apostolic role without the requirement of solemn papal enclosure (clausura). Simultaneously, Pagani established lay fraternities for men, such as the Compagnia di San Bartolomeo and the Fratelli della Croce (often designated as Lupi or Oblati), aimed at deepening lay piety and social charity.Following a life of unrelenting ascetical rigor, tireless preaching, and prolific authorial labor, Antonio Pagani died in Vicenza on January 4, 1589, surrounded by his Franciscan brothers and spiritual disciples. His death prompted an immediate wave of popular veneration throughout the Venetian hinterland. In the centuries following his death, the cause for his beatification was formally introduced in Rome, leading to his designation as Venerable within the Catholic Church. Modern historiography—spearheaded by twentieth- and twenty-first-century scholars of Franciscan history, Venetian church history, and gender studies—has re-evaluated Pagani not merely as a pious author, but as a crucial architect of post-Tridentine lay spirituality and a pioneer of active female religious life in early modern Europe.
