publishers.name: Bodoni Giambattista
publishers.biography: Giambattista Bodoni (Saluzzo, February 26, 1740 – Parma, November 30, 1813) stands as the undisputed titan of Neoclassical typography, widely celebrated across early nineteenth-century Europe as the Princeps Typographorum—the 'Printer of Kings and King of Printers.' Operating at the precise historical conjunction where the Age of Enlightenment gave way to the Napoleonic Empire, Bodoni orchestrated a radical paradigm shift in the material culture of the book. Rather than viewing typography as a mere mechanical vehicle for the passive transmission of text, he elevated matrix-cutting, presswork, and page layout into an autonomous architectural art form. Alongside his Parisian contemporary and rival Firmin Didot, Bodoni stripped the printed page of the lingering Baroque and Rococo ornamentation that had dominated European printing presses since the seventeenth century. In its place, he instituted a severe, pristine aesthetic characterized by absolute geometric symmetry, unyielding verticality, hyper-calibrated margins, and an unprecedented contrast between razor-thin hair serifs and heavy, jet-black vertical stems. His monumental editions of classical Greek, Latin, and Italian literature redefined European bibliophilia, converting the printed volume into a Neoclassical monument of monumentality, clarity, and structural purity that embodied the intellectual aspirations of the late eighteenth-century Republic of Letters.Born into a modest family of provincial craftsmen in Saluzzo, within the Principality of Piedmont (then part of the Kingdom of Sardinia), Bodoni was immersed in the mechanics of printing from his earliest childhood. His father, Francesco Agostino Bodoni, and his grandfather, Domenico Pedro Bodoni, were both established printers and engravers who taught the young Giambattista the fundamentals of setting movable type, preparing relief woodcuts, and operating hand presses. Displaying an exceptional precocity for fine metal engraving and counterpunch design, the eighteen-year-old Bodoni departed Piedmont in February 1758, bound for Rome in the company of his schoolmate Dominic Tonetti. In the Papal Capital, his extraordinary artistic aptitude secured him an appointment at the prestigious press of the Stamperia della Sacra Congregazione de Propaganda Fide, the Vatican's missionary publishing institute founded in 1622. Under the patronage of Cardinal Giuseppe Spinelli, then Prefect of the Congregation, and the direct mentorship of the press director, Father Ruggero Costantini, Bodoni was entrusted with the extraordinary task of organizing, cleaning, and recasting ancient matrices for oriental and exotic typefaces, including original punches engraved in the sixteenth century by Robert Granjon and Claude Garamond. During his eight-year tenure at the Propaganda Fide, Bodoni mastered the structural nuances of non-Latin scripts—ranging from Syriac, Coptic, and Arabic to Armenian, Hebrew, and Tibetan—while simultaneously expanding his intellectual horizons by studying oriental languages at the Sapienza University. This intense Roman formation imbued him with a profound respect for typographic scholarship, structural variation, and the global heritage of letterforms.The decisive turning point in Bodoni's career occurred in early 1768. Following a severe illness that shattered his plans to travel to London to establish an independent press, Bodoni accepted a fateful invitation from Duke Ferdinand I of Bourbon and his enlightened French Prime Minister, Guillaume du Tillot, to relocate to the Duchy of Parma. Du Tillot, eager to transform Parma into an intellectual and artistic rival to Paris, Rome, and Florence, appointed Bodoni as the Director of the newly established Stamperia Reale (Royal Printing House), housed in the sprawling complex of the Palazzo della Pilotta. Initially utilizing imported type matrices purchased from the Parisian typefounder Pierre-Simon Fournier, Bodoni produced brilliant ceremonial books, such as the Descrizione delle feste celebrate in Parma per le nozze del Serenissimo Infante D. Ferdinando di Borbone (1769). However, Bodoni soon grew dissatisfied with French Rococo types and began cutting his own original steel punches, gradually founding his own private type foundry within the ducal palace. In 1791, with the official permission of the Duke and the financial sponsorship of the Spanish diplomat and Neoclassical connoisseur Don José Nicolás de Azara, Bodoni was granted permission to establish his private press, the Officina Bodoniana. From this private press issued his absolute masterpieces: breathtaking folio editions of Horace (1791), Virgil (1793), Catullus, Tibullus, and Propertius (1794), Torquato Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata (1794), Dante Alighieri's Divina Commedia (1795), and Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1791). His production culminated in the majestic three-volume Greek edition of Homer's Iliad (1808), dedicated directly to Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte, who hailed Bodoni as a supreme national treasure of the Empire and bestowed upon him pensions, honors, and imperial patronage.From a technical and typographical perspective, Bodoni's innovations reshaped the chemistry and physics of early modern printing. In his seminal treatise, the Manuale Tipografico—first issued as a modest specimen book in 1788 and subsequently expanded into the monumental, posthumous two-volume edition of 1818 edited by his devoted widow, Margherita Dall'Aglio—Bodoni systematically articulated the four fundamental pillars of typographical beauty: regularità (uniformity and consistency across the alphabet), chiarezza (sharp clarity and legibility), buon gusto (good taste through harmonic proportion), and grazia (grace achieved through flawless execution and finish). Mechanically, Bodoni altered the geometry of the letterform by abandoning the diagonal stress and sloped serifs of traditional Old Style typefaces (such as Bembo or Garamond) in favor of a strictly vertical mathematical axis, flat unbracketed serifs, and extreme contrast between ultra-delicate hairlines and thick structural stems. To showcase these extreme typographic lines, Bodoni revolutionized the physical materials of printing: he discarded rough hand-made rag papers in favor of ultra-smooth, highly calendered woven paper (papier vélin) supplied by English mills like Whatman and Italian mills in Fabriano; he reformulated printing ink using purified lampblack, nut oil, and boiled linseed oil to achieve an unprecedented obsidian-black density; and he modified the wooden hand press to deliver immensely powerful, uniform impressions. Eliminating decorative headpieces, tailpieces, and floral borders, Bodoni relied exclusively on generous interline spacing (interlineatura), wide architectural margins, and pristine white space to generate a dramatic visual rhythm.The critical reception of Bodoni's work spans centuries of artistic fervor, intense debate, and enduring institutional legacy. In his own lifetime, Bodoni was venerated by the international cultural elite; sovereigns, popes, diplomats, and literary figures—including Pope Pius VI, Joachim Murat, Vincenzo Monti, Antonio Canova, and Stendhal (who immortalized the printer's perfectionism in *La Chartreuse de Parme*)—made pilgrimages to his Parma workshop to marvel at his presses. However, with the advent of the Industrial Revolution and the late nineteenth-century Gothic Revival, Bodoni's work faced fierce ideological criticism. Scholars and craft revivalists such as William Morris, John Ruskin, and the leaders of the Kelmscott Press castigated Bodoni's modern typefaces as cold, mechanical, overly rational, and destructive to the organic legibility of traditional humanist type. Despite these Victorian detractors, the twentieth century witnessed a massive global rehabilitation of Bodoni's legacy. Renowned type foundries—including American Type Founders (ATF under Morris Fuller Benton), Bauer, Linotype, and Haas—redesigned and digitized the Bodoni family, transforming it into the quintessential typeface for modern editorial design, high-fashion journalism (such as Vogue and Harper's Bazaar), and corporate branding. In 1963, the Museo Bodoniano was officially inaugurated inside the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma, preserving thousands of Bodoni's original steel punches, copper matrices, presses, trial sheets, and archival correspondence. Bodoni remains a foundational pillar of graphic design history, celebrated for turning the printed letter into a timeless monument of Neoclassical geometry and aesthetic perfection.

academic_description: Large 4to (286x207 mm). [4], 35, [1 blank] pp. Frontispiece with a portrait of Livia Doria Carafa engraved by Raffaello Morghen after a design by Fedele Fischetti. Fine engraved initials, head- and tailpieces. Contemporary mottled half calf, smooth spine decorated with gilt foliate tools, gilt title on a red morocco lettering piece, panels covered with marbled paper, red edges (some losses to the headcaps, slightly worn and rubbed). Some occasional very light foxing. A very good copy printed on strong paper. A separate edition of the Elogio storico written by Bertola de’ Giorgi as an introduction to the collection Prose e versi per onorare la memoria di Livia Doria Caraffa. This work was printed in 1784 by Giambattista Bodoni at the behest of the Neapolitan prince Vincenzo Carafa della Roccella (1739-1814), in honour of his late wife, Livia Carafa Doria del Carretto (1745-1779).For the offprint publication of the Elogio, Bodoni inserted a preliminary two-leaf quire, including a new title page and a short address to the readers by Bertola de’ Giorgi. As in the collection Prose e versi of 1784, the frontispiece features a portrait of Livia Carafa designed by Fedele Fischetti (1732-1792) and engraved by Raffaello Morghen (1758-1833). The separate edition bears no printing date, but it may have been issued in 1785, coinciding with Bertola de’ Giorgi’s stay in Parma.To date, we have identified only one copy of the Elogio on the market. This copy once belonged to Hugh Cecil Brooks -author of the well-known Compendiosa bibliografia di edizioni bodoniane (1927)- and was sold at the auction of his collection of Bodoni books.Bertola de’ Giorgi was born in Rimini into a noble family. At 16 he entered the Siena monastery of Monte Oliveto, but a few years later we find him fighting in Hungary against the Turks. His early life was quite an adventurous one until the age of 24, when in 1776 he began teaching. He taught first in Naples and later universal history in Pavia, whose university at the time was one of the most celebrated in Italy: Volta, Spallanzani, and Scarpa, among many others, hold a chair there (E. Bigi, Bertola de’ Giorgi, Aurelio, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 9, 1967, s.v.).

authors.name: Antolini Giovanni
authors.biography: Giovanni Antonio Antolini (1756–1841) stands as one of the most visionary figures of Italian Neoclassical architecture, urban planning, and architectural theory during the tumultuous transition from the late Ancien Régime through the Napoleonic Era to the Restoration. As an architect, hydraulic engineer, archaeologist, and academic professor, Antolini reconfigured the classical idiom not merely as a decorative revivalism, but as a monumental, functional, and political apparatus designed to structure modern civic life. His historical trajectory encapsulates the ideological transformation of Northern and Central Italy under French Hegemony, bridging the Enlightenment rationalism of the late eighteenth century with the civic grandiosity of the Cisalpine Republic and the Kingdom of Italy. Most celebrated for his colossal, unbuilt urban masterplan for the Foro Bonaparte in Milan, Antolini’s intellectual output extended into groundbreaking archaeological surveys, major hydraulic infrastructure projects along the Po and Tiber rivers, and an influential critical translation and commentary of Vitruvius’s De architectura. Through his dual commitments to rigorous classical draftsmanship and progressive civic engineering, Antolini codified a distinctively Italian strand of revolutionary Neoclassicism that profoundly influenced nineteenth-century European urbanism.Born on June 25, 1756, in the Emilian township of Castel Bolognese, situated within the Legation of Ravenna under Papal sovereignty, Giovanni Antonio was the son of Gioacchino Antolini and Caterina Tosi. Raised in an environment steeped in regional artisanal and hydraulic traditions, he displayed an early aptitude for mathematics, geometry, and technical drawing. His formal education commenced in nearby Faenza under the guidance of the eminent architect and engineer Giuseppe Pistocchi, whose interest in Enlightenment functionalism and structural clarity deeply impacted the young scholar. Recognizing Antolini's exceptional talents, his mentors encouraged him to migrate to Rome in 1776, the unrivaled epicenter of archaeological scholarship and architectural theory in late eighteenth-century Europe. In the Holy City, Antolini frequented the circles of the Accademia di San Luca and immersed himself in the direct study of Roman antiquities, working alongside leading engravers, topographers, and architects who were actively dismantling Baroque caprice in favor of a rigorous, archaeologically grounded Antiquity.Antolini’s formative Roman decade (1776–1796) was marked by intensive field research, practical engineering commissions, and theoretical publication. Under the patronage of Pope Pius VI (Giannangelo Braschi), who was undertaking vast infrastructural modernization across the Papal States, Antolini engaged in complex hydraulic surveys, most notably contributing to the ambitious enterprise to drain the Pontine Marshes (Paludi Pontine). This engineering practice instilled in him a permanent synthesis of utilitarian infrastructure and formal aesthetic grandeur. Concurrently, Antolini pursued meticulous archaeological investigations south of Rome. In 1785, he published his foundational treatise, Il Tempio di Ercole in Cori, printed in Rome with splendid copperplate engravings. This work showcased his masterful capacity to measure, reconstruct, and theoretically analyze archaic Roman Doric architecture, establishing his reputation throughout European academic circles as a premier scholar of classical antiquity.The geopolitical earthquake of the French Revolution and Napoleon Bonaparte’s Italian Campaign of 1796 radically reoriented Antolini’s political and artistic alignment. Embracing radical Jacobin ideals and Republican enlightenment principles, Antolini left Rome for Lombardy, which had been transformed into the Cisalpine Republic. Settling in Milan, the capital of the new Napoleonic state structure, he emerged as the paramount architectural interpreter of Republican ideology. In 1800, following Napoleon’s victory at Marengo, Antolini conceived his absolute masterpiece: the Foro Bonaparte. Designed as a monumental circular urban complex measuring over 500 meters in diameter around the medieval site of the Castello Sforzesco, the Foro Bonaparte was designed to integrate the administrative, cultural, and economic institutions of the new Republic into a singular, unified spatial order. The proposal featured a grand central piazza encircled by majestic colonnades, public assembly halls, a national theater, a museum, a pantheon for illustrious citizens, custom houses, and maritime basins connected to the city’s canal network.The political and formal symbolism of the Foro Bonaparte represented the apotheosis of Neoclassical civic utopia. Drawing inspiration from Roman forums, Greek agoras, and French revolutionary projects by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and Étienne-Louis Boullée, Antolini envisioned an urban architecture that rejected feudal spatial hierarchies in favor of egalitarian civic transparency. Though Napoleon initially approved the grand plan with enthusiasm, the colossal projected costs and political reorientations of the French administration—which shifted from revolutionary republicanism toward imperial autocracy—led to the project’s eventual abandonment in 1802. The Italian authorities instead opted for more modest urban interventions led by Luigi Cagnola and Giovanni Canonica. Nevertheless, Antolini’s elaborate portfolio of copperplate engravings illustrating the Descrizione del Foro Bonaparte (published in Milan in 1806) circulated widely across Europe, cementing the project as one of the definitive benchmarks of Neoclassical urban design.Despite the cancellation of the physical forum, Antolini’s prestige propelled him to the highest academic positions in Northern Italy. In 1803, he was appointed Professor of Architecture at the prestigious Accademia di Belle Arti di Brera in Milan, where he trained a generation of Lombard architects. He maintained close intellectual networks with prominent Neoclassical luminaries, including the poet Vincenzo Monti, the archaeologist Ennio Quirino Visconti, the painter Andrea Appiani, and the decorator Felice Giani. In 1812, Antolini relocated to Emilia to assume the Chair of Architecture at the University of Bologna and the Accademia Clementina (later the Accademia di Belle Arti di Bologna), a position he held with immense distinction for nearly three decades until his death. During his tenure in Bologna, he produced pivotal theoretical texts, including his highly regarded Italian translation and commentary on Vitruvius (L'Architettura di Marco Vitruvio Pollione, published in 1814), as well as monographic studies on the Temple of Minerva in Assisi and major essays on bridge construction, hydraulic dynamics, and urban surveying.The printing history of Antolini’s published output reflects the supreme craftsmanship of early nineteenth-century architectural publishing. His works were executed in grand folio formats, requiring sophisticated typographic composition and high-precision copperplate etching. Printed by elite publishing establishments such as the Stamperia Reale in Milan and the Tipografia delle Belle Arti in Bologna, Antolini personally supervised the engraving of his technical plates, collaborating with master engravers like Michele Dien and Francesco Rosaspina. These publications served a dual purpose: as pedagogical manuals for academy students and as luxury intellectual manifestos distributed to royal societies, foreign academies, and European heads of state. His treatises were celebrated for their extraordinary typographical clarity, meticulous orthographic projections, and rigorous textual commentary that synthesized ancient architectural theory with modern engineering mathematics.Following the Restoration of 1815 and the return of Austrian and Papal control over Northern Italy, Antolini navigated the conservative political climate by focusing increasingly on theoretical, educational, and public utility projects. He designed public buildings, bridges, and canalizations across Romagna and the Venetian territories while maintaining his academic professorship in Bologna. Giovanni Antonio Antolini passed away in Bologna on March 11, 1841, at the advanced age of eighty-four. His death was commemorated by solemn eulogies delivered at the Accademia Clementina and published by leading intellectuals of the Restoration period, such as Pietro Giordani. In the historiography of modern architecture, Antolini remains canonized as a key transitional master whose theoretical brilliance and urban vision demonstrated how ancient architectural forms could be deployed to serve the modern democratic state.

academic_description: Folio (454x329 mm). 40, [2] pp. and XXIV engraved plates. Etched vignette on title page. Contemporary half vellum (rubbed and worn, spine edges missing). Some foxing and occasional marginal staining, all in all a good, wide-margined copy. First edition published in conjuction with the brothers Masi, whose name appears in certain copies instead of that of Marsigli. A second, enlarged edition was issued soon after in the same year at the author’s expenses. A third edition was printed in Milan in 1829. It is a manual of civil architetcture conceived as a teaching tool for the students of architectural drawing.Giovanni Antonio Antolini was professor of civil and military architecture, hydraulics, and practical geometry at the University of Bologna between 1803 and 1815, then he moved to Milan to teach at the Brera Academy until his death. He is the author of several theoretical works. His major project was the urban plan, presented to Napoleon in 1801, for the area around the Sforza Castle in Milan, which was given the name “Foro Bonaparte”.“La critica ha veduto nell’Antolini più il teorico, il professore, lo studioso degli antichi monumenti che non l’architetto e l’urbanista: la sua meritoria e complessa attività di studioso e insegnante non deve tuttavia farci dimenticare il significato almeno del suo progetto per il Foro Bonaparte, espressione non solo nei singoli edifici del gusto neoclassico, al quale egli pure partecipa, ma anche di quelle aspirazioni ad un rigido funzionalismo e razionalismo che avevano trovato in Italia un sostenitore in Carlo Lodoli e in Francia più diretta applicazione nell’opera degli architetti ‘illuministi’ e ‘rivoluzionari’, in particolare in E.-L. Boullée e C.-N. Ledoux” (M. Pepe, Antolini, Giovanni Antonio, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 3, 1961, s.v.).

title: Il problema estetico in San Tommaso

authors.name: Eco Umberto
authors.biography: Umberto Eco (born January 5, 1932, in Alessandria, Piedmont; died February 19, 2016, in Milan) stands as one of the most formidable polymaths of modern European intellectual history. Operating seamlessly across the domains of medieval aesthetics, structural semiotics, narrative theory, literary criticism, and creative fiction, Eco reconstituted the relationship between high academic philosophy and global popular culture. As Chair of Semiotics at the University of Bologna—the oldest continuously operating university in the Western world—and founder of the Scuola Superiore di Studi Umanistici, Eco established a paradigm of semiotic inquiry that synthesized Charles Sanders Peirce’s pragmatic triadic sign model, Ferdinand de Saussure’s structural linguistics, and the scholastic rigorousness of Thomas Aquinas. Beyond his foundational theoretical texts, Eco achieved an unprecedented global literary stature through his debut novel, Il nome della rosa (1980), a medieval murder mystery that simultaneously operated as a dense semiotic treatise on intertextuality, heresy, and laughter. His lifelong immersion in the material history of the printed book, incunabula, and the mechanics of textual transmission made him not only a monumental scholar but also one of the premier bibliophiles and cultural critics of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.Born to Giulio Eco, an accountant, and Giovanna Bisio, Eco spent his early years in the Piedmontese city of Alessandria, an environment whose regional topography and dialectal culture would later color his novel Baudolino (2000). Raised under the fascist regime of Benito Mussolini, the young Eco experienced the ideological indoctrination of the era alongside the brutal reality of the Second World War and the Italian Resistance, experiences he would later dissect in his celebrated essay on "Ur-Fascism" (1995). At the urging of his father, who envisioned a legal career for his son, Eco initially enrolled at the University of Turin (Università degli Studi di Torino) to study law. However, his profound humanistic inclinations led him to abandon legal studies in favor of philosophy and medieval humanities, studying under the direction of the eminent aesthetic philosopher Luigi Pareyson. In 1954, Eco defended his doctoral dissertation (laurea) on the aesthetic problem in Thomas Aquinas, published two years later as Il problema estetico in Tommaso d'Aquino (1956). Pareyson’s philosophy of formativity—which viewed artistic creation as a process of dynamic production rather than static reflection—exerted a formative influence on Eco’s emerging theories of art, interpretation, and reader reception.Following his graduation, Eco entered a vibrant period of media experimentation and cultural activism. From 1954 to 1959, he served as a cultural producer for the newly established Italian state broadcaster, RAI (Radiotelevisione Italiana) in Milan, collaborating with an extraordinary cohort of young intellectuals—including Luciano Berio, Bruno Maderna, Gianni Vattimo, and Furio Colombo—who came to be known as the "corsari" (corsairs) of cultural television. This immersion in mass communications sparked Eco's lifelong fascination with pop culture, television narrative codes, and comic strips. During the same period, Eco joined the avant-garde literary collective Gruppo 63, contributing to radical debates on narrative structure, linguistic experimentation, and the subversion of bourgeois literary conventions. His academic career advanced rapidly: after holding lectureships in aesthetics and architecture at the University of Turin, the University of Florence, and the Politecnico di Milano, Eco was named Professor of Semiotics at the University of Bologna in 1971, where he founded the first university program in Communication Sciences (DAMS - Discipline delle Arti, della Musica e dello Spettacolo) and held the world's first chair dedicated explicitly to semiotics.Eco's theoretical output during the 1960s and 1970s fundamentally reconfigured modern aesthetic and semiotic theory. In Opera aperta (1962; expanded English edition *The Open Work*, 1989), he argued that modern and avant-garde works of art (such as the music of Karlheinz Stockhausen or the literature of James Joyce) are characterized by an inherent openness that demands the active interpretive participation of the receiver, contrasting them with closed, conventional narratives. This was followed by Apocalittici e integrati (1964), a groundbreaking study that subjected mass media, comic strips (from *Superman* to *Peanuts*), and pop music to the same rigorous analytical scrutiny previously reserved for high literature. In 1968, Eco published La struttura assente, a foundational critique of Claude Lévi-Strauss’s rigid structuralism, asserting that structure is not an ontological reality hidden within the world, but an operational model constructed by the semiotic researcher. This line of thought culminated in his magnum opus of sign theory, Trattato di semiotica generale (1975; published simultaneously in English as A Theory of Semiotics, 1976), which provided a unified general framework for understanding codes, sign production, iconism, and the cultural mechanics of lying—famously defining semiotics as "the discipline studying everything which can be used in order to lie."In the late 1970s, Eco shifted his focus toward the pragmatic dynamics of reception and reader-response theory. In Lector in fabula (1979; translated in part in The Role of the Reader, 1979), he introduced the concept of the "Model Reader" (lettore modello)—a structural text-internal strategy generated by the text to guide interpretation. Distinguishing between the *intentio auctoris* (authorial intention), *intentio operis* (textual intention), and *intentio lectoris* (readerly intention), Eco grew increasingly critical of extreme post-structuralist and deconstructive approaches to reading that legitimized infinite or unchecked interpretation. In his Tanner Lectures at Cambridge, published as Interpretation and Overinterpretation (1992), and his collection I limiti dell'interpretazione (1990; *The Limits of Interpretation*), Eco argued that while texts permit a wide range of readings, they nevertheless impose boundaries, exercising a veto power against arbitrary or paranoiac misreadings. This theoretical framework was further expanded in Kant e l'ornitorinco (1997; *Kant and the Platypus*, 1999), where Eco probed the cognitive foundations of semiotics, exploring how human perception categorizes unknown phenomena through schema and cultural conventions.Eco’s transition into world fame as a novelist came in 1980 with the publication of Il nome della rosa (The Name of the Rose) by the Milanese publisher Bompiani. Set in a northern Italian Benedictine abbey in November 1327, the novel combines a classic detective narrative—starring the Franciscan friar William of Baskerville and his novice Adso of Melk—with deep historical erudition regarding the Franciscan poverty controversy, the Avignon papacy, medieval heresy, and the Aristotelian corpus. At the heart of the plot lies the search for the legendary lost second book of Aristotle's Poetics, dedicated to comedy and laughter, which the blind librarian Jorge da Burgos seeks to destroy out of fear that laughter will annihilate fear and destabilize religious authority. The novel proved to be an astounding international publishing phenomenon, selling over 50 million copies worldwide and winning the prestigious Premio Strega in 1981. Eco continued his novelistic exploration of semiotics, historical paranoia, and hermetic drift in Il pendolo di Foucault (1988; *Foucault's Pendulum*, 1989), a monumental satire of secret societies, Rosicrucianism, and Templar conspiracy theories. His subsequent fiction included L'isola del giorno prima (1994; *The Island of the Day Before*), set in the seventeenth century around the search for the secret of longitude; Baudolino (2000), a picaresque tale set during the Third Crusade and the sack of Constantinople; La misteriosa fiamma della regina Loana (2004; *The Mysterious Flame of Queen Loana*), an illustrated autobiographical meditation on memory and popular culture; Il cimitero di Praga (2010; *The Cemetery of Prague*), an investigation into nineteenth-century anti-Semitism and the forging of *The Protocols of the Elders of Zion*; and Numero zero (2015), a biting satire of yellow journalism and Italian political conspiracies in the post-Gladio era.Throughout his career, Eco maintained an intimate relationship with the material book and the history of printing. A legendary bibliophile, his private personal library contained over 30,000 volumes in his Milanese residence overlooking the Castello Sforzesco, alongside a collection of 20,000 volumes at his country home in Montecerignone. Eco possessed an extraordinary collection of rare books, incunabula, and early modern imprints, focusing specifically on false sciences, occultism, and mnemonic systems, which he meticulously cataloged and discussed in works such as La memoria vegetale (2006). He was an ardent defender of paper books against digital ephemeral media, famously asserting that the book belongs to the same category of ultimate technological perfection as the wheel or the scissors. In his final years, Eco demonstrated his uncompromising editorial commitment: when the giant Mondadori group acquired Rizzoli-Bompiani in 2015, creating a mega-publishing conglomerate, Eco, along with Mario Andreose, Elisabetta Sgarbi, and other prominent writers, founded the independent publishing house La nave di Teseo in late 2015 to safeguard intellectual freedom and editorial diversity. Eco passed away in Milan on February 19, 2016, shortly before the official launch of the house's literary program. His legacy endures as a towering monument to the human capacity for critical reflection, linguistic creation, and textual passion.

related_names.name: Flores d’Arcais Giuseppe
related_names.biography: Giuseppe Flores d'Arcais (Cagliari, June 22, 1908 – Padua, November 13, 2004) stands as one of the defining figures of twentieth-century Italian educational philosophy, pedagogical epistemology, and Christian personalism. As the long-tenured Chair of Pedagogy at the University of Padua (Università degli Studi di Padova), Flores d'Arcais spearheaded what scholars universally recognize as the Paduan School of Pedagogy (Scuola Padovana di Pedagogia). Operating at the vital intersection of moral philosophy, historical hermeneutics, and theoretical education, he systematically liberated pedagogy from its long-standing subjection to Giovanni Gentile's neo-idealist hegemony, constructing instead an autonomous epistemological architecture centered on the irreducible dignity, freedom, and transcendent vocation of the human person. Across more than six decades of intense intellectual production, institutional leadership, and journal editing, Flores d'Arcais articulated a sophisticated personalist framework that profoundly reshaped post-World War II Italian educational discourses, offering a rigorous third way between Marxist functionalism and Anglo-American empirical pragmatism.Born into an ancient aristocratic family of Sardinian and Spanish heritage—the Flores d'Arcais lineage—in Cagliari in 1908, the young Giuseppe developed early intellectual inclinations toward philosophical speculation and the humanities. Moving to mainland Italy for higher academic training, he completed his university studies at Padua, a historic center of learning that was then undergoing a profound transformation under the shadow of the Fascist regime and the prevailing neo-idealist philosophy of Gentile and Benedetto Croce. During his formative years in the late 1920s and 1930s, Flores d'Arcais immersed himself in classical philosophy, scholastic metaphysics, and the burgeoning Christian personalism championed across Europe by thinkers such as Jacques Maritain, Emmanuel Mounier, and Étienne Gilson. Crucial to his intellectual orientation was his close association with Luigi Stefanini, the eminent Paduan philosopher who pioneered metaphysical personalism in Italy. Under Stefanini's guidance, Flores d'Arcais recognized that the crisis of modern European civilization was fundamentally an anthropological crisis, requiring a radical re-examination of the educational process as the primary locus of human self-realization and moral awakening.The core of Flores d'Arcais's theoretical contribution resides in his formulation of Personalismo Pedagogico (Pedagogical Personalism). In groundbreaking treatises such as Il problema pedagogico (1940), L'ambiente nella pedagogia contemporanea (1947), Il personalismo (1950), and the monumental Pedagogia e personalismo (1988), he argued that education cannot be reduced to socio-political indoctrination, psychological conditioning, or mere vocational training. Against the Marxist reduction of education to socio-economic class mechanics, and against John Dewey's functionalist instrumentalism, Flores d'Arcais maintained that the human being is fundamentally a person (persona)—an ontologically unique, relational, and self-transcending subject. In his profound hermeneutic engagements with historical figures—most notably Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Saint Augustine, and Antonio Rosmini—Flores d'Arcais demonstrated how educational theory must navigate the dynamic tension between nature and grace, liberty and authority, individual interiority and social solidarity. His critical study Rousseau (1980) remains a milestone in modern Italian scholarship, deconstructing the paradoxes of Émile to reveal how natural education requires an implicit transcendent teleology to avoid devolving into totalitarian social engineering.As a key academic strategist and publishing visionary, Flores d'Arcais transformed the University of Padua into an international hub for educational research and editorial activity. Heading the Institute of Pedagogy for decades, he cultivated a vibrant network of scholars, journal editors, and publishing houses across Northern and Central Italy. He worked in close collaboration with premier educational publishing firms such as CEDAM in Padua, La Scuola in Brescia, Liviana, and La Nuova Italia in Florence. In 1941, he founded the authoritative academic journal Rassegna di Pedagogia (later Revue de Pédagogie), serving as its chief editor for over half a century. Through this periodical, Flores d'Arcais published cutting-edge essays on theoretical pedagogy, history of education, comparative school systems, and theoretical psychology, maintaining rigorous peer-review standards that elevated Italian educational scholarship to international prominence. Furthermore, his directorial leadership of multi-volume reference works, including monumental pedagogical encyclopedias and specialized book series, created an enduring infrastructure for academic distribution across Europe.The critical reception of Flores d'Arcais's work reflects the complex ideological shifts of late twentieth-century Europe. During the intense ideological debates of the 1960s and 1970s, when secularism, structuralism, and neo-Marxist critical theory dominated Western universities, his firm insistence on personalist metaphysics, spiritual transcendence, and ethical realism made him a central target of secular and empiricist critique. However, his unyielding commitment to rigorous philosophical argumentation earned him immense respect across political divides. Critics and allies alike acknowledged that Flores d'Arcais had successfully established pedagogy as an autonomous, scientifically valid academic discipline in Italian universities, equipped with its own distinct methodology and normative horizon. Upon his passing in Padua in 2004 at the age of ninety-six, he was universally eulogized as a grand patriarch of Italian education. Today, his theoretical legacy endures in contemporary debates on humanistic ethics, digital educational personalism, and the defense of human dignity within democratic educational systems.

academic_description: 4to (250x176 mm). 157, [3] pages. Original publisher’s wrappers. A good copy, uncut and mostly unopened, leaves slightly uniformly browned. Provenance: Giuseppe Flores d’Arcais, considered the founder of the school of personalized pedagogy (his large signature on the front cover and the label of his library on the spine). First edition of the first book by the famous Italian semiotician and novelist Umberto Eco. Il problema estetico in San Tommaso consists of an enlargement of Eco’s thesis developed with the historian and philosopher Luigi Pareyson (1918-1981) on the theme of the complex and original aesthetic theories advanced by the influential medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274).Umberto Eco, a native of Alexandria, graduated in 1954 from the University of Turin with a thesis on St. Thomas Aquinas. After teaching at the Faculty of Letters of the University of Milan, at the Faculty of Architecture in Florence and at the Polytechnic of Milan, in 1975 he was appointed professor of semiotics at the University of Bologna.Eco was awarded many honorary titles by universities from all over the world. Since 1989 he was the president of the International Center for Semiotic and Cognitive Studies and since 1994 of the International Association for Semiotic Studies.Contributor to many Italian newspapers and magazines such as “Il Corriere della Sera”, “La Repubblica” and “L’Espresso”, in his long career and vast bibliography he dealt in particular with aesthetics, artistic avant-garde, linguistics, and mass communication. After the extraordinary success of his debut novel Il nome della rosa (1980), Eco published other works of fiction, among which Foucault’s Pendulum (1988), The Island of the Day Before (1994), Baudolino (2000), and The Prague Cemetery (2010) (cf. P.E. Bondanella, The Cambridge Companion to Umberto Eco, Cambridge, 2013; S.G. Beardsworth & R.E. Auxier, eds., The philosophy of Umberto Eco, Chicago, 2017).Giuseppe Flores d’Arcais (1908-2004) was among the pioneers in the teaching of the history of entertainment and audiovisuals. Graduating from Padua with a degree in musical aesthetics in 1929, Flores d’Arcais, who joined Fascism as a young man, was not only a professor of pedagogy but also of didactics, aesthetics, philosophy, history of theater, of which he held one of the first chairs in Italy (1959-1972), and method and didactics of audiovisual arts until his retirement (1983). He greatly contributed to giving didactic dignity to the disciplines of entertainment, radio communication and cinema, to whose interaction he dedicated his first course “The Problem of Relations between Cinema and Theater”. He gave equal space to the history of theater and cinema, supplementing courses on Luigi Pirandello and the birth of filmaking with sections devoted to the European cinema between 1930 and 1960 or Neorealism. He was a full member of the Accademia Patavina di Scienze, Lettere ed Arti, and a corresponding member of the Istituto Veneto. In addition to his many pedagogical writings, mention should also be made of Il film nella scuola (1963) and Note per una estetica del cinema (in: “Rivista del cinematografo”, 1, 1953, pp. 6-10) (cf. A.M. Bernardinis, Scritti di Giuseppe Flores D’Arcais, in: “Studi in onore di Giuseppe Flores d’Arcais”, Padua, 1985, pp. XXXVII-LXXVII).Considering that Eco and Flores d’Arcais knew each other well and copies of later Eco’s pubblications bearing Eco’s dedication to him are known, it is possible that Eco himself gave this copy to Flores d’Arcais, but did not dedicate it to him as at the time the latter was already a reknown professor while Eco had graduated from university only a few years earlier.

authors.name: Valdés Juan de
authors.biography: Juan de Valdés (ca. 1490/1500–1541) stands as one of the most enigmatic, subtle, and profoundly influential figures of early modern European intellectual and religious history. A Spanish humanist of noble Castilian lineage, Valdés operated at the crossroads of northern Erasmian humanism, Spanish mystical reform (alumbradismo), and the clandestine Italian Reformation (the movement of the Spirituali or Italian Evangelismo). Through his vernacular dialogues, personal letters, and informal spiritual directorship, Valdés exerted a monumental influence over sixteenth-century religious discourse. His unique theology—which emphasized internal spiritual illumination, the radical justification of the soul by faith through the grace of Christ, and a disdain for rigid external ecclesiastic ceremonies—served as the ideological cornerstone for a sophisticated network of Italian aristocrats, intellectuals, and prelates seeking a spiritual renewal within the Catholic Church prior to the rigid dogmatism of the Council of Trent.Born in the Castilian city of Cuenca into an influential family of municipal administrators (his father, Hernando de Valdés, served as a regidor), Juan de Valdés was the twin brother of Alfonso de Valdés (c. 1490–1532), who rose to prominence as Latin secretary to Emperor Charles V. The brothers were raised within an environment marked by intellectual ambition and the complex socio-religious reality of early modern Spain, where Jewish converso heritage frequently intersected with humanistic aspiration. Around 1526, Valdés matriculated at the University of Alcalá de Henares, an institution founded by Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros as a bastion of Renaissance philology and trilingual scholarship. At Alcalá, Valdés immersed himself in the study of Greek and Hebrew under the tutelage of eminent scholars such as Pedro de Lerma and Diego de Eguía. It was during these formative years that Valdés absorbed the critical, biblically grounded humanism of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, whose works were actively being translated and published in Alcalá by the printer Miguel de Eguía. Concurrently, Valdés came into contact with the circles of the Alumbrados (Illuminists) in Escalona and Toledo, particularly absorbing the spiritual inwardness advocated by figures like Pedro Ruiz de Alcaraz and Isabel de la Cruz, though he ultimately developed a far more refined and biblically anchored theological structure than his illuminist contemporaries.In 1529, while still at Alcalá, Valdés anonymously published his first major work, the Diálogo de la doctrina cristiana, printed at Miguel de Eguía’s press. Formally structured as a pedagogical conversation between an archbishop, a parish priest, and a nobleman, the text sought to reform lay instruction by replacing scholastic formulas with direct scriptural readings, heavily drawing upon Erasmian catechisms and Luther’s early commentary on the Decalogue. The book immediately attracted the suspicion of the Spanish Inquisition. Inquisitor General Alonso Manrique de Lara, despite his initial Erasmian sympathies, permitted a formal trial against the work. Recognizing the impending danger of arrest and trial, Valdés abandoned Castile in 1531, fleeing to Italy, never to return to his homeland. He initially settled in Rome, where he secured a position as a papal chamberlain under Pope Clement VII, benefiting from the diplomatic protection and status previously established by his late brother Alfonso.Following the death of Clement VII in 1534, Valdés moved permanently to Naples, a city under Spanish viceregal rule, where he spent the remaining seven years of his life. It was in Naples, specifically at his residence in the coastal neighborhood of Chiaia, that Valdés inaugurated one of the most remarkable intellectual salons of the Renaissance. The Valdesian circle (il circolo valdesiano) brought together the elite of Italian humanism, noble society, and church reform. Among those who frequented his gatherings or engaged in intense spiritual direction were the noblewoman Giulia Gonzaga, the poet Marcantonio Flaminio, the general of the Capuchin order Bernardino Ochino, the Augustinian canon Pietro Martire Vermigli, the Florentine patrician Pietro Carnesecchi, Vittoria Colonna, and Galeazzo Caracciolo. For this circle, Valdés composed his most enduring theological, spiritual, and literary works. In his masterly philological dialogue, the Diálogo de la lengua (composed in Naples ca. 1535, though circulated strictly in manuscript), Valdés laid the foundations for modern Spanish linguistics and vernacular prose style, advocating for naturalness, clarity, and vernacular elegance summarized in his famous maxim: "Escribo como hablo" ("I write as I speak").Valdés’s spiritual writings during the Neapolitan period represented a shift from traditional Erasmian moral satire toward a deeply mystical, Christocentric pneumatology. In works such as the Alfabeto cristiano (written for Giulia Gonzaga), the Ciento i diez consideraciones (One Hundred and Ten Considerations), and his extensive commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew, the Gospel of John, the Epistle to the Romans, and First Corinthians, Valdés delineated a path of individual salvation based on the direct, experimental action of the Holy Spirit upon the soul. He argued that true Christian faith was not acquired through intellectual assent to scholastic dogmas or external rituals, but through an internal, experiential transformation wrought by Christ’s sacrifice on the Cross. This radical doctrine of justification—which shared striking affinities with Protestant soteriology while remaining within an ecclesiastical structure—found its most widespread popularization in the anonymous bestseller Il Beneficio di Cristo (1543), authored by Benedetto da Mantova and revised by Marcantonio Flaminio, which relied heavily upon Valdés's Neapolitan lectures and notes.The typographical and editorial history of Juan de Valdés’s oeuvre is extraordinary for its underground, posthumous, and transnational character. Because of the aggressive surveillance of the Inquisition, none of Valdés’s Neapolitan spiritual works were published during his lifetime. Upon his death in August 1541, his manuscripts were preserved by Giulia Gonzaga and Marcantonio Flaminio. The Italian translation of the Alfabeto cristiano was published anonymously in Venice in 1546, likely through the agency of Marco Antonio Magno. The defining moment for the international dissemination of Valdés’s thought occurred in Basel, Switzerland, where the Italian Protestant exile Celio Secondo Curione edited and published the first edition of Le cento & dieci divine considerationi in 1550, printed by the renowned press of Pietro Perna and Johannes Oporinus. Curione’s edition introduced Valdés to Northern European Protestantism, leading to subsequent French, English (translated by Nicholas Ferrar in 1638 with notes by George Herbert), and Dutch translations. Conversely, Valdés’s linguistic masterpiece, the Diálogo de la lengua, remained hidden in manuscript form for over two centuries until it was finally edited and published in Madrid in 1786 by the Spanish Enlightenment scholar Gregorio Mayans y Siscar.The death of Juan de Valdés in 1541 spared him from the fierce persecution that soon dismantled his circle. With the establishment of the Roman Inquisition (Sacrum Officium) in 1542 under Pope Paul III and the promulgation of Paul IV's Index Librorum Prohibitorum in 1559, all writings by Valdés were explicitly condemned and placed in the highest class of prohibited books. Many of his closest followers met tragic fates: Bernardino Ochino and Pietro Martire Vermigli were forced into permanent exile in Northern Europe, Pietro Carnesecchi was eventually tried and beheaded by the Inquisition in Rome in 1567, and Giulia Gonzaga’s private papers were seized upon her death, triggering further inquisitorial trials. In nineteenth- and twentieth-century historiography, Valdés emerged as a crucial subject of debate. Scholars such as Marcel Bataillon viewed him as the supreme exponent of Spanish Erasmianism, whereas José C. Nieto and Massimo Firpo demonstrated his autonomy from Erasmus, emphasizing his original synthesis of Spanish illuminism and Pauline theology. Today, Juan de Valdés is celebrated not only as a master of Renaissance Spanish prose, but as an intellectual titan who redefined early modern European spirituality and bridged the cultural worlds of Habsburg Spain and Renaissance Italy.

related_names.name: Herbert George
related_names.biography: George Herbert (1593–1633), whose surname appears inverted in early regional registers as Herbert, George, stands as one of the supreme figures of early modern English literature, Caroline devotional theology, and Jacobean academic rhetoric. Born into an elite Welsh march line during the zenith of the Elizabethan era, Herbert traversed the highest strata of academic preferment at Cambridge and courtly political ambition before deliberately renouncing worldly advancement to embrace the humble life of a parish priest at Fugglestone St Peter with Bemerton, Wiltshire. His posthumously published masterpiece, The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations (1633), represents an unsurpassed flowering of the Metaphysical poetic tradition, fusing rigorous theological sophistication, formal inventive brilliance, architectural symbolism, and deep psychological intimacy. Situated at the historical intersection of late Renaissance humanism, High Anglican ceremonialism, and Calvinist soteriology, Herbert’s life and artistic production reflect the profound spiritual and political anxieties of early Stuart England.Born on 3 April 1593 at Montgomery Castle, Wales, George Herbert was the fifth son of Richard Herbert of Montgomery (d. 1596) and Magdalen Newport (d. 1627), a woman of extraordinary intellect, piety, and literary patronage who famously maintained a lifelong friendship with John Donne. The Herbert family was exceptional in its cultural and political influence: George’s eldest brother, Edward Herbert (later 1st Baron Herbert of Cherbury), became a pioneering philosopher of Deism, a diplomat, and a historian, while another brother, Henry Herbert, served as the long-tenured Master of the Revels under Kings Charles I and Charles II. Following the premature death of his father in 1596, George was raised under the meticulous personal tutelage and intellectual oversight of his mother in London and Oxford. In 1604, he entered the prestigious Westminster School as a King’s Scholar under the headmastership of Richard Ireland and the spiritual directorship of Lancelot Andrewes, then Dean of Westminster. Andrewes’s profound mastery of classical rhetoric, oriental languages, and patristic theology left an indelible mark on the young Herbert, instilling in him a lifelong veneration for linguistic precision and the liturgical beauty of the reformed Church of England.In 1609, Herbert matriculated at Trinity College, Cambridge, beginning an academic tenure of singular distinction. He graduated Bachelor of Arts in 1613 and Master of Arts in 1616, whereupon he was elected a Major Fellow of Trinity College. Exhibiting unmatched mastery of Latin and Greek verse and humanistic rhetoric, Herbert was appointed Praelector in Rhetoric at Cambridge in 1618. His academic ambition culminated in 1620 with his election to the prestigious office of Public Orator of the University of Cambridge, a position he retained until 1628. As Public Orator, Herbert served as the official Latin voice of the university, composing formal epistles, panegyrics, and addresses to royal visitors, foreign ambassadors, and powerful court patrons. During this period, Herbert cultivated close relationships with key figures of the Jacobean court, including King James I, the royal favorite George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, and the philosopher-statesman Francis Bacon. Bacon held Herbert’s judgment in such immense esteem that he dedicated his 1625 translation of Certaine Psalmes to him and sought Herbert’s assistance in rendering his philosophical treatise De Dignitate et Augmentis Scientiarum into Latin. Herbert’s courtly prospects were further enhanced by his election to the English Parliament as Member for Montgomery in 1624 and 1625.However, the mid-1620s witnessed a profound existential and spiritual crisis in Herbert’s life, catalyzed by the successive deaths of his chief political patrons—including the Duke of Richmond, the Marquess of Hamilton, and King James I himself in 1625—as well as the death of his beloved mother in 1627, whose funeral sermon was preached by John Donne alongside Herbert’s own published Latin and Greek elegies, Memoriae Matris Sacrum. Disillusioned with the impermanence of secular advancement and long suffering from chronic respiratory illness (likely pulmonary tuberculosis), Herbert retreated from court politics to fulfill a burgeoning religious vocation. He had been ordained a deacon by 1626, receiving the prebend of Layton Ecclesia in the diocese of Lincoln, where he led the structural restoration of the ruined parish church of St Mary at Leighton Bromswold. In 1629, he married Jane Danvers, a relative of his stepfather Sir John Danvers. In April 1630, under the patronage of his kinsman Philip Herbert, Earl of Pembroke, and with the encouragement of William Laud, then Bishop of London, Herbert was ordained to the priesthood and instituted as Rector of St Andrew’s Church in Fugglestone with Bemerton, near Salisbury. For the remaining three years of his life, Herbert devoted himself wholeheartedly to the cure of souls, exemplifying the pastoral ideal he articulated in his celebrated prose treatise, A Priest to the Temple, or, The Country Parson (composed during his ministry but printed posthumously in 1652).It was during his tenure at Bemerton that Herbert brought to completion his supreme literary legacy, The Temple. The collection is structured as a complex theological and spiritual narrative, divided into three distinct structural sections: "The Church-porch" (a didactic, moralistic prologue setting forth rules for ethical conduct), "The Church" (the heart of the volume, containing over 160 devotional lyrics exploring the intricate drama of the individual Christian soul in dialogue with God), and "The Church Militant" (an apocalyptic historical poem depicting the movement of the Gospel from East to West). Herbert’s verse in "The Church" is renowned for its astonishing stanzaic variety—employing over 140 different meter and rhyme schemes—its deceptive simplicity of tone, and its masterful employment of metaphysical conceits, musical cadence, and visual typography. Notable among his poetic innovations are his pattern or shape poems, such as "The Altar" and "Easter Wings," wherein the physical arrangement of the printed text on the page reflects the physical and iconographic subject of the poem. Through poems such as "The Collar," "Love (III)," "Jordan (I) & (II)," and "The Pulley," Herbert probed the tension between human vanity and divine grace, spiritual rebellion and quiet submission, with an emotional vulnerability and structural control unparalleled in seventeenth-century lyric poetry.Herbert’s health precipitously deteriorated in early 1633. Realizing his death was imminent, he entrusted the fair manuscript notebook of The Temple to his close friend Edmund Duncon, instructing him to deliver it to Nicholas Ferrar, the founder of the saintly religious community at Little Gidding, Huntingdonshire. Herbert instructed Ferrar to examine the verses: if he believed they might turn to the advantage of any dejected poor soul, he should publish them; if not, he should burn them. Herbert succumbed to consumption on 1 March 1633, at the age of thirty-nine, and was buried beneath the altar of St Andrew’s Church in Bemerton. Ferrar immediately recognized the divine genius of the manuscript and oversaw its passage through the press. The Temple was published later that same year, printed at Cambridge by Thomas Buck and Roger Daniel, printers to the University. The initial edition faced brief censorship hurdles regarding lines in "The Church Militant" referencing the church's movement to America, but Vice-Chancellor Samuel Ward intervened to authorize its release. The book achieved immediate, extraordinary commercial and devotional success, undergoing thirteen re-editions throughout the seventeenth century alone and becoming a foundational text for personal devotion across diverse Protestant factions, admired equally by King Charles I in his captivity and by Puritans such as Richard Baxter.The critical reception and scholarly legacy of George Herbert have undergone dramatic evolutions over the centuries. In 1670, Izaak Walton published his classic biography, The Life of Mr. George Herbert, which idealized Herbert as an unblemished Anglican saint and established an enduring hagiographic lens that dominated readers' interpretations for over two centuries. While the Neoclassical taste of the eighteenth century temporarily eclipsed Herbert’s reputation, preferring the polished couplets of Pope, the nineteenth century witnessed a major resurgence of interest, led by Samuel Taylor Coleridge—who praised Herbert’s exquisite purity of language—and later by the Oxford Movement and Hopkins. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, scholarly work by Rosemond Tuve, Joseph Summers, Louis Martz, Helen Vendler, and Stanley Fish reframed Herbert not merely as a pious parson, but as a supremely sophisticated literary craftsman, a master of self-subverting rhetoric, and a profound voice in the history of English religious consciousness. Today, Herbert is universally celebrated as a central pillar of early modern literature, whose verse uniquely bridges the sacred and the poetic with unmatched formal elegance.

academic_description: 4to (197x146 mm). [32], 311, [13] pp. Collation: *-****4 A-Rr4 Ss2. Woodcut initials and printer’s decorations. Blind-tooled leather boards, with raised bands and gilt title on spine (boards scuffed, with significant edgewear, small losses to leather and cracking at joints, light cracking at front hinge, binding still sturdy). From the collection of Prof. Roberto Severino, Washington, D.C. Pages lightly toned with minimal foxing and occasional small chip or frayed bottom edge, light damp staining throughout, small ink stains in the lower margins of pp. 252-253 not affecting the text. A good, genuine copy. Extremely rare first English edition of this collection of letters and essays put together by the author’s friends, in the translation of Nicholas Ferrar (1592-1637), the founder of Little Gidding, the ‘Arminian Nunnery’, where the Ferrar family lived under a definite religious rule from 1625 to 1646. The edition also contains a publisher’s note to the reader, the Considerations by George Herbert (1593-1633) with remarks concerning the dubious and offensive passages in the text, Curione’s introduction (dated from Basle, May 1st, 1550), Thomas Jackson’s approbation, a commendatory letter of Herbert to his friend Ferrar, the dedicatory epistle of Valdes to his Commentary upon the Romans addressed to Giulia Gonzaga, and the errata.The Spanish humanist and religious reformer Juan de Valdés was mostly active in Naples, where he became the spiritual center of a group of prominent men and women anxious for reform and spiritual revival in the church, to whom belonged, among others, Giulia Gonzaga and Vittoria Colonna. Though he remained a Catholic, he paved the way for Protestant ideas by his emphasis on religious feeling and his disregard of ecclesiastical authority; and after his death, many of his friends, among them Peter Martyr and Bernardino Ochino, left the Catholic Church.“The Spanish original [Ciento y diez Consideraciones] of Juan de Valdés Hundred and ten divine considerations is lost, but there have been published twelve editions of translations. From Italian [Le Cento e dieci divine Considerazioni, first printed in 1550] they have been translated into five other languages. Three editions appeared in English. To the editor of the first English translation, who scrupulously hesitated to publish it, on account of certain passages in the book, George Herbert wrote in 1638: ‘I wish you by all means to publish it, for these three eminent things observable therein: First, that God in the midst of Popery should open the eyes of one to understand and express so clearly and excellently the intent of the gospel in the acceptation of Christ’s righteousness (as he sheweth through all his Considerations), a thing strangely buried and darkened by the adversaries, and their great stumbling block. Secondly the great honour and reverence which he every where bears towards our dear master and lord, concluding every Consideration almost with his holy name, and setting his merit forth so piously, for which I do so love him, that, were there nothing else, I would print it, that with it the honour of my lord might be published. Thirdly, the many pious rules of ordering our life, about mortification and observation of God’s kingdom within us and the working thereof, of which he was a very diligent observer. These three things are very eminent in the author, and overweigh the defects (as I conceive), towards the publishing thereof’ […] Soon, after the death of Valdés, Vermiglio and Occhino left Italy, where liberty of preaching was no longer left them. For a short period the press at Venice was still suffered to spread evangelical literature. The Benefit of Christ was printed there and circulated in tens of thousands of copies. About the year of the opening of the Council of Trent several works of Juan de Valdés were published at Venice. Together with his brother’s dialogue on the sack of Rome, there appeared Juan’s Dialogue between Mercury and Charon, his Christian Alphabet, and seven of his tracts on the fundamental doctrines of spiritual Christendom. In 1548 such a licentiousness of the press was stopped. Valdés’ Considerations were printed at Basle, where they appeared in 1550 in Italian. The Commentaries on the Romans and on the first epistle to the Corinthians were edited in 1556 and ‘57 at Geneva. One of the tracts was twice published, in 1554 and 56, in Germany in a Latin translation, of which a German and a Polish translation were made and very soon printed. In the Neapolitan realm persecution grew heavy ; some withdrew beyond the Alps, many recanted, many suffered capital punishment. Giulia Gonzaga, who strictly kept to the faith imbibed by the guidance of Valdés and to the practice recommended her by him, was summoned to Rome, but death released her from more painful and fearful experience, at her retreat in the Neapolitan convent, in the year 1566. Probably the Roman Inquisition seized, after her death, the letters which Carnesecchi had written to her. He was imprisoned. In vain he urged, that the doctrine of Valdés on justification could not be considered to have been heretical, as long as the Council had not determined otherwise; that high authorities and dignitaries had adhered to it; that he himself, after always fluctuating in his mind, had at last acquiesced in what the Council had ultimately decreed and the Pope had approved. He ingenuously confessed, it is true, as for the relation of inherent justice to that which is imputed, that he, not knowing exactly to discern the difference between the opinion of Valdés and the determination of the Council, was not yet quite resolved, whether he ought to condemn Valdés’ doctrine on this point or not; but he declared he would submit to his judges, his intention being, entirely to conform himself in this as well as in all other articles to the orthodox catholic faith. On some captious question he also reminded them of his not being a theologian. He was beheaded and burnt, in 1567. Soon every spark of evangelical life was choked within the reach of the Inquisition” (E. Boehmer, Bibliotheca Wiffeniana. Spanish Reformer of two centuries from 1520. Strassburg-London, 1874, I, pp. 73 and 79-81).

title: Emblemata

authors.name: Maccio Paolo
authors.biography: Paolo Maccio (known in the Latinized Republic of Letters as Paulus Maccius; c. 1576 – 1638) is an Italian humanist. Operating at the vibrant intersection of late Renaissance classical philology, Counter-Reformation moral philosophy, and Baroque visual culture, Maccio carved out a prominent legacy as a professor of Greek and Latin rhetoric at the University of Bologna (the Archiginnasio), a neo-Latin poet, an academic orator, and a master emblem theorist. While his scholarly output encompassed extensive pedagogical manuals on Latin prosody and topical panegyrics on European geopolitics, his enduring monument in the annals of European print history remains his masterpiece, the Pauli Maccii Emblemata, published in Bologna in 1628 by the press of Clemente Ferroni. This monumental volume represented a pinnacle of collaborative Baroque book production, uniting Maccio's polyglot verses and erudite commentaries with copperplate engravings executed by the foremost artists of the Bolognese school, including Giovanni Battista Coriolano, Oliviero Gatti, Bernardino Curti, and Agostino Parisini. Through his teaching and published works, Maccio embodied the transformation of classical humanist erudition into an instrument of Counter-Reformation moral synthesis and visual rhetoric, exerting a lasting influence on early modern Italian emblem literature and academic discourse.Born in Milan around 1576 into a family of modest mercantile standing, Maccio demonstrated an early aptitude for classical letters and philological study. His formative education occurred within the rigorous intellectual environment of early seventeenth-century Lombardy, where the educational reforms of Cardinal Carlo Borromeo had established a powerful synthesis of Latinity, Christian moral theology, and rhetorical discipline. Maccio immersed himself in the classical canon, mastering ancient Greek, classical Latin poetry, patristic literature, and scholastic philosophy. Seeking greater academic opportunities and a broader platform for his scholarly talents, Maccio relocated to Bologna in the opening decade of the seventeenth century. Bologna at this juncture was a preeminent center of European intellectual and artistic life, boasting its ancient University, a thriving printing industry, and a vibrant community of visual artists led by the legacy of the Carracci academy. Maccio rapidly integrated himself into the city's elite intellectual networks, winning the esteem of local aristocrats, ecclesiastics, and university authorities through his public lectures and Latin compositions. His formal incorporation into the faculty of the Studio di Bologna marked the beginning of a distinguished academic career that would span nearly three decades, during which he trained multiple generations of Italian and foreign students in the arts of classical eloquence and poetic composition.As a public academician and holder of the chair of Greek and Latin humanities at the Archiginnasio, Maccio produced a diverse corpus of published scholarship that reflected the intellectual imperatives of his era. Among his major pedagogical contributions was his Prosodia in quinque libros divisa (first published in Bologna in 1617 and subsequently reissued in expanded editions in 1623 and beyond). Designed as a comprehensive textbook for university students and humanistic academies, the Prosodia offered an exhaustive systematic analysis of Latin meter, verse structure, accentuation, and poetic diction, illustrating its precepts with hundreds of classical and neo-Latin examples. Beyond his pedagogical manuals, Maccio earned renown as an official orator for academic and civic occasions. His academic discourses, such as the celebrated opening lecture Ilyssus, sive De laudibus philosophiae, articulated a lofty vision of humanistic education as the essential prerequisite for civic virtue and Christian piety. Furthermore, Maccio engaged directly with the turbulent geopolitical events of his day through neo-Latin poetry; his historical epic fragment De Bello Bohemico (1621) offered a panegyric celebrating the Imperial and Catholic victories in the early stages of the Thirty Years' War, aligning his literary pen with the ideological aims of the Papacy and the Habsburg monarchy. Throughout his tenure in Bologna, Maccio was an active participant in literary academies, including the Accademia dei Gelati and the Accademia degli Indominati, where he engaged in debates on poetics, iconology, and classical antiquities alongside leading intellectuals such as Cesare Ripa, Ridolfino Campeggi, and Claudio Achillini.The capstone of Maccio's scholarly and artistic career was the publication of his monumental emblem book, the Pauli Maccii Emblemata, printed at Bologna in 1628 by the distinguished typographer Clemente Ferroni. Issued as a luxurious quarto volume, the work stands as one of the most iconographically complex and aesthetically refined emblem books produced in Seicento Italy. The typographical execution by Ferroni was exceptional, employing elegant Roman and Italic types set within spacious margins to accommodate Maccio's multi-layered textual apparatus. The volume comprises eighty-four distinct emblems (including eighty-one numbered emblem plates and decorative frontispieces), each constructed according to a sophisticated tripartite and polyglot architecture. Every entry opens with a Latin motto (lemma), followed by an exquisite engraved copperplate illustration (pictura). Below the image, Maccio provided an original Latin epigram composed in elegiac couplets, accompanied by his own vernacular Italian verse paraphrase—a deliberate strategy designed to bridge the Latinate academic readership with broader vernacular literary culture. Following the epigrams, Maccio appended an extensive Latin prose commentary (commentarius) packed with dense citations from ancient Greek and Roman authors, Church Fathers, classical mythographers, and Renaissance naturalists. The visual component of the work was executed by an extraordinary team of Bolognese printmakers: Giovanni Battista Coriolano contributed numerous refined compositions characterized by expressive shading; Oliviero Gatti provided dynamic allegorical figures; while Bernardino Curti and Agostino Parisini executed intricate decorative borders and landscape backgrounds. The themes of the Emblemata range from moral stoicism, the transience of worldly ambition, and the harmony of the virtues, to complex theological allegories on divine providence, original sin, and the redemption of the soul, effectively translating post-Tridentine moral theology into visual and poetic emblems.Paolo Maccio died in Bologna in 1638, leaving behind a reputation as one of the city's most respected university professors and literary figures. His death was commemorated by eulogies and academic memorial verses composed by his colleagues at the Archiginnasio. In the decades following his passing, Maccio's Prosodia remained a standard reference work in Italian educational institutions, while his Emblemata acquired an enduring prestige among European bibliophiles, print collectors, and emblem scholars. In eighteenth-century literary historiography, pioneer bibliographers such as Pellegrino Antonio Orlandi (1714) and Giovanni Fantuzzi (1786) documented Maccio's biography and publication history, praising his erudition and the high artistic quality of his illustrated volumes. In twentieth and twenty-first-century scholarship, Maccio has undergone a significant critical reevaluation. Scholars of Baroque literature and visual culture, led by Mario Praz, John Landwehr, and Peter M. Daly, have recognized Maccio's 1628 volume as a pivotal monument in the evolution of the Italian emblem tradition, marking the transition from the concise moralizing devices of Andrea Alciato and Scipione Bargagli to the lavish, theatrical visual rhetoric characteristic of the High Baroque. Modern iconographers continue to study Maccio's work for its profound integration of word and image, its reflection of Seicento university culture, and its invaluable documentation of the collaborative artistic synergy between Bolognese humanists and the printmaking workshops of the Carracci circle.
