related_names.name: Colbert Jean-Baptiste
related_names.biography: Jean-Baptiste Colbert (1619–1683), one of the principal ministers of Louis XIV and one of the most consequential administrators of the French Grand Siècle, was the chief architect of a vast programme of fiscal, administrative, commercial, naval, colonial, artistic, and scholarly reorganization. His career coincided with the transformation of the French monarchy from a composite and fiscally fragmented early-modern state into a more centralized system of royal government. As Controller-General of Finances, Secretary of State for the Navy and the King's Household, Superintendent of the Royal Buildings, Arts, and Manufactures, and a central patron of academies, libraries, archives, and learned scholarship, Colbert exercised an exceptionally wide range of powers.The economic system later called Colbertism—a retrospective term rather than a doctrine that Colbert himself formulated as a systematic theory—combined protectionist tariffs, regulation of production, state privileges, encouragement of domestic manufactures, commercial companies, colonial expansion, and close administrative supervision. Yet Colbert's historical importance cannot be reduced to mercantilism. He was equally a builder of institutions, an administrator of information, a patron of scholarship, and one of the great bibliophiles of seventeenth-century Europe.Born on 29 August 1619 at Reims, Colbert came from a prosperous family of merchants, financiers, and municipal office-holders. His father, Nicolas Colbert, sieur de Vandières, belonged to the commercial elite of Reims, while his mother was Marie Asselin. The family's social trajectory is important for understanding Colbert himself: he was not born into the high nobility or the traditional judicial aristocracy, but emerged from the urban and commercial world whose financial techniques he would later incorporate into royal administration. Jean-Louis Bourgeon's study of the Colbert family has demonstrated the importance of this mercantile background for understanding the family's rise.Colbert's early career was therefore administrative rather than traditionally academic. He entered the orbit of Michel Le Tellier and acquired experience within the royal financial and administrative apparatus. During the Fronde, the crisis of the French monarchy exposed the weaknesses of fiscal administration, the dependence of the Crown upon financiers, and the political importance of credit and information. Colbert's association with Cardinal Jules Mazarin became decisive. He entered Mazarin's service and eventually became responsible for the administration of the cardinal's enormous private fortune. Through this position he acquired an intimate knowledge of royal finance, tax farming, credit networks, office-holding, patronage, and the mechanisms by which wealth circulated between the Crown, financiers, and political society. The later legend of Colbert as an incorruptible financial reformer should nevertheless be treated critically: modern scholarship, particularly that of Daniel Dessert, has emphasized the extent to which his own power depended upon networks of family, clients, financiers, and office-holders.Colbert also acquired property and social status during these years. In 1657 he purchased the barony of Seignelay in Burgundy; in 1668 Louis XIV elevated Seignelay to a marquisate. Colbert himself did not consistently use the marquisal title, which became especially associated with his eldest son, Jean-Baptiste Antoine Colbert, marquis de Seignelay, who succeeded him in the administration of the navy. Colbert subsequently acquired Sceaux and other properties, transforming them into centres of architectural, horticultural, and artistic patronage. His rise thus illustrates the rapid social transformation of a wealthy administrative family into one of the most powerful ministerial dynasties of the reign of Louis XIV.The death of Mazarin on 9 March 1661 transformed Colbert's position. Louis XIV decided to govern without appointing another chief minister, and Colbert became one of the most powerful figures in the new system of personal monarchy. His first great political campaign was directed against Nicolas Fouquet, Superintendent of Finances. Colbert accumulated and transmitted information concerning Fouquet's finances and political networks, contributing decisively to the latter's arrest at Nantes in September 1661 by Charles de Batz de Castelmore, comte d'Artagnan. Fouquet was subsequently tried by the Chambre de Justice. The office of Superintendent of Finances was abolished, and Colbert emerged as the principal architect of the subsequent financial administration.Colbert became Intendant of Finances in 1661 and Controller-General of Finances in 1665. His programme aimed to increase the Crown's effective revenues, improve accounting and administrative supervision, restrain abuses associated with tax farming and financial intermediaries, and strengthen the authority of the central government over provincial fiscal administration. He sought to rationalize the taille, improve the collection of indirect taxes such as the aides and gabelle, supervise state expenditure, and obtain greater regularity in royal accounts. The Chambre de Justice of 1661–1663 was used against financiers accused of illicit enrichment and fiscal abuses. Colbert's financial administration was energetic and interventionist, but it did not abolish the structural contradictions of the Ancien Régime fiscal system: privilege, venality, tax exemptions, regional diversity, and dependence upon financiers continued to shape the French state.His economic policy is conventionally described as Colbertism. The term, however, is retrospective, and Colbert never formulated a coherent economic treatise comparable to a modern economic doctrine. His policy was instead expressed through memoranda, instructions, regulations, tariffs, administrative correspondence, and practical interventions. Its central objectives included the encouragement of domestic production, limitation of certain imports, development of French exports, attraction of foreign skilled workers, improvement of manufactures, and the strengthening of the fiscal and commercial resources of the monarchy. The tariffs of 1664 and especially 1667 were important instruments of this protectionist policy.Manufacturing was one of the principal fields of intervention. Colbert encouraged the establishment and regulation of privileged manufactures producing textiles, tapestries, furniture, ceramics, glass, arms, naval equipment, and luxury goods. The Gobelins complex was reorganized as a major centre of royal production under the artistic direction of Charles Le Brun; the Beauvais manufactory received royal support; and the Manufacture royale des glaces de miroirs was established in 1665, eventually becoming the historical predecessor of Saint-Gobain. Colbert sought to recruit foreign craftsmen and techniques while imposing standards of production, apprenticeship, inspection, and quality control. The purpose was not simply economic: manufactures supplied the court and contributed to the international representation of French royal magnificence.Commerce and overseas expansion formed another part of the same programme. In 1664 Colbert promoted the foundation of the Compagnie française des Indes orientales and the Compagnie française des Indes occidentales, alongside companies concerned with trade in the Levant, northern Europe, and other commercial regions. These corporations received royal privileges intended to compete with Dutch and English commercial power. Colbert also strengthened French colonial administration in Canada and the Caribbean and promoted the integration of colonial production into the wider commercial strategy of the monarchy. His colonial policy was inseparable from the expansion of plantation slavery. In 1681 he initiated the process that led to the royal regulation of slavery in the French Caribbean; however, the ordinance known today as the Code Noir was not promulgated until March 1685, two years after his death, under Louis XIV and with his son Seignelay playing a decisive role in its completion. It is therefore historically misleading to describe Colbert as the sole author of the Code Noir, although his administration unquestionably initiated and supervised the process that produced it.Colbert's reorganization of the navy was equally ambitious. In 1669 he became Secretary of State for the Navy, and he subsequently transformed naval administration, shipbuilding, recruitment, arsenals, and maritime finance. Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, and other ports were developed as major naval centres. The maritime registration system, or inscription maritime, provided the monarchy with a more systematic mechanism for identifying and recruiting seamen. Naval administration was linked to a wider system of regulations concerning shipbuilding, forests, timber supplies, ports, arsenals, and maritime commerce. Colbert's objective was to create not merely a larger fleet but a permanent administrative and industrial infrastructure capable of sustaining French naval power. The French navy expanded dramatically during his ministry, although estimates of its size vary according to whether one counts ships of the line, smaller vessels, galleys, and vessels in reserve; claims of a simple rise from fewer than twenty to more than two hundred fully operational warships are therefore too crude.The same administrative logic extended to legislation. Colbert's ministry was associated with a remarkable sequence of royal ordinances that sought to standardize major areas of French law and administration. These included the Ordonnance civile touchant la réformation de la justice of 1667, the Ordonnance criminelle of 1670, the Ordonnance de commerce of 1673, commonly associated with the name of Jacques Savary and therefore known as the Code Savary, and the Ordonnance de la marine of 1681. These texts did not create a unified national legal system in the modern sense, but they represented a major effort to impose greater regularity and royal supervision upon civil procedure, criminal procedure, commerce, and maritime law. Colbert's contribution to this process was institutional and administrative as much as legislative: he used memoranda, commissions, expert consultation, inspection, and centralized review to turn knowledge of existing practices into instruments of government.Colbert's conception of government depended fundamentally upon information. He demanded reports, statistical statements, financial accounts, inventories, correspondence, technical descriptions, commercial intelligence, and reports from provincial officials. His ministry generated an extraordinary documentary archive, much of which survives in the French national collections. Manuscript evidence preserves his autograph instructions, memoranda, correspondence, and administrative papers, including instructions to his son concerning naval affairs. The documentary character of Colbert's government has led Jacob Soll to describe him as an “information master”: a minister who attempted to convert archives, libraries, scholarly knowledge, accounting techniques, and administrative correspondence into a practical technology of political power.This information culture was inseparable from Colbert's bibliophilia. He was one of the great book collectors of seventeenth-century France and assembled the Bibliotheca Colbertina, one of the most important private libraries of the Grand Siècle. At his death it contained roughly 20,000 printed books, accompanied by an exceptionally important collection of manuscripts, charters, papers, and other documentary materials. The library was managed in part by the learned scholar Étienne Baluze, whose scholarly expertise helped give the collection its extraordinary historical and juridical character. Colbert's collecting interests were not limited to literary prestige: books, manuscripts, legal documents, historical records, scientific works, and oriental materials could all serve the intellectual infrastructure of government.Colbert simultaneously transformed the Bibliothèque du Roi. In 1666 he arranged for the royal library to move from the rue de la Harpe to the rue Vivienne, close to his own hôtel. The royal collections were substantially enlarged under his administration. The library acquired major collections, including that of Gaston d'Orléans, while agents and missionaries were sent abroad to obtain Greek, Arabic, Persian, Hebrew, Syriac, and other manuscripts. The BnF records that under Colbert the number of manuscripts doubled and the printed collections quadrupled. The distinction between the Bibliothèque du Roi and Colbert's private Bibliotheca Colbertina is therefore essential: they were distinct collections, although they were closely connected through personnel, intellectual networks, acquisition strategies, and eventually provenance. After Colbert's death, his personal library passed through his family. The printed books were dispersed in sales, most notably the great sale of 1728, while the manuscripts followed a different trajectory. In 1732 approximately 6,117 ancient manuscripts, including hundreds of oriental, Greek, and Latin manuscripts, together with charters and modern papers, were acquired for the Bibliothèque du Roi. This later integration made the Colbertine provenance one of the most important strata in the history of the French national manuscript collections.The bibliographical significance of Colbert's collections is therefore immense. His manuscripts are now distributed among the holdings of the Bibliothèque nationale de France, while the catalogues and provenance records of the former Colbertine collection remain fundamental for reconstructing the intellectual history of seventeenth-century France. The BnF preserves, among other resources, the Cinq cents de Colbert and Mélanges de Colbert, while later cataloguing has allowed scholars to reconstruct the provenance of individual manuscripts. Colbert's collecting activity should consequently be understood not simply as aristocratic bibliomania but as part of a broader early-modern culture in which the possession, classification, transmission, and interpretation of written information constituted a form of power.The same conception of knowledge shaped Colbert's patronage of scholarship and the arts. He supported the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres, established in 1663 as the Petite Académie; he played a decisive role in the reform of the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture, which received new statutes and stronger royal support in 1663; he founded or promoted the Académie des Sciences in 1666; he was instrumental in establishing the Académie de France à Rome in the same year; and he founded the Académie royale d'Architecture in 1671. These institutions were not independent manifestations of a modern “research system”: they were closely connected to royal patronage, artistic production, technical expertise, public ceremony, and the symbolic representation of Louis XIV's monarchy. Colbert's objective was to place artistic and scholarly production within a coordinated system of royal institutions.His relationship with the Académie des Sciences was especially significant. Colbert helped recruit and pension scholars, including Christiaan Huygens, and supported the development of the Paris Observatory, where Giovanni Domenico Cassini became a central figure. Scientific knowledge was valuable to the monarchy not only for theoretical reasons but because it could contribute to navigation, cartography, engineering, astronomy, surveying, medicine, military technology, and the systematic description of the kingdom's resources. Colbert's scientific patronage thus belonged to the same administrative logic as his financial reports and naval memoranda: knowledge was to be collected, verified, organized, and put to use.Colbert was also deeply involved in the culture of royal printing. The Imprimerie Royale, founded in 1640 under Louis XIII, already possessed a distinguished history before Colbert; he did not found it. Under his administration, however, royal printing became increasingly integrated into the broader programme of state representation and learned publication. Colbert's patronage of scholarship, typography, engraving, royal iconography, and monumental publication contributed to the development of the extraordinarily sophisticated visual and typographical culture of Louis XIV's reign. The celebrated Romain du Roi, however, must not be attributed directly to Colbert as a completed typeface: the project was initiated only in 1692, almost a decade after his death, under the direction of a commission of the Académie des Sciences, with Philippe Grandjean subsequently responsible for cutting the type. It represents the continuation of a typographic and scientific programme associated with Colbert's cultural administration rather than a work executed during his lifetime.Colbert's cultural policy was closely connected with Versailles and the broader system of royal representation. As Superintendent of the King's Buildings from 1664, he exercised authority over architecture, royal residences, decorative programmes, gardens, artistic commissions, and manufactures. He worked closely with figures such as Charles Le Brun, André Le Nôtre, Louis Le Vau, Claude Perrault, and other artists, architects, engineers, and craftsmen. The aim was to make royal magnificence materially visible and intellectually legible. Painting, sculpture, architecture, tapestry, gardens, medals, inscriptions, books, scientific instruments, and ceremonial architecture all contributed to the same political language of monarchy.The last phase of Colbert's career exposed the limits of his programme. The Franco-Dutch War of 1672–1678 and Louis XIV's increasingly expensive military policy placed enormous pressure upon royal finances. Colbert's ideal of fiscal regularity and economic balance could not withstand the escalating cost of warfare. Extraordinary taxation, borrowing, the creation and sale of offices, and other expedients became increasingly necessary. At the same time, France experienced poor harvests and serious agrarian distress, demonstrating the limits of an economic programme centred upon manufacturing, commerce, and state-directed production within a predominantly agrarian society. Colbert's relationship with François-Michel Le Tellier, marquis de Louvois, also deteriorated as military expenditure and the interests of the War Ministry gained increasing priority.Colbert's final years were marked by illness, especially gout, and by declining political influence. He remained a central minister until his death in Paris on 6 September 1683. He was succeeded in the naval and colonial administration by his son Jean-Baptiste Antoine Colbert, marquis de Seignelay, although the political dominance enjoyed by the Colbert family during the earlier decades of Louis XIV's personal government did not survive intact. After Colbert's death, Louvois succeeded him as Superintendent of the Royal Buildings, and the institutional balance of the court shifted decisively.Colbert's historical legacy is consequently more complex than the traditional portrait of the infallible founder of French mercantilism. He did not create a modern centralized state in the strict sense, nor did he eliminate the fiscal, social, and institutional pluralism of the Ancien Régime. His economic interventions could be inefficient or contradictory; his protectionism provoked commercial retaliation; his fiscal reforms remained dependent upon established mechanisms of privilege and finance; and the enormous cost of Louis XIV's wars undermined the financial equilibrium he sought to establish. Yet his achievement was extraordinary. He created or strengthened administrative procedures, manufactures, naval institutions, academies, libraries, archives, and systems of documentary control that continued to shape French government long after his death.Above all, Colbert should be understood as a statesman of administration and knowledge. His financial memoranda, letters, instructions, administrative papers, and documentary collections constitute a remarkable record of seventeenth-century government. His personal library and the subsequent history of the Bibliotheca Colbertina make him equally important to the history of collecting, bibliography, manuscript provenance, and the formation of the French national library. The publication of his papers by Pierre Clément in the nineteenth century, the survival of his manuscripts in the BnF and Archives nationales, and the modern reconstruction of his intellectual and administrative networks have made Colbert one of the best-documented ministers of the ancien régime. His significance lies therefore not simply in “Colbertism,” but in the larger system through which finance, administration, commerce, naval power, scientific knowledge, libraries, archives, printing, and artistic patronage were brought together in the service of Louis XIV's monarchy.

related_names.name: Heber Richard
related_names.biography: Richard Heber (5 January 1773 – 4 October 1833) stands as one of the most colossal and enigmatic figures in the annals of bibliomania and private library formation. A Member of Parliament, classical scholar, and co-founder of the prestigious Roxburghe Club, Heber amassed what was undoubtedly one of the largest private collections of printed books and manuscripts in Western history. Operating at the zenith of the British aristocratic book-collecting craze during the early nineteenth century, his insatiable passion for acquisition transformed his life into a relentless crusade across the auction houses, booksellers' shops, and private muniment rooms of Great Britain and Continental Europe. Immortalized as Atticus in Thomas Frognall Dibdin’s celebrated bibliographical dialogue Bibliomania (1809), Heber’s philosophy of collecting extended far beyond aesthetic appreciation or speculative investment; it was an all-consuming commitment to textual preservation that ultimately consumed his personal fortune, political standing, and psychological well-being.Born in Westminster, London, Heber belonged to an affluent and well-connected landed gentry family from Shropshire and Yorkshire. He was the eldest son of the Reverend Reginald Heber, rector of Marton in Craven and co-heir to the ancient estate of Hodnet Hall, and his first wife, Elizabeth Davenport. Following her death, his father married Mary Baylie, producing Richard’s half-brother, Reginald Heber (1783–1826), who would gain international renown as the Anglican Bishop of Calcutta and a celebrated hymnographer. Raised in an environment steeped in Anglican piety, classical erudition, and Tory political sentiment, young Richard demonstrated an extraordinary precocity for Latin scholarship and textual criticism. Educated privately under the tutelage of George Parker and later at Brasenose College, Oxford—where he matriculated in 1790—Heber quickly distinguished himself within Oxford’s elite antiquarian circles. While still an undergraduate, he published critical editions of the classical poets Silius Italicus (Punica, 2 vols., 1792) and Persius (1790), demonstrating an advanced grasp of philological method, manuscript collation, and typographical history.During his tenure at Oxford, where he earned his Bachelor of Arts in 1793 and his Master of Arts in 1797, Heber was drawn into the intellectual orbits of the prominent scholars and bibliophiles of the late Georgian era. He cultivated close friendships with figures such as Richard Porson, the brilliant Cambridge Grecian; Edmond Malone, the pioneering Shakespearean editor; and Thomas Tyrwhitt. It was during these formative years that Heber’s focus shifted from classical philology to the uncharted domain of early English literature, drama, and poetry. Recognizing that the printed heritage of the Elizabethan, Jacobean, and Caroline eras was rapidly disappearing or being neglected, Heber began purchasing rare black-letter quartos, early plays, original broadside ballads, and rare continental imprints with unprecedented fervor. His inheritance of substantial family estates upon his father’s death in 1804 provided him with the vast financial resources required to scale his acquisitions to an unprecedented degree.Heber’s prominence in literary society was further solidified through his intimate friendship with Sir Walter Scott. The two men met around 1800 through their shared enthusiasm for border ballads and early Scottish romance. Heber rendered invaluable assistance to Scott by supplying him with rare printed sources and medieval manuscripts for the Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802–1803) and Sir Tristrem (1804). In recognition of his generosity and erudition, Scott dedicated the sixth canto of his epic poem Marmion (1808) to Heber, crafting famous lines that paid homage to Heber’s vast library at Hodnet and his encyclopedic mind: 'How lingering pacing to and fro / Like ghost, I moulder length of woe / While Heber’s library, enriched with store / Of ancient lore, unlocks its door.' Beyond Scott, Heber was an influential nexus in conservative intellectual circles, contributing to the establishment of the Quarterly Review in 1809 alongside William Gifford, George Canning, and Robert Southey, thereby marrying his antiquarian pursuits with active participation in Tory literary politics.The defining moment of early nineteenth-century British bibliophilia occurred in May and June 1812 with the forty-two-day auction of the library of John Ker, 3rd Duke of Roxburghe. The sensational bidding wars at this sale—culminating in the Marquis of Blandford paying the record sum of £2,260 for the 1471 Valdarfer edition of Boccaccio’s Decameron—led directly to the founding of the Roxburghe Club. Heber was one of the eighteen founding members who gathered at the St. Alban’s Tavern on 17 June 1812, alongside George John, 2nd Earl Spencer, and Thomas Frognall Dibdin. As a central figure within the Roxburghe Club, Heber championed the private reprinting of extremely rare early English texts for distribution among its aristocratic members, setting a precedent for nineteenth-century bibliographical societies and textual publishing clubs.Heber’s collecting philosophy was unique in its scope, scale, and disregard for conventional physical limitations. Unlike contemporaries such as Earl Spencer or Thomas Grenville, who sought pristine copies, exquisite bindings by Roger Payne or Charles Lewis, and immaculate incunabula on vellum, Heber was driven by a totalizing textual imperative. He sought to assemble every edition of every work of literary, historical, or philological significance printed in Britain or Europe from the invention of movable type through the seventeenth century. Famous for his dictum—'No gentleman can be without three copies of a book: one for show, one for use, and one for borrowers'—Heber systematically purchased duplicate and triplicate copies of extraordinarily rare works. When questioned regarding this practice, he maintained that multiple copies were necessary to compare typographical variants, marginalia, and textual alterations introduced during early printing presses' press-runs.To accommodate an accumulation that eventually surpassed 150,000 printed volumes and tens of thousands of manuscripts, Heber established a sprawling network of library repositories across Britain and the Continent. His ancestral home, Hodnet Hall in Shropshire, was expanded until its rooms were overflowing with books stacked in double and triple rows. In London, he bought and filled a large house in Pimlico, another in York Street, Westminster, and held additional quarters in the Albany. As his hunting grounds expanded to the Continent following the conclusion of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815, Heber acquired residences or rented multi-room storage facilities in Paris, Brussels, Antwerp, Ghent, and Cologne. Booksellers across Europe—most notably Thomas Thorpe, Payne & Foss, and De Bure in Paris—acted as his constant agents, securing entire private collections and bidding aggressively on his behalf at foreign auctions.In 1821, Heber reached the pinnacle of his public career when he was elected to the House of Commons as a Member of Parliament representing Oxford University, a highly prestigious constituency that reflected his standing as a gentleman scholar and high Tory. He was awarded an honorary Doctor of Civil Law (DCL) by the university in 1822. However, his parliamentary service was brief and largely inactive, as his time remained dominated by the pursuit of books and the management of his far-flung collection. His public career came to a sudden and tragic end in 1826. Allegations of a homosexual scandal involving a young man—believed to be Charles Henry Hartshorne, a young Cambridge graduate and fellow bibliophile—were brought to light by the scandal-mongering newspaper The Age, edited by L. M. Westmacott. In the homophobic climate of Regency and Georgian England, such accusations meant social ruin and potential criminal prosecution.To escape the scandal, Heber abruptly resigned his parliamentary seat in 1826 and fled to Continental Europe, embarking on a prolonged period of self-imposed exile. For five years, he roamed between France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, taking refuge in his obsession. Rather than abating, his collecting mania intensified during exile. He purchased vast quantities of continental incunabula, early French romances, Neo-Latin poetry, and Dutch typographical rarities, shipping hundreds of crates back to his already overburdened properties in England. He lived in virtual seclusion, alienating many former friends, though he maintained correspondence with a select group of loyal antiquaries and booksellers. He returned quietly to England in 1831, living as a reclusive hermit in his book-choked house in Pimlico, surrounded by mountains of uncatalogued volumes, unopened parcels, and crumbling bindings.Richard Heber died unmarried on 4 October 1833 at his house in Pimlico, at the age of sixty. He died intestate regarding his personal library, leaving behind an unprecedented logistical challenge for his executors. The sheer scale of his holdings overwhelmed the British book trade. Between 1834 and 1837, the dispersal of the Bibliotheca Heberiana was carried out across sixteen separate auction sales—thirteen in London conducted by Sotheby and Son and R. H. Evans, along with major sales in Paris and Ghent. The London auctions alone encompassed 208 days of selling, featuring over 117,000 individual auction lots representing more than 200,000 volumes. The sales realized a total sum of over £56,000—a staggering figure for the period, though representing only a fraction of Heber's financial expenditure.The dispersal of Heber’s library acted as a major catalyst for nineteenth-century scholarship and institutional collecting. The sales drew institutional buyers, private collectors, and booksellers from across the globe. Vast tranches of early English drama, Tudor poetry, and rare continental printing were acquired by the British Museum, the Bodleian Library, and major private collectors such as William Henry Miller (whose acquisitions formed the core of the famous Britwell Court Library), Sir Thomas Phillipps, and later American magnates like Henry E. Huntington and Henry Clay Folger. Today, items bearing the distinct small stamp or manuscript ownership inscription 'Bibliotheca Heberiana' are preserved in the world's most prestigious research libraries. Richard Heber’s legacy endures as the ultimate archetype of the heroic, tragic, and monumental bibliophile, whose personal obsession permanently rescued countless literary treasures of Western civilization from destruction and oblivion.

academic_description: 4to (mm 203x140). 331, [5] pp. With frontispiece, portrait of the Madonna di San Luca and 81 full-page emblems, all engraved by Giovanni Battista Coriolano (1595-1649), Oliviero Gatti (1598-1646) and Agostino Parisini (fl. 1625-1636) after drawings by Florio Macchi and Giovanni Battista Coriolano. 18th-century full calf, panels within a triple fillet in gilt, spine with five raised bands and gilt title on morocco label, marbled endleaves, gilt edges (joints and top of the spine partially restored). Provenance: Jean-Baptiste Colbert (1619-1683), minister of finances of France under King Louis XIV, also renown for his celebrated library which was sold at Paris in 1728 (his ownership's inscription on the title-page); Richard Heber (1773-1833), English book-collector and founder of the Roxburghe Club of bibliophiles, whose library of 105,000 volumes was sold by auction at London in 1835 (his stamp on the front flyleaf); and Beckford Library (pencil note on the front flyleaf, dated Dec. 20, 1882). Small repair to the lower margin of pp. 121/122 not affecting the text, otherwise a very good, fresh copy.First edition of this lively and richly illustrated emblem book, which often offers an interesting iconography on contemporary life in Bologna.Giovanni Battista Coriolano and Oliviero Gatti, pupils of G.L. Valesio, are responsible for the majority of the illustrations. The engraved title and 26 of the emblems were engraved by Coriolano. The dedicatory plate and 52 of the emblems are the work of Gatti. The remaining plates were engraved by Agostino Parisini after Florio Maccio, a pupil of Lodovico Carracci.Paolo Maccio (o Macchi o Mazzi), born in Modena, studied in Bologna, where he was later appointed professor in the local university. He published several orations and occasional texts related to academic life (cf. G. Tiraboschi, Biblioteca modenese, Modena, 1783-'86, III, pp. 103-104 AND VI, p. 131; see also S. Mazzetti, Repertorio di tutti i professori dell'Università e dell'Istituto delle Scienze di Bologna, Bologna, 1848, p. 207).

authors.name: Speckle Daniel
authors.biography: Daniel Speckle (frequently Latinized as Daniel Specklinus and rendered in French scholarship as Daniel Specklin; 1536 – August 15, 1589) stands as one of the most significant and innovative military architects, cartographers, and urban engineers of the Northern Renaissance. Operating at the crucial historical juncture where Italian Renaissance fortificatory theory intersected with the pragmatic defensive needs of Northern and Central European polities, Speckle transformed the science of permanent fortification. His practical work across the Holy Roman Empire and his monumental treatise, Architectura von Festungen (1589), laid the theoretical and geometric groundwork for the Old German Fortress School (Altdeutsche Befestigungskunst), directly influencing subsequent generations of military engineers, including Wilhelm Dilich, Matthias Dögen, and ultimately the defensive paradigms of Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban and Menno van Coehoorn.Born in the Free Imperial City of Strasbourg in 1536, Speckle belonged to a family deeply embedded in the vibrant artistic and craft traditions of the Alsatian metropolis. His father, Veit Speckle (died 1555), was an acclaimed woodcutter (Formschneider) celebrated for executing the exquisite woodcuts designed by Albrecht Meyer and Heinrich Füllmaurer for Leonhart Fuchs’s landmark botanical treatise, De Historia Stirpium commentarii insignes (Basel: Michael Isengrin, 1542). Raised in an atmosphere of rigorous draughtsmanship and technical discipline, young Daniel was initially apprenticed as a silk embroiderer (Seidensticker) and punch-cutter. This formative artistic education endowed him with remarkable graphic precision, spatial visualization, and draftsmanship—skills that would later prove indispensable for both his cartographic surveys and his detailed architectural and engineering copperplates.Following the completion of his initial apprenticeship in the mid-1550s, Speckle embarked upon extensive Wanderjahre (journeyman travels) that lasted nearly a decade (c. 1555–1564) and fundamentally reshaped his career trajectory. Travelling through the Low Countries, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, Prussia, Austria, Hungary, and Italy, Speckle transitioned from decorative crafts to practical building engineering and military design. Crucially, during his time along the imperial frontier in Ottoman-threatened Hungary, Speckle observed and participated in field fortification works at Komárno (Komorn). There, he gained direct exposure to the devastating impact of heavy siege artillery and the practical shortcomings of medieval masonry walls. In Italy, Speckle studied the advanced bastioned trace (tracé italien) pioneeringly deployed by Michele Sanmicheli, Baldassarre Peruzzi, and Giovan Giacomo Paleari d'Allio. He absorbed the geometric principles of low-profile angular bastions, integrated casemates, and deep dry ditches, synthesizing Italian theoretical treatises with the practical demands of Northern European terrain and artillery warfare.Upon his return to Alsace in the mid-1560s, Speckle re-established himself in Strasbourg as a master craftsman, surveyor, and engraver. His talent as a cartographer achieved imperial renown with the publication in 1576 of his monumental map of Alsace, titled Alsatiae Superioris et Inferioris Nova Descriptio (commonly known as the Chorographia Elsassia). Printed from three large woodblocks that Speckle himself carved, this masterwork represented the most detailed, scientifically accurate, and visually stunning regional survey of Alsace produced in the sixteenth century. Dedicated to the estates of Upper and Lower Alsace, the map secured Speckle’s status as a preeminent technical authority across the Upper Rhine basin.Speckle’s growing reputation as an expert engineer led to widespread recruitment by princes and imperial cities throughout the Holy Roman Empire. In 1573, he was summoned to Vienna to advise on the modernization of the imperial capital’s fortifications, specifically contributing to the reconstruction of the Schottenbastei and surrounding bastioned fronts. Over the next decade, his consultancies spanned the length and breadth of Southern Germany and the Rhineland. He designed or renovated fortifications, arsenals, and municipal works for Duke Louis of Württemberg at Schorndorf and Stuttgart, Elector Palatine Johann Casimir at Heidelberg and Mannheim, the Margrave of Baden, the Duke of Bavaria at Ingolstadt and Lichtenberg, as well as the Free Imperial Cities of Ulm, Nuremberg, Regensburg, Amberg, and Frankfurt am Main. Speckle’s defensive architecture emphasized wide, straight curtains, spacious bastions with heavy flanks (Orillons), elevated cavaliers for long-range counter-battery fire, and sophisticated subterranean casemates ventilated to disperse gunpowder smoke.In October 1577, the City Council of Strasbourg appointed Speckle to the prestigious post of Stadtbaumeister (City Master Builder and Chief Engineer). In this capacity, Speckle assumed total responsibility for the civil architecture, hydraulic engineering, and military preparedness of one of the empire's most strategically vital Protestant bastions. During his twelve-year tenure as Stadtbaumeister, Speckle thoroughly overhauled Strasbourg’s medieval defenses, constructing modern earthwork ramparts, advanced ravelins, and water-filled ditches. Beyond fortifications, he engineered municipal grain stores, flour mills along the Ill River, public water conduits, and directed major structural renovations on the Frauenhaus (Maison de l'Œuvre Notre-Dame), leaving an indelible imprint on Strasbourg's urban landscape.The culmination of Speckle’s life work occurred in 1589 with the publication of his treatise, Architectura von Festungen (Architecture of Fortifications), printed at Strasbourg by the distinguished press of Bernhard Jobin. A magnificent folio volume lavishly illustrated with 36 double-page copperplate engravings designed and etched under Speckle’s direct supervision, the book was the first comprehensive fortification manual written in the German language. Divided into three exhaustive parts, the work provided systematic instruction on practical geometry, the design of regularity in fortresses, the construction of earthen versus stone ramparts, siege tactics, counter-mine networks, and urban layout within fortified enclosures. Speckle argued passionately for adapting fortresses to specific local topography rather than blindly applying rigid theoretical shapes, advocating for wide bastions capable of accommodating massive defensive artillery.Tragically, Daniel Speckle died in Strasbourg on August 15, 1589, just months after the initial printing of Architectura von Festungen. However, the posthumous influence of his publication was immense. The treatise went through numerous subsequent editions—notably those published in Strasbourg by Lazar Zetzner in 1599, 1608, and 1628, as well as later Dresden reissues in 1658—serving as the fundamental textbook for military officers and engineers across Protestant and Catholic Europe during the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).In addition to his published architectural work, Speckle was an avid historian and chronicler. He compiled a massive manuscript chronicle of his native city, known as the Collectanea, which recorded Strasbourg’s political, social, architectural, and military history from ancient times up to 1589. Remaining in manuscript for centuries, the Collectanea was edited and published in the late nineteenth century by the historian Rodolphe Reuss, revealing Speckle to be not only an engineering genius but also a astute observer of sixteenth-century urban society and political culture. Today, Daniel Speckle is recognized as a quintessential Northern Renaissance polymath whose synthesis of geometry, art, cartography, and military science profoundly shaped the early modern European built environment.

publishers.name: Jobin Bernhardt
publishers.biography: Jobin Bernhardt (also rendered in contemporary German typographical registers as Bernhard Jobin, Bernhart Jobin, or in Latinized colophons as Bernhardus Jobinus; fl. 1570–1593/1594) stands as one of the most versatile, intellectually vibrant, and commercially influential printmakers, engravers, and typographers of the Northern Renaissance. Active in the Imperial Free City of Strasbourg during the crucial decades of the late sixteenth century, Jobin inhabited the dynamic intersection where Protestant humanism, vernacular satirical literature, fine art engraving, and musical publication converged. Operating in an era characterized by intense confessionalization, rapid expansion of the book market, and profound artistic cross-pollination between the Swiss Confederation and the Holy Roman Empire, Jobin elevated the Strasbourg press from a localized engine of evangelical pamphlet production into an international center for illustrated literature, instrumental music books, and sophisticated woodcut iconography.The precise origins and early formative years of Jobin Bernhardt remain partially shrouded in the archival record of the Upper Rhine, though early genealogical registers suggest roots in Belfort (Beffert) or the surrounding Alsatian hinterlands before his permanent establishment in Strasbourg. Trained initially in the meticulous craft of the Formschneider (woodblock cutter and engraver), Jobin mastered the mechanical and artistic techniques required to translate complex painterly designs onto high-relief wooden matrixes. His decisive integration into the intellectual and cultural elite of Strasbourg was formalized around 1566 through his marriage to Anna Fischart, the sister of the renowned humanist polymath, satirist, and legal scholar Johann Fischart (c. 1546–1590). This matrimonial alliance forged an extraordinary creative partnership between printer and author that would define the landscape of late sixteenth-century German vernacular literature. Settling in Strasbourg, Jobin acquired citizenship, matriculated into the local guild of painters and printers, and established an independent printing house equipped with multiple presses, casting matrices, and specialized woodcut workshops.The editorial program of Jobin Bernhardt was distinguished by his close, symbiotic relationship with Johann Fischart, whose sprawling, polyphonic, and linguistic-experimental works Jobin printed, illustrated, and distributed across the Holy Roman Empire. Jobin was the exclusive publisher responsible for issuing Fischart's most radical literary achievements, including the celebrated Geschichtklitterung (1575, expanded in 1582 and 1590)—an extraordinary, highly creative adaptation and radical transformation of François Rabelais's Gargantua. Through Jobin’s meticulous typography and typographic design, Fischart’s complex linguistic puns, neologisms, and layered marginal commentaries were organized into readable, visually dynamic printed pages. Jobin also manufactured and published Fischart’s biting anti-papal and anti-Jesuit satires, such as Nachtrab oder Nebelkräh (1570), Das Podagrammisch Trostbüchlein (1577), and Ehezucht (1578), alongside moralizing domestic treatises and translated histories. These publications established the Jobin press as the preeminent mouthpiece of vibrant, combative Lutheran and Reformed vernacular culture in Southwestern Germany.Parallel to his literary publications, Jobin Bernhardt achieved international renown through his collaborative artistic ventures with the master Swiss painter and illustrator Tobias Stimmer (1539–1584). Recognizing Stimmer’s genius in Mannerist block design, Jobin engaged Stimmer to produce monumental series of woodcuts that Jobin himself cut into wood or oversaw through his studio assistants. Among their most celebrated achievements was the magnificent Neue Künstliche Figuren Biblischer Historien (printed by Jobin in 1576), an emblem-like pictorial Bible featuring intricate architectural borders, expressive figural groupings, and accompanying poetic verses in German and Latin written by Fischart. Jobin was also instrumental in printing and publishing Stimmer's famous portrait series, including the Icones sive Imagines Vivae Literis Claris Virorum (1589), which provided iconic, authoritative visual likenesses of Protestant Reformers, contemporary European scholars, legal minds, and political rulers. Jobin’s precise cutting technique—preserving the delicate cross-hatching, calligraphic fluidity, and dramatic chiaroscuro of Stimmer’s drawings—set a new standard for Northern European book illustration, challenging the dominance of Nuremberg and Frankfurt presses.Beyond vernacular satire and visual arts, Jobin Bernhardt holds a monumental position in the history of Renaissance music printing and instrumental pedagogy. A skilled lutenist himself, Jobin recognized the growing demand among urban patricians, university students, and noble amateurs for printed instrumental music in German lute tablature (Deutsche Lautentabulatur). In 1572, Jobin printed and published his landmark anthology Das erste Buch der Lauten, followed swiftly in 1573 by Das ander Buch der Lauten. These monumental volumes featured intricate woodcut music types and contained elaborate arrangements of vocal chansons, motets, madrigals, and German lieds by European masters such as Orlando di Lasso, Clemens non Papa, and Jacques Arcadelt, alongside original dances (passamezzi, gagliarde, padovane) composed by leading lutenists including Sixt Kargel, Melchior Neusidler, and Valentin Bakfark. Jobin designed a clear, highly legible system for printing the complex numeric and alphabetical grids of lute tablature alongside elaborate woodcut initial letters and ornamental headpieces, making his music books highly prized across the Continent.The operational infrastructure of Jobin's printing office reflected the sophisticated business strategies required by late sixteenth-century print capitalism. Situated in Strasbourg—a key trade node connecting the Rhineland, Switzerland, France, and the Low Countries—Jobin actively sought Imperial Privileges (Privilegia Caesarea) from Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolf II to protect his costly music books and illustrated editions from piracy by rival printers in Basel, Nuremberg, and Frankfurt. Jobin maintained an active presence at the biannual Frankfurt Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse), where he distributed his catalogues, bartered unbound sheets with international booksellers, and acquired paper stock. His pressmarks frequently featured symbolic allegories of industry, faith, and artistic truth, including motifs of the anvil, celestial globes, and personifications of Veritas and Fides, signaling the intellectual integrity and technical precision of his shop.Following Jobin Bernhardt’s death in Strasbourg around late 1593 or early 1594, his extensive printing establishment, inventory of copperplates and woodblocks, and editorial privileges were inherited and carried on by his son, Tobias Jobin, who continued publishing under the family name into the early seventeenth century. The legacy of Jobin Bernhardt remains an essential pillar of early modern bibliographical study. His presses preserved the seminal literary output of Johann Fischart, defined the visual landscape of late Renaissance German art through the woodcuts of Tobias Stimmer, and revolutionized the dissemination of lute repertoire across Western Europe. Scholars of typography, musicology, and art history continue to regard Jobin as an exemplar of the early modern master craftsman—a publisher who seamlessly synthesized artistic mastery, mechanical innovation, and humanist erudition.

related_names.name: Greuter Matthias
related_names.biography: Matthias Greuter (also known in Italian historiography as Matteo Greuter and in French records as Matthieu Greuter; c. 1566 – 4 December 1638) stands as one of the most versatile, technically prolific, and intellectually pivotal printmakers, engravers, cartographers, and globe makers operating in Western Europe during the transition from late Mannerism to the high Baroque. Born in the Imperial Free City of Strasbourg (Strassburg) during the height of the Upper Rhenish graphic renaissance, Greuter synthesized Northern European printmaking precision—characterized by rigorous line burin technique, dense hatching, and sophisticated ornamental design—with the theatrical visual rhetoric and monumental spatial demands of Counter-Reformation Rome. Over a career spanning more than five decades across Strasbourg, Lyons, Avignon, and Rome, Greuter established himself not merely as an reproductive engraver of artistic compositions, but as a central agent in the diffusion of scientific knowledge, papal propaganda, urban cartography, and academic broadsheets (tesi laureali). His workshop in Rome became a critical node in an international intellectual network that connected Jesuit astronomers like Christoph Scheiner, natural philosophers such as Galileo Galilei, Roman publishers like Giacomo Mascardi, and the grand patronal ambitions of Pope Paul V Borghese and Pope Urban VIII Barberini.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Training in the Upper RhineGreuter was born in Strasbourg around 1564–1566 into a vibrant artisan milieu deeply steeped in goldsmithing, typography, and relief and intaglio printmaking. Strasbourg at the close of the sixteenth century was a major intellectual crossroad between the German Holy Roman Empire and the Kingdom of France, housing a renowned Protestant Gymnasium and a thriving printing industry led by figures such as Bernhard Jobin. Greuter received his initial artistic training within the Rhenish tradition of small-scale ornamental engraving (Kleinmeister style), absorbing the design vocabularies of Tobias Stimmer, Étienne Delaune, and the Mannerist pattern books circulated across Central Europe. His earliest signed prints, dating from the late 1580s and early 1590s, demonstrate an extraordinary mastery of the burin on copperplate, featuring delicate grotesques, allegorical figures of the Virtues and Vices, architectural frames, and moralizing genre scenes. These early plates reveal Greuter’s early mastery of micro-engraving, spatial framing, and complex iconographical program design, skills that would later make him the engraver of choice for intricate scientific diagrams and multi-panel broadsheets.The French Interlude: Migration to Lyons and Avignon (c. 1592–1603)Political tensions, religious instability, and the economic lure of Catholic patronal markets prompted Greuter to depart the Upper Rhine around 1592. He migrated south into France, settling initially in Lyons, then one of Europe’s premier centers for international book publishing and trade fair distribution. In Lyons, Greuter collaborated with prominent printers and humanists, executing elegant frontispieces, title pages, emblematic illustrations, and royal portraits, including effigies of King Henry IV of France. By the late 1590s, Greuter had established himself in Avignon, a papal enclave within French territory. This geographic transition was of paramount importance: it integrated Greuter into Catholic ecclesiastical patronage networks and familiarized him with Roman Catholic devotional iconography. In Avignon, he produced large devotional prints, thesis sheets for Jesuit colleges, and commemorative engravings that caught the attention of visiting prelates. The technical fluidity of his etching technique combined with his crisp Rhenish engraving burin work allowed him to produce high volumes of copperplates with remarkable speed and crispness, facilitating his eventual migration to the capital of the Catholic world.The Roman Workshop: Scientific Collaboration, Jesuit Patronage, and Academic BroadsheetsIn 1603 or early 1604, Greuter relocated permanently to Rome, establishing a prosperous workshop near the church of San Marcello along the Via del Corso, later operating under the emblem of the Sun (Bottega del Sole). Rome under the pontificates of Clement VIII Aldobrandini, Paul V Borghese, and Urban VIII Barberini was undergoing a colossal artistic and architectural transformation. Greuter quickly identified a lucrative niche by specializing in complex multi-plate engravings, academic thesis prints (tesi), astronomical plates, and ephemeral festival decorations. His workshop became the premier destination for scholars, aristocrats, and religious orders seeking to publish visually authoritative texts. Most notably, Greuter played a fundamental role in the visual dissemination of early modern science. In 1613, he was commissioned by the Accademia dei Lincei and printer Giacomo Mascardi to engrave the copperplates for Galileo Galilei’s landmark treatise, Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle macchie solari (History and Demonstrations Concerning Sunspots). Greuter’s meticulous plates faithfully rendered Galileo’s telescopic observations of the sunspot migrations across the solar disk, translating delicate ink wash drawings into highly precise engraved stippling and hatching. Later, Greuter was engaged by the Jesuit astronomer Christoph Scheiner to engrave plates for his monumental counter-argument on solar physics, the Rosa Ursina sive Sol (1626–1630), showcasing his unique ability to navigate competing scientific camps while maintaining absolute technical impartiality and graphic perfection.Cartographic Monumentality: The Plan of Rome and Globe ProductionWhile Greuter’s reputation as an illustrator of scientific and academic texts was secure, his most lasting contribution to European visual culture lies in his monumental cartographic enterprises. In 1618, Greuter surveyed, designed, and engraved a massive multi-sheet bird’s-eye perspective view of Rome, titled Disegno della città di Roma con tutti gli edificii et vie di essa. Republished and updated in 1629 to reflect the grand architectural projects of Urban VIII, this plan remains one of the supreme masterpieces of Baroque cartography. It captured every street, church, palace, ruin, and garden with astounding spatial accuracy and artistic elegance, serving as both an administrative document and a triumphal celebration of Papal urbanism. Expanding his cartographic enterprise in his final decade, Greuter turned to globemaking, an art form previously dominated by Dutch cartographers such as Willem Janszoon Blaeu. In 1632, Greuter published a monumental 50-centimeter terrestrial globe, followed in 1636 by a matching celestial globe. Dedicating these works to Pope Urban VIII and Cardinal Francesco Barberini, Greuter engraved the globe gores with remarkable calligraphic precision, incorporating the latest geographic discoveries in the Americas and Asia alongside refined classical constellations. These globes represented the pinnacle of Italian Baroque globe production and established Rome as a competitive center for cartographic manufacturing.Legacy, Family Dynasty, and Historiographical ImpactMatthias Greuter died in Rome on 4 December 1638, leaving behind a massive artistic legacy and a fully functioning printmaking enterprise that was continued by his talented son, Johann Friedrich Greuter (Giovanni Federico Greuter, c. 1590–1662), and later his grandson Giancarlo. Johann Friedrich inherited his father’s technical virtuosity, working closely with leading Baroque painters such as Pietro da Cortona, Gian Lorenzo Bernini, and Guido Reni to produce some of the most dramatic reproductive prints of the High Baroque. Early art historians, including Giovanni Baglione in his Le vite de' pittori, scultori et architetti (1642) and Joachim von Sandrart in his Teutsche Academie (1675), lauded Greuter as a master who successfully united Northern Rhenish mechanical discipline with the grand style of Roman classicism. Modern scholarship, ranging from Roberto Almagià’s cartographic studies to contemporary histories of early modern science, recognizes Matthias Greuter as a figure of central importance whose copperplates defined the visual landscape of seventeenth-century Rome and laid the groundwork for Baroque graphic arts.

academic_description: Folio. [8], 112, [i.e. 114: 1-66, (1), 66-112], [1: errata] leaves. Title printed in red and black within an engraved architectural border by Matthias Greuter, woodcut coat of arms of Julius Duke of Brunswig, 21 (20 double-page) engravings (sometimes appearing as two single leaves; one is also signed by Matthias Greuter), and numerous woodcut illustrations in the text. Contemporary limp vellum (a bit smutty), with later added supralibros and spine label, from the library of Walter Hawken Tregellas (1831-1894), an English writer of historical and biographical works and a professional draughtsman (with his presentation label on the pastdown), and from the Royal Engineers Library (gilt stamp on binding, and small ink stamp on title-page and on a few other places). Some very light browning and marginal dampstains, but a very nice genuine copy.Rare first edition of this magnificent work on fortification and town-planning, the first important contribution in the German-speaking world on the subject since Dürer's Etliche Underricht zur Befestigung der Stett (1527). It was to become the standard reference work on the construction of fortresses until there was a decisive change in the manner in which wars where fought. Further editions were published in 1599, 1608, 1705 and 1756.''Speckle writes his treatise from a strongly national motivation as is clear from his preface. He wishes to prove that the Germans are not completely without imagination, and that their invention of printing and of a 'grausam Geschütz' ('fearsome artillery') shows them to be the 'the greatest in the world' in these fields. He attacks, above all, the Italian theorists for their academic disputes, declaring their rules to be outmoded and openly ridiculing their approach ('when someone has no Latin, he cannot understand it, and so has no business to talk about it'). He demonstrates the urgency of fortification, as Dürer has done, by reference to the Turkish threat. Speckle claims to be familiar with fifty or sixty types of fortification, but restricts himself to a few only. He writes in German and avoids foreign words, 'so that every German - such as I too have the honour to call myself - can understand' '' (H.-W. Kruft, A History of Architectural Theory from Vitruvius to the Present, London & New York, 1994, p. 115).In addition to Dürer, whose work Speckle considered very important, he had adopted the work of Francesco de Marchi from Bologna, Della architettura militare, thus proving that he kept abreast of the latest trends. But he was no less a pragmatist, who in his teaching methods took into account whether a fortress was located in flat countryside, in hills or in mountainous terrain. Mathematics and geometry, in conjunction with practical skills and a knowledge of mechanical laws were also the art of building fortresses. Some of his retreats and mountain castles appear on the other hand as fantastic visions of a world that had rid itself of enemies. In a copy of the 1608 edition in the Strasbourg library these castles are labeled by hand and identified as based on reality. In the second part of the treatise Speckle presents plans whose forms are dictated by terrain. He describes inter alia, in great detail, the Turkish siege of Malta (1565) and the rebuilding of La Valetta, and in so doing provides us with one of the most detailed plans we have of Francesco Laparelli's project (cf. J. Zimmer, Daniel Speckle Architectura Von Vestungen, in: ''Architectural Theory from the Renaissance to the Present'', B. Evers & C. Thoenes, eds., Köln, 2003, pp. 511-519).The twenty-eighth chapter of the first part of the treatise contains the essence of Speckle's thinking on town planning. He starts with a description of a regular plan with six bastions, of which he gives a perspective view and which reveals the priority he accords to defensive considerations. He then describes in great detail an ideal type of town plan with eight bastions, in which his political and social ideas are revealed. In the tradition of all military architects of the second half of the sixteenth century, he uses a strict radial pattern. Around the central square are situated the church, royal palace, town hall and staple inn. Religious, secular and economic power are concentrated in this area. The military, on the other hand, are removed to the areas around the bastions. It is interesting that Speckle expressly sets civil law above martial law. Speckle aims overall at a very ordered community: 'mercenaries should be done away with'. Defensive considerations determine the city to the last detail (cf. K. Krüger, Albrecht Dürer, Daniel Speckle und die Anfänge frühmoderner Städteplanung in Deutschland, in: ''Mitteilungen des Vereins für deutsche Geschichte Nürnbergs'', 67, 1980, pp. 79-97; and H. de la Croix, Military Architecture and the Radial City Plan in Sixteenth Century Italy, in: ''The Art Bulletin'', 427/ 4, 1960, pp. 263-290).''Later in the sixteenth century, the instruments and surveying techniques essential to the preparation of ichnographic city plans were made available to an increasingly large circle of northern artists and topographers through a number of publications. One of the most interesting of these books is Daniel Speckle's treatise on fortifications, published in 1589. Speckle's method of surveying, which permitted a ground plan of 'any building, city or castle' to be drawn, is closely related to Hirschvogel's procedure. Unlike Hirschvogel's confusing description of his own invention, however, Speckle's chapter on surveying is a model of clarity and verbal economy. Speckle's straightforward and step-by-step exposition of surveying techniques parallels those of Tartaglia and Bartoli earlier in the century. It permitted any interested artist or architect to learn and apply them easily'' (J.A. Pinto, Origins and Development of the Ichnographic City Plan, in: ''Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians'', 35, 1, 1976, p. 49).In the Architectura are also described several instruments of his invention, especially his set of six reduction compasses (cf. I. Schneider, Der Proporzionalzirkel. Ein universelles Analogrecheninstrument der Vergangenheit, München, 1970, pp. 31-32).Daniel Speckle (Specklin), a native of Strasbourg, was the son of the eminent carver Veit Rudolph Speckle. After completing his apprenticeship as a silk embroiderer, he left Strasbourg in 1552 to go on a study tour, which took him to the fortress of Komorn and Györ in Hungary. By 1555 he was in Vienna, where he first trained as a master mason and later became an architect. The influence of the chief builder in Vienna, Hermes Schallautzer, could well have played a role in influencing Speckle's decision to concentrate in the future on the construction of fortresses. He soon achieved success in this field and was employed as head of constructions for various fortress projects. He visited Antwerp in 1560 and subsequently travelled to Denmark, Sweden, Poland, and Russia. In 1564 he returned to Strasbourg, married and worked again as a silk embroiderer. Having been involved with the construction of fortifications in Düsseldorf and Regensburg in 1567, he was once again in Hungary, this time with his patron, the Imperial general Lazarus von Schwendi, where he was instrumental in the planning of fortifications in VaraÅ¾din, Kashau, and Tokai. During this time he must also have acquired a reputation as a mapmaker, since as a result of Schwendi's connections he was commissioned in 1573 by Archduke Ferdinand to produce a map of Alsace, which he worked on until 1576. He also was engaged in producing an overall plan for fortifying the city of Ulm. To this end he drew up extensive plans and models, as well as a builder's journal, the first of its kind. There followed a journal for Colmar (1579) and a building code for Basle (1589). By now he had also produced elaborate pieces of work for the city of Strasbourg, including a large-scale wooden model of the city. On October 5, 1577 Speckle was appointed City Architect with an annual salary of 250 Guilders, 6 tuns of wine and 1000 bundles of wood. With the authorization of the city council he continued to work for other domains and towns, such as Schlettstadt, Ensisheim, Colmar, Basle, Veldens, Belfort, Cologne, Heidelberg, and Hanau. After being sent on a study trip to Antwerp, he brought back several plans of the fortifications of towns in Brabant and Holland. In September 1587 he submitted his Architectura to the council of Strasbourg. Finally, the city of Heilbronn requested his advice and later sent him the ground plans of a planned fortress for his appraisal, but he was not able to air his opinions on it, as he died on October 18, 1589, aged 53 (cf. K.E. Mayer, Die Lebensgeschichte des Strassburger Stadt- und Festungsbaumeisters Daniel Specklin, Stuttgart, 1928, passim; and A. Fischer, Daniel Specklin aus Strassburg, 1539-1589: Festungsbaumeister, Ingenieur und Kartograph, Sigmaringen, 1996, passim).
