authors.name: Aesopus
authors.biography: Aesop (Greek Αἴσωπος, Aisōpos), conventionally dated to the sixth century BC, is the legendary figure to whom one of the most influential traditions of animal fable in Greek and European literature has been attributed. His historical existence cannot be established with certainty, and the dates c. 620–560 BC should be treated as conventional rather than securely documented. What can be traced with greater confidence is the development of an Aesopic literary tradition in which short narratives involving animals, humans, and other personified beings are used to illuminate recurrent problems of conduct, power, prudence, deception, justice, and human limitation. The name “Aesop” therefore designates both a figure of archaic Greek cultural memory and a large, composite corpus of fables transmitted through Greek, Latin, Byzantine, and early modern traditions.The ancient evidence for Aesop's life is fragmentary and heterogeneous. Herodotus is the earliest substantial source to mention him: in Histories 2.134 he describes Aesop as a slave of Iadmon, a Samian, and uses the Delphians' payment of compensation for Aesop's killing as evidence that Aesop had indeed belonged to Iadmon. Herodotus does not, however, give the elaborate narrative of Aesop's trial and execution found in later biographies. The familiar story of his quarrel with the Delphians, the accusation of sacrilege, the hidden sacred vessel, and his death by being thrown from the cliffs belongs to the later biographical tradition and should not be presented as Herodotean fact.The ancient tradition variously associates Aesop with Samos, Thrace, Phrygia, Lydia, and other regions. His alleged servile status is considerably better attested than his ethnic or geographical origins, although even the later biographical narratives elaborate the historical tradition with legendary material. The etymology of the name has sometimes encouraged an association between Aesop and Ethiopia, but this does not constitute evidence for an Ethiopian historical identity. Modern interpretations of Aesop as a deliberately constructed “outsider” or subaltern figure are valuable for understanding the cultural symbolism of the tradition, but should be distinguished from demonstrable biographical facts.Aesop's association with the political and intellectual world of the Greek archaic period was considerably elaborated by later authors. Plutarch's Banquet of the Seven Wise Men presents Aesop as a guest associated with Croesus and as a participant in a conversation involving figures such as Solon, Thales, and Chilon. Plutarch also represents him as having been sent by Croesus to Periander and to consult the oracle at Delphi. These episodes belong to the literary construction of Aesop as a figure of practical wisdom and witty counsel rather than constituting independent evidence for a historically verifiable diplomatic career.The famous Delphic episode likewise developed considerably beyond the information supplied by Herodotus. The later Vita Aesopi, transmitted in several Greek recensions and especially influential in the Byzantine and Renaissance periods, transforms Aesop into a paradoxical hero: physically unattractive and socially marginal, yet extraordinarily intelligent, verbally inventive, and capable of defeating supposedly superior opponents through wit. The surviving biographical traditions are therefore better understood as part of the Aesopic literary corpus than as reliable chronological biography. The Planudean Life of Aesop, composed in the Byzantine period and preserved in the manuscript tradition associated with Maximus Planudes, became particularly influential in the subsequent history of the fable.The fables themselves cannot be regarded as the work of Aesop in the modern authorial sense. No writings by Aesop survive, and there is no secure evidence that he himself committed a collection of fables to writing. The ancient tradition instead represents him as the exemplary fabulist to whom stories circulating in oral and literary form could be attributed. A collection of Aesopic tales was associated in antiquity with Demetrius of Phalerum, who lived in the late fourth and early third centuries BC; the collection itself is lost. Later Greek collections derive from a complicated process of compilation, adaptation, and transmission. The so-called Augustana collection, the Vindobonensis tradition, and the Planudean-Accursian tradition represent different stages of this process rather than successive editions of a single original book.Aesopic fable is characterized by narrative brevity, concentration on a single conflict or reversal, and a close relationship between story and moral interpretation. The moral may be explicit, normally in the form of an epimythion, or left to the reader's inference. Animals such as the fox, lion, wolf, lamb, ass, crow, tortoise, and mouse function not simply as allegorical symbols but as recurring narrative types whose actions expose mechanisms of power, deception, self-interest, and social hierarchy. The genre was especially suited to rhetorical and pedagogical use because the fable could provide a compact paradeigma, or illustrative example, in an argument. Aristotle explicitly discusses the fable in Rhetoric II.20, where he cites an Aesopic story as a form of rhetorical proof.The literary prestige of Aesop in classical Greece is also reflected in Plato. In the Phaedo 60c–61b, Socrates explains that while in prison he had begun to put Aesopic fables into verse, together with a hymn to Apollo. Plato's passage does not imply that Aesop's fables formed a fixed written canon in the sixth century BC; rather, it demonstrates that by the fourth century BC “Aesop” had become an established cultural authority for a recognizable type of morally instructive narrative.Aesopic fable subsequently acquired a major Latin tradition. Phaedrus, probably a Thracian or Macedonian freedman writing under the early Roman Empire, transformed Aesopic material into Latin verse, chiefly in iambic senarii. His five-book collection, together with later material, constitutes one of the principal channels through which Greek fable entered Latin literary culture. Phaedrus should not, however, be reduced to a simple political satirist of Tiberius: although his fables contain reflections on power, inequality, and the vulnerability of the weak, the surviving corpus is formally and thematically more varied. Babrius, probably active in the Roman imperial period, subsequently composed a substantial Greek collection in choliambic verse. Both poets became crucial sources for the later history of the Aesopic tradition.Late antique and medieval transmission multiplied the number of texts circulating under Aesop's name. Latin collections associated with Romulus incorporated material ultimately connected with Phaedrus; Avianus composed a collection of forty-two fables in elegiac verse; and medieval Latin school culture preserved, adapted, and moralized fable collections in a variety of forms. The Greek Byzantine tradition developed independently alongside these Latin lines of transmission. By the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the recension associated with Maximus Planudes and the Vita Aesopi had become particularly important for the later Western reception of Greek Aesop.The transition from manuscript to print transformed the scale of the Aesopic tradition. Several Latin and vernacular Aesopic texts were printed during the 1470s. In Milan, editions of the Vita et fabulae in the Latin translation of Rinuccio d'Arezzo appeared in 1474 and 1476, followed by another Milanese edition in 1479. In Verona, Accio Zucco's Aesopus moralisatus, a Latin-Italian adaptation of the anonymous Neveletian fable tradition, was printed on 26 June 1479. These editions demonstrate that the printed Aesop was from the beginning a composite phenomenon: “Aesop” could designate Greek fables, Latin adaptations, medieval collections, vernacular translations, moralizations, and illustrated compilations.Among the most influential early printed manifestations was Heinrich Steinhöwel's bilingual Esopus, printed by Johann Zainer at Ulm around 1476–1477. The edition presented Latin texts together with Steinhöwel's German translation and was accompanied by an exceptionally rich programme of woodcuts. The Morgan Library copy contains 288 leaves and 191 woodcuts; other bibliographical descriptions distinguish different states or versions of the printing, and the edition became one of the principal visual and textual models for subsequent European Aesop editions. Its influence extended far beyond Germany, contributing to the transmission of a standardized illustrated conception of the fabulist and his animal narratives.The Greek printed tradition developed along a different path. The edition prepared by Bonus Accursius in Milan, generally dated 1478–1479, is traditionally regarded as the editio princeps of the Greek Aesopic fables. It presented the Greek text together with the Latin translation of Rinuccio and included the biographical material now known as the Vita Accursiana. The collection represented a particular recension of the Greek tradition and contained approximately 147 fables in the form transmitted by its manuscript source. It should therefore not be confused with the much later critical reconstruction of the ancient Aesopic corpus.The fifteenth-century Italian tradition was particularly important. Francesco Del Tuppo's Neapolitan edition of 1485 provided a new Italian version of the Vita and fables and was accompanied by eighty-eight woodcuts, twenty-three illustrating the life of Aesop and sixty-five the fables. Its text combined the Latin tradition of Rinuccio with the medieval collection associated with Gualterus Anglicus, while the illustrations constituted an independent and highly original contribution to the visual history of Aesop.The sixteenth century brought a decisive expansion and diversification of Aesopic publishing. The most important scholarly landmark was Aldo Manuzio's Venetian edition of October 1505, Vita & Fabellae Aesopi cum interpretatione Latina, the first Aldine edition of Aesop. It presented Aesop in Greek and Latin and placed the fables within a much larger collection of texts concerned with fable, allegory, and proverbial wisdom. Alongside Aesop it included the forty-three fables of Babrius, printed under the name “Gabrius”, Aphthonius's De fabula, Philostratus's De fabula, Hermogenes as transmitted by Priscian, Phurnutus, Palaephatus, Heraclides Ponticus, Horapollo, collections of proverbs, and other related material. The edition is therefore important not merely as a printing of Aesop but as an ambitious reconstruction of the Greek literary environment of fable and allegory.Aesop's sixteenth-century reception was not confined to scholarly Greek editions. In 1520 Alexander and Benedictus de Bindonis printed at Venice a large Latin collection containing 214 fables of Aesop, the thirty-three fables translated by Lorenzo Valla, sixty-three attributed to “Salone Parmensis”, forty-two fables of Avianus, and the two Hecatomythia of Lorenzo Astemio. This type of composite collection is characteristic of Renaissance Aesop: the name of the ancient fabulist functioned as an organizing principle for a much broader anthology of ancient, medieval, and humanist fable.The vernacular tradition developed with equal intensity. An important anonymous Italian collection, Favole d'Esopo Greco elegantissime, e de molti altri, was printed at Venice by Michele Tramezzino in 1551. It belongs to a line of sixteenth-century Italian translations and adaptations that increasingly detached Aesopic material from the strictly humanist Latin-Greek environment and made it available to readers of the Italian vernacular.Particularly influential was Giulio Landi's Italian translation of the Vita Aesopi, first published in Venice by Gabriele Giolito de' Ferrari in 1545. Landi translated and reshaped the Byzantine life attributed to Maximus Planudes, while Lodovico Domenichi supervised its passage into print. The work enjoyed an exceptionally long afterlife and was repeatedly reprinted during the sixteenth century. A second Giolito edition appeared in 1550; later editions included those of 1561, 1569, 1575, 1580, 1585, and 1592. It is important, however, to distinguish the Vita from the fables themselves: the 1550 Giolito printing, for example, contains the Life of Aesop but not the fables. Moreover, the attribution to Landi of all the fables that subsequently accompanied his Vita is not secure and has been questioned by modern scholarship.The 1569 Dilettevoli favole di Esopo e di altri elevati ingegni, printed in Venice by Giovanni Bariletto, belongs to this expanding vernacular tradition. The work was associated with Landi but, as with the later collections, the precise attribution of all individual fables to him should not be assumed. The 1575 edition printed by Francesco Ziletti was substantially more ambitious: Vita di Esopo Frigio, prudente et faceto favolatore was accompanied by the fables attributed to Aesop and by numerous additional fables of other authors, with interpretations and illustrations, and the collection claimed approximately four hundred pieces. This edition illustrates the characteristic Renaissance tendency to enlarge “Aesop” into an anthology of morally instructive narratives rather than to reproduce a fixed ancient corpus.A parallel and highly original development was the transformation of Aesopic material into Italian verse. Cesare Pavesi, under the name Pietro Targa, published Cento e cinquanta favole in 1569, while Giovanni Mario Verdizzotti published his Cento favole morali in Venice with Giordano Ziletti in 1570. Verdizzotti's collection contained one hundred fables in verse, plus the introductory fable “Del padre, e del figliuolo, che menavan l'asino”, effectively making 101 pieces in the volume. The work was richly illustrated, with woodcuts designed by Verdizzotti himself. Its sources included not only Aesop but also other ancient and Renaissance fabulists, notably Gabriele Faerno. The collection enjoyed a long series of reprints and became an important link between Renaissance Aesopic literature and the later European fabulistic tradition.The scholarly Latin tradition remained active alongside these vernacular transformations. A particularly important Venetian edition appeared in 1561 from Francesco Rampazetto: Aesopi Phrygis Fabellae graece et latine, cum aliis opusculis. It contained the Vita Aesopi attributed to Planudes, 150 Aesopic fables, forty-three fables of Babrius, and treatises by Aphthonius, Philostratus, and Hermogenes, together with several other Greek texts. Its compact octavo format and bilingual presentation made it both a scholarly and pedagogical book. Another major illustrated Latin collection was the 1572 Venetian edition printed by the heirs of Melchiorre Sessa, Aesopi Phrygis, et aliorum Fabulae, a 12mo volume of 214 leaves with woodcut illustrations, explicitly intended “in gratiam studiosae iuventutis”.The sixteenth-century history of Aesop thus cannot be reduced to a sequence of editions reproducing a stable text. Renaissance printers and editors repeatedly reshaped the corpus by combining Greek and Latin recensions, medieval collections, Phaedrian and Avianian material, Planudean biography, humanist translations, new vernacular adaptations, and newly composed fables. The category “Aesop” consequently functioned as both an authorial name and a bibliographical category. The history of the printed Aesop is therefore inseparable from the history of compilation, translation, illustration, school culture, and the growing market for vernacular moral literature.The intellectual transformation of Aesop continued into the seventeenth century and beyond. The ancient fable became a vehicle for moral education, political observation, social satire, and literary experimentation. Jean de La Fontaine's Fables choisies, mises en vers, whose first collection appeared in Paris in 1668, did not simply translate Aesop but transformed material from Aesopic, Phaedrian, Oriental, and other traditions into a sophisticated poetic form. The modern history of the fable is consequently best understood not as a direct line from a historical sixth-century author to La Fontaine, but as a continuous process of adaptation in which “Aesop” served as a durable cultural model.Modern philology has progressively separated the historical question of Aesop from the textual history of the fables. Richard Bentley's Dissertation upon the Fables of Aesop, published in 1699 as part of his Dissertations upon the Epistles of Phalaris, was an important early demonstration that the surviving collections could not simply be attributed to the sixth-century fabulist. The decisive modern synthesis was Ben Edwin Perry's Aesopica (1952), which assembled Greek and Latin texts, testimonia, biographies, proverbs, and 725 numbered fable types, while carefully distinguishing the various strands of the Aesopic tradition. Perry's work remains fundamental for the study of the corpus, although subsequent scholarship has continued to refine the chronology, relationships, and cultural contexts of individual collections.The modern conception of Aesop should therefore be fundamentally historical rather than biographical. There may have been an archaic Greek fabulist whose reputation gave rise to the tradition, but the surviving “Aesopic corpus” is the product of centuries of oral transmission, compilation, translation, moralization, literary imitation, and editorial reconstruction. From the Greek collections of antiquity through Phaedrus and Babrius, Byzantine Planudes, the incunabular printers, the Aldine press, the vernacular translators of the Italian Renaissance, and ultimately La Fontaine and modern children's literature, Aesop has functioned less as a single author than as one of the most durable authorial personae in European literary history.

publishers.name: Tournes Jean de
publishers.biography: Jean I de Tournes (1504 – 7 September 1564) stands as one of the most transcendent figures in the history of early modern European typography, humanism, and print culture. Operating in sixteenth-century Lyon—a city that served as the dynamic, unregulated economic crossroads of international commerce, artistic innovation, and intellectual freedom between Northern Europe and Italy—De Tournes elevated the craft of printing from a mere mechanical trade into a sublime form of aesthetic and scholarly expression. Born in Noyon in Picardy, the very hometown of his contemporary John Calvin, Jean de Tournes migrated south during his youth to Lyon, a metropolis unencumbered by the restrictive censorship of the Sorbonne and the Parisian Guild of Booksellers. There, he established a press whose aesthetic brilliance, typographical precision, and editorial sophistication rivaled the Venetian workshop of Aldus Manutius and the Parisian press of the Estienne family, permanently shaping the visual and textual landscape of the French Renaissance.De Tournes's formative training took place within the renowned Lyonnese workshop of Sebastian Gryphius (Sébastien Gryphe), a German-born master printer who had introduced the compact italic format and rigorous scholarly editing of Latin classics to the Rhone valley. Serving as a compositor and press corrector under Gryphius during the 1530s, De Tournes was immersed in a vibrant sodalitas literaria—an informal academy of humanist scholars, translators, and poets that included Étienne Dolet, Rabelais, and Clement Marot. Through this rigorous apprenticeship, De Tournes acquired not only impeccable Latinity and proofreading discipline but also an acute understanding of the emerging market for elegant, small-format vernacular texts. Around 1542, having secured his own equipment and press credentials, he established an independent printing house at the sign of the Deux-Têtes (later associated with his iconic printer's mark of the Vraie Chimère, featuring two vipers entwined around a rod, symbolizing prudence and eloquence).The middle decades of the sixteenth century marked the golden age of the De Tournes press, characterized by an unprecedented synthesis of poetic literature, typographic invention, and graphic arts. De Tournes became the undisputed publisher of the École lyonnaise, a brilliant constellation of Renaissance poets whose work demanded a visual presentation capable of matching its formal complexity. In 1544, he printed Maurice Scève's masterwork, Délie, objet de plus haulte vertu, an enigmatic sequence of 449 dizains organized around 50 complex woodcut emblems (emblemes). De Tournes's layout for Délie—framing the geometric woodcuts with delicate architectural and floral borders—established a new benchmark for emblem literature across Western Europe. He subsequently published the groundbreaking Euvres de Louïze Labé Lionnoize (1555), giving physical form to the fierce, passionate voice of one of the Renaissance's greatest female poets, as well as works by Pernette du Guillet, Antoine du Moulin, and Guillaume Guéroult.Central to the aesthetic signature of the De Tournes press was his extraordinary partnership with the illustrator and engraver Bernard Salomon, popularly known as Le Petit Bernard. Salomon’s delicate, Mannerist woodcuts—characterized by slender, elongated figures, dynamic movement, and extraordinarily fine cross-hatching—were perfectly calibrated to match De Tournes's light, refined typography. Together, De Tournes and Salomon produced a series of illustrated masterpieces that set the aesthetic standard for European book design. Chief among these was the Metamorphose d'Ovide figurée (1557), in which Salomon’s 178 intricate wood engravings were paired with elegant French octosyllabic verses framed by intricate arabesque, grotesque, and strapwork borders. Their collaboration extended to the Quadrins historiques de la Bible (1554), Claude Paradin's Devises heroïques (1557), and Jean Lemaire de Belges's historical treatises. To complete his visual program, De Tournes commissioned and deployed the exquisite italic typefaces cut by Robert Granjon, as well as Granjon's revolutionary caractères de civilité (a type design imitating French cursive handwriting) and an unprecedented array of typographical ornaments, vignettes, and intricate lace-like fleurons.Beyond his contributions to vernacular poetry and visual arts, Jean de Tournes was a deeply committed intellectual whose publishing house served as an engine for religious reform and humanist pedagogy. While publicly maintaining his standing as a respected citizen and printer to the crown (being named Imprimeur du Roi in Lyon in 1559), De Tournes harbored strong sympathies for the Evangelical and Calvinist movements. He systematically printed French translations of the Holy Scriptures, metric psalters translated by Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze, and works of Protestant devotional theology, often issuing them anonymously or under discreet imprints to evade inquisitorial scrutiny. His mottoes—Son art en Dieu ("His art is in God") and Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris ("Do not unto others what you would not have done unto you")—reflected a personal theology rooted in Christian humanism, ethical integrity, and spiritual devotion.The escalating religious tensions of the French Wars of Religion severely disrupted the tranquility of Lyon and De Tournes's business. Following the Protestant seizure of Lyon in April 1562, the printing trade suffered cataclysmic financial losses due to disrupted trade routes, hyperinflation, and political instability. Though De Tournes survived the immediate violence of the conflicts, he succumbed to the catastrophic outbreak of the bubonic plague that ravaged Lyon in the late summer of 1564, dying on September 7 of that year. His intellectual and typographic legacy was carried on by his son, Jean II de Tournes (1539–1615), who maintained the family press under increasingly hostile counter-reformation pressures until 1585, when escalating religious persecution forced the family to relocate the press to Geneva. Today, the imprints of Jean I de Tournes are revered by bibliophiles, printing historians, and literary scholars as the absolute pinnacle of sixteenth-century French book production, exemplifying a harmonious equilibrium between textual scholarship, typographical innovation, and artistic genius.

related_names.name: Salomon Bernard
related_names.biography: Bernard Salomon, frequently referenced in earlier bibliographical literature under the inverted nomenclature Salomon Bernard and affectionately dubbed « Le Petit Bernard » by seventeenth- and eighteenth-century connoisseurs, stands as one of the most sublime and prolific graphic artists, draftsmen, and wood engravers of the Northern Renaissance. Flourishing in Lyon during the mid-sixteenth century—a golden era in which the city on the Rhône served as the undisputed intellectual, commercial, and typographical bridge between Italian Mannerism and Northern European Humanism—Salomon fundamentally transformed the medium of book illustration. Operating at the epicenter of the Lyonnese publishing boom, his artistic vision became intrinsically bound to the legendary printing house of Jean de Tournes. Together, author, printer, and artist forged an aesthetic identity characterized by exquisite ornamental borders, slender Italianate figures, intricate architectural frames, and a breathtaking mastery of micro-woodcut engraving that set the standard for European illustrated books for generations.Extremely little survives in the way of documentary archival evidence regarding the precise origins and formative years of Bernard Salomon. It is generally deduced by art historians that he was born in Lyon or its immediate environs between 1506 and 1510. Early municipal records from Lyon mention various artistic commissions, indicating that by the late 1530s he was already established as an accomplished painter and master decorator within the city's guild structures. Unlike his Parisian contemporaries who relied heavily on royal patronage, Salomon’s artistic development was conditioned by the unique sociopolitical climate of Lyon—a free city unencumbered by a permanent university or royal court, but thriving on banking, silk manufacturing, international trade fairs, and above all, an unbridled print industry. During the 1540s, Salomon received prestigious public commissions for municipal festival decorations, most notably participating in the elaborate ephemeral architecture and triumphal arches erected for the Joyous Entry of King Henri II and Catherine de' Medici into Lyon in September 1548. These large-scale projects allowed him to absorb and digest the visual language of the School of Fontainebleau, particularly the dramatic Mannerist compositions of Rosso Fiorentino, Francesco Primaticcio, and Niccolò dell'Abbate, as well as the elegant draftsmanship of Parmigianino, which he would later translate into miniature print forms.The decisive turning point in Salomon’s career occurred around 1545, when he entered into an exclusive and extraordinarily synergistic partnership with the master printer Jean de Tournes. De Tournes, who had trained under the celebrated Sebastian Gryphius, sought to elevate the artistic quality of Lyonnese presswork to rival the grand Italian houses of Aldus Manutius and the Parisian master presses of Geoffroy Tory and Robert Estienne. In Salomon, De Tournes found an illustrator of unprecedented genius who could adapt to the rigorous spatial constraints of the printed page without sacrificing decorative exuberance or narrative clarity. Salomon’s output for De Tournes was monumental in scope, encompassing hundreds upon hundreds of bespoke woodblocks. Among his earliest masterpieces for De Tournes were the illustrations for the 1547 edition of Marguerites de la Marguerite des princesses by Marguerite de Navarre, followed by his celebrated series for Andrea Alciato’s Emblemata (Les Emblemes de M. André Alciat, 1547) and Aesop’s Fables (Les Fables d'Ésope phrygien, 1547). Salomon’s ability to condense complex allegorical, moral, and mythical narratives into tiny woodcut blocks—often measuring no more than a few centimeters—astonished his contemporaries and established a new visual vernacular for emblem books.Salomon’s crowning artistic achievements materialized in the 1550s through two monumental publishing ventures: the visual illustration of the Holy Scriptures and the woodcut cycle for Ovid’s Metamorphoses. In 1553, De Tournes published the Quadrins historiques de la Bible, featuring a breathtaking series of wood engravings by Salomon, accompanied by poetic quatrains written by the Lyonnese humanist Claude Paradin. This Biblical suite was an instant international sensation, undergoing dozens of re-editions, expanded printings, and translations into Italian, Spanish, English, German, and Flemish. Salomon re-envisioned Old Testament narratives with dynamic foreshortening, theatrical gestural language, and vast, atmospheric spatial depth. Building upon this triumph, De Tournes and Salomon released La Métamorphose d'Ovide figurée in 1557. In this work, Salomon reached the absolute pinnacle of Mannerist graphic refinement. His depiction of classical mythology—replete with elongated, ethereal nymphs, muscular deities, serpentine line work, and lavish grotesque borders composed of satyrs, arabesques, and strapwork—became the definitive visual interpretation of Ovid for the late sixteenth century.The technical execution of Salomon’s illustrations represents a high-water mark in the history of relief printing and typography. Working on high-density fruitwood blocks, Salomon (and the skilled artisan engravers operating under his direct studio supervision) achieved an extraordinarily fine, hairline relief line that mimicked the delicacy of copperplate engraving while maintaining the durability required for letterpress integration. His woodcuts were designed to interact seamlessly with De Tournes’ elegant typography, which utilized the magnificent italic types of Robert Granjon and refined Roman fonts. Furthermore, Salomon introduced a revolutionary system of modular, interchangeable ornamental frames—featuring intricate cartouches, Mannerist grotesques, flora, fauna, and architectural motifs—which enabled De Tournes to frame both text blocks and illustrations dynamically. This harmonious synthesis of image, ornament, and type defined the signature 'Lyonnese Style', which was eagerly imitated across print shops in Frankfurt, Geneva, Antwerp, Venice, and Strasbourg.Beyond the realm of paper and ink, Bernard Salomon’s designs exercised a monumental influence on the decorative and decorative arts of the European Renaissance. His compositions were immediately seized upon as primary source material by master artisans working in diverse media. The enamelers of Limoges (such as Pierre Courteys and the Limosin family) transcribed Salomon’s Ovidian and Biblical woodcuts directly onto polychrome and grisaille enamel plates and ewers. Similarly, majolica painters in Urbino and Faenza, woodcarvers crafting cabinet furniture, tapestry weavers in Flanders, and damascene armorers across Northern Europe utilized Salomon’s prints as master pattern books. Though Salomon died around 1561—likely falling victim to the catastrophic plague epidemic that devastated Lyon or the early religious conflicts that engulfed the city on the eve of the French Wars of Religion—his artistic legacy endured long after his death. His work bridged the gap between Italian high style and Northern European graphic arts, leaving an indelible mark on book design, Mannerist iconography, and the history of visual culture.

academic_description: 16mo (122x70 mm). 375, [9] pp. Collation: a-z8 A8. Greek portion of title romanized. Greek and Latin text in parallel columns from p. 3 to p. 279, on opposite pages from p. 280 to p. 375. Woodcut printer’s device on title page and prism device to verso of otherwise blank final leaf. With 40 woodcut illustrations in text illustrating the fables of Aesopus, of which 37 are ascribed to Bernard Salomon and 3 (fables 46, 100, 118) are repeated from Tournes edition of La Perrière’s Theatre des bons engines (1545). Woodcut head- and tail-pieces and decorative initials. Early 17th-century blind-stamped panelled calf, spine in compartments, covers with fleur-de-lys centre-pieces, central panel with floral corner-pieces, blue (faded) edges (joints, spine ends, and corners partly skillfully restored). Later ink underlining and occasional marginalia in Greek and Latin (the latter mostly at end, including more extensive notes around prism device). Small restoration to lower margin of title, some occasional spotting and marginal staining, slightly browned, all in all a very good, genuine copy, nicely bound and with a strong impression of the woodcuts. First de Tournes edition in Greek and Latin, edited by Adam Knopff (cf. Typographus Lectori, p. [382]), of Aesop’s fables. A second edition, with sixty-one woodcuts and the addition of the fables of Avianus, was issued by De Tournes in 1570 (cf. R. Brun, Le livre français illustré de la Renaissance, Paris, 1969, pp. 77-81 and 184).The volume also includes the Aesopi fabulatoris vita (pp. 7-118) by Maximus Planudes (c. 1260-1330), the fables (Fabellae) by Babrius or Gabrias (2nd cent.), the Batrachomiomachia by Homerus (8th cent. BC), and the Galeomyomachia by Theodorus Prodromus (12th cent.).

title: Saggio filosofico e critico sulli giuochi di azzardo
academic_description: 8vo (205x 127 mm). VIII, 232, [4] pp. The first leaf, a blank, is included in the pagination. The name of the printer can be found in the printing license at the end of the volume. Typographic ornament on the title page. Decorative head- and tailpieces. Contemporary half calf, gilt spine with lettering piece, marbled boards, sprinkled edges (some minor restoration to spine and corners). On the title page manuscript initials “N.C.”. Contemporary manuscript note at p. 39. Some scattered foxing due to the quality of the paper, all in all a good, genuine copy. Rare first edition, dedicated by the author to John Acton (1736-1811), commander of the navy of the Kingdom of Naples, of this work dealing with gambling from every possible angle: mathematical, statistical, ethical, economical, legal, psychological, and social.In 1790, at the age of twenty-five, Francesco Bernardino Cicala published in Naples the Saggio filosofico e critico sulli giuochi di azzardo, echoing in its title another work on the same subject by P.R. Montmort (Essai d’analyses sure les jeux de hazard, Paris, 1708). The treatise is not a mere examination of mathematical operations, but a series of insights on gambling interpreted in the context of human action and from a historical perspective. The author does not hide his personal involvement, having personally known the gambling tables. His personal experience acquires, however, through introspective analyses a public dimension. Indeed, the self-inquiry broadens to include groups, social classes and the entire nation. Gambling is investigated not only as an individual issue, but also in its collective dimension. The spreading of gambling is seen as a political problem to be dealt with through the critical lenses of the rationalist culture of the Enlightenment.The Saggio consists of two sections, each comprising eight chapters: Human Sensibility, The Passion for the Game, Moral Effects, Consequences, Vicious Habits, Address to the Beautiful Sex, Time, its Use and Abuse, Physical Effects, Origins, Subject of Disputes, Matter of Calculation, Political Aims, Theory of Justice, Legislation, Law of Proscription, Linguet on Examination.In addition to the usual classical and Christian authors, quotations from French, German and English thinkers are particularly numerous in the work: J. De la Bruyère, F. de la Rochefoucauld, H. Grotius, Cl.-A. Helvetius, S. Pufendorf, Ch.-L. Montesquieu, D. Diderot, F.-M. Voltaire, J.J. Rousseau, P.L. Maupertuis, É. Condillac, J. Locke, and W. Balckstone. Significant are also the references to Italian Enlightenment philosophers like A. Genovesi, G. Filangieri and C. Beccaria, remembered for his article on gambling published in the journal “Il Caffè”.In describing the physical effects of gambling, Cicala achieves a remarkable effectiveness by using with confidence his medical knowledge of the functioning of the human organism. Ethical-philosophical reflections, on the other hand, intersect with mathematical theories and the calculus of probability. Cicala is well aware of the latest scientific-mathematical achievements in this field, and quotes Montmort, Bernoulli and Moivre.Cicala also does not forget the role of women in gambling, providing an in-depth analysis of individual male and female behaviors. For Cicala gambling concerns both sexes, but he feels the need to directly addresses the female audience traditionally excluded from the debate of ideas. Concluding his analysis, Cicala also assesses the positive and recreational aspects of gambling if practiced in moderation, considering gambling as permissible when it creates healthy conditions of recreation and sociability that are positive both for the individual and the community (cf. E. Filieri, Francesco Bernardino Cicala 1765-1815, tra passione e ragione: il gioco d’azzardo nella pubblica armonia, in: “Il Canone e la Biblioteca, costruzioni e decostruzioni della tradizione letteraria italiana”, A. Quondam, ed., Rome, 2002, II, pp. 353-360).When he wrote the present work, Cicala was a young man of 25, living in Naples at a time when gambling was a defining moment in society life. He had been for years very sensitive to both social gatherings and the passion for gambling. When he wrote the essay he had long avoided the now hated gambling tables: for him they had become only places to stay away from, because they evoked in him atmospheres and memories of a pathology that were still too vivid in his memory. It is precisely this pathology and the states of mind associated with it that Cicala analyzes in detail, with a particular attention to the interpersonal and social fallout of the gambler’s behaviors. Cicala is at the same time a man of his time and a forerunner of a knowledge that was not yet widespread scientific patrimony at his time. His interpretation of the compulsion for gambling is no more in moralistic terms, but rather in the broader framework of ethics, medicine and psychic introspection. He goes beyond his time by separating the cultural and social dimension of gambling from the individual dimension of the gambler (F.B. Cicala, Il gioco d’azzardo. Saggio filosofico e critico sulli giuochi di azzardo, G. Corrivetti & M.R. Pelizzari, eds., Cava de’ Tirreni, 2006, pp. 11-18).Francesco Bernardino Cicala, born in Lecce in 1765, began writing at a very young age. At 20 he had already composed two tragedies, Marcantonio in Egitto (which remained unpublished) and Gli Arsacidi, which was successfully performed in Naples, replicated in various Italian cities and first published in 1789. His tragedies also include Merope, La dinastia degli Eraclidi, Meride, Erode (remained unpublished), and Ermione, first performed in 1797 and published in 1798. Admitted, at only 22, to the Academy of Arcadia under the name Melindo Alitreo, at 27 he was accepted into the Royal Academy of Sciences and Fine Letters in Naples. He was also a member of the Accademia del Buon Gusto in Palermo and the Accademia dei Pastori Ereini-Imerei. Most of his poems and tragedies were published in the two volumes of the Opere (Lecce, 1814). In 1799 Cicala joined the Republic of Naples. When the Bourbons returned, he was imprisoned for two years, then forced to flee outside the kingdom. Returning home with the arrival of the Napoleonids, he settled in Lecce, where he died in 1815.

title: Epistolae

authors.name: Antiquari Jacopo
authors.biography: Jacopo was probably the son of the physician Stefano Antiquari. After studying under Giovanni Antonio Campano, who taught at Perugia from 1452 to 1459, he entered the service of the papal governor of that city, Giovanni Battista Savello, and accompanied him to Bologna when he was transferred there in 1468. In the early 1470s he moved to Milan, possibly on the invitation of Bartolomeo Caldo, secretary to duke Galeazzo Maria Sforza. Antiquari served as secretary to the dukes, with supervision over appointments to ecclesiastical benefices. He chose to remain at Milan even after the French removed Lodovico (il Moro) Sforza in 1500. Antiquari was a protector, adviser, and confidant of the greatest literary figures of his day, most notably Angelo Poliziano. He is mentioned in Erasmus’ Ciceronianus as one of the many writers who could not meet the exacting standards of the Ciceronians.

publishers.name: Bianchini Cosimo
publishers.biography: Printer from Verona who worked in Perugia, son of Bernardo. In 1497, the city of Perugia entrusted him with the task of caring for two lions donated to the city by Giampaolo Baglioni; from then on, he was nicknamed Bianchino del Leone. In Perugia, he had a home and workshop near the fish market and the church of St. Henry. He partnered with Girolamo Cartolari for a single edition. In addition to being a printer, he was a publisher, bookbinder, and creator of woodcuts. From 1527 to 1531, his output ceased. He may have died in 1544, although the names of his sons appear on the city’s payment documents as early as 1536. He was succeeded by his son Girolamo.

authors.name: Morata Olympia Fulvia
authors.biography: Olympia Fulvia Morata (1526–1555) stands as one of the most formidable intellectual figures of the sixteenth-century European Republic of Letters. A prodigy of Italian humanism, a pioneer of female classical scholarship, and an uncompromising voice of the Protestant Reformation, Morata embodied the dramatic convergence of Renaissance philology and transalpine evangelical theology. Operating at the intersection of the Ferrarese court of the Este dynasty and the radical printing houses of Basel and the Palatinate, her brief life captured both the zenith of Italian Renaissance learning and the tragic violence of early modern religious upheaval. Her surviving writings—comprising Latin and Greek dialogues, Greek psalm paraphrases, humanist declamations, and an expansive epistolary network spanning Europe—attest to an extraordinary intellectual synthesis that bridged classical antiquity, courtly humanism, and radical Reformation soteriology.Born in Ferrara in 1526, Olympia was raised in an environment saturated with humanistic rigor and political significance. She was the daughter of Fulvio Pellegrino Morato (Fulvius Peregrinus Moratus), a distinguished scholar of grammar, rhetoric, and classical literature who served as tutor to the young princes of the Este court, including Alfonso and Ercole d'Este. Pellegrino Morato was deeply embedded in the intellectual networks of Northern Italy, maintaining active correspondence with eminent humanists such as Celio Secondo Curione and Bembo. From her earliest childhood, Olympia demonstrated an extraordinary aptitude for classical philology. Her father personally directed her foundational studies in Latin grammar and syntax, instilling in her a deep devotion to Ciceronian rhetoric and classical poetry. The intellectual milieu of Ferrara during the 1530s was uniquely positioned to foster such precocity; under Duke Ercole II d'Este and his wife, Renée of France (Renata di Francia), the court of Ferrara became a vibrant nexus for intellectual experimentation and international diplomacy.In 1539, at approximately thirteen years of age, Morata's remarkable intellectual gifts earned her an invitation to enter the ducal court of Ferrara. She was appointed as the formal academic companion and tutor to the young Anna d'Este, the eldest daughter of Duke Ercole II and Renée of France (who would later marry François de Guise and subsequently Jacques de Savoie, Duke of Nemours). At court, Morata was afforded unprecedented access to the highest echelons of classical scholarship. Her education was placed under the supervision of the renowned German humanist brothers Johannes Sinapius (Johann Senf) and Kilian Sinapius (Chilianus Sinapius), who had been recruited to Ferrara to lecture on Greek language and medicine. Under their tutelage, alongside continued guidance from Celio Secondo Curione, Morata achieved absolute fluency in ancient Greek and Latin. By her mid-teens, she was delivering formal Latin lectures on Cicero’s Paradoxa Stoicorum, composing original Greek epigrams, and translating portions of Homer’s Iliad into Latin prose. Contemporary observers, including foreign ambassadors and visiting scholars, marveled at her capacity to debate complex philosophical problems in refined classical Latin, earning her recognition as a true virago literata and docta puella.The court of Renée of France was not merely a sanctuary for classical philology, but also the epicenter of evangelical dissent in Counter-Reformation Italy. Duchess Renée, the daughter of King Louis XII of France, maintained strong sympathies for the Reformation and transformed her Ferrarese household into an asylum for exiled French and Italian evangelicals. In 1536, John Calvin visited Ferrara under the pseudonym Charles d'Espeville, leaving an indelible imprint on the duchess's courtly circle, which also included the French poet Clément Marot and the reformer Bernardino Ochino. Morata’s exposure to this environment precipitated a profound internal spiritual metamorphosis. While her early youth had been dominated by the aesthetic and rhetorical ideals of classical pagan antiquity, her engagement with the writings of Martin Luther, Philip Melanchthon, and Calvin redirected her scholarly energies toward biblical exegesis and soteriology. Morata increasingly came to regard classical erudition not as an end in itself, but as a philological instrument to be consecrated to the understanding of Sacred Scripture and the defense of the doctrine of justification by faith alone (sola fide).This period of intellectual and spiritual maturity was soon disrupted by political and personal crises. In 1548, her father Fulvio Pellegrino Morato passed away. Concurrently, political pressure from the Roman Papacy and the Holy Office of the Inquisition intensified upon Duke Ercole II d'Este to purge his court of heresy. As Ercole II moved to suppress evangelical conventicles and curtail his wife’s Protestant network, Morata was compelled to leave the ducal court to care for her ailing mother, Lucrezia, and her younger siblings. Deprived of courtly patronage and facing growing suspicion from local inquisitorial authorities, her situation in Ferrara became increasingly precarious. However, during this period of distress, she met Andreas Grundler (Andreas Grundlerus), a young German physician, classicist, and committed Protestant from Schweinfurt in Franconia, who had come to the University of Ferrara to complete his medical doctorate. The two shared an intense intellectual and religious affinity and were married in late 1549 or early 1550.Fearing active persecution by the Inquisition in Northern Italy, Morata and Grundler resolved to flee across the Alps to the Holy Roman Empire in the summer of 1550, accompanied by Olympia's eight-year-old brother, Emilio Morato. Their journey into exile marked the beginning of a perilous transalpine odyssey. Upon arriving in Southern Germany, the couple sought refuge in Augsburg, where Morata’s reputation as a scholar preceded her. She was warmly received by prominent patricians and patrons of learning, including Johann Jakob Fugger and Antonius Fugger, as well as the humanist Bishop of Augsburg, Urbanus Rhegius's associates. Through these contacts, Grundler was offered a post as municipal physician in his hometown of Schweinfurt, an Imperial Free City in Franconia. Settling in Schweinfurt in late 1550, Morata devoted herself to intense study, translating the Psalms into elegant Greek verse, composing theological dialogues, and maintaining a vast epistolary network with leading figures of the Protestant Reformation, including Matthias Flacius Illyricus, Hieronymus Wolf, Hubert Languet, and her lifelong mentor Celio Secondo Curione, who was by then established in Basel.The violent realities of early modern European warfare shattered this brief period of academic tranquility. In 1553, the Imperial Free City of Schweinfurt became embroiled in the catastrophe of the Second Margrave War (Markgrafenkrieg). The mercenary armies of Albert Alcibiades, Margrave of Brandenburg-Kulmbach, occupied Schweinfurt and converted it into a military stronghold. Subsequently, the city was subjected to a brutal fourteen-month siege by the combined forces of the Bishop of Würzburg, the Duke of Brunswick, and the Elector of Saxony. Schweinfurt was subjected to continuous artillery bombardment, starvation, and a rampant outbreak of pestilence. Morata and her family were forced to live for months in underground cellars to escape the shellfire, during which time Grundler contracted severe epidemic fever. In June 1554, the besieging forces breached the city walls, plundered Schweinfurt, and set fire to the municipality. Morata and her husband escaped the burning city on foot, barefoot and destitute, having lost all their personal possessions, money, and—most devastatingly for Morata—her entire personal library and manuscript collection.Following their traumatic flight across Franconia, during which Grundler was briefly seized and held for ransom by rogue soldiers, the refugees found sanctuary in the territory of Count Erbach, who provided them with clothing, shelter, and medical care. News of their plight rapidly spread through the German scholarly community. Through the intervention of influential patrons and the recommendation of the Protestant Elector Palatine Frederick II (and subsequently Elector Otto Henry, or Ottheinrich), Grundler was appointed Professor of Medicine at the University of Heidelberg in late 1554. Recognizing Morata's phenomenal erudition, the university authorities and imperial administrators took the extraordinary step of offering her a formal academic appointment to deliver public lectures in Greek literature—a proposal almost unprecedented for a woman in sixteenth-century Europe. However, Morata’s physical constitution had been permanently shattered by the horrors of the siege of Schweinfurt and the subsequent flight. Suffering from severe pulmonary consumption (tuberculosis), she was unable to assume full lecturing duties, focusing instead on reconstructing her lost literary corpus from memory and draft letters.Olympia Fulvia Morata died in Heidelberg on October 26, 1555, at the age of twenty-nine. Her husband, Andreas Grundler, and her young brother, Emilio, succumbed to the plague only weeks later, in November 1555, and were buried beside her in the Church of St. Peter (Sankt Peter) in Heidelberg, where her funerary monument remains to this day. Prior to her death, aware of her impending end, Morata entrusted her remaining papers, dictate fragments, and reconstructed letters to her faithful friend and correspondent in Basel, Celio Secondo Curione, entreating him to collect and publish her literary legacy.Curione orchestrated a magnificent editorial crusade to immortalize Morata's life and intellectual achievements. Enlisting the printing press of Pietro Perna in Basel—the premier publishing house for Italian Protestant émigrés—Curione edited and released the first edition of her collected works in 1558 under the title Olympiae Fulviae Moratae Mulieris omnium eruditissimae Latina et Graeca, quae haberi potuerunt, Scripta. This monumental edition included her Latin and Greek dialogues, her Greek translation of the Psalms, her philosophical essays, her funeral orations, and her extensive correspondence with contemporary European intellectuals. The volume was dedicated to Queen Elizabeth I of England, framing Morata as an exemplar of Protestant female piety and supreme humanist learning. Perna’s press issued subsequent expanded and corrected editions in 1562, 1570, and 1580, ensuring the wide distribution of her writings throughout Transalpine Europe, England, and the Low Countries.The historical and critical significance of Olympia Fulvia Morata resides in her unique dual identity as a master of Renaissance classical philology and an articulate theologian of the Transalpine Reformation. In the history of women's writing, she represents a crucial transitional figure between the Quattrocento tradition of Italian female courtly humanists (such as Isotta Nogarola, Laura Cereta, and Cassandra Fedele) and the mid-sixteenth-century confessional polemicists of Protestant Europe. Her correspondence provides invaluable historiographical insight into the transalpine networks of refugee scholars, the internal political dynamics of the Ferrarese court, the reception of classical texts among early modern women, and the devastating human cost of the German wars of religion. Celebrated by her contemporaries as the "fourth Grace" and the "tenth Muse," Morata remains a titan of early modern intellectual history, whose erudition and tragic destiny continue to illuminate the complex intersections of gender, humanism, and religious reform in sixteenth-century Europe.

publishers.name: Perna Pietro
publishers.biography: Pietro Perna (c. 1519 – 16 August 1582) stands as one of the most seminal, audacious, and influential printer-publishers of the European High Renaissance and the Age of Confessionalization. Operating from the free imperial city of Basel during the second half of the sixteenth century, Perna transformed his typographical workshop into the vibrant epicenter of the radical Reformation, Italian evangelical exile literature, early modern political philosophy, and Paracelsian medical reform. Born in Villa Basilica, a small rural township within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Lucca, Perna belonged to that extraordinary generation of Italian intellectual emigrés—including Celio Secondo Curione, Bernardino Ochino, Lelio Sozzini, and Matteo Gribaldi—who fled the mounting repression of the Roman Inquisition to reshape the intellectual contours of Northern Europe. Through his press, marked by the iconic printer's emblem of the glowing lamp (Lucerna) bearing the motto Veritas filia temporis or Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, Perna acted as a crucial bridge between Italian Renaissance humanism and the Northern European Republic of Letters (Respublica literaria), pioneering the publication of heterodox theology, religious tolerance treatises, clandestine political philosophy, and revolutionary scientific texts.The formative years of Pietro Perna were deeply intertwined with the unique socio-religious and commercial milieu of sixteenth-century Lucca. The Lucchese Republic, famous for its thriving international silk trade and close commercial ties to Lyons, Antwerp, and Venice, served as a fertile breeding ground for evangelical ideas during the 1530s and 1540s. The presence of reform-minded humanists such as Peter Martyr Vermigli at the monastery of San Frediano and the circulation of heterodox texts by Juan de Valdés, Martin Bucer, and Philip Melanchthon profoundly impacted the young Perna. Raised in a family of modest background in Villa Basilica, Perna acquired early technical knowledge of commerce and manuscript culture before embracing the evangelical doctrines of justification by faith. However, following the formal reorganization of the Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Roman and Universal Inquisition by Pope Paul III in 1542 (via the bull Licet ab initio) and the subsequent crackdown on Lucchese heterodoxy, Perna was forced to abandon his homeland. By late 1544 or early 1545, he had crossed the Alps into Switzerland, seeking asylum in the Protestant canton of Basel, which had already established itself as a paramount center of international printing and humanist scholarship under the influence of Desiderius Erasmus, Johann Froben, and Johannes Oporinus.Upon his arrival in Basel, Perna systematically embedded himself within the city's academic and typographical ecosystem. In 1549, he officially matriculated at the University of Basel (Universitas Basiliensis), an institution that offered him both legal protection and direct access to an elite international network of scholars, philologists, and physicians. During his initial years in exile, Perna worked as a corrector, compositor, and commercial agent for established Basel printers, most notably Johannes Oporinus and Robert Winter. These apprenticeships provided him with invaluable technical mastery over Greek, Latin, and vernacular typography, as well as an intimate understanding of international book distribution networks centered around the semi-annual Frankfurt Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse). In 1558, having demonstrated financial independence and civic loyalty, Perna took the formal oath of citizenship in Basel and established his own independent printing shop. His workshop quickly became a sanctuary and operational hub for Italian religious refugees, humanists, and radical thinkers who found the rigid confessional orthodxies of both Roman Catholicism and Calvinist Geneva equally oppressive.Perna’s editorial program was defined by extraordinary intellectual bravery and an unyielding commitment to freedom of thought. At a time when Europe was dividing into rigid confessional camps, Perna served as the principal publisher for the proponents of religious toleration and radical anti-Trinitarianism. He worked in intimate collaboration with the Savoyard humanist Sebastian Castellio (Sébastien Châteillon), who had famously broken with John Calvin over the execution of Michael Servetus in 1553. Perna printed and clandestinely distributed key works by Castellio and his circle, promoting the radical idea that coercion in matters of faith was inherently un-Christian. Furthermore, Perna published the highly controversial Dialogi XXX (1563) by the former Capuchin vicar-general Bernardino Ochino. The publication of this work, which contained radical discussions on polygamy and the Trinity, ignited an international theological firestorm, leading to Ochino's banishment from Zurich and placing Perna under severe surveillance by the Basel municipal authorities (the Rat) and the university’s theological faculty.Beyond heterodox theology, Pietro Perna executed a monumental cultural operation by introducing the core masterpieces of Italian Renaissance political and historical thought to Northern Europe. Recognizing the profound European appetite for realistic statecraft, Perna undertook the publication of the works of Niccolò Machiavelli and Francesco Guicciardini. Because Machiavelli's writings had been placed on the papal Index Librorum Prohibitorum in 1559, Perna adopted ingenious editorial strategies. In 1560, he published the first Latin translation of Machiavelli's Il Principe (as Princeps) alongside the Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio, translated by the Italian humanist exile Silvestro Tegli. By rendering Machiavelli into Latin—the universal language of European scholarship—Perna detached the Florentine thinker from localized Italian politics and inaugurated the broader European debate over Machiavellianism, reason of state (ragione di Stato), and political realism. Similarly, Perna printed expansive, elegant editions of Guicciardini’s Storia d'Italia, providing Northern European intellectuals with an unvarnished analytical history of the Italian Wars and Renaissance diplomacy.Perna’s press was equally decisive in the history of science, philosophy, and medicine. He became the premier European publisher of the works of Paracelsus (Theophrastus von Hohenheim), playing a central role in the Paracelsian medical revolution of the late sixteenth century. Collaborating closely with the Basel physician and polymath Theodor Zwinger, as well as the French Paracelsian scholar Jacques Gohory (Leo Suavius) and Michael Toxites, Perna collected, edited, and published massive multi-volume Latin editions of Paracelsus’s medical, chirurgical, and alchemical treatises. These publications systematically converted Paracelsus's chaotic, obscure German manuscripts into structured Latin texts, allowing chemical medicine (iatrochemistry) to infiltrate university curricula across Europe. In the realm of philosophy, Perna printed seminal Renaissance Neoplatonic and Aristotelian works, including texts by Marsilio Ficino, Pietro Pomponazzi (notably his controversial De naturalium effectuum causis sive de incantationibus), and the contemporary Paduan Aristotelian Jacopo Zabarella, thereby bridging the Paduan natural philosophy tradition with Northern European academic circles.The operational reality of Perna's workshop was characterized by intense financial precariousness and constant geopolitical risk. Operating a major press required enormous capital investments in rag paper, high-quality metal type (Roman, Italic, and Greek fonts), ink, and labor. To fund his ambitious publication projects, Perna formed complex commercial partnerships with wealthy merchants and scholars, including the Basel physician Guglielmo Grataroli, the Polish nobleman Jan Łaski, and various Frankfurt financiers. His books were distributed across vast networks stretching from London, Antwerp, and Lyons to Venice, Kraków, and Transylvania. To evade regional censorship and book confiscations at imperial customs posts, Perna frequently resorted to pseudonymous imprints, fictitious publishing locations (such as claiming a book was printed in 'Palermo', 'Perna', or 'Utopia'), and secret distribution networks managed by trusted itinerant peddlers and student messengers.Throughout his career, Perna walked a treacherous tightrope between civic compliance and ideological defiance. He was repeatedly summoned before the Basel City Council and censors to face interrogation regarding illicit publications. In several instances, his books were impounded, and he faced heavy fines and brief periods of imprisonment. The orthodox Calvinist establishment in Geneva, led by Theodore Beza, repeatedly denounced Perna as a dangerous vector of heresy, atheism, and anti-Trinitarian subversion. Despite these relentless pressures, Perna maintained his press through astute diplomatic maneuvering, the protection of influential patrons within the Basel city governance, and his indispensable status as an economic engine for the city's book trade. His workshop remained active until his very last days.Pietro Perna died in Basel on 16 August 1582, during an outbreak of the plague, and was buried in the cemetery of Saint Peters Church (Peterskirche). Following his death, his son-in-law, the printer Konrad Waldkirch, took over management of the press, continuing to publish heterodox and philosophical literature using Perna’s typographical stock. Today, Perna is recognized by historians of the book, the Reformation, and early modern philosophy as a pivotal historical figure. He was not merely a mechanical printer, but a true intellectual impresario whose editorial vision preserved the most radical currents of Italian humanism and provided the structural foundation for the European Enlightenment’s commitment to religious toleration, empirical science, and political realism.

related_names.name: Celio Secondo Curione
related_names.biography: Celio Secondo Curione (1503–1569) stands as one of the most compelling, multifaceted, and intellectually audacious figures of the Italian Renaissance and the European Reformation. A classicist of extraordinary philological erudition, an unyielding religious dissident, a bold satirist, and an influential educator, Curione embodied the tragic yet vibrant phenomenon of the Italian evangelical exile (*fuoruscitismo*). Situated at the turbulent crossroads where Erasmian humanism collided with Protestant theology and radical free-thought, Curione traversed the major intellectual capitals of northern Italy before fleeing across the Alps to escape the clutches of the Roman Inquisition. In his mature years as Professor of Rhetoric at the University of Basel, he transformed the Rhine metropolis into a sanctuary for heterodox scholarship, challenging both Catholic dogma and Calvinist orthodoxy with his expansive, almost universalist conception of divine grace. His career encapsulates the heroic efforts of sixteenth-century scholars who sought to reconcile classical *humanitas* with evangelical faith in an era increasingly defined by confessional dogmatism and inquisitorial violence.Born on May 1, 1503, in Ciriè, a small town near Turin in the Duchy of Savoy, Celio Secondo was the twenty-third child of Jacomino Curione, a nobleman and high-ranking administrator in the Savoyard court, and Charlotte de Montrotier, a noblewoman of French origin. Tragically orphaned of both parents by the age of nine, the young Celio was entrusted to the care of his older siblings and relatives in Turin. He received a rigorous humanist education at the University of Turin, where he immersed himself in classical philology, rhetoric, and jurisprudence under the guidance of renowned masters such as Giorgio Coassolo and Giovanni Cervi. It was during these formative years in Turin that Curione encountered the radical religious currents sweeping across Western Europe. A crucial turning point occurred when he inherited a magnificent, illuminated manuscript Bible from his father, alongside an early copy of Agostino Steuco's commentary and the early reformist writings of Desiderius Erasmus, Martin Luther, and Philip Melanchthon. Inspired by these texts, the young scholar formed an evangelical study circle with his close friends, Giacomo della Manta and Francesco della Rovere. Driven by a fervent desire to witness the German Reformation firsthand, the trio set out for Germany around 1520, but their youthful zeal led to their arrest by order of the Bishop of Turin, Bonifacio Ferrero. Imprisoned in the Benedictine Abbey of San Benigno Canavese, Curione executed a daring and emblematic escape: he managed to break open the abbey's reliquary, removed the sacred bones of Saints Agapitus and Tiburtius, and replaced them with a copy of the Holy Scriptures inscribed with a message urging the monks to venerate the Word of God rather than dead bones. This dramatic act of defiance marked the permanent rupture between Curione and the traditional ecclesiastical structure.Following his escape, Curione sought refuge in Milan, where he dedicated himself to teaching humanities and providing charitable relief during the devastating plague of 1530. It was in Milan that he married Margherita Bianca Isachi of Monferrato, a woman of noble lineage who would remain his steadfast companion throughout decades of exile and hardship. For the next decade, Curione led the precarious life of an itinerant humanist professor, moving between the vibrant academic centers of northern Italy. In Casale Monferrato and Pavia, his lectures on Cicero, Virgil, and classical rhetoric attracted enormous audiences of enthusiastic students. At the University of Pavia, where he was appointed to the chair of eloquence, his openly evangelical readings of sacred and profane texts alarmed the local Dominican inquisitors. When officers were dispatched to arrest him, the university students formed a physical shield around their beloved professor, driving the papal delegates out of the city. Nevertheless, as the climate of religious tolerance rapidly deteriorated in the Italian peninsula, Curione was forced to flee once again. He found temporary asylum in Venice, the capital of print and intellectual liberty, and subsequently in Ferrara, where he was warmly received at the court of Duchess Renée of France, a celebrated patroness of evangelical refugees and Calvinist sympathizers. By 1541, Curione had moved to Lucca, joining the brilliant circle of humanist reformers gathered around Peter Martyr Vermigli at the *Studio Lucchese*, which included scholars like Girolamo Zanchi and Immanuel Tremellius. However, the promulgation of the papal bull Licet ab initio in July 1542 by Pope Paul III, which established the Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Roman Inquisition, shattered the evangelical networks of Italy. Warned of an imminent warrant for his execution, Curione narrowly escaped an inquisitorial ambush in Lucca and fled across the Alps to Switzerland, leaving behind his native land forever.Arriving in the Swiss Confederation, Curione settled initially in Lausanne, where, through the recommendation of Heinrich Bullinger and Pierre Viret, he was appointed rector of the Latin College (*Collège de Lausanne*) in 1542. His pedagogical talent quickly earned him widespread acclaim across the Helvetic cantons. In 1546, he accepted a prestigious invitation from the magistracy and university senate of Basel to occupy the Chair of Rhetoric and Classics at the University of Basel—a position he would hold with distinction for nearly twenty-four years until his death. Basel was at that time the capital of European humanist publishing, a refuge for religious dissidents, and a melting pot of radical theological debate. In Basel, Curione became the central figure of an international intellectual network that spanned from England to Poland and from Italy to Transylvania. He maintained an extensive correspondence with leading scholars and monarchs, including Queen Elizabeth I of England (to whom he dedicated several of his works), Philip Melanchthon, Sebastian Castellio, Lelio Sozzini, and Theodor Bibliander. Unlike many of his fellow exiles who conformed strictly to the magisterial Calvinism of Geneva or the Zwinglianism of Zurich, Curione preserved an independent, highly critical theological stance. He aligned himself closely with Sebastian Castellio in opposing the execution of Michael Servetus in 1553, fiercely advocating for religious liberty, liberty of conscience, and the complete abolition of capital punishment for heresy.Curione’s theological output was deeply interwoven with his philological mastery. In 1544, he published anonymously his celebrated satirical dialogue, Pasquillus Ecstaticus (The Ecstatic Pasquin), a scathing attack on the papacy, the monastic orders, and the corruptions of the Roman Curia. Written in the tradition of Lucian and Erasmus, the work described a visionary journey through the heavens, exposing the papal hierarchy as a tyrannical engine of spiritual deception. The book became an immediate European bestseller, translated into German, English, and French, and solidified Curione’s reputation as an uncompromising polemicist. However, his most profound and controversial theological work was published in Basel in 1554: De Amplitudine Beati Regni Dei Dialogi IIII (Four Dialogues on the Vast Extent of God’s Blessed Kingdom). Dedicated to King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, this masterpiece challenged the dominant Augustinian and Calvinist doctrines of double predestination and the narrow limitation of the elect. Drawing upon biblical exegesis, classical philosophy, and Hermetic traditions, Curione argued that God’s infinite mercy, love, and redemption far exceed His wrath. He asserted that the number of the saved throughout human history—including righteous pagans, infants, and those who had never heard the Christian Gospel—would vastly outnumber the damned. This vision of an overwhelmingly victorious divine kingdom bordered on universal reconciliation (*apokatastasis*) and sent shockwaves through the Reformed establishment. John Calvin and Theodore Beza condemned the work as a dangerous heresy that undermined ecclesiastical discipline, while the Basel city council subjected Curione to rigorous interrogation, narrowly refraining from banning him from the university due to his immense international prestige and the intervention of his academic colleagues.Beyond his theological writings, Curione made monumental contributions to print culture and classical scholarship as a literary editor, lexicographer, and press supervisor. Working in intimate partnership with Basel’s greatest printer-publishers—most notably Johannes Oporinus and the fellow Lucchese exile Pietro Perna—Curione orchestrated the publication of an astonishing array of classical, historical, and pedagogical texts. He produced landmark critical editions and commentaries on the works of Cicero (including the *Orator* and *De Officiis*), Sallust, Tacitus, Seneca, Juvenal, and Aristotle’s *Rhetoric*. His massive three-volume lexicographical work, Forum Romanum (1561), became an indispensable reference tool for Latinists across Western Europe for generations. Furthermore, Curione played a pivotal role in disseminating contemporary historical and political knowledge: he translated and published the history of the Portuguese discoveries in the Indies by Manuel I, edited Francesco Guicciardini's *Storia d'Italia*, and composed De Bello Melitensi Historia (1567), an eyewitness-based chronicle of the Siege of Malta. His home in Basel functioned as a vibrant academy and salon where students, foreign diplomats, itinerant scholars, and printers gathered to discuss literature, philosophy, and theology free from the constraints of confessional dogmatism.Celio Secondo Curione passed away in Basel on November 24, 1569, succumbing to an epidemic fever alongside several of his children, and was buried in the cloister of the Basel Minster (*Münster*). His legacy is vast and complex. In the historiography of the Reformation, as outlined by scholars such as Delio Cantimori, Antonio Rotondò, and Valerio Marchetti, Curione occupies a monumental position as a bridge between Italian Renaissance humanism and early modern European freethought. He refused to replace Roman Catholic dogmatism with a Protestant equivalent, instead championing an open, tolerant, and rationalist reading of Christian revelation. His bold defense of the infinite scope of divine salvation in *De Amplitudine* laid intellectual foundations that would later nourish Arminianism, Socinianism, the Enlightenment critique of confessional dogma, and modern religious liberalism. As an editor and educator, his meticulous editions of classical texts and his pedagogical treatises helped shape the humanist curriculum of Northern Europe. Celio Secondo Curione remains an enduring symbol of the triumph of humanistic inquiry, intellectual courage, and spiritual freedom over the forces of tyranny and intolerance.

With Morata's epitaph by Johannes Herold within a full-page woodcut border. 18th century calf with gilt fillets and floreal ornaments on the panels, gilt back and edges, marbled endpapers. With the book-plates of the French linguist and book-collector Pierre-Alexandre Gratet-Duplessis (1792-1853) and of the architect Jules-Édouard Potier de la Morandière (1813-1905).Second, greatly enlarged edition, published by the Italian emigrant scholar Celio Secondo Curione (1503-1569) with a new dedication to Queen Elizabeth of England, dated Basel, September 1, 1562.The first edition was published in 1558 and contained thirty letters by and to Morata as well as some letters by others. In the present edition the number of letters was raised to 74, of which 50 were by Morata, 14 to her and 10 by others. In the third edition (1570), which was reprinted in 1580, two Italian letters by Morata were added.The volume contains furthermore a declamation on Cicero's Stoic Paradoxes and another In Praise of Mutius Scaevola (the latter in both Greek and Latin), a Latin translation of the first two stories of Boccaccio's Decameron,two dialogues in Latin, eleven poems (eight in Greek and three in Latin), and the translation into Greek of seven Psalms, as well as several poems in Greek and Latin in her praise and some epitaphs (cf. O.F. Morata, Briefe, R. Kössling, ed., Leipzig, 1990, pp. 215-216).At the end of the volume is printed the famous letter in form of an elegy variously attributed to Ippolita Torelli (1499-1520), wife of Baldassarre Castiglione, who was one of the most influential representatives of courtly culture in Italy and author of the Courtier (1528). This poem was first included in his Latin poetry as by himself. It was written in 1518, when Baldassarre was ambassador to the Gonzaga at Rome. In it she laments his absence from home and calls his attention to the dangers of the court of Leo X. She mentions as a great comfort the portrait Raphael had painted of him. Added is also her epitaph by Pietro Bembo, which is found on her tomb in the Santuario delle Grazie near Mantua (cf. J.D. Falvo, The Economy of Human Relations: Castiglione's ‘Libro del Cortegiano', New York, 1992, pp. 159-166).“Es ist eine bunte Vielfalt von Begegnungen und Verbindungen zwischen italienischen sowie deutschen und in einem Falle auch schweizerischen Gelehrten, die sich in Olympia Moratas Korrespondenz widerspiegelt. Diese gründete im wesentlichen auf der Gemeinsamkeit Renaissance-humanistischer Bildung und - mehr oder weniger ausgeprägt - auf reformatorischer Glaubenshaltung. Möglicherweise hatte der deutsche Dichter Goethe auch diese Kontakte im Blick, als er unter dem 30. Januar 1828 in seinem Tagebuch notierte: ‘Las in den Briefen der Olympia Fulvia Morata, und es ging mir über den eigentlichen, damaligen, protestantischen Zustand ein ganz neues Licht auf. Meine Bemerkungen denke niederzuschreiben' ” (R. Kössling, Die Korrespondenz der Olympia Fulvia Morata (1526-1555) als Dokument italo-deutscher Begegnungen, in: “Acta Conventus Neo-Latini Bariensis”, Tempe, AZ, 1998, p. 377).Celio Secondo Curione was born the youngest of twenty three children in Moncalieri in the province of Turin. He first studied law and humanities at Turin and continued his studies in Milan, where he also started to teach in 1528. He became more and more interested in the writings of the German reformers. He taught at Pavia and Venice, where he met Bernardino Ochino. He lived for a short time at the court of Ferrara and in Lucca. After several narrow escapes from the Inquisition he fled to Switzerland via the Grisons where he met with Camillo Renato, an Antitrinitarian, and became rector of the newly founded University of Lausanne in 1542. In 1546 he went to Basel, where he taught ancient classics at the University until his death. He gained a wide reputation and attracted many students coming from foreign countries. He declined invitations by the Pope to Rome, by the Duke of Savoy to Turin, from the Emperor to the University of Vienna, and from the prince of Transylvania to the new college established at Alba Julia. He was not a confessed theologian, nevertheless he wrote a treatise Christianae religionis institutio (1549), from which he omitted any mention of the Trinity or the deity of Christ as a doctrine necessary for salvation. In 1550 he attended the Anabaptist Council at Venice and in 1554 wrote a work dedicated to the Polish king, De amplitudine beati regni Dei, in which he opposed Calvin's doctrine of predestination. He was accused by Vergerio in 1559 of heresy, but was exonerated by the University of Basel. Curione was very careful not to commit himself to any compromising doctrinal position, nevertheless his writings and his association with Castellio, Ochino, and Lelio Sozzini make him one of the precursors of the Unitarian-Socinian movement (cf.
