authors.name: Erasmus Desiderius
authors.biography: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (born c. 27 October 1466 in Rotterdam, County of Holland; died 12 July 1536 in Basel, Swiss Confederacy) stands as the undisputed Princeps Humanistarum ("Prince of the Humanists") and the towering intellectual titan of the Northern Renaissance. Operating at the luminous crossroads where classical philology intersected with Christian theology, Erasmus redefined early modern European intellectual culture. Through an unprecedented mastery of Latin and Greek classical literature, paired with a relentless dedication to textual criticism, he forged an intellectual movement known as Christian Humanism. This paradigm sought to revitalize Western Christendom by stripping away medieval scholastic accretions and returning directly to the pristine sources of classical antiquity (bonae litterae) and the early Church Fathers (ad fontes). In an era fractured by religious dogmatism, dynastic conflict, and institutional corruption, Erasmus established himself as the supreme architect of the Respublica Literaria (the Republic of Letters)—a transnational, irenic community of scholars bound by erudition, moral philosophy, and open correspondence. His extraordinary literary output, disseminated through the revolutionary technology of the printing press, exercised an indelible influence on European biblical scholarship, educational reform, satire, and political theory.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationThe circumstance of Erasmus's birth was shadowed by social illegitimacy, a condition that deeply impacted his psychological development and legal standing throughout his early life. Born Desiderius Erasmus—the name Desiderius being a humanistic Latin addition he later adopted—he was the second illegitimate son of Gerard, a Catholic priest from Gouda, and Margaretha Rogerius, a physician's daughter from Zevenbergen. Despite the canonical stigma of his birth, his parents ensured he received a rigorous education. Around 1475, Erasmus was sent to the Latin school of St. Lebuin's in Deventer, an institution governed by the chapter of St. Lebuin's and profoundly influenced by the Devotio Moderna—a religious movement emphasizing personal piety, meditative reading, and practical Christian ethics. Under the headmastership of the pioneering humanist Alexander Hegius (c. 1433–1498), a pupil of Rudolf Agricola, the school curriculum began incorporating Greek and classical Latin, exposing the young Erasmus to genuine Renaissance humanism.The tragic deaths of both his parents to the bubonic plague around 1483 disrupted Erasmus's formal studies. Placed under the care of guardians who squandered his modest inheritance, he was pressured into entering a religious order. In 1487, Erasmus took his vows as a Canon Regular of St. Augustine at the monastery of Emmaus at Steyn, near Gouda. Though he harbored a lifelong disdain for monastic asceticism, formal rituals, and the intellectual isolation of the cloister, Steyn provided him with invaluable access to an extensive library of classical authors, including Cicero, Terence, Ovid, and the early Church Fathers, particularly Saint Jerome. On 25 April 1492, Erasmus was ordained to the priesthood by the Bishop of Utrecht. Recognizing his brilliant Latinity, Henri de Bergues, Bishop of Cambrai, appointed Erasmus as his Latin secretary in 1493, liberating the young monk from the confines of the monastery and granting him dispensation to travel across Europe.Securing permission from the Bishop of Cambrai to pursue formal theological studies, Erasmus matriculated at the University of Paris in 1495, residing at the austere Collège de Montaigu under the principalship of the strict reformer Jan Standonck. Erasmus found the dominant scholastic theology of Paris—dominated by Scotist dialectics, pedantic disputations, and rigid syllogisms—profoundly repellent. He famously caricatured the scholastic doctors as pedants lost in abstract hair-splitting while remaining blind to the ethical essence of the Gospel. In Paris, to supplement his meager income, Erasmus began working as a private tutor for wealthy foreign students, including the young English noble William Blount, 4th Baron Mountjoy. It was through Mountjoy that Erasmus made his epochal first visit to England in the summer of 1499, an journey that would fundamentally alter the trajectory of his intellectual mission.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksIn England, Erasmus was welcomed into the luminous intellectual circle centered around Oxford and London. He established deep, lifelong friendships with the theologian John Colet (later Dean of St. Paul's), the lawyer and humanist Thomas More, and the scholars William Grocyn and Thomas Linacre. Colet's contextual, historical-grammatical lectures on the Epistles of St. Paul inspired Erasmus to abandon pure secular poetry and turn his philological acumen toward biblical studies. Realizing that a true restoration of theology required direct access to the original Greek text of the New Testament, Erasmus devoted the following decade to mastering the Greek language with obsessive discipline.Erasmus's literary career exploded in the early 16th century with a series of works that transformed European literature. In 1500, he published his Adagiorum Collectanea (printed in Paris by Johann Philippi), a modest collection of 818 Latin proverbs extracted from classical authors, accompanied by brief commentary. This work was designed as a practical handbook for scholars seeking to cultivate elegant Latin style. Over the next three decades, as Erasmus gathered new classical manuscripts across Europe, the collection expanded exponentially into the Adagiorum Chiliades (first definitive edition published by Aldus Manutius in Venice, 1508), containing over 4,000 adages accompanied by extensive essays on politics, war, philosophy, and social critique. Proverbs such as Dulce bellum inexpertis ("War is sweet to those who have not experienced it") and Festina lente ("Make haste slowly") became sweeping humanist treatises condemning warmongering princes and tyranny.In 1503 (dated 1504), while residing in the Low Countries, Erasmus published the Enchiridion Militis Christiani (Handbook of the Christian Soldier). Written as a manual of lay piety, the Enchiridion articulated Erasmus's central religious concept: the Philosophia Christi (the Philosophy of Christ). He argued that true Christianity did not consist in external rituals, pilgrimages, fasting, or the veneration of relics, but in the internal transformation of the heart through love, humility, and the direct imitation of Christ's life as revealed in Scripture. This work served as a manifesto for the spiritual democratization of the Laity.During his return journey from Italy to England in 1509, while crossing the Alps and staying at the London home of Thomas More, Erasmus composed his most famous masterpiece of satirical literature: Moriae Encomium (In Praise of Folly, published in Paris by Gilles de Gourmont in 1511). Written in the voice of Folly (Moria) personified, the work is a brilliant double-entendre that parodies every stratum of Renaissance society. Folly begins by lightheartedly claiming that human life would be impossible without her gifts of illusion, self-love, and passion. However, the satire gradually deepens into a scathing indictment of corrupt popes, worldly cardinals, superstitious monks, autocratic princes, and arrogant scholastic theologians. In the final, visionary section of the book, Erasmus shifts tone entirely, presenting true Christian faith as a holy, ecstatic "folly" that defies worldly logic—a divine foolishness rooted in the self-sacrificial love of the Cross.The pinnacle of Erasmus's scholarly achievement arrived in February 1516 with the publication of the Novum Instrumentum omne by the Basel publisher Johann Froben. This monumental work presented, for the first time in print, the complete Greek text of the New Testament, established from a synthesis of late Byzantine manuscripts, accompanied by Erasmus's original, elegant Latin translation—which corrected over a thousand mistranslations in the venerable Vulgate—and extensive critical Annotationes. Accompanied by his methodological essays, the Paraclesis and the Ratio verae theologiae, Erasmus urged that Scripture be translated into every vernacular language so that "the farmer might sing snippets of them at the plow, the weaver hum them to the movement of his shuttle." Erasmus's Greek New Testament served as the textual foundation for Martin Luther's German translation of the Bible (the September Testament of 1522) and William Tyndale's English New Testament (1526), thereby unwittingly laying the philological dynamite that would shatter the medieval Western Church.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationErasmus was the first European intellectual to fully understand, master, and exploit the transformative power of the print media. He was not merely an author; he was an editor, textual critic, proofreader, and publishing strategist who worked in intimate collaboration with the greatest printing houses of the Renaissance. The circulation of his works achieved numbers hitherto unimaginable in Western history, with hundreds of thousands of copies of his treatises, schoolbooks, and translations circulating across the continent.During his early Parisian period, Erasmus published primarily with Josse Bade (Jodocus Badius Ascensius), whose press at the sign of the Praelum Ascensianum became a hub of humanist printing. However, Erasmus's typographic trajectory reached an artistic turning point during his Italian journey (1506–1509). In 1507, Erasmus traveled to Venice to collaborate directly with the legendary master printer Aldus Manutius (Aldo Manuzio). For nearly ten months in 1508, Erasmus lived in the household of Aldus, sharing a room with the Greek scholar Marcus Musurus. Working within the environment of the Aldine Neacademy, Erasmus revised and vastly expanded the Adagia. The resulting 1508 Aldine folio edition of the Adagiorum Chiliades was a typographic masterpiece, set in Aldus's famous cursive italic types and utilizing rare Greek manuscripts from the library of Cardinal Bessarion. The Aldine anchor-and-dolphin device became inextricably linked with Erasmian erudition.From 1514 until his death in 1536, Erasmus's primary publishing sanctuary was Basel, centered around the printshop of Johann Froben (Froben Press). Froben's workshop, which employed master artists such as Hans Holbein the Younger for woodcut title pages, borders, and initials, became the physical engine of the Erasmian enterprise. Erasmus took up physical residence in Basel, serving effectively as Froben's editorial director and literary advisor. Together, Erasmus and Froben produced a magnificent series of monumental folio editions of the early Church Fathers: Saint Jerome (9 volumes, 1516), Cyprian (1520), Arnobius (1522), Hilary of Poitiers (1523), Irenaeus (1526), Ambrose (1527), Augustine (10 volumes, 1528–1529), and John Chrysostom (1530). These editions represented a revolution in scholarly typography, featuring clear Roman types, systematic paragraphing, marginal glosses, and comprehensive thematic indexes.Erasmus also revolutionized European pedagogy through his educational textbooks, printed in vast press-runs across Paris, Strasbourg (by Matthias Schürer), Cologne, and Antwerp. His De Duplici Copia Verborum ac Rerum (1512), commissioned by John Colet for St. Paul's School, taught students how to cultivate rhetorical abundance. His Colloquia Familiaria (Familiar Colloquies), which began as simple Latin dialogue exercises in 1518, evolved through dozens of expanded editions into a masterwork of social commentary, dramatizing contemporary life, gender roles, religious hypocrisy, and moral philosophy through vivid, conversational Latin.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyThe outbreak of the Protestant Reformation following Martin Luther's 95 Theses in 1517 placed Erasmus in an increasingly perilous intellectual position. Initially, Erasmus sympathized with Luther's critiques of papal indulgences, clerical corruption, and ceremonialism, writing letters to high church officials pleading for moderation and reform. Consequently, ultra-conservative Catholic theologians, particularly the faculty of theology at the University of Paris (the Sorbonne) led by Noël Béda, and the Spanish Inquisition accused Erasmus of laying the intellectual foundations for the schism, coining the famous adage: "Erasmus layd the egge, and Luther hatched it."However, Erasmus steadfastly refused to align himself with the Lutheran movement, deeply dreading the destruction of Christian unity, civil disorder, and the rise of a new form of religious dogmatism that he feared would destroy bonae litterae. As Luther grew increasingly radical, rejecting papal authority and the Catholic sacramental system, the pressure on Erasmus from popes, emperors, and Catholic princes to write against Luther became overwhelming. In September 1524, Erasmus published his theological manifesto on human agency: De Libero Arbitrio DIA-TRIBE sive Collatio (On Free Will). Utilizing a measured, skeptical-probabilist methodology, Erasmus defended the freedom of the human will to cooperate with divine grace in the process of salvation, drawing upon scriptural texts and patristic consensus.Luther responded in late 1525 with his ferocious, uncompromising treatise De Servo Arbitrio (On the Bondage of the Will), in which he asserted total divine predestination, denied human free will in salvation, and denounced Erasmus as a worldly Lucianist who preferred peace and human philosophy to divine truth. Erasmus replied with the two-part Hyperaspistes (1526–1527), but the rift between the humanist irenicist and the Protestant reformer was absolute. Erasmus found himself trapped in a tragic middle ground: condemned by Protestants as a cowardly traitor who shrank from the implications of his own scholarship, and denounced by Catholic zealots as a dangerous heretic.When the Protestant Reformation conquered Basel under the leadership of Johannes Oecolampadius in 1529, Erasmus packed his library and moved to the Catholic imperial city of Freiburg im Breisgau. He returned to Basel in 1535 to oversee the printing of his last major work, the Ecclesiastes (a massive treatise on the art of preaching), and died there on 12 July 1536. His final whispered words, according to tradition, were in his native Dutch: "Lieve God" ("Dear God"). He was buried with great honor in Basel Minster, despite remaining a Catholic priest in a Protestant city.The post-mortem reception of Erasmus was marked by severe censure from the Counter-Reformation Catholic Church. At the Council of Trent, his entire body of work was placed in the highest category of prohibition on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum issued by Pope Paul IV in 1559 and modified by Pope Pius IV in 1564. In Protestant lands, his works were mined for philological utility but often viewed with theological suspicion. It was not until the Enlightenment and the modern historiographical revolution—led by scholars such as Pierre Bayle, Wilhelm Dilthey, Pierre de Nolhac, Johan Huizinga, and Marcel Bataillon—that Erasmus was fully re-evaluated as the seminal progenitor of modern European liberalism, religious tolerance, historical-critical methodology, and irenic diplomacy. Today, Erasmus stands as an enduring monument to the power of humane learning, scholarly independence, and the unyielding pursuit of peace through reason.

publishers.name: Westheimer Bartholomaeus
publishers.biography: Bartholomäus Westheimer (latinized as Bartholomaeus Westhemerus or Westmerus; c. 1499 – c. 1567) stands as one of the pivotal, if frequently underappreciated, conduits of biblical humanism, Protestant hermeneutics, and typographic scholarship during the Northern Renaissance. Operating at the dynamic intersection of South German humanism, Basel’s golden age of print, and the institutionalization of the Protestant Reformation, Westheimer synthesized classical philology with patristic erudition. His comprehensive reference works—ranging from seminal concordances and lists of scriptural idioms to monumental harmonies reconciling biblical passages with the writings of the Early Church Fathers—exerted a profound, lasting influence on sixteenth-century homiletics, biblical exegesis, and pedagogical practice throughout the Holy Roman Empire, Switzerland, and the Republic of Letters.Born around 1499 in the imperial city of Pforzheim—the renowned incubator of German Renaissance humanism that also produced Johannes Reuchlin and Philipp Melanchthon—Westheimer was steeped from early youth in the linguae tres (Latin, Greek, and Hebrew). Pforzheim’s famed Latin school provided him with an rigorous grounding in classical rhetoric and grammar. Seeking advanced academic training, Westheimer matriculated at the University of Heidelberg around 1514–1515, completing his Bachelor of Arts in 1517. Heidelberg at this juncture was undergoing a decisive transformation, as traditional scholastic scholasticism gave way to the evangelical humanism sparked by Martin Luther’s Heidelberg Disputation (1518) and the circulating works of Erasmus of Rotterdam. Westheimer’s academic formation was defined by this shift, blending formal logical rigor with an urgent commitment to the recovery of primary sacred texts.Attracted by the vibrant intellectual climate of Basel—which had become the preeminent center of northern European publishing under the aegis of Johann Froben, Heinrich Petri, and Johannes Oporinus—Westheimer relocated to the Swiss city in the mid-1520s. There he entered the immediate orbit of the reformer Johannes Oecolampadius, the scholar Simon Grynaeus, and the humanist circle surrounding Erasmus. Basel provided the ideal atmosphere for Westheimer’s unique talents. Recognizing that the success of the Reformation depended as much on the meticulous quality of its printed texts as on theological dogma, Westheimer assumed the crucial role of corrector typographicus (scholarly proofreader and editor) for several of the city's premier printing houses, most notably those of Johann Herwagen (Heragius) and Johannes Bebel.In the early modern print shop, the scholarly corrector was far more than a technical proofreader; he was an active editor, collator of manuscript variants, and intellectual architect of the volume. Westheimer’s work in Herwagen’s press brought him into daily contact with complex Greek and Latin manuscripts, Old Testament Hebrew texts, and patristic codices. This intimate familiarity with printing typography and textual criticism directly informed his own literary production. Between 1530 and 1536, Westheimer compiled his first monumental work, the Phrases seu modi loquendi divinae scripturae, which was subsequently expanded into the masterwork titled Conciliatio Scripturae divinae et patrum orthodoxorum (first published in Basel, 1536). This ambitious compendium sought to demonstrate the foundational harmony between Protestant biblical interpretation and the testimony of the early Church Fathers, systematically arranging scripture passages Alongside parallel citations from Augustine, Jerome, John Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, and Gregory of Nazianzus.The publication of the Conciliatio established Westheimer as an authority on sacred rhetoric and patristic florilegia. Protestant theologians praised the work for providing preachers and scholars with an indispensable arsenal against Roman Catholic accusations of theological novelty, proving that evangelical doctrines regarding justification, grace, and the sacraments had deep roots in patristic antiquity. Westheimer followed this success with his Troporum, schematum, idiomatumque communium liber (Basel, 1561), a pioneering textbook of biblical rhetoric. In this work, Westheimer systematically classified the figurative language, tropes, allegories, and Hebraic idioms found throughout the Old and New Testaments. Grounded in the rhetorical theories of Quintilian and Melanchthon’s Elementa Rhetorica, Westheimer’s manual became a standard university and gymnasium textbook for decoding the stylistic nuances of the Latin Vulgate and the original biblical tongues.In addition to his hermeneutical dictionaries and concordances, Westheimer produced extensive original commentaries and annotations on large portions of the Old Testament. His biblical exegesis—including detailed volumes on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, the Book of Psalms, Daniel, and the Minor Prophets—focused on grammatical-historical exposition. Rejecting excessive medieval scholastic allegorization, Westheimer prioritized the literal-historical sense of the Hebrew text, while drawing upon Jewish commentators, classical philology, and early Christian historical contexts. Published in elegant folio and quarto editions by Basel's leading printers, these commentaries circulated widely across Protestant Europe, finding their way into the personal libraries of pastors, professors, and civic magistrates.Alongside his literary work in Basel, Westheimer maintained a dedicated career as a Protestant pastor and educator. In the 1540s, he accepted pastoral appointments in South Germany, serving as minister in Eppingen (1542–1546) and Bretten, before taking up ecclesiastical responsibilities in the Palatinate (Pfalz-Zweibrücken) and Nördlingen. His dual career as a rural/municipal pastor and an international scholarly author allowed him to tailor his reference books to the practical, day-to-day needs of parish clergy. He recognized that parish ministers often lacked large personal libraries or extensive university training; thus, his handbooks were deliberately engineered as comprehensive, single-volume reference tools for sermon preparation and catechetical instruction.From a material and typographical perspective, Westheimer’s publications represent the pinnacle of mid-sixteenth-century Swiss presswork. Printed using crisp Roman types, interspersed with clear italic for commentary and expertly cut Greek and Hebrew founts, these books showcased the technical sophistication of Basel’s printing industry. Title pages were frequently decorated with elaborate woodcut borders, printer’s devices (such as Herwagen’s three-headed Hermes or Oporinus’s Arion), and detailed analytical tables designed to facilitate quick reference. The commercial success of Westheimer's titles prompted multiple printings across major publishing hubs, including Zurich, Strasbourg, Frankfurt, and Nuremberg, ensuring their widespread international diffusion.The broad dissemination of Westheimer’s writings inevitably attracted the scrutiny of Counter-Reformation authorities. Despite his heavy reliance on canonized Church Fathers, Westheimer’s evangelical hermeneutics and explicit critiques of medieval papal scholasticism led to his inclusion in Roman Catholic indexes of prohibited books. The Tridentine Index Librorum Prohibitorum and subsequent expurgatory indexes produced in Spain and the Spanish Netherlands listed his works under the class of primary Protestant authors (auctores primae classis), ordering the total suppression or rigorous expurgation of his volumes. Nevertheless, Catholic polemicists quietly consulted his exhaustively indexed patristic concordances while publicly condemning his evangelical conclusions.Bartholomäus Westheimer passed away around 1567, likely in Eppingen or Nördlingen, leaving behind a profound legacy within the landscape of early modern scholarship. Modern historiographical assessments, particularly within the field of Renaissance history and book history, recognize Westheimer as a quintessential representative of the humanist-Reformation nexus. By transforming complex biblical philology and vast patristic literature into highly structured, accessible reference handbooks, he performed a vital service for early modern literacy, ministerial education, and textual scholarship. His works remain essential historical markers for understanding how the sixteenth-century Republic of Letters assembled, organized, and transmitted sacred knowledge across confessional boundaries.

academic_description: 8vo. [16], 477 [i.e. 479], [1] pp. Collation: α8, a-z8, A-G8. With the printer's device on the verso of the last leaf. Contemporary blindstamped pigskin over wooden boards, one clasp.First edition of this selection of Erasmus' letters made from his Opus epistolarum of the same year. The whole volume was intended for school boys as a manual of model letters. The volume opens with the announcement of Erasmus' death and a short biography of the latter by Beatus Rhenanus, and also contains some laudatory verses on Erasmus by Henricus Glareanus and Johannes Sapidus, and an epitaphium by Andrea Alciati. Westheimer reprinted the volume in 1551. The present edition was possibly, although there is no direct evidence, also edited by Johannes Gast (d. 1552), who in 1546 published Desiderii Erasmi Roterodami epistolae familiares in tres centurias divisae.“Il a une haute idée de la lettre considerée comme un genre littéraire qui ‘peint les moeurs, le destin, les sentiments, les conditions de la vie publique et de la vie privée' tout en maintenenant le ton de la conversation: colloquium inter absentes. Ses préférences vont à la simplicité, au style naturel et familier, à tout ce qui s'écarte résolument des expressions conventionelles, artificielles et impersonnelles. Sans doute, Erasme lui-même n'a-t-il pas toujours suivis ces sages recommandations? Il n'en reste pas moins qu'il n'aurait pu écrire un tel traité épistolaire s'il n'avait été d'abord un gran épistolier. Ajoutons pour mémoire, qu'Erasme n'a pas publié lui-même un recueil de ses plus belles lettres familières. Le volume intitulé Desiderii Erasmi Roterdami epistolae familiares est une édition posthume, chez B. Westhemerus à Bâle en 1538” (L.-E. Halkin, Erasmus ex Erasmo. Erasme éditeur de sa correspondence, Aubel, 1983, pp. 127-128).Bartholomaeus Westheimer (1499-1567/68) was born at Pforzheim and educated in the Latin school of Johann Sapidus at Schlettstadt. Around 1525 he lived in Rastatt and came into contact with the circle of Reformed theologians like Johannes Brenz and Dietrich von Gemmingen. A year later he settled in Basle as a proofreader, became a citizen and married a former nun. In Basel he issued his first theological works being printed by Thomas Wolff, whose printing shop he eventually took over in 1536. During some of his business trips, he met in Strasbourg the theologian Konrad Hubert with whom he remained in correspondence over a longer period. In 1546 he ceased his activities as a printer and became pastor of Therwil (near Basel) and in 1547 of Mulhouse. In 1551 he returned to Basel and his name is found in the university register. In 1553 he was called as a preacher to Horbourg (near Colmar). With a short stay in Montbéliard (Burgundy) he returned permanently to Horbough.As a printer he published over one hundred works: classical authors, theological and philological treatises as well as medical tracts, mostly in Latin. As theologian (he had converted from Calvinism to Lutheranism in his later years), he tried to show, combining humanism, biblical studies, and the Church Fathers, that the Reformation is indeed a return to the spirit of the early Church. If he ever had contacts with Erasmus is not known, but it is very probable (cf. H. Rissel, Dem Buch und der Kanzel gedient: Bartholomäus Westheimer aus Pforzheim, 1499?-1567, in: “Neue Beiträge zur Pforzheimer Stadtgeschichte”, Ch. Groh, ed., Stuttgart, 2006, pp. 13-24). Gerrit Gerritszoon (better known as Desiderius Erasmus) was born at Rotterdam, apparently on October 28, 1466, the illegitimate son of a physician's daughter and a future monk. At Deventer he attended the local school run by the German humanist Alexander Hegius, learning Latin and Greek. On his parents' death he entered the Augustinian College of Stein near Gouda, where he spent six years. At length the Bishop of Cambrai, Henry of Bergen, made him his private secretary. In order to allow him to accept that post, he was given a temporary dispensation from his monastic vows, dispensation that later was made permanent by Pope Leo X.After taking priest's orders Erasmus went to Paris, where he studied at the Collège Montaigu. He resided there until 1498, gaining a livelihood by teaching. Among his pupils was Lord Mountjoy, on whose invitation probably Erasmus made his first visit to England in 1498. He lived chiefly at Oxford, making the acquaintance of John Colet and Thomas More.In 1500 he was again in France, living for the next six years mainly at Paris. During this period he wrote the Adagia (Paris, 1500) and the Enchiridion Militis Christiani (Antwerp, 1503). After a short visit to England, in 1506 Erasmus carried out a long-desired journey to Italy, staying chiefly at Padua as tutor to Alexander Stewart, Archbishop of St. Andrews, and Venice, collaborating to the publishing house of Aldo Manuzio. His visit closed with a short stay in Rome.In 1509 the accession of Henry VIII and the invitation of Lord Mountjoy induced Erasmus once more to settle in England. In this period he wrote the famous Encomium Moriae (first published at Strasbourg or Paris in 1511) and resided mainly at Cambridge, where he was appointed Margaret professor of Divinity and professor of Greek.After 1514 he lived alternatively in Basel and England, and from 1517 to 1521 at Louvain. In 1516 at Basel appeared the first edition of the Colloquia, usually regarded as his masterpiece, and the first edition of his annotated New Testament. After the explosion of Lutheran revolution, he found himself in the most embarrassing position, assailed on the one side by the Catholic who considered him as the cause of all the new troubles, and criticized on the other side by the Lutherans who accused him for his cowardice and inconsistency in refusing to follow up his opinions to their legitimate conclusions.In 1521 he left Louvain, where the champions of the old faith had made his stay unendurable and, with the exception of six years in Freiburg, he spent the rest of his life at Basel. In those years he continued publishing a long succession of classical and patristic writers, as well as new augmented and corrected editions of his main works, especially the Adagia, the Colloquia and his epistolary. At the same time he was engaged in continual controversies, on the one side with Protestants thinkers like Ulrich von Hutten and Martin Luther, with whom he exchanged a series of pamphlets about the free will (starting with Erasmus' De Libero Arbitrio, Antwerp, 1524), on the other side with the Catholic theologians of the Sorbonne.With the publication of the dialogue Ciceronianus (Basel, 1528), he then ruined some old friendships, like that with Guillaume Budé, and raised against himself new adversaries, those humanists, namely, who he accused to set style above matter. Nevertheless during his last years Erasmus enjoyed great fame and consideration all over Europe. He died at Basel on July 12, 1536 and was buried there in the cathedral (cf. C. Augustijn, Erasmus: His Life, Works, and Influence, Toronto, 1991; J. McConica, Erasmus, Oxford, 1991; and L.-E. Halkin, Erasmus: A Critical Biography, Oxford, 1993).

authors.name: Doni Anton Francesco
authors.biography: Anton Francesco Doni (1513–1574) stands as one of the most eccentric, innovative, and multifaceted literary figures of the Italian High Renaissance. A quintessential exponent of the mid-sixteenth-century phenomenon of the poligrafi—professional vernacular men of letters who sustained their livelihoods through the booming Venetian publishing market—Doni operated at the volatile intersection of humanist scholarship, print capitalism, visual art, and social satire. As an author, compiler, typographer, iconographer, and proto-bibliographer, he exerted a transformative influence on the evolution of Italian prose, bibliographical science, and utopian literature. His landmark publications, most notably La Libraria (1550)—widely acknowledged as the first systematic printed bibliography of Italian vernacular literature—and I Mondi (1552–1553), a visionary blend of satire, anti-academic dialogue, and speculative urban design, bridged the medieval encyclopedic tradition with early modern print culture. Situated within the aesthetic currents of Mannerism and the socio-religious anxieties of the pre-Tridentine era, Doni's career captures the intellectual dynamism, economic precarity, and editorial experimentation of sixteenth-century Italian humanism.Born in Florence in 1513 into modest circumstances, Doni was the son of Bernardo di Miniato, a artisan forbiciaro (scissors-maker). Despite his humble lineage, his early exposure to the intellectual atmosphere of Florence enabled him to pursue an ecclesiastical career. In his youth, he entered the Servite Order at the famous convent of the Santissima Annunziata in Florence, taking the monastic name Fra Giuliano. His monastic education provided him with a rigorous foundation in Latin grammar, scholastic philosophy, and classical literature. However, Doni's tempestuous personality and acute fascination with the vibrant secular culture of his age led to severe friction with religious discipline. Around 1540, he abandoned the Servite habit without obtaining formal papal secularization—an act of apostasy that would haunt his social standing for the remainder of his life and expose him to vicious attacks from personal rivals. Upon leaving the monastery, Doni embarked on a period of restless migration across Northern and Central Italy. He settled temporarily in Piacenza, where he became a key figure in the prestigious Accademia degli Ortolani under the academic pseudonym "Il Bizzarro." Subsequent sojourns in Pavia, Milan, Venice, and Rome exposed him to courtly patronage networks, humanistic academies, and the practical operations of commercial printing shops, cementing his vocation as an independent author-entrepreneur.Doni's literary production is renowned for its genre-defying versatility, Mannerist discursiveness, and structural ingenuity. In 1550, while residing in Venice, he published La Libraria through the famous press of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari. Designed to catalog and defend vernacular literature against the entrenched hegemony of Latin humanism, the work offered an exhaustive inventory of Italian printed books, complete with biographical notes, critical appraisals, and thematic classifications. Recognizing the vast reservoir of unprinted texts, Doni followed this success with La Seconda Libraria (1551), dedicated exclusively to unpublished manuscripts, anonymous tracts, and suppressed writings—an pioneering effort in bibliographical archaeology. His philosophical and satirical genius reached its pinnacle in I Mondi (1552–1553), issued by the master printer Francesco Marcolini. Composed of complex dialogues between allegorical figures, artisans, and celestial spirits, I Mondi divided the universe into distinct realms ("Mondo Piccolo," "Mondo Grande," "Mondo Massimo"), concluding with "Il Mondo Savio e Pazzo," a remarkable depiction of a star-shaped utopian city built on radical social equality, communal property, gender parity, and architectural symmetry. Preceding Tommaso Campanella's Città del Sole by half a century, Doni's utopian vision combined socio-political critique with radical anti-clericalism. Parallel to I Mondi, Doni published I Marmi (1552–1553), a collection of nocturnal conversations set upon the marble steps of the Florence Cathedral, capturing the authentic voices of Florentine citizens, intellectuals, and craftsmen. His passion for moral philosophy and narrative folklore manifested in La Moral Filosoffia (1552), an adaptation of the ancient Indian fable collection Panchatantra (derived from John of Capua's Latin Directorium Humanae Vitae), which introduced Eastern apologues to Italian vernacular readers. Furthermore, Doni was deeply attuned to the visual arts, authoring Il Disegno (1549), an early theoretical treatise on theoretical and practical draftsmanship that elevated disegno as the intellectual foundation of painting, sculpture, and architecture, reflecting his intimate friendships with visual masters such as Bronzino, Enea Vico, and Tintoretto.Doni's engagement with typography extended far beyond authorial manuscript production; he was an active printer, typographer, and book designer. In 1546, having returned to Florence, Doni established his own printing office under the official aegis of the Accademia Fiorentina. Operating near the Piazza del Duomo, his press issued important vernacular editions, including works by Luigi Alamanni, Niccolò Machiavelli's Clizia, and his own epistolary collection, Lettere di M. Anton Francesco Doni (1547). However, administrative incompetence, inadequate financial backing, and fierce competition from the official ducal printer Lorenzo Torrentino, alongside bitter factional strife with academic rivals like Pier Francesco Giambullari and Lodovico Domenichi, led to the bankruptcy and closure of Doni's shop in 1547. Forced to relocate to Venice—the undisputed capital of European typography—Doni established fruitful partnerships with the city's foremost publishing houses, particularly those of Gabriel Giolito and Francesco Marcolini. Marcolini, famed for his sophisticated typographical layouts and exquisite woodcut illustrations, collaborated closely with Doni to produce visually stunning volumes. Works like I Mondi and I Marmi were designed as integrated visual-textual experiences, featuring intricate architectural title pages, emblematical printer's marks, woodcut portraits, and complex diagrams executed by engravers such as Enea Vico. Doni was among the first Italian authors to treat the printed page as an interactive spatial medium, meticulously directing font selections, marginal notes, frontispieces, and visual emblems to engage the dynamic expectations of the sixteenth-century reading public.Throughout his career, Doni's fiery temperament involved him in fierce literary and personal controversies. His most notorious feud was with his former intimate friend and fellow poligrafo, Lodovico Domenichi. What began as an editorial collaboration collapsed into decades of mutual accusations of plagiarism, financial fraud, and heresy. Doni launched devastating written attacks against Domenichi in works such as I Tre Libri delle Lettere and the Inferni, accusing his rival of corrupting texts and harboring Protestant sympathies. In retaliation, Domenichi exposed Doni's uncanonical departure from the Servite Order, accusing him of apostasy and impiety. Doni's biting anti-clericalism, fascination with heterodox and utopian ideas, and uncensored satirical style inevitably attracted the hostile attention of the Roman Inquisition during the Counter-Reformation. Following the Council of Trent, several of his publications, including I Mondi and La Libraria, were listed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum or subjected to severe expurgation in post-Tridentine reeditions (such as those prepared by Antonio Possevino and Publico Pietro Altamura). In the nineteenth century, scholars such as Girolamo Tiraboschi and Emmanuele Antonio Cicogna initiated a critical reappraisal of Doni's bibliographical and literary legacy. In the twentieth century, landmark studies by Benedetto Croce, Delio Cantimori, Paul F. Grendler, Mario Costanzo, and Giorgio Masi re-established Doni as a crucial Mannerist thinker, a pioneer of modern bibliography, and a visionary voice in early modern political philosophy. Doni died in retreat at Monselice near Padua in 1574, leaving behind a monumental legacy that redefined the intersection of print technology, vernacular literature, and intellectual freedom.

publishers.name: Marcolini Francesco
publishers.biography: Francesco Marcolini (c. 1500 – c. 1559), frequently designated as Francesco Marcolini da Forlì, stands as one of the most inventive, versatile, and artistically sophisticated printer-publishers of the Italian High Renaissance. Operating primarily in Venice during the vibrant golden age of the vernacular press, Marcolini was far more than a mere technician of type; he was a polymathic cultural entrepreneur, architect, engraver, mechanician, and writer whose press became the epicenter of Venetian literary avant-gardism. Working in close collaboration with seminal figures such as Pietro Aretino, Sebastiano Serlio, Anton Francesco Doni, and Giuseppe Porta (known as Giuseppe Salviati), Marcolini redefined the aesthetics of the printed book through innovative visual layouts, complex architectural illustrations, music engraving, and intricate emblematic iconographies. His masterpiece, Le Sorti intitolate giardino d'i pensieri (1540), remains a landmark in the history of fortune-telling books, emblem literature, and woodcut illustration. Through his celebrated printer's mark depicting Veritas Filia Temporis (Truth as the Daughter of Time), Marcolini linked his typographical program to humanistic ideals of intellectual freedom, artistic innovation, and critical truth.Born in Forlì in the Romagna region around the turn of the sixteenth century, Marcolini received a formative education that combined artisan craftsmanship with practical mathematics, architecture, and visual arts. Little is recorded regarding his immediate lineage, but his early training in Forlì instilled in him a proficiency in woodworking, mechanics, and design that would later distinguish his publishing endeavor from purely philological printing houses like that of the Aldine dynasty. By the late 1520s or early 1530s, Marcolini migrated to Venice, the undisputed capital of the European book trade. This migration coincided with the dramatic political and intellectual realignment following the Sack of Rome in 1527, which drove a wave of Roman humanists, artists, and literary figures northward to the Venetian Republic. In this dynamic, cosmopolitan environment, Marcolini quickly integrated himself into the artistic and literary circles surrounding the satirical genius Pietro Aretino, whose patronage and friendship would define the first major phase of Marcolini's printing career.Marcolini established his independent printing press in Venice around 1534, located initially in the parish of San Giuliano and later near the Ponte de' Baffi in the district of Santa Giustina. His initial typographical output was dominated by the works of Pietro Aretino, with whom he entered into a symbiotic professional partnership. Marcolini became Aretino's exclusive printer for over a decade, publishing first editions of his Ragionamenti, religious prose (such as L'Umanità di Cristo and I Sette Salmi), theatrical comedies including La Cortigiana and Il Marescalco, and the groundbreaking volumes of Aretino's Lettere (1538). Aretino frequently praised Marcolini in his correspondence, describing him as a man of extraordinary genius, skilled in architecture, clockmaking, and woodcutting. This collaboration established a new model for vernacular literary celebrity, wherein author and publisher worked in tandem to craft a highly marketable, modern intellectual persona. Marcolini's press was instrumental in establishing the vernacular Italian language as a prestigious vehicle for contemporary satire, drama, and personal epistolary collections.Beyond vernacular literature, Marcolini made groundbreaking contributions to the printing of architectural treatises and technical manuals. In 1537, he published Book IV of Sebastiano Serlio's Regole generali di architectura, followed by Book III in 1540. These volumes represented a revolutionary moment in architectural typography. Serlio's texts were designed from their inception to fuse text and image seamlessly, utilizing expansive folio formats, elaborate full-page woodcut illustrations, and intricate architectural diagrams. Marcolini's precise presswork, deep understanding of spatial proportion, and technical skill in woodblock printing allowed Serlio's codification of Vitruvian orders to achieve unprecedented clarity and visual elegance. This work established a precedent for architectural publishing across Europe, directly influencing later masters such as Andrea Palladio and Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola. Simultaneously, Marcolini demonstrated extraordinary versatility by entering the field of music printing. In 1536, he published the Intabolatura di liuto by the famous lute virtuoso Francesco Canova da Milano, utilizing a newly devised single-impression music printing system that showcased his technical ingenuity in press design.In 1540, Marcolini authored and printed his undisputed visual and typographical masterpiece, Le Sorti intitolate giardino d'i pensieri. A monumental folio edition devoted to the game of fortune-telling, the work utilized a complex combinatorial apparatus involving playing cards, abstract virtues, allegorical figures, and astrological influences. Readers navigated the book by drawing cards that directed them to specific pages, allegorical figures, and philosophical triplets (terzine) written by Ludovico Dolce. What set Le Sorti apart was its astounding visual program, designed largely by the Mannerist artist Giuseppe Porta (Giuseppe Salviati). The book featured a famous full-page frontispiece showing a crowd of figures surrounding an architectural garden of thought, along with dozens of intricate woodcuts depicting allegories of virtues, vices, and astrological personifications. The printer's mark featured on the final page—a dramatic woodcut depicting Time rescuing his daughter Truth from the clutches of Envy and Calumny—became one of the most celebrated allegorical devices of the Italian Renaissance, symbolizing Marcolini's artistic conviction and his resistance to intellectual censorship.Between 1545 and 1550, Marcolini's printing activity experienced a mysterious hiatus. Evidence suggests he left Venice during this period, traveling to Cyprus and possibly Rome to undertake engineering, architectural, and design commissions for noble patrons. During his absence, his press lay dormant, but he returned to Venetian publishing around 1550 with renewed vigor. Upon his return, he expanded his publishing repertoire to include philosophical works, military treatises, historical texts, and works by leading members of the Accademia dei Pellegrini and the Accademia Venetiana (also known as the Accademia della Fama), founded by Federico Badoer in 1557. Marcolini was appointed as the official printer to the short-lived Accademia Venetiana, printing their ambitious prospectuses and scholarly treatises with exceptional typographical refinement. His late output displayed a move toward greater classical elegance, maintaining high standards of typographical composition until his death in Venice around late 1559 or early 1560.The historical and critical legacy of Francesco Marcolini is immense. He bridged the gap between the intellectual humanism of early 16th-century Venice and the visual dynamism of late Mannerist book design. Unlike many commercial printers of his era who prioritized quantity over quality, Marcolini treated each edition as a holistic work of art, integrating typography, spatial architecture, and woodcut illustration into a unified aesthetic experience. His close associations with Aretino, Serlio, Salviati, and the Venetian academies situate him at the very center of the Italian Renaissance cultural network. In modern typographical scholarship, Marcolini is celebrated not only as a master printer but as a pioneering visual communicator whose works fundamentally reshaped the possibilities of the printed page in early modern Europe.

academic_description: 8vo. [16], 405 [i.e. 395], [5] pp. Collation: A-Z8, AA-CC8. With the printer's device on the title-page and at the end and the woocut arms of the Vitelli Baglioni family on leaf A3v, the third part has a separate title-page (leaf S1) with a different device. 18th century marbled calf, gilt back, tinted edges and endpapers, stamp on the title-page and on p. 1: Ex Bibliotheca J. Richard D.M. (Jacques Richard, 1744-1812, physician and book-collector from Lyon). Rare first edition of all three books of Doni's collected letters. The first book was published in 1544 by Girolamo Scotto with dedications to Federico Cesi and Lodovico Domenichi (dated Venice, May 9, 1544). It was reprinted with a few additions and modifications in 1545 by the same printer. In 1546 Doni had its own printing of a revised edition in Florence dedicated to Francesco de' Medici and a year later he printed the Libro secondo, dedicated to Agostino Bonucci, general of the Servite Order.The present edition is dedicated to Costanza Vitelli Baglioni (Venice, July 27, 1552). The dedication to Domenichi of the first book of the first edition was retained but addressed now to the reader. It contains sixty-six letters. The second books is still dedicated to Bonucci, and contains sixty-two letters. Most of these letters had already been published in the earlier editions, many were omitted, and several reprinted from Doni's Disegno (1549). The newly added third book is dedicated to Jacopo de Nores (Venice, July 13, 1552). It contains fifty-two letters, of which fifteen had been previously published in the Libro secondo, and eight in the first part of the Medaglie (1550) (cf. S. Re Fiorentin, I ‘libri di lettere' di Anton Francesco Doni, in: “Levia Gravia”, II, 2000, pp. 65-95). At the end of the volume are printed thirty-two sonnets exchanged between Doni and his correspondents, twenty-three of which had already been published in the 1544-edition of his letters.Doni expressly emphasizes the burlesque and playful character of his letters in a letter addressed to the printer Gabriele Giolito (Padova, February 15, 1544, p. 205), where he writes that “tutte le cose che si dicono e si scrivono non sono vere. Ma bisogna spregnar la fantasia. Dove voi troverete molte delle mie lettere piacevoli; dette & scritte solamente per dare spasso à chi le leggerà” (cf. G. Genovese, La lettera oltre il genere. Il libro di lettere, dall'Aretino al Doni, e le origini dell'autobiografia moderna, Roma & Padova, 2009, pp. 193-200).“Le lettere di Doni si pongono sin dall'inizio sotto il segno della ‘piacevolezza': se nella dedica alla ‘Signora Gostanza Vitella de' Baglioni' Doni non esita a dichiarare che esse ‘furono ristampate per la seconda volta, per la piacevolezza che tengono nel dir loro' (l. Aiir), poco più avanti nella dedica ‘Ai Lettori' del ‘Libro Primo' sostiene di ‘darle fuori' perché ha ‘piacere di dar piacere al mondo' (p. 3). Nelle lettere del Doni la tradizione comica toscana e il modello aretiniano sono riassimilati e per così dire forzati con un costante lavoro di dilatazione e manipolazione formale dei materiali a disposizione. La tensione linguistica e stilistica, l'uso marcato di una sintassi che rifugge da criteri di armonia e di misura in direzione dell'aggressività e dell'espressivismo sono piegati al gioco della deformazione e dell'invenzione. L'accumulo di materiali diversi, il gusto della variazione, sintomi di un'insofferenza nei confronti di soluzioni letterarie classiche connotate dalla ripetizione invariata di moduli e temi, riflettono un'adesione agli aspetti più incongrui del reale, di cui si privilegiano gli elementi ‘bassi' e stravaganti. Nelle lettere doniane l'universo narrativo si offre al lettore in un'esuberante varietà divertita e piacevole, dove non mancano, tuttavia, momenti fortemente polemici” (M.C. Figorilli, ‘Meglio ignorante che dotto'. L'elogio paradossale in prosa nel Cinquecento, Napoli, 2008, pp. 165-166).Doni's letters were put on the Roman Indices of 1559 and 1564, and in the Parma Index of 1580 all his writings were condemned to be expurgated (cf. Venezia, 1552 (p. 385) Anton Francesco Doni was born in Florence, the son of a scissors-maker and second hand dealer. The first reliable information is that, after 1535, he joined the religious order of the Servi di Maria in the Florentine convent of the Santissima Annunziata, taking the name of brother Valerio. During his years there Doni became a friend of the sculptor Giovannangelo Montorsoli, a disciple of Michelangelo.In 1540 they both left Florence and the convent and moved to Genoa; the following year Doni transferred to Alessandria, where he stayed with Antonio Trotti and Isabella Guasco. In 1542 he spent shorter periods in Pavia and Milan, and then moved to Piacenza to begin the study of law. Very soon, however, he gave up juridical studies and followed his inclination for literature. In Piacenza Doni joined the Accademia degli Ortolani, a group of intellectuals with whom he shared a very polemical, anti-classical attitude. Among its most prominent members were Giuseppe Betussi, Girolamo Parabosco, and Lodovico Domenichi.To Domenichi, in particular, Doni was bound by a very close friendship, following him to Venice, where he was introduced to Pietro Aretino and where he published the first book of his Lettere, as well as the Dialogo della Musica (1544). Soon afterwards Doni travelled back to Florence, where he began to take part in the meetings of the Accademia degli Umidi. In 1546 he became secretary of the Accademia Fiorentina and, with the aid of Cosimo I de' Medici, duke of Florence, tried to establish a printing house of his own. The business turned out to be disastrous, however, and lasted only from 1546 to 1548. In this period Doni published approximately twenty texts closely connected with the activities of the Accademia Fiorentina, among which should be mentioned Gli spiriti folletti (1546) and the Prose antiche di Dante, Petrarcha e Boccaccio (1547). In 1548, after the failure of his printing house, Doni broke off his relations with the Florentine milieu leaving Florence once and for all and, after a violent quarrel, whose reasons remain obscure, ended his personal relationship with Domenichi.Back in Venice, Doni edited the first Italian version of Thomas More's Utopia, translated by Ortensio Lando (1548). In 1549 his eldest son, Silvio, was born from an extramarital relationship with Lena Gabbia; to him Doni dedicated the Epistole di Seneca ridotte nella lingua toscana, issued in the same year. This is the first example of Doni's penchant for plagiarism, since what he actually did was to publish under this title his own adaptation of Sebastiano Manilio's translation of Seneca's Moral Epistles (1494).Meanwhile, he had begun a close collaboration with the printer Gabriele Giolito with the publication of the Disegno (1549), a book concerned with the primacy of figurative art. In 1550 Giolito published three further volumes by Doni: Fortuna di Cesare, Prima Libraria, and Medaglie.In his writings from 1549 onwards Doni often mentions the Accademia Pellegrina. However, this is neither the name of an existing institution (as it was believed until recently), nor the designation of a project for the creation of a new community of intellectuals; Doni's Accademia Pellegrina is simply a literary fiction and an important element of the setting of his works. Ercole Bentivoglio, Titian, Francesco Sansovino, Lodovico Dolce, Pietro Aretino, Francesco Marcolini, and other alleged members of the Accademia often appear as characters in, or even co-authors of, Doni's output.Doni's most productive period coincided with the years 1551-1553, when he was a collaborator of the printer Francesco Marcolini, who during this triennium printed many of Doni's major works: the Seconda Libraria (1551), the Zucca (1551-52), the Moral Filosofia (1552), the Marmi (1552-53), the diptych Mondi-Inferni (1552-53), the Pistolotti amorosi (1552), a collection of letters written by various fictional lovers.In 1555 Doni suddenly left Venice and went to Urbino, where he wanted to obtain the patronage of Duke Guidobaldo II della Rovere with the aid of Pietro Aretino. Aretino, however, refused, and to take revenge for what he considered a betrayal, in 1556 Doni wrote a very aggressive book, the Terremoto (Earthquake), in which he predicted that his former friend would die before the end of the year – exactly as happened. In 1556 he also published Le Ville, a work devoted to the features of country houses.Between 1557 and 1558 Doni stayed in Ancona, where he tried to open a new printing house, but he was soon compelled to leave because of an edict of Pope Paul IV which ruled that all those who had left the priesthood should return to their convents. There is no clarity regarding the details of the following three years of Doni's life. However, between 1562 and 1563 he was certainly in Arquà, where he planned a monument in honour of Petrarch, which was never built. In 1562 Giolito printed Il Cancellieri dell'Eloquenza, Il Cancellieri della Memoria, the Dichiarazione sopra il XIII cap. dell'Apocalisse, and the second revised edition of the diptych Mondi-Inferni with the new title Mondi terrestri, celesti e infernali.In 1564, Le Pitture was published in Padua by the printer Grazioso Percaccino. This work collects the invenzioni, or allegorical descriptions of love, fortune, time, sleep, and death, which Doni had created to adorn the projected monument dedicated to Petrarch. In 1567 Doni and his son Silvio moved to Monselice, near Padua. In the same year he composed the Lumiera, a short poem that takes up themes from the main works of the 1550s. The following year, Giorgio de' Cavalli printed an updated edition of the Mondi in Venice, the last before Doni's death.Doni's works enjoyed great success throughout Europe and were soon translated into other major European languages: Spanish (Zucca en español, 1552), English (The Moral Philosophy of Doni, 1570), and French (Les Mondes célestes, terrestres et infernaux, 1578, 1580, 1583).In July 1574 Doni returned to Venice, where he offered Henry III of Valois the precious manuscript of a poem in ottava rima, the Guerra di Cipro. This is the last known fact of Doni's life. He died soon after, in September 1574 – still in Venice, according to some sources, or back in Monselice, according to other (cf. P. Pelizzari, Nota biografica, in: A.F. Doni, “I Mondi e gli Inferni”, Torino, 1994, pp. LXIX-LXXXIV; and G. Masi, Appunti su Anton Francesco Doni e sull'edizione dei ‘Mondi' e degli ‘Inferni', in: “Filologia e Critica”, XXII, 1997, pp. 264-293).

authors.name: Camerarius Joachim
authors.biography: Joachim Camerarius the Elder (1500–1574) stands as one of the most brilliant, versatile, and influential humanists of the Northern European Renaissance. A scholar of extraordinary linguistic erudition, pivotal university reformer, and tireless textual critic, Camerarius occupied a central position within the intellectual and confessional matrix of sixteenth-century Germany. Alongside his lifelong companion and intellectual collaborator, Philipp Melanchthon, Camerarius served as a primary architect of the Praeceptio Germaniae—the systematic transformation of Northern European education through the integration of classical Greek and Latin philology with evangelical theology. His monumental contributions to classical scholarship, ranging from groundbreaking critical editions of Plautus, Sophocles, and Homer to translations of Galen and Claudius Ptolemy, established standards of textual rigor that bridged the methodology of Italian humanists like Piero Vettori with the emerging philological traditions of early modern Germany. Beyond his textual corpus, Camerarius was an instrumental figure in the institutionalization of the Reformation, drafting foundational documents at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 and orchestrating the overhaul of major universities, including Nuremberg, Tübingen, and Leipzig.Born on April 12, 1500, in the Franconian imperial city of Bamberg, Camerarius hailed from a patrician family originally named Liebhard. The surname Camerarius was adopted by his ancestors in reference to their hereditary title of Kämmerer (hereditary chamberlain) to the Prince-Bishops of Bamberg. His early educational foundation was established in Bamberg under the guidance of local schoolmasters before he matriculated at the University of Leipzig in 1512 at the exceptionally early age of twelve. At Leipzig, the young scholar came under the profound influence of the English Hellenist Richard Croke and the renowned Latinist Peter Mosellanus (Peter Schade), whose instruction ignited Camerarius’s lifelong devotion to ancient Greek grammar and Neo-Latin eloquence. Seeking an environment more receptive to the new humanist learning, Camerarius transferred in 1518 to the University of Erfurt. There, he entered the celebrated literary circle gathered around Conrad Mutianus Rufus and Helius Eobanus Hessus, immersing himself in the study of classical rhetoric, poetry, and ancient history. In 1521, drawn by the radical intellectual ferment surrounding the early Protestant movement, Camerarius relocated to the University of Wittenberg. This move proved decisive: at Wittenberg, he established an intimate, lifelong friendship with Philipp Melanchthon and entered the immediate circle of Martin Luther. Under Melanchthon’s guidance, Camerarius deepened his command of Greek syntax, began lecturing publicly on Quintilian and Cicero, and engaged directly with the critical translation of Biblical texts.Camerarius’s career as an institutional administrator and educational reformer commenced in 1526, when, upon Melanchthon’s direct recommendation, the Senate of the Imperial City of Nuremberg appointed him rector of the newly established Aegidien-Gymnasium. In Nuremberg, working in close concert with the reformer Lazarus Spengler, Camerarius designed a pioneering humanist curriculum that served as a blueprint for secondary education throughout Protestant Europe. His diplomatic and theological capabilities were put to a severe test in 1530, when he accompanied Melanchthon to the Imperial Diet of Augsburg. Camerarius actively assisted in the redaction, translation, and diplomatic negotiations surrounding the Confessio Augustana (Augsburg Confession), playing a subtle yet critical role in maintaining irenic dialogue with Catholic imperial representatives. Recognizing his institutional genius, Duke Ulrich of Württemberg summoned Camerarius in 1535 to reorganize the University of Tübingen along humanist and evangelical lines, a task he accomplished with remarkable speed by revitalizing the faculties of arts and theology. In 1541, Duke Maurice of Saxony enticed Camerarius to accept the professorship of Greek and Latin literature at the University of Leipzig. For the remaining thirty-three years of his life, Camerarius transformed Leipzig into the premier center of classical philology and humanist erudition in Northern Europe, navigating the immense political and military turmoil of the Smalcaldic War (1546–1547) and the contentious Adiaphoristic controversies with remarkable diplomatic tact and scholarly detachment.The philological legacy of Joachim Camerarius is immense, characterized by unprecedented critical acumen, stemmatological intuition, and deep linguistic sensitivity. His edition of the comedies of Plautus (M. Accii Plauti Comoediae XX), printed at Basel in 1552, represented a watershed moment in Latin textual scholarship. Utilizing the famous Codex Vetus (Vaticanus Lat. 3870), which he examined with meticulous care, Camerarius purged centuries of scribal corruptions, restored ancient metrical structures, and established a text that remained standard for generations. His labor in Greek letters was equally groundbreaking: he produced critical editions and Latin translations of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey, Sophocles’ tragedies, Hesiod, Theocritus, Demosthenes, Xenophon, and Herodotus. Camerarius did not limit his erudition to literary classics; he was deeply fascinated by ancient science, astronomy, and medicine. In 1535, he published the editio princeps of the Greek text of Claudius Ptolemy’s astrological treatise, the Tetrabiblos (or Quadripartitum), alongside his own Latin translation, accompanied by an edition of the Karbos (Centiloquium). His medical interest led him to translate and annotate works by Galen and Aetius of Amida. In the realm of contemporary history and biography, Camerarius authored two masterworks that remain indispensable primary sources for the Renaissance and Reformation eras: his Narratio de Helios Eobano Hesso (1553) and his monumental De vita Philippi Melanchthonis narratio (1566). The latter represents the first comprehensive biography of Melanchthon, offering an insider’s view of the intellectual dynamics, personal struggles, and theological debates of the Reformation inner circle.The dissemination of Camerarius’s vast literary output was made possible through his intimate, highly strategic relationships with the leading printing houses of Northern Europe. He maintained close working alliances with the great Basel presses, most notably those of Johannes Herwagen, Johann Oporinus, and Hieronymus Froben. These Basel publishers possessed the specialized Greek fonts and scholarly correctors necessary to produce Camerarius’s complex Greek commentaries and critical texts. In Nuremberg, he collaborated extensively with Johannes Petreius, who printed several of his grammatical and astronomical works, while in Leipzig, his texts issued regularly from the presses of Ernst Voegelin, Michael Blum, and Valentin Papa. Camerarius was also a central node in an international republic of letters (*Respublica Literaria*). His voluminous epistolary correspondence—comprising well over one thousand extant Latin and Greek letters—demonstrates active textual exchanges with Italian humanists such as Piero Vettori (Victorius) in Florence and Cardinal Pietro Bembo, as well as Northern scholars like Erasmus of Rotterdam, Johannes Sturm in Strasbourg, and Joachim Vadianus in St. Gallen. Through these networks, Camerarius facilitated the exchange of rare manuscripts, collations, and codicological data across confessional divides, maintaining a steadfast commitment to the universal fellowship of humanist learning despite the religious wars fracturing Europe.Camerarius passed away in Leipzig on April 17, 1574, leaving behind a family that would continue his scholarly legacy, most notably his son, Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a celebrated physician, botanist, and emblem author. In the centuries following his death, Camerarius’s reputation as a giant of classical philology remained unshakeable. Polyhistors of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, including Daniel Georg Morhof and Johann Albert Fabricius, praised him as the ultimate exemplar of Northern erudition—a scholar who combined the stylistic elegance of the Italian Renaissance with German textual thoroughness. Modern historiography, led by scholars such as Heinz Scheible, Thomas Fuchs, and Volkhard Wels, has re-evaluated Camerarius not merely as a passive transmitter of classical antiquity, but as an indispensable agent of cultural transformation who shaped the institutional structures of early modern German universities, pioneered modern philological methodologies, and preserved the intellectual coherence of Protestant Humanism during a period of acute ideological crisis.

publishers.name: Wechel Andreas
publishers.biography: Andreas Wechel (also known in French as André Wechel and in Latin typographical imprints as Andreas Wechelus; d. 1581) stands as one of the most pivotal and culturally consequential scholar-printers of the late Northern Renaissance. Active during a period of profound religious fracturing, intellectual revolution, and geopolitical instability, Wechel operated at the very heart of early modern European book history. His career bridges two of the sixteenth century’s paramount typographical and intellectual capitals: Paris, where he inherited and expanded the humanist printing house established by his father Christian Wechel, and Frankfurt am Main, where he re-established his firm following his flight from the sectarian violence of the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre in 1572. Through his meticulous typographical standards, his deployment of sophisticated Greek and italic founts, and above all his close alliances with the leading lights of French, German, and international Humanism—most notably the philosopher-reformer Petrus Ramus (Pierre de la Ramée) and the diplomat Hubert Languet—Wechel functioned not merely as a commercial manufacturer of books, but as a primary architect of the trans-European Republic of Letters (Respublica Literaria).Born into a distinguished dynasty of printers originating from the Low Countries (Brabant), Andreas received a rigorous humanist education that equipped him with a fluent command of Latin, Greek, and the mechanics of textual scholarship. His father, Christian Wechel (Chrétien Wechel), had established a formidable reputation in Paris during the 1520s and 1530s at his shop on the Rue Saint-Jean-de-Beauvais, publishing under the famous printer's mark of the Pegasus (and occasionally the Basilisk). Christian Wechel had been an early champion of humanist pedagogy, printing works by Erasmus of Rotterdam, Guillaume Budé, and early medical humanists, while maintaining a delicate balance amid rising religious tensions. Following Christian’s death around 1554, Andreas Wechel assumed full leadership of the Parisian enterprise. Inheriting a well-equipped workshop with access to superior founts—including types influenced by Claude Garamont and Pierre Haultin—Andreas immediately consolidated the firm’s reputation for typographical elegance and textual accuracy. During his Parisian period (circa 1554–1572), Wechel’s press became the principal publishing vehicle for the intellectual circle surrounding Petrus Ramus, whose radical restructuring of Aristotelian logic, rhetoric, and mathematics demanded an agile, visionary publisher capable of translating complex pedagogical diagrams and pedagogical trees into printed format.Wechel’s association with Petrus Ramus transformed his printing shop into an ideological and philosophical nerve center. The Wechel atelier issued numerous first and definitive editions of Ramus’s works, including his Dialectique, Institutiones Dialecticae, and various treatises on classical authors and mathematics. Beyond Ramism, Wechel’s Parisian catalogue reflected a deep commitment to natural philosophy, medicine, and philology. He published the authoritative medical writings of Jean Fernel (such as the Universa Medicina), which became standard university texts across Europe, as well as works by the polymath Guillaume Postel and the jurist Jean Bodin. However, this intellectual dynamism unfolded against the darkening backdrop of the French Wars of Religion. As Paris grew increasingly hostile to Protestant sympathizers and humanist reformers, Wechel’s output and personal ties drew the scrutiny of the Sorbonne and Catholic authorities. Despite maintaining a degree of commercial discretion, Wechel’s intimate personal and business connections with leading Huguenots and foreign Protestants rendered his position in the French capital precariously unstable by the early 1570s.The turning point of Wechel’s life and career occurred in August 1572 during the horrifying events of the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre. As Catholic mobs targeted Protestant scholars, merchants, and citizens across Paris, Ramus was brutally murdered in his quarters at the Collège de Presles. Wechel himself narrowly escaped assassination, surviving only through the intervention of the diplomat Hubert Languet, the representative of the Elector of Saxony, who sheltered the printer in his official residence. Stripped of much of his domestic security and recognizing the impossibility of continuing his work in Paris, Wechel fled the Kingdom of France, joining the tragic exodus of Huguenot artisans and intellectuals. Strikingly, Wechel managed to transport a significant portion of his typographical capital—including matrices, punches, and printing blocks—out of France, demonstrating extraordinary foresight and logistical resourcefulness in the face of violent displacement.Wechel chose as his refuge the Free Imperial City of Frankfurt am Main, a strategic decision that fundamentally altered the geography of European publishing. While many Huguenot exile printers gathered in Geneva, Basle, or Strasbourg, Wechel recognized Frankfurt’s unique position as the financial and commercial crossroads of the Holy Roman Empire and the home of the bi-annual International Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse). Establishing his new printing house in Frankfurt in late 1572 or early 1573, Wechel quickly gained citizenship and imperial privileges. The Frankfurt office of Wechel immediately distinguished itself from local competitors by importing the refined aesthetic of Parisian typography—characterized by generous margins, balanced title pages, superior ink quality, and French Renaissance ornament—to the German market. In exile, Wechel rebuilt his business with astonishing speed, establishing a vast international distribution network that spanned Germany, Switzerland, the Low Countries, England, and Eastern Europe.In Frankfurt, Wechel’s press became an intellectual sanctuary and a major hub for international Protestant humanism. He maintained his close relationship with Hubert Languet, through whom he entered the circle of the young English polymath and poet Sir Philip Sidney. During Sidney’s continental tour, the Englishman lodged at Wechel’s home in Frankfurt, fostering a famous friendship that left an indelible mark on Elizabethan literary culture and English Protestant diplomacy. Under Wechel’s guidance, the press embarked on ambitious multi-volume scholarly initiatives. He employed brilliant philologists as correctors and editors, most notably Friedrich Sylburg, whose masterly editions of Greek classics, patristic texts, and Byzantine historians set new standards for German classical scholarship. Wechel’s Frankfurt catalogue expanded to encompass comprehensive series of Neo-Latin poetry, legal compilations, historical compendia, and essential works of Protestant theology, while continuing to serve as the global clearinghouse for the posthumous dissemination of Ramist philosophy.Andreas Wechel died in Frankfurt am Main in November 1581, leaving behind an enterprise that had redefined the mechanics of the international book trade. His legacy was maintained and further expanded by his sons-in-law, Claude de Marne (Claudius Marnius) and Jean Aubry (Johann Aubry), who published under the famous imprint Heredes Andreae Wecheli (The Heirs of Andreas Wechel). Under their direction, and later in collaboration with the printer Johann Karl Unckel in Frankfurt and Hanau, the Wechel press continued its devotion to high humanist scholarship, famously publishing works by Giordano Bruno during his travels through Central Europe in the late 1580s and early 1590s. Today, book historians and scholars of Renaissance intellectual culture recognize Andreas Wechel not merely as a master craftsman, but as a central figure in the transmission of French Renaissance learning to Northern Europe, whose resilience in the face of religious persecution ensured the preservation and proliferation of early modern humanist thought.

academic_description: 8vo. [8] leaves, 562 pp., 1 leaf (errata). Collation: (:)8, a-z8, A-L8, M10. With the printer's device on the title-page. Marbled boards, with the entry of ownership ‘inservio studijs Gerhardi Conradi. 1626' on the title-page and a handwritten alphabetical index of the main recipients at the end. First edition of an important part of Camerarius' correspondence published by his sons Joachim the Younger (1534-1598), physician and botanist, and Philip (1537-1624), professor of law at Altdorf.The volume, which opens with a dedication to Joachim Ernest of Anhalt dated from Nuremberg, December 21, 1582, contains 446 letters. It is provided with an index of the over fifty recipients and an index of names appearing in the letters. A second volume, also published by Camerarius' sons, appeared at Frankfurt/Main in 1595.The greatest number of letters (135) are addressed to the Reformer of Nürnberg, Hieronymus Baumgartner (1498-1565), who was also for a longer period major of that city (cf. E. van Hout, Zum Briefwechsel des älteren Hieronymus Baumgartner, Bonn 1877, passim).Fifty-nine letters are addressed to Christoph von Carlowitz (1507-1578), a notable representative of that group of German politicians committed to the ideals of Erasmus. He was most influential under the Duke and Elector Maurice of Saxony and was also employed on many domestic assignments and foreign missions by the Elector Augustus of Saxony, as well as the emperors Ferdinand I and Maximilian II (cf. T. Woitkowitz, Die Briefe von Joachim Camerarius d. Ä. an Christoph von Karlowitz bis zum Jahr 1553, Stuttgart, 2003, passim, esp. pp. 27-32).To Hieronymus Wolf (1516-1580) are addressed forty-two letters. Wolf was a teacher, an editor and translator of ancient Greek authors for the Basel printer Johannes Oporin, librarian to Hans Jakob Fugger and the city of Augsburg.Georg Fabricius (1516-1571), poet, historian and archaeologist is the recipient of thirty-one letters, and the addressees of more than ten letters were the poet Helius Eobanus Hessus, Hieronymus Herold, a Nuremberg physician, Hermann von Neuenahr, humanist and chancellor of the University of Cologne, and Johannes Stigel, poet and professor of rhetoric at the University of Jena. Leipzig, May 21, 1565 (p. 534) Joachim Camerarius, a native of Bamberg, was the son of a nobleman, episcopal official and councillor of Bamberg in Franconia. He studied at Leipzig and Erfurt. In 1521, after receiving a master of arts degree, he went to Wittenberg, where his close and lasting friendship with Philipp Melanchthon developed, and where he was quickly drawn into the orbit of Luther, whose cause he espoused and supported throughout his life.He then pursued a successful academic career. In 1526 he became rector of the newly founded Latin school in Nuremberg. Attending the diet of Augsburg with Melanchthon in 1530, he faced the Catholic theologians in a basically conciliatory spirit. In 1535 he was asked to help to reorganize the University of Tübingen, where he stayed until 1541. Thereafter he joined the University of Leipzig and to the end of his life served recurrently as dean of arts and rector.A devoted classical scholar, Camerarius edited, annotated and translated many ancient authors, among them Homer, Sophocles, Cicero, and Plautus. He also wrote works on grammar and style, and numerous poems. He assisted Albrecht Dürer in the publication of some of his books and composed a poem on the occasion of his death. Indeed, contemporaries regarded Camerarius as the greatest German philologist of his time and as the successor of Desiderius Erasmus (cf. F. Baron, ed., op.cit., passim).
