title: Le rime di M. Agnolo Firenzuola fiorentino

authors.name: Firenzuola Agnolo
authors.biography: Agnolo Firenzuola (born Michelangelo Girolamo Giovannini da Firenzuola; September 28, 1493 – June 27, 1543) stands as one of the most brilliant, versatile, and stylistic exemplars of High Renaissance Italian vernacular literature. Operating at the turbulent intersection of monastic devotion, Roman courtly sociability, and Tuscan humanist philology, Firenzuola synthesized the linguistic doctrines of Pietro Bembo with an uninhibited, vivid Tuscan idiom rooted in spoken vitality and stylistic elegance (sprezzatura). Best known for his masterly adaptation of Apuleius’s Metamorphoses (L’Asino d’oro), his theoretical treatise on aesthetic perfection (Dialogo delle bellezze delle donne), his Boccaccian frame-novella collection (I Ragionamenti), and his classicizing vernacular comedies (I Lucidi and La Trinuzia), Firenzuola embodied the quintessential sixteenth-century Tuscan man of letters. His literary output bridges the formal rigor of early Cinquecento classicism with the burgeoning Mannerist fascinations for dialogue, metamorphosis, psychological nuance, and eroticized naturalism.Born in Florence to Bastiano de’ Giovannini and Lucrezia del Barbigia, Firenzuola belonged to a respectable family originally hailing from the border town of Firenzuola in the Tuscan-Emilian Apennines—a origin reflected in the surname adopted by his grandfather and maintained by the author. His early intellectual formation took place in the buoyant scholarly environment of Florence before he matriculated at the University of Siena and subsequently the University of Perugia to pursue legal studies. In Perugia, Firenzuola formed pivotal, lifelong intellectual alliances with figures who would dominate Cinquecento literary culture, most notably Pietro Aretino, Claudio Tolomei, and Giovanni Matteo Giberti. Despite his legal preparation, Firenzuola felt drawn to the ecclesiastical path and the world of letters. Around 1517 or 1518, he entered the Vallombrosan Order—a reformed Benedictine congregation deeply rooted in Tuscany—taking the monastic name Agnolo. His monastic profession, far from cloistering his intellect, opened avenues for diplomatic and administrative advancement within the papal curia, propelling him into the vibrant, hedonistic atmosphere of Medicean Rome.During the pontificate of Clement VII (Giulio de' Medici), Firenzuola resided in Rome as the procurator general for the Vallombrosan Order. There, he immersed himself in the intellectual life of the Roman academies, particularly the Accademia dei Vignaioli, mingling with humanists and poets such as Francesco Berni, Blosio Palladio, Mauro Lugano, and Annibale Caro. This Roman period was marked by intense literary experimentation, courtly networking, and a notoriously worldly lifestyle that contrasted sharply with his monastic vows. It was also during this period that Firenzuola contracted the virulent strain of syphilis (morbo gallico) that would torment him for the remainder of his life. Suffering from excruciating physical decline, he sought treatment at the thermal baths of Pozzuoli near Naples. This period of severe health crises prompted his temporary retreat to Florence and Siena, ultimately leading to his appointment around 1538 as the commendatory abbot of the monastery of San Salvatore at Vaiano, near Prato, and later of Santa Maria a Spoleto. The quiet, idyllic surroundings of Prato provided Firenzuola with a sanctuary where, despite ongoing illness, he spent his final years surrounded by a circle of cultured friends and devoted himself to composing his mature literary masterpieces.Firenzuola’s literary corpus represents a brilliant exploration of vernacular prose styles, theoretical debates, and creative adaptations of classical and Oriental models. In the sphere of linguistic debate, he actively engaged in the Cinquecento Questione della lingua. In 1524, he published the Discacciamento delle lettere inutilmente aggiunte nei nodi della lingua toscana, a fierce, witty polemic directed against Gian Giorgio Trissino's proposal to introduce Greek letters (such as epsilon and omega) into Italian orthography. Firenzuola championed the innate phonetic authority and historical supremacy of the Tuscan vernacular. His creative prose reached its apex in Prato. I Ragionamenti d'amore, designed on the structural framework of Boccaccio's Decameron, features a group of noble youths gathered in the garden of Costanza Amaretta to discuss the nature of love, interspersed with six vibrant novelle and lyric verse. His aesthetic dialogue, Dialogo delle bellezze delle donne (often referred to as Celso, after the author’s textual alter ego), represents one of the most sophisticated treatments of female beauty in Renaissance literature. Set at the monastery of Santa Grata in Prato, the dialogue meticulously dissects the concept of physical harmony, proposing precise mathematical and visual proportions for the female body while coining refined stylistic terms such as grazia, vaghezza, venustà, and maestà.Equally groundbreaking was Firenzuola’s work as a translator and re-creator of classical and Near Eastern narrative structures. His L'Asino d'oro is not a literal translation of Apuleius’s Metamorphoses, but a radical *volgarizzamento* that transplants the ancient narrative into contemporary Cinquecento Italy. Firenzuola replaces Apuleius’s Lucius with himself (Agnolo), relocating the transformation and picaresque adventures to the Tuscan landscape, thereby weaving autobiography, satirical observation of contemporary clergy, and Neoplatonic allegory into a fluid vernacular idiom. Similarly, his La Prima Veste de' Discorsi degli Animali adapted the ancient Indian fable tradition of the Panchatantra (derived via John of Capua's Latin Directorium humanae vitae), recasting moral fables of animal wisdom into elegant Tuscan dialogues. In the dramatic sphere, Firenzuola authored two major vernacular comedies: I Lucidi, a brilliant reworking of Plautus's Amphitruo that adapts the classical motif of mistaken identity to a contemporary Florentine domestic setting, and La Trinuzia, a complex comedy of romantic entanglements and social satire. His poetry, collected in Le Rime, demonstrates a masterly command of Petrarchan lyrical forms infused with Bernesque wit and Mannerist sensibility.The printing and transmission history of Firenzuola’s oeuvre is intimately tied to the premier printing houses of mid-sixteenth-century Florence and Venice. While a few minor works were printed during his lifetime, the vast majority of his writings were edited and published posthumously through the tireless efforts of his brother, Girolamo Firenzuola, and his literary executor, Giovan Battista Gelli. In 1548, the renowned Florentine press of Bernardo Giunta published the princeps editions of the Prose di M. Agnolo Firenzuola (containing the Discorsi degli Animali, I Ragionamenti, and Le Bellezze delle Donne) as well as Le Rime di M. Agnolo Firenzuola. In the same year, the ducal printer Lorenzo Torrentino issued competing Florentine imprints, establishing Firenzuola’s prose as a touchstone of mid-Cinquecento Tuscan typography. Subsequently, the Venetian publishing giant Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari released numerous popular octavo editions of L'Asino d'oro and the comedies, ensuring their rapid dissemination across the Italian peninsula and beyond. Typographically, these editions served as exemplars of readable, elegant italic characters (*corsivo*) designed for a sophisticated lay reading public.The critical reception of Agnolo Firenzuola has undergone significant evolution from the early modern period to contemporary scholarship. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, lexicographers of the Accademia della Crusca cited Firenzuola extensively as a primary stylistic authority (*testo di lingua*) for the purity, naturalness, and richness of his Tuscan vocabulary. Literary historians such as Giovan Maria Crescimbeni, Girolamo Tiraboschi, and Pier Antonio Serassi praised his narrative fluidity while wrestling with the moral ambiguity of his monastic vocation and worldly writings. In the nineteenth century, Francesco De Sanctis recognized Firenzuola as a quintessential figure of the late Renaissance, whose formal perfection and linguistic hedonism reflected the brilliant, albeit politically declining, Italian court culture. Twentieth-century scholarship, led by seminal studies from Giuseppe Fatini, Mario Bonfantini, Giuliano Innamorati, and Franco Pignatti, contextualized Firenzuola within the wider sociological dynamics of Roman humanism, anti-Trissinian linguistic nationalism, and the complex stylistic shifts toward Mannerism. Today, Firenzuola is celebrated not merely as a master of prose style, but as a pivotal cultural theorist whose writings on female aesthetics, classical adaptation, and vernacular comedy defined the artistic consciousness of the Italian High Renaissance.

publishers.name: Giunta Bernardo
publishers.biography: Bernardo Giunta (fl. 1551–1596), often designated by bibliographers as Bernardo II Giunta to distinguish him from his illustrious grandfather Bernardo I, stands as one of the quintessential printer-publishers of the late Italian Renaissance. Operating at the intersection of Grand Ducal autocratic patronage, Counter-Reformation textual regulation, and pan-European book commerce, Bernardo II carried the Florentine workshop of the Giunti (or Junta) press to the apex of its institutional authority during the second half of the sixteenth century. While the roots of the Giunti dynasty traced back to the fifteen-century mercantile enterprise of Filippo I and Lucantonio I Giunti, Bernardo II’s tenure encapsulated a pivotal transition in European print culture: the metamorphosis of humanistic editorial freedom into highly regulated, state-sponsored, and academically vetted publishing enterprises. Active primarily in Florence from 1551 through 1596, while simultaneously extending his commercial and typographical operations into Venice (1559–1577) and Bologna (1591), Bernardo II embodied the archetype of the late Renaissance typographus academicus, serving as official printer to the Medici court and executing landmark publications that defined the visual and literary canon of Mannerist Italy.Born into the premier typographical family of Florence, Bernardo II was steeped from his youth in the rigorous operational mechanics and commercial strategies of early modern printing. Following the death of Bernardo I Giunta in 1551, the stewardship of the Florentine press devolved upon his descendants, notably Bernardo II and his brother Filippo II Giunta. The young Bernardo received an intensive humanist education, acquiring fluency in classical Latin, vernacular Italian philology, and the technical intricacies of typefounding, ink chemistry, and paper procurement. The Giunti family maintained an unparalleled network of printing houses and distribution depositories spanning Florence, Venice, Lyons, Madrid, and Medina del Campo. This international infrastructure provided Bernardo II with immediate access to vast capital reserves, high-grade rag paper from Tuscan and Venetian mills, and a steady stream of international manuscript sources. His formative years coincided with the consolidation of Cosimo I de' Medici’s rule over the Duchy (later Grand Duchy) of Florence, an autocratic regime that recognized the printing press as a supreme instrument of cultural diplomacy, state propaganda, and linguistic hegemony.The scholarly and literary legacy of Bernardo Giunta is inextricably linked to his close alignment with the Accademia Fiorentina and the intellectual circle surrounding the Benedictine scholar Don Vincenzio Borghini. Among the most monumental achievements of Bernardo’s press was the second, radically expanded edition of Giorgio Vasari’s Le Vite de' più eccellenti pittori, scultori, e architettori, issued in three lavish quarto volumes in 1568. Known to bibliophiles as the definitive Giuntina edition, this masterpiece of artistic historiography was meticulously overseen by Bernardo II. The publication was rendered visually iconic through the inclusion of over one hundred ornate woodcut portrait frames designed by Vasari himself and engraved by Master Cristoforo Coriolano. Bernardo’s shop engineered a complex typographical layout that seamlessly combined roman text types, italic commentaries, woodcut initials, and inserted portrait cuts. Equally monumental was Bernardo’s role in navigating the fierce censorship of the Post-Tridentine era. When Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron was placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, Bernardo Giunta, under the editorial guidance of Borghini and the official mandate of the Deputati appointed by Grand Duke Cosimo I, printed the famous expurgated 1573 edition. This edition served as a landmark compromise between Roman inquisitorial orthodoxy and Florentine linguistic pride, establishing the text as a standardized model of Tuscan prose.Materially and typographically, the imprints produced under Bernardo Giunta’s direction showcased extraordinary technical virtuosity. The Florentine workshop, prominently situated near the Piazza della Signoria, utilized the famous printer's mark depicting the Florentine Red Lily (Giglio), often flanked by the initials B. G. or accompanied by elaborate Mannerist cartouches and allegorical figures of Justice and Fortitude. Bernardo expanded the firm's font inventory, acquiring crisp italic types inspired by Ludovico Vicentino degli Arrighi and robust roman fonts cut by leading European punchcutters. Beyond vernacular masterpieces, Bernardo’s press maintained a lucrative monopoly on legal, medical, and liturgical printing. He produced massive folio volumes of civil and canon law, official Grand Ducal edicts (Bandi e Provvisioni), and sacred texts tailored to the liturgical reforms mandated by the Council of Trent. His enterprise in Venice between 1559 and 1577 allowed him to exploit the vastly superior maritime trade channels and paper markets of the Venetian Republic, while his temporary establishment in Bologna in 1591 catered directly to the academic demand of the University of Bologna, producing authoritative legal and philosophical commentaries.The historical significance of Bernardo Giunta has been consistently recognized by analytical bibliographers and cultural historians from the eighteenth century to the present. Early bibliographical topographers such as Angelo Maria Bandini and Antoine-Augustin Renouard highlighted Bernardo’s role in preserving the aesthetic integrity of Tuscan printing during an era increasingly dominated by commercial speed and cheap paper. Modern archival research by Paolo Camerini and William A. Pettas has illuminated Bernardo’s sophisticated financial arrangements, including his reliance on consortiums, advance privileges (copyrights) granted by the Pope and the Grand Duke, and cross-border book exchange networks (cambio di libri) connected to the Frankfurt Book Fair. Bernardo Giunta’s long career, terminating around 1596, marked the sunset of the golden age of Florentine Renaissance typography. By synthesizing technical mastery, scholarly rigor, and shrewd political alignment, Bernardo II preserved the cultural primacy of Florence and bequeathed to posterity some of the most beautiful and textually influential books of the sixteenth century.

academic_description: 8vo (mm 150x90). 135, [1] ll. Collation: A-R8. Printer's device on title page and on last leaf recto. Late 17th-centry or early 18th-century Italian morocco, panels within a triple gilt fillet, flat spine richly gilt with gilt title, marbled endleaves, inside gilt dentelles, gilt edges (small repair to spine and back panel, corners and hinges a bit worn). Minor scattered foxing, but a very good copy.First edition, published posthumously by Lorenzo Scala and by him dedicated to Francesco Miniati, of this fortunate collection of poetry.The poems are addressed to Selvaggia (from the Prato family of the Buonamici, the woman loved by the poet), Annibal Caro, Camillo Tonti, Dada Buonvisa, to the women from Prato, Filippo Ciconini (in death of Bartolomeo Gerardacci), Vincenzo Visconti, Giovanfrancesco Buonamici, Domenico Perini, Verdespina, Santi Quattro, Clemenza Buonamici, Lucrezia Tornabuoni, Martinozzo, Inghirano, Pandolfo Pucci, Giovanni Lanciolina, Giovanbattista del Milanese, Leo Villani (a bricklayer), Guido Antonio Adimari, Lasca, and Gualterotto de Bardi. The volume contains also imitation poems from Horace, two elegies, a canzone in praise of the sausage, a song in praise of the holy wood, a chapter in praise of thirst, and one in the death of an owl.At p. 60 it opens with a separate title-page the section Lagrime di Messer Agnolo Firenzuola nella violenta morte d'un giovane nobile napoletano, dedicated to the noblewoman from Prato Clemenza Roca. At p. 89 begins Il Sacrificio pastorale (cf. D. Maestri, Le rime di Agnolo Firenzuola: proposta di un ordinamento del testo e valutazione critica, in: “Italianistica”, III, 1974, pp. 78-96).Agnolo Firenzuola, a native of Florence, following in the footsteps of his father, a notary, studied law at Siena and Perugia, where he met Claudio Tolomei and Pietro Aretino. Upon graduation, he took the holy habit at Vallombrosa and in 1518 moved to Rome, where he became the procurator of the order at the Curia. In Rome, he formed a literary circle with his Sienna and Arezzo friends and made the acquaintance of P. Bembo, A. Caro and G. Della Casa. In 1526 he was dispensed from his vows and contracted syphilis, a disease that plagued him for a long time. The main reason why he decided to give up the habit was the meeting with a cultivated Roman noblewoman, wife of a lawyer, whom Firenzuola praises in many of his works under the pseudonym of Costanza Amaretta. In 1538 he moved to Prato, where he founded the Accademia dell'Addiaccio and embraced again the monastic life, becoming abbot of the Monastery of San Salvatore. In the last years he went through a legal dispute with his sister over their father's legacy and various quarrels with local families. Firenzuola died in absolute solitude at Prato on June 27, 1543.All his works, except the Discacciamento de le lettere inutilmente aggiunte ne la lingua toscana (‘Expulsion of the letters unnecessarily added to the Tuscan language') published at Rome in 1524, were posthumously edited by his brother Girolamo, who entrusted L. Scala and L. Domenichi with the publication of Agnolo's papers: the Prose appeared in 1548; the comedies I Lucidi and Trinunzia in 1549; and the Asino d'oro (‘Golden Ass'), an adaptation from Apuleius' masterpiece, in 1550 (cf. F. Pignatti, Firenzuola, Agnolo, in: “Dizionario biografico degli Italiani”, XLVIII, 1997, s.v.).

title: La navigation aérienne en Chine. Relation d’un voyage accompli en 1860 entre Foutcheou et Nant-Chang par Delaville-Dedreux
publisher_data: Paris, Chez Desloges (Imprimerie de Ch. Bonnet), 1863
academic_description: 8vo (183x116 mm). 71, 3 (catalogue of the bookseller Desloges) pp. Half-title, wood-engraved plate depicting a fantastical Chinese-style balloon, some foxing and staining, partly unopened, original printed wrappers. Rare first edition of this curious work in which the author expounds his ideas on airships by way of an imaginary balloon voyage to China. Mareschal begins by citing the claim that a balloon was launched at Peking in 1306, enabling him to propose that aerial navigation in China had achieved a state of perfection that was unknown in Europe. The narrative that follows, partly in the form of a dialogue with the author’s fellow balloonist, Kié-Fo, allows Mareschal to make various observations on aeronautics at a time of considerable development in airship technology: only a few years after Henri Giffard’s pioneering engine-powered flight of 1852. There is also a notably early suggestion that the North Pole could be reached by aerostat, which would entail a journey of about 600 miles each way and which, given favourable winds, could be covered in two days.

publishers.name: Ciotti Giovanni Battista
publishers.biography: Giovanni Battista Ciotti (Siena, c. 1560 – Palermo, c. 1625) stands as one of the most dynamic, commercially innovative, and intellectually consequential publisher-booksellers (librari) operating in late Renaissance and early Baroque Europe. Active across the chief intellectual capitals of the Italian peninsula and connected directly to Northern European trade hubs through the Frankfurt Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse), Ciotti occupied a central node in the international transmission of philosophy, literature, and scientific thought. Operating primarily under his famous printer's mark depicting Pallas Athena/Minerva holding a shield and olive branch (All'insegna della Minerva), Ciotti bridged the elite humanist networks of Venice with the burgeoning book markets of the Kingdom of Naples, Sicily, and the Holy Roman Empire. His publishing house was intimately entangled with some of the most influential and controversial figures of the era, most notably the philosopher Giordano Bruno, the epic poet Torquato Tasso, the dramatist Battista Guarini, and the Baroque poet Giambattista Marino.Born in Siena shortly after 1560, Ciotti spent his early youth in a Tuscan city navigating political integration into the Grand Duchy of Tuscany under the Medici dynasty. Recognizing the limited commercial scope of the Sienese book market, Ciotti migrated in his late adolescence or early adulthood to Venice, the indisputable capital of European typography and international book trade. In Venice, Ciotti underwent a rigorous apprenticeship within the dense network of workshops situated around the Rialto and the parish of San Giuliano. He mastered not only the physical mechanics of presswork and font selection but also the intricate financial mechanisms of early modern publishing, including credit management, international bill exchanges (lettere di cambio), joint-venture publishing partnerships, and the complex legal negotiations required to secure printing privileges (privilegi) from the Venetian Senate and the Council of Ten.By 1583–1584, Ciotti established his independent shop in Venice, adopting the device of Minerva—a figure symbolizing wisdom, strategic intellect, and editorial vigilance. Rather than relying exclusively on maintaining a massive printing office with personal presses, Ciotti operated as a high-level publisher and distributor. He frequently commissioned typography from specialized Venetian printing shops—such as those of Bernardo Giunti, Giacomo Franceschi, and the Bindoni family—while retaining full editorial control, financing, and trademark distribution. His production was characterized by elegant typography, clear roman and italic fonts, well-executed woodcut initials, and ornate architectural title pages. Ciotti was quick to identify the emerging taste for Mannerist and early Baroque literature, publishing authorized and unauthorized editions of Torquato Tasso's epic poetry and theoretical treatises, as well as multiple editions of Battista Guarini's pastoral drama Il Pastor Fido, engaging in fierce commercial competition with rival Venetian publishers to secure peninsula-wide distribution.Ciotti's international reputation was cemented by his active, biannual attendance at the Frankfurt Book Fair, where Italian publishers exchanged Italian vernacular and Latin titles for Northern European scholarly, legal, and theological texts. It was during his visits to Frankfurt in 1590 that Ciotti developed a close relationship with the excommunicated Dominican philosopher Giordano Bruno. Ciotti took charge of importing and selling Bruno's complex Latin treatises printed in Germany, such as De minimo, De monade, and De innumerabilibus. In 1591, Ciotti acted as the primary intermediary who introduced Bruno to the wealthy Venetian patrician Zuan Mocenigo, who desired instruction in the art of memory (mnemonica). Ciotti facilitated Bruno's fateful return to Venice in late 1591, even providing the philosopher with lodging and studio space near his shop. Following Mocenigo's denunciation of Bruno to the Venetian Inquisition in May 1592, Ciotti was summoned as a key witness before the Holy Office. His detailed depositions before the inquisitorial tribunal remain one of the most vital historical sources for understanding Bruno's final European movements, reading habits, and publication history.Following the ordeal of the Bruno trial, Ciotti continued to expand his publishing enterprise, entering into a highly lucrative partnership with the poet Giambattista Marino. Ciotti published several early collections of Marino's poetry, helping to shape the emerging Baroque poetic style across Italian literary academies, including the Sienese Accademia dei Filomati and the Venetian circles that presaged the Accademia degli Incogniti. However, by the second decade of the seventeenth century, shifts in Venetian economic dominance, rising paper costs, and tightening ecclesiastical censorship prompted Ciotti to diversify his commercial operations southward. Between 1614 and 1617, Ciotti relocated his main operations to Palermo, the viceregal capital of Sicily.In Palermo, Ciotti filled a major structural void in the Sicilian printing landscape, bringing advanced Venetian typographical standards and international distribution channels to the island. He secured prestigious official appointments, becoming printer to the Senate of Palermo and to the Spanish Viceroy of Sicily. In his Sicilian workshop, situated near the Cassaro, Ciotti printed authoritative legal codes, municipal decrees, historical chronicles, religious works, and literary outputs for local academies, such as the Accademia dei Riaccesi. He maintained his publishing business in Palermo until his death, which occurred after 1625. Modern bibliographical scholarship—from Dennis E. Rhodes to Tiziana Pesenti and Angela Nuovo—regards Giovanni Battista Ciotti as a monumental figure in early modern publishing history, an entrepreneur whose vision linked Northern European academia with the Mediterranean world and whose press served as an essential engine of late Renaissance intellectual culture.

Woodcut decorative ornaments and initials. Later flexible vellum. On the last leaf verso manuscript dedication “Alla Serenis.ma Sig.ra Palazzina Anconitana” signed with the letter “G” and followed by the drawing of a heart within a square. Some light marginal staining. Rare first edition of this tragicomedy in five acts in verse dedicated to Giovanni Badoer on the occasion of his wedding with Maria Contarini.In the dedication, dated Venice, 20 September 1597, the author states that with this play he introduced something new into drama by bringing love stories far away from woods and rivers (i.e., pastoral and piscatorial dramas) and setting them for the first time in a urban landscape (Rome is the scene): “nel prendere argomento io della mia favola, Cittadino, & nell’introdurre Città, e Cittadini, forsi non ho fatto male” (l. A3v) (cf. L. Riccò, Minotauri, centauri, ermfroditi: misti e mostri teatrali italiani, in: “Norme per lo spettacolo, norme per lo spettatore: teoria e prassi del teatro intorno all’ ‘Arte Nuevo’ ”, G. Poggi & M.G. Profeti, Florence, 2011, p. 89).“Due secoli più tardi per condizione dei personaggi, non principi, non gente d’altissimo affare, ma semplici borghesi, il dramma del Turamini si sarebbe chiamato tragedia urbana” (E. Bertana, La tragedia, Milan, a. 1905, pp. 210-212).Born in Siena to a wealthy family, Bernardino Turamini decided to take the vows as an observant minor and to change his name to Giacomo. After the conversion his literary activity focused exclusively on religious themes. He later moved to Rome, where he entered the circle of the Barberini family and printed a series of sacred dramas based on the life of saints and biblical heroines.

authors.name: Clenardus Nicolaus
authors.biography: Clenardus Nicolaus (also known in his native Dutch as Nicolaas Cleynaerts or Cleynaert, and in French as Nicolas Clénard; 5 December 1495 – 5 November 1492) stands as one of the most enigmatic, original, and globally minded figures of Northern Renaissance Humanism. A consummate philologist, pedagogue, Hebraist, and pioneering Western Arabist, Clenardus transformed the pedagogical landscape of early modern Europe through his widely reprinted Greek and Hebrew grammars while simultaneously charting a radical, irenic path of interreligious dialogue. Operating at the vibrant intersection of the Erasmian trilingual movement in Brabant, the imperial courtly culture of Renaissance Spain and Portugal, and the Islamic scholastic centers of the Wattasid Sultanate in Fez, Clenardus embodied the ultimate expansion of humanist philology: a conviction that the rigorous, objective study of semitic and classical languages could transcend dogmatic violence, replace military crusade with scholarly persuasion, and forge intellectual bridges across the deeply divided Mediterranean world.Born in the Brabantine town of Diest in the Burgundian Netherlands, Clenardus hailed from a respectable middle-class family. In 1512, he matriculated at the University of Louvain (Leuven), entering the Pedagogium Porci (the College of the Pig), where he pursued the traditional arts curriculum, graduating as Licentiate of Arts in 1515. Rather than confining himself to traditional scholastic theology, Clenardus was captured by the intellectual revolution radiating from the newly established Collegium Trilingue (Collegium Buslidianum). Founded in 1517 under the spiritual aegis of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam and funded through the testament of the magistrate Jérôme de Busleyden, the Trilingue revolutionized Northern European education by institutionalizing the formal study of Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Clenardus immersed himself in these studies, receiving rigorous training in Greek from the humanist publisher and scholar Rutger Rescius, and in Hebrew from a succession of distinguished specialists including Matthaeus Adrianus, Robert Wakefield, Robert Shirwood, and Johannes Campensis. Concurrently appointed regent at the Pig College, Clenardus combined intensive theological studies with active teaching, rapidly recognizing that existing medieval grammatical manuals were bogged down in opaque terminology and inefficient scholastic taxonomy.Clenardus's period at Louvain culminated in a series of pedagogical masterpieces that established his international reputation. In 1529, he authored the Tabula in grammaticam Hebraeam, a revolutionary, single-sheet synoptic presentation of Hebrew grammar designed to grant students immediate visual clarity over complex verbal conjugations and declensional patterns. This was immediately followed by his crowning pedagogical achievements: the Institutiones in linguam Graecam (1530) and the Meditationes Graecanicae (1531). Clenardus approached Greek instruction not as an abstract speculative exercise, but as a dynamic, accessible craft. By streamlining declensions, standardizing paradigm tables, and prioritizing practical reading over endless theoretical exceptions, his Institutiones demystified Greek for generations of students. In the Meditationes, he paired systematic syntax rules with a running textual commentary on an epistle of Saint Basil the Great, guiding the novice step-by-step from elementary morphology to complex prose analysis. These works transformed Louvain into a premier center for Greek studies and earned Clenardus the admiration of humanist scholars throughout the Low Countries and Germany.Despite his academic success in Louvain, Clenardus felt an unquenchable wanderlust and an urgent intellectual impulse to master Arabic. In 1531, enticed by reports of rich manuscript holdings and the personal invitation of Hernando Colón (Ferdinand Columbus, son of Christopher Columbus), Clenardus departed the Netherlands for the Iberian Peninsula alongside his friend and fellow scholar Johannes Vasaeus (Jan Vaes). Reaching Spain in 1532, Clenardus served as librarian to Ferdinand Columbus in Seville, helping catalog and organize the legendary Biblioteca Colombina. He subsequently moved to the University of Salamanca to lecture on Greek and Latin, inserting himself into the brilliant intellectual milieu of Spanish humanists and scholastic reformers like Francisco de Vitoria and Hernán Núñez de Guzmán (El Pinciano). In 1533, his stellar reputation caught the attention of the Royal Court of Portugal; King João III and his court invited Clenardus to Évora and Lisbon to serve as preceptor to Prince Dom Henrique (the future Cardinal-King of Portugal). For five years (1533–1538), Clenardus moved within the highest courtly and ecclesiastical circles of Portugal, tutoring royal youths while systematically preparing for his ultimate life mission: the scholarly conquest of the Islamic world.Clenardus’s intellectual evolution during his Iberian years marked a decisive break with contemporary Christian attitudes toward Islam. Rejecting both the military ethos of the Reconquista and the coercive methods of the Inquisition, Clenardus argued that Islam could only be confronted through peaceful theological debate grounded in linguistic mastery of classical Arabic. However, learning Arabic in 16th-century Spain and Portugal presented monumental obstacles; printed grammars were non-existent, Arabic books were routinely seized and burned as suspected heresy, and qualified native teachers were suppressed. Undeterred, Clenardus deployed extraordinary methods: he purchased several enslaved Arabic native speakers—most notably a highly educated Moorish captive named Michel—who served as his personal scribes, teachers, and linguistic informants. Having achieved working proficiency in Arabic script and syntax, Clenardus resolved to journey to North Africa to study at the source. In 1540, he crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and took up residence in Fez, the cultural and academic heart of the Wattasid Sultanate. For fifteen months (1540–1541), Clenardus lived among Muslim scholars, frequented local madrasas, scoured book markets for rare classical codices, and engaged in candid, respectful theological disputations, compiling notes for an ambitious Arabic grammar, dictionary, and annotated Latin translation of the Qur'an.The publishing history and typographical circulation of Clenardus's works represent a monumental chapter in early modern print culture. His initial works were printed in Louvain by Rutger Rescius using elegant Greek fonts that modeled the best Venetian styles. Following Clenardus's departure for Spain and subsequent death, his Institutiones in linguam Graecam became the single most widely published Greek grammar in 16th- and 17th-century Europe, undergoing over five hundred editions across the continent. Master printers in every major typographical hub seized upon Clenardus's text: in Paris, Christian Wechel, Robert Estienne, and Adrien Turnèbe printed countless revised octavos; in Lyons, Sebastianus Gryphius and Jean de Tournes disseminated portable student editions; in Basel, Johann Froben and Nicolaus Episcopius issued heavily annotated versions; and in Antwerp, Christopher Plantin produced definitive editions corrected by leading philologists such as Petrus Antesignanus and Friedrich Sylburg. Furthermore, Clenardus's vibrant, witty, and deeply candid personal letters—collected and published posthumously as Epistolarum libri duo (first fully issued in Louvain in 1550 and later by Plantin in 1566)—became immediate classics of Renaissance epistolary prose, offering invaluable ethnographic insights into early modern Spanish, Portuguese, and Moroccan society.Exhausted by intense physical hardship, financial deprivation, and political hostility in Morocco, Clenardus returned to Spain in 1542 with the dream of establishing a specialized trilingual academy in Granada dedicated to training Christian scholars in Arabic, Greek, and Hebrew. Before his visionary project could materialize, he succumbed to illness and died in Granada on November 5, 1542, at the age of forty-six; he was laid to rest within the grounds of the Alhambra in the Church of Santa María. Though his proposed Arabic college died with him and many of his prized Arabic manuscripts were scattered or lost, Clenardus's legacy endured powerfully. His Greek grammar remained the standard university textbook throughout Europe for over two centuries, shaping the classical education of thinkers from Justus Lipsius and Joseph Scaliger to Isaac Casaubon. In modern historiography, Clenardus is celebrated not only as a master pedagogue of the Northern Renaissance, but as a prophetic visionary of comparative philological orientalism and peaceful cross-cultural engagement.

publishers.name: Plantin Christophe
publishers.biography: Christophe Plantin (c. 1520 – 1 July 1589) stands as one of the most monumental figures in the history of Western typography, textual transmission, and early modern scholarly publishing. Operating at the commercial and intellectual epicenter of sixteenth-century Europe, Plantin transformed the craft of printing into an international industrial enterprise and a cornerstone of Northern Renaissance Humanism. As the founder of the legendary Officina Plantiniana in Antwerp, Plantin orchestrated an unprecedented synthesis of typographic aesthetics, textual accuracy, and commercial distribution. Appointed Architypographus Regius (Arch-printer to the King) by Philip II of Spain, Plantin produced some of the most intricate typographical monuments of the Renaissance—most notably the magnificent eight-volume Antwerp Polyglot Bible (Biblia Regia). His career traversed the violent political, religious, and socio-economic upheavals of the Low Countries during the Eighty Years' War, requiring an extraordinary capacity for ideological navigation between Catholic Habsburg authority and clandestine heterodox spiritualist movements.Born in the hamlet of Saint-Avertin near Tours, France, around 1520, Plantin’s early life was overshadowed by tragic dislocation. Following the death of his mother during a devastating plague outbreak, his father Jean Plantin relocated the family to Lyon. Plantin was subsequently sent to Paris and later to Caen in Normandy, where he entered his formative apprenticeship under the renowned master bookbinder and bookseller Robert Macé II during the late 1530s. In Caen, Plantin mastered the meticulous disciplines of leatherbinding, gilding, and codicological architecture, while acquiring a solid working knowledge of Latin, French, and classical literature. Around 1545, he returned to Paris, marrying Jeanne Rivière, with whom he would raise a family deeply integrated into his publishing empire. In search of dynamic economic expansion and seeking to escape the oppressive religious censorship imposed by the Sorbonne in Paris, Plantin relocated with his wife to Antwerp in 1548 or 1549. At that time, Antwerp was the unchallenged financial and mercantile capital of Northern Europe, boasting a thriving community of international merchants, engravers, papermakers, and humanist intellectuals.Upon establishing residency in Antwerp, Plantin registered as a citizen (poorter) and quickly gained a stellar reputation as a master craftsman of decorated leather caskets and luxury bookbindings for the high nobility. However, a violent encounter in 1555 fundamentally altered his career trajectory: while walking through the streets of Antwerp at night to deliver an ornate leather casket commissioned for Gabriel de Çayas, secretary to King Philip II, Plantin was ambushed by masked assailants who mistook him for another individual. Plantin suffered a severe shoulder and arm wound inflicted by a sword, which rendered heavy physical labor such as leather binding exceedingly difficult. Adapting with characteristic resilience, Plantin pivoted entirely to typographical printing. In May 1555, he issued his inaugural publication: Giovanni Michele Bruto’s La Institutione di una fanciulla nata nobilmente (The Education of a Noble Maiden), presented with parallel Italian and French translations. From this modest beginning, Plantin rapidly assembled capital, acquired high-quality punch-cuts, and hired master compositors, giving birth to the Officina Plantiniana. He adopted his famous printer's mark—a hand holding a pair of compasses emerging from a cloud, accompanied by the Latin motto Labore et Constantia ("By Labor and Constancy"), in which the fixed leg symbolized constancy and the moving leg represented labor.Beneath his public image as a devout Roman Catholic subject of the Spanish Empire, Plantin engaged in complex, highly secret affiliations with radical heterodox spiritualist networks. Throughout the 1550s and 1560s, he became a central figure in the Familia Caritatis (Family of Love or Familists), a mystical, non-dogmatic spiritual movement founded by the Westphalian merchant Hendrick Niclaes. Plantin served as the secret printer for Niclaes’s esoteric writings, which advocated an internal, non-confessional spiritual rebirth while advising external conformity to established ecclesiastical authorities. Following a rift within the movement in the 1570s, Plantin aligned himself with the dissident Familist prophet Hiël (Hendrik Jansen van Barrefelt), printing Hiël's allegorical mystical treatises under cryptic pseudonyms. Concurrently, Plantin cultivated open and immensely productive relationships with leading Humanist scholars, scientists, and philologists across Europe. The Officina Plantiniana functioned as an intellectual academy, hosting intellectual luminaries such as the neo-Stoic philosopher Justus Lipsius, the Flemish cartographer Abraham Ortelius, the pioneering botanists Carolus Clusius (Charles de l'Écluse), Rembert Dodoens, and Matthias de l'Obel, and the diplomat Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq. Plantin revolutionized scientific publishing by commissioning detailed botanical and anatomical woodcuts and copperplate engravings, while publishing authoritative critical editions of ancient classical texts edited by scholars such as Lipsius and Theodor Poelman.Plantin’s undisputed typographical masterpiece was the publication of the monumental Biblia Sacra Hebraice, Chaldaice, Graece et Latine, commonly known as the Antwerp Polyglot Bible or Biblia Regia. Produced between 1568 and 1572 with substantial financial backing and official patronage from King Philip II of Spain, this massive eight-volume folio set was conceived to supersede the earlier Complutensian Polyglot and establish a standardized, philologically precise text for biblical research. To direct the editorial enterprise, Philip II sent his chief court chaplain, the eminent Spanish theologian and orientalist Benito Arias Montano, to Antwerp. Montano and Plantin developed an extraordinarily close scholarly partnership, coordinating an international team of linguists and proofreaders including Guy Le Fèvre de La Boderie, Andreas Masius, and Franciscus Raphelengius (Plantin’s brilliant son-in-law, who was a master of Near Eastern languages). The printing of the Polyglot required unprecedented technical resources: thousands of pounds of specialized lead types cast in Hebrew, Aramaic (Chaldean), Greek, Syriac, and Latin, designed by legendary typefounders such as Robert Granjon, Claude Garamond, Pierre Haultin, and François Guyot. Printed on high-grade royal paper with magnificent copperplate frontispieces executed by artists such as Philip Galle and Pieter van der Heyden, the Antwerp Polyglot solidified Plantin’s international reputation as the undisputed premier printer of Christendom.Recognizing Plantin's unmatched operational capacity, Philip II granted him the prestigious title of Architypographus Regius in 1570, accompanying the appointment with an exclusive royal privilege (monopoly) for printing standardized Roman Catholic liturgical books—including the Missale Romanum, Breviarium Romanum, Diurnale, and Officium Beatae Mariae Virginis—for Spain and its global territories in the Americas. To fulfill these staggering production quotas, Plantin scaled up the Officina Plantiniana into the largest printing establishment in the world, running up to twenty-two printing presses concurrently and employing over eighty pressmen, compositors, proofreaders, and engravers. Plantin was a pioneer in industrial workflow, introducing standardized typographical design, innovative musical notation printing using custom musical fonts cut by Pierre Haultin and Guillaume Le Bé, and rigorous scholarly proofreading. He employed eminent internal correctors such as Cornelis Kiliaan, who compiled the foundational dictionary of the Dutch language (Dictionarium Teutonico-Latinum) under Plantin's direct editorial patronage.The devastating socio-political cataclysms of the Dutch Revolt severely tested Plantin's administrative genius. During the disastrous "Spanish Fury" of November 1576, when unpaid Spanish soldiers sacked Antwerp, Plantin was forced to pay enormous ransoms on nine separate occasions to prevent his workshop from being looted and burned. Facing financial distress, broken supply chains, and mounting unpaid debts owed by the Spanish Crown, Plantin demonstrated astonishing political adaptability. While maintaining his Antwerp operations under the Protestant Calvinist Republic that governed the city between 1577 and 1585, he expanded his enterprise northwards. In 1583, leaving the management of his main Antwerp press to his capable son-in-law Jan Moretus (Jan Moerentorf), Plantin established a branch in Leiden. Appointed official printer to the newly founded University of Leiden and the States-General of Holland, Plantin published scholarly works for prominent Protestant humanists such as Joseph Justus Scaliger and Justus Lipsius, insulating his enterprise from regional devastation.Following the siege and reconquest of Antwerp by the Duke of Parma, Alexander Farnese, in August 1585, Plantin returned to his primary Antwerp establishment, leaving the Leiden branch under the direction of his son-in-law Franciscus Raphelengius. Although his final years were burdened by heavy financial debts resulting from royal arrears, Plantin preserved the high scholarly rigor and typographical distinction of his press until his death on July 1, 1589. He was interred in the Cathedral of Our Lady in Antwerp. Having no surviving sons, Plantin devised his enterprise to his daughters and sons-in-law: Jan Moretus took ownership of the main Antwerp press, which continued to trade as the Officina Plantiniana for centuries, while Raphelengius directed the scholarly press in Leiden. The Antwerp establishment remained in the continuous possession of the Moretus family until 1876, when Edward Moretus sold the fully preserved complex—complete with historical presses, punches, matrices, manuscripts, and archives—to the City of Antwerp. Today, preserved as the UNESCO-listed Plantin-Moretus Museum, Plantin’s legacy stands as an immortal monument to humanistic scholarship, typographical perfection, and the transformative power of the early modern book trade.

related_names.name: Clusius Carolus
related_names.biography: Carolus Clusius (the Latinized moniker of Charles de l'Écluse, born 19 February 1526 in Arras; died 4 April 1609 in Leiden) stands as one of the most transcendent figures in Northern Renaissance natural philosophy, serving as a primary architect of modern empirical botany, floristics, and descriptive plant morphology. Operating at the vibrant intersection of late sixteenth-century humanist philology and observational natural history, Clusius liberated the study of plants from its subservience to classical pharmacological compendia, such as those of Dioscorides and Galen. Through an immense international epistolary network spanning the entirety of the Respublica Literaria, Clusius facilitated the global exchange of botanical specimens, seeds, and woodcut illustrations, fundamentally reshaping early modern European horticulture, agronomy, and medical botany. His foundational role in introducing exotic flora—most famously the tulip (Tulipa gesneriana), the potato (Solanum tuberosum), the horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), and the crown imperial (Fritillaria imperialis)—to Western and Central Europe laid the empirical and aesthetic foundations for the Golden Age of Dutch horticulture and early modern botanical garden architecture.Born into a prosperous and influential patrician family in Arras (then part of the French-speaking Southern Netherlands under Habsburg sovereignty), Clusius was educated in an atmosphere saturated with legal erudition and Christian humanism. His father, Michel de l'Écluse, served as a seigneurial councillor at the Abbey of Saint-Vaart. Clusius commenced his academic trajectory at the famed Latin school in Ghent before matriculating at the University of Louvain (Leuven) to study jurisprudence and humanities at the Collegium Trilingue. Driven by an insatiable intellectual restlessness and growing sympathies for Protestant reformist thought, he ventured to Germany in 1548, enrolling at the University of Marburg under the distinguished jurist Johann Oldendorp. However, his pivotal intellectual epiphany occurred during his subsequent sojourn at the University of Wittenberg, where he studied under the charismatic humanist reformer Philipp Melanchthon. Melanchthon’s pedagogical philosophy, which emphasized the direct observation of the physical cosmos as an exercise in divine order, steered Clusius away from the dry legal codices toward the study of the natural world.In 1551, Clusius migrated to Southern France to enter the renowned Faculty of Medicine at the University of Montpellier. There, he was admitted into the household of the legendary physician and ichthyologist Guillaume Rondelet. Rondelet’s domestic circle functioned as an informal academy for the leading lights of Renaissance naturalism, bringing Clusius into contact with contemporary cohorts such as Laurent Joubert, Mathias de Lobel (Lobelius), and Pierre Pena. Under Rondelet’s rigorous mentorship, Clusius developed an extraordinary eye for field observation, anatomical dissection, and comparative specimen analysis. Rather than remaining within the parameters of clinical medical practice, Clusius gravitated entirely toward descriptive botany and botanical translation. Returning to the Low Countries, he published his first major contribution: a masterly French translation of Rembert Dodoens’s Cruydeboeck, entitled Histoire des plantes (Antwerp: Jean Loë, 1557), which established his reputation as a formidable translator capable of mediating complex vernacular natural history into elegant scholarly prose.During the 1560s and 1570s, Clusius embarked upon extensive botanical expeditions across Western and Central Europe. In 1564–1565, while serving as preceptor to the young Fugger brothers (Jakob and Anton Fugger, scions of the immense Augsburg banking dynasty), Clusius traversed the Iberian Peninsula. Over nineteen months of arduous field research across Spain and Portugal, he surveyed alpine regions, coastal zones, and arid plateaus, identifying over two hundred previously undescribed plant species. The results of this pioneering expedition were published by the press of Christopher Plantin in Antwerp as Rariorum aliquot stirpium per Hispanias observatarum historia (1576). This landmark text was notable not only for its precise Latin descriptions but also for its exceptionally detailed woodcut illustrations, setting a new standard for floristic surveys of specific geographical regions.Clusius’s extraordinary expertise brought him to the attention of the Habsburg imperial court. In 1573, Emperor Maximilian II summoned Clusius to Vienna to serve as the imperial court botanist and director of the newly projected imperial botanical garden (Hortus Medicus). Clusius retained this prestigious post under Emperor Rudolf II until 1588. During his fifteen years in Vienna, Clusius transformed the imperial capital into an epicentre of botanical research. He undertook exhaustive field explorations of the Austrian Alps, Styria, Carinthia, and the Pannonian plains of Hungary. These travels culminated in his groundbreaking publication Rariorum aliquot stirpium, per Pannonias, Austriam, & alias quasdam vicinas provincias observatarum historia (Antwerp: Plantin, 1583). Within this work, Clusius appended the Fungorum in Pannoniis observatorum brevis historia—the very first dedicated monograph on regional mycology in European history, in which he systematically categorized and illustrated dozens of edible and poisonous fungal species.It was during his Viennese period that Clusius received living specimens of central Asian and Ottoman flora from his close friend and correspondent Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, the Habsburg ambassador to the Sublime Porte in Constantinople. Busbecq dispatched bulbs of tulips, lilies, and sweet chestnuts to Clusius, who successfully cultivated and propagated them in the imperial soil of Vienna. Following political and religious tensions at the Catholic court of Rudolf II, Clusius resigned his post in 1588 and relocated to Frankfurt am Main. However, in 1593, the Curators of the newly established University of Leiden extended an irresistible invitation, appointing Clusius as Professor of Botany and founding prefect of the Hortus Botanicus Leiden. Though advanced in age and suffering from severe physical infirmities incurred during his field travels, Clusius transformed Leiden into the premiere botanical research facility of Northern Europe. He designed the physical arrangement of the garden's four quadrangles, organizing plants according to systematic structural characteristics rather than mere alphabetical or therapeutic criteria.The publishing history of Clusius’s major works represents one of the most celebrated chapters in early modern typography, defined by his decades-long symbiosis with the printer Christopher Plantin and Plantin’s successor Jan Moretus of Antwerp. Plantin recognized Clusius’s genius and spared no expense in producing his works. Plantin commissioned master draftsmanship from artists such as Peeter van der Borcht, whose drawings were subsequently engraved into high-relief woodblocks by premier woodcutters including Arnold Nicolai, Gerard van Kampen, and Cornelis Muller. Clusius’s ultimate achievements culminated in two massive, masterwork folios published by the Officina Plantiniana: the Rariorum plantarum historia (1601), which brought together his Iberian and Pannonian flora along with expanded mycological and horticultural studies, and the monumental Exoticorum libri decem (1605). In the Exoticorum, Clusius collected, translated, annotated, and illustrated all known information regarding global exotic natural history, incorporating his Latin translations of Garcia de Orta’s Indian medical treatise, Nicolás Monardes’s New World flora, and Cristóbal Acosta’s oriental materia medica, alongside empirical reports from Dutch and English maritime voyages (including items brought back by Sir Francis Drake and Sir Walter Raleigh).The critical reception and enduring legacy of Carolus Clusius are immense. By severing botany from classical authority and grounding it in direct morphological observation, precise artistic rendering, and transatlantic specimen exchange, Clusius laid the empirical groundwork for the later taxonomical syntheses of Caspar Bauhin, Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, and ultimately Carl Linnaeus. His introduction of the tulip to the Low Countries directly fueled the horticultural craze that culminated in the Dutch Tulipmania of the 1630s, while his meticulous documentation of New World species such as the potato, tobacco, and cocoa provided Europe with its earliest systematic scientific accounts of global biodiversity. Clusius passed away in Leiden in April 1609, leaving behind an indelible monument in the history of science as the true patriarch of early modern descriptive botany.

academic_description: 8vo. 258 [i.e. 242, with errors in the pagination], [4] pp., [1 blank] leaf. Collation: A-F8, G-H4, I-Q8, R4. Blank R4. With the printer's device on the title-pages of both parts. 18th-century calf, richly gilt back, marbled edges and endpapers. With the printed ex-libris: Bibliothèque de la Bastide-Pomme. First edition, edited by the humanist physician and pioneering botanist Carolus Clusius (1526-1609) from the originals he found in Granada and Salamanca. This is the only edition printed in the 16th century (cf. Correspondance de Nicolas Clénard publié par Alphonse Roersch, Bruxelles, 1940-1941).Book I contains 24 letters, Book II 21. On the verso of the title-page is a preface to the reader by Christopher Plantin dated Antwerp, March 1, 1566. At the beginning of the second part is a letter by Carolus Clusius to Thomas Rediger dated Bruges, January 1, 1566.Most notable are the letters to Johannes Latomus of July 1539 and April 1541, which contain quotations in Arabic, and the Epistola ad Christianos de professione Arabica, militiaque constituenda adversus Machometum, in which Clenardus describes his method of learning Arabic and reports his observation on Islam. Granada, January 17, 1542 (p. 212)Epistola ad Christianos de professione Arabica, militiaque constituenda adversus Machometum (p. 218) Nicolaus Clenardus, a native of Diest in Brabant, matriculated in 1512 at the University of Louvain. After graduating in 1515 he taught arts courses in his college, the Pig, while taking up the study of theology under Jacobus Latomus, who was to remain his friend for life.A priest from about 1521, Clenardus succeeded Jan Driedo as president of Houterlee's College. This appointment permitted him to pursue his humanistic studies with the help of Goclenius, Rescius, and Jan van Campen, professors at the Collegium Trilingue.During Erasmus' years at Louvain Clenardus did not took up any personal ties with him, although he owed a considerable debt to Erasmus's epistolary style and general views. He taught privately and established his reputation as a Hebrew scholar with Tabula ad grammaticam hebraeam (1529). He also published two textbooks for students of Greek, Institutiones in linguam graecam (1530) and Meditationes graecanicae in artem grammaticam (1531), both of which met with great success and were used by generations of students.When his terms as president of Houterlee's college had ended and Louvain did not seem to offer any further prospects for the time being (probably by a lack of reverence and prudence), Clenardus was compelled to look elsewhere.Juan Luis Vives seems to have convinced him that Muslims could be converted to the Christian faith by force of persuasion, and he resolved to learn Arabic. He then entered the service of Hernando Colón, the son of the discoverer of America, whom he accompanied back to Spain towards the end of 1531. He taught Greek and Latin at Salamanca until 1533, when he joined Prince Henry of Portugal, who at the age of twenty-one was already archbishop of Braga. Under Henry's auspices, Clenardus founded a humanist college at Braga, which he directed until 1538. Thereafter Henry's support enabled him to study Arabic in Granada and for a while in 1540 at Fez in Morocco. He was still in Granada at the time of his death (cf. H. de Vocht, History of the Foundation and the Rise of the Collegium Trilingue Lovaniense, 1517-1550, Louvain, 1951-1955, II, pp. 220-234).

title: Les Lettres

authors.name: Pasquier Étienne
authors.biography: After graduating from the renowned Collège de Presle in 1546, Étienne Pasquier studied with the greatest legal humanists of his day. From François Hotman, François Baudouin, Jacques Cujas, and Andrea Alciati, he acquired a profound sense of the reality of laws and institutions, which led him assert the importance of the French political and cultural inheritance over and against classical Roman and modern Italian models. His public career and private scholarship advanced apace.In 1549 he was called to the Paris bar. In 1558 he became very ill through eating poisonous mushrooms, and did not recover fully for two years. This compelled him to occupy himself with literary work. In 1564 he represented the University of Paris in a famous lawsuit with the Jesuits, whom he portrayed as agents of Romanist tyranny seeking to undermine the liberties of the Gallican church. In 1585 he became advocate general of the Chambre des Comptes in Paris, one of the sovereign courts, and in 1588 he left the city as a deputy to the meeting of the Estates General at Blois.A Politique and staunch opponent of the ultramontane Catholic League that just seized control of Paris, he did not return to his magistracy until Henry IV officially entered the city in 1594. During his absence from public life, he assembled a new six-book edition of his Recherches. He continued his work in the Chambre des Comptes until 1604 and then retired. He survived this retirement more than ten years, producing much literary work.
authors.bibliography: D. Thickett, Estienne Pasquier: The Versatile Barrister of Sixteenth-Century France, London, 1979, passim.

publishers.name: L'Angelier Abel
publishers.biography: Abel L'Angelier (ca. 1553 – 1610) stands as one of the most transformative figures in the history of early modern French publishing, typography, and intellectual culture. Operating from his famed boutique in the Grand'Salle of the Palais de Justice in Paris during the turbulent decades of the French Wars of Religion and the reign of Henri IV, L'Angelier was not merely a merchant of bound sheets, but a master orchestrator of late Renaissance humanism, Neo-Stoicism, Italianate vernacular literature, and early Baroque aesthetics. His publishing house functioned as a crucial nexus for the French Politiques—the moderate political and legal thinkers who sought peace through state sovereignty and religious tolerance—and served as the primary launching pad for some of the most enduring monuments of European literature, most notably the expanded 1588 edition of Michel de Montaigne’s Essais and the esoteric, antiquarian treatises of Blaise de Vigenère.Born into a prominent dynasty of Parisian University booksellers (libraires jurés de l'Université de Paris), Abel was the son of Arnoul L'Angelier, a well-established publisher active in the mid-sixteenth century. Steeped from infancy in the mechanics of the book trade, young Abel received a rigorous humanist education, acquiring fluency in Latin and Italian alongside his native French. Upon entering the Parisian booksellers' guild in the mid-1570s, he quickly positioned himself at the cutting edge of modern vernacular publishing. His professional and social standing was further solidified in 1578 by his marriage to Françoise de Louvain, the daughter of a respected printing family. Françoise proved to be an indispensable intellectual and managerial partner, running the business alongside Abel and continuing its operation for a decade after his death in 1610 under the imprint of Veuve Abel L'Angelier.The literary and philosophical significance of L'Angelier’s catalog can hardly be overstated. In 1588, Montaigne selected L'Angelier to publish the monumental fifth edition of his Essais (the famous quarto edition), which marked the first appearance of the third book of essays and contained over six hundred additions to the first two books. Montaigne traveled specifically to Paris to supervise the printing in L'Angelier’s orbit, forging an intellectual alliance that would shape the history of Western philosophy. Following Montaigne’s death, L'Angelier, in collaboration with the publisher Michel Sonnius and under the passionate editorial stewardship of Marie de Gournay—Montaigne's "fille d'alliance"—published the definitive post-humous 1595 folio edition of the Essais. Beyond Montaigne, L'Angelier was the chief publisher of Blaise de Vigenère, ushering into print his groundbreaking Traicté des Chiffres (1586), his translations of Thucydides and Livy, and his magnificent, illustrated commentary on Philostratus, Les Images ou Tableaux de platte peinture. L'Angelier also nurtured the burgeoning genre of French prose fiction and Mannerist literature, issuing major works by François Béroalde de Verville (including Le Leat de la Constance and the alchemical romance Le Tableau des riches inventions), Nicolas de Montreux, Pierre de Larivey’s Italianate comedies, and Guillaume Bouchet’s Les Sérées.In terms of printing history and topographical dynamics, L'Angelier operated primarily as a libraire-éditeur rather than a master printer who owned press equipment. His shop was strategically located "au premier pilier de la Grand'Salle du Palais"—the heart of the judicial and administrative life of Paris. This location guaranteed direct access to an affluent, highly educated clientele comprising magistrates of the Parlement de Paris, royal officers, humanists, and visiting nobles. L'Angelier sub-contracted the physical printing of his editions to top-tier Parisian typography workshops, such as those of Jean Le Blanc, Denis Binet, and Pierre Le Mur, exercising meticulous oversight over paper quality, font selection (frequently utilizing elegant French Cicéro and Augustin Roman and Italic types), and layout design. He was an early pioneer in the artistic integration of copperplate engravings into vernacular texts, commissioning renowned artists like Jacques Granthomme to produce intricate frontispieces, allegorical portraits, and emblem books that defined the visual vocabulary of the French late Renaissance.The legacy of Abel L'Angelier remains central to the historiography of the book. Navigating the treacherous ideological terrain of the Catholic League's siege of Paris and the eventual restoration of monarchical stability under Henri IV, L'Angelier maintained a editorial program rooted in intellectual cosmopolitanism, political moderation, and literary innovation. He effectively popularized Italian Renaissance masterpieces in French translation through scholars like Gabriel Chappuys, while simultaneously establishing a canon of native French prose. Following Abel's death in late November 1610, Françoise de Louvain maintained the house's prestige until her own passing in 1620. Modern bibliographical scholarship, led by pioneer historians such as Michel Simonin and Jean Vignes, recognizes L'Angelier not simply as a bookseller, but as a central architect of early modern French literary culture who bridged the world of High Humanism and the nascent classical era.

Pasquier's collection of 149 letters (in 10 books) published during his lifetime (a sequel - books XI-XXII - was published posthumously in 1619).“In Pasquier's epistolary practice, moreover, the exercise of the literary imagination is largely a function of an engaged historical consciousness. Pasquier the historian is attentive to the particular in both his own life and the life of his nation: childbirth, the marriage of a son, and various incidents in the wars of religion are equally worthy of original tropes. In putting together the first ten books of his letters, published in a single handsome quarto volume when he was fifty-seven years old, Pasquier rejoices in the diversity of the book […] Pasquier publishes as an accomplished, independent, mature writer, seeking chiefly to encourage other writers to do the same in their own language and way. Accordingly Pasquier infuses his letters with a strong personal style, making his book into a collection of highly autobiographical essays that could be read alongside those of his friend Montaigne” (J.G. Altman, The Letter Book as a Literary Institution 1539-1789: Toward a Cultural History of Published Correspondences in France, in: “Yale French Studies”, 71, 1986, pp. 22-23).“Considérées une à une, les Lettres de Pasquier peuvent être rattachées à différent genres, qui d'ailleurs ne révèlent pas toujours de l'épistolaire, d'où la tentation de les classer autrement que l'a voulu l'écrivain. Mais lorsqu'on les envisage dans la perspective du projet éditorial, on constate qu'elles constituent un tableau dont chaque coup de pinceau est indispensable à l'équilibre de l'ensemble. Il ne s'agit pas ici d'une publication d'archives ou de mise en recueil posthume. Pasquier entreprend de peindre les méandres d'un mou sur lequel pèsent des tabous séculaires avec une pudeur qui s'évanouit au fil du temps et une cohérence qui ne cesse de croître. Il prend ses lettres comme des matériaux bruts qu'il assemble et modifie au gré de sa fantaisie, tantôt dans un savant désordre, tantôt en reconstituant la succession chronologique ou en procédant à un regroupement thématique. Si toutes les lettres du recueil ne sont pas familières, l'œuvre, elle relève indéniablement du genre familier” (L. Vaillancourt, La lettre familière au XVIe siècle. authors.name: Sabellico Marco Antonio
authors.biography: Marcantonio da Coccio, better known as Marcantonio Sabellico, was born of poor parents in Vicovaro (northeast of Rome). He received his early schooling in his native town and then continued his studies in Rome under Pomponio Leto, Gasparino Barzizza, Domizio Calderini, and Porcelio Pandone. While in Rome he took part in the life of Leto's Roman Academy and adopted his humanistic ‘nom de plume': Sabellico. In 1473 he was called to Udine to teach rhetoric but also continued his studies in dialectics, mathematics, and Greek. In 1482 appeared his first work in print De vetustate Aquileiae patriae. He was dismissed from his employment in Udine, and spent over a year in Verona, where he completed twenty-two of the thirty-three books of his history of Venice. In 1487 he presented this work (printed in 1487) to the doge and senate, and soon afterwards he was appointed to the second public lectureship in the humanities at the school of San Marco (cf. F.Lepori, La scuola di Rialto dalla fondazione alla metà del Cinquecento, in: “Storia della cultura veneta. Dal primo Quattrocento al Concilio di Trento”, G. Arnaldi & M. Pastore Stocchi, eds., Vicenza, 1980/81, pp. 600-605).On the death of Giorgio Valla (1500), who had the first lectureship, Sabellico took over his position. He also served as librarian to the collection of books which Cardinal Bessarion had given Venice, but which was as yet without a permanent home. Sabellico repaid the republic's largesse by writing and publishing further works in praise of Venice as well as a description of the city in three books and a dialogue on the Venetian magistrates (1489). In addition he continued his literary studies and produced commentaries on Pliny the Elder, Valerius Maximus, Livy, Horace, and other classical authors. Several of his orations and his philosophical, moral, and historical minor works attest to both his productiveness and his rise to considerable prominence in Venice. Toward the end of his life he published his historical magnum opus, a universal history from the Creation, under the title Enneades seu rhapsodiae historiarum (1498). A second part was printed in 1504.

publishers.name: Da Lessona Albertino
publishers.biography: The Venetian press at the juncture of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries represented the apex of European print culture, serving as a cosmopolitan nexus where humanist scholarship, mercantile enterprise, and typographical innovation converged. Within this vibrant ecosystem, Albertino da Lessona (frequently designated in Latin colophons as Albertinus Vercellensis, Albertinus de Lessona Vercellensis, or Albertino Vercellese) operated as an energetic printer and publisher whose active production spans the crucial transitional era from 1499 to 1506. This period witnessed the definitive maturation of the incunabula era into the dynamic, highly competitive post-incunabula market. Originating from the small settlement of Lessona in the Biellese region—historically tied to the ecclesiastical and political sphere of Vercelli in eastern Piedmont—Albertino belonged to a crucial diaspora of Northern Italian craftsmen who migrated to the Venetian Lagoon. These artisans brought technical ingenuity and regional financial alliances to the printing shops surrounding the Rialto and San Marco. While his independent typographic career was relatively condensed, spanning roughly seven years, Albertino da Lessona played an indispensable role in disseminating classical Latin literature, humanist treatises, vernacular poetry, legal compendia, and liturgical volumes, thereby entrenching the reputation of Venetian workshops across the broader European Republic of Letters.To fully understand Albertino da Lessona's formative background, one must examine the socio-economic topography of late fifteenth-century Piedmont. The territory of Lessona, nestled in the foothill zone of the Biellese within the broader diocese and district of Vercelli, was characterized by modest agrarian economies and specialized artisan guilds. During the final decades of the Quattrocento, young men from Vercelli, Trino, Lessona, and surrounding communes migrated in significant numbers to Venice, attracted by the insatiable demand for labor in the city's burgeoning printing industry. This regional network included illustrious figures such as Bernardino Stagnino, Giovanni Tacuino, Bernardino Vercellese, and the Giolito family. Albertino’s early life was shaped by this regional solidarity; upon arriving in Venice during the late 1490s, he underwent an intensive apprenticeship within established Venetian workshops where he mastered the complex mechanics of punch-cutting, type-casting, page composition, press operation, and ink chemistry. His colophons consistently retained the demonym Vercellensis or de Lessona Vercellensis, a clear indication that regional identity functioned both as a mark of pride and as a branding mechanism within the competitive Venetian trade guild structure.The operational debut of Albertino da Lessona's press occurred in 1499, a year that marked the final phase of the XVth-century incunabula tradition. From his workshop, located in the traditional publishing district of Venice, Albertino issued a carefully selected sequence of texts designed to appeal to both university faculties and humanistically educated patricians. Among his earliest and most notable achievements were high-quality editions of classical Latin authors. He undertook the printing of Publius Vergilius Maro's Opera, accompanied by the authoritative late-antique commentaries of Servius and Aelius Donatus. This monumental undertaking demonstrated his press's capability to manage intricate page layouts, surrounding a central classical text with dense, multi-column scholarly commentary in smaller type sizes. Beyond Vergil, Lessona printed works by Ovid, Terence, Martial, and the historical narratives of Appian of Alexandria as translated into Latin by Pier Candido Decembrio. Nor did he restrict his catalog exclusively to classical antiquity; his press actively catered to contemporary Renaissance humanism and vernacular letters. He issued editions of Giovanni Boccaccio's Genealogia Deorum Gentilium and De Montibus, Silvis, Fontibus, essential reference tools for Renaissance mythography and geography, as well as vernacular poetic collections. To maintain high textual integrity, Albertino cultivated professional relationships with notable humanist scholars, editors, and proofreaders (castigatores) active in Venice, ensuring that his editions were recognized not merely for their typographical clarity, but also for their philological precision.From a material and typographical perspective, the output of Albertino da Lessona reveals a sophisticated understanding of book design tailored to specific market reader demographics. For legal treatises, scholastic commentaries, and liturgical texts, his shop utilized robust Gothic types (rotunda), which offered the density and traditional authority expected by canon lawyers, theologians, and monastic orders. Conversely, for classical humanities and Renaissance literature, Lessona employed a clear, elegant Roman typeface modeled after the classical proportions refined by Nicolas Jenson and Erhard Ratdolt. His volumes were frequently embellished with decorative woodcut initials—ranging from delicate white-on-black criblé initials to intricate foliate and historiated capitals—and, in select literary editions, delicate contour woodcut illustrations executed in the classic Venetian style. Operating in an environment characterized by fierce commercial rivalry, Lessona navigated the complex regulatory framework of the Venetian Senate, occasionally seeking short-term printing privileges (privilegi di stampa) to protect his financial investments in major titles from unauthorized reprinting by rival presses. He sourced high-grade rag paper from the renowned paper mills (cartiere) of Treviso and the Riviera del Garda, ensuring that his books possessed physical durability and aesthetic appeal.The sudden conclusion of Albertino da Lessona's independent printing activity around the year 1506 reflects the volatility of the Venetian publishing enterprise during the early sixteenth century. The catastrophic political crisis caused by the War of the League of Cambrai (1508–1516), combined with recurrent economic recessions, price wars, and plagues, forced many mid-sized Venetian print shops to liquidate, consolidate, or transition into subcontracted printing for larger publishing conglomerates like those of Aldus Manutius, Lucantonio Giunta, or the Sessea family. Whether Lessona succumbed to financial hardship, returned to his native Piedmont, or entered into an uncredited partnership with other Vercellese printers remains a subject of ongoing historical inquiry. Nevertheless, his legacy within early modern European printing history is firmly secured. Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century bibliographers such as Georg Wolfgang Panzer and Ludwig Hain systematically recorded his imprints, while twentieth-century analytical bibliographers—including Victor Scholderer in the monumental Catalogue of Books Printed in the XVth Century Now in the British Museum (BMC), Konrad Haebler, Fernanda Ascarelli, and Marco Menato—have cataloged his distinct typographical fonts and press marks. Today, surviving copies of Albertino da Lessona's incunabula and post-incunabula are preserved in major national and university libraries worldwide, standing as monumental testimonies to the technical skill, intellectual ambition, and entrepreneurial vigor of the Piedmontese printing diaspora during Venice's golden age of typography.
