publisher_data: Colophon: Venice, Albertino da Lessona, 24 December 1502
academic_description: Folio. Two parts in one volume. 136 [i.e. 138] leaves; [72] leaves. Collation: a-i6, K8, l8, m-x6, y8; A-M6. Old vellum over boards, some contemporary marginal annotations. Restoration to lower outer corner of the title page not affecting the text. First collected edition of Sabellico's works and first edition of his twelve books of letters (occupying leaves a1v-l1v), which are a most important source for his biography. The Epistolae, dedicated to Marcantonio Morosini, are followed by Orationes, De situ Venetae urbis (a topographical description of the city of Venice as it was during the author's life), De Venetiis magistratibus, De praetoris officio, De reparatione Latinae linguae (considered the first historical and connected narrative of the Renaissance movement in Italy), De officio scribae (on the office of a government secretary), and De vetustate Aquileiae. The whole second part consists of his neo-Latin poetry, of which the poem De rerum et artium inventoribus, in which he enumerates the inventions of mankind and their inventors, is the most interesting (cf. R. Chavasse, ‘De inventoribus rerum': Marcantonio Sabellico and Polydore Virgil, in: “Polidoro Virgilio e la cultura umanistica europea”, R. Bacchielli, ed., Urbino, 2003, pp. 207-224).W.A. Copinger (Supplementum, London, 1895-1902, no. 5196) attributes the first part to a printer from Brescia around 1490. In fact there is some visible difference in the typographical material and woodcut initials between the two parts of the volume (cf. M. Sabellico, De latinae linguae reparatione, G. Bottari, ed., Messina, 1999, p. 72).Among Sabellico's correspondents were members of his family, especially his son Mario and his brother Catalucio da Coccio, and a wide range of personalities: fellow humanists, church dignitaries, political leaders and noblemen, e.g. Giovanni Stefano Emiliano, Pomponio Leto, Giovanni Antonio Flaminio, Ermolao Barbaro, Antonio, Benedetto and Tommaso Trevisan, Giorgio Merula, Angelo Sabino, Jacopo Filippo Foresti, Sebastiano Badoer, Leonardo Loredan, Palladio Negri, Giovanni Battista Cantalicio, Paolo Santonino, Pietro Barozzi, Angelo Poliziano, Antonio Bonfini, Gasparino Barzizza, Pietro and Paolo Marsi, Andrea Mocenigo, Carlo Barbavero, Agostino and Marco Barbarigo, Francesco Piccolomini, Girolamo Donà, Domenico Grimani, Lodovico Sforza, Ercole d'Este, Giovanni Bentivoglio, Lodovico Odasi, Antonio Bonfini, Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, Bernardo Bembo, Girolamo Squarzafico, Fabio and Giovanni Pontano, Coriolano Cippico, Antonio Corner, Antonio Moretto.One letter is addressed to a woman: the learned Cassandra Fedele. The collection also contains some letters addressed to him (e.g. Pomponio Leto). That his letters became models of an elegant style is shown nine years later after its first publication by a selection of letters entitled Breviores epistolae, ‘for teaching the rudiments of the Latin language to adolescents', which were published at Leipzig in 1511 (two editions in that year, reprinted in 1513 and 1520). They could be classified by topics such as family, sons' education, editing and publishing, dedication and patronage, classical texts, Venetian life and ceremony.The letter at p. 52 is addressed to the poet and playwright Marco Armonio (1477-c. 1552), who in 1500 had written and staged in Venice a neo-Latin comedy entitled Stephanium, which was greeted with great enthusiasm. In the letter, Sabellico, who had the chance to read the comedy before it was published around 1503 and had attended first-hand its first staging, praises the work for the ‘argumentum, dignitas personarum, sententiarum gravitas, verba cum vetusta, tum figura et lepore Plautinis simillima”, using a terminology that is clearly taken from Aristotle's Poetics, whose first edition had appeared in Venice only a few years earlier (1498) in the Latin translation by Lorenzo Valla. This may well be one of the very first mentions of Aristotle's principles on poetics and their application to a contemporary literary text (cf. W. Ludwig, Einleitung, in: G. Armonio, “Ioannis Harmonii Marsi Comoedia Stephanium”, Munich, 1971, pp. 12-17).“Marcantonio Sebellico's Epistolae familiares were collected by his amanuensis, Giovanni Carsio, and published in Venice in 1502. The indispensable Carsio was like a ‘family member' in the extended households of Venice and Vicovaro [...] He was not an ideal humanist editor, but he did include much that reveals Sabellico's network, household and family bonds. The letters are generally undated, the years are never given, though occasionally the day and the month are added [...] The letters, in Alison Holcroft's words [Going Public: Marcantonio Sabellico and the 1502 Collection of his Letters, unpublished paper] ‘if a little lacking in hard data on education, are wonderful as soap opera!' [...] His Letters reveal lived emotion as well as ideal or exemplary emotion. Further Sabellico felt an emotional bond with his creative work and spoke of his own books as his children or servants, thereby conveying something of his sense of household bonds. He played on the dual meaning of familiares as servants or with epistolae as informal or domestic newsletters” (R. Chavasse, Humanist Educational and Emotional Expectations of Teenagers in Late Fifteenth-Century Italy, in: “Emotions in the Household, 1200-1900”, S. Broomhall, ed., New York, 2008, pp. 70-71).“Le [lettere le] aveva messe assieme e stampate nel 1502 il Sabellico medesimo, benchè nella graziosa dedica a Marco Antonio Morosin abbia voluto far credere che la raccolta, la divisione in libri e la stampa si dovevano all'antico suo amanuense, allora maestro di scuola Giovanni Carsio, e che egli solamente non l'avesse impedita: ciò che gli avremmo forse potuto credere, se si fosse ricordato di togliere dall'epistolario qualche lettera che lo smentisce recisamente” (G. Mercati, Ultimi contributi alla storia degli umanisti, Città del Vaticano, 1939, II, pp. 1-2).“In late Quattrocento Venice the foremost manipulator of the power of print publication among writers was Marcantonio Sabellico. He, it has been suggested, probably deserves the title usually reserved for Erasmus - that of being the first writer to make a career from the new medium. When he came to have his twelve books of letters printed, he professed lack of enthusiasm about releasing what he termed these base slaves from his house. Yet the academies success which he enjoyed in Venice owned much to the ways in which he took advantage from the press” (B. Richardson, op. cit., p. 83).“Some good descriptions of the work at the School of San Marco can be found in the letters of Sabellico, who taught there for twenty years - from 1486 to 1506, longer than any other humanist. However, a remark on one of these letters suggests that not only the heavy burden of work, but also another reason might have limited the attractiveness of the School of San Marco: the low, or at least uncertain, position of a professional humanist in Venetian social structure. Sabellico mentioned with pride that not only the sons of citizens but also from members of the Venetian nobility attended his language classes; he added that although they were frequently held at his house he never heard from his pupils anything about Venetian politics” (F. Gilbert, Humanism in Venice, in: “Florence and Venice: Comparisons and Relations. I: Quattrocento”, Firenze, 1979, p. 16).Marcantonio da Coccio was born of poor parents in Vicovaro (northeast of Rome). He received his early schooling in his native town and then continued his studies in Rome under Pomponio Leto, Gasparino Barzizza, Domizio Calderini, and Porcelio Pandone. While in Rome he took part in the life of Leto's Roman Academy and adopted his humanistic ‘nom de plume': Sabellico. In 1473 he was called to Udine to teach rhetoric but also continued his studies in dialectics, mathematics, and Greek. In 1482 appeared his first work in print De vetustate Aquileiae patriae. He was dismissed from his employment in Udine, and spent over a year in Verona, where he completed twenty-two of the thirty-three books of his history of Venice. In 1487 he presented this work (printed in 1487) to the doge and senate, and soon afterwards he was appointed to the second public lectureship in the humanities at the school of San Marco (cf. F.Lepori, La scuola di Rialto dalla fondazione alla metà del Cinquecento, in: “Storia della cultura veneta. Dal primo Quattrocento al Concilio di Trento”, G. Arnaldi & M. Pastore Stocchi, eds., Vicenza, 1980/81, pp. 600-605).On the death of Giorgio Valla (1500), who had the first lectureship, Sabellico took over his position. He also served as librarian to the collection of books which Cardinal Bessarion had given Venice, but which was as yet without a permanent home. Sabellico repaid the republic's largesse by writing and publishing further works in praise of Venice as well as a description of the city in three books and a dialogue on the Venetian magistrates (1489). In addition he continued his literary studies and produced commentaries on Pliny the Elder, Valerius Maximus, Livy, Horace, and other classical authors. Several of his orations and his philosophical, moral, and historical minor works attest to both his productiveness and his rise to considerable prominence in Venice. Toward the end of his life he published his historical magnum opus, a universal history from the Creation, under the title Enneades seu rhapsodiae historiarum (1498). A second part was printed in 1504 (cf. R. Chavasse, The ‘Studia Humanitatis' and the Making of a Humanist Career: Marcantonio Sabellico's Exploitation of Humanist Literary Genres, in: “Renaissance Studies”, 17/1, 2003, pp. 27-38; see also G. Rita, Da Vicovaro a Venezia: introduzione a Marcantonio Sabellico, Vicovaro, 2004, passim).

title: Tavola di quanto è stato raccolto per M. Alessandro Canobbio intorno la nobiltà, antichità, e fatti della città di Verona

authors.name: Canobbio Alessandro
authors.biography: Alessandro Canobbio, a native of Milan, was first active in the wool manufacture and trade at Verona and was for several years head of the local wool spinning mill. But he was more attracted by the profession of a notary and obtained his patent in 1562. He then worked for the city administration in various important positions. In 1570 he became secretary to Niccolò Ormaneto, bishop of Verona. Between 1572 and 1577 he resided for longer periods at Padua, where he wrote an account of the plague, which ravaged there in 1576. He also wrote a history of the academies of Verona (1571, reprinted in 1590) and a Discorso a i presidenti della carità di Verona (1572), on poor relief. From 1589 to 1596 he helped to organize several archives, public and private. His last major work was a code of behavior for the true Christian with advice on the conjugal life, the education of children, the employment of money and social intercourse.

publishers.name: Discepolo Girolamo
publishers.biography: Girolamo Discepolo (fl. 1584–1599), known in Latin imprints as Hieronymus Discepolus, stands as one of the most distinguished and technically innovative master printers and publishers of the late Italian Renaissance and Counter-Reformation period. Active across key intellectual and administrative centers of central and southern Italy—most notably Rome, Viterbo, and Naples—Discepolo operated at the crucial intersection of humanist scholarship, post-Tridentine ecclesiastical printing, and the emerging empirical sciences. In the broader landscape of late sixteenth-century European typography, as documented in authoritative bibliographic repertories such as the Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani published by the Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana (Treccani), Discepolo represents the ideal model of the itinerant master craftsman-publisher (tipografo-editore). Through shrewd commercial acumen, sophisticated aesthetic judgment, and alliances with preeminent scholars, he transformed regional presses into vital nodes of international book circulation.Discepolo’s early career and vocational formation took shape in the dense, highly competitive typographic ecosystem of Rome during the pontificates of Gregory XIII (Ugo Boncompagni) and Sixtus V (Felice Peretti). During the 1570s and early 1580s, Rome was undergoing a massive expansion in print production driven by the mandates of the Council of Trent, requiring vast quantities of liturgical volumes, papal bulls, legal commentaries, and counter-reformatory theological treatises. In this demanding environment, Discepolo acquired a comprehensive mastery of the typographic trade, learning the intricacies of punch-cutting, typefounding, ink composition, matrix setting, and press operation. He was deeply influenced by the structural clarity and elegant proportions of Roman and Venetian typography, absorbing the classical aesthetic traditions established by Aldus Manutius and Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari while adapting to the monumental, architectural title-page designs popularized by Roman printing dynasties such as the Blado press and the Stamperia Vaticana under Domenico Basa. Recognizing the market saturation in the papal capital, Discepolo sought an opportunity to establish an independent press where he could exercise total creative control over his catalog.In 1584–1585, Discepolo established his printing office in Viterbo, a strategic city within the Papal States possessing a rich humanist tradition and favored by influential patrons, including members of the Farnese cardinalate and the local municipal oligarchy. Discepolo’s Viterbo period, though relatively brief (spanning approximately 1585 to 1590), proved to be historically epoch-making. The crowning achievement of his career occurred in 1586 with the publication of the editio princeps of Giambattista Della Porta’s revolutionary treatise, De humana physiognomonia libri IIII. This masterwork of Renaissance natural philosophy and proto-scientific inquiry sought to establish systemic correspondences between human facial features, moral temperaments, and animal characteristics. The publication was a monumental technical undertaking: Discepolo oversaw the integration of elaborate letterpress typography with dozens of intricate, highly detailed copperplate engravings and woodcut illustrations. The technical challenge of combining heavy-pressure intaglio plate printing with relief letterpress composition on high-grade rag paper demonstrated Discepolo’s extraordinary mechanical precision and aesthetic brilliance. The 1586 Viterbo edition immediately achieved European celebrity, solidifying Della Porta’s reputation and establishing Discepolo as a printer capable of executing the most complex illustrated scholarly books of the late Renaissance.Following his monumental success in Viterbo, Discepolo recognized the vast commercial potential of Naples, the sprawling capital of the Spanish Viceroyalty and one of the largest metropolitan centers in Europe. Around 1588–1590, Discepolo relocated his primary operations southwards to Naples, establishing a prominent printing shop in the heart of the city’s intellectual and commercial district, near San Domenico Maggiore and the viceregal tribunals. In Naples, Discepolo entered a vibrant and competitive publishing landscape, operating alongside notable Neapolitan printers such as Giuseppe Cacchi, Orazio Salviani, and the Carlino and Vitale presses. Discepolo quickly integrated into the Neapolitan intellectual elite and regional academic circles, including the Accademia degli Svegliati. His Neapolitan production catalog reflected a remarkably broad intellectual spectrum: he issued major treatises on civil and canon law (ius commune), medical texts, vernacular poetry, historical chronicles, and extensive devotional and theological literature required by the post-Tridentine religious orders. He maintained his close working relationship with Giambattista Della Porta, publishing subsequent scientific and philosophical works, while simultaneously serving as an official printer for regional ecclesiastical authorities and municipal magistrates.The material culture and typographical aesthetic of Discepolo’s press are distinguished by an exceptionally high standard of craftsmanship. His shop employed clean, well-cast Roman (rotunda and antiqua) and Italic types, frequently complemented by exquisite woodcut historiated initials, baroque tailpieces, headpieces, and elaborate woodcut or engraved architectural title borders. Discepolo’s printer's mark (marca tipografica)—which frequently featured emblematic allegorical figures representing Virtue, Prudence, or Justice accompanied by Latin moral mottos—served across early modern Europe as a hallmark of editorial integrity and typographical elegance. Analytical bibliography of surviving copies reveals that Discepolo carefully sourced superior paper stock from major paper mills in Lazio, Campania, and the Venetian terraferma, ensuring that his editions possessed structural durability and optical clarity. His adept management of supply chains, complex labor division within the workshop, and distribution logistics through international book fairs in Venice and Frankfurt demonstrated a sophisticated grasp of early modern capitalism.Operating within both the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples required Discepolo to navigate the rigid and complex apparatus of Counter-Reformation censorship. The enforcement of the Index Librorum Prohibitorum by the Sacred Congregation of the Index and the Roman and Neapolitan Inquisition meant that every manuscript submitted to Discepolo’s press had to undergo rigorous vetting by ecclesiastical and viceregal censors. Natural philosophical works—particularly those touching upon natural magic, astrology, or physiognomy, such as those by Della Porta—were subjected to intense scrutiny. Discepolo proved remarkably adept at securing the necessary ecclesiastical approvals (imprimatur) and privilege declarations from viceregal authorities, ensuring that his press operated strictly within the boundaries of orthodoxy without sacrificing intellectual sophistication or scientific innovation. His pragmatic navigation of state and church authorities enabled his business to prosper continuously without suffering the confiscations or inquisitorial prosecutions that plagued more radical contemporary contemporaries.Girolamo Discepolo’s enduring legacy is enshrined in the annals of early modern European printing and bibliographical history. Scholars of historical bibliography, from early chroniclers like Lorenzo Giustiniani and Cristoforo Belli to modern specialists such as Dennis E. Rhodes, Fernanda Ascarelli, and Marco Santoro, have recognized Discepolo as a pivotal figure who elevated provincial printing to international prominence. Copies of his editions, particularly the magnificent 1586 Viterbo De humana physiognomonia, are today held in the world's most prestigious bibliographical institutions, including the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, the Biblioteca Nazionale Vittorio Emanuele III in Naples, the British Library, the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and major university research collections throughout Europe and North America. Through his dedication to typographical excellence, mastery of complex multi-media printing technologies, and active participation in the intellectual networks of late sixteenth-century Italy, Girolamo Discepolo remains a monumental figure in the transition from Renaissance humanism to early modern scientific print culture.

academic_description: 4to (195x144 mm). [24] leaves. Collation: A-F4. With the woodcut arms of the city of Verona on the title page. Late 18th-century red morocco, panels with gilt floral borders, gilt edges, decorated endpapers (a few scratches). Some very light occasional foxing. A very good copy. Very rare first edition of the table of contents of a comprehensive chronicle of the city of Verona, intended by Canobbio to show the plan of his Historia intorno la nobiltà e l’antichità di Verona, to which he worked from 1577 to 1604 and which should cover 3436 years of history of the territory. The work was never finished, only the present index and a summary, Breve compendio cavato dalla sua historia di Verona (1598), were published during his lifetime. Apparently the manuscript of the larger work got lost (cf. A. Viviani, Alessandro Canobbio e la sua opera storica, in: “Nova historia”, VII/1-2, 1955, pp. 42-52).“Se l’interesse archeologico è prevalente in Torello Saraina ed esclusivo in Onofrio Panvinio, accanto all’archeologia in Alessandro Canobbio si può riscontrare anche una qualificante ricerca archivistica svolta in un’area che talora comprende le città confinanti con Verona. Canobbio stesso nella Tavola data alle stampe nel 1587 per far conoscere quanto aveva raccolto in vista della compilazione di un lavoro che illustrasse ‘la nobiltà, antichità, et fatti della città di Verona’, elenca gli archivi che ha frequentato, esitenti presso le istituzioni civili ed ecclesiastiche più significative per la millenaria storia di Verona. La Tavola secondo il Canobbio aveva lo scopo di anticipare la conoscenza del suo capolavoro Gli Annali, contenenti ‘cose avvenute nello spatio di tremila quattrocento trentasei anni alla comune patria’. Alla Tavola fece seguire un Breve compendio dei suoi annali che pubblicò nel 1598 dedicandolo a Girolamo Giuliari. Tavola e Compendio furono provvidenziali per i posteri, perché il Canobbio morì prima di poter stampare gli Annali, che, dopo la sua morte andarono perduti […] [Canobbio] merita tuttavia molta considerazione per aver egli fatto uscire la ricerca storica dalla fredda oggettivazione lapidaria, che bloccava lo studioso nell’ambito delle antichità classiche ed ecclesiastiche, per avviarlo invece ai depositi archivistici, naturalemente più vicini alla vita politica, sociale ed economica” (L. Vecchiato, La vita politica, economica e amministrativa a Verona durante la dominazione Veneziana, in: “Verona tra Cinque e Seicento”, V/1, Verona, 1995, pp. 68-70).Alessandro Canobbio, a native of Milan, was first active in the wool manufacture and trade at Verona and was for several years head of the local wool spinning mill. But he was more attracted by the profession of a notary and obtained his patent in 1562. He then worked for the city administration in various important positions. In 1570 he became secretary to Niccolò Ormaneto, bishop of Verona. Between 1572 and 1577 he resided for longer periods at Padua, where he wrote an account of the plague, which ravaged there in 1576. He also wrote a history of the academies of Verona (1571, reprinted in 1590) and a Discorso a i presidenti della carità di Verona (1572), on poor relief. From 1589 to 1596 he helped to organize several archives, public and private. His last major work was a code of behavior for the true Christian with advice on the conjugal life, the education of children, the employment of money and social intercourse (cf. E. Rossini, Un notatio del secolo XVI: Alessandro Canobbio, in: “Atti e memorie dell’Accademia di agricoltura, scienze e lettere di Verona”, s. 6, XIX, 1967/68, pp. 157-198).

authors.name: Castiglione Sabba da
authors.biography: Sabba da Castiglione was an instance of the self-fashioned courtier-knight of the later Renaissance who combines an unusual set of roles: Hospitaller commander, canon regular, art collector, courtier, poet, and preceptor of knightly rules. He was born in Milan around 1480, where he also became his first. education. He pursued post-secondary studies at the University of Padua, studying jurisprudence from about 1500 to late spring 1505, but did not finish his legal education. After a brief stay in Mantua, in 1505, at the age of 25, he decided to join the Order of the Knights of Jerusalem (later called Knights of Malta), of which he soon became Deputy Attorney General. He lived in Rhodes until 1508, then moved to Rome, where he sojourned seven years as legal aide-de-camp to the admiral of the Order of the Knights Hospitaller (and later Grand Master), Fabrizio del Carretto, cultivating his interest in the arts and literature. In Rome he also met his cousin, Baldassare Castiglione, author of Il Cortegiano. Fra Sabba was a passionate forerunner of archaeology and, during his stay on the Aegean Sea, he was able to procure several ancient marble pieces to Isabella d'Este in Mantua. In 1515, at the age of thirty-five, Fra Sabba became a Hospitaller commander, accepting a post previously held by his friend Giulio de’ Medici, the future Pope Clement VII. He took up residence at the Order’s Commenda, or commandery, a district headquarters similar to a feudal estate, in Faenza, Romagna, part of the Papal States. He accepted this post to better dedicate himself to the studies he loved so much, away from mundane affairs, the intrigues of courts and military life. His residence in Faenza was the Church of Commenda (Saint Mary Magdalene), also called ‘Magione’, dating back to the XII century. It was not in good conditions when Fra Sabba came. This was due to the fact that previous commanders had not chosen the complex of the Commenda as their own living place, employing their revenues for other purposes. In 1533, Fra Sabba entrusted Girolamo da Treviso with the task to embellish the church with a fresco portraying the ‘Enthroned Madonna between Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Catherine of Alexandria’. Another work of art of great importance, accomplished in the year of his death, is the one painted by Francesco Menzocchi from Forlì: a monochrome fresco depicting him as an old man presented by Saint Joseph to the Virgin. Underneath this image lies Fra Sabba’s sepulchre, with a Latin epigraph composed by himself. His interests as a man of study and collector gave birth to a library, unfortunately lost, and to a collection of pieces of art, whose surviving items are to be seen in the Pinacoteca Comunale of Faenza.

academic_description: 4to (214x152 mm). [8], 135, [1] leaves. Collation: *4 †4 a-z4 A-L4. With the large woodcut portrait of the author on the title page and the printer’s device on last leaf verso. Contemporary limp vellum, inked title on the spine and lower edge, remnants of ties (new endpapers, small stains). On title page manuscript ownership’s inscription Ballybay Library. Inner margin of the title page reinforced, small holes to the gutter of the first two leaves with no loss of text, small ink stain on the upper blank margin at the end of the volume, otherwise a very good genuine copy. First complete edition. First published in Bologna in 1546, containing only seventy-two chapters, the Ricordi appeared in an enlarged edition in 1549 (124 chapters) also in Bologna. The present, definitive, edition containing 133 ‘ricordi’ was edited by Zaccaria Bellenghi, Fra Sabba’s chaplain in Faenza, shortly after the latter’s death. The work became very popular and between 1546 and 1613 twenty-five editions were published.In the present edition is also found for the first time the title woodcut showing Fra Sabba in his study. Ugo Rozzo (Lo studiolo nella silografia italiana, 1479-1558, Udine, 1998, pp. 90, 114), deems this frontispiece to be remarkable for the mid-sixteenth century both for its Hospitaller imagery and its display of books within the study. The woodcut is emblematic of Sabba’s monastic life conducted within the Order’s parameters of social utility. He presents an iconographic image of the devout humanist knight who prefers the tranquility of his Commenda to the bustle of the city (see also D. Thornton, The Scholar in his Study: Ownership and Experience in Renaissance Italy, New Haven, CT, 1997, pp. 106-114).The work consists of two series of “avvertimenti” (advices), each closely related to Castiglione’s initial idea of providing to his grandnephew Bartolomeo Righi useful hints on how to become a perfect knight Hospitaller, but its numerous printings in the sixteenth century and its breadth of scope suggest a wider target audience. The other ‘ricordi’, were developed into true small treatises or essays, that Castiglione expanded and augmented in every new edition. Despite not having a wide-ranging extent, nevertheless they present a considerable interest, especially when compared to the works of contemporaries on the same topics, i.e. the life of a courtier, the government of a city, the prince and the tyrant, men of arms and religion, marriage, how to decorate a house, clothes, food and drink, physical exercise, travel, etc. But included were also his life in Faenza, his political aspirations, linguistic experiments, ideas on religious reform. Geopolitical issues of the day are vigorously engaged and farcical passages replete with colloquial phrasing appear alongside passionate theological discourse expressing a strident anti-Lutheran viewpoint (cf. C. Scarpati, Per il testo dei ‘Ricordi’, in: “Studi sul Cinquecento italiano”, Milano, 1982, pp. 68-82; see also D.F. Allen, The Hospitaller Castiglione’s Catholic Synthesis of Warfare, Learning and Lay Piety on the Eve of the Council of Trent, in: “The Hospitallers, the Mediterranean, and Europe: Festschrift for Anthony Luttrell”, K. Borchardt & al. eds., London, 2016, pp. 286-298).The Ricordi is also very interesting from the point of view of art history and criticism, showing Fra Sabba’s antiquarian efforts for Isabella d’Este, his admiration for Dürer’s prints, and the artists he had known at Rome, e.g. Gian Cristoforo Romano, Bramante, Raphael, Cristoforo Foppa, ‘Il Caradosso’, the San Gallo family, just to mention a few (cf. M. Collareta, Il mondi dell’arte dei ‘Ricordi’ di Fra Sabba, in: “Sabba da Castiglione, 1480-1554. Dalle corti rinascimentali alls Commenda di Faenza. Atti del Covegno, Faenza, 19-20 maggio 2000”, A.R. Gentilini, ed., Florence, 2004, pp. 297-312).At the end of the volume is reprinted another work by Fra Sabba, the Consolatoria, written during his stay at Rhodes (November 25, 1517). This consolatory epistle, addressed to the Milanese poet Camilla Scarampi for the death of her husband Ambrogio Guidoboni. This letter was published at Bologna in 1529. From the dedication dated March 15, 1527 to Giacomo Guicciardini, vice-president of Romagna, we learn that Fra Sabba had submitted the work, in the last ten years, to Niccolò Machiavelli and Panfilo Sassi asking them if they considered it worthy of being published (M.C. authors.name: Ridolfi Luca Antonio
authors.biography: Luc’Antonio Ridolfi was born and had his early education in Florence. At the beginning of the thirties he settled to Rome and became to be known in the literary circles of that city. After the mur- der of Alessandro de’ Medici he took refuge at Lyon as many of his ‘Republican’ compatriots, but maintained close relations with many Florentine, which remained in Italy as Claudio Tolomei, Niccolò Martelli, Pietro Vettori and Benedetto Varchi. He had come to Lyon as a merchant, but started around 1542 to work for the printing house of Gauillaume Rouillé as editor and translator of Italian texts. He spent the last years before his death in Florence.

publishers.name: Rouillé Guillaume
publishers.biography: Guillaume Rouillé (c. 1518 – June 20, 1589), known in Latin as Gulielmus Rovillius and in Italian as Guglielmo Rovillio, stands as one of the most visionary, prolific, and culturally influential printer-publishers of the sixteenth-century European Renaissance. Operating from the vibrant commercial metropolis of Lyon, Rouillé was a central figure alongside Sebastian Gryphius and Jean de Tournes in establishing the city as the primary rival to Paris and Venice in the global republic of letters. Positioned at the geographical and intellectual crossroads between Italy, France, the Low Countries, and the Iberian Peninsula, Rouillé functioned not merely as a commercial printer, but as an astute cultural entrepreneur and humanist impresario. His press specialized in small-format vernacular editions, lavishly illustrated emblem books, monumental legal folios, authoritative botanical encyclopedias, and medallic iconographies. By fusing the typographical elegance and marketing innovations of Venetian vernacular printing with the rigorous scholarship of French humanism, Rouillé reshaped the visual and textual landscape of Early Modern Europe.Born in Touraine—most likely in or near Tours—around the year 1518, Rouillé received a formative education in the mechanical and intellectual arts of typography through an early migration to Venice. In the 1530s and early 1540s, he entered the renowned Venetian printing house of Gabriele Giolito de' Ferrari, the undisputed pioneer of vernacular publishing (*libri volgari*) in Italy. In Giolito’s workshop, Rouillé absorbed cutting-edge typographical methodologies: the usage of sleek italic founts, compact octavo (*8vo*) and sextodecimo (*16mo*) formats designed for portability, ornate architectural woodcut borders, floral cartouches, and aggressive marketing strategies targeted at a broadening lay readership. This Venetian immersion permanently imprinted itself upon Rouillé’s aesthetic sensibility and business acumen. Around 1543 to 1545, recognizing the burgeoning economic potential and intellectual liberty of Lyon—a city free from the rigid guild restrictions of Paris and the ideological surveillance of the Sorbonne—Rouillé relocated to the Rhône valley. His integration into the Lyonnese elite was solidified through his marriage to Madeleine de Portonaris, daughter of the prominent Piedmontese-born Lyonnese publisher Vincent de Portonaris. This alliance granted Rouillé crucial financial backing, established commercial credit, and direct access to an extensive distribution network spanning Northern Italy, Southern France, and Spain.Rouillé established his establishment under the sign of L'Écu de Venise (*The Venetian Shield*) on the bustling Rue Mercière, the epicenter of Lyon's book trade. From this base, he orchestrated an extraordinary publishing program that bridged humanist erudition and popular appeal. A cornerstone of his enterprise was his engagement with visual humanism and emblem literature. In 1548, Rouillé initiated a famous collaboration with the scholar Barthélemy Aneau, principal of the Collège de la Trinité in Lyon, to produce groundbreaking editions of Andrea Alciato’s Emblemata. Rouillé reimagined the emblem book format by encasing every page within intricate, highly styled woodcut frames depicting grotesques, arabesques, and architectural motifs, accompanied by translations in French, Italian, and Spanish. In 1552, he published Aneau’s own original emblematic masterwork, Picta Poesis. Rouillé’s mastery of illustrated history culminated in his celebrated Promptuarii Iconum Insigniorum (*Promptuary of the Medals of the Most Famous Men*), first issued in 1553. This ambitious medallic encyclopedia presented over eight hundred woodcut medallion portraits of historical, biblical, and mythological figures from Adam and Eve to contemporary monarchs, accompanied by concise biographical summaries. Designed for multi-lingual international dissemination, Rouillé simultaneously published the work in Latin, French (*Promptuaire des medalles*), Italian, and later Spanish, demonstrating his unmatched expertise in localized market adaptation.Beyond emblem literature and visual iconographies, Rouillé was a crucial catalyst in the dissemination of Renaissance literature, medicine, jurisprudence, and science. He maintained an extensive intellectual network that included the foremost humanists, physicians, and translators of the era, such as Jacques Daléchamps, Antoine Du Verdier, Gabriel Chappuys, and Pierre de Ronsard. In the realm of natural philosophy and medicine, Rouillé achieved an monumental publishing triumph with the publication of Jacques Daléchamps’s Historia generalis plantarum (1586–1587). Issued in two massive folio volumes containing nearly three thousand detailed woodcut illustrations, this monumental botanical compendium synthesized ancient botanical authority with empirical Early Modern observation, marking a watershed moment in botanical taxonomy. Simultaneously, Rouillé dominated the European market for vernacular Italian literature, printing crisp, pocket-sized editions of Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron, Francesco Petrarca’s Canzoniere, Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso, and Dante Alighieri’s Divina Commedia, alongside French translations that popularized Italian Renaissance culture among French nobility and bourgeoisie. In the domain of legal humanism, Rouillé issued colossal, multi-volume folio editions of civil and canon law texts by Bartolus de Saxoferrato, Baldus de Ubaldis, Andrea Alciato, and Charles Du Moulin, securing lucrative long-term institutional contracts across European universities.Typographically, the press of Guillaume Rouillé was defined by meticulous layout composition, typographical clarity, and exceptional ornamental quality. Rouillé made signature use of small, elegant cursive and italic typefaces directly influenced by Venetian models, allowing him to squeeze maximum text into aesthetically pleasing pocket formats. His printer’s device—a majestic eagle perched atop a pedestal or globe, flanked by a coiled serpent, and bearing the motto In virtute, et fortuna (*In Virtue and Fortune*) or In virtute, fortuna comes—became a universally recognized trademark of typographical excellence. To produce his magnificent woodcut illustrations and decorative borders, Rouillé employed top-tier Lyonnese artists and engravers, including Pierre Eskrich (also known as Pierre Vase) and Georges Reverdy, while drawing stylistic inspiration from Bernard Salomon. His commercial strategy relied on an unprecedented international distribution web. Rouillé established direct supply chains and agency agreements in Venice, Florence, Rome, Frankfurt, Antwerp, Medina del Campo, and Salamanca, effectively making his Lyonnese shop a primary export engine for scholarly books bound for Spain and the New World.During the tumultuous years of the French Wars of Religion (1562–1598), when Lyon fell under Protestant control in 1562 and experienced severe economic and socio-political dislocation, Rouillé demonstrated remarkable pragmatic resilience. Maintaining a Catholic confessional identity while preserving commercial neutrality, he successfully navigated political purges, censorship decrees, and trade disruptions, maintaining continuous output when many rival printing houses collapsed. By the time of his death in Lyon on June 20, 1589, Rouillé had directed his press for over four decades, accumulating immense wealth, civic prestige, and international renown. His sons, Guillaume II and Philippe Rouillé, together with his extended heirs (*Heredes Gulielmi Rovillii*), continued the operations of the firm well into the seventeenth century. In modern historical and bibliographical scholarship—from the pioneering studies of Henri Baudrier to the work of Natalie Zemon Davis, Ruth Mortimer, and Ian Maclean—Guillaume Rouillé is recognized not merely as a master typographer, but as a seminal architect of Renaissance print culture who dynamically fused textual scholarship, artistic design, and global commerce.

academic_description: 4to (204x150 mm). 100, [4] pp. The last leaf is a blank. Collation: A-N4. Title-page within an elaborate woodcut border with at the center Rouillé’s device. 18th-century vellum over boards, gilt spine, marbled endpapers, red edges. Slightly browned throughout. A good copy. First edition (it was reprinted in 1558 and in 1560). The publisher Guillaume Rouillé (1518?-1588), who, starting with an Italian translation of De viris illustribus urbis Romae, published at the Sign of Venice in Lyons during his life over seventy book in Italian. These were addressed not only to the Italians residing in France, but also to the many Frenchmen, who had learned Italian in the course of war, study, or business. Rouillé had apprehended the book business in Venice with Giovanni and Gabriello Giolito and established himself at Lyons in 1543. His book production exceeded that of Robert Estienne, Gryphius and de Tournes, and his learning at least equalled theirs. His firm gained European reputation and his books were also sold in Antwerp, Frankfurt, Medina del Campo, Saragossa, as well as in Venice and Naples (cf. N. Zemon Davis, Publisher Guillaume Rouillé, Businessman and Humanist, in: “Editing Sixteenth Century Texts. Papers given at the Editorial Conference University of Toronto”, R.J. Schoeck, ed., Toronto, 1966, pp. 72-112; see also J. Balsamo, L’italianisme lyonnais et l’illustration de la langue française, in: “Lyon et l’illustration de la langue française à la Renaissance”, Lyon, 2003, pp. 211-229).Rouillé dedicated his Decamerone to Marguerite du Bourg, dame du Cange, wife of a high French financial officer, a very learned lady, to whom he was later to dedicate also his 1558-edition of Petrarch (cf. M.-M. Fontaine, ‘Un couer mis en gage’. Pontus de Tyard, Marguerite du Bourg et le milieu lyonnais des années 1550, in: “Nouvelle Revue du XVIe siècle”, 1984/2, p. 76-77; see also É. Picot, Les français italianisants au XVIe siècle, Paris, 1906, I, pp. 201-202).“Il Ridolfi, che collaborò con il Rouillé anche all’edizione del Petrarca (1550) e pubblicò presso lo stesso editore il dialogo l’Aretefila (1560), contribuì con una Vita di M. Giovanni Boccaccio brevemente descritta e con il Raccoglimento di tutte le sentenze a quella che viene considerata come la prima edizione stampata in Francia del Decameron in lingua italiana, la quale uscì dai torchi del Rouillé in formato tascabile nel 1555” (cfr. E. Giudici, Luc’Antonio Ridolfi et la Renaissance Franco-Italienne, in: “Quaderni di Filologia e Lingue Romanze”, n.s. 1, Rome, 1985, pp. 115-150).As clearly can also be presumed from the title, the Ragionamento is intended as a page by page commentary to Rouillé’s edition of the Decamerone. “Le text est anonyme, mais il est sûrement de Ridolfi, ainsi qu’en témoigne une lettre de son ami Alfonso Cambi. Herberé est un Français féru d’italien, qui a été inspiré par un séjour de deux ans dans le cercle de Marguerite de Berry, où tous cultivent le toscan. Herberé cherche à perfectionner son italien à l’aide du Décaméron, et se met à interroger Degli Uberti sur le text. Ce Degli Uberti est basé probablement sur quelque parent d’Antonio di Niccolò degli Uberti, éditeur du Décaméron en 1527, mais ce qu’il dit reflète les opinions de Ridolfi lui-même, qui n’oublie pas quelques allusions désobligeantes sur d’autres éditeurs, dont Girolamo Ruscelli (Venise 1552). Ces allusions valurent à Ridolfi quelques médisances de la part d’autres exilés florentins, dont Ludovico Castelvetro dans une lettre à Francsco Giuntini. Mais l’intérêt du dialogue réside dans ce qu’il nous apprend sur la fortune en France de Boccace, ainse que dans les multiples allusions dans le text à la Divina Commedia” (R. Cooper, Le cercle de Lucantonio Ridolfi, in: “L’émergence littéraire des femmes à Lyon à la Renaissance, 1520-1560”, M. Clément & J. Icadorna, eds., Saint-Étienne, 2008, p. 43).“Lucantonio Ridolfi publie également chez Guillaume Rouillé des dialogues qui mettent en scène une société franco-italienne, riche de débats. Tel est le cas de celui qui oppose un Français (Claude de Herberay) et un Florentin (Alessandro degli Uberti) discutant du Decamerone de Boccacce et de questions linguistiques à propos des trois auteurs canoniques, Dante, Pétrarque et Boccacce, et qu’il rapporte dans le Ragionamento havuto in Lione, da Claudio de Herberè gentil’huomo franzese, et da Alessandro degli Uberti gentil’huomo fiorentino, sopra alcuni luoghi del Cento novelle di Boccaccio (1557)” (M. Huchon, Louise Labbé. Une créature de papier, Genève, 2006, p. 42).Luc’Antonio Ridolfi was born and had his early education in Florence. At the beginning of the thirties he settled to Rome and became to be known in the literary circles of that city. After the mur- der of Alessandro de’ Medici he took refuge at Lyon as many of his ‘Republican’ compatriots, but maintained close relations with many Florentine, which remained in Italy as Claudio Tolomei, Niccolò Martelli, Pietro Vettori and Benedetto Varchi. He had come to Lyon as a merchant, but started around 1542 to work for the printing house of Gauillaume Rouillé as editor and translator of Italian texts. He spent the last years before his death in Florence (cf. E. Guidici, op. cit., pp. 115-150).

authors.name: Eder Georg
authors.biography: Georg Eder was born in Freising (Bavaria) and studied at Cologne and later law at Vienna, where he held for several times the position of rector of the university and of the dean of the faculty of law. He also became a member of the imperial court of justice. His repeated sharp attacks on the fundamental principles of Lutheranism created some stir even in circles of the imperial court for its harsh language and caused him the prohibition to publish works on religious matter. His most important work, however, remains the first history of the University of Vienna (1559).

publishers.name: Hofhalter Raphael
publishers.biography: Raphael Hofhalter (c. 1525 – c. 1568), also recorded in historical sources as Raphael Pruckner, Raphael Printz, and in Polish-Hungarian contexts as Raphael Skarga, stands as one of the most dynamic, artistically accomplished, and religiously contentious master printers, typographers, and punchcutters of the Central European High Renaissance. Operating across a turbulent geographical arc that encompassed the Imperial capital of Vienna, the Calvinist stronghold of Debrecen, the Transylvanian court of Nagyvárad (Oradea), and the Western frontier domain of Csáktornya (Čakovec), Hofhalter’s itinerant career reflects the complex interplay between Renaissance humanism, imperial patronage, confessionalization, and the rapid spread of the print medium across multi-confessional borderlands. Renowned for his exquisite punchcutting, sophisticated typographic layouts, and mastery of woodcut illustration, Hofhalter elevated the aesthetic standards of Central European book production while simultaneously placing his press at the explosive vanguard of the Protestant and Anti-Trinitarian Reformations.Early Life, Origins, and Technical ApprenticeshipThe precise origins of Raphael Hofhalter remain a subject of nuanced historiographical discussion, though evidence points to a Germanic or Swiss regional background, with early typographical training likely received in the major print centers of the Upper Rhine or Switzerland—most notably Zurich or Basel—before his emergence in Southern Germany and Poland. Early archival references occasionally link him to the surname Pruckner or Printz, suggesting that 'Hofhalter' may have been an assumed name or a title reflecting status acquired through courtly or guild connections. Unlike many contemporary shop-managing printers who relied entirely on hired craftsmen for letterform design, Hofhalter was a complete master of the typographic art: he was a skilled punchcutter (schneidkünstler), matrix caster, press builder, and engraver. This comprehensive technical mastery granted his publications a distinct visual identity, characterized by crisp Roman and Italic typefaces, balanced proportion, and intricate woodcut initials and borders that rivaled the finest productions of Venice, Basel, and Nuremberg.The Viennese Golden Age (1555–1562): Imperial Patronage and Humanist NetworksHofhalter arrived in Vienna around 1555, a moment when the imperial capital was undergoing a intellectual transformation under the patronage of King (later Emperor) Ferdinand I and the surrounding circle of Habsburg humanists. Establishing his printing house in the heart of Vienna, Hofhalter quickly secured an imperial privilege (Privilegium Impressorium) and positioned himself as the primary printer for the city's intellectual elite. Between 1555 and 1562, Hofhalter’s Viennese workshop produced over one hundred known titles, encompassing monumental legal codes, astronomical treatises, medical compendia, historical chronicles, and Latin humanist poetry. Among his most prestigious commissions were works by the imperial physician and historian Wolfgang Lazius, including the celebrated Rerum Viennensium commentarii (1556), as well as publications for the eminent scholar Johannes Sambucus and the court astronomer Paulus Fabricius.Visual presentation was the hallmark of Hofhalter’s Viennese press. He introduced sophisticated Renaissance architectural title-borders, elaborate coat-of-arms woodcuts for the nobility, and large-format fold-out anatomical and cartographic plates. Hofhalter also made significant contributions to multilingual printing, cutting types for Latin, German, Hungarian, and Slavic scripts. His printer’s emblem during this period—frequently featuring the allegorical figure of Spes (Hope) anchored amid stormy seas, accompanied by the motto In spe contra spem—served not only as a mark of aesthetic pride but also as a subtle declaration of spiritual resilience amid growing religious tensions.Confessional Shift, Flight, and the Hungarian-Transylvanian Itinerancy (1562–1567)Despite his commercial success and official standing in Vienna, Hofhalter harbored deep sympathies for the Protestant Reformation. Beneath the surface of his official imperial commissions, Hofhalter engaged in the clandestine printing of evangelical, Lutheran, and Reformed polemics, distributing them throughout Austria, Hungary, and Bohemia. By late 1562, under mounting pressure from the Counter-Reformation authorities and facing imminent judicial prosecution and confiscation of his equipment by Habsburg officials, Hofhalter staged a dramatic escape from Vienna. Packing his punches, matrices, woodblocks, and disassembled presses onto carts, he fled eastward into the Kingdom of Hungary and the Principality of Transylvania, where regional magnates offered protection and religious tolerance.In 1563, Hofhalter established his press in Debrecen, the center of Hungarian Calvinism, at the invitation of the prominent Reformed theologian Péter Melius Juhász. In Debrecen, Hofhalter’s press became the primary engine of the Hungarian Reformation, printing foundational vernacular Bibles, catechisms, hymnbooks, and theological treatises that shaped the Hungarian language and national identity. Moving between Debrecen and Nagyvárad (Oradea) under the patronage of Prince John Sigismund Zápolya (János Zsigmond), Hofhalter adapted his output to the shifting theological landscape of Transylvania. As the Transylvanian court drifted from Calvinism toward Radical Reformation and Unitarianism under the influence of figures such as Ferenc Dávid and Giorgio Biandrata, Hofhalter was commissioned to print some of the most radical theological texts of the sixteenth century, including the seminal Anti-Trinitarian treatise De falsa et vera unius Dei Patris, Filii et Spiritus Sancti cognitione (1567–1568), a masterpiece of typography printed under conditions of intense international scrutiny.The Final Chapter: Csáktornya (1567–1568) and Typographical LegacyIn 1567, seeking new patronage and operational stability, Hofhalter accepted the invitation of Count Juraj IV Zrinski (György Zrínyi) to relocate his printing equipment to Csáktornya (modern Čakovec, Croatia). Count Zrinski, a powerful Protestant nobleman, sought to establish a regional printing house to promote the Reformation across Northern Croatia, Slavonia, and Southwestern Hungary. Hofhalter’s arrival in Csáktornya marked the introduction of the first permanent printing press in the region of Međimurje. At Csáktornya, Hofhalter produced crucial Protestant devotional literature, Croatian and Hungarian vernacular texts, and polemical works, including writings by Mihály Sztárai.Hofhalter’s tireless career was cut short by his death in late 1568 or early 1569 in Csáktornya. Following his death, his widow Brigitta and his son, Rudolf Hofhalter (who had inherited his father’s technical mastery and punchcutting skill), continued the operations of the family press. Rudolf Hofhalter subsequently carried the press to Alsólendva (Lendava) and later back to Debrecen, preserving the artistic and typographical lineage established by his father.

On the title page ownership’s inscriptions “Conventus S. Wenceslai Egrensis” and “Ex libris Joannis Sedleckij”. Contemporary limp vellum (soiled), ties, new endpapers, some light damp stains throughout, but a good copy. Rare first edition. Soon after the death of the humanist and poet Konrad Celtes in 1508, the Collegium Poetarum, which was called into being by him in Vienna and which had the right of conferring the laureateship, came to an end. Efforts were made in the middle of the century to restore the Collegium, especially by some influential imperial councillors such as Jacob Jonas, Georg Sigmund Seld, Sigmund von Herberstein and Georg Eder. It was finally re-established in 1558 under the head of Nathanael Balsmannus, a member of the Collegium Archiducale.The first important publication of the new Collegium Poetarum was printed on the occasion of the coronation of Ferdinand as emperor in Frankfurt. His son Maximilian organized him a pompous reception at Vienna, followed by various festivities. A deputation of the university met the newly created emperor on sumptuously decorated ships on the Danube near Klosterneuburg and welcomed him with poetical eulogies. The emperor was then escorted to Vienna and enthusiastically welcomed in the cathedral of St. Stephen by the inhabitants of Vienna. The following festivities also included the coronation of several poets, e.g. Hieronymus Lauterbach from Bohemia and Vitus Jacobaeus from Nuremberg. Not only verses from both the newly created poets laureate are included in this volume, but also from numerous professors from various faculties of the university such as Georg Mitkreuz Petrus a Rotis, Bartholomäus Reisacher, Paul Fabricius, Johannes Sambucus, Johannes Heber, etc. (cf. authors.name: Estienne Henri
authors.biography: Henri Estienne (also known by his Latinized name Henricus Stephanus, and conventionally designated as Henri II Estienne; c. 1528/1531–1598) was one of the most important scholar-printers, Hellenists, philologists, lexicographers, and vernacular polemicists of sixteenth-century Europe. The eldest surviving son of the celebrated Parisian printer and humanist Robert I Estienne and Perrette Bade, daughter of the printer and scholar Josse Bade, he belonged to one of the great European dynasties of Renaissance printing. His career extended across the principal centres of the Republic of Letters—Paris, Geneva, Italy, the Low Countries, Germany, and France—and united the functions of printer, editor, textual critic, translator, lexicographer, author, and bibliographical entrepreneur. The BnF records his period of activity as 1554–1598 and identifies him both as a printer-bookseller and as the printer of the Augsburg humanist and banker Ulrich Fugger between 1558 and 1568.The precise year of Estienne's birth is not entirely secure. Older and many modern reference works give 1531, whereas the Bibliothèque nationale de France retains 1528? as the probable date. He was certainly born in Paris and was the eldest son of Robert Estienne and Perrette Bade. For scholarly purposes, therefore, c. 1528/1531 is preferable to presenting 1531 as absolutely certain.Family, education, and formationEstienne grew up within an exceptional multilingual and scholarly environment. His father's Parisian printing house employed correctors and scholars from different countries, and Henri later recalled that Latin functioned as the common language of the household. This does not mean that he acquired classical Latin in a wholly “native” sense, but it does explain the extraordinary linguistic environment in which his philological formation took place. His own account emphasizes the unusual decision to begin his serious literary education with Greek rather than Latin. He read Greek authors from an early age and received instruction from leading French Hellenists, notably Pierre Danès, Jacques Toussain, and Adrien Turnèbe.His education was inseparable from the practical world of Renaissance printing. The young Estienne learned not merely the languages of classical antiquity but also the material and editorial techniques by which Greek and Latin texts were transmitted, corrected, compared, and disseminated. This combination of philological learning and typographical practice became the defining characteristic of his career.During the late 1540s and early 1550s Estienne travelled extensively. Italy was particularly important: he visited major intellectual and manuscript centres, including Florence, Rome, Naples, and Venice, and acquired first-hand knowledge of manuscript traditions. Older biographical accounts associate these journeys with his study and collation of manuscripts of Greek authors, including Sextus Empiricus, Appian, Xenophon, Diogenes Laertius, and the poems attributed to Anacreon. He subsequently travelled in England and the Low Countries before returning to Paris. The traditional chronology should nevertheless be treated with some caution, since the surviving evidence does not support reducing these years to a single continuous “humanistic pilgrimage.”The Parisian beginnings and the AnacreonteaEstienne's independent publishing career is conventionally associated with the celebrated 1554 edition of the poems attributed to Anacreon: Ἀνακρέοντος Τηΐου μέλη. Anacreontis Teii odae ab Henrico Stephano luce & Latinitate nunc primum donatae (Paris, 1554).This was the first printed edition of the collection subsequently known as the Anacreontea, and it established Estienne's reputation as a Greek textual scholar and editor. The edition combined Greek text, Latin translation, and scholarly apparatus and exemplified the characteristic Estiennian fusion of philology and typography. The importance of the volume lies not merely in its status as an editio princeps, but in the fact that Estienne made the recovery and presentation of Greek literary texts the central vocation of his printing career.The 1554 publication was followed by an increasingly ambitious programme of classical editions. Estienne's Greek printing rapidly acquired a reputation for textual accuracy, elegant typography, and scholarly intervention, making the name Stephanus one of the most recognizable signatures of Renaissance Greek scholarship.Geneva and the Estienne printing houseThe religious conflicts of sixteenth-century France profoundly affected the Estienne family. Robert Estienne, who had moved increasingly toward the Reformed cause, left Paris and established himself in Geneva. Henri's career likewise became associated with the Genevan centre of Reformed printing, although his movements between France, Geneva, and other European cities remained extensive.After Robert Estienne's death in September 1559, Henri succeeded him in the Genevan workshop and became one of the principal printers of the Republic of Geneva.The French government's earlier association of Robert with the royal Greek printing programme had resulted in the famous Grecs du Roi, the Greek types designed by Ange Vergèce and cut by Claude Garamont. Robert brought a series of matrices to Geneva, and these types became part of the typographical heritage inherited by Henri. The surviving evidence, however, does not justify reducing the matter to a simple testamentary prohibition that mechanically “bound” Henri to Geneva. The history of the matrices, the family inheritance, and the transfer of the workshop is more complicated.At Geneva Estienne operated simultaneously as printer, publisher, editor, and author. His workshop produced Reformed theological works as well as classical and humanistic texts. He printed works associated with Théodore de Bèze and other Reformed scholars, but his programme was never confined to theology. The classical Greek corpus remained at the centre of his intellectual and commercial activity.Classical philology and the Greek printing programmeEstienne's Genevan career produced an extraordinary sequence of editions of Greek authors. Among the most important were:Aeschyli Tragoediae (1557);Diodori Siculi Bibliothecae historicae (1559);Xenophontis opera (1561);Sexti Empirici adversus mathematicos and related works (1562);Thucydidis historiae (1564);Herodoti historiarum libri IX (1566);Sophoclis tragoediae (1568);Pindari Olympia, Pythia, Nemea, Isthmia (1560s);editions and commentaries on other Greek authors;and, ultimately, the monumental edition of Plato in 1578.His editorial method combined comparison of earlier printed editions, consultation and collation of manuscripts, conjectural emendation, linguistic analysis, and extensive annotation. The importance of these editions lies not simply in their typographical elegance but in their contribution to the establishment of Renaissance textual criticism as a systematic scholarly discipline.His edition of Sextus Empiricus was particularly important for the history of European intellectual culture. Estienne was the first to publish a complete Latin translation of the Hypotyposes pyrrhoniennes, thereby contributing substantially to the transmission of ancient Pyrrhonian scepticism into early modern Europe.His edition of Herodotus was also closely connected with one of his most famous literary works, the Apologie pour Hérodote. The relationship between the classical historian and Estienne's contemporary satire became one of the most characteristic expressions of his humanist polemic.Ulrich Fugger and the economics of scholar-printingEstienne's publishing programme required substantial financial resources. One of his most important patrons was Ulrich Fugger of Augsburg, the wealthy bibliophile and member of the Fugger banking dynasty. Between 1558 and 1568 Estienne enjoyed Fugger's financial support and styled himself in his imprints as Fugger's printer. The BnF explicitly identifies him as imprimeur de l'illustre (H)ul(d)r(e)ich Fugger during this period.The Fugger connection illustrates the economic structure underlying Renaissance humanist scholarship. The production of large Greek editions required expensive paper, skilled compositors, specialized type, manuscript acquisition, editorial labour, and international distribution. Estienne's work therefore depended upon a network extending well beyond Geneva and France. The eventual loss of Fugger's support contributed to the financial instability of Estienne's later career. The economic burden was intensified by his most ambitious undertaking, the Thesaurus Graecae Linguae.The Thesaurus Graecae Linguae (1572)Estienne's supreme achievement as a lexicographer was the monumental: Thesaurus Graecae Linguae, Geneva, 1572. The first edition consisted of five folio volumes, the fifth containing the Appendix libellorum ad Thesaurum Graecae linguae pertinentium and additional lexicographical material. Contemporary bibliographical records confirm the five-volume structure of the first edition.The Thesaurus represented a culmination of the Greek lexicographical tradition available to sixteenth-century scholars. It drew on ancient lexica, scholia, grammarians, classical authors, manuscript evidence, and previous lexicographical compilations, while vastly expanding the amount of Greek linguistic material made accessible to European scholars. Its entries did not merely provide isolated Greek–Latin equivalents: Estienne organized evidence concerning forms, derivations, meanings, usages, and textual attestations, producing an enormously rich record of ancient Greek vocabulary.The Thesaurus remained fundamental to European Greek scholarship for centuries. Its scale, philological ambition, and documentary richness made it one of the monuments of Renaissance humanism and a major ancestor of modern historical lexicography. Later nineteenth-century Greek lexicography continued to depend heavily upon it.The financial consequences were severe. The enormous costs of producing such a work placed Estienne under considerable financial pressure, contributing to the deterioration of his economic position. His financial difficulties were compounded by the appearance of Johann Scapula's Lexicon Graeco-Latinum in Basel in 1579. Scapula's lexicon was substantially dependent upon the materials of the Thesaurus but presented them in a much more compact and commercially accessible form. The book became a highly successful competitor and was repeatedly reprinted. The first identifiable edition is the Basel edition of 1579. It is safer, however, to describe Scapula's work as a commercially formidable abridgement and competitor than to state categorically that it “stole” Estienne's work or directly caused his financial collapse.The Apologie pour HérodoteAmong Estienne's most extraordinary works was the Apologie pour Hérodote, first published at Geneva in 1566 under the full Latin title Apologia pro Herodoto, sive Herodoti historia fabulositatis accusata and accompanied by the French work later known as the Traité préparatif à l'Apologie pour Hérodote.The work ostensibly defended Herodotus against charges of credulity and historical fabulism. Its real scope, however, was much broader. Estienne used the extraordinary stories found in Herodotus as a framework for a vast satirical comparison between the alleged marvels of antiquity and the equally astonishing realities of sixteenth-century Europe.The work became one of the most powerful pieces of anti-Catholic and anti-clerical satire of the French Reformation. It contains anecdotes concerning religious superstition, ecclesiastical corruption, sexuality, violence, social hypocrisy, and popular credulity. Its polemical force brought it into conflict with Genevan authorities, and portions of the text were subject to censorship.The modern critical study of the preparatory treatise has demonstrated that the relationship between the Latin Apologia and the French Traité préparatif is more complex than that of a straightforward translation: Estienne substantially reworked, expanded, transformed, and adapted the material in French. Bénédicte Boudou's critical edition of the Traité préparatif is therefore an essential resource for understanding this part of his oeuvre.French language and linguistic nationalismEstienne was not exclusively a classical scholar. He was also one of the most energetic sixteenth-century defenders of the French language. In the Traité de la conformité du langage françois avec le grec (Geneva, 1565), he argued for profound affinities between French and Greek and presented French as a language capable of attaining a degree of expressive and rhetorical power comparable to that of the classical languages. The work belongs to the broader intellectual movement of Renaissance vernacular language defence, but Estienne's argument is unusually learned because it is grounded in comparative linguistic observation.His Deux dialogues du nouveau langage françois italianizé (Geneva, 1578) attacked the fashionable Italianisms of contemporary French speech, particularly those associated with courtly culture. The work is simultaneously linguistic criticism, social satire, and cultural polemic.In 1579 appeared the Projet du livre intitulé De la précellence du langage françois, commonly cited as La Précellence du langage françois. Here Estienne developed his defence of French on a still broader scale, arguing for its suitability to eloquence, history, jurisprudence, and literary expression. These works make him an important figure in the emergence of early modern French linguistic consciousness. Treccani and Larousse both identify the Traité de la conformité, the Deux dialogues, and the Précellence as central components of this linguistic programme.The Francofordiense Emporium and the European book tradeEstienne's international commercial activity is vividly documented by his Francofordiense Emporium, sive Francofordienses nundinae, published at Geneva in 1574. The work is an encomium and description of the Frankfurt Book Fair, based on Estienne's experience of the fair and its commercial environment. It is important not only as a literary curiosity but also as a rare first-person document concerning the international circulation of books in sixteenth-century Europe. The first edition was printed at Geneva in 1574 and is an exceptionally scarce work.The Francofordiense Emporium reveals Estienne's understanding of the book as an international commodity. His commercial network extended across Geneva, Frankfurt, Basel, Paris, Heidelberg, and other centres, demonstrating that the Renaissance printing house was simultaneously a scholarly institution and an international business.The 1578 edition of Plato and the “Stephanus pagination”Estienne's most enduring contribution to the modern study of Plato was his monumental three-volume edition: Platonis opera quae extant omnia, Geneva, 1578. The edition was printed by Estienne and incorporated a Greek text based on the comparison of earlier printed editions and available manuscript evidence. The accompanying Latin translation was newly produced by Jean de Serres and subsequently revised and corrected by Estienne. The three volumes contain the complete Platonic corpus as it was then understood, including works that modern scholarship subsequently determined to be spurious.The extraordinary afterlife of this edition lies in its pagination. Modern references to Plato—for example, Symposium 172a, Republic 514a, or Phaedo 118a—use the page-and-letter system derived from Estienne's 1578 edition. This is conventionally called Stephanus pagination, from the Latinized form of Estienne's name, Henricus Stephanus. The system was not created as a modern scholarly citation scheme, but the pagination of the 1578 edition became the stable reference framework subsequently adopted by generations of editors and scholars.Few Renaissance editions have therefore exercised such a direct and permanent influence on modern scholarship: virtually every modern scholarly citation of Plato continues to preserve the physical pagination of Estienne's sixteenth-century edition.Later scholarly activity and intellectual mobilityThe later decades of Estienne's life were increasingly unstable. His financial difficulties, the demands of his printing business, disputes with Genevan authorities, and his desire to maintain access to international markets led him to spend increasing periods outside Geneva. The Swiss Historical Dictionary records that his absences became particularly frequent after about 1590.His relationship with Geneva was complicated by the tension between his identity as a Reformed printer and his extraordinarily independent literary temperament. His satirical writings, especially those dealing with religion, morality, and contemporary society, repeatedly brought him into conflict with ecclesiastical authorities. The censorship of some of his writings illustrates the limits imposed upon even a major Protestant intellectual within the Genevan political and religious order.Estienne nevertheless continued to publish and revise classical and humanistic works. His later bibliography includes, among other things, Schediasmatum variorum, a collection of philological observations and emendations, and his 1585 edition of Aulus Gellius, whose prefatory material contains one of the most valuable autobiographical accounts of his intellectual formation and the Estienne household. His work therefore continued to oscillate between textual criticism, linguistic analysis, classical scholarship, satire, and the practical world of printing.Final years and deathEstienne's final years were marked by financial insecurity and increasingly extensive travel. The old image of the endlessly wandering humanist has some basis in reality, but his movements should be understood primarily in relation to the economic and intellectual geography of the European book trade. He died at Lyon in 1598. His son Paul Estienne, born in 1567, succeeded him in the continuation of the family's Genevan printing tradition. Estienne's death thus did not terminate the Estienne printing dynasty, although the scale and intellectual authority of Henri's enterprise were never fully reproduced.Historical significanceHenri Estienne occupies an exceptional position in the history of European scholarship because he united several functions that were increasingly specialized in later centuries. He was at once printer, publisher, editor, textual critic, lexicographer, translator, philologist, classical scholar, vernacular polemicist, and international bookseller.
