publishers.name: Estienne Henri
publishers.biography: Henri Estienne (also known by his Latinized name Henricus Stephanus, and conventionally designated as Henri II Estienne; c. 1528/1531–1598) was one of the most important scholar-printers, Hellenists, philologists, lexicographers, and vernacular polemicists of sixteenth-century Europe. The eldest surviving son of the celebrated Parisian printer and humanist Robert I Estienne and Perrette Bade, daughter of the printer and scholar Josse Bade, he belonged to one of the great European dynasties of Renaissance printing. His career extended across the principal centres of the Republic of Letters—Paris, Geneva, Italy, the Low Countries, Germany, and France—and united the functions of printer, editor, textual critic, translator, lexicographer, author, and bibliographical entrepreneur. The BnF records his period of activity as 1554–1598 and identifies him both as a printer-bookseller and as the printer of the Augsburg humanist and banker Ulrich Fugger between 1558 and 1568.The precise year of Estienne's birth is not entirely secure. Older and many modern reference works give 1531, whereas the Bibliothèque nationale de France retains 1528? as the probable date. He was certainly born in Paris and was the eldest son of Robert Estienne and Perrette Bade. For scholarly purposes, therefore, c. 1528/1531 is preferable to presenting 1531 as absolutely certain.Family, education, and formationEstienne grew up within an exceptional multilingual and scholarly environment. His father's Parisian printing house employed correctors and scholars from different countries, and Henri later recalled that Latin functioned as the common language of the household. This does not mean that he acquired classical Latin in a wholly “native” sense, but it does explain the extraordinary linguistic environment in which his philological formation took place. His own account emphasizes the unusual decision to begin his serious literary education with Greek rather than Latin. He read Greek authors from an early age and received instruction from leading French Hellenists, notably Pierre Danès, Jacques Toussain, and Adrien Turnèbe.His education was inseparable from the practical world of Renaissance printing. The young Estienne learned not merely the languages of classical antiquity but also the material and editorial techniques by which Greek and Latin texts were transmitted, corrected, compared, and disseminated. This combination of philological learning and typographical practice became the defining characteristic of his career.During the late 1540s and early 1550s Estienne travelled extensively. Italy was particularly important: he visited major intellectual and manuscript centres, including Florence, Rome, Naples, and Venice, and acquired first-hand knowledge of manuscript traditions. Older biographical accounts associate these journeys with his study and collation of manuscripts of Greek authors, including Sextus Empiricus, Appian, Xenophon, Diogenes Laertius, and the poems attributed to Anacreon. He subsequently travelled in England and the Low Countries before returning to Paris. The traditional chronology should nevertheless be treated with some caution, since the surviving evidence does not support reducing these years to a single continuous “humanistic pilgrimage.”The Parisian beginnings and the AnacreonteaEstienne's independent publishing career is conventionally associated with the celebrated 1554 edition of the poems attributed to Anacreon: Ἀνακρέοντος Τηΐου μέλη. Anacreontis Teii odae ab Henrico Stephano luce & Latinitate nunc primum donatae (Paris, 1554).This was the first printed edition of the collection subsequently known as the Anacreontea, and it established Estienne's reputation as a Greek textual scholar and editor. The edition combined Greek text, Latin translation, and scholarly apparatus and exemplified the characteristic Estiennian fusion of philology and typography. The importance of the volume lies not merely in its status as an editio princeps, but in the fact that Estienne made the recovery and presentation of Greek literary texts the central vocation of his printing career.The 1554 publication was followed by an increasingly ambitious programme of classical editions. Estienne's Greek printing rapidly acquired a reputation for textual accuracy, elegant typography, and scholarly intervention, making the name Stephanus one of the most recognizable signatures of Renaissance Greek scholarship.Geneva and the Estienne printing houseThe religious conflicts of sixteenth-century France profoundly affected the Estienne family. Robert Estienne, who had moved increasingly toward the Reformed cause, left Paris and established himself in Geneva. Henri's career likewise became associated with the Genevan centre of Reformed printing, although his movements between France, Geneva, and other European cities remained extensive.After Robert Estienne's death in September 1559, Henri succeeded him in the Genevan workshop and became one of the principal printers of the Republic of Geneva.The French government's earlier association of Robert with the royal Greek printing programme had resulted in the famous Grecs du Roi, the Greek types designed by Ange Vergèce and cut by Claude Garamont. Robert brought a series of matrices to Geneva, and these types became part of the typographical heritage inherited by Henri. The surviving evidence, however, does not justify reducing the matter to a simple testamentary prohibition that mechanically “bound” Henri to Geneva. The history of the matrices, the family inheritance, and the transfer of the workshop is more complicated.At Geneva Estienne operated simultaneously as printer, publisher, editor, and author. His workshop produced Reformed theological works as well as classical and humanistic texts. He printed works associated with Théodore de Bèze and other Reformed scholars, but his programme was never confined to theology. The classical Greek corpus remained at the centre of his intellectual and commercial activity.Classical philology and the Greek printing programmeEstienne's Genevan career produced an extraordinary sequence of editions of Greek authors. Among the most important were:Aeschyli Tragoediae (1557);Diodori Siculi Bibliothecae historicae (1559);Xenophontis opera (1561);Sexti Empirici adversus mathematicos and related works (1562);Thucydidis historiae (1564);Herodoti historiarum libri IX (1566);Sophoclis tragoediae (1568);Pindari Olympia, Pythia, Nemea, Isthmia (1560s);editions and commentaries on other Greek authors;and, ultimately, the monumental edition of Plato in 1578.His editorial method combined comparison of earlier printed editions, consultation and collation of manuscripts, conjectural emendation, linguistic analysis, and extensive annotation. The importance of these editions lies not simply in their typographical elegance but in their contribution to the establishment of Renaissance textual criticism as a systematic scholarly discipline.His edition of Sextus Empiricus was particularly important for the history of European intellectual culture. Estienne was the first to publish a complete Latin translation of the Hypotyposes pyrrhoniennes, thereby contributing substantially to the transmission of ancient Pyrrhonian scepticism into early modern Europe.His edition of Herodotus was also closely connected with one of his most famous literary works, the Apologie pour Hérodote. The relationship between the classical historian and Estienne's contemporary satire became one of the most characteristic expressions of his humanist polemic.Ulrich Fugger and the economics of scholar-printingEstienne's publishing programme required substantial financial resources. One of his most important patrons was Ulrich Fugger of Augsburg, the wealthy bibliophile and member of the Fugger banking dynasty. Between 1558 and 1568 Estienne enjoyed Fugger's financial support and styled himself in his imprints as Fugger's printer. The BnF explicitly identifies him as imprimeur de l'illustre (H)ul(d)r(e)ich Fugger during this period.The Fugger connection illustrates the economic structure underlying Renaissance humanist scholarship. The production of large Greek editions required expensive paper, skilled compositors, specialized type, manuscript acquisition, editorial labour, and international distribution. Estienne's work therefore depended upon a network extending well beyond Geneva and France. The eventual loss of Fugger's support contributed to the financial instability of Estienne's later career. The economic burden was intensified by his most ambitious undertaking, the Thesaurus Graecae Linguae.The Thesaurus Graecae Linguae (1572)Estienne's supreme achievement as a lexicographer was the monumental: Thesaurus Graecae Linguae, Geneva, 1572. The first edition consisted of five folio volumes, the fifth containing the Appendix libellorum ad Thesaurum Graecae linguae pertinentium and additional lexicographical material. Contemporary bibliographical records confirm the five-volume structure of the first edition.The Thesaurus represented a culmination of the Greek lexicographical tradition available to sixteenth-century scholars. It drew on ancient lexica, scholia, grammarians, classical authors, manuscript evidence, and previous lexicographical compilations, while vastly expanding the amount of Greek linguistic material made accessible to European scholars. Its entries did not merely provide isolated Greek–Latin equivalents: Estienne organized evidence concerning forms, derivations, meanings, usages, and textual attestations, producing an enormously rich record of ancient Greek vocabulary.The Thesaurus remained fundamental to European Greek scholarship for centuries. Its scale, philological ambition, and documentary richness made it one of the monuments of Renaissance humanism and a major ancestor of modern historical lexicography. Later nineteenth-century Greek lexicography continued to depend heavily upon it.The financial consequences were severe. The enormous costs of producing such a work placed Estienne under considerable financial pressure, contributing to the deterioration of his economic position. His financial difficulties were compounded by the appearance of Johann Scapula's Lexicon Graeco-Latinum in Basel in 1579. Scapula's lexicon was substantially dependent upon the materials of the Thesaurus but presented them in a much more compact and commercially accessible form. The book became a highly successful competitor and was repeatedly reprinted. The first identifiable edition is the Basel edition of 1579. It is safer, however, to describe Scapula's work as a commercially formidable abridgement and competitor than to state categorically that it “stole” Estienne's work or directly caused his financial collapse.The Apologie pour HérodoteAmong Estienne's most extraordinary works was the Apologie pour Hérodote, first published at Geneva in 1566 under the full Latin title Apologia pro Herodoto, sive Herodoti historia fabulositatis accusata and accompanied by the French work later known as the Traité préparatif à l'Apologie pour Hérodote.The work ostensibly defended Herodotus against charges of credulity and historical fabulism. Its real scope, however, was much broader. Estienne used the extraordinary stories found in Herodotus as a framework for a vast satirical comparison between the alleged marvels of antiquity and the equally astonishing realities of sixteenth-century Europe.The work became one of the most powerful pieces of anti-Catholic and anti-clerical satire of the French Reformation. It contains anecdotes concerning religious superstition, ecclesiastical corruption, sexuality, violence, social hypocrisy, and popular credulity. Its polemical force brought it into conflict with Genevan authorities, and portions of the text were subject to censorship.The modern critical study of the preparatory treatise has demonstrated that the relationship between the Latin Apologia and the French Traité préparatif is more complex than that of a straightforward translation: Estienne substantially reworked, expanded, transformed, and adapted the material in French. Bénédicte Boudou's critical edition of the Traité préparatif is therefore an essential resource for understanding this part of his oeuvre.French language and linguistic nationalismEstienne was not exclusively a classical scholar. He was also one of the most energetic sixteenth-century defenders of the French language. In the Traité de la conformité du langage françois avec le grec (Geneva, 1565), he argued for profound affinities between French and Greek and presented French as a language capable of attaining a degree of expressive and rhetorical power comparable to that of the classical languages. The work belongs to the broader intellectual movement of Renaissance vernacular language defence, but Estienne's argument is unusually learned because it is grounded in comparative linguistic observation.His Deux dialogues du nouveau langage françois italianizé (Geneva, 1578) attacked the fashionable Italianisms of contemporary French speech, particularly those associated with courtly culture. The work is simultaneously linguistic criticism, social satire, and cultural polemic.In 1579 appeared the Projet du livre intitulé De la précellence du langage françois, commonly cited as La Précellence du langage françois. Here Estienne developed his defence of French on a still broader scale, arguing for its suitability to eloquence, history, jurisprudence, and literary expression. These works make him an important figure in the emergence of early modern French linguistic consciousness. Treccani and Larousse both identify the Traité de la conformité, the Deux dialogues, and the Précellence as central components of this linguistic programme.The Francofordiense Emporium and the European book tradeEstienne's international commercial activity is vividly documented by his Francofordiense Emporium, sive Francofordienses nundinae, published at Geneva in 1574. The work is an encomium and description of the Frankfurt Book Fair, based on Estienne's experience of the fair and its commercial environment. It is important not only as a literary curiosity but also as a rare first-person document concerning the international circulation of books in sixteenth-century Europe. The first edition was printed at Geneva in 1574 and is an exceptionally scarce work.The Francofordiense Emporium reveals Estienne's understanding of the book as an international commodity. His commercial network extended across Geneva, Frankfurt, Basel, Paris, Heidelberg, and other centres, demonstrating that the Renaissance printing house was simultaneously a scholarly institution and an international business.The 1578 edition of Plato and the “Stephanus pagination”Estienne's most enduring contribution to the modern study of Plato was his monumental three-volume edition: Platonis opera quae extant omnia, Geneva, 1578. The edition was printed by Estienne and incorporated a Greek text based on the comparison of earlier printed editions and available manuscript evidence. The accompanying Latin translation was newly produced by Jean de Serres and subsequently revised and corrected by Estienne. The three volumes contain the complete Platonic corpus as it was then understood, including works that modern scholarship subsequently determined to be spurious.The extraordinary afterlife of this edition lies in its pagination. Modern references to Plato—for example, Symposium 172a, Republic 514a, or Phaedo 118a—use the page-and-letter system derived from Estienne's 1578 edition. This is conventionally called Stephanus pagination, from the Latinized form of Estienne's name, Henricus Stephanus. The system was not created as a modern scholarly citation scheme, but the pagination of the 1578 edition became the stable reference framework subsequently adopted by generations of editors and scholars.Few Renaissance editions have therefore exercised such a direct and permanent influence on modern scholarship: virtually every modern scholarly citation of Plato continues to preserve the physical pagination of Estienne's sixteenth-century edition.Later scholarly activity and intellectual mobilityThe later decades of Estienne's life were increasingly unstable. His financial difficulties, the demands of his printing business, disputes with Genevan authorities, and his desire to maintain access to international markets led him to spend increasing periods outside Geneva. The Swiss Historical Dictionary records that his absences became particularly frequent after about 1590.His relationship with Geneva was complicated by the tension between his identity as a Reformed printer and his extraordinarily independent literary temperament. His satirical writings, especially those dealing with religion, morality, and contemporary society, repeatedly brought him into conflict with ecclesiastical authorities. The censorship of some of his writings illustrates the limits imposed upon even a major Protestant intellectual within the Genevan political and religious order.Estienne nevertheless continued to publish and revise classical and humanistic works. His later bibliography includes, among other things, Schediasmatum variorum, a collection of philological observations and emendations, and his 1585 edition of Aulus Gellius, whose prefatory material contains one of the most valuable autobiographical accounts of his intellectual formation and the Estienne household. His work therefore continued to oscillate between textual criticism, linguistic analysis, classical scholarship, satire, and the practical world of printing.Final years and deathEstienne's final years were marked by financial insecurity and increasingly extensive travel. The old image of the endlessly wandering humanist has some basis in reality, but his movements should be understood primarily in relation to the economic and intellectual geography of the European book trade. He died at Lyon in 1598. His son Paul Estienne, born in 1567, succeeded him in the continuation of the family's Genevan printing tradition. academic_description: 8vo (158x93 mm). [4], 228 pp. Collation: *2 a-n8 o-p4 q2. With the printer’s device on the title-page. Later stiff vellum, ink title on the spine, sprinkled edges. Slightly uniformly browned, some marginal foxing, but a fine copy. First edition of the second attack of Henri Estienne on Ciceronianism. The first was published a year previously under the title De latinitate falso suspecta expostulation (with an appendix on the style of Plautus). The last volume of his critic, aimed especially at Mario Nizolio’s Thesaurus as a kind of bible of Ciceronianism, appeared as Nizoliodidascalus, sive Monitor Ciceronianorum in 1578.“Il est hors de doute qu’à un ‘degré zero’, pour ansi dire, de lecture, il s’agit d’un exercice promotionel: fustigeant les incorrections des éditions de Cicéron d’un Bade, d’un Lambin, d’un Manuce, et de tant d’autres, Estienne ne fait que souligner, par ricochet, la qualité des siennes. Rappelons en effet que qu’Estienne, ruiné par la publication de son Thesaurus, sortait, en 1577, l’année même de la publication du Pseudocicero, une edition des Epistolae ad familiares, pour laquelle le Pseudocicero pouvait fare figure d’une sorte d’avant-coureur ou d’accompagnement publicitaire, afin d’assurer, si possible, les revenues don’t Estienne avait si existentiellement besoin. Mais il y a plus... [Estienne] developpe un système parfaitement cohérent et remarquablement moderne de critique textuelle et de pratique éditoriale. Si les éditions d’Estienne sont supérieures à celles de ses rivaux, c’est parce que sa méthode est supérieure à la leur, sin bien qu’à un ‘degré dérivé’ de lecture, on pourrait interpréter le Pseudocicero comme un traité de méthode critique, dans lequel s’articule, avec force et précision, le canon des règles à suivre par un bon éditeur” (L. Deitz, Le ‘Pseudocicero’ d’Henri Estienne, ou: Du bon usage de la critique, in: “La philologie humaniste et ses representations dans la théorie et dans la fiction”, P. Galand-Hallyn, & al. eds., Genève, 2005, pp. 562-563; see also P. Mesnard, Le ‘Pseudocicero’ de Henri Estienne et l’avènement du cicéronianisme critique, in: “Bulletin de l’Association G. Budé”, octobre, 1967, pp. 283-292).Henri Estienne was a member of the prominent family of French printers. He succeeded his father Robert in the Geneva publishing house in 1557 and became one of the most distinguished scholar-publishers the world has ever known. By the terms of his father’s will, he had to keep the precious equipment from publishing Greek texts in Geneva. He obtained subsidies from a variety of sources, including Ulrich Fugger, a Protestant member of the great German banking family, and king Henry of France. His most important single publication is his five-volume Thesaurus of the Greek language (1572), a monumental reference work that, in updated versions, remains useful to scholars today. He never succeeded, however, in recovering all of its enormous cost. Henri also published a number of standard edition of Greek writers, including Herodotus, Thucydides, and Plato. He continued his father’s involvement in Calvinist publishing, producing a number of standard works including Théodore de Bèze’s version of the New Testament and Geoge Buchanan’s paraphrase of the Psalms. He also published his own philological investigations as well as polemical and satirical pieces, all in all about 170 titles (cf. J. Kecskeméti, & al., eds., La France des Humanistes. Henri II Estienne, editeur er écrivain, Turnhout, 2003, passim).

authors.name: Patrizi Francesco
authors.biography: Francesco Patrizi da Siena (1413–1494), known in Latin scholarly circles as Franciscius Patricius Senensis, stands as one of the most authoritative political theorists, humanists, and ecclesiastical figures of the Italian Quattrocento. Occupying a crucial historiographical node between classical civic humanism and early modern monarchical political philosophy, Patrizi authored two of the most widely circulated systematic treatises on statecraft of the Renaissance: De institutione reipublicae ('On the Institution of the Republic') and De regno et regis institutione ('On the Kingdom and the Education of the King'). His life reflected the intense political volatility, intellectual mobility, and patronal realignments of fifteenth-century Italy, bridging the republican traditions of his native Siena, the diplomatic corridors of the Roman Curia under Pope Pius II, and the royal court of the Aragonese dynasty in Naples.Born in Siena in 1413 to the patrician family of the Patrizi—a lineage traditionally affiliated with the aristocratic faction of the Monte dei Nove—young Francesco received a rigorous education in Latin grammar, classical rhetoric, moral philosophy, and jurisprudence. During the 1430s and 1440s, he embedded himself deeply within the civic and intellectual fabric of Siena, occupying various public magistracies, serving on diplomatic missions, and actively participating in the Sienese humanist network alongside figures like Enea Silvio Piccolomini (the future Pope Pius II) and Agostino Dati. However, the internal factional turmoil of Siena severely disrupted his career. In 1456, following an unsuccessful political conspiracy aimed at restoring the power of the suppressed noble factions against the ruling populist government, Patrizi was arrested, interrogated, and condemned to perpetual exile, accompanied by the confiscation of his family estates.Forced into exile, Patrizi sought refuge first in Ferrara and subsequently in Rome, where his longstanding friendship with Enea Silvio Piccolomini proved transformative. Following Piccolomini's elevation to the papacy as Pius II in 1458, Patrizi was integrated into the papal court and cleared of remaining canonical impediments. In 1460, through papal provision, he was appointed Bishop of Gaeta, a strategic coastal see within the Kingdom of Naples. This ecclesiastical elevation relocated Patrizi to the southern sphere of Aragonese patronage, where he served for over three decades until his death in 1494. In Gaeta and Naples, Patrizi effectively combined his pastoral duties with intensive scholarly activity, acting as a counselor, orator, and intellectual advisor to King Ferdinand I of Naples (Ferrante) and his son, Alfonso, Duke of Calabria.Patrizi's seminal political treatise, De institutione reipublicae, composed in nine comprehensive books between approximately 1465 and 1471, represents one of the most elaborate systematic syntheses of republican political philosophy produced in fifteenth-century Europe. Deeply grounded in Cicero, Livy, Aristotle's Politics, and Polybius, the work offers an exhaustive examination of civic virtue, constitutional balance, public magistracies, judicial integrity, military organization, and urban planning. Patrizi argued that the stability of a republic relies fundamentally upon the moral elevation and classical education of its ruling class, emphasizing that civic liberty (libertas) cannot subsist without strict adherence to justice, legal equity, and the active suppression of private factionalism.In his subsequent masterwork, De regno et regis institutione (likewise structured in nine books and dedicated to Alfonso, Duke of Calabria), Patrizi shifted his theoretical paradigm to address the realities of monarchical governance. Rather than viewing republic and monarchy as mutually exclusive, Patrizi adapted his humanist pedagogical framework to the prince (speculum principis). He outlined the cardinal and theological virtues required of a sovereign, arguing that a true king is distinguished from a tyrant by his dedication to the common good, respect for fundamental law, patronage of letters, and self-mastery over his passions. The work meticulously detailed the ideal curriculum for royal princes, covering physical discipline, military strategy, historical analysis, moral philosophy, and eloquence.Beyond his principal political works, Patrizi was a prolific poet, epistolarian, and translator. He composed Latin elegies and epics, most notably the Eridanus (written during his Ferrarese exile), and translated classical Greek texts into Latin, including speeches by Aeschines and treatises by Xenophon. He also wrote in the Italian vernacular, producing devotional verse, political discourses regarding the civic defense of Siena, and humanist dialogues. His literary style was characterized by a refined, ciceronian Latinity that earned him high praise among his contemporary humanists, including Cristoforo Landino, Mario Filelfo, and Hermolaus Barbarus.The print history of Patrizi's treatises demonstrates their immense early modern European impact. Though widely circulated in manuscript form during his lifetime, the work achieved global prominence through sixteenth-century print culture. The editio princeps of De institutione reipublicae was produced in Paris in 1518 by the printer Pierre Vidoue for the publisher Jean Petit, followed immediately by Jean Petit's 1519 Paris edition of De regno et regis institutione. These handsome folio and quarto editions triggered an explosion of re-editions in Paris, Strasbourg, Basel, and Venice throughout the sixteenth century. Vernacular translations quickly followed, including the French renderings by Jean Le Blond (1544 and 1550), the Italian translations by Giovanni Fabrini da Fobine (Venice, 1545 and 1553), and English adaptations that directly informed Thomas Elyot's The Boke Named the Gouernour (1531) and Richard Robinson's Elizabethan political treatises.In modern historiography, Patrizi da Siena's legacy has been re-evaluated as an essential bridge between Quattrocento civic humanism and modern state theory. Scholars such as Felice Battaglia, Claudio Finzi, Diego Quaglioni, and James Hankins have emphasized that Patrizi provided the early modern world with its most comprehensive, accessible textbook on classical political wisdom prior to Jean Bodin and Niccolò Machiavelli. His dual legacy as a theorist of both republican civic virtue and prince-centered statecraft highlights the profound adaptability and enduring structural power of Renaissance humanist thought.

publishers.name: Manuzio Aldo heirs of
publishers.biography: Aldo's heirs were his sons, Marco Manuzio, Antonio and Paolo, who were all minors at the time of their father's death. The company was therefore initially managed by Andrea Torresano the Elder, Aldo's partner and father-in-law, and his sons, Giovanni Francesco and Federico. Once Paolo, the youngest son of Aldo, had come of age, the company continued with the Torresano family until 1540; subsequently, the Manuzio and Torresano families continued to work separately.

publisher_data: Colophon: In Vinegia, In casa de’ figliuoli di Aldo, 1545
academic_description: 8vo (151x102 mm). 278, [4] leaves. Collation: A-Z8 AA-LL8 MM10. Colophon at l. MM9r. Printer’s device on title page and last leaf verso. Contemporary limp vellum, inked title on spine and on the lower edge (soiled, traces of ties). On the front panel and on title page ownership’s inscription “Jo: Petri Clericij”. Marginal rust spots on leaves AA1-8, a few very light damp stains. A very good, genuine copy. First edition in Italian of one of the most important documents for the history of political and educational thought of fifteenth century Humanism. It was begun around 1462, completed in 1468 and first published by Jean Savigny in 1518 under the title De institutione reipublicae libri novem. It has often been seen as a precursor of Machiavelli’s Principe and had a great influence on Thomas Elyot’s Gouvernour (cf. J. Schlotter, Thomas Elyot’s ‘Governor’ in seinem Verhältnis zu Francesco Patrizi, Freiburg/Br., passim).The work covers the whole field of civic Humanism discussing all questions of state administration, law (moral and civil), town and country planning (cf. P.N. Pagliara, Vitruvio: da testo a canone, in: “Memoria dell’antico nell’arte italiana”, S. Settis, ed., Torino, 1986, III, pp. 28-30), and the management of a family (the duties of a husband and of a wife, the education of children, cf. G. Müller, Bildung und Erziehung im Humanismus der italienischen Renaissance, Wiesbaden, 1969, pp. 117, 36). Patrizi recommends protection for merchants and tradesmen who contribute to the enriching of a country, considers that the state should provide the means of subsistence to the population if necessary, and also deals with the importance of culture (fine arts, music, theatre, literature, libraries), medicine and the great physicians of the past, gymnastic exercises, etc. (cf. M. Capelli, ‘Ad actionem secundum virtutem tendit’. La passione, la sapienza e la prudenza: ‘vita activa’ e ‘vita contemplativa’ nel pensiero umanistico, in: “The ways of life in classical political philosophy”, F. Lisi, ed., Sankt Augustin, 2004, pp. 203-30).“Patrizi’s text deals with the disposition and government of a city-state Republic, understood in the terms of the contemporary political reality of fifteenth-century Italy, describing and analyzing the political, social and economic conditions that prevail in such an urban context. Significantly, the treatise does not confine itself to a theoretical discussion of the city as locus of government, but examines the urban fabric itself, giving ample space to a discussion of the role of the architect in planning the city, and the disposition of streets, piazzas and individual buildings, both public and private. Architecture and government are thus bound together, so that a well-governed city will be architecturally well-ordered, and vice versa [...] While, in some respects, the most original feature of Patrizi’s treatise is the way in which he links social and political issues of government to the question of urban life. Patrizi viewed the city-state as the natural resolution of man’s need to be a ‘social animal’, and in Book I he outlines the ways in which urban society should be ordered to maintain equality among citizens. While Book II deals with the varieties of professions that should exist in the city, Book III instead focuses on public offices and the procedures that should be observed in nomination and election... Indeed the core three books relate specifically to the family, in its public and private role. While Book IV discusses the function of the family and the paterfamilias in the government of private affairs, Book V and VI project the family onto the public scene. So that virtues honed in the family setting are given a public purpose. It is thus in Book V that the public virtues of government, discussed in Book III, are revealed as being an attribute to the patrician class, showing that these families are naturally suited to rule. A clear statement in favor of the ancestral aristocracy’s capacity to rule come in chapter One of Book VI, where Patrizi provides a definition of urban society as being made up of three classes: the ancient nobility, a middle-ranking group of worthy citizens, and a majority suited only to being governed... However, it is in the last section of the treatise that Patrizi addresses themes relevant to an understanding of the Pope’s architectural patronage in Siena. Specifically, chapter Eleven of Book VIII discusses private architecture in the urban context. Patrizi advises the families in public office should invest in a palace suited to their status, but this should be a ‘beautiful home’. He recommends the use of ‘sancta mediocritas’ (a golden mean), so that a building will display neither the opulence nor the avarice of its owner, but rather that the palace will beautify the collective image of the city” (F. Nevola, Siena, Constructing the Renaissance City, New Haven, CT & London, 2007, pp. 87-88).The translator Giovanni Fabbrini, who dedicated the volume to the sons of the Roman nobleman Antonio Massimi, to whom he was the tutor, was born at Figline Valdarno in 1516 and studied at Florence under Lorenzo Amadei and Gaspare Marescotti. In 1544 he settled in Rome, where he published his first work, Della interpretation della lingua latina. In 1546 he returned to Florence and finished the translation of Patrizi’s second important work, the De regno et regis institutione. A year later he was called by the Senate of Venice to teach in the public schools. His activities as a merchant brought him some wealth and allowed him to concentrate more on his literary activities. He published numerous translations into the vernacular, commentaries and grammatical and linguistic studies, among them in 1565, Teoria della lingua, dedicated to Cosimo de’ Medici. He died in Venice in 1580 (cf. F. Sarri, Giovanni Fabbrini da Figline (1516-1580?), in: “La Rinascita”, II, 1939, pp. 617-640; III, 1940, pp. 233-270; IV, 1941, pp. 361-408).“In his translation of a section following the list of artisans in which Patrizi discusses the ancient respect for certain works of art […] Fabrini adds a reference to Michelangelo in the chapter on artists per se (p. 36v) […] Fabrizi’s inclusion of the example of Michelangelo suggests that the rise in status of the artist could indeed have promoted the rise in status of the artisan in general” (G.W. McClure, The Culture of Profession in Late Renaissance Italy, Toronto, 2004, p. 230).Francesco Patrizi received his early education at the Studio of Siena, his native city. He became a friend of the bishop of Siena Enea Silvio Piccolomini (later Pope Pius II). In 1452 was to be a member of a Sienese embassy which accompanied the Emperor Frederick III to Rome. For a certain time he served as podestà of Montalcino. A few years later his fortunes had changed dramatically for the worse- He was among the notables who were arrested in 1456 and tried for conspiring to hand Siena over to Jacopo Piccinini, who was in the service of Alfonso of Naples. Only the intervention of Enea Silvio, then a cardinal, could prevent his death. Patrizi was instead sentenced to exile, leaving his wife and for sons in the charge of their grandparents. Later he was admitted into Holy Orders and, still favored by Enea Silvio, now pope Pius II, was elected bishop of Gaeta in the kingdom of Naples, without the duty to reside in his diocese. Still in 1461 he took up residence in Foligno as papal governor. His experience as governor as well as his originally first-hand knowledge of the ups and downs of politics in his native Siena certainly furthered his interest in political science and the Institutione reipublicae was written during his stay at Foligno. Apparently he released his post of governor of Foligno in 1471, settled at Gaeta for the rest of his life, apart from occasional missions for the House of Aragon, attending to his episcopal duties. At Gaeta he wrote his second great work on political science De regno & regis institutione (cf. F. Battaglia, Enea Silvio Piccolomi e Francesco Patrizi: Due politici senesi del Quattrocento, Siena, 1936, pp. 76-100; F.C. Nardone, Francesco Patrizi umanista senese, Empoli, 1996, passim; and P. Benedetti Bertoldi, Francesco Patrizi the Elder: the Portrait of a Fifteenth Century Humanist, thesis, Oxford, 1996, passim).

authors.name: Rasch Johann
authors.biography: Johann Rasch (ca. 1540 – 1612) stands as one of the most remarkably versatile figures of the late Renaissance in Central Europe—a polymathic mind whose administrative, musical, bibliographical, and scientific endeavors epitomized the intellectual climate of the Holy Roman Empire during the transitional era between Humanism and the Counter-Reformation. Serving for over four decades as organist, bibliographer, and administrator at the Benedictine Abbey of Our Dear Lady of the Scots (Schottenstift) in Vienna, Rasch occupied a unique nexus within the Habsburg capital. His output spanned polyphonic sacred music published by the prestigious Munich press of Adam Berg, ground-breaking vernacular treatises on viticulture and enology, complex chronological and astronomical studies regarding calendar reform and comets, and elaborate genealogical compilations dedicated to the House of Habsburg. Far from being a mere institutional functionary, Rasch represented the early modern ideal of the practical scholar who seamlessly integrated monastic librarianship, musical artistry, agronomic empiricism, and civic record-keeping.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationJohann Rasch was born around the year 1540, likely in the town of Pöchlarn in Lower Austria, or within the adjacent Bavarian-Austrian borderlands along the Danube basin. The region, heavily influenced by both Danubian Humanism and the trade routes connecting Passau, Linz, and Vienna, provided a fertile environment for his early intellectual growth. While precise documentation regarding his parentage remains sparse, biographical clues embedded in his later publications indicate that he received rigorous early schooling in choral music, Latin grammar, and basic arithmetic within a monastic or collegiate environment. Scholars have suggested that his musical talents as a soprano or organ pupil brought him into contact with regional ecclesiastical centers in Upper Austria and Bavaria, where the polyphonic traditions of the Franco-Flemish school were being actively synthesized with South German sacred practice.During the 1560s, Rasch pursued higher academic studies, absorbing the mathematical, astronomical, and chronological disciplines then transforming Central European university curricula. His formative years coincided with profound religious and political realignments across the Holy Roman Empire following the Peace of Augsburg (1555). Rasch spent crucial years in Munich during the late 1560s and early 1570s, a period when the court chapel of Duke Albert V of Bavaria was becoming one of Europe's premier musical centers under the leadership of Orlando di Lasso. In Munich, Rasch established vital connections with court musicians, humanists, and printers—most notably the ducal printer Adam Berg—which deeply influenced his double career as a composer and publisher of practical treatises. This Bavarian exposure exposed him not only to the highest standards of Counter-Reformation liturgical art but also to advanced typographical techniques that would later characterize his own bibliographic projects.The Viennese Period and Institutional Leadership at the SchottenstiftIn 1570, Rasch was formally engaged as organist (Organist) at the prestigious Benedictine Abbey of the Scots (Schottenstift) in Vienna, an institution of ancient lineage founded in 1155 by Duke Henry II Jasomirgott. By the late sixteenth century, the abbey had become a vital spiritual and cultural bastion for the Catholic Restoration in Lower Austria, navigating the complex socio-religious tensions between the Lutheran sympathies of the Austrian landed estates (Landstände) and the ardent Catholic orthodoxy of the Habsburg imperial court under Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolf II. Rasch’s role at the Schottenstift quickly expanded far beyond his musical duties at the organ loft. Recognizing his meticulous administrative capabilities, classical erudition, and organizational acumen, the monastic authorities appointed him abbey bibliographer, librarian, and clerk of the fabric (Kirchenprobst).In his capacity as librarian, Rasch cataloged and reorganized the monastic archive and library, imposing systematic order on centuries of accumulated codices, incunabula, and legal charters. His intimate knowledge of the abbey's holdings enabled him to draft comprehensive inventories and historical registers that protected the monastery's feudal rights and territorial revenues. Furthermore, as Kirchenprobst, Rasch managed the financial accounts of the abbey's urban properties and agricultural estates, particularly its extensive vineyard holdings in and around Vienna, Grinzing, and the Wachau valley. This administrative responsibility directly sparked his scientific interest in viticulture, turning the monastic scholar into one of Central Europe's pioneer enological authors.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksRasch’s publication record reflects a staggering breadth of interests, divided into four major domains: sacred polyphony, viticulture and practical agronomy, calendrics and astronomy, and dynastic genealogy. His earliest major published work was a collection of polyphonic vocal compositions entitled Cantiunculae paschales (Munich: Adam Berg, 1572), written for four to six voices. These Easter motets demonstrate a masterful command of imitative counterpoint and expressive text-setting directly indebted to the Munich style of Orlando di Lasso and Jacobus de Kerle. Rasch continued his musical output with collections of German spiritual songs and devotional hymns, such as Gartentrost (1589), designed to promote Catholic piety through accessible, melodic polyphony suitable for both church choir and domestic sacred recreation.Rasch’s most enduring scientific achievement is undoubtedly his treatise on viticulture, titled Von Bwen, Pflanzen und Pflegen des Weins, commonly referred to as the Weinreich or Weinbuch, first published in Vienna in 1580 by Blasius Pusch and subsequently expanded in 1582, 1589, and 1599. The Weinreich is widely celebrated as one of the very first comprehensive manuals on enology and viticultural economy written in the German language. Structurally divided into systematic chapters, the work covers soil classification, vine grafting, seasonal pruning, trellis construction, grape harvesting, barrel cooperage, cellar hygiene, and the chemical remediation of spoiled wines. Combining classical authorities such as Pliny the Elder, Columella, and Virgil with empirical observations gathered from Austrian and Bavarian winegrowers, Rasch produced a work of immense practical value. Beyond technical instruction, the Weinreich offers a fascinating window into early modern economic philosophy, detailing municipal wine taxation, trade routes along the Danube, social customs surrounding wine consumption, and moral admonitions against drunkenness.In the realm of mathematics, astronomy, and chronology, Rasch was equally prolific. His Gegennebenrechenbüchlein (1586) provided commercial merchants and monastic stewards with practical methods for double-entry bookkeeping, currency exchange, and interest calculations. Intrigued by the passage of time and divine providence, he published several astronomical and apocalyptic works, including the Cometen-Buch (1577/1582), written in response to the Great Comet of 1577 that captivated European intellectuals like Tycho Brahe. Rasch interpreted celestial phenomena through a dual lens of natural philosophy and Christian eschatology. His calendrical treatises, such as the Chronologia (1582) and Passagier, actively engaged in the fiery contemporary debates surrounding the Gregorian calendar reform promulgated by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582, advocating for mathematical accuracy while defending Catholic ecclesiastical authority against Protestant calendar detractors.Finally, Rasch served the historical ambitions of the imperial dynasty through elaborate genealogical and historiographical treatises. Works such as his Genealogia der Hochlöblichen Landesfürsten in Oesterreich compiled chronological lines, armorial bearings, and biographical summaries of the Babenberg and Habsburg rulers. By linking local Austrian saint veneration—particularly the cult of Saint Leopold—with the political legitimacy of the reigning house, Rasch aligned his historical scholarship with the broader ideological program of the imperial court in Vienna.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe printing history of Johann Rasch’s oeuvre reveals a sophisticated understanding of the early modern publishing market and typographical networks. Rather than relying on a single printing firm, Rasch strategically leveraged top-tier presses in both Bavaria and Austria. His major musical works were issued from the renowned press of Adam Berg in Munich. Berg’s workshop was famous throughout the Holy Roman Empire for its superb music typography, utilizing elegant movable metal types, woodcut historiated initials, and crisp layout formats that accommodated complex polyphonic part-books.For his vernacular practical, mathematical, and historical treatises, Rasch turned to prominent Viennese printers, including Blasius Pusch, Michael Zimmermann, and Leonhard Nassinger. These publications were typically produced in sturdy quarto formats using sharp German Fraktur typefaces, adorned with woodcut title borders, architectural frames, and technical diagrams. The Weinreich featured woodcut illustrations depicting agricultural implements, vineyard pruning knives, barrel designs, and seasonal vineyard labor, rendering the technical knowledge accessible to literate guild masters, vineyard bailiffs, and monastic cellarers. The wide distribution of Rasch’s books across Lower Austria, Styria, Bohemia, and Bavaria demonstrates an effective commercial network that relied on Danubian trade channels and the annual book fairs in Frankfurt and Leipzig.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyDuring his lifetime, Johann Rasch was widely esteemed across Central Europe as an exemplar of the humanist ideal—the homo universalis who integrated sacred music, classical learning, and empirical science into the service of church and state. Contemporaries praised his administrative rigor at the Schottenstift and consulted his mathematical and calendrical works for practical governance. However, as the Baroque period progressed and scientific disciplines became increasingly specialized, Rasch’s multi-faceted output was temporarily obscured by the shifting intellectual currents of the seventeenth century.Interest in Rasch experienced a major resurgence in the nineteenth century during the rise of modern Austrian historiography, bibliographical science, and musicology. Pioneering bibliographers such as Anton Schmid and Emil von Ottenthal re-discovered Rasch’s seminal role in early German music printing and monastic archival science. In the twentieth century, musicologists such as Othmar Wessely reassessed Rasch’s musical compositions, emphasizing his position as a key bridge between the Franco-Flemish polyphony of Lasso and the early Baroque Catholic church style in Vienna. Concurrently, historians of science and agriculture recognized the Weinreich as an invaluable primary document for early modern enology, economic history, and historical linguistics.When Johann Rasch passed away in Vienna in 1612, he left behind a monumental legacy embedded within the archival holdings of the Schottenstift and the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek. Today, he is remembered not only as a distinguished organist and monastic librarian, but as a pioneering figure who brought the empirical spirit of early modern science to the ancient vineyards and scholarly traditions of Austria.

publishers.name: Berg Adam
publishers.biography: Adam Berg (c. 1540–1610) stands as one of the most pivotal figures in early modern South German typography and book culture, serving for nearly half a century as the primary official court printer (Bayerischer Hofdrucker) to the Catholic Dukes of Bavaria—Albrecht V (r. 1550–1579), Wilhelm V "the Pious" (r. 1579–1597), and Maximilian I (r. 1597–1651). Operating at the intellectual, political, and artistic epicenter of the Counter-Reformation in Wittelsbach Bavaria, Berg transformed Munich from a modest regional printing center into an international powerhouse of Catholic publishing, legal humanism, and luxurious music typography. His press was instrumental in formulating and disseminating the theological tenets of the Council of Trent, the anti-Protestant polemics of the Society of Jesus, and the imperial administrative apparatus of the Bavarian state. Most notably, Berg’s workshop produced monumental, lavishly illustrated choir books for the Bavarian court chapel (Hofkapelle), setting unprecedented standards for music printing in Northern Europe through his legendary collaboration with the composer Orlando di Lasso (Orlandus Lassus). By synthesizing technological mastery in movable music type, elegant Fraktur and Antiqua founts, fine paper sourcing, and artistic partnerships with leading Renaissance engravers, Berg defined the visual and material culture of Counter-Reformation Central Europe.Born around 1540 in Nittenau, a small market town in the Upper Palatinate (Oberpfalz), Berg grew up in a region fraught with confessional instability following the rapid spread of Lutheranism across the Holy Roman Empire. Though raised in an Evangelical environment, Berg sought technical training in the book trades during the 1550s, serving an apprenticeship in composition, presswork, and bookselling within the vibrant typographic networks of Franconia and Swabia. His definitive breakthrough occurred in 1564, when he relocated to Munich, the residential capital of Duke Albrecht V. At the time, the dominant printing enterprise in Munich had been operated by Alexander Weißenhorn II, whose sudden death left the workshop under the administration of his family. To secure ownership of the press and establish legal standing within the strictly Catholic Duchy of Bavaria, Berg executed two strategic decisions: he formally converted to Catholicism in early 1564 and married Katharina Weißenhorn, the widow of Alexander Weißenhorn II. This marital alliance granted Berg immediate control over the established Weißenhorn workshop, including its standing inventory, press machinery, type foundries, and civic privileges. Recognizing his technical competence, Duke Albrecht V formally appointed Berg as the official Bavarian Ducal Court Printer on March 29, 1564, initiating an extraordinarily productive career that spanned over forty-six years.Among Adam Berg’s most monumental historical achievements was his revolutionary work in music typography, which elevated Munich to equal standing with premier European music publishing centers such as Venice, Paris, and Nuremberg. Central to this achievement was Berg’s close, multi-decade partnership with Orlando di Lasso, the world-renowned maestro di cappella of the Munich court chapel. In 1573, under the direct patronage of Duke Albrecht V and later Duke Wilhelm V, Berg initiated the publication of the Patrocinium musices, a colossal multi-volume series of choir books in grand folio format (Folio grande). Unlike the smaller, utilitarian oblong partbooks standard in sixteenth-century music publishing, the Patrocinium musices was designed for grand performance and liturgical ostentation: an entire choir could stand around a single, massive opened volume displayed on a central choir desk. To execute this project, Berg employed custom-cast, single-impression music type of extraordinary clarity, framed by elaborate woodcut borders, historiated initials, and heraldic engravings created by master artists such as Jost Amman, Hans Mielich, and Alexander Mair. Spanning twelve volumes published between 1573 and 1598, the series contained Lasso’s masses, motets, magnificats, and passion settings, alongside compositions by court figures such as Antonius Gosswin, Ivo de Vento, and Jakob Lechner. Berg’s music editions were celebrated across Europe for their technical perfection, heavy rag paper, and magnificent layout, serving as tangible symbols of Wittelsbach piety and Renaissance grandeur.Beyond music, Adam Berg’s press functioned as the chief intellectual engine for the Catholic Restoration across Southern Germany, Austria, and the Swiss Cantons. Following the expansion of the Society of Jesus in Munich and the establishment of the Jesuit College, Berg became the primary publisher for Jesuit scholars and controversialists. He produced numerous editions of Peter Canisius’s famous Catechismus in Latin, German, and polyglot versions, which served as the foundational pedagogical tool for Catholic instruction across Central Europe. Berg’s workshop printed polemical treatises opposing Lutheran and Calvinist theologians, including major works by Martin Eisengrein, Jakob Gretser, Georg Scherer, and Jakob Feucht, as well as hagiographies, devotional manuals, and prominent treatises against witchcraft (Hexenliteratur). Furthermore, as imperial and ducal printer, Berg held an absolute monopoly over official Bavarian state documents. He printed the landmark Bairische Landtsordnung (Bavarian Territorial Code) of 1553 and its 1578 revisions, Wiguleus Hund’s foundational genealogical history Bayrisch Stammenbuch (1585–1587), territorial police ordinances, tax registers, and official public decrees. His press was also a prominent source for broadsheets and early news pamphlets (Neue Zeitungen), disseminating official reports on the Ottoman wars, celestial events, royal weddings, and state executions across the Empire.The commercial success of Berg’s enterprise rested upon an astute combination of technical refinement, artistic collaboration, and extensive commercial distribution. Berg invested heavily in acquiring diverse type specimen collections, maintaining an exceptionally rich inventory of German Fraktur, Schwabacher, Roman (Antiqua), Italic, and Hebrew founts, alongside specialized liturgical red-and-black printing capabilities. He fostered close working relationships with leading South German graphic artists: Jost Amman designed intricate title-page borders populated by allegorical representations of Faith, Justice, and the Wittelsbach lion; Alexander Mair provided delicate copperplate engravings; and Peter Candid contributed designs for devotional illustrations. To sustain his vast production output, Berg operated multiple hand-presses concurrently and maintained an active presence at the bi-annual book fairs (Buchmessen) in Frankfurt am Main and Leipzig. He established distribution networks extending from Vienna and Prague to Cologne and Venice. His financial prosperity was immense, allowing him to purchase multiple municipal properties in Munich, acquire rural estate holdings, and maintain a elevated socio-economic standing among the city's patrician class.In his declining years, Adam Berg gradually transferred operational management of his printing house to his son, Adam Berg the Younger (d. 1625), and his son-in-law, while maintaining editorial and financial oversight until his death in Munich in November 1610. Following his passing, the workshop continued under his heirs before being integrated into the distinguished Munich printing firm of Nikolaus Heinrich, ensuring the unbroken continuation of ducal typography in Bavaria throughout the seventeenth century. Today, Adam Berg is recognized by bibliographers, musicologists, and cultural historians as one of the towering masters of early modern European print culture. His surviving imprints—numbering over 1,000 distinct titles recorded in the Verzeichnis der im deutschen Sprachbereich erschienenen Drucke des 16. Jahrhunderts (VD 16)—are preserved in major national libraries worldwide, including the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, the British Library, and the Library of Congress. Berg’s career exemplifies the synthesis of early modern media technology, royal patronage, and confessional propaganda, representing a monumental chapter in the history of the printed book.

academic_description: 4to (178x134 mm). [6] leaves. Collation: A4 B2. With a woodcut illustration on the title page. Later boards. On the front pastedown bookplate Ex-libris Franz Pollack Parnau. Slightly uniformly browning, a good copy. First edition. Presented as a ‘Practica’, i.e. a booklet containing astrological predictions, it is in reality a mocking poem on the genre, about which Rasch holds forth in even greater detail in his Gegenpractic of 1584. In the rhymed dedication poem to Duke Albrecht V of Bavaria Rasch mentions two of his works to be published, his Weinbuch (1580) and the Cometen Buch (1582). Under the woodcut on the title page is a Latin citation on predictions from Lucas Panaetius, a humanist from Ulcinj (Montenegro) active in Venice, probably taken from his prefatory letter ad- dressed to Rosello de Rosellis printed in Caesar’s Commentary (Venezia, 1511).For him there are three kinds of prognostication: there are first of all, prophecies for no specific year, perhaps dealing with the end times, but most of them are mere dreams; then there are prognosti- cations based on conjunctions and eclipses that treat multiple years, but most of them are mere fanta- sies; and then there are the prognostications for a single year, called ‘practicas’, of which there are so many that no one gains much honor from them, and most are held (for good reason) to be full of false-hood. Rasch states that the ‘practicas’ usually include, first of all, the astrologers’ mumbo jumbo based on equinoxes, eclipses, and ruling planets, followed by six sections: first, agricultural fertility; second, illness; third, war and peace; fourth, the good and ill fortunes of human estates; fifth the good and ill fortune of lands and cities; and sixth, the weather of each season and moon phase (cf. J. Green, Printing the Future: The Origin and Development of the ‘Practica Teütsch’ to 1620, in: “Archiv für Geschichte des Buchwesens”, 67, 2012, pp. 1-18).As a ‘catholic’ polemicist Rasch denounced ‘practicas’ as Lutheran propaganda (cf. R.B. Barnes, Astrology and Reformation, Oxford, 2016, pp. 179-180). Just one name occurs in the poem, that of the Bohemian astronomer, mathematician, and astrologer Cyprian Leovitius (d. 1574), who was the author of several ‘practicas’. Unnamed Rasch addresses his scorn also to Leonhard Thurneysser (1531-1596), who since 1571 had regularly published some ‘practicas’ (cf. T. Odebrecht, Beiträge zur richtigen Würdigung Leonhard Thurneyssers, in: “Märkische Forschungen”, 7, 1861, pp. 201-202).Johann Rasch was born around 1540 in Pöchlarn on the Danube in Lower Austria. In his childhood he studied as a choirboy at the collegiate high school of the Benedictine abbey of Mondsee. From there he turned to the university in Wittenberg. He felt repulsed by the squabbles and quarrels’ prevailing there, so that he left Wittenberg after only a short stay and returned again as a cleric from 1561 to 1563 to Mondsee Abbey. In 1565 But he also left this place and enrolled at the University of Vienna, where he studied astronomy and mathematics with Bartholomaeus Reisacher. After graduation, he went to Munich, where he met the printer Adam Berg, but did not found livelihood there and returned to Vienna in 1570 as schoolmaster and organist in the Schottenstift, and also run a bookshop as ‘catholic’ bookseller . He probably received citizenship in Vienna around 1580. In historical research, Rasch was first recognized primarily as a musician (cf. A. Rausch, Johann Rasch (Rassius), in: “Österreichisches Musiklexikon”, R. Flotzinger, ed., Wien, 2005, vol. 4, p. 1869). In the early 1570s he had several compositions printed by Adam Berg in Munich. In addition to the sacred composi- tions, Rasch also created astronomical, astrological, calendar, prognostic, economic, historical, theo- logical, ethical, and poetic-literary works. He also was the author of one of the earliest German-language wine books Von Baw, Pflege und Brauch des Weins (1580) (cf. B. Sutter, Johannes Keplers Stellung innerhalb der Grazer Kalendertradition des 16. Jahrhunderts, in: “Johannes Kepler 1571-1971. Gedenkschrift der Universität Graz”, 1975, pp. 281-288; see also M. Schilling, Johann Rasch, in: “Frühe Neuzeit in Deutschland 1520‒1620. Literaturwissenschaftliches Verfasserlexikon”, W. Kühlmann & al., eds, Berlin, 2016, vol. 5, cols. 191-197).

authors.name: Corner Andrea
authors.biography: Andrea Corner (1610–1686) stands as one of the most distinguished patrician administrators, military coordinators, and senior statesmen of the Serene Republic of Venice (Serenissima Repubblica di Venezia) during the high Seicento. Operating within a century defined by dramatic geopolitical realignments and protracted military existential crisis in the Eastern Mediterranean, Corner’s life encapsulated the ethos, structural governance, and imperial ambitions of the Venetian ruling class. Belonging to one of the most venerable case vecchie (the ancient noble houses) of Venice, his public trajectory spanned the pivotal decades of the War of Candia (1645–1669) against the Ottoman Empire and the opening salvos of the Morean War (1684–1699). As a Senator, military magistrate, Provveditore, and eventually Procuratore di San Marco—the highest civic dignity below the Doge—Corner served as an anchor of oligarchic governance, balancing financial stewardship with active command and strategic diplomacy.Born in Venice on November 14, 1610, into the wealthy and influential branch of the Corner family, Andrea was steeped from early childhood in the traditions of state service and classical humanism. The Corner lineage had provided the Republic with doges, cardinals, generals, and scholars, establishing a family tradition that demanded rigorous civic dedication. His early education was meticulously structured around classical rhetoric, civil and canon law, history, political philosophy, and military engineering. He immersed himself in classical historiography—particularly the works of Polybius, Livy, and Tacitus—seeking insights into republican civic virtue, defensive strategy, and state preservation (ragion di Stato). This humanist grounding was systematically paired with practical instruction in maritime commerce, naval tactics, and public accounting, preparing him for rapid entry into the Venetian cursus honorum.Upon entering the Maggior Consiglio (Great Council) at the mandatory age, Corner quickly established himself as an insightful and energetic magistrate within the Venetian administrative network. He progressed steadily through the required preliminary offices, serving as Savietto del Collegio and Savio di Terraferma, positions that exposed him to the day-to-day administrative machinery of the Venetian state. To refine his executive capabilities, he accepted appointments as podestà and capitano in major cities of the Venetian Terraferma, including pivotal mainland centers such as Brescia and Padua. In these positions, Corner exercised judicial authority, oversaw public finances, managed military garrisons, and negotiated between local municipal elites and the central authority of the Venetian Signoria, proving his skill as an even-handed and resolute administrator.The outbreak of the War of Candia in 1645 drastically altered the trajectory of Corner’s career, thrusting him into high-stakes military and logistical management. As the Ottoman Empire launched its massive invasion of Crete, Venice mobilized all available administrative and financial resources to defend its prize overseas possession (Stato da Màr). Corner was appointed to critical emergency magistracies, serving as Provveditore and military coordinator responsible for directing troop movements, securing grain supplies, managing naval munitions, and fortifying maritime transit routes. His administrative dispatches and official reports (relazioni) submitted to the Venetian Senate reveal an exceptionally detailed strategist wrestling with severe financial deficits, naval supply bottlenecks, and the immense human cost of defending the besieged city of Candia (modern Heraklion). His steadfastness during these crucial years secured his reputation as an indispensable pillar of state defense.In recognition of his extraordinary civic devotion, administrative mastery, and immense personal financial contributions to the war-depleted state treasury, Andrea Corner was elevated to the prestigious lifetime dignity of Procuratore di San Marco (specifically assigned to the branch of de Citra or de Ultra). Second in social and political prestige only to the Doge, the Procuratorship granted Corner monumental influence over civic administration, the management of wealthy charitable trusts (commissarie), major public works, and the architectural maintenance of the Piazza San Marco complex. In this high office, Corner became a primary advisor within the Senate (Pregadi), shaping post-war diplomatic relations, fiscal restructuring, and naval reorganization following the tragic fall of Candia in 1669.Beyond his political and military leadership, Corner was a key participant in the vibrant intellectual and cultural life of Seicento Venice. The 17th century saw Venice emerge as the capital of European opera, public theater, and sophisticated academic debate, spearheaded by institutions like the Accademia degli Incogniti. Corner acted as an influential patron to contemporary historiographers, poets, mapmakers, and musical composers. He commissioned elaborate historical treatises, political pamphlets, and commemorative engravings that glorified Venetian republican liberty and his family's historical contributions. His patronage extended to prominent Venetian printers and typographers, who produced elegant folio editions of military histories and panegyrics under his dedicated sponsorship.In the final decade of his life, Corner remained an active and influential senior statesman. When the Republic joined the Holy League in 1684 and embarked on the Morean War under the military leadership of Captain General (and later Doge) Francesco Morosini, Corner provided crucial political backing and financial strategy in the Senate, championing the campaign to reconquer the Peloponnese from Ottoman rule. He continued to attend senate debates and fulfill his duties as Procurator until his death in Venice on March 10, 1686. His passing was commemorated with elaborate public funeral rites in Venice, honoring a life dedicated entirely to the service, defense, and preservation of the Venetian Republic.In contemporary historiography, Andrea Corner is evaluated as an archetypal representative of the 17th-century Venetian patriciate. Modern historians, including Gino Benzoni, Gaetano Cozzi, and Giuseppe Gullino, have highlighted how Corner's career illustrates the institutional flexibility, diplomatic pragmatism, and systemic resilience of Venice during its long era of confrontation with the Ottoman Empire. His extensive body of archival documents, official dispatches, and financial records, preserved primarily within the Archivio di Stato di Venezia (ASVe), continues to provide scholars with an indispensable empirical window into the political, naval, and socio-economic history of early modern Europe.

academic_description: 405x277 mm. Text within a typographic border. Woodcut decorative initial. Traces of folding, restorations along the folding, some foxing, all in all well preserved. Celebratory broadsheet printed on the occasion of a dinner party given by the vice-podesta of Brescia Andrea Cornaro (or Corner), containing a laudatory sonnet signed by Pietro dalla Curte.Andrea Corner, born in Venice in 1610 into a noble Venetian family, became a member of the Maggior Consiglio at only 20 in 1630. He had a very successful and long career as a politician, diplomat and galley captain, both in Venice and in the Venetian islands. On February 6, 1668 he married Marina Barbaro, widow of Girolamo Corner, who brought him a dowry of 6,000 ducats. On July 14, 1669 he was elected podesta in Brescia. He made his entrance in town in January 1670. Among the various problems connected with the administration of a territory as vast and relevant as that of Brescia, he had to reorganize the local possessions of the Church, to provide new oarsmen for the Venetian fleet by punishing to the galley even those convicted for a period of less than eighteen months, to overcome the difficult grain supply for the the city, and to more stringently control the smuggling of foreign goods into the Brescia territory (cf. C. Povolo, Corner, Andrea, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, 29, 1983, s.v.).As the broadsheet is addressed to Corner as vice-podesta of Brescia, it is presumable that it was printed before July 1669, the year of his appointment as podesta.

authors.name: Raulin Jean
authors.biography: Jean Raulin (1443–1514) stands as one of the most compelling and transitional figures in late fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century French intellectual history. Positioned at the complex intersection of late scholastic theology, monastic reform, and early northern Renaissance humanism, Raulin achieved renown as a formidable academic administrator, an austere Benedictine reformer, and one of the most popular and evocative preachers of the pre-Reformation era. Operating within the vibrant ecosystem of the University of Paris and the monastic networks of the Order of Saint Benedict, Raulin's life and published corpus illuminate the intellectual anxieties, moral rigorism, and typographical culture of France on the precipice of the Protestant Reformation and the Italian Wars.Born in the diocese of Toul in Lorraine in 1443, Raulin was dispatched at an early age to Paris to pursue his higher education at the prestigious Collège de Navarre. Founded in 1304 by Joan I of Navarre, the college was a premier crucible for royal administrators, canonists, and theologians. Raulin excelled in the liberal arts before matriculating into the Faculty of Theology. Under the tutelage of prominent scholastic masters, he mastered the subtleties of Thomistic and Nominalist dialectic, distinguishing himself by a rigorous commitment to moral theology and spiritual discipline. He earned his licentiate and was subsequently capped as a Doctor of Theology at the Sorbonne in 1479. His extraordinary erudition, combined with an unimpeachable moral reputation, led to his election in 1481 as the Grand Master (Grand Maître) of the Collège de Navarre. In this capacity, Raulin presided over the academic and spiritual formation of an entire generation of scholars, fostering an environment where traditional scholastic disputation began to encounter the initial currents of the devotio moderna and Christian humanism.During his tenure at the Collège de Navarre, Raulin established close intellectual ties with prominent academic reformers, including Jean Standonck (the austere principal of the Collège de Montaigu) and early humanists like Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples. However, despite reaching the pinnacle of Parisian academic prestige, Raulin experienced a profound personal and spiritual crisis regarding the worldly ambitions and spiritual complacency of university life. In 1497, at the age of fifty-four, Raulin made the radical decision to resign his high academic office at Navarre. Renouncing his university honors, he withdrew from Paris to take the monastic vows of the Benedictine Order at the historic Abbey of Cluny. This dramatic retreat from academic power to monastic asceticism made a profound impression on contemporary French society and cemented Raulin's reputation as a figure of extraordinary moral authority.At Cluny, Raulin did not retreat into complete obscurity; rather, his intellectual talents were immediately redirected toward the urgent cause of monastic reform. Recognizing his administrative genius and spiritual zeal, Cardinal Georges d'Amboise, Archbishop of Rouen and Prime Minister to King Louis XII, enlisted Raulin to assist in reforming the Benedictine institutions across France. Working alongside fellow reformers such as Guy Jouenneaux (abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés), Raulin sought to restore strict observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict, eliminate simony, and revive scholarly devotion within monastic scriptoria and libraries. It was during this late Benedictine period that Raulin composed his most influential treatises and compiled his massive homiletic cycles. His literary output includes the celebrated allegorical treatise Itinerarium Paradisi (The Itinerary to Paradise), first published in Paris in 1512, the Doctrinale de triplici morte (1518), and extensive collections of Latin sermons: the Sermones de Adventu, Sermones de Quadragesima, Sermones de Dominica, and Sermones de Sanctis.As a preacher, Raulin was legendary for his ability to bridge high scholastic erudition with vivid, popular communication. His sermons were characterized by an incisive social critique, targeting the vices of the clergy, the venality of magistrates, and the corruption of the royal court. Raulin frequently employed exempla—moral fables, rustic allegories, and popular folklore—to make complex theological doctrines accessible to broad audiences. One of his most famous homiletic fables involved a widow deliberating whether to remarry, who misinterprets the sound of church bells as confirming her earthly desires ("Prends ton valet, prends ton valet"), only to realize her folly when the bells later seem to chime a warning ("Ne le prends pas, ne le prends pas"). This iconic narrative caught the attention of later Renaissance authors, most notably François Rabelais, who adapted Raulin's bell allegory in the Tiers Livre (1546) during Panurge's deliberations on marriage.The dissemination of Raulin's works represents a landmark chapter in early French printing history. His writings were eagerly seized upon by the premier humanist printers of Paris and Lyon. Chief among his publishers was the renowned scholar-printer Jodocus Badius Ascensius (Josse Bade), who, often in collaboration with Jean Petit (Johannes Parvus) and Berthold Rembolt, brought out multi-volume folio editions of Raulin's sermons and letters (Epistolae, posthumously published in 1521). These editions were produced with exceptional typographical care, featuring elegant Roman and Gothic fonts, woodcut title borders, and comprehensive analytical indexes designed for preachers. The popularity of Raulin's printed works quickly spread beyond France; major printing houses in Lyon (Jacques Myt, Jean de Vingle), Antwerp, and Venice issued repeated editions throughout the first half of the sixteenth century, establishing his sermons as standard handbooks for Catholic homiletics across Western Europe.Jean Raulin died on February 6, 1514, leaving behind a profound legacy that straddled two eras. In the decades following his death, he was venerated by Catholic reformers as a model of pre-Reformation piety and academic integrity. Humanists admired his epistolary style and dedication to educational reform, while Protestant polemicists paradoxically cited his fierce denunciations of clerical abuses as evidence of the necessity of the Reformation. In modern historiography, particularly in the foundational studies of Augustin Renaudet and Larissa Taylor, Raulin is recognized as a central figure in the spiritual awakening of pre-Reformation France—a scholar who seamlessly united the intellectual rigor of the Sorbonne with the ascetic devotion of Cluny.
