publishers.name: Petit Jean
publishers.biography: Jean Petit (fl. 1492–1530; Latinized in imprints as Johannes Parvus), known in early English and French vernacular documentation as Petit Jean or Master Jean Petit, stands as one of the most formidable, prolific, and influential figures in the history of the early modern European book trade. Operating from the vibrant heart of the Latin Quarter in Paris during the crucial transition from the late incunabular period to the golden age of Renaissance humanism, Petit transformed the structural mechanics of academic, legal, and literary publishing. As a sworn bookseller (librarius juratus) to the prestigious University of Paris (the Sorbonne), Petit occupied a paramount position within the intellectual infrastructure of northern Europe. Rather than confining his operations strictly to the physical mechanics of the printing press, he operated as a master publisher, financial entrepreneur, and paper distributor who commissioned, financed, and organized the production of over a thousand distinct editions, dictating textual taste and scholarly standards across the Western World for nearly four decades.Early Life, Lineage, and the Establishment of the Parisian EmporiumWhile the exact details of Jean Petit's early birth date remain obscure, archival records indicate his emergence into the active Parisian book market around 1492, coinciding with the rapid maturation of French typography following its initial introduction by Ulrich Gering, Michael Friburger, and Martin Crantz in 1470. Establishing his primary shop on the iconic Rue Saint-Jacques—the central arterial highway of Parisian book culture—he initially adopted the sign of the Fleur-de-Lys (In intersignio Lilii) before expanding his enterprise to the famed Lion d'Argent (In intersignio Leonis Argentei). Petit’s social and financial capital expanded swiftly due to his strategic integration into the commercial guilds of Paris and his acquisition of the coveted status of librarius juratus. This official university appointment granted him significant tax exemptions, immunity from civic duties, and privileged rights over the distribution of academic texts, enabling him to forge an unparalleled commercial network that linked Paris with printing centers in Lyon, Basel, Cologne, Venice, and London.Intellectual Networks, Editorial Strategy, and Humanist PublishingJean Petit’s commercial genius lay in his ability to cater simultaneously to traditional scholastic orthodoxy and the emerging currents of Northern Renaissance humanism. His publishing program was colossal in scope. In the realm of classical antiquity, Petit published landmark editions of Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Cicero, Terence, and Lucan, often accompanied by extensive commentaries from contemporary Italian and French scholars. Recognizing the profound cultural shift spearheaded by early humanism, Petit established collaborative relationships with premier scholars and correctors of the era, most notably Jodocus Badius Ascensius (Josse Bade), before Badius set up his own press, as well as Guillaume Budé, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, and early works associated with Desiderius Erasmus. Concurrently, Petit retained a virtual monopoly on essential academic textbooks, canon law treatises (including the Corpus Juris Canonici and the decretals), civil jurisprudence, and the scholastic summae of Thomas Aquinas, John Duns Scotus, and Albertus Magnus. His list also embraced vernacular literature, chivalric romances, and liturgical works tailored for both clerical and lay markets, demonstrating a total mastery of early modern consumer demand.Typographical Partnerships, Production Mechanics, and Printing InnovationsA defining aspect of Jean Petit's methodology was his reliance on a dynamic network of specialized master printers whom he employed as subcontractors or business partners. Because the volume of his enterprise far exceeded the physical capacity of a single workshop, Petit funded print runs executed by the finest typographers in Paris, including Thielman Kerver, Gui Marchand, Pierre Le Dru, Antoine Chappiel, Robert Gourmont, Gilles de Gourmont, and Antoine Vérard. Typographically, Petit's publications reflect the shift from heavy medieval Gothic fonts (such as lettre de forme and lettre bâtarde) toward elegant Roman and Italic typefaces designed to reflect humanist aesthetic values. His books are renowned for their visual majesty, often decorated with elaborate woodcut title borders, historiated initials, and his famous, highly recognizable printer’s marks (marques typographiques). These devices usually featured two heraldic lions supporting a shield emblazoned with the lilies of France and his stylized monogram (I.P.), a visual signature that functioned as a early modern seal of textual authority and brand authenticity across Europe.Legal Privileges, Market Monopolies, and International DistributionPetit was at the forefront of early copyright history, frequently securing royal privileges (privilèges du Roi and privilèges du Parlement) to protect his massive capital investments from pirated reprints by rival booksellers in Lyon or the Low Countries. His distribution apparatus was unprecedented: Petit maintained branch agencies, commission agents, and wholesale trade agreements that ensured his books were available at the St. Bartholomew’s Fair in Frankfurt, the trade marts of Leipzig, and the bookshops of London and Oxford. Indeed, Petit exercised such dominance over the English market that a significant percentage of Latin textbooks and liturgical volumes imported into Tudor England during the reigns of Henry VII and Henry VIII bore the imprint of Jean Petit from Paris. His enterprise was further strengthened by his control over the raw materials of the trade, particularly the wholesale paper supply, which allowed him to dictate terms to smaller Parisian printing shops.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyThe legacy of Jean Petit is synonymous with the Golden Age of the early French printed book. Upon his passing around 1530, he left behind one of the most prosperous print dynasties in European history, continued and adapted by his widow, his sons (including Oudin Petit and Jean Petit II), and his sons-in-law, who maintained the family's typographical empire well into the late sixteenth century. Modern analytical bibliographers, from Anatole Claudin and Philippe Renouard to contemporary book historians, view Jean Petit as the quintessential prototype of the early modern publisher-capitalist. He bridged the medieval scriptorium culture, the scholastic university model, and the commercial print capitalism of the Renaissance. His imprints remain prime artifacts for bibliophiles, institutions, and scholars worldwide, embodying the artistic brilliance, intellectual vitality, and commercial sophistication of early Renaissance typography.

Eighteenth century marbled calf, gilt spine with five raised bands, red morocco label, red edges, marbled endpapers.First edition of this collection of 56 letters published by the author's nephew Robert Raulin. “On trouve, dans la correspondence de Raulin, la même doctrine de réforme par le retour aux vertus monastiques: chasteté du corps, ‘abstinence' de l'esprit, devotion, paix et concorde, obéissance ou plus simplement ‘la pauvreté et la charité' ” (G.T. Bedouelle, Jean Raulin, in: “Dictionaire de Spiritualité”, Paris, 1932-1995, 13, pp. 156). These ideas are clearly expressed in the letter to the friars of St. Alban in Basel (ll. LVv-LIXr).“Several ideas may be drawn from his correspondence. First, Raulin relied heavily upon his long term relationships in the clerical milieu, bishops and heads of monasteries, to push his reform efforts forward. He labored primarily with and among the Benedictines, with a few exceptions, and crossed into other monastic orders only as the need arose. Second, many of Raulin's correspondents were relationships that he had developed during his time as chancellor of Navarre; many were former colleagues and students. It is possible that Raulin had begun to sow the seeds of clerical reform among colleagues and students while at Navarre. Later, as his ideas matured and his plan unfolded, those relationships proved useful and strategic for clerical reform. A third idea we can draw from his correspondence is that he appears to have had a precise strategy - he wrote those in positions of leadership who might more successfully accomplish reform in the monasteries. The majority of his letters are addressed to those in ecclesiastical authority, bishops, abbots, and priors, who had greater authority to bring reform to the monasteries. Fourth, his reliance on political help to accomplish reform was minimal, although he did use civil authority to force entry into a few monasteries and to impose his reforms. Fifth, the College of Navarre was a center of reformist and humanist activity since the time of Gerson, early in the fifteenth century. Twenty-five letters of the fifty-six were addressed to former Navarrists, nine former graduates and professors of Navarre during the twenty-five plus years that Raulin was associated with the school. Eight letters were addressed to the like-minded principle of the College of Montaigu and close friend, Jean Standonck, who was also involved in clerical reform. A sixth idea is seen in the nature of Raulin's letters. They fall into three main categories: 1) letters of encouragement to continue in the struggle for reform; 2) letters of admonishment to those who were not taking an active enough of approach in the reform; and 3) letters asking for help or influence to push the reform forward. Based on the existing correspondence, clerical reform, both monastic and episcopal reform was the central theme in Raulin's Epistolae” (H.K. Foreman, Jean Raulin, 1443-1515, and the ‘Ideal Clergy': a Study of Clerical Reform in Early Sixteenth Century France, Thesis, Aberdeen, 2008, pp. 69-70).Added is a speech Raulin held at the Collège de Navarre and the famous oration on church reform held in the monastery of Cluny, Collatio de perfecta religionis plantatione, incremento, et instauratione, published for the first time at Basel by Sebastian Brant in 1498. CLIIIr., i.e. CLVIIr) Jean Raulin, a native of Toul, studied theology under Martinus de Magistris at the University of Paris and graduated there in 1479. Two years later he became grand-master of the Collège de Navarre. He was considered one of the most prominent exponents of the Nominalist school and a skilled popular preacher convinced of the necessity of a reform of the church. In 1497 he entered the Benedictine monastery of Cluny, a step he explains in a letter (ll. XLVIv-XLIv) to Christoph von Utenheim, then guardian of the Franciscans of Basel and later rector of the university and bishop. He worked for reform, not without the resistance of the local clergy, also in southern France, but especially in the monasteries of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and Saint-Germain-des-Prés until his death (cf. A. Renaudet, Préréforme et humanisme à Paris pendant les premières guerres d'Italie (1494-1517), Paris, 1916, pp. 165-170 and 234-236).“Raulin apparait comme un exemple intéressant des grandeurs et limites des réformateurs de la fin du quinzième siècle. Ardent et ingénieux prédicateur, infatigable dénonciateur des vices des évêques et des moines, il est tributaire des représentations eschatologiques de son temps, qu'il developpe longuement. Pourtant on trouve, dans son oeuvre, parfois implicitement, les éléments dont se servira la Réforme catholique” (G.T. Badouelle, op. cit, p. 156).

authors.name: Sabinus (Schuler) Georg
authors.biography: Georgius Sabinus (Schuler) was educated at Wittenberg under Melanchthon. In 1530 he accompanied the latter to the diet of Augsburg and published a volume of poetry, Elegiae, which immediately attracted the attention of the literary world. In 1533 he left for Italy, where Pietro Bembo came to take interest in him and his work. In August 1534, as he was preparing to return to Germany from Venice, he persuaded Giambattista Egnazio to give him a letter of introduction to Erasmus. By October he was in Freiburg and obtained from Erasmus some flattering letters to take back to Melanchthon.In 1536 he married Melanchthton's daughter Anna and in 1538 he was appointed to the chair of rhetoric at the University of Frankfurt an der Oder. In 1544 Albert, duke of Prussia, invited him to Königsberg, were he became the rector of the ducal college, which was quickly promoted to the status of a university (cf. L. Mundt, Die Lehrtätigkeit des Georg Sabinus an der Universität Königsberg, in: “Die Universität Königsberg in der Frühen Neuzeit”, H. Marti & M. Komorosowski, eds., Köln, 2008, pp. 77-115).In 1553 Sabinus was crowned with laurels and dubbed a knight by none other than the papal ‘count palatine' Girolamo Aleandro, Luther's antagonist at the diet of Worms. In 1555 he returned to Frankfurt and was again appointed professor and councillor to Elector Joachim II of Brandenburg, for whom he undertook several diplomatic missions in Italy and Poland.Sabinus was a fried of Joachim Camerarius and of his fellow poets Eobanus Hessus and Johannes Dantiscus. He corresponded occasionally with Bembo, in whose entourage at Padua he also met Damião de Gois. Apart his poetry he also contributed to classical and historical scholarship, such as a commentary on Ovid and a work on emperor Maximilian.

The letters written by Pietro Bembo and Battista Egnazio to Sabinus were already printed in the first edition of the Poemata of 1538. The Epistolarum liber first appeared in 1544 in the augmented edition of the Poemata and was reprinted in 1558. The most complete edition of Sabinus' collected works, published posthumously by his son-in-law Eusebius Menius, was issued by Vögelin at Leipzig in 1563, and all subsequent editions (1568, 1578, 1581, 1589, and 1597) are based on it.The volume opens with a dedicatory letter by Menius to Sigismund of Brandenburg, archbishop of Magdeburg, dated from Wittenberg, April 29, 1563, and is followed by a letter by Joachim Camerarius to Menius, dated from Lipsia, May 15, 1563. Also reprinted is Sabinus dedicatory epistle to the archbishop of Madgeburg, dated from Frankfurt/Oder, November 13, 1558 (cf. G. Ellinger, Geschichte der neulateinischen Literatur Deutschlands im 16. Jahrhundert, Berlin & Leipzig, 1929-1933, II, pp. 65-75; see also J. Voight, Mitteilungen aus der Korrespondenz des Herzogs Albrecht von Preussen mit Martin Luther, Philipp Melanchthon und Georg Sabinus, Königsberg, 1841, pp. 56-77).“Ebenso glänzte er [Sabinus] im Lateinisch-Schreiben. Seine Briefe, seine Abhandlungen, so viele wir noch haben, tragen alle das Gepräge der klassischen Form. Er brauchte sich nicht zu scheuen und zu schämen, mit den grössten Latinisten seiner Zeit, mit einem Pietro Bembo, Caspar Contareni, Baptista Egnatio, Christoph Türk, Joachim Camerarius, u. A. zu correspondieren, und Alle an welche er schrieb, mit welchen er in brieflichen Verkehr stand, lobten und bewunderten die Nettigkeit, die Glätte, die Leichtigkeit der Sprache” (M.W. Heffter, Erinnerungen an Georg Sabinus, den trefflichen Dichter, akademischen Lehrer und Diplomaten, den Mitstifter der Universität zu Königsberg in Preussen, Leipzig, 1844, p. 78).The volume furthermore contains: Elegiarum libri VI; Caesares Germanici; De nuptiis Regis Poloniae carmen Heroicum; Ecloga de Gallo ad Ticinum capto; Ecloga de nuptiis Illustrissimi Principis Alberti Marchionis Brandeburgensis; Epigrammatum & Hendecasyllaborum libri II; Liber Carminum Adoptivus; and De carminibus ad veterum imitationem artificiose componendis. Frankfurt/O., September 1, 1556 (p. 474) Georgius Sabinus (Schuler) was educated at Wittenberg under Melanchthon. In 1530 he accompanied the latter to the diet of Augsburg and published a volume of poetry, Elegiae, which immediately attracted the attention of the literary world. In 1533 he left for Italy, where Pietro Bembo came to take interest in him and his work. In August 1534, as he was preparing to return to Germany from Venice, he persuaded Giambattista Egnazio to give him a letter of introduction to Erasmus. By October he was in Freiburg and obtained from Erasmus some flattering letters to take back to Melanchthon.In 1536 he married Melanchthton's daughter Anna and in 1538 he was appointed to the chair of rhetoric at the University of Frankfurt an der Oder. In 1544 Albert, duke of Prussia, invited him to Königsberg, were he became the rector of the ducal college, which was quickly promoted to the status of a university (cf. L. Mundt, Die Lehrtätigkeit des Georg Sabinus an der Universität Königsberg, in: “Die Universität Königsberg in der Frühen Neuzeit”, H. Marti & M. Komorosowski, eds., Köln, 2008, pp. 77-115).In 1553 Sabinus was crowned with laurels and dubbed a knight by none other than the papal ‘count palatine' Girolamo Aleandro, Luther's antagonist at the diet of Worms. In 1555 he returned to Frankfurt and was again appointed professor and councillor to Elector Joachim II of Brandenburg, for whom he undertook several diplomatic missions in Italy and Poland.Sabinus was a fried of Joachim Camerarius and of his fellow poets Eobanus Hessus and Johannes Dantiscus. He corresponded occasionally with Bembo, in whose entourage at Padua he also met Damião de Gois. Apart his poetry he also contributed to classical and historical scholarship, such as a commentary on Ovid and a work on emperor Maximilian (cf. I. Irmscher, Georgius Sabinus, Schüler und Schwiegersohn Melanchthons, in: “Sileno. Rivista di studi classici e cristiana”, XVII, 1991, pp. 299-306; and H. Scheible, Georg Sabinus, 1508-1560: ein Poet als Gründungsrektor, in: “Die Albertus-Universität zu Königsberg und ihre Professoren”, Berlin, 1995, pp. 17-31).

title: Classicarum epistolarum lib. III. Sive Scholae Argentinenses restitutae

authors.name: Sturm Johann
authors.biography: Johann Sturm was born at Schleidan in the Rhineland (near Aachen) and had his early education in Liège at Saint Jerome's, a school conducted by the Brethren of the Common Life. At the University of Louvain, he and his professor of Greek, Rutger Regius, prepared and published Greek texts for students, thus establishing a pattern for Sturm's life.In 1529 he went to Paris to study medicine, rhetoric and dialectic. His patrons included Guillaume Budé, Marguerite de Navarre, and Cardinal Jean Du Bellay. By 1534 he was lecturing at the new Collège de France. His commentaries on Cicero and on logic earned for him fame as a humanist scholar and an outstanding teacher. Drawn into Cardinal du Bellay's effort to ally Francis I with the German Protestants, Sturm's position became precarious. In December 1536 he fled France for Strasbourg, where he was hired to teach rhetoric and dialectic in a newly founded school. Two years later the Latin schools and lower theological classes were combined into one institution, the Strasbourg Gymnasium. Sturm was appointed rector.The goal of the gymnasiums was to create a Christian citizen and also to train young patricians for their future role as magistrates and civil servants. Sturm believed the curriculum must also provide the knowledge of the nature and of the mind so fully cultivated by the ancients. For over forty years Sturm directed the Strasbourg Gymnasium, but as a Calvinist lost his position during the religious struggles in 1582.
authors.bibliography: B. Schröder, ed., Johannes Sturm (1507–1589), Pädagoge der Reformation, Jena, 2009, passim.

publishers.name: Rihel Josias
publishers.biography: Josias Rihel (1525–1609) stands as one of the most distinguished and prolific printer-publishers of the late Northern Renaissance, occupying a central position in the intellectual and typographical landscape of sixteenth-century Strasbourg (Strassburg). Operating at the vital geopolitical and cultural crossroads between the Holy Roman Empire and the French kingdom, Rihel’s press served as a primary engine for Alsatian Humanism, Protestant pedagogical reform, classical philology, and transnational book distribution. Over a career spanning more than five decades, from the mid-1550s until his death in 1609, Josias Rihel transformed his family’s printing house into an international publication house that supplied university faculty, gymnasium scholars, humanistic academies, and reform-minded elites across Europe with immaculate editions of classical texts, Protestant theology, historiography, and legal science.Born into a prominent Strasbourgeois printing dynasty around 1525, Josias was the son of Wendelin Rihel the Elder (d. 1555), a master typographer who had established one of Strasbourg's most successful presses during the early decades of the Protestant Reformation. Raised within the vibrant atmosphere of an active printing shop, Josias received a rigorous education in Latin, Greek, and the mechanics of typography, serving his apprenticeship under his father's tutelage alongside his brothers, Theodosius Rihel (c. 1530–1607) and Wendelin Rihel the Younger. Following the death of Wendelin the Elder in 1555, the press briefly operated under the collective imprint of the Haeredes Wendelini Rihelii (Heirs of Wendelin Rihel). However, by the late 1550s, Josias and his brother Theodosius reorganized the family enterprises, establishing distinct yet interconnected printing workshops in Strasbourg that would dominate the regional book trade for the next half-century.The cornerstone of Josias Rihel’s publishing program was his intimate collaboration with the renowned humanist educator Johannes Sturm (1507–1589), the founding rector of the Strasbourg Gymnasium Protestanticum (later the Academy of Strasbourg). Sturm’s revolutionary educational curriculum, which emphasized elegant Ciceronian Latinity, dialectic, and moral philosophy, required an unprecedented volume of standardized, high-quality textbooks. Josias Rihel became the primary printer for Sturm and the Gymnasium, issuing dozens of critical schoolbook editions, classical commentaries, and pedagogical manuals. Rihel’s press issued definitive, beautifully formatted editions of Marcus Tullius Cicero—including the Epistolae ad Familiares, De Officiis, Orator, and the complete philosophical dialogues—often accompanied by Sturm’s meticulous scholia and introductory lectures. Beyond Cicero, Rihel published works by Demosthenes, Quintilian, Aristotle, Hermogenes, and Terence, actively shaping the humanist educational curriculum of Central and Western Europe.Beyond pedagogical textbooks, Josias Rihel played a pivotal role in disseminating major historical, theological, and political texts of the Reformation era. He maintained close ties with key Protestant scholars, including the historian Johann Sleidanus (Jean Sleidan), whose masterwork De statu religionis et reipublicae, Carolo Quinto Caesare, commentarii became one of the most influential contemporary histories of the Reformation. Rihel published numerous legal treatises, natural philosophy texts, emblem books, and theological works by authors aligned with both Lutheran and Melanchthonian (Philippist) traditions, such as Philip Melanchthon, Girolamo Zanchi, Caspar Peucer, and Michael Toxites. Furthermore, leveraging Strasbourg’s status as a sanctuary for French Huguenot refugees, Rihel printed a significant corpus of French-language Protestant texts, serving as an intellectual conduit between the German-speaking Holy Roman Empire and the French Protestant underground.From a typographical and aesthetic perspective, the output of Josias Rihel represents the pinnacle of late sixteenth-century Strasbourgeois book design. His shop maintained an extensive inventory of elegant humanist Roman types, sharp Aldine-style Italics, robust Greek fonts for complex philological apparatuses, and refined Fraktur and Schwabacher faces for vernacular publications. Rihel’s editions were frequently adorned with intricate woodcut borders, historiated initials, and his famous printer’s devices. His primary mark depicted Pallas Athena (Minerva), the goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare, holding a spear and shield, often accompanied by an olive branch or owl, and framed by Latin mottos such as Vigilantia et Labore ("Through Vigilance and Labor") or Ingenio et Constantia. This iconographic choice explicitly highlighted the firm's devotion to scholarly rigor, civic virtue, and humanist erudition.Rihel's commercial operation was exceptionally sophisticated. He maintained an expansive distribution network that relied heavily on the biannual Frankfurt Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse), where he traded sheets with printers and booksellers from Basel, Zurich, Geneva, Cologne, Lyon, and Frankfurt. Despite navigating period political upheavals, confessional tensions between strict Gnesio-Lutherans and Sturm's Calvinist-leaning circle, and severe economic fluctuations, Josias Rihel sustained continuous production until his death in Strasbourg in 1609. Following his passing, the enterprise was carried forward by his descendants, including his son Josias Rihel II, ensuring that the Rihel typographical legacy persisted well into the seventeenth century. Today, bibliographers and historians of the book recognize Josias Rihel as a quintessential master of Renaissance typography whose press preserved and multiplied the intellectual monuments of European Humanism.

authors.biography: Luigi Antonio Santorelli was born at Monteforte and practised as a lawyer. The De perscribendis epistolis libellus was reprinted at Naples in 1653.

publishers.name: Cacchi Giuseppe
publishers.biography: Cacchi worked as a printer in Naples, L'Aquila and Vico Equense. Born in L'Aquila around 1533 or 1535, he learnt the art of typography in Naples from Orazio Salviani. In 1565 he returned to L'Aquila to open his own printing press and bookshop. In 1569 he brought printing to Vico Equense. He probably died in 1593.

academic_description: 4to. [8], 145, [3] pp. Collation: *4, A-S4, T². With the woodcut arms of Giovanni Battista Loffredo, Marquis of Monteforte, on the title-page and the printer's device on the verso of the last leaf. Contemporary limp vellum. First edition. The work opens with a dedicatory letter by Santorelli to Giovanni Battista Loffredo (d. 1609), Marquis of Monteforte, dated January 13, 1590. This is followed by a preface to the reader by a relative of Santorelli, Tommaso Aniello Schiavo, in which are enumerated the most elegant letter writers of the past, e.g. Angelo Poliziano, Christophe de Longueil, Pietro Bembo, Jacopo Sadoleto, and Paolo Manuzio.Santorelli gives the definition of twenty kind of letters (from nunciatoria to conquestatoria). At the end of these definitions are cited some sources from ancient authors where such letters can be found, and some definitions are accompanied by examples from his own correspondence.At the end of the volume are found some rhetorical rules to be observed in letter writing and a list with forms of address, De superscriptione epithetorum: “Le répertoire placé sous cette rubrique correspond tout à fait aux listes d'états du XVe siècle, bien que le mot ne soit jamais prononcé. Après le clergé, du Pape à l'abbesse (ce qui peut passer pour un progrès), on trouve un laïcat, ou la noblesse d'épée disparaît au profit de la magistrature: après l'empereur, le roi, le prince et le duc, on va du consul au juge; vient un tiers-état qui est encore conduit par les intellectuels, théologiens en tête, les simples ‘citoyens' passeront après le scholasticus et le tabellarius; un repentir bénéficiera au chevalier et au soldat (on croirait à une influence d'Érasme), mais aussi à l'orateur. Comme dans les méthodes du XVe siècle allemand, mais aussi chez Pontanus, la famille vient en fin. Reste que les laboratores (sauf l'artisan) sont oublié, ou exclus” (G. Gueudet, L'art de la lettre humaniste, Paris, 2004, p. 439).Luigi Antonio Santorelli was born at Monteforte and practised as a lawyer. The De perscribendis epistolis libellus was reprinted at Naples in 1653 (cf. C. Minieri Riccio, Memorie storiche degli scrittori nati nel regno di Napoli, Napoli, 1844, p. 319).

title: Epistolae, et praefationes quae dicuntur

authors.name: Manuzio Paolo
authors.biography: Paolo Manuzio (known in Latin as Paulus Manutius; Venice, June 12, 1512 – Rome, April 6, 1574) stands as one of the most decisive intellectual and typographical figures of the European High Renaissance and Counter-Reformation. As the third son of the legendary scholar-printer Aldus Manutius the Elder (Aldo Manuzio il Vecchio) and Maria Torresano, Paolo inherited not merely a celebrated family name and the famous printer's mark of the anchor and dolphin (festina lente), but the profound historical responsibility of sustaining the humanist Republic of Letters through rigorous textual criticism, classical philology, and elegant typography. Operating at the crucial nexus where Venetian civic humanism intersected with the centralized ecclesiastical reforms of Tridentine Rome, Paolo redefined the Aldine enterprise. While his father had earned immortal fame by rescuing ancient Greek literature from potential destruction through his pioneering Greek editio princeps editions and italic octavos, Paolo directed his immense scholarly energies toward Latin antiquity, emerging as the undisputed supreme authority on Marcus Tullius Cicero in sixteenth-century Europe. His life's work represents a monument to the synthesis of rigorous philological erudition, typographical mastery, and diplomatic negotiation across the shifting religious and geopolitical landscape of early modern Europe.The early life of Paolo Manuzio was marked by familial tragedy and complex legal dynamics. Following the death of his father Aldus in February 1515, when Paolo was barely three years old, the management of the Aldine Press in Venice fell under the direction of his maternal grandfather, Andrea Torresano da Asola, assisted by Paolo's uncles, Gian Francesco and Federico Torresano. Raised in the Venetian parish of San Paternian, Paolo's delicate physical constitution was matched by an extraordinary precocity for Latin letters. His initial education was supervised by eminent Venetian humanists, most notably Giovanni Battista Egnazio (Giambattista Egnazio), a former collaborator of his father and friend of Desiderius Erasmus, alongside Benedetto Ramberti. Under their instruction, Paolo developed an obsessive devotion to the style, syntax, and political thought of classical Rome, viewing the Latin language not as a dead medium, but as an living, sacred instrument of cultural renewal. Tensions regarding the administration and financial distribution of the family printing business eventually led to a formal rupture between the Manutius heirs and the Torresani family. Following protracted negotiations and legal settlements, the partnership was dissolved in 1533, enabling the twenty-one-year-old Paolo to assume full personal control of the re-established Academia Aldina at the sign of the Anchor and Dolphin.Upon assuming the helm of the Aldine Press in 1533, Paolo inaugurated a new editorial era characterized by an unprecedented concentration on Latin literature, epigraphy, and Roman constitutional history. His intellectual project was anchored in an uncompromising Ciceronianism, aligning him philosophically with the stylistic doctrines articulated by Cardinal Pietro Bembo. Paolo viewed Cicero's prose as the absolute zenith of human eloquence and civic wisdom. Over three decades in Venice, he authored, edited, and published monumental commentaries on the Ciceronian corpus that redefined early modern classical philology. His editions of the Epistolae ad Atticum, ad Brutum, ad Quintum fratrem (1540, with expanded commentaries in 1547), the Epistolae ad Familiares (1552), and the Orationes (1554) set new standards for textual accuracy, collating manuscripts, eliminating medieval corruptions, and providing exhaustive historical notes on Roman law, prosopography, and republican institutions. Paolo was not merely an editor of ancient texts; he was a formidable scholar-antiquarian in his own right. His landmark historical treatises—including De Civitate Romana (1558), De Comitiis Romanis (1585), and De Senatu Romano (1581)—provided groundbreaking reconstructions of Roman constitutional mechanics, administrative assemblies, and legal frameworks, laying foundational stones for modern classical archaeology and political history. His own Latin epistles, published across multiple volumes as Epistolarum libri, were celebrated across European universities as unsurpassed masterpieces of modern Neo-Latin prose.To sustain these scholarly endeavors, Paolo cultivated an expansive, prestigious international network of intellectual and political patrons. He maintained close correspondence and scholarly alliances with leading figures of the Sacred College and the European Republic of Letters, including Cardinals Pietro Bembo, Jacopo Sadoleto, Reginald Pole, Marcello Cervini (later Pope Marcellus II), Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, and Cristoforo Madruzzo. He collaborated closely with prominent foreign and Italian humanists such as Marc-Antoine Muret (Muretus), Gabriel Faerno, Latino Latini, Gian Vincenzo Pinelli, Annibale Caro, and Benedetto Varchi. Paolo's printing house in Venice remained a vibrant intellectual salon, attracting international scholars who sought his exquisite editions and critical judgment. From a typographical perspective, Paolo refined the aesthetic identity of the press. He perfected the italic typefaces originally cut for his father by Francesco Griffo, introducing greater regularity, harmonious proportions, and elegant capital letters. Furthermore, his Roman types (tondo) achieved a clarity and balanced dignity that influenced presswork throughout northern Italy and France. Despite these typographical triumphs, Paolo faced persistent economic hardship caused by the rising costs of paper, fierce pirating of Aldine editions by Lyon and Florentine printers, and the declining economic dominance of Venice in international book trade networks.The turning point of Paolo Manuzio's career occurred in the early 1560s against the backdrop of the Counter-Reformation. Following the election of Pope Pius IV (Giovanni Angelo Medici) in 1559, the Roman Curia sought to establish an official, highly sophisticated printing press in Rome to publish authoritative, uncorrupted texts of Holy Scripture, the Church Fathers, and the forthcoming decrees of the Council of Trent. Recognizing Paolo's unequaled typographical prestige and philological rigor, Pius IV formally invited him to Rome in 1561 to direct the newly established Stamperia del Popolo Romano (Typographia Apostolica Civitatis Romae), located near the Palazzo della Sapienza. Accompanied by a lucrative papal salary, privileges, and quarters in the Holy City, Paolo relocated his primary operations to Rome, while leaving his Venetian press under the management of his supervisors and eventually his son, Aldus Manutius the Younger (Aldo il Giovane). In Rome, Paolo orchestrated one of the most ambitious publishing programs of the sixteenth century. Under his direct oversight, the Roman press produced the official edition of the decrees of Trent, Canones et decreta Concilii Tridentini (1564), followed by the official Catholic catechism, Catechismus ex decreto Concilii Tridentini (1566), the revised Breviarium Romanum (1568), and the monumental Missale Romanum (1568). Simultaneously, he brought his philological expertise to bear on massive patristic projects, printing critical editions of Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, Saint Ambrose, and Saint Cyprian.The final decade of Paolo Manuzio's life was defined by intense physical suffering, severe bouts of illness, financial anxieties, and personal dilemmas regarding his separation from Venice. Despite these hardships, he remained devoted to his scholarly pursuits until his final days. He made periodic return journeys to Venice and Padua between 1569 and 1572 to restore his failing health and oversee his family's affairs, but ultimately returned to Rome, where he enjoyed the continued esteem of Popes Pius V and Gregory XIII. Paolo passed away in Rome on April 6, 1574, at the age of sixty-one, and was buried with high honors in the church of San Lorenzo in Lucina. His legacy is immense: he successfully navigated the transition of Renaissance typography from a tool of humanist rediscovery into an instrument of institutional rigor and confessional standardization. Through his unsurpassed Ciceronian commentaries, his pioneering constitutional treatises on ancient Rome, and his typographical leadership in both Venice and Rome, Paolo Manuzio secured a permanent place in the pantheon of Western bibliography, embodying the highest ideals of the scholar-printer.

publishers.name: Academia Veneta
publishers.biography: The Academia Veneta—known variously in contemporary documents and modern historiography as the Accademia Veneziana or the Accademia della Fama—represents one of the most intellectually ambitious, structurally complex, and institutionally revolutionary cultural initiatives of the Italian High Renaissance. Flourishing in Venice between 1557 and 1561 under the visionary direction of the patrician Federico Badoer (1529–1593), the institution was conceived not merely as a private literary salon or a localized humanistic sodality, but as a grandiose, state-aligned, encyclopedic mega-structure. It combined an academy of sciences, letters, civil jurisprudence, philosophy, and political theory with a state-of-the-art scholarly press (officina tipografica). By attempting to centralize, standardize, and disseminate human knowledge through the printed medium under the aegis of the Venetian Republic, the Academia Veneta served as a critical evolutionary bridge between classical Renaissance sodalities and the early modern national academies of science and letters that would emerge across Europe in the seventeenth century, such as the Accademia dei Lincei in Rome or the Académie des Sciences in Paris.The genesis of the institution was rooted in the extraordinary intellectual and socio-political climate of mid-sixteenth-century Venice. Following the traumatic political shifts of the Italian Wars and the intellectual readjustments brought about by the Protestant Reformation and the Council of Trent, the Venetian ruling class sought to reaffirm the Myth of Venice (Mito di Venezia)—the idealization of the Republic as an incorruptible bastion of order, liberty, wisdom, and divine favor. Born into an ancient and influential Venetian patrician family, Federico Badoer had received an elite humanistic education under the celebrated scholar Battista Egnazio at the Scuola di San Marco. Badoer gained diplomatic experience as the Venetian ambassador to the court of Emperor Charles V and King Philip II of Spain. Driven by an intense Neoplatonic conviction regarding the unity of all knowledge and a profound sense of civic duty, Badoer envisioned an institution that would harness the Republic's mercantile wealth and its unrivaled typographical infrastructure to construct a systematic, universal library of human wisdom. In 1557, Badoer formally established the academy in his ancestral palace, assembling an unparalleled coalition of Venetian patricians, foreign diplomats, university professors, polymaths, and master printers.The internal architecture of the Academia Veneta was staggering in its administrative rigor and utopian scope. Badoer structured the academy into eleven distinct faculties or chambers, each dedicated to a specific discipline: Theology, Moral Philosophy, Natural Philosophy, Mathematics, Medicine, Civil and Canon Law, Rhetoric, History, Poetry, Politics/Military Strategy, and Printing/Typography. Each faculty was headed by prominent scholars who served as original researchers, translators, editors, and peer-reviewers. Among the extraordinary intellectual figures affiliated with the academy were the celebrated poet Bernardo Tasso (father of Torquato Tasso), who served as the academy’s chancellor for Italian letters; the political theorist Bartolomeo Cavalcanti; the Neoplatonic philosopher Francesco Patrizi da Cherso; the prolific editor and polymath Girolamo Ruscelli; the Venetian patrician scholar Domenico Venier; and the diplomat Antonio Milledonne. Members were divided into administrative categories, including reggenti (directors), lettori (lecturers), and correttori (textual editors), operating under a strict set of statutes designed to turn intellectual endeavor into a public, institutional duty.At the very heart of the academy's mission was its printing press, the officina tipografica, which Badoer intended to make the undisputed epicenter of European scholarly publishing. To head this monumental printing enterprise, Badoer recruited Paolo Manuzio (1512–1574), the brilliant scholar-printer and son of the legendary founder of the Aldine Press, Aldus Manutius the Elder. Under Paolo Manuzio’s direction, the press adopted the iconic device of the academy: an allegorical figure of Fama (Fame), depicted as a winged woman standing atop a globe, blowing a long trumpet, surrounded by the Neoplatonist motto derived from Petrarch: Io volo al ciel per riposarmi in Dio ("I fly to heaven to rest in God"). It was this ubiquitous typographical mark that earned the institution its popular moniker, the Accademia della Fama. The press was supplied with custom-cast Greek, Latin, and Hebrew typefaces, superior paper stocks, and employed teams of philologists tasked with collating ancient manuscripts from private Venetian collections and the Biblioteca Marciana.The bibliographical output of the Academia Veneta during its brief four-year operational lifespan remains one of the most remarkable chapters in early modern book history. In 1558 and 1559, the press published its programmatic manifesto, titled the Summa Librorum quos in omnibus facultatibus explicandos, et in lucem edendos sibi Academia Veneta sumpsit, alongside its vernacular equivalent, the Sommario delle opere che l'Accademia Veneta ha dato ordine con la gratia di Dio che si stampino. These bibliographical manifestos outlined an astonishing publishing agenda of over 1,000 proposed titles, encompassing critical editions of Aristotle, Plato, Cicero, and the Church Fathers, alongside bilingual editions of classical legal codes, mathematical treatises by Archimedes and Euclid, anatomical works, geographical maps, and contemporary political tracts. Among the monumental works actually produced and completed by the press were Bernardo Tasso's epic poem L'Amadigi (1560)—a typographic masterpiece in folio—along with major legal treatises by Federico Lauretanus, editions of Thomas Linacre's grammatical treatises, and extensive collections of contemporary Venetian state orations and diplomatic discourses.Philosophically, the Academia Veneta represented a synthesis of Venetian civic humanism and Counter-Reformation orthodoxy, laced with Neoplatonic encyclopedism. Badoer and his circle believed that the restoration of political stability and religious harmony in Christendom depended on the systematic organization and dissemination of purified, authoritative knowledge. The academy sought to bridge the traditional divide between Latinate academic scholarship and vernacular popular culture, publishing works in both languages to educate the ruling elite and the broader reading public. Furthermore, the academy served as a de facto think tank for the Venetian Senate, preparing reports on monetary policy, naval architecture, agricultural reform, and diplomatic protocol. This intimate link between scholarly production, typographical innovation, and statecraft made the academy a uniquely Venetian phenomenon, unmatched by contemporary Italian academies such as the Accademia degli Intronati of Siena or the Accademia Florentina.Despite its brilliance and monumental achievements, the Academia Veneta collapsed in spectacular fashion in 1561 due to catastrophic financial mismanagement and political controversy. Federico Badoer’s utopian vision was undermined by his complete disregard for budgetary reality. In his zeal to expand the academy's scope, Badoer accrued staggering debts exceeding 60,000 ducats—an immense sum for the era. He mismanaged public funds entrusted to him, defaulted on payments to paper suppliers, typographers, and scholars, and unlawfully appropriated revenues from state grain offices and trust funds. As creditors inundated the Venetian magistrate courts with lawsuits, the Venetian government recognized that Badoer’s ruinous financial practices threatened to embroil the patriciate in a public scandal. On August 19, 1561, the powerful Council of Ten (Consiglio dei Dieci) intervened decisively, issuing an arrest warrant for Badoer, seizing the academy’s headquarters, impounding its printing presses, and placing its paper stock and manuscript library under state receivership.The sudden dissolution of the Academia Veneta sent shockwaves throughout the European Republic of Letters. Paolo Manuzio, financially damaged but exonerated of personal wrongdoing, was subsequently invited to Rome by Pope Pius IV to take charge of the Vatican Press (Typographia Vaticana), carrying with him the typographical standards and scholarly methodologies honed during his time with Badoer. Badoer himself suffered legal prosecution, imprisonment, and permanent political disgrace, living out his remaining years in relative obscurity. Nevertheless, the legacy of the Academia Veneta endured. Its publishing program demonstrated the unprecedented power of a dedicated institutional press to organize humanistic knowledge, and its structural organization provided a direct blueprint for subsequent early modern scientific and literary academies across Europe. Today, surviving imprints bearing the winged figure of Fama are prized as monumental masterpieces of sixteenth-century Venetian typography and monuments to a magnificent, tragic vision of universal humanism.

academic_description: 8vo. [12], 5-148 leaves. Collation: A8, a8, B-S8, T4. With the engraved emblem of the Accademia della Fama on the title-page. Old manuscript annotations on the margins. Later ownership entry by Guilelmus Meys. Early ninteenth century red half-calf, gilt spine, marbled edges. First edition, dedicated to Alberico Cibo Malaspina, of the first collection of Paolo Manuzio's Latin letters (overall 84), to which are also added the most important dedication letters (praefationes, overall 21) to his hitherto published works.“On comprend alors l'importance des lettres-préfaces que Manuce place en tête de ses principales éditions, en particulier celles de Cicéron, où l'on aurait tort de voir un répertoire de lieux communs. En s'adressant aux membres éminents de la Curie et de la noblesse italienne qu'il sait favorable aux disciplines libérales, l'érudit s'efforce de parfaire dans ce grands âmes l'idéal politique et spirituel qu'elles diffuseront dans leur propre circle pour qu'il devienne le ciment de la Cité et de son organisation hiérarchique. Tel est le programme qu'expose emblématiquement l'épître dédicatoire des Lettres et Préfaces (1558), jointe à tous les rééditions, où Manuce célèbre Laurent de Médicis, modèle du princeps cicéronien alliant iustitia, temperantia et liberalitas, et se conciliant par la gloire de ses mérites la faveur de ses concitoyens et des nations étrangères” (C. Mouchel, Paul Manuce épistolier: grandeur et misère de l'écrivain cicéronien, in: “Bibliothèque d'Humanisme et Renaissance”, LIV/3, 1992, p. 647).An augmented edition in four books appeared in 1560, followed by one in five books in 1561, one in eight books in 1569, one in ten books in 1571, and a final one in eleven books in 1573. Posthumously were published collections in twelve books in 1580 and in fourteenth books by Andreas Schott in 1624.“C'est la première édition des élégantes lettres et préfaces de Paul Manuce, si souvent réimprimées depuis; elle ne contient que celles des lettres qui, dans les éditions suivantes, forment les trois premiers livres, et un petit nombre de préface. Ces lettres n'ont pas été réimprimées sans altération. Dès la deuxième édition faite en 1560, le nom de Flaminius disparoît d'une lettre adressée à Stephano Saulio, fol. 4. Dans des éditions ultérieures, d'autres noms ont été supprimés ou remplacés” (Renouard, op. cit., p. 271).“Nel 1558 [Paolo Manuzio] fu coinvolto da Federico Badoer nel prestigioso progetto dell'Accademia della Fama, con l'incarico di stampare tutte le opere che l'istituzione avrebbe pubblicato. L'ambizioso programma del patrizio veneziano dovette ancora una volta dargli l'illusione di poter avere un ruolo importante in un'accademia che, nei desideri del fondatore, avrebbe dovuto avere un rapporto privilegiato con le istituzioni veneziane. Il segno di tale nuova progettualità lo conferma il fatto che nel 1558 Paolo pubblicò un'antologia delle sue lettere in latino, in un'elegante edizione all'insegna dell'Accademia della Fama, che conteneva in appendice una raccolta di praefationes: si trattava di ventuno dedicatorie che avevano accompagnato alcune delle sue più importanti edizioni e che, ancora una volta, testimoniavano le sue relazioni, non solo ai vertici della gerarchia ecclesiastica, ma anche tra i rappresentanti della diplomazia francese, con i quali era entrato in contatto tra gli anni trenta e quaranta” (L. Braida, Libri di lettere. Le raccolte epistolari del Cinquecento tra inquietudini religiose e ‘buon volgare', Bari, 2009, pp. 172-173).“Das gedruckte Corpus der Briefe des Paulus Manutius [...] scheint als wichtiges Bindeglied zwischen italienischer und transalpiner Epistolographie zur Zeit des Späthumanismus eine Schlüsselstellung eingenommen zu haben. Offenbar fand es als epistolographisches Schulbuch weite Verbreitung” (B.R. Jenny, Die Amerbachkorrespondenz. Von der humanistischen Epistolographie zur bürgerlichen Briefstellerei, in: “Der Brief im Zeitalter der Renaissance”, F.J. Worstbrock, ed., Weinheim, 1983, pp. 204-205).“Mais la fin du genre épistolaire n'est nullement de poursuivre une recherche spécifique, parallèle à celle des traités érudits. Chaque lettre est une méditation, c'est-à-dire un exercice et un effort de l'auteur pour témoigner de sa puissance à donner formulation excellente aux principes excellents de l'humanistas, ramenée à la réalisation toujours plus parfaite des quatre personae que définit le De officis. Manuce n'a jamais eu d'autre objectif que de faire coïncider à la cime de l'âme la part la plus généreuse de la philosophie de Cicéron – son platonisme et son stoïcisme – avec la noblesse et la suavité de son style, reconquises de l'intérieur” (C. Mouchel, op. cit., p. 641).The Accademia della Fama or Accademia Veneta was founded in 1558 by the Venetian noblemen Federico Badoer, Domenico Venier, and Girolamo Molino, and was dissolved only three years later due to conflicts with the Venetian authorities. This extravagant organization was a large, ambitious, and fatally costly undertaking designed formally along the lines of the Aldine Neacademia to serve the public needs of scholarship in science, arts, and letters. Its separate departments, the Consiglio Iconomico, Consiglio Politico, Consiglio delle Scientie, and Oratorio, were intended collectively to embrace the whole of the Renaissance encyclopaedia and thereby ensure the moral and scientific education of the state. As announced in a series of three published constitutions, various suppliche, and letters, it aimed to cover the full range of disciplines, since all pertained “to the public and private interests”. The academy was defunct after less than four years. Charged with the publication of the academician's literary activities was the printer Paolo Manuzio (cf. P. Venezia, [September 11 a.], 1558 (l. 147v) Paolo was the youngest son of Aldo Manuzio the Elder. He had the misfortune to lose his father at the age of two. After this event his grandfather and two uncles, the three Asolani, carried on the Aldine Press, while Paolo prosecuted his early studies at Venice. Excessive application hurt his health, which remained weak during the rest of his life. At the age of twenty-one he had acquired a solid reputation for scholarship and learning.In 1533 Paolo undertook the conduct of his father's business, which has latterly been much neglected by his uncles. Paolo determined to restore the glories of the house, and in 1540 he separated from his uncles. The field of Greek literature having been well night exhausted, he devoted himself principally to the Latin classics. He was a passionate Ciceronian, and perhaps his chief contributions to scholarship are the corrected editions of Cicero's letters and orations, his own epistles in a Ciceronian style, and his Latin version of Demosthenes. Throughout his life he combined the occupations of a scholar and a printer, winning an even higher celebrity in the former field than his father had done. Four treatises from his pen on Roman antiquities deserve to be commemorated for their erudition no less than for the elegance of their Latinity.Several Italian cities contended for the possession of so rare a man. He also received tempting offers from the Spanish court. Although his publications were highly esteemed, their sale was slow. Thus his life was a permanent struggle with pecuniary difficulties. In 1556 he received for a time external support from the Accademia Veneta, founded by Federico Badoer, who failed disgracefully in 1559, and the academy was extinct in 1562. Meanwhile Paolo had established his brother Antonio, a man of good parts but indifferent conduct, in a printing office and book shop at Bologna. Antonio died in 1559, having been a source of trouble and expense to Paolo during the last four years of his life. Other pecuniary embarrassment arose from a contract for supplying fish to Venice, into which Paolo had somewhat strangely entered with the government.In 1561 Pius IV invited him to Rome, offering him a yearly stipend of 500 ducats, and undertaking to establish and maintain his press there. The profits were to be divided between Paolo Manuzio and the Apostolic Camera. Paolo accepted the invitation, and spent the larger portion of his life, under three papacies, with various fortunes in the city of Rome. The works published by the Stamperia del Popolo Romano were mostly Latin works of theology and Biblical or patristic literature. Meanwhile his eldest son, the younger Aldo, had succeeded him in the management of the Venetian printing house. Overtaxed with studies and commercial worries Paolo died at Rome in his sixty-second year (cf. T. Sterza, Paolo Manuzio editore a Venezia (1533-1561), in: “ACME. Annali della Facoltà di lettere e filosofia dell'Università degli studi di Milano”, 61/2, 2008, pp. 123-168; and F. Barberi, Paolo Manuzio e la stamperia del popolo romano (1561-1570): con documenti inediti, Roma, 1942, passim).

authors.name: Lauro Pietro
authors.biography: Pietro Lauro (also known as Pietro Lauro Modenese, ca. 1510 – 1568) stands as one of the most versatile, industrious, and influential poligrafi—professional translators, press correctors, and vernacular editors—active in Venice during the golden age of Renaissance print culture. Operating at the dynamic intersection of humanist erudition and the commercial book market, Lauro played a paramount role in democratizing classical, scientific, philosophical, and foreign literature for the rapidly expanding Italian vernacular readership of the mid-sixteenth century. While often overshadowed in romanticized literary histories by more flamboyant contemporaries such as Pietro Aretino, Ludovico Dolce, or Niccolò Franco, Lauro’s monumental corpus of translations provided the intellectual foundation for early modern European cross-cultural transfer. His linguistic agility allowed him to bridge Latin, Greek, Spanish, and vernacular Italian, turning the printing shops of the Venetian lagoon into international hubs of knowledge dissemination.Born in Modena around the first decade of the sixteenth century, Lauro received a rigorous humanist education grounded in classical philology, rhetoric, and moral philosophy. Though precise details regarding his early domestic lineage remain sparse, his early writings reveal a deep familiarity with scholastic Latin traditions, ancient Greek syntax, and the emerging prestige of the Tuscan vernacular as canonized by Pietro Bembo. Drawn to the economic vitality and intellectual liberty of the Republic of Venice, Lauro migrated to the lagoon around the late 1530s or early 1540s. Venice was then experiencing an unprecedented expansion in its typographical industry. The city's printers were shifting from expensive, Latin-dominated folios toward accessible, vernacular octavos and duodecimos aimed at merchant elites, educated women, civic administrators, and provincial scholars. Recognizing that his classical training could be converted into economic subsistence within the print shop, Lauro integrated himself into the flourishing networks of Venetian publishing houses.Lauro’s bibliography of translations is extraordinary in its thematic breadth, spanning botany, medicine, agronomy, history, Christian humanism, and romance literature. One of his most celebrated contributions to early modern science was his translation of Leonhard Fuchs’ landmark botanical treatise, De historia stirpium octo commentarii. Published in Venice by Vincenzo Valgrisi in 1544 under the title Historia de le piante, Lauro’s translation brought Northern European botanical classification and medical herbalism directly to Italian apothecaries, physicians, and natural philosophers. In doing so, Lauro had to navigate not only complex Latinized botanical nomenclature but also the subtle theological risks associated with translating Protestant authors like Fuchs into post-Tridentine Italy. His work in the natural sciences extended to classical agriculture; his Italian vernacularization of Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella’s De re rustica (published by Michele Tramezzino in 1544) provided Renaissance landowners with a practical, vernacular handbook on estate management, soil cultivation, and animal husbandry.Beyond scientific literature, Lauro was a central agent in translating the Northern European Renaissance and Iberian humanism for Italian readers. He undertook vernacular renderings of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, including popular editions of the Enchiridion militis christiani and selections from the Apophthegmata, framing Erasmian moral piety for Italian devotional contexts before such works faced strict censorship under the Roman Index of Prohibited Books. Equally significant was his introduction of Spanish moral and chivalric literature to the Venetian press. Lauro translated Juan Luis Vives’ treatises on female education and domestic duty (such as De institutione feminae christianae, rendered as De l'ufficio del marito and related moral guides) and Antonio de Guevara’s celebrated mirror-for-princes, the Reloj de príncipes (as Horologio de' principi). Furthermore, Lauro was instrumental in catalyzing the immense Italian craze for Iberian chivalric romances. Working in close collaboration with the publisher Michele Tramezzino, Lauro translated significant portions of the Amadís de Gaula cycle, Palmerín de Oliva, and Primaleón, adapting the courtly ethics and fantastic geography of Spanish romance into fluid, elegant Italian prose that captivated Italian aristocratic readers.The operational locus of Lauro’s career was inextricably linked to the typography and business strategies of Venice’s premier publishing dynasties, notably those of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari, Vincenzo Valgrisi, and Michele Tramezzino. Working as an editor and translator for Giolito, Lauro contributed directly to the publisher's famous series of vernacular classics and educational treatises. The physical format of Lauro’s translations reflected cutting-edge Venetian book design: clean italic fonts, woodcut initials, elegant architectural title pages, and detailed thematic indexes compiled by Lauro himself to maximize usability for non-scholarly readers. His prefatory epistles, addressed to prominent Venetian patricians, noblewomen, and intellectual patrons, offer invaluable insight into the economic realities of sixteenth-century authorship, where translators navigated tight printing deadlines, rival unauthorized editions, and the patronal patronage system.Pietro Lauro died in Venice around 1568, leaving behind a legacy that fundamentally shaped the Italian Renaissance vernacular revival. Modern bibliographical scholarship has reassessed Lauro not merely as a passive translator for hire, but as an active cultural mediator who helped construct the vernacular encyclopedia of the sixteenth century. By translating complex Latin science, classical historiography, Erasmian philosophy, and foreign fiction into clear, accessible Italian, Lauro expanded the boundaries of vernacular literacy and literary culture. His work paved the way for the institutionalization of Italian as a global language of print, solidifying Venice’s reputation as the vibrant capital of the early modern European book trade.

publishers.name: Tramezzino Michele
publishers.biography: Michele Tramezzino (fl. 1539–1579) stands as one of the most intellectually versatile and commercially innovative publisher-booksellers of the Italian High and Late Renaissance. Operating primarily from the typographical capital of Venice, while maintaining an unprecedented, symbiotic business axis with his brother Francesco Tramezzino in Papal Rome, Michele forged a publishing empire that bridged the world of popular vernacular literature, monumental humanistic historiography, specialized legal jurisprudence, and revolutionary cartographic engraving. Famous for his ubiquitous printer's device featuring the Sibylla Cumaea or Tiburtina accompanied by the stoic motto Fato prudentia major ("Wisdom is greater than fate"), Tramezzino transformed the Venetian print trade by combining commercial savvy in the distribution of Spanish chivalric romances with an unyielding commitment to high-end copperplate printmaking and scientific geography.The exact historical origins and early lineage of the Tramezzino family remain partially shrouded in the archival lacunae of early modern Italy, though scholarship indicates roots connecting Rome and the Venetian Republic. Active from approximately 1536/1539 through 1579, Michele established his primary workshop and bookstore (bottega) in Venice, situated in the commercial heart of the city near the Rialto Bridge and the parish of San Giuliano, under the sign of the Sibyl (All'insegna della Sibilla). Simultaneously, his brother Francesco directed the Roman office located near Campo de' Fiori and the Via del Pellegrino. This dual-node enterprise allowed the Tramezzino firm to capitalize on the complementary strengths of the two great Italian printing centers: Venice's vast international merchant distribution network, maritime trade connections, and laxer preliminary censorship; and Rome's concentration of antiquarian scholars, papal curial patronage, Roman ruin topographers, and master engravers.Michele Tramezzino's publishing program was characterized by an extraordinary breadth of genre, reflecting both the shifting tastes of the sixteenth-century reading public and the intellectual imperatives of Italian Humanism. A central pillar of his early commercial success was his systematic introduction of Iberian chivalric romances into the Italian vernacular market. Entrusting the prolific translator Mambrino Roseo da Fabriano, Tramezzino secured long-term privileges from the Venetian Senate to translate, publish, and disseminate the monumental cycles of Amadís de Gaula, Palmerín de Oliva, Primaleón, Platir, Flortir, and Silves de la Selva. These narrative works, published in elegant octavo and duodecimo formats, catered to a burgeoning lay reader demographic and generated the steady capital required to fund Tramezzino's far more speculative and costly artistic and scientific ventures.Parallel to his romance enterprise, Tramezzino established himself as a premier publisher of classical antiquity, contemporary history, and political philosophy. He issued seminal vernacular translations of classical historians, including Diodorus Siculus, Polybius, Plutarch, Xenophon, and Appian of Alexandria, alongside contemporary historical narratives such as Paolo Giovio's Historiarum sui temporis, Francesco Guicciardini's political treatises, and early Italian editions of Johannes Sleidanus's history of the Protestant Reformation. Tramezzino worked closely with leading humanists and editors of his day, such as Dionigi Atanagi, Alfonso de Ulloa, and Girolamo Ruscelli, creating a vibrant network of editorial collaborators who provided meticulous text-critical apparatuses, indexes, and marginalia that set his editions apart from those of rival Venetian houses like Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari or Vincenzo Valgrisi.Where Michele Tramezzino achieved undisputed immortality in the annals of graphic art and science, however, was in the realm of cartography and fine copperplate printmaking. Moving away from the traditional, coarse woodcut illustration that dominated early sixteenth-century book production, Tramezzino invested heavily in intaglio copperplate engraving. He collaborated with the most brilliant cartographers, artists, and engravers of the Renaissance, including the Piedmontese cosmographer Giacomo Gastaldi, the antiquarian Pirro Ligorio, and master engravers such as Enea Vico, Giulio Sanuto, Sebastiano di Re, and Jacob Bos. Through these partnerships, Tramezzino published groundbreaking maps of the world, continental landmasses, and specific regions, including Gastaldi's monumental 1546 world map, detailed topographies of the British Isles, Flanders, the Kingdom of Naples, Greece, and the Holy Land, as well as complex architectural plans of ancient and modern Rome. These maps, printed on high-quality broadsheets, were sold individually or bound into customized composite atlases (often referred to by modern cartobibliographers as IATO or Italian-Assembled To-Order atlases, closely linked to the Roman network of Antonio Lafreri).The typographical execution of Tramezzino's books reflected a refined Aesthetic standard. His shop employed clean, highly legible Roman and Italic types, often supplied by the top typefounders of Venice and Lyon. The title pages of his imprints were meticulously structured, featuring the prominent, elegantly woodcut or engraved vignette of the Cumaean Sibyl sitting upon a tripod or holding a book, framed by intricate Renaissance grotesque borders. Furthermore, Tramezzino was an early master of legal protection within the fragmented Italian print market. He aggressively petitioned the Venetian Senate and the Papal Chancellery for privilegi (monopolistic copyrights) covering his maps, translations, and specialized texts, frequently entering into fierce litigations against unauthorized pirate printers in Florence, Milan, and Naples who attempted to copy his lucrative cartographic prints and chivalric translations.By the time of his cessation of activity around 1579, Michele Tramezzino had built a legacy that profoundly reshaped early modern print culture. He demonstrated that a print publisher could balance mass-market vernacular fiction with high-culture antiquarian scholarship and cutting-edge geographical science. Modern analytical bibliography and cartobibliography recognize the imprints of the Insegna della Sibilla as supreme specimens of sixteenth-century Italian graphic art. His cartographic output remains a cornerstone for the study of Renaissance geography, while his vast output of translated romance and historical literature provided the foundational reading material for generations of early modern European readers.

academic_description: 8vo. [16], 240 pp. Collation: a8, A-P8. Printer's device on title-page. Italic types. Later full vellum.First edition, second issue (the first bears the date 1552), dedicated by the author to Francesco Chimenti.“Pietro Lauro presentava la sua raccolta di lettere al dedicatario Francesco Chimenti, 'nobile fiorentino', come una raccolta di ‘concetti', frutto di conversazioni: ‘Vengo dunque con le mie lettere, ne le quali vostra Signoria leggerà molti bei discorsi e piacevoli ragionamenti e vi sovvenirà di molti similari parlari, che voi et meco ne la casa vostra, e in più altri luochi con diverse persone virtuose havete trattato. Et io tenendone memoria, me ne sono in molte mie lettere servito' ” (L. Braida, Libri di lettere. Le raccolte epistolari del Cinquecento tra inquietudini religiose e ‘buon volgare', Bari, 2009, p. 243).“Le recueil contient 125 lettres [including the dedicatory] non datées, écrites, de l'aveu de l'auteur, à partir d'études et de conversations. D'après la Tavola delle materie, il y aurait 6 l. ‘consolatorie', 3 d' 'esortatione', 1 ‘giocosa', 1 ‘famigliare', etc. Plus que les destinataires (des noms apparemment fictifs se mêlent à d'autres de personnes connues: Ortensio Lando, Fausto da Longiano, Lucrezia Gonzaga da Gazuolo,…) comptent les sujets, un par lettre: aux plus nombreux traités dans la ligne de la morale traditionelle (le mariage, l'éducation des enfants, la consolation,…), s'opposent quelques attitudes inhabituelles ou paradoxales: Lauro se déclare contre la pauvreté puisque la société n'estime pas les qualités du pauvre; il invite l'écrivain à justifier son oeuvre et à la louer lui-même, il engage à douter de la rhétorique en se fondant sur une des règles de la rhétorique,…). Non sans raison, ce recueil est parfois attribué à O. Lando” (J. Basso, Le genre épistolaire en langue italienne, 1538-1662, Roma, 1999, I, pp. 170-171).“Il Sanesi [Tre epistolari del Cinquecento, in: “Giornale storico della Letteratura italiana”, 23, 1894, pp. 26-32] accosta l'epistolario di Lucrezia Gonzaga a quello di Pietro Lauro: mentre il primo potrebbe essere opera del Lando (e il Sanesi ne è convinto) per via dello stile, ricco di ‘citazioni della storia e della mitologia' e caratterizzato da ‘una certa maniera di filosofare tutta propria del Lando', è proprio questo stile, paradossale e basato sull'accostamento di contrari, che il Lauro vuole apertamente imitare in quelle che, secondo l'opinione di Sanesi, sono lettere fittizie scritte à la Lando. Certo è che la dedicatoria a Francesco Chimenti, nobile fiorentino del primo libro di Lettere del Lauro si può considerare esattamente speculare a quella appena vista al Manfrone [Pietro Paolo Manfrone, dedicatee of Lucrezia Gonzaga's letters, see p. XXX]: laddove nella prima il dedicatario veniva liquidato con la titolazione della soprascritta, qui l'autore si diffonde in numerose variazioni sul tema della generosità del Chimenti nei confronti dei virtuosi, ma soprattutto nei confronti del dedicante, tanto che il Lauro lo vedeva ‘tanto disposto ai suoi comodi, che lui à saper desiarli'. Altro aspetto sottolineato in più riprese è il piacere provato dal Chimenti nell'intrattenersi in dotte conversazioni, conversazioni che il Chimenti ritroverà in parte divenute materiale per queste lettere (‘Et io tenendone memoria, me ne sono in molte mie lettere servito')” (C. Schiavon, Una via d'accesso agli epistolari. Le dediche dei libri di lettere d'autore nel Cinquecento. Prima parte, in: “Margini. Giornale della dedica e altro”, 3, 2009, p. 28).Lauro published a second volume of letters seven years later, Delle lettere di messer Pietro Lauro. Libro secondo (Venice, 1560), dedicated to Johann Jakob Fugger.All the letters in the collection are without place and date. A certain number of recipients can certainly be considered as fictitious. For that we have decided to render their names exactly as they are given in the printed text. In brackets is found the modern spelling of the names of the identified recipients. Born in Modena around 1510, he probably made medical studies in Bologna or Padua, considering the many translations of medical works he did during his career.Around 1542 he moved to Venice, where he started collaborating with some local typographers (mainly Giolito, Tramezzino, and Valgrisi) as a translator from Greek and Latin. He continued this activity until 1568, together with those of schoolmaster and scribe.Among the many works he translated into Italian stand out the De inventoribus rerum by Polidoro Virgili (1543) and Erasmus' Colloquia (1545), which were both subsequently put on the Index. He also translated De officio mariti by Juan Luis Vives (1546) and Leon Battista Alberti's De re aedificatoria (1546).The relationships Lauro had with several Italian figures close to the Evangelical movement, like Ortensio Lando, Lucrezia Gonzaga, and Renée of France (to whom he dedicated his Colloqui famigliari di Erasmo), and the many letters he addressed to German correspondents, (all found in his letter collections), testify to his sympathy for the Lutheran doctrines (cf. S. Seidel Menchi, Erasmus als Ketzer: Reformation und Inquisition im Italien des 16. Jahrhunderts, Leiden & New York, 1992, pp. 435, 467). Besides that, the friar Ambrogio da Milano referred to him as a Lutheran in a deposition made before the Inquisition in 1557. So did a certain Ettore Donati during another trial. Lauro died in Modena after 1568 (cf. G. Dini, Lauro, Pietro, in: “Dizionario biografico degli Italiani”, Roma, 2005, LXIV, pp. 119-122).

authors.name: Martelli Nicolò
authors.biography: Nicolò (or Niccolò) Martelli was the scion of a wealthy family of merchants from Florence. At the age of fourteen he was sent to Rome to make practice in the trade. Here he met his idol, Pietro Aretino, who encouraged him to compose poems. Back in Florence he took over the family business.In 1531, exiled for a few months in Prato, he met the “letterati” Baldinaccio Martellini, Pandolfo Martelli, and Agnolo Firenzuola, and had a love affair with Maria Minerbetti, wife of Tommaso Minerbetti, Duke Cosimo de' Medici's local representative. In 1536 he married Lucrezia di Francesco Ciampelli. In 1540 he founded, together with Giovanni Mazzuoli, Antonio Grazzini and many others, the Accademia degli Umidi (cf. M. Maylender, Storia delle Accademia d'Italia, Bologna, 1930, V, pp. 363-367), which a year later was transformed into the more institutional Accademia Fiorentina (cf. Plaisance, Une première affirmation de la politique culturelle de Côme Ier: la trasformation de l'Academie des ‘Humidi' en Académie Florentine (1540-1542), in: “L'Accademia e il suo principe”, Roma, 2004, p. 140, 185-186).Martelli remained member of the academy with the name of “Gelato” and in 1544-45 was appointed consul. In 1543 he travelled to France in search of business venture, following the footsteps of his friend Luigi Alamanni, but already after a month he returned to Florence to assume the new position as mayor of Impruneta. He died in Florence in 1555.Martelli was the author of many occasional pieces dedicated to members of the Medici family. He also wrote love verses addressed to Maria Minerbetti and several comical compositions. His entire poetic production remained unpublished, except the Stanze sopra le nozze del duca Cosimo Medici secondo (Firenze, 1539).
