publishers.name: Doni Anton Francesco
publishers.biography: Anton Francesco Doni (1513–1574) stands as one of the most eccentric, innovative, and multifaceted literary figures of the Italian High Renaissance. A quintessential exponent of the mid-sixteenth-century phenomenon of the poligrafi—professional vernacular men of letters who sustained their livelihoods through the booming Venetian publishing market—Doni operated at the volatile intersection of humanist scholarship, print capitalism, visual art, and social satire. As an author, compiler, typographer, iconographer, and proto-bibliographer, he exerted a transformative influence on the evolution of Italian prose, bibliographical science, and utopian literature. His landmark publications, most notably La Libraria (1550)—widely acknowledged as the first systematic printed bibliography of Italian vernacular literature—and I Mondi (1552–1553), a visionary blend of satire, anti-academic dialogue, and speculative urban design, bridged the medieval encyclopedic tradition with early modern print culture. Situated within the aesthetic currents of Mannerism and the socio-religious anxieties of the pre-Tridentine era, Doni's career captures the intellectual dynamism, economic precarity, and editorial experimentation of sixteenth-century Italian humanism.Born in Florence in 1513 into modest circumstances, Doni was the son of Bernardo di Miniato, a artisan forbiciaro (scissors-maker). Despite his humble lineage, his early exposure to the intellectual atmosphere of Florence enabled him to pursue an ecclesiastical career. In his youth, he entered the Servite Order at the famous convent of the Santissima Annunziata in Florence, taking the monastic name Fra Giuliano. His monastic education provided him with a rigorous foundation in Latin grammar, scholastic philosophy, and classical literature. However, Doni's tempestuous personality and acute fascination with the vibrant secular culture of his age led to severe friction with religious discipline. Around 1540, he abandoned the Servite habit without obtaining formal papal secularization—an act of apostasy that would haunt his social standing for the remainder of his life and expose him to vicious attacks from personal rivals. Upon leaving the monastery, Doni embarked on a period of restless migration across Northern and Central Italy. He settled temporarily in Piacenza, where he became a key figure in the prestigious Accademia degli Ortolani under the academic pseudonym "Il Bizzarro." Subsequent sojourns in Pavia, Milan, Venice, and Rome exposed him to courtly patronage networks, humanistic academies, and the practical operations of commercial printing shops, cementing his vocation as an independent author-entrepreneur.Doni's literary production is renowned for its genre-defying versatility, Mannerist discursiveness, and structural ingenuity. In 1550, while residing in Venice, he published La Libraria through the famous press of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari. Designed to catalog and defend vernacular literature against the entrenched hegemony of Latin humanism, the work offered an exhaustive inventory of Italian printed books, complete with biographical notes, critical appraisals, and thematic classifications. Recognizing the vast reservoir of unprinted texts, Doni followed this success with La Seconda Libraria (1551), dedicated exclusively to unpublished manuscripts, anonymous tracts, and suppressed writings—an pioneering effort in bibliographical archaeology. His philosophical and satirical genius reached its pinnacle in I Mondi (1552–1553), issued by the master printer Francesco Marcolini. Composed of complex dialogues between allegorical figures, artisans, and celestial spirits, I Mondi divided the universe into distinct realms ("Mondo Piccolo," "Mondo Grande," "Mondo Massimo"), concluding with "Il Mondo Savio e Pazzo," a remarkable depiction of a star-shaped utopian city built on radical social equality, communal property, gender parity, and architectural symmetry. Preceding Tommaso Campanella's Città del Sole by half a century, Doni's utopian vision combined socio-political critique with radical anti-clericalism. Parallel to I Mondi, Doni published I Marmi (1552–1553), a collection of nocturnal conversations set upon the marble steps of the Florence Cathedral, capturing the authentic voices of Florentine citizens, intellectuals, and craftsmen. His passion for moral philosophy and narrative folklore manifested in La Moral Filosoffia (1552), an adaptation of the ancient Indian fable collection Panchatantra (derived from John of Capua's Latin Directorium Humanae Vitae), which introduced Eastern apologues to Italian vernacular readers. Furthermore, Doni was deeply attuned to the visual arts, authoring Il Disegno (1549), an early theoretical treatise on theoretical and practical draftsmanship that elevated disegno as the intellectual foundation of painting, sculpture, and architecture, reflecting his intimate friendships with visual masters such as Bronzino, Enea Vico, and Tintoretto.Doni's engagement with typography extended far beyond authorial manuscript production; he was an active printer, typographer, and book designer. In 1546, having returned to Florence, Doni established his own printing office under the official aegis of the Accademia Fiorentina. Operating near the Piazza del Duomo, his press issued important vernacular editions, including works by Luigi Alamanni, Niccolò Machiavelli's Clizia, and his own epistolary collection, Lettere di M. Anton Francesco Doni (1547). However, administrative incompetence, inadequate financial backing, and fierce competition from the official ducal printer Lorenzo Torrentino, alongside bitter factional strife with academic rivals like Pier Francesco Giambullari and Lodovico Domenichi, led to the bankruptcy and closure of Doni's shop in 1547. Forced to relocate to Venice—the undisputed capital of European typography—Doni established fruitful partnerships with the city's foremost publishing houses, particularly those of Gabriel Giolito and Francesco Marcolini. Marcolini, famed for his sophisticated typographical layouts and exquisite woodcut illustrations, collaborated closely with Doni to produce visually stunning volumes. Works like I Mondi and I Marmi were designed as integrated visual-textual experiences, featuring intricate architectural title pages, emblematical printer's marks, woodcut portraits, and complex diagrams executed by engravers such as Enea Vico. Doni was among the first Italian authors to treat the printed page as an interactive spatial medium, meticulously directing font selections, marginal notes, frontispieces, and visual emblems to engage the dynamic expectations of the sixteenth-century reading public.Throughout his career, Doni's fiery temperament involved him in fierce literary and personal controversies. His most notorious feud was with his former intimate friend and fellow poligrafo, Lodovico Domenichi. What began as an editorial collaboration collapsed into decades of mutual accusations of plagiarism, financial fraud, and heresy. Doni launched devastating written attacks against Domenichi in works such as I Tre Libri delle Lettere and the Inferni, accusing his rival of corrupting texts and harboring Protestant sympathies. In retaliation, Domenichi exposed Doni's uncanonical departure from the Servite Order, accusing him of apostasy and impiety. Doni's biting anti-clericalism, fascination with heterodox and utopian ideas, and uncensored satirical style inevitably attracted the hostile attention of the Roman Inquisition during the Counter-Reformation. Following the Council of Trent, several of his publications, including I Mondi and La Libraria, were listed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum or subjected to severe expurgation in post-Tridentine reeditions (such as those prepared by Antonio Possevino and Publico Pietro Altamura). In the nineteenth century, scholars such as Girolamo Tiraboschi and Emmanuele Antonio Cicogna initiated a critical reappraisal of Doni's bibliographical and literary legacy. In the twentieth century, landmark studies by Benedetto Croce, Delio Cantimori, Paul F. Grendler, Mario Costanzo, and Giorgio Masi re-established Doni as a crucial Mannerist thinker, a pioneer of modern bibliography, and a visionary voice in early modern political philosophy. Doni died in retreat at Monselice near Padua in 1574, leaving behind a monumental legacy that redefined the intersection of print technology, vernacular literature, and intellectual freedom.

publisher_data: Florence, (at the author's expenses) [Anton Francesco Doni], 1546
academic_description: 4to. [4], 5-91, [1] leaves. Collation: A-Z4 (lacking Z4, a blank). With the woodcut portrait of the author on the title-page. Seventeenth century vellum over boards, marbled edges. First edition, published at the author's expenses, of this collection of 209 letters arranged in chronological order. The second book, which was almost ready when the first appeared, was never published. It is preserved in a manuscript of the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale of Florence (cf. C. Marconcini, ed., Dal primo e dal secondo libro delle lettere di Niccolò Martelli, Lanciano, 1916, pp. 5-12).The present edition, variously attributed to the Guinta press, has more recently been assigned to Anton Francesco Doni. “Il nome del Doni non si legge nella data, ma apparisce chiarissimo che ne fosse lo stampatore, non solo per la forma de' caratteri, ma per esservi detto in una lettera del Martelli, a pag. 84, e per altri certi riscontri: onde si vede quanto sbagliassero il Bandini ed il Renouard, nei loro cataloghi Giuntini, quando attribuirono questa edizione ai Giunti. Il Doni, quale ne fosse la causa, dopo avere dato mano alla stampa di questo libro, lo criticò nella Prima Libreria” (S. Bongi, Catalogo delle opere di A.F. Doni, in: A.F. Doni, “I marmi”, P. Fanfani, ed., Firenze, 1863, II, p. 303).Bongi does not seem, however, to have noticed the letter addressed to a certain Gian Francesco da Pavia (“car. e bidello della sacra Accademia Fiorentina”, l. 63v), in which the author invites the unidentified recipient (called “virtuoso giovane”) to undertake the printing of his letters, to choose a nice paper and elegant types, and to accept a remuneration for the edition.“Anche Nicolò Martelli, che stampò il suo libro di lettere presso la stamperia di Doni a Firenze, dedica la sua raccolta a una donna: si tratta di Maddalena Bonaiuti, moglie di Luigi Alamanni. Nell'incipit lo scrittore ricorda subito il noto marito, dicendo di aver pensato in un primo momento di dedicare a lui il libro, ma aggiunge: ‘facendolo errava, & tale errore meritava riprensione: ma haveria risposto, che non meno si conveniva alle sue nobili qualitati & magnanime Eccellenze d'esser sacrati purissimi inchiostri, che egli stesso s'habbia fatto si divinamente quelle d'altri'; così Martelli si rivolge a Maddalena: ‘ma ecco che voi per essere il cuore dell'anima sua; come egli l'animo de l'anima vostra: indirizzandole alla candidezza di quello splendore: che vi adorna il pellegrino spirito di si pregiate lodi: ci haverà parte in ogni modo'. Con la donna, in ogni caso, Martelli ha debiti personali diretti: di lei infatti viene lodato ‘l'offitio di cortesia' e la sua capacità di intercedere efficacemente ‘dalle gran Madame & dalle persone deputate, à ciò per le vie ch'ella sa più brevi & migliori', sostenendo che, vista l'influenza che già esercita alla giovane età di ventidue anni, è facile pensare che ‘tutte le faccende importanti di cotesto Christianissimo Regno, si guideranno un giorno nel dignissimo cospetto vostro per conferirle nella Maestà della Sereniss. Madama Caterina unica vostra Signora & mia sempiterna Patrona, acciò ch'ella ne risolva poi col grande Arigo Marito suo, quello che Dio gli spirerà'. In effetti la Bonaiuti era dama di compagnia della potente Caterina de' Medici, futura regina di Francia. Il Martelli, ricorda poi un episodio preciso: ‘quando non havendo di me à gran pena conoscenza vi degnaste introdurme a villa Cutrea la vigilia del Batista hora ha due anni, davanti al sacro cospetto della Giovane Reale: per presentarle il libro delle Donne Illustri, che presto verrà a luce'. Le lettere che le vengono donate, inoltre, sostiene Martelli, parlano in più punti delle dame di compagnia della regina, che Maddalena stessa gli ha permesso di conoscere. La dedica si conclude unendo negli auspici la dedicataria ‘insieme con l'Eccellenza del suo gran Consorte in quella Realissima di Madama la Dalfina, unica sua Regina'. Grazie alla mediazione della Bonaiuti, Martelli aveva ottenuto dalla Delfina di Francia, prima della pubblicazione del libro di lettere, una donazione di cento scudi d'oro e delle raccomandazioni per il granduca Cosimo I. Non sembra invece che questa dedica sia stata particolarmente gradita alla dama di compagnia di Caterina de' Medici, visto che in una lettera al marito di lei, Alamanni, Martelli si lamenta: ‘Meritava un certo che, se non d'altro, di gratitudine di parole, dove io non ho mai havuto risposta alcuna, né da V. S., né da Lei, né dal Sr abate vostro figlio'; lo stralcio, riportato da Hauvette [Luigi Alamanni (1495-1556). Sa vie et son oeuvre, Paris, 1903, p. 133] è tratto da una lettera dell'epistolario inedito, destinato probabilmente a diventare il secondo libro di lettere, poi mai stampato e conservato nella Biblioteca Nazionale di Firenze (cl. VIII, cod. 1447); se non ci sono errori nella data indicata da Hauvette (10 gennaio 1545) si tratterebbe di un pentimento piuttosto precoce, visto che il Primo libro verrà stampato nel 1546” (C. Schiavon, Una via d'accesso agli epistolari. Le dediche dei libri di lettere d'autore nel Cinquecento. Prima parte, in: “Margini. Giornale della dedica e altro”, 3, 2009, pp. 36-37).“Le lettere di Niccolò Martelli […] costituiscono il più coerente esempio di ortodossia al modello aretini ano […] Sin dallo strato più esterno – l'apparato paratestuale – è evidente la volontà, esplicitamente dichiarata, di ricalcare il modello. Sono infatti presenti gli elementi caratterizzanti dei volumi aretiniani: l'inclusione, già nel titolo della prima raccolta, del numero ordinale (Il primo libro delle lettere) e un ritratto dell'autore, di buona fattura, in posa di tre quarti. Aretino aveva usato il libro di lettere per imporsi definitivamente come il più influente ‘uomo di penna' del proprio tempo; analogamente, anche se in tono minore, Martelli, che proviene da una famiglia di mercanti, affida alla stampa delle proprie epistole la speranza di essere accolto nel novero dei letterati ‘illustri'. Un desiderio che stenta a realizzarsi, come egli stesso ammette con amarezza in diverse occasioni […] L'immagine che Martelli vuol dare di sé […] è quella del letterato che insegue con un certo grado di successo una vocazione difficile. È in questo senso significativa la scelta di proporre un primo blocco di epistole che sono per la maggior parte accompagnatorie o dedicatorie di scritti occasionali […] Si tratta di un insieme che, pur tradendo l'imperativo aretiniano della varietas che allontana il ‘tedio', risulta funzionale per lanciare in limine uno sguardo retrospettivo sulla propria biografia intellettuale […] Per saldare la frammentarietà di questa sezione suggerendo una lettura di essa in chiave autobiografica, Martelli inserisce tra le prime una lettera indirizzata all'Aretino, anch'essa fondamentalmente concepita per accompagnare alcuni versi, che riassume in poche righe la storia della propria vocazione” (G. Genovese, La lettera oltre il genere. Il libro di lettere, dall'Aretino al Doni, e le origini dell'autobiografia moderna, Roma & Padova, 2009, pp. 153-159). Marguerite de Navarre. Firenze, June 10, 1546 (l. 91r) Nicolò (or Niccolò) Martelli was the scion of a wealthy family of merchants from Florence. At the age of fourteen he was sent to Rome to make practice in the trade. Here he met his idol, Pietro Aretino, who encouraged him to compose poems. Back in Florence he took over the family business.In 1531, exiled for a few months in Prato, he met the “letterati” Baldinaccio Martellini, Pandolfo Martelli, and Agnolo Firenzuola, and had a love affair with Maria Minerbetti, wife of Tommaso Minerbetti, Duke Cosimo de' Medici's local representative. In 1536 he married Lucrezia di Francesco Ciampelli. In 1540 he founded, together with Giovanni Mazzuoli, Antonio Grazzini and many others, the Accademia degli Umidi (cf. M. Maylender, Storia delle Accademia d'Italia, Bologna, 1930, V, pp. 363-367), which a year later was transformed into the more institutional Accademia Fiorentina (cf. Plaisance, Une première affirmation de la politique culturelle de Côme Ier: la trasformation de l'Academie des ‘Humidi' en Académie Florentine (1540-1542), in: “L'Accademia e il suo principe”, Roma, 2004, p. 140, 185-186).Martelli remained member of the academy with the name of “Gelato” and in 1544-45 was appointed consul. In 1543 he travelled to France in search of business venture, following the footsteps of his friend Luigi Alamanni, but already after a month he returned to Florence to assume the new position as mayor of Impruneta. He died in Florence in 1555.Martelli was the author of many occasional pieces dedicated to members of the Medici family. He also wrote love verses addressed to Maria Minerbetti and several comical compositions. His entire poetic production remained unpublished, except the Stanze sopra le nozze del duca Cosimo Medici secondo (Firenze, 1539) (cf. E. Stumpo, Nicolò Martelli, in: “Dizionario biografico degli Italiani”, Roma, 2008, LXXI, pp. 61-64).

authors.name: Aventinus (Thurmair) Johannes
authors.biography: Johannes Aventinus (born Johannes Thurmair or Turmair; July 4, 1477 – January 9, 1534) stands as one of the most formidable figures of Northern European humanism, universally acclaimed as the pioneer of modern scientific historiography within the Holy Roman Empire and revered as the 'Bavarian Herodotus.' Operating at the volatile intersection of Renaissance philology, Germanic archaism, and the early confessional ruptures of the Protestant Reformation, Aventinus transformed the writing of history from medieval annalistic compilation into a critical, source-driven, and epigraphically verified discipline. His monumental dual historiographical achievements—the Latin Annales Boiorum and its vernacular counterpart, the Bayerische Chronik—redefined the cultural and political self-consciousness of the Duchy of Bavaria and the wider German-speaking lands. By subjecting monastic charters, ancient inscriptions, numismatic evidence, and medieval chronicles to rigorous philological scrutiny, Aventinus established a new methodology for territorial history while simultaneously articulating a fiercely anti-curial, proto-nationalist political philosophy that deeply impacted the intellectual landscape of early modern Europe.Born in the Lower Bavarian town of Abensberg—from whose Latinized name, Aventinum, he adopted his humanist pseudonym—Aventinus was the son of Peter Thurmair, a prosperous and respected innkeeper of the establishment 'Zum Rothaase.' From his early youth, Thurmair exhibited an extraordinary intellectual capacity, receiving his initial schooling at the Latin school of Abensberg before matriculating at the University of Ingolstadt in 1495. The academic environment at Ingolstadt, though still dominated by scholastic traditions, was beginning to absorb the fresh currents of Italian humanism. Seeking a broader engagement with classical studies, Aventinus relocated in 1498 to the University of Vienna, which had recently become the undisputed epicenter of German humanism following the arrival of Conrad Celtis (1459–1508). Under Celtis’s charismatic tutelage, Aventinus was initiated into the Sodalitas Litteraria Danubiana, absorbing Celtis’s vision of a revitalized Germanic culture capable of rivalling Italian intellectual supremacy through the rediscovery of native antiquities and classical poetry.Aventinus’s educational pilgrimage continued across the major university centers of Central and Western Europe. In 1503, he spent time at the University of Kraków, then a renowned center for mathematical and astronomical studies, where he deepened his knowledge of geography and classical science under humanists such as Laurentius Corvinus. In 1504, he traveled to the University of Paris, enrolling at the Collège de Lemoine. In Paris, Aventinus came under the profound influence of Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (Jacobus Fabricius Stapulensis, c. 1455–1536), whose Christian humanism, Aristotelian commentaries, and irenic pedagogical reform left an indelible mark on the young Bavarian scholar. Obtaining his Master of Arts degree from Paris in 1507, Aventinus returned to Bavaria equipped with an unrivaled mastery of Latin philology, Greek literature, pedagogical theory, and historical method, positioning himself as one of the premier intellectuals of the Wittelsbach realm.Upon his return to Munich in 1507, Aventinus was quickly integrated into the courtly and academic circles of the House of Wittelsbach. In 1509, Duke William IV and his brother Duke Louis X of Bavaria entrusted Aventinus with the prestigious responsibility of serving as private tutor to their younger brother, Duke Ernest of Bavaria (1500–1560), who would later become the Prince-Bishop of Passau and Archbishop of Salzburg. Establishing his residence at the ducal court in Burghausen, Aventinus devised an innovative pedagogical curriculum based on classical philology, music theory, mathematics, and geography, rejecting the dry scholastic manuals of the medieval schoolmen. To facilitate this elite education, Aventinus authored a series of groundbreaking educational manuals, including the Rudimenta grammaticæ (1512), the Musica monographia (1516), and the Grammatica nova (1517), which synthesized Latin grammar with humanistic elegance.Aventinus’s pedagogical success in Burghausen solidified his reputation among the German intelligentsia. In 1516, he orchestrated the establishment of the Sodalitas Litteraria Angilostadensis at the University of Ingolstadt, an academic society designed to foster humanist scholarship, publish classical texts, and coordinate historical research across Bavaria. Through this network, Aventinus maintained an extensive correspondence with the leading luminaries of European humanism, including Willibald Pirckheimer (1470–1530), Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547), Hieronymus Gebwiler (1473–1545), and Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536). Recognized by the Wittelsbach dukes as a scholar of exceptional promise, Aventinus was officially appointed in February 1517 as the official Bayerischer Geschichtsschreiber (Historiographer of the Duchy of Bavaria)—a groundbreaking institutional appointment that liberated him from pedagogical duties and provided him with the financial patronage necessary to execute a comprehensive history of the Bavarian state.As official historiographer, Aventinus initiated an unprecedented research project that anticipated the modern archival revolution. Armed with ducal letters of authorization, he spent years traveling across the Holy Roman Empire, conducting extensive field research in imperial archives, municipal registries, and monastic libraries. He systematically examined and transcribed manuscript collections at major Benedictine and Augustinian abbeys, including St. Emmeram in Regensburg, Tegernsee, Niederaltaich, Weltenburg, Mondsee, Passau, Freising, and Salzburg. Unlike medieval chroniclers who uncritically copied mythic genealogies, Aventinus interrogated his primary sources with rigorous philological skepticism. He pioneered the use of auxiliary historical sciences in Germany, meticulously collecting Roman stone inscriptions (epigraphy), ancient coins (numismatics), medieval charters (diplomatics), and geographical landmarks. In 1523, he produced the Bavariae Descriptio, the very first printed geographical and topometrical map of Bavaria, printed via woodblock in Landshut.The culmination of this exhaustive archival labor was his Latin magnum opus, the Annales Boiorum (Annals of the Bavarians), composed between 1517 and 1521. Spanning seven massive volumes, the Annales provided a panoramic history of Bavaria from its legendary antique origins under the mythical king Tuisco and Celtic-Germanic tribes down to the imperial Diet of Worms in 1521 and the death of Emperor Maximilian I. Aventinus framed Bavarian history within the broader narrative of the Holy Roman Empire and European geopolitics, displaying an astonishing mastery of classical prose modeled on Livy, Tacitus, and Sallust. Recognizing that his Latin masterpiece remained inaccessible to the broader German public, Aventinus spent the years between 1526 and 1533 translating, recasting, and expanding the text into the vernacular, producing the Bayerische Chronik. Written in a powerful, evocative Early New High German (Frühneuhochdeutsch), the Bayerische Chronik transcended mere translation to become a vibrant piece of vernacular literature, rich in cultural detail, social commentary, and political polemic.Aventinus’s historiography was defined by a fiercely critical political and ecclesiastical ideology. Imbued with the irenic humanism of Erasmus and affected by the early developments of the Lutheran Reformation, Aventinus utilized his historical narratives to deliver a scathing critique of medieval papal overreach, monastic corruption, and ecclesiastical encroachment upon secular authority. He argued that the political decline of the German Empire was directly linked to the interference of the Roman Curia, detailing historical instances of papal interdicts, simony, and financial exploitation of the German populace. While Aventinus never formally severed his ties with the Catholic Church nor officially embraced the Lutheran church structure, his trenchant anti-clericalism and published critiques of ecclesiastical privileges aroused the intense hostility of conservative Catholic theologians in Munich and Ingolstadt, notably Johannes Eck (1486–1543).The intensifying confessional polarization of the Holy Roman Empire eventually engulfed Aventinus in severe persecution. In October 1528, while residing in Abensberg, he was abruptly arrested by the local inquisitorial authorities on charges of suspected Lutheran heresy, anti-clerical agitation, and violating fast laws. He was imprisoned in the castle of Abensberg, facing potential execution or life imprisonment. However, his high-ranking academic prestige and the immediate intervention of his former pupil, Prince Ernest of Bavaria, alongside Duke William IV, secured his prompt release after eleven days of confinement. Shaken by his imprisonment and realizing that his intellectual freedom was untenable in Catholic Munich or Ingolstadt, Aventinus sought sanctuary in the Free Imperial City of Regensburg, a municipal republic that was increasingly receptive to humanist reform and intellectual independence.In Regensburg, Aventinus spent the final years of his life in scholarly retreat, continuing his historical, linguistic, and musical investigations. In November 1529, at the age of fifty-two, he married Barbara Kraseis, the daughter of a Regensburg burger, with whom he had two children. Despite ongoing financial hardships and the persistent threat of confiscation of his manuscript collection, Aventinus refined his historical manuscripts until his sudden death on January 9, 1534, at the age of fifty-six. He was solemnly interred in the church of St. Rupert adjacent to the famous Benedictine Monastery of St. Emmeram in Regensburg, where his grave monument remains a testament to his enduring legacy.Because of their radical anti-curial content and the sensitive political environment of the Counter-Reformation in Bavaria, neither the Annales Boiorum nor the Bayerische Chronik could be published unexpurgated during Aventinus’s lifetime. The manuscript of the Annales Boiorum underwent a highly contentious publishing history. The editio princeps was printed posthumously at Ingolstadt in 1554 by the press of Alexander and Samuel Weissenhorn; however, this edition was heavily censored and expurgated by the Catholic humanist Hieronymus Ziegler, who excised hundreds of passages attacking the papacy and medieval clergy. It was not until 1580 that the complete, uncensored Latin text was published in the Protestant printing hub of Basel by Pietro Perna, meticulously edited by the Lutheran theologian and historian David Chytraeus (1530–1600). Similarly, the vernacular Bayerische Chronik was first published in Frankfurt am Main in 1566 by Georg Rab and Han Weigand, quickly becoming a central text for Protestant humanists and early modern political theorists across Central Europe.In the nineteenth century, the intellectual legacy of Aventinus underwent a massive revival, led by the emergence of modern professional historical science in Germany. The Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences (Königliche Bayerische Akademie der Wissenschaften) recognized Aventinus as the founding father of Bavarian national history and undertook the monumental publication of his complete works. Between 1881 and 1908, the Academy published the definitive critical edition, Johannes Aventinus' Sämmtliche Werke, in six monumental volumes under the editorial direction of Sigmund von Riezler, Matthias von Lexer, and Gotthold Oldenbourg. Today, Aventinus is celebrated not only as a master of Renaissance Latinity and German prose, but as an indispensable architect of historical empiricism whose archival rigor, epigraphical precision, and courageous intellectual independence permanently transformed the writing of history in the Western tradition.

publishers.name: Grimm Sigmund
publishers.biography: In partnership with Marx Wirsung, the distinguished municipal physician and humanist scholar Dr. Sigmund Grimm (Sigismundus Grymm) established the celebrated Augsburg printing workshop known in Latin colophons as In officina Sigismundi Grymm Medici & Marci Wirsung.The historical significance of Grimm & Wirsung’s publishing endeavor extends far beyond mere commercial print production. Their press served as a vital engine for early sixteenth-century German intellectual life, fusing medical-scientific erudition with radical humanist satire, classical translations, and early Lutheran theology. Furthermore, the press of Grimm & Wirsung became the primary patron and canvas for Hans Weiditz (famously designated by art historians as the Petrarch Master or Petrarkameister), one of the supreme graphic artists of the German Renaissance.

publishers.name: Wirsung Marx
publishers.biography: Marx Wirsung (also Latinized as Marcus Wirsung or recorded in early modern vernacular orthography as Marx Wyrssung; fl. 1510–1520s) stands as one of the most intellectually compelling, if historically elusive, figures operating at the confluence of vernacular humanism, pharmaceutical science, and high Renaissance typography in the Free Imperial City of Augsburg. Active during the explosive transitional period between the late Northern Renaissance and the onset of the Protestant Reformation, Wirsung occupied a unique socio-cultural niche. By primary trade an apothecary (Apotheker) of considerable repute and civic standing, he successfully crossed the boundary into master publishing and typography. In partnership with the distinguished municipal physician and humanist scholar Dr. Sigmund Grimm (Sigismundus Grymm), Wirsung established the celebrated Augsburg printing workshop known in Latin colophons as In officina Sigismundi Grymm Medici & Marci Wirsung.The historical significance of Marx Wirsung’s publishing endeavor extends far beyond mere commercial print production. His press served as a vital engine for early sixteenth-century German intellectual life, fusing medical-scientific erudition with radical humanist satire, classical translations, and early Lutheran theology. Furthermore, the press of Grimm & Wirsung became the primary patron and canvas for Hans Weiditz (famously designated by art historians as the Petrarch Master or Petrarkameister), one of the supreme graphic artists of the German Renaissance. Through this synergistic alliance of apothecary-publisher, physician-scholar, and master woodcutter, Wirsung helped transform Augsburg into a principal epicenter of visual and typographical innovation within the Holy Roman Empire, leaving an indelible imprint on the history of European print culture.To contextualize Marx Wirsung’s emergence, one must examine the socio-economic and intellectual milieu of Imperial Augsburg during the reign of Emperor Maximilian I. By the early sixteenth century, Augsburg had established itself alongside Nuremberg, Basel, and Strasbourg as a paramount financial, commercial, and typographical metropolis. Situated along the vital trade routes connecting Northern Europe with Northern Italy, the city was dominated by mega-merchant dynasties such as the Fuggers and Welsers, while simultaneously harboring a vibrant community of humanist scholars, artists, and craftsmen.Marx Wirsung’s foundational career was rooted in pharmacy. In the early modern urban structure, the apothecary was not merely a retail merchant of drugs, but a highly skilled practitioner of natural philosophy, botanical taxonomy, and chemical distillation. The pharmaceutical workshop served as a locus of scientific inquiry, closely aligned with medicine, alchemy, and academic humanism. Wirsung’s deep immersion in the apothecary’s art provided him with both the capital required to invest in print technology and a network of learned contacts, most notably medical practitioners seeking to publish professional and vernacular treatises.Wirsung’s family lineage was intimately tied to the intellectual and literary life of Augsburg. Most notably, he was closely related to—and widely considered the father or primary mentor of—Christof Wirsung (c. 1500–1571), who achieved enduring fame as a medical writer and translator. Christof Wirsung produced the definitive sixteenth-century German translation of Fernando de Rojas’s Spanish masterpiece La Celestina (published by the Wirsung press in 1520), as well as monumental pharmaceutical compendia like the General Artzney-Buch. The Wirsung household epitomized the rising urban patriciate-bourgeoisie that bridged practical science, vernacular literature, and typographical enterprise.Around the year 1517, Marx Wirsung formed his historic printing partnership with Dr. Sigmund Grimm, a highly educated physician who had studied at the University of Freiburg and served as a town doctor in Augsburg. The alliance between a physician and an apothecary in a publishing venture was uniquely suited to the intellectual demands of the era. Together, they acquired typographical materials, recruited skilled compositors, and commissioned custom woodcut blocks, setting up an ambitious officina that operated with remarkable vigor between 1517 and 1523.The editorial policy of the Grimm & Wirsung press was characterized by extraordinary range, ideological boldness, and aesthetic rigor. Their catalog was organized around several core thematic pillars:Humanist Polemics and Anti-Clerical Satire: Grimm and Wirsung became the chief publishers for the radical imperial knight and humanist polemicist Ulrich von Hutten. They issued first editions of Hutten’s most explosive Latin and German dialogues, including Phalarismus (1517), Vadiscus, sive Trias Romana (1520), and In Hieronymum Aleandrum et Marinum Caracciolum... satirae (1521). These works violently attacked papal corruption, church taxation, and Roman hegemony, galvanizing nationalist and reformist sentiments across Germany.Vernacular Literature and Translations: In 1520, the press published the landmark work Ain schön wolgestalt Spiel creaturischen Conplexion..., Christof Wirsung’s masterful German adaptation of Rojas’s La Celestina. This release marked a watershed moment in the transmission of Spanish Renaissance drama into the German-speaking world, combining nuanced psychological dialogue with exquisite illustrative art.Early Reformation Pamphlets (Flugschriften): As the Lutheran storm broke across the empire following the Diet of Worms (1521), the Grimm & Wirsung press acted as a crucial distribution channel for the nascent Protestant movement. They printed short treatises, sermons, and open letters by Martin Luther, Andreas Karlstadt, and Johannes Eberlin von Günzburg, alongside anti-Lutheran counter-polemics by Johannes Eck, demonstrating both commercial opportunism and an engagement with contemporary theological debates.Classical Philology and Philosophy: The press produced pristine editions of classical texts, including works by Cicero, Terence, and Prudentius, tailored for school curricula and scholarly humanists.The defining glory of Marx Wirsung’s typographical career lies in his press’s unparalleled visual culture, achieved through an exclusive collaboration with the artist Hans Weiditz. Between 1518 and 1522, Weiditz served as the primary draughtsman for Grimm & Wirsung, producing hundreds of intricate woodcuts that set new standards for German book ornament and narrative illustration.Weiditz’s work for Wirsung was characterized by breathtaking realism, dynamic movement, and acute socio-historical observation. His woodcuts did not merely mirror the text; they provided a running visual commentary on early modern society, depicting peasants, mercenaries, merchants, clergy, and artisans with unsparing detail. Among the most extraordinary projects commissioned during Wirsung’s tenure was the series of woodcuts intended for the German translation of Petrarch’s moral treatise De remediis utriusque fortunae (later published as the Trostspiegel in Glück und Unglück) and Cicero’s De Officiis (*Von den Tugentfachen Tuggenden*).Typographically, the imprints of Grimm & Wirsung are recognized by their elegant balance of heavy German Schwabacher and early Fraktur types alongside crisp Latin Antiqua founts. Wirsung and Grimm invested heavily in monumental architectural title-borders (*Titelbordüren*), heraldic devices, and decorative historiated initials (*Initialen*). The press's title pages frequently featured intricate multi-block woodcuts that functioned as visual manifestos for the texts contained within.Despite their artistic and critical triumphs, the enterprise of Grimm & Wirsung was plagued by severe economic instability. The capital-intensive nature of high-end illustrated book production, combined with over-expansion and the volatile economic landscape caused by the Social and Religious Wars of the 1520s, severely strained the press's financial resources. The death or withdrawal of Marx Wirsung around 1521–1522 deprived the firm of vital management and financial backing.Following Wirsung’s departure, Dr. Sigmund Grimm attempted to maintain the workshop alone, but spiraling debts led to total insolvency. In 1527, Grimm’s property and printing materials were formally confiscated by creditors and sold at auction. The vast stock of woodcut blocks, matrices, and founts was acquired by the prolific Augsburg printer Heinrich Steiner (Heinrich Stayner). Steiner built a vast publishing empire throughout the 1530s and 1540s almost entirely upon the typographical assets and unpublished woodcut collections created under Wirsung and Grimm, including the famous 1532 edition of Petrarch's Trostspiegel.In modern bibliographical historiography, Marx Wirsung has received rigorous re-evaluation. Early nineteenth-century scholars like Georg Wilhelm Zapf and Georg Wolfgang Panzer cataloged his imprints as rare typographical curiosities. However, twentieth-century scholars—including Robert Proctor, Campbell Dodgson, Josef Benzing, and Heinrich Theodor Musper—recognized Wirsung as a pivotal catalyst in Northern Renaissance art and printing. Contemporary book historians identify the Grimm & Wirsung press as a quintessential example of early modern intellectual entrepreneurship, where the worlds of medicine, pharmacy, humanist scholarship, and visual art converged to reshape European print culture.

Although Aventinus had contacts with many fellow humanists and noblemen, his extant correspondence with them is surprisingly small. Among a little more than twenty extant letters written by and addressed to him we find among others the names of Konrad Celtis, Urbanus Rhegius, Beatus Rhenanus, Joachim Vadian, Philipp Melanchthon, Conrad Peutinger, and Willibald Pirckheimer.Aventinus' letters in this volume mostly concern the publication of the life of emperor Henry VI from a codex in the library of the monastery of Saint Emmeram. The first three letters, to the prior of Saint Emmeram, Ambrosius Münzer, to the librarian of the monastery Dionysius Menger and to the priest Ulrich Preu of Pföring, are letters of thanks for their help in the publishing venture. The letter to Leonard von Eck (1480-1550), a powerful figure in the political life of the time and an important councillor to duke William VI of Bavaria, and the two letters by Frederick III the Wise of Saxony to Aventinus are about a project of a chronicle of Saxony and Thuringia the Elector had entrusted to the humanist Georg Spalatin (1484-1545) (cf. Johannes Aventinus, Briefwechsel, in: “Sämmtliche Werke”, S.v. Riezler, ed., München, 1881, I/2, pp. 632-654).This work also testifies of the short lived Sodalitas literaria Angilostadiensis, an association of men of letters and learning from the environment of the University of Ingolstadt. The society benefited of the patronage of Duke Ernst of Bavaria and was presided by Leonard von Eck. It was licensed by the University (its statutes having been approved by the philosophical faculty), and it drew some local talent into the circle of companionship and scholarly activities. Most members, however, returned to other pursuits when the first flush of enthusiasm had subsided. The organisation languished for a while, then dissolved without formalities. But it was an interesting group while it lasted, and it provided stimulating companions for Aventinus. His first close acquaintance with Leonard von Eck came at this time. Another member, the Greek and Hebrew scholar Matthias Kretz, was destined to play an important part as opponent of Luther. Melchior Seuter was the author of several books on the Turkish wars, which Aventinus read with profit. Urbanus Rhegius lectured on poetry and rhetoric at the University before he was drawn to the side of the reformers and became a preacher in North Germany. A distinguished member was Georg Spies, or Cuspinus, a well-known jurist. There must have been good talk and lively debates, but in Aventinus' eyes the group's essential function was not discussion but publication. However, only the present edition of a medieval life of Emperor Henry IV was published under the auspices of the Sodalitas (cf. G. Strauss, Historian in an Age of Crisis. The Life and Work of Johannes Aventinus, Cambridge, MA, 1963, pp. 67-68).The present volume opens with the already mentioned biography (attributed to Erlung von Würzburg) of emperor Henry IV (1050-1106), who was chosen German King at Tribur in 1053, crowned at Aix-la-Chapelle in 1054, and appointed duke of Bavaria in 1055, and inherited after his father's death the kingdoms of Germany, Italy and Burgundy. Because of his early age these territories were governed in his name by his mother Agnes. In 1069 Henry took the reins of government into his own hands. No historical incident had more impressed the imagination of the western world than his abasement at Canossa, which represented the king as standing in the courtyard of the castle for three days in the snow, clad as a penitent, and entreating to be admitted to the presence of pope Gregory VII. It was, however, a move of policy to weaken the pope's position at the cost of a personal humiliation to himself. Henry was seen as a friend of the lower orders, was capable of generosity and gratitude, and showed considerable military skill. Unfortunate in the time in which he lived, and in the troubles with which he had to contend, he holds an honourable position in history as a monarch who resisted the excessive pretensions both of the papacy and of the ambitious feudal lords of Germany. Henry's biography is followed by nine of his letters. The volume closes with some Latin poems by the members of the Ingolstadt Sodalitas, i.e. Georg Spies, Johannes Kneissel, Urbanus Rhegius, Otto von Pack, Hieronymus Anfang, Melchior Soiter, Matthias Kretz, Magnus Haldenberger, David Rotmund, Georg Bossus, Georg Schack, and Augustinus Merbolt. Torgau, October 4, 1514 (l. e3v)Eck, Leonhard von (l. f1v) Johannes Aventinus was the son of an innkeeper in Abensberg, Lower Bavaria. He attended the local school of the Carmelite monastery and matriculated at the University of Ingolstadt in 1495. In 1496 he received the lower orders and pursued his humanistic studies in Vienna, Cracow and Paris. In 1517 he was appointed tutor to the dukes Louis and Ernest of Bavaria and was named historiographer to the dukes of Bavaria. His Annales Boiorum were severely anticlerical and thus unsuited for publication under the auspices of the Catholic dukes, and the Church set them on the Index. Not until 1554 was an expurgated version of the Annales published at Ingolstadt. Later in his life Aventinus continued to work on a chronicle of all Germany, of which, however, only the first book and an index were completed. He spent the rest of his life in the free imperial city of Regensburg, which remained aloof when the dukes of Bavaria began to repress all Lutheran tendencies. All of Aventinus' works were put on the Venetian Index in 1554 (cf. C. März, op. cit., cols. 72-77).

authors.name: Borghesi Diomede
authors.biography: Diomede Borghesi was born in Siena around 1540. He was a pupil of Ludovico Meneghini, professor at the local “Studio”. At an early age he was banned from the city for unknown reasons and confined for two years to Portoferraio on the island of Elba. He managed to escape to Mantua, where he gained the protection of Cardinal Federico Gonzaga.After the latter's death in 1564, he moved to Padua, and completed there his literary apprenticeship under Sperone Speroni, Francesco Piccolomini and Scipione Gonzaga. Although Borghesi had established his home in Padua, he nevertheless did not cease to roam through Italy. Between 1564 and 1587 he visited Venice, Bergamo, Verona, Rome, Viterbo, Perugia, Siena, Florence, Bologna, Ferrara, Reggio Emilia, Correggio, and Turin, where he became particularly known as a poet, composing various occasional poems for Carlo Emanuele of Savoy. Between 1566 and 1571 he published five volumes of Rime.In 1588 Borghesi entered the service of Ferdinando de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, who established a chair of ‘lingua Toscana‘, the very first in any Italian university. This chair was especially created for Borghesi to teach Tuscan to the many German and North Italian students present in Siena at that time (cf. A. Cappagli, Diomede Borghesi e Celso Cittadini lettori di toscana favella, in: “Tra Rinascimento e strutture attuali. Atti del primo convegno della Società Internazionale di Linguistica e Filologia Italiana, Siena, 28-31 marzo 1989”, Torino, 1991, I, pp. 23-35; and P. Rossi, La prima cattedra di lingua toscana dai ruoli allo studio senese, 1588-1743, Torino, 1910, passim).“His lecture notes, which are now in the Siena library and his tenure of the chair have been described by Rossi in his paper on the Tuscan language chair [see supra]. There are also two inaugural lectures by him delivered in connection with his academic duties [published respectively in 1589 and 1590], to which may be added an Oratione intorno agli onori della poesia e della eloquenza, printed in Siena in 1596. Most of Borghesi's extant philological works were written by him in epistolary form, and appear to have enjoyed some degree of popularity [...] Borghesi published some Lettere famigliari, the first [and only] volume bears the Padua imprint and the date 1578. In 1868 an edition of Borghesi's [unpublished] correspondence, edited by G. Campori, saw the light in Bologna from the press of G. Romagnoli” (R. Weiss, The Sienese Philologists of the Cinquecento. A Bibliographical Introduction, in: “Italian Studies” 3, 1946, pp. 44-45). From then on until his death on January 28, 1598, he lived in Siena, completely devoting himself to the study of grammar and language.

publishers.name: Pasquati Lorenzo
publishers.biography: Lorenzo Pasquati (active in Padua between circa 1562 and 1521; Latinized as Laurentius Pasquatus) stands as one of the pivotal figures in late Renaissance and early Baroque typography in Northern Italy. Operating primarily within the intellectual orbit of the University of Padua (the historic Bo), Pasquati elevated the academic press from a local municipal utility to an international engine of scientific, medical, and humanist scholarship. During a transformative era marked by the decline of purely scholastic Aristotelianism and the birth of experimental science, Pasquati’s workshop served as the physical conduit through which seminal thinkers—most famously Galileo Galilei, Girolamo Fabrici d'Acquapendente (Hieronymus Fabricius ab Aquapendente), Ercole Sassonia (Hercules Saxonia), and Lorenzo Pignoria—disseminated their discoveries across the Republic of Venice and the broader European Respublica Literaria. His output bridges the refined typographic elegance of late sixteenth-century Venetian printing with the rigorous technical demands of early seventeenth-century scientific illustration, placing his press at the very epicenter of early modern natural philosophy and academic culture.While specific details regarding Pasquati’s exact birth date and early childhood remain unrecorded in municipal parish registers, his surname and early typographical marks connect him to the Venetian hinterland and the thriving network of artisan printers operating across the Veneto. Appearing in Paduan archival records by the early 1560s, Pasquati established his workshop at a critical juncture when the University of Padua was solidifying its status as Western Europe’s premier center for medical, anatomical, and mathematical studies. Unlike major Venetian publishing houses that focused on high-volume commercial production, literary vernacular works, and devotional texts for pan-European book fairs, Pasquati strategically aligned his press with the institutional and intellectual needs of Padua's two primary academic corporations: the Universitas Iuristarum (Jurists) and the Universitas Artistarum (Artists, which encompassed students and professors of philosophy, medicine, astronomy, and mathematics). Through rigorous training in Latin, Greek, and vernacular composition, as well as mastering the complex layout of academic commentaries and intricate woodcut and copperplate matrices, Pasquati secured a near-monopoly over official university printing, academic orations, disputation broadsides, and faculty treatises in Padua for nearly six decades.Pasquati’s printing history is inextricably linked to some of the most influential scientific and humanistic publications of the late Renaissance. Most prominent among these is his intimate collaboration with Galileo Galilei during Galileo’s tenure as Professor of Mathematics at Padua. In 1606, Pasquati printed Galileo’s rare and foundational treatise, Le Operazioni del Compasso Geometrico e Militare. Printed in a limited run of approximately sixty copies directly inside Galileo’s private residence in Padua to protect the intellectual property of the instrument and control its distribution, Pasquati managed the complex typographical setting of mathematical diagrams, geometrical scale layouts, and operational tables, demonstrating exceptional technical flexibility. Equally monumental was Pasquati’s collaboration with the renowned anatomist Girolamo Fabrici d'Acquapendente. Between 1600 and 1604, Pasquati produced Fabrici’s pioneering folio treatises on embryology, comparative anatomy, and physiology, including De visione, voce, auditu (1600), De locutione et eius instrumentis (1601), De venarum ostiolis (1603), and De formato foetu (1604). These anatomical works required an unprecedented level of typographical sophistication, integrating elaborate full-page copperplate engravings of anatomical dissections alongside dense Latin commentary. Pasquati's press was also responsible for major medical texts by Ercole Sassonia (De phoenigmis, 1593; Pantheum medicinae, 1603) and Roderigo de Castro, as well as humanistic and antiquarian masterworks such as Lorenzo Pignoria’s Characteres Aegyptii (1608), an early landmark in Egyptology and emblem studies. His shop became a vibrant intellectual hub where professors, foreign students from the German and English nationes, and visiting scholars congregated to review proofs, discuss natural philosophy, and engage in academic debate.Typographically, Pasquati’s production reflects the transition from Renaissance classical design to early Baroque functionalism. His imprints, frequently bearing colophons such as In Padova, per Lorenzo Pasquati or Padova, Appresso Lorenzo Pasquati, are characterized by crisp Roman types for main texts, refined Italic fonts for dedications and annotations, and distinctive woodcut printer's devices—often depicting allegorical figures of Justice, Prudence, or civic emblems of Padua. Recognizing the capital-intensive nature of publishing lavishly illustrated scientific folios, Pasquati established strong financial and distribution partnerships with prominent Venetian booksellers and publishers, most notably Francesco Bolzetta. While Pasquati provided the typographic craftsmanship and supervised presswork in Padua, Bolzetta and Venetian merchant networks funded paper supplies and arranged distribution across Italy, Germany, France, and England. This collaborative framework allowed Pasquati’s Paduan imprints to bypass local distribution limits and enter the international scientific canon, reaching figures such as William Harvey, Johannes Kepler, and Francis Bacon.Pasquati’s press was frequently situated at the heart of intense academic and intellectual controversies. The printing of Galileo’s Compasso in 1606 immediately ignited the famous plagiarism dispute involving the Milanese nobleman Baldassarre Capra and his tutor Simon Mayr. Capra published a Latin translation claiming ownership of the invention, prompting Galileo to initiate legal proceedings before the Venetian authorities. Pasquati’s testimony and press records served as vital forensic evidence in proving Galileo’s priority and securing Capra’s expulsion from the university. Beyond legal disputes, Pasquati’s precise rendering of anatomical plates and mathematical treatises established new standards for scientific printing, proving that scholarly accuracy depended as much on typographical rigour as on empirical observation. By the time of his passing around 1621, after six decades of continuous activity, Lorenzo Pasquati had established a typographical dynasty and laid the technical groundwork for Paduan scientific publishing throughout the seventeenth century, cementing his reputation as an indispensable architect of early modern intellectual history.

With the printer's device on the title-page, ornamental woodcut initials. 18th century vellum over boards, red label with gilt title on spine, marbled endpapers, contemporary marginal annotations, entry of ownership by count Leonardo Trissino (1780-1841) dated 1837 (cf. D. Bortolan, Leonardo Trissino, celebre avventuriero, in: “Nuovo Archivio Veneto”, 1892, pp. 5-46). First edition, edited by Francesco Salce and dedicated by the author to Bianca Cappello (Padua, August 11, 1578), first lover and then from 1579 wife of Ferdinando de' Medici, of Diomede Borghesi's Lettere famigliari, so called to distinguish them from the Lettere discorsive, which he published in three parts (La prima [-II, -III] parte delle lettere, Padua, Lorenzo Pasquati, 1584; Venice, Francesco de' Franceschi, 1584; Siena, Luca Bonetti, 1603) and in which he exposed his grammatical theories on the Italian language.The collection contains 158 letters, arranged more or less in chronological order. “Un certain nombre est daté, de 1564 à 1578; leur classement est chronologique à l'exception de la première lettre du livre, du 1er juillet 1578, la plus récente, et des dernières qui marquent un retour en arrière. La plupart des lettres sont de compliment et assez brèves. Parmi les exceptions, on relèvera la première lettre du livre addressée à Scipion Gonzague prince d'Empire pour souligner l'estime attachée ‘oggidì' à ‘il parlar nobilmente et lo scriver con vaghezza et regolatamente' en général, et en particulier à la forme épistolaire, puis une lettre qui traite de la supériorité de la nature sur l'art c'est-à-dire de la poèsie sur les sciences (pp. 26-39) et une longue lettre de consolation (pp. 51-58). Le commerce littérarire tient aussi une certaine place dans ce recueil. Les destinataires principaux, parmi lesquels Bianca Capello, reçoivent entre 5 et 6 lettres” (J. Basso, Le genre épistolaire en langue italienne (1538-1662). Répertoire chronologique et analytique, Rome-Nancy, 1990, I, p. 279).“La reputazione del Borghesi assai più che alle Rime e alle Orazioni si raccomanda alle Lettere familiari e discorsive. Infatti mentre queste vanno lodate dei buoni precetti che porgono su vocaboli e frasi e su la più retta intelligenza della lingua nostra, quelle si pregiano di eleganza non artificiosa né studiata. Esse possono offrirsi ad esempio ai giovani e a chi voglia perfezionarsi in tal sorta di componimenti così necessaria ad ogni condizione di persone, perché non si discostano dall'uso moderno se non in quanto la purezza della lingua che negli scrittori moderni così raramente s'incontra scompagnata dall'artifizio e dalla fatica, appare nel Borghesi affatto naturale e spontanea” (Diomede Borghesi, Lettere, G. (p. 130) Diomede Borghesi was born in Siena around 1540. He was a pupil of Ludovico Meneghini, professor at the local “Studio”. At an early age he was banned from the city for unknown reasons and confined for two years to Portoferraio on the island of Elba. He managed to escape to Mantua, where he gained the protection of Cardinal Federico Gonzaga.After the latter's death in 1564, he moved to Padua, and completed there his literary apprenticeship under Sperone Speroni, Francesco Piccolomini and Scipione Gonzaga. Although Borghesi had established his home in Padua, he nevertheless did not cease to roam through Italy. Between 1564 and 1587 he visited Venice, Bergamo, Verona, Rome, Viterbo, Perugia, Siena, Florence, Bologna, Ferrara, Reggio Emilia, Correggio, and Turin, where he became particularly known as a poet, composing various occasional poems for Carlo Emanuele of Savoy. Between 1566 and 1571 he published five volumes of Rime.In 1588 Borghesi entered the service of Ferdinando de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, who established a chair of ‘lingua Toscana‘, the very first in any Italian university. This chair was especially created for Borghesi to teach Tuscan to the many German and North Italian students present in Siena at that time (cf. A. Cappagli, Diomede Borghesi e Celso Cittadini lettori di toscana favella, in: “Tra Rinascimento e strutture attuali. Atti del primo convegno della Società Internazionale di Linguistica e Filologia Italiana, Siena, 28-31 marzo 1989”, Torino, 1991, I, pp. 23-35; and P. Rossi, La prima cattedra di lingua toscana dai ruoli allo studio senese, 1588-1743, Torino, 1910, passim).“His lecture notes, which are now in the Siena library and his tenure of the chair have been described by Rossi in his paper on the Tuscan language chair [see supra]. There are also two inaugural lectures by him delivered in connection with his academic duties [published respectively in 1589 and 1590], to which may be added an Oratione intorno agli onori della poesia e della eloquenza, printed in Siena in 1596. Most of Borghesi's extant philological works were written by him in epistolary form, and appear to have enjoyed some degree of popularity [...] Borghesi published some Lettere famigliari, the first [and only] volume bears the Padua imprint and the date 1578. In 1868 an edition of Borghesi's [unpublished] correspondence, edited by G. Campori, saw the light in Bologna from the press of G. Romagnoli” (R. Weiss, The Sienese Philologists of the Cinquecento. A Bibliographical Introduction, in: “Italian Studies” 3, 1946, pp. 44-45).From then on until his death on January 28, 1598, he lived in Siena, completely devoting himself to the study of grammar and language (cf. Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, Rome, 1970, XII, pp. 643-646; and S. Valente, Diomede Borghesi, lirico e grammatico del secolo XVI, Bari, 1905, passim).

title: Lettere amorose di madonna Celia gentildonna romana, scritte al suo amante

authors.name: Celia Romana
authors.biography: Celia Romana (fl. second half of the sixteenth century) represents one of the most compelling and enigmatic figures within the landscape of Italian High Renaissance lyric poetry, situated at the vibrant intersection of mid-sixteenth-century Petrarchism, aristocratic female authorship, and the material history of early modern print culture. Writing during the pivotal decades of the Counter-Reformation and the consolidation of Bemban poetic orthodoxy, the author published under the intriguing designation of "M. Celia, gentildonna romana" (Madonna or Madama Celia, Roman noblewoman). Her sole surviving literary monument—a slender yet intensely expressive collection entitled Amorose rime di M. Celia, gentildonna romana, issued from the Emilian presses of Piacenza in 1562—occupies a singular place in the canon of petrarchismo al femminile. Alongside illustrious female contemporaries such as Vittoria Colonna (1492–1547), Veronica Gambara (1485–1550), Gaspara Stampa (1523–1554), Laura Terracina (1506–c. 1575), Tullia d'Aragona (c. 1510–1556), Chiara Matraini (1515–1604), and Laura Battiferri (1523–1589), Celia Romana contributed significantly to the democratization and diversification of early modern vernacular lyricism. However, unlike the spiritualized Neoplatonism of Colonna or the courtly panegyrics of Battiferri, Celia's verse is characterized by an unvarnished, visceral intensity, charting the psychological disintegration and emotional agony of an unrequited, agonizing passion with unmatched dramatic urgency.The biographical identity of Celia Romana has constituted one of the most enduring historical and philological puzzles in Renaissance literary scholarship. Operating in mid-sixteenth-century Rome—a city undergoing profound sociopolitical and religious transformations under the pontificates of Julius III (Giulio III Ciocchi del Monte, r. 1550–1555), Paul IV (Gian Pietro Carafa, r. 1555–1559), and Pius IV (Giovanni Angelo Medici, r. 1559–1565)—the poet moved within an environment where aristocratic female intellectual expression was tightly policed by patrician family structures and the tightening moral strictures of the Tridentine Church. Philologists and bibliophiles have long debated whether "Celia" was a baptismal name, a family surname (such as the Roman Debbia or Celli lineages), or an elaborate poetic pseudonym. Nineteenth-century archival hypotheses occasionally suggested that Celia might have been a high-ranking cortigiana onesta (an educated courtesan) operating within the elevated humanistic salons and papal diplomatic circles of Rome, drawing structural comparisons to Tullia d'Aragona or Veronica Franco. Conversely, competing theories hold that she was an authentic Roman patrician living in enforced social seclusion or religious retreat, whose highly personal manuscript notebook (scartafaccio) was surreptitiously obtained and transmitted to the printing press without her explicit public sanction. While early twentieth-century skepticism occasionally pondered whether the collection was an exercise in male prosopopoeia—a heteronym created by a male humanist constructing a female voice—modern scholarship, led by Italianists such as Carlo Dionisotti, Francine Daenens, Tatiana Crivelli, and Virginia Cox, overwhelmingly affirms the authenticity of her distinct female agency and subjective perspective.Literarily and stylistically, the Amorose rime consists of forty-five sonnets and several madrigals that together form an exceptionally tight, narrative-driven lyric sequence. Philological analysis demonstrates that Celia Romana operated with complete technical mastery over the Italian vernacular as codified by Pietro Bembo in his seminal Prose della vulgar lingua (1525). She adopted the traditional hendecasyllabic meter and Petrarchan rhyme schemes (primarily ABBA ABBA CDE CDE or CDC DCD), yet radically subverted the conventional emotional dynamics of the Petrarchan tradition. Where Petrarca and his male emulators constructed an idealized, distant female object of desire (the inaccessible Laura) viewed through a reflective, Neoplatonic lens, Celia inverted the gaze: she positioned herself as the agonized female subject, addressing a distant, cruel, or unfaithful male lover. Her poetry eschews the transcendent, sublime resolution typical of mainstream Renaissance Neoplatonism, refusing to convert earthly heartbreak into divine contemplation. Instead, her verses delve into the raw psychological realities of jealousy, betrayal, temporal decay, and existential despair. Intertextually, her work displays deep thematic affinities with the elegiac tradition of Catullus and Ovid, as well as the impassioned, immediate lyric voice of Gaspara Stampa, whose Rime had been posthumously printed in Venice in 1554. Celia's sonnets frequently utilize dramatic apostrophe, urgent interrogatives, and stark antitheses to articulate the claustrophobic confinement of a woman bound by societal decorum while consumed by an unquenchable internal fire.The material and printing history of Celia's work provides crucial insights into the editorial transmission of sixteenth-century vernacular poetry outside major publishing capitals. The princeps edition was issued in 1562 in Piacenza with the title Amorose rime di M. Celia, gentildonna romana. The choice of Piacenza—a key urban center within the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza under the rule of Ottavio Farnese—as the place of publication highlights the decentralized nature of Emilian print culture during the 1560s. Printing operations in Piacenza, represented by typographers such as Seth Viotti, Francesco Conti, and Giovanni Bazachi, frequently catered to elite manuscript circulation and regional humanistic academies, offering a discreet alternative to the massive commercial printhouses of Venice (such as those of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari or Vincenzo Valgrisi). The publication of Celia's work reflects a broader mid-century publisher strategy: capitalizing on the immense public appetite for female-authored lyric collections, which were viewed as modern marvels of vernacular eloquence. However, unlike the widely reprinted anthologies of Vittoria Colonna or Laura Terracina, the print run of Celia's Amorose rime was exceptionally modest. The work was never granted a contemporary second edition, rendering original copies extraordinarily rare in European research libraries. Today, surviving exemplars are preserved in elite institutions, including the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze, and the British Library.The critical reception and historiographical legacy of Celia Romana underwent a dramatic evolution across four centuries. Following its initial appearance in 1562, the collection fell into relative obscurity during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, overshadowed by the dominant counter-reformation religious poetry and the baroque extravagances of the Seicento. The literary re-emergence of Celia Romana began in the late nineteenth century, driven by the rise of scientific bibliography and historical philology in unified Italy. In 1888, the Venetian scholar Giuseppe Giuriati published a pioneering critical study and re-edition of her poetry, bringing her back to the attention of Renaissance specialists. This was followed in 1895 by Emilio Teza's rigorous textual analysis presented to the Reale Accademia dei Lincei. The decisive turning point in her critical fortunes arrived in 1945, when the eminent philosopher and literary critic Benedetto Croce dedicated an influential essay to her in his Poeti e scrittori del Pieno e Tardo Rinascimento. Croce praised Celia's verse for its psychological authenticity, emotional directness, and freedom from artificial rhetorical ornamentation, establishing her as one of the most original poetic voices of the Italian Cinquecento. In contemporary scholarship, Celia Romana is recognized as a vital component of the early modern female canon. Feminist literary historians and bibliographers, including Louise George Clubb, Laura Benedetti, Brian Richardson, and Abigail Brundin, continue to examine her work as a primary exemplar of female self-fashioning, subversion of patriarchal literary codes, and the complex mechanics of manuscript-to-print transmission in Renaissance Italy.

publishers.name: Cornetti Giacomo
publishers.biography: Giacomo Cornetti (active in Rome between 1584 and 1593) is bibliographically elusive, printer-publishers (librari e stampatori) operating in the papal capital during the twilight of the late Italian Renaissance. Emerging at the height of the Counter-Reformation—a period shaped by the rigorous ecclesiastical decrees of the Council of Trent, the administrative transformations of Pope Sixtus V (Felice Peretti), and the intellectual consolidation under Clement VIII (Ippolito Aldobrandini)—Cornetti occupied a crucial crossroads where humanistic erudition, political theory, visual art, and commercial print culture converged. Far from being a mere mechanical artisan who pressed ink to paper, Cornetti operated as a sophisticated publishing entrepreneur. He actively scouted, financed, and circulated works that reshaped European intellectual history, most notably issuing the early landmark editions of Giovanni Botero’s political treatises and the historic editio princeps of Cesare Ripa’s allegorical manual, the Iconologia.The precise early life, geographical origins, and typographical apprenticeship of Giacomo Cornetti remain largely unrecorded in surviving civil registers, a common fate for mid-level print entrepreneurs of the late sixteenth century. However, typographical analysis of his presswork suggests strong material connections to the dominant printing networks of Northern Italy, particularly Venice, Ferrara, and Bologna. By the mid-1580s, Cornetti had established his publishing quarters in the heart of Rome’s bustling commercial and literary district, concentrated around the Parione quarter, Campo de' Fiori, and the Via Pellegrino. This neighborhood served as the vibrant epicenter of the Roman book trade, where bookshops double-functioned as intellectual salons, scriptoria, and political gathering spots. Establishing his shop under his own mark—often characterized by allegorical figures, cornucopiae, or religious motifs—Cornetti successfully integrated himself into the tight-knit network of Roman librari, competing and collaborating with prominent contemporaries such as Vincenzo Accolti, Guglielmo Facciotti, Bartolomeo Bonfadino, Giovanni Martinelli, and the workshop of the late Giovanni Gigliotti.The apex of Giacomo Cornetti’s career occurred between 1588 and 1593, a golden decade during which he published several foundational texts of early modern European thought. In 1588, Cornetti brought forth Giovanni Botero’s pioneering urbanological and demographic study, Delle cause della grandezza e magnificenza delle città. Recognizing the immense intellectual appetite for Botero’s political analysis, Cornetti followed this success in 1589 by publishing the definitive Roman edition of Botero’s masterpiece, Della ragion di Stato libri dieci. This work, designed to counter Machiavellian political pragmatism with a Christian doctrine of governance, became an instantaneous international bestseller, undergoing dozens of reprintings across Europe and defining Tacitist political debate for over a century. Cornetti’s press was also instrumental in disseminating contemporary epic and lyric poetry, maintaining close ties with the literary circles surrounding Torquato Tasso. In 1591, Cornetti printed the fourth part of Tasso’s Rime alongside prose dialogues such as Il Cataneo, overo de gli idoli, cementing his reputation as a favored publisher for high-status literary figures seeking prestigious Roman imprints.Equally monumental was Cornetti’s role in the birth of early modern visual theory. In 1593, working in association with the estate of Giovanni Gigliotti, Cornetti published the unillustrated editio princeps of Cesare Ripa’s Iconologia overo Descrittione dell'Imagini universali cavate dall'antichità et da altri luoghi. Ripa, a nobleman from Perugia and household steward (scalco) to Cardinal Antonio Maria Salviati, compiled an exhaustive alphabetical dictionary of personifications, virtues, vices, passions, and celestial concepts drawn from classical literature, Egyptian hieroglyphics, and Renaissance numismatics. Cornetti’s elegant small-quarto edition provided the foundational textual blueprint that would govern European visual arts, emblem design, theatrical staging, and Baroque painting throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, directly inspiring artists from Bernini and Pietro da Cortona to Vermeer and Nicolas Poussin.From a material and bibliographical perspective, the imprints issuing from the press of Giacomo Cornetti demonstrate a high degree of typographical craftsmanship tailored to the strict regulatory demands of Counter-Reformation Rome. His books were characterized by well-cut Roman (tondo) and Italic (corsivo) typefaces—often sourced from French and Venetian punchcutters such as Robert Granjon—balanced with ornate woodcut initials (capilettera historiati), architectural title-page borders, and expressive tailpieces. Operating in close proximity to the Curia, Cornetti expertly navigated the complex censorship apparatus enforced by the Master of the Sacred Palace (Magister Sacri Palatii) and the Congregation of the Index. Every major publication issued from his shop carried the explicit legal protection of papal privileges (cum gratia et privilegio SS. D. N.) alongside formal ecclesiastical permissions, ensuring both commercial monopoly within the Papal States and protection against pirated editions in competing print centers like Venice and Florence.Following 1593, Giacomo Cornetti’s name disappears from Roman imprint colophons, indicating either his death, retirement, or the sale of his typographical equipment to other Roman publishing houses. Despite his brief active period of less than a decade, his historical and bibliographical legacy is monumental. Modern book historians and scholars of political thought, including Luigi Firpo, Francesco Barberi, Fernande Ascarelli, and Dennis E. Rhodes, have highlighted Cornetti as a model of the high-end Counter-Reformation publisher who bridged the gap between elite ecclesiastical patronage and commercial print culture.

academic_description: 8vo. 76 leaves. A-I8, K4. With the printer's device on the title-page. Printed in italic. Eighteenth-century vellum over boards, lettering piece on spine, marbled edges. Ownership entries on the title page including "Mario de Candia", possibly the great Sardinian tenor with the same name (1810-1883).Fifth edition of this collection of sixty-eight fictitious love letters signed by Madonna Celia under her name or the pseudonym of Zima. First published in Venice by Antonio degli Antonii for Francesco Rampazzetto in 1562, it was reprinted 10 times until 1628.Towards the end of the century the book was put in the Index as all the works related to profane love, and therefore could be printed only donec expurgetur. “Lo stesso [Fabrizio] Zanetti ripubblicò nel 1600 le Lettere amorose di Madonna Celia Romana, con numerose variazioni rispetto alla prima edizione del 1562: veniva soppressa la dedica dell' ‘Amante alla Signora Lisa', sostituita con una lettera dedicatoria firmata dallo stesso Zanetti a Ottavio Sfoglio, ‘gentiluomo trevigiano'. In un avviso ai lettori, lo stampatore giustificava la sua operazione con il fatto che la raccolta da molti anni non aveva avuto riedizioni, eccetto alcune ‘mal corrette'. Anche in questo caso numerosi erano gli interventi sul testo: in modo particolare l'espurgatore eliminava tutti i termini religiosi usati per esprimere la passione amorosa […]” (L. Braida, Libri di lettere. Le raccolte epistolari del Cinquecento tra inquietudini religiose e “buon volgare”, Bari, 2009, pp. 284-285).The letters are all addressed by Celia to her anonymous lover, who is also the editor of the collection. In the dedication to Signora Lisa, he says that from the thousand letters he had received in the fifteen-year-long love affair with Celia, he had decided to select some of them in order to warn all men and all women against the dangers of love, and to demonstrate the intellectual and human qualities of Celia which, despite she had not received a proper education, leaked clearly even from her hasty letters. Most of the letters are dated. The earliest date is February 2, 1549; the latest December 30, 1560.“As the sixteenth century progressed, early modern writers continue to capitalize on the converging trends of epistolary literature and widespread interest in describing the female experience, turning increasingly to manuals and repertories for guidance. On the one hand, popular epistolary narratives such as the Lettere amorose of Madonna Celia and those of Girolamo Parabosco began to codify representations of the woman writer as an epistolary character motivated by passion and lovesickness. Models for such fictionalized and generalized female narrators, who fell from grace as they abandoned the feminine ideals of chastity and silence to follow their hearts, abounded” (M.K. Ray, Writing Gender in Women's Letter Collections of the Italian Renaissance, Toronto, 2009, p. 123).“The genre, and the pseudonymous publication, would lead us to suspect that the author was a fictional creation, though the fact that a sonnet by a Celia Romana appears in a verse collection of the period (Tempio, 1568, l. 31v) leaves open the possibility that she may have existed” (V. Cox, Women's Writing in Italy 1400-1650, Baltimore, MD, 2008, p. 317, no. 5).
