related_names.name: Caldara Antonio
related_names.biography: Antonio Caldara (c. 1670 – December 28, 1736) stands as one of the most prolific, versatile, and historically influential composers of the European High Baroque. Positioned at the monumental crossroads where the lush, melodic expressivity of the late Venetian and Roman schools coalesced with the rigorous, august contrapuntal architecture of the Habsburg Imperial Court in Vienna, Caldara embodied the consummate early eighteenth-century maestro di cappella. Over a career spanning nearly five decades, his creative output—encompassing more than eighty operas, forty-three oratorios, one hundred and fifty masses, and hundreds of cantatas, motets, and instrumental works—served not only as a pinnacle of late Baroque synthesis but also as a primary musical instrument of counter-reformation theology and Habsburg imperial ideology. His structural mastery of the stile antico and stile moderno forged an indelible link between the late seventeenth-century Venetian polyphonic tradition and the emergent Classical style cultivated by next-generation masters such as Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.Born in Venice around 1670, Caldara was nurtured within the dense musical ecosystem of the Venetian Republic, a city whose ecclesiastical and civic institutions functioned as dynamic laboratories for European art music. He was the son of Giuseppe Caldara, a professional violinist who provided his initial instruction in the rudiments of string playing and solfège. Recognizing the young Antonio's exceptional talent, his family secured his admittance as a choirboy at the iconic Basilica di San Marco, the institution long renowned for its polychoral tradition established by Willaert, Gabrieli, and Monteverdi. Under the tutelage of the venerable maestro di cappella Giovanni Legrenzi, Caldara received an uncompromising grounding in counterpoint, liturgical composition, and organ performance. Concurrently, he developed an extraordinary virtuosity on the violoncello, studying under the cellist-composer Domenico Gabrielli. Caldara's dual mastery of vocal polyphony and the low string continuum proved foundational: the cello's expressive bass lines and counter-melodic possibilities would permanently inform the rich linear counter-textures of his mature vocal and instrumental scores. By the late 1680s, Caldara was active in Venetian musical life as both a sought-after instrumentalist and an emerging composer, debuting his first opera, L'Argene, in 1689, followed by instrumental sonatas that circulated among Venetian noble salons.The turn of the eighteenth century marked Caldara's transition from the Venetian orbit to major courtly appointments across Western Europe. In 1699, he was appointed maestro di cappella di camera to Ferdinando Carlo Gonzaga, the last Duke of Mantua. This tenure, which lasted until 1707, allowed Caldara to refine his dramatic style, composing several operas and sacred works for the Gonzaga court. However, the political turmoil of the War of the Spanish Succession and the subsequent downfall of the Mantuan duchy forced Caldara into a nomadic phase that ultimately transformed his international standing. In 1708, he traveled to Barcelona, where he entered the service of Archduke Charles of Austria (the Habsburg pretender to the Spanish throne, later Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI). For the archducal court in Spain, Caldara composed L'Atenaide (1708), widely recognized as the first Italian opera seria performed on the Iberian Peninsula. This initial encounter with the future Emperor Charles VI established a crucial patronal bond that would define the final, most glorious phase of Caldara's career.Before his eventual move to the imperial capital, Caldara spent seven highly formative years in Rome (1709–1716) as maestro di cappella to Prince Francesco Maria Ruspoli, one of the most magnificent patrons of the High Baroque. Residing at the Palazzo Bonelli, Caldara worked alongside the preeminent figures of the era, including Arcangelo Corelli, Alessandro Scarlatti, and the young Georg Friedrich Händel. Free from the immediate demands of public opera production—owing to papal bans on theatrical spectacles—Caldara turned his creative energies toward the chamber cantata and the sacred oratorio. Under Ruspoli's patronage, he produced over two hundred solo cantatas and a series of dramatic oratorios, including La castità al cimento (1705) and Santa Francesca Romana (1710). In these Roman works, Caldara synthesized Corellian instrumental texture with an expansive, emotionally subtle vocal line, perfecting the da capo aria form and developing an intricate approach to obbligato instrumental accompaniment that raised the cello, oboe, and trumpet to concertante partners with the human voice.The decisive summit of Caldara's career arrived in 1716, when Emperor Charles VI summoned him to Vienna to assume the exalted position of Imperial Vice-Kapellmeister (Kaiserlicher Vize-Kapellmeister) at the Habsburg court. Working alongside the senior Imperial Kapellmeister Johann Joseph Fux, Caldara was tasked with managing the vast musical apparatus of the Holy Roman Empire. While Fux focused primarily on imperial administrative duties and grand liturgical contrapuntal works, Caldara became the imperial court's primary dramatic and chamber composer. The collaboration between Caldara and the imperial court poets Apostolo Zeno and, subsequently, Pietro Metastasio gave birth to the golden age of Viennese opera seria and sacred sepolcro oratorios. Caldara set Metastasio’s earliest canonical libretti, including La clemenza di Tito, Demetrio, Olimpiade, and Achille in Sciro, creating a musical-dramatic aesthetic characterized by noble restraint, structural clarity, and profound emotional resonance tailored specifically to glorify the Habsburg dynasty and its divine mandate.From a musicological and typographical perspective, Caldara's Viennese tenure represents an astonishing era of centralized manuscript culture and selected print circulation. While his early instrumental chamber works—such as the Suonate da camera a tre, Op. 1 (1693) and Op. 2 (1699)—were published in Venice by Giuseppe Sala and subsequently reprinted in Amsterdam by the famed music printer Estienne Roger, the vast majority of his Viennese operas, oratorios, masses, and motets were preserved in hand-copied manuscript scores produced by the official imperial copyists. Charles VI, a passionate musician and skilled contrapuntalist himself, maintained an exhaustive archive of Caldara's scores within the Imperial National Library (now the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek). Caldara's Viennese sacred works, such as the Missa Sanctificationis St. Joannis Nepomuceni and his celebrated Stabat Mater, demonstrate a breathtaking fusion of the strict stile antico vocal canon with the dynamic, instrumentally driven stile moderno, featuring chromatic expressivity, dramatic pauses, and soaring contrapuntal fugues that astounded his contemporaries.Antonio Caldara died in Vienna on December 28, 1736, leaving behind a colossal artistic legacy that deeply resonated throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. His counterpoint exerted a direct influence on the highest echelons of European musical composition. Johann Sebastian Bach personally transcribed Caldara's Magnificat in C major, inserting his own structural revisions to study Caldara's melodic economy and structural fugal technique. Georg Philipp Telemann, Jan Dismas Zelenka, and Joseph Haydn studied his sacred works as authoritative models of contrapuntal balance. In the twentieth century, groundbreaking musicological archival research by scholars such as Ursula Kirkendale, Brian W. Pritchard, and Andrea Garavaglia systematically reconstructed Caldara’s biography and cataloged his immense output, securing his historic standing not merely as an imperial craftsman, but as one of the quintessential architects of European late Baroque musical culture.

authors.name: Viscardi Giovanni Andrea
authors.biography: Little is know about the life of Giovanni Andrea Viscardi, lawyer and historian, native of Bergamo. He studied in Padova, where he became friend of Torquato Bembo, the son of the famous humanist Pietro. Before 1555 he entered the service of the Grimaldi, lords of Monaco. Later on he accompanied the bishop of Bergamo to the Council of Trent. Viscardi spent most of his life in Bergamo, even though he briefly served as podestà in Lovere. In 1590 he published the Dialogo della miseria della vita humana et della certezza della vita eterna, which deals with death and the reversals of fortune topics that are extensively discussed also in his letters. In 1597 he dedicated to the doge Marino Grimani his Precetti morali e civili con molti et varii essempi. He is also said to have been loved by the poetess Gaspara Stampa, whose Rime (1554) contain four poems dedicated to him.

publishers.name: Ventura Comino
publishers.biography: Giacomino Venturetti, son of Venturino, was a printer active in Bergamo. Born in Sabbio Chiese near Brescia around 1550, he worked for some time in Lyon under Bartolomeo Gabiano. In 1578, he purchased the printing shop of Vincenzo Sabbio, where he had previously worked as an apprentice, and was granted the title of official printer of the city. He had a workshop in the San Cassiano neighborhood. In 1585, he bought Giuseppe Pigoccio’s bookstore in Piazza Vecchia. He also worked in partnership with Cristoforo Corbelli, Felice Olmo, and Battista Mageni. He married Cassandra Colonei and had the following children: Ventura, Valerio, Pietro, Massimo, Vittoria, Prudenzia, and Romualdo. He died on January 7, 1617; his sons Valerio and Pietro succeeded him.

related_names.name: Imperiali Giuseppe Renato
related_names.biography: Giuseppe Renato Imperiali (29 April 1651 – 15 January 1737) stands as one of the most formidable figures of the Roman Curia during the transitional epoch bridging the late Baroque Counter-Reformation with the early Italian Enlightenment (Illuminismo). Elevated to the Sacred College of Cardinals in 1690, Imperiali exerted an extraordinary influence over the temporal administration, diplomatic posture, and intellectual life of the Papal States for nearly half a century. As Prefect of the Sacra Congregazione del Buon Governo for over four decades, he oversaw the municipal finances, public works, and fiscal administration of the entire pontifical territory, operating at the very center of Roman administrative statecraft. Simultaneously, Cardinal Imperiali achieved international renown within the European Republic of Letters (Res publica literaria) as an unexcelled bibliophile and cultural patron. His private library, housed in the Palazzo Imperiali at Piazza Santi Apostoli in Rome and cataloged by the eminent scholar Giusto Fontanini in 1711, served as a vital institutional nexus for European humanists, antiquarians, theologians, and natural philosophers, embodying the ideal of the open, public-facing aristocratic library.Born in the Apulian fiefdom of Francavilla Fontana in the Kingdom of Naples on 29 April 1651, Giuseppe Renato was the eldest son of Michele II Imperiali, Prince of Francavilla and Marquis of Oria, and Brigida Grimaldi, daughter of the Prince of Gerace. The Imperiali family, belonging to the ancient Genoese patriciate (the Albergo Imperiali), had successfully expanded its economic and feudal influence into Southern Italy during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries while maintaining crucial ties to the Holy See. Young Giuseppe Renato was earmarked early for an ecclesiastical career in Rome under the direct mentorship and protection of his paternal uncle, Cardinal Lorenzo Imperiali (1612–1673), himself a prominent Curial prelate and Governor of Rome. Sent to the Papal capital at a young age, Giuseppe Renato received a rigorous education in canon and civil law (utroque jure) under private tutors, complemented by studies in classical humanities, theology, and diplomatic history. Following his uncle’s death in 1673, the young nobleman inherited substantial wealth and political connections, which facilitated his rapid integration into the prelatial ranks during the pontificates of Clement X (Altieri) and Innocent XI (Odescalchi). He entered the Curial hierarchy as a Referendary of the Supreme Tribunals of the Apostolic Signatura of Justice and Grace in 1679, subsequently obtaining the lucrative office of Cleric of the Apostolic Camera in 1683.Imperiali’s administrative capabilities came to full fruition under Pope Alexander VIII (Ottoboni), who appointed him General Treasurer of the Apostolic Camera (Tesoriere Generale) in 1689. In this role, Imperiali demonstrated remarkable financial acumen in reorganizing the Papal treasury, managing debt obligations (luoghi di monte), and reforming tax collection procedures across the Papal provinces. Impressed by his administrative efficiency and aristocratic pedigree, Alexander VIII elevated him to the cardinalate in the consistory of 13 February 1690, assigning him the deaconry of San Giorgio in Velabro (which he later exchanged for the title of Santa Pudenziana, and ultimately the presbyterial title of San Lorenzo in Lucina). Immediately following his elevation, Imperiali was appointed Papal Legate to Ferrara (1690–1696). His legation in Ferrara proved to be a masterclass in territorial governance: he actively mediated territorial and hydraulic disputes concerning the diversion of the Po River, implemented agricultural stabilization measures, modernised local grain reserves (annona), and checked the territorial encroachments of the neighboring Duchy of Modena and the House of Habsburg.Upon his return to Rome in 1696, Pope Innocent XII (Pignatelli) appointed Cardinal Imperiali to the presidency of the Sacra Congregazione del Buon Governo, a position he retained continuously under five successive popes (Innocent XII, Clement XI, Innocent XIII, Benedict XIII, and Clement XII) until his death in 1737. In this capacity, Imperiali became the de facto minister of internal affairs for the Papal States. He conducted extensive investigations into municipal corruption, restructured local taxation, enforced rigorous auditing standards for communal budgets, and promoted public works, such as the drainage of marshlands and the construction of roads and granaries. His long tenure was marked by an uncompromising defence of central Papal authority against local feudal oligarchies and municipal privileges, earning him both widespread respect for his impartiality and bitter enmity from regional aristocracies. Within the Sacred College, Imperiali aligned himself with the zelanti—the faction of independent cardinals committed to defending the spiritual liberty and administrative integrity of the Church against the interference of the European dynastic monarchies (Spain, France, and Austria).Imperiali’s political prestige reached its absolute zenith during the dramatic Conclave of 1730, convened following the death of Pope Benedict XIII. Supported by the zelanti and the imperial faction aligned with the Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI, Imperiali emerged as the leading candidate for the Papal throne. He secured a formidable consensus, coming within a mere two votes of the required two-thirds majority necessary for election. However, his uncompromising stance on Papal sovereignty and his past political disputes with the House of Bourbon led King Philip V of Spain to exercise the royal right of veto (exclusive), delivered formally by Cardinal Cornelio Bentivoglio. This diplomatic intervention blocked Imperiali’s accession, leading ultimately to the election of Cardinal Lorenzo Corsini as Pope Clement XII. Despite this bitter political reversal, Imperiali maintained his immense influence in Curial affairs, serving as a trusted senior advisor to Clement XII and continuing his oversight of internal Papal administration.Beyond his political and curial duties, Giuseppe Renato Imperiali achieved enduring historical distinction as one of the preeminent literary patrons and bibliophiles of early eighteenth-century Europe. In his residence at the Palazzo Imperiali at Piazza Santi Apostoli, he assembled the Bibliotheca Imperialis, a legendary collection comprising over 25,000 printed volumes and thousands of rare manuscripts spanning theology, canon law, patristics, classical literature, civil history, and natural philosophy. Unlike many contemporary aristocratic collections, Imperiali transformed his library into an active research institution open to scholars, foreign visitors, and young academics regardless of their social standing or political affiliation. To manage this vast repository, Imperiali employed the friar and scholar Giusto Fontanini as his domestic chaplain and chief librarian. In 1711, Fontanini published the celebrated catalog Bibliothecae Josephi Renati Imperialis Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae Diaconi Cardinalis Sancti Georgii Catalogus secundum auctorum cognomina ordine alphabetico dispositus (Rome: Typis Francisci Gonzagae), a monumental folio volume that became an indispensable reference work for librarians, book collectors, and bibliographers across Enlightenment Europe due to its innovative cross-referencing system and meticulous typographical descriptions.Imperiali’s salon at Piazza Santi Apostoli functioned as a primary gathering place for the intellectual elite of Rome and a key node in the international Republic of Letters. He was a generous protector of the Accademia degli Arcadi (in which he was enrolled under the Arcadian pseudonym Cleante Focide), sponsoring poetry recitals, antiquarian debates, and historical studies. He maintained an extensive correspondence with international scholars, including the Maurist monk Jean Mabillon, the historian Ludovico Antonio Muratori, the bibliographer Domenico Silvio Passionei, and the antiquarian Bernard de Montfaucon. Imperiali was also a major patron of the visual arts, commissioning works from prominent Baroque and Rococo masters such as Francesco Trevisani, Sebastiano Conca, and Tommaso Chiari, and expanding his family’s collection of ancient Greco-Roman sculpture. In matters of ecclesiastical scholarship, he leaned toward learned Augustinian and Dominican erudition, providing protection to scholars accused of rigorism or Jansenist sympathies, such as Gian Lorenzo Berti, while maintaining a strict orthodoxy in his public acts.Cardinal Giuseppe Renato Imperiali died in Rome on 15 January 1737 at the advanced age of eighty-five. His death was mourned across Europe as the passing of a statesman of majestic stature and an incomparable champion of learning. In accordance with his testament, he was buried in the Basilica of Sant'Agostino in Rome, where his executors erected a monumental funerary monument designed by the architect Paolo Posi and sculpted in polychrome marbles by Pietro Bracci, featuring an allegorical representation of Fame and Charity. Imperiali bequeathed his magnificent library in trust (fideicommissum) for public utility, ensuring that it remained open to the citizens of Rome. Although the collection suffered partial dispersal during the political upheavals of the late eighteenth century and the French occupation of 1798, the legacy of the Bibliotheca Imperialis and Imperiali's administrative reforms enduringly influenced the institutional and cultural history of the Papal State throughout the Enlightenment.

authors.name: Manfredi Muzio
authors.biography: Manfredi Muzio (1535–1608) stands as a pivotal yet often understated figure in late sixteenth-century Italian letters, operating at the dynamic intersection of humanist epistolary culture, courtly diplomacy, and Counter-Reformation editorial management. The legitimated son and primary literary executor of the renowned Renaissance courtier, polemicist, and poet Girolamo Muzio (1496–1576)—author of the celebrated chivalric and moral treatises Il Duello (1550) and Il Gentilhuomo (1571)—Manfredi navigated the increasingly rigid ideological and religious landscape of post-Tridentine Italy. His historic significance in early modern intellectual history resides in a dual achievement: first, as an energetic curator and editor of his father's vast epistolary and polemical estate, and second, as an authorial biographer whose foundational account, the Vita di Girolamo Muzio, shaped the posthumous memory of one of the mid-Cinquecento's most fierce defenders of Catholic orthodoxy and aristocratic ethics. By organizing, editing, and ushering through the Venetian presses the voluminous correspondence (*Lettere*) and anti-heretical works of his father, Manfredi transformed private familial memory into a public monument of Counter-Reformation piety and literary authority.Born in 1535 into a turbulent and nomadic household, Manfredi spent his formative years in the shadow of his father’s peripatetic career across the principal courtly centers of Northern and Central Italy, including Milan, Ferrara, Urbino, Rome, and Venice. Girolamo Muzio, himself born in Padua to a Capodistrian notary and later knighted for his literary and diplomatic service to various Italian princes, spared no effort in providing Manfredi with a comprehensive humanist and courtly education. Formed in the classicized curriculum of Latin rhetoric, vernacular poetics, canon law, and political protocol, young Manfredi was directly exposed to the high-stakes patronage dynamics of the mid-sixteenth century. His youth was deeply influenced by his father's diplomatic missions and literary ties with major patrons, most notably Duke Ercole II d'Este, Duke Guidobaldo II della Rovere of Urbino, and Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. Legitimated and formally integrated into his father's intellectual household, Manfredi absorbed the moral and religious imperatives of the Counter-Reformation, developing a deep familiarity with the administrative, legal, and secretarial machinery of Italian courts and ecclesiastical chancelleries.Manfredi’s principal original literary creation is his authoritative life of his father, the Vita di Girolamo Muzio, a work that functions simultaneously as a filial tribute, a historical chronicle, and a sophisticated exercise in Tridentine life-writing. In this biography, Manfredi constructs a carefully calibrated narrative that presents Girolamo not merely as an accomplished man of letters, but as an unyielding defender of the Roman Catholic Church against Northern European Protestantism, a master theorist of courtly honor, and an exemplary servant to the Holy See. Beyond his biographical narrative, Manfredi operated as a prolific editor. Following Girolamo's death in 1576 at the estate of Paneretta near Florence, Manfredi assumed full responsibility for his father's extensive archive. He systematically collected, arranged, and published several substantial volumes of Girolamo’s Lettere, offering early modern readers a sweeping window into the political, theological, and literary debates of the mid-Cinquecento. His editorial method involved careful textual selection, thematic organization, and rhetorical refinement of epistolary exchanges involving popes, cardinals, Italian dukes, and eminent literary figures such as Pietro Aretino, Bernardo Tasso, and Sperone Speroni. Furthermore, Manfredi oversaw the post-mortem compilation of Girolamo’s theological and anti-heretical writings, ensuring their strict alignment with the emerging censorship frameworks overseen by the Sacred Congregation of the Index.The printing history of Manfredi Muzio's editorial and biographical output offers a compelling case study in the dynamics of late sixteenth-century publishing, particularly within the bustling print ecosystem of Venice. Working during an era marked by the rigorous enforcement of the Index Librorum Prohibitorum and heightened State-Church negotiations over intellectual property, Manfredi forged strategic partnerships with leading Venetian printing houses, including those of Giacomo Vincenti, Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari, and Giovanni Battista Ciotti. The physical typography of the volumes edited by Manfredi reflects the formal shift from the open, unadorned layouts of earlier Renaissance printing to the densely structured, highly annotated, and paratextually rich editions characteristic of Counter-Reformation publishing. Manfredi personally managed the complex process of securing ecclesiastical permissions (*imprimaturs*) and dogal privileges across the Venetian Republic and the Papal States to protect his publications against pirated reproductions. His editions were consistently outfitted with elaborate paratexts—including ornate woodcut devices, formal dedicatory letters to high-ranking prelates and aristocrats, analytical tables of contents, and extensive marginal glosses—designed to frame the reading experience for a pious, aristocratic audience across Catholic Europe.The critical reception of Manfredi Muzio's work has undergone a significant evolution from the early modern period down to contemporary scholarship. In the eighteenth century, pioneering encyclopedists and bio-bibliographers such as Giammaria Mazzuchelli in his Gli scrittori d'Italia and Girolamo Tiraboschi in his monumental Storia della letteratura italiana recognized Manfredi as an indispensable biographical authority, relying heavily on his narrative while acknowledging its inherent panegyric and apologetic tendencies. In nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Italian historiography, scholars frequently examined Manfredi's editorial interventions critically, noting how he smoothed over personal rivalries and suppressed sensitive theological nuances in Girolamo's correspondence to present an image of unblemished orthodoxy compatible with Tridentine decorum. In contemporary Renaissance and early modern studies, scholars of epistolary culture, family memory, and print history—such as Maria Luisa Doglio, Antonio Sorella, and Valerio Sanzotta—have re-evaluated Manfredi Muzio not simply as a dutiful son or passive editor, but as an active, conscious agent of early modern literary self-fashioning. His biographical and editorial efforts are now studied as pivotal examples of how early modern families manipulated the print medium to secure social prestige, preserve intellectual lineages, and navigate the complex political realities of post-Tridentine Italy.

publishers.name: Viani Andrea
publishers.biography: Andrea Viani was a printer and a publisher active in Pavia and in Piacenza. In Pavia, he served as a janitor at the law school at least until 1620. In Piacenza, he used Giovanni Bazachi’s printing press.

academic_description: 8vo. [10], 105, [5] pp. Collation: A-G8, H4. Bound in nineteenth century yellow paper (on the front cover manuscript ownership entry by the famous collector Leonardo Trissino, dated Firenze 1839). First and only edition of this collection of one hundred letters written to accompany copies of his tragedy Semiramis and of his pastoral play Semiramis boschereccia, to be sent to the addressees of the letters. Both plays were printed in Bergamo in 1593. This is confirmed in the dedication to Agostino Gambarelli (Nancy, January 1, 1594). Manfredi says that he obtained from the typographer Comin Ventura one hundred copies of these two works, and that he decided to present them to friends and patrons jointly with a letter. Many secretaries at that time used to send identical letters to different recipients, whereas Manfredi preferred to personalize each accompanying letter. Seen the novelty of the enterprise and the great variety of the letters, he considered them worthy of being published, also in view of obtaining a critic of his plays.In addition to the one hundred letters, “une dernière lettre est ajoutée à la fin du livre, addressée, come l'épître dédicatroire, au responsable des deux Semiramis, et datée du 1er août 1593: elle accompagne l'expédition des 100 lettres precedents, qu'Agostino Gambarelli devra faire parvenir à leurs destinataires, le plus souvent jointes aux exemplaires qu'il a la charge de distribuer” (J. Basso, Le genre epistolaire en langue italienne (1538-1662). Répertoire chronologique et analytique, Roma & Nancy, 1990, II, p. 345).In a letter addressed to Veronica Franco (Nancy, July 20, 1593), Manfredi thanks her for the sonnet she had sent to him in praise of the tragedy Semiramis, and announces his gift of the two volumes. He also asks her to keep him informed about the imminent publication of an epic poem by her, which, however, was never published and remained totally unknown. This letter seems to have escaped to the attention of M.F. Rosenthal, who quotes only another letter of Manfredi to Franco dated Nancy, October 30, 1591, which was published in 1606 in Manfredi's Lettere brevissime (cf. The Honest Courtesan. Veronica Franco, Citizen and Writer in Sixteenth-Century Venice, Chicago & London, 1992, pp. 152 and 318).All the letters are arranged in alphabetical order by the first name of the addressees, and are dated Nancy, July 1593, except for the last one. August 1 (p. 103) Muzio Manfredi, a nobleman born in Cesena, after a short stay at the Roman court, moved around 1580 to Parma, where he entered the service of the Farnese family. As a member of the Accademia degli Innominati, he knew the playwrights Pomponio Torelli and Giovan Battista Guarini. In Parma he published an important edition of Tasso's Gerusalemme liberata (1581). In 1584 he found a patron in the person of Ferrante II Gonzaga at Guastalla, and in 1591 became secretary to the Duchess Dorothea of Lorraine, first at Tortona (where he got married with Ippolita Benigni, one of the Duchess' court ladies), and later at Nancy (cf. M.E. Briard, Le poète Muzio Manfredi et Dorothea de Lorraine, duchesse de Brunswick, in: “Journal de la Société d'archéologie lorraine”, XXXVIII, 1889, pp. 29-35).“Intrapresa una brillante carriera di poeta cortigiano e galante animatore di salotti, che lo vede protagonista nelle Corti romana, parmense e guastallese, il poeta giunge ai vertici della sua fortuna di artista e ‘gentiluomo' intorno alla metà degli anni '80. Ma dopo quella data, una serie di vicissitudini e di gravi incidenti con la classe signorile che fino ad allora lo aveva sostenuto e gratificato, lo porterà, fra momenti travagliati e dolorosi, ad una vecchiaia di emarginazione e di miseria” (L. Denarosi, Il principe e il letterato: due carteggi inediti di Muzio Manfredi, in: “Studi italiani”, 1997, 9, no. 1, p. 153).His bitter diatribe against the Duke of Mantua, Vincenzo Gonzaga, contained in the dedication of the Semiramis boschereccia, costed him the latter's favour, which Manfredi tried in vain to regain after his return from France. He spent his last years in extreme poverty plying between Pavia, Ravenna, and Rome (cf. M.A. Bertolotti, Muzio Manfredi e Passi Giuseppe letterati in relazione col duca di Mantova, in: “Il Buonarroti”, Roma, 1888, III, p. 119 ff.).Manfredi was a prolific writer and a member of various important academies (Accademia dei Confusi in Bologna, Accademia degli Invaghiti in Ferrara, and Accademia Olimpica in Vicenza). His numerous madrigals (1587) were very popular among contemporary musicians, who set many of them to music. Among his others publications, are poems (Rime, 1575), a work called Sogno amoroso (1596), the poetic garland Cento donne cantate (1580), and the collection Lettere brevissime (1606), in which he discusses topics related to tragedy.

authors.name: Eobanus Hessus Helius
authors.biography: Helius Eobanus Hessus (born Eoban Koch; 6 January 1488 – 5 October 1440) stands as one of the most luminous and prolific figures of Northern European Neo-Latin humanism. Revered by his contemporaries as the Rex poetarum ('King of Poets') within the German lands, Hessus occupied a monumental position at the intersection of Italian Renaissance stylistic elegance, German civic humanism, and the intellectual transformations of the Lutheran Reformation. Operating across pivotal academic centers—most notably Erfurt, Nuremberg, and Marburg—he elevated Latin verse composition to an unprecedented level of formal mastery, forging a synthesis between classical Ovidian poetics, Christian biblical exegesis, and contemporary pedagogical reform. His vast poetic corpus, encompassing elegies, bucolics, epic paraphrases, pedagogical treatises, and epistolary verse, served as a vital cultural bridge that mediated between the sodalities of early sixteenth-century German humanists and the emerging confessional structures of Protestant academia.Born in the Hessian village of Halgehausen, near Frankenberg, Hessus was the son of a modest rustic family named Koch. Adopted into a tradition of self-fashioning characteristic of Northern humanism, he constructed his classicized nomenclature from his native region (Hessus), his birth on a Sunday (Helius, evoking the sun god Helios), and his patron saint, Saint Eoban (Eobanus). His early education unfolded at Gemünden and Frankenberg before he matriculated at the University of Erfurt in 1504. Under the intellectual mentorship of Jakob Muttmann and Maternus Hatten, the young scholar rapidly immersed himself in the study of classical philology and rhetoric. Erfurt at the dawn of the sixteenth century was the crucible of German humanist agitation, dominated by the intellectual sodality gathered around Conradus Mutianus Rufus (Mutian) at nearby Gotha. Hessus was quickly absorbed into this Sodalitas Erphordiensis, forging intimate bonds with scholars and satirists such as Crotus Rubeanus, Ulrich von Hutten, Justus Jonas, and Euricius Cordus. By the time he received his Master of Arts degree in 1508, Hessus had emerged as the undisputed poetic prodigy of the Erfurt circle.The early public career of Hessus reflected the precarious mobility required of early modern men of letters. After serving briefly as rector of the St. Severus school in Erfurt (1509–1513) and undertaking a diplomatic journey to Riesenburg in Prussia under the patronage of Bishop Job von Dobeneck (1514–1516), Hessus returned to Erfurt in 1517 to assume the prestigious chair of Poetry and Eloquence (Professor poeseos et elocutionis) at the University of Erfurt. It was during this Erfurt professorship that Hessus solidified his status as the leader of the local humanist sodality. He played a central, supportive role during the famous Reuchlin controversy, championing Johann Reuchlin against the Cologne theologians and aligning himself with the ideological vanguard that produced the satirical Epistolae Obscurorum Virorum ('Letters of Obscure Men'). When Martin Luther passed through Erfurt in April 1521 on his epochal journey to the Diet of Worms, Hessus organized a triumphant public reception, cementing his alignment with the evangelical reform movement and transforming Erfurt into a bastion of Lutheran humanism.Economic instability and academic decline in Erfurt prompted Hessus to accept an invitation in 1526 from the Nuremberg City Council, mediated by Philip Melanchthon, to join the faculty of the newly established Aegidianum Gymnasium. In Nuremberg, Hessus entered one of his most artistically fertile periods. Surrounded by an exceptional intellectual circle that included Melanchthon, Joachim Camerarius, the polymath Willibald Pirckheimer, the statesman Lazarus Spengler, and the artist Albrecht Dürer, Hessus composed his celebrated poetic topography, Urbs Norimberga (1532), an exquisite panegyric in Latin hexameters that immortalized the city's architecture, civic order, and artistic genius. Despite his professional success in Franconia, nostalgia drew him back to Erfurt in 1533 in an arduous attempt to revive the university's fortunes. Finding the institution fundamentally diminished by political and religious strife, he accepted a permanent call in 1536 from Landgrave Philip I of Hesse ('Philip the Magnanimous') to become Professor of History and Poetry at the newly founded Protestant University of Marburg. He remained in Marburg as a celebrated academic patriarch until his death on October 5, 1540.In terms of literary output and philosophical orientation, Hessus was a master of Ovidian metric flexibility, which he applied to both secular and sacred themes. His early masterpiece, the Heroidum Epistolae ('Epistles of Heroines', first published 1514 and extensively revised in 1528), explicitly modeled itself on Ovid's Heroides, yet boldly expanded the genre by introducing Christian, biblical, and contemporary female figures—such as the Virgin Mary, Saint Catherine, and contemporary women of the Reformation—alongside classical heroines. His didactic medical poem, De tuenda bona valetudine ('On Preserving Good Health', 1524), featuring extensive commentaries by Euricius Cordus and later Johann Dryander, fused classical dietary advice with humanist verse and became an enduring pedagogical textbook across European universities. Hessus reached the zenith of his literary fame with his metric Latin paraphrase of the Psalms, the Psalterium Davidis carmine elegiaco redditum (1537). This monumental work translated the Hebrew Psalter into classical Latin elegiac couplets, creating a devotional bestseller that saw over forty editions across Europe, used widely in Protestant Latin schools to teach both classical prosody and evangelical piety. Shortly before his death, he completed a monumental Latin verse translation of Homer's Iliad (1540), demonstrating his extraordinary philological range and poetic stamina.The printing history and typographical circulation of Hessus's oeuvre reflect the dynamic commercial networks of early modern Northern European publishing. His works were produced by the premier printers of the Holy Roman Empire, including Wolfgang Stürmer in Erfurt, Hieronymus Formschneider and Petreius in Nuremberg, Johann Setzer in Hagenau, Hans Lufft in Wittenberg, and preeminently Christian Egenolff in Frankfurt am Main. Egenolff, in particular, recognized the immense commercial viability of Hessus's medical and poetic works, reissuing the De tuenda bona valetudine and the Psalterium in elegant, octavo and duodecimo formats complete with woodcut illustrations, marginal commentary, and academic indices. The widespread adoption of Hessus's texts within the Protestant Gymnasia and universities guaranteed his publishers substantial, long-term returns, making Hessus one of the first German authors to achieve financial viability primarily through the print medium.The critical reception of Helius Eobanus Hessus highlights his pivotal position in early modern intellectual history. Upon his passing in 1540, funeral orations and mourning elegies were composed by the foremost intellectuals of Europe, led by Philip Melanchthon and Joachim Camerarius, the latter publishing a comprehensive biography of Hessus in 1553 (Narratio de Eobano Hesso), which stands as one of the earliest full-length humanist biographies in German historiography. While later Baroque and Enlightenment critics sometimes dismissed Neo-Latin poetry as derivative mimicry, nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholarship—pioneered by Carl Krause and expanded by modern scholars such as Harry Vredeveld—has re-evaluated Hessus as an original, creative genius of the Northern Renaissance. His ability to synthesize pagan classical form with Protestant evangelical theology defined the aesthetic identity of early modern Lutheran culture, establishing a pedagogical and poetic standard that dominated Central European academia for over two centuries.

publishers.name: Vögelin Ernst
publishers.biography: Ernst Vögelin (1529–1589), Latinized in scholarly imprints as Ernestus Voegelinus or Voegelius, stands as one of the most intellectually ambitious, typographically refined, and politically controversial master printers and publishers of the Holy Roman Empire during the second half of the sixteenth century. Operating primarily from the vibrant mercantile and academic hub of Leipzig, and later from Frankfurt am Main and Constance, Vögelin transformed a modest printing enterprise into the celebrated Officina Voegeliniana, a cultural engine that propelled the intellectual dissemination of Northern Protestant Humanism, late Renaissance philology, legal jurisprudence, and neo-Aristotelian philosophy throughout Europe. Situated historically at the precarious intersection of humanistic erudition and intense confessionalization (Konfessionalisierung), Vögelin’s publishing career exemplifies the pivotal role played by printer-scholars in defining the doctrinal, literary, and academic contours of the post-Reformation era. His output not only shaped the curriculum of Protestant universities such as Leipzig and Wittenberg, but also situated him at the center of the explosive theological controversies surrounding Philippism and Crypto-Calvinism that rocked Electoral Saxony in the 1570s.Born on August 10, 1529, in the imperial city of Constance (Konstanz), Vögelin belonged to an established civic family deeply integrated into the urban patriciate and the intellectual currents of Southwestern Germany. His early formative education was steeped in the classical humanities, combining rigorous training in Latin and Ancient Greek with exposure to the emerging evangelical theology of the Swiss and Upper Rhenish Reformation. Seeking advanced scholarly opportunities in Northern Germany, Vögelin migrated to Saxony and matriculated at the University of Leipzig during the late 1540s. It was in Leipzig that Vögelin made the decisive transition from academic student to print entrepreneur. He gained intimate entry into the elite publishing apparatus of the city by forming a close professional alliance with Valentin Bapst the Elder (also rendered Papst), one of Leipzig’s leading civic printers. Following Bapst’s death, Vögelin cemented his social and commercial position by marrying Bapst’s daughter (and heiress), thereby acquiring ownership of the established printing house, its presses, typographical fonts, and active publishing privileges around 1559. Through this strategic inheritance and his own formidable capital investments, Vögelin rapidly expanded the shop into a premier printing house, securing imperial printing privileges (privilegia impressoria) from Imperial authorities as well as territorial protections from Elector Augustus of Saxony.The scholarly orientation of the Officina Voegeliniana was defined by Vögelin’s intimate integration into the elite intellectual networks of Melanchthonian Humanism—frequently designated as Philippism after the influential Wittenberg reformer Philipp Melanchthon. Vögelin maintained extraordinarily close intellectual and personal ties with Melanchthon’s primary disciples and intellectual heirs, most notably Joachim Camerarius the Elder, the celebrated classicist and rector at Leipzig; Caspar Peucer, Melanchthon’s son-in-law and physician-philosopher at Wittenberg; Esrom Rüdinger; Viktorin Strigel; and David Chytraeus. Under their editorial guidance, Vögelin issued monumental editions of classical Greek and Latin literature, advanced philological treatises, legal commentaries, and academic textbooks that became standard across European faculties of arts and law. His press printed authoritative editions of Demosthenes, Cicero, Aristotle, Homer, and Hesiod, frequently embellished with parallel Latin translations and detailed scholarly commentary by Camerarius. Furthermore, Vögelin became the principal printer for major legal compilations and municipal codes, establishing Leipzig’s primacy in European legal publishing. His theological production focused on irenic, humanistically oriented Lutheran scholarship, avoiding the vitriolic polemicism of the rigid Gnesio-Lutheran party and emphasizing dialectical rigor, pedagogical clarity, and civic morality.From a technical and typographical perspective, Vögelin raised the standards of Saxon printing to levels that rivaled the supreme continental workshops of Johannes Oporinus in Basel, Plantin in Antwerp, and the Estienne family in Paris. The material production of the Officina Voegeliniana was characterized by exceptional presswork, pristine paper Sourced from top Rhenish and Bohemian mills, and meticulous proofreading executed by university-trained correctors. Vögelin acquired and commissioned extensive sets of high-grade Antiqua and Italic types cut after Italian and French punches, alongside exquisite Greek fonts and specialized Hebrew characters designed to handle complex polyglot apparatuses. His books were frequently adorned with elaborate Renaissance woodcut title borders, elegant architectural frames, historiated initial letters, and striking printers' devices. Vögelin’s primary printer's emblem was a vivid visual pun on his surname (derived from Vögelin, meaning 'little bird'): it typically depicted a bird soaring toward the sun or perched resiliently beside a palm tree, accompanied by moralizing Latin or Greek mottos emphasizing perseverance, divine favor, and scholarly devotion. To ensure the rapid distribution of his massive print runs, Vögelin operated a sophisticated commercial distribution network anchored in the bi-annual Leipziger Buchmesse and the Frankfurter Buchmesse, where he maintained dedicated sales vaults and traded sheets with book merchants from Venice, Lyon, London, and Basel.The trajectory of Vögelin’s life took a tragic and dramatic turn in the mid-1570s, as the latent doctrinal rift between radical Gnesio-Lutherans and moderate Philippists erupted into open political warfare within Electoral Saxony. Elector Augustus, initially supportive of the Philippist faculty, became convinced that his court physicians and theologians—including Caspar Peucer and printer networks associated with Leipzig and Wittenberg—were secretly undermining Lutheran orthodoxy by orchestrating a clandestine movement toward Reformed Calvinism, a crisis known as the Crypto-Calvinist Controversy (Kryptocalvinismus). In 1574, the publication and covert distribution of controversial Calvinistic Eucharistic treatises, such as the anonymous Exegesis perspicua controversiae de Coena Domini, ignited an electoral purge. Vögelin, who had printed, financed, and distributed numerous works by Peucer, Rüdinger, and other suspected Philippist theologians without obtaining strict territorial censorial clearance, was identified as a primary instrument of the alleged conspiracy. In 1576, electoral inquisitors suppressed Vögelin’s Leipzig workshop; his presses were impounded, his books confiscated, and he was subjected to intense legal interrogation and temporary imprisonment.Stripped of his Saxon privileges and forced into exile, Vögelin displayed remarkable resilience by relocating his family and remaining capital to the Free Imperial City of Frankfurt am Main, the undisputed capital of the international book trade. Re-establishing his printing operations in Frankfurt and maintaining close operational links with his native Constance, Vögelin resumed publishing under his own name and through cooperative ventures with Rhenish and Palatine pressmen. Free from Saxon censorship, he continued to issue critical scholarly editions, humanistic compendia, and Protestant literature until his death around 1589. His monumental legacy was actively maintained and extended into the seventeenth century by his sons—most notably Gotthard Vögelin and Ernst Vögelin the Younger—who established celebrated printing firms in Frankfurt, Heidelberg, and Neustadt an der Haardt, remaining central suppliers to the Palatine Calvinist and pan-European humanist republic of letters. Today, Ernst Vögelin is remembered by historians of the book and scholars of the Reformation as a quintessential Renaissance printer-publisher whose commitment to humanistic learning and intellectual freedom withstood the fierce storms of confessional intolerance.

related_names.name: Camerarius Joachim
related_names.biography: Joachim Camerarius the Elder (1500–1574) stands as one of the most brilliant, versatile, and influential humanists of the Northern European Renaissance. A scholar of extraordinary linguistic erudition, pivotal university reformer, and tireless textual critic, Camerarius occupied a central position within the intellectual and confessional matrix of sixteenth-century Germany. Alongside his lifelong companion and intellectual collaborator, Philipp Melanchthon, Camerarius served as a primary architect of the Praeceptio Germaniae—the systematic transformation of Northern European education through the integration of classical Greek and Latin philology with evangelical theology. His monumental contributions to classical scholarship, ranging from groundbreaking critical editions of Plautus, Sophocles, and Homer to translations of Galen and Claudius Ptolemy, established standards of textual rigor that bridged the methodology of Italian humanists like Piero Vettori with the emerging philological traditions of early modern Germany. Beyond his textual corpus, Camerarius was an instrumental figure in the institutionalization of the Reformation, drafting foundational documents at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 and orchestrating the overhaul of major universities, including Nuremberg, Tübingen, and Leipzig.Born on April 12, 1500, in the Franconian imperial city of Bamberg, Camerarius hailed from a patrician family originally named Liebhard. The surname Camerarius was adopted by his ancestors in reference to their hereditary title of Kämmerer (hereditary chamberlain) to the Prince-Bishops of Bamberg. His early educational foundation was established in Bamberg under the guidance of local schoolmasters before he matriculated at the University of Leipzig in 1512 at the exceptionally early age of twelve. At Leipzig, the young scholar came under the profound influence of the English Hellenist Richard Croke and the renowned Latinist Peter Mosellanus (Peter Schade), whose instruction ignited Camerarius’s lifelong devotion to ancient Greek grammar and Neo-Latin eloquence. Seeking an environment more receptive to the new humanist learning, Camerarius transferred in 1518 to the University of Erfurt. There, he entered the celebrated literary circle gathered around Conrad Mutianus Rufus and Helius Eobanus Hessus, immersing himself in the study of classical rhetoric, poetry, and ancient history. In 1521, drawn by the radical intellectual ferment surrounding the early Protestant movement, Camerarius relocated to the University of Wittenberg. This move proved decisive: at Wittenberg, he established an intimate, lifelong friendship with Philipp Melanchthon and entered the immediate circle of Martin Luther. Under Melanchthon’s guidance, Camerarius deepened his command of Greek syntax, began lecturing publicly on Quintilian and Cicero, and engaged directly with the critical translation of Biblical texts.Camerarius’s career as an institutional administrator and educational reformer commenced in 1526, when, upon Melanchthon’s direct recommendation, the Senate of the Imperial City of Nuremberg appointed him rector of the newly established Aegidien-Gymnasium. In Nuremberg, working in close concert with the reformer Lazarus Spengler, Camerarius designed a pioneering humanist curriculum that served as a blueprint for secondary education throughout Protestant Europe. His diplomatic and theological capabilities were put to a severe test in 1530, when he accompanied Melanchthon to the Imperial Diet of Augsburg. Camerarius actively assisted in the redaction, translation, and diplomatic negotiations surrounding the Confessio Augustana (Augsburg Confession), playing a subtle yet critical role in maintaining irenic dialogue with Catholic imperial representatives. Recognizing his institutional genius, Duke Ulrich of Württemberg summoned Camerarius in 1535 to reorganize the University of Tübingen along humanist and evangelical lines, a task he accomplished with remarkable speed by revitalizing the faculties of arts and theology. In 1541, Duke Maurice of Saxony enticed Camerarius to accept the professorship of Greek and Latin literature at the University of Leipzig. For the remaining thirty-three years of his life, Camerarius transformed Leipzig into the premier center of classical philology and humanist erudition in Northern Europe, navigating the immense political and military turmoil of the Smalcaldic War (1546–1547) and the contentious Adiaphoristic controversies with remarkable diplomatic tact and scholarly detachment.The philological legacy of Joachim Camerarius is immense, characterized by unprecedented critical acumen, stemmatological intuition, and deep linguistic sensitivity. His edition of the comedies of Plautus (M. Accii Plauti Comoediae XX), printed at Basel in 1552, represented a watershed moment in Latin textual scholarship. Utilizing the famous Codex Vetus (Vaticanus Lat. 3870), which he examined with meticulous care, Camerarius purged centuries of scribal corruptions, restored ancient metrical structures, and established a text that remained standard for generations. His labor in Greek letters was equally groundbreaking: he produced critical editions and Latin translations of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey, Sophocles’ tragedies, Hesiod, Theocritus, Demosthenes, Xenophon, and Herodotus. Camerarius did not limit his erudition to literary classics; he was deeply fascinated by ancient science, astronomy, and medicine. In 1535, he published the editio princeps of the Greek text of Claudius Ptolemy’s astrological treatise, the Tetrabiblos (or Quadripartitum), alongside his own Latin translation, accompanied by an edition of the Karbos (Centiloquium). His medical interest led him to translate and annotate works by Galen and Aetius of Amida. In the realm of contemporary history and biography, Camerarius authored two masterworks that remain indispensable primary sources for the Renaissance and Reformation eras: his Narratio de Helios Eobano Hesso (1553) and his monumental De vita Philippi Melanchthonis narratio (1566). The latter represents the first comprehensive biography of Melanchthon, offering an insider’s view of the intellectual dynamics, personal struggles, and theological debates of the Reformation inner circle.The dissemination of Camerarius’s vast literary output was made possible through his intimate, highly strategic relationships with the leading printing houses of Northern Europe. He maintained close working alliances with the great Basel presses, most notably those of Johannes Herwagen, Johann Oporinus, and Hieronymus Froben. These Basel publishers possessed the specialized Greek fonts and scholarly correctors necessary to produce Camerarius’s complex Greek commentaries and critical texts. In Nuremberg, he collaborated extensively with Johannes Petreius, who printed several of his grammatical and astronomical works, while in Leipzig, his texts issued regularly from the presses of Ernst Voegelin, Michael Blum, and Valentin Papa. Camerarius was also a central node in an international republic of letters (*Respublica Literaria*). His voluminous epistolary correspondence—comprising well over one thousand extant Latin and Greek letters—demonstrates active textual exchanges with Italian humanists such as Piero Vettori (Victorius) in Florence and Cardinal Pietro Bembo, as well as Northern scholars like Erasmus of Rotterdam, Johannes Sturm in Strasbourg, and Joachim Vadianus in St. Gallen. Through these networks, Camerarius facilitated the exchange of rare manuscripts, collations, and codicological data across confessional divides, maintaining a steadfast commitment to the universal fellowship of humanist learning despite the religious wars fracturing Europe.Camerarius passed away in Leipzig on April 17, 1574, leaving behind a family that would continue his scholarly legacy, most notably his son, Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a celebrated physician, botanist, and emblem author. In the centuries following his death, Camerarius’s reputation as a giant of classical philology remained unshakeable. Polyhistors of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, including Daniel Georg Morhof and Johann Albert Fabricius, praised him as the ultimate exemplar of Northern erudition—a scholar who combined the stylistic elegance of the Italian Renaissance with German textual thoroughness. Modern historiography, led by scholars such as Heinz Scheible, Thomas Fuchs, and Volkhard Wels, has re-evaluated Camerarius not merely as a passive transmitter of classical antiquity, but as an indispensable agent of cultural transformation who shaped the institutional structures of early modern German universities, pioneered modern philological methodologies, and preserved the intellectual coherence of Protestant Humanism during a period of acute ideological crisis.

academic_description: 8vo. [152] leaves (the last is a blank). Collation: A-T8. With the printer's device on the title-page and Camerarius' coat-of-arms on the verso. Contemporary blind-stamped pigskin over boards, spine with three raised bands. Contemporary entry of ownership dated 1581 by Christophorus Sella (Sessel), a Nuremberg theologian (fl. 2nd half of the 16th century). Due to sticking together of some leaves, the printed surface of the pages is not clearly readable; these pages have been added in photostate from another copy (A2r, A5v, A6r, L5v, L6r, M1v, M2r, M2v, M3r, M5v, M6r, M7v, M8r, N1v, N2r). First edition of the third part of Eobanus' correspondence published by Joachim Camerarius (1500-1574). A first, rather negligent and disorderly collection of Eobanus' letters (Epistolarum familiarium libri XII) was published two years after his death by Johannes Draconites at Marburg in 1542. But it was Eobanus' lifelong friend and correspondent Camerarius, who published a first series of letters in Narratio de H. Eobano Hesso (Eobanus' biography) in 1553. This was followed by Libellus alter in 1557, the present Tertius libellus, and Libellus novus in 1568 (cf. C. Krause, op. cit, II, pp. 264-266).Of the 169 letters contained in the volume only seven are by Eobanus, all the other are by former pupils and friends. The volume is furthermore interspersed with some of Eobanus' verses and numerous poetic compositions by his friends. The volume actually represents an act of reverence originated by Camerarius shown through letters of numerous contemporary scholars and noble men (cf. G. Huber-Rebenich. Officium amicitiae. Beobachtungen zu den Kriterien frühneuzeitlichen Briefsammlungen am Beispiel der von Joachim Camerarius herausgegebenen Hessus-Korrespondenz, in: “Menti amore legati. Lateinische Freundschaftsdichtung und Dichterfreundschaft in Mittelalter und Neuzeit”, Heidelberg, 2001, pp. 145-156).“Seit seiner ersten Zeit in Erfurt hat Hessus bis zum Ende seines Lebens einen regen Briefwechsel mit Freunden, Gönnern und anderen einflussreichen Personen gepflegt, nicht zuletzt mit den Wittenberger Reformatoren. Die Korrespondenz enthält viel Persönliches aus seinem Umfeld. Gegenstand sind ebenso familiäre Angelegenheiten und Verabredungen mit Freunden, die Aufschluss über das gesellige Leben innerhalb des Humanistenzirkels geben, wie Beziehungen zu (potentiellen) Förderern und Dienstherren. Des weiteren tauschte man sich über literarische Fragen aus, über die Beschaffung von Büchern, eigene Arbeiten oder die Werke anderer - klassischer oder zeitgenössischer - Autoren. Jedoch nahm Hessus in seinen Briefen auch zu aktuellen politischen, religiösen und sozialen Fragen Stellung; seine Urteile sind freilich in der Regel eher emotional geprägt denn als kohärente programmatische Äusserungen zu verstehen. Insgesamt gibt sich Hessus in seinem Briefwechsel als gutmütige Persönlichkeit ohne scharfe Kanten zu erkennen. Ein aggressiver Tonfall wird allenfalls laut, wenn Hessus seine Dichtkunst nicht angemessen gewürdigt sieht, oder im Konflikt mit radikalen Gegnern der klassischen Bildung. Mit fortschreitendem Alter nimmt in den persönlichen Äusserungen die Klage über finanzielle Nöte und gesundheitliche Probleme immer mehr Raum ein. Mag Hessus Briefen auch die intellektuelle Tiefe und Kohärenz etwa der Korrespondenz eines Melanchthons abgehen, so stellen sie doch eine wertvolle zeithistorische Quelle dar und geben durch die oft sehr spontan wirkenden Äusserungen Einblick in das Alltagsleben einen humanistischen Dichters” (G. Huber-Rebenich & S. Lütkemeyer, Helius Eobanus Hessus, in: “Deutscher Humanismus 1480-1520. Verfasserlexikon”, F.J. Worstbrock, ed., Berlin & New York, 2008, I/4, pp. 1110). T6r) Eobanus Koch (Coccius) was born at Halgehausen, near Frankenberg (Hassia), the son of a peasant in the service of the Cistercian abbey of Haina, north of Marburg. He adopted his first name Helius on account of being born on a Sunday. He was educated at first by Abbot Dietmar of Haina and subsequently by Johann Mebes in the Latin school of Gmünden, which he attended until 1502. After further schooling at Frankenberg under Jakob Horle, he registered at the University of Erfurt, where he was introduced to Latin poetry by Maternus Pistoris. The humanist Crotus Rubeanus took an affectionate interest in him from the time of his arrival.A feud in 1505 between the artisans of Erfurt and the students offered Eobanus the opportunity of publishing his first work, De pugna studentium erphordiensium (1506). After graduating in September 1506, he was appointed headmaster of the school of St. Severus in Erfurt. In 1508 he published De amantium infoelicitate and a year later his Bucolicon and was recognized at once by Mutianus Rufus and Ulrich von Hutten to be unrivalled among the Latin poets of Germany.In autumn of 1509 Eobanus entered the service of a former pupil, Job von Dobeneck, who had since become bishop of Pomesiana in East Prussia and resided in the latter's residence at Riesenburg. In 1514 were published at Leipzig his Sylvae, a collection of local, historical and military poems, idylls, epigrams and occasional pieces he wrote in the preceding years in Prussia. In the same year appeared his best work of poetry, a most original volume with the title Heroides in imitation of Ovid, consisting of letters from holy women, from the Virgin Mary down to Kunigunde, wife of Emperor Henry II.After his return to Erfurt in July 1514, he was soon the center of a circles of humanists. Jointly with Mutianus, Crotus, and Johannes Petrejus he spoke in support of Reuchlin. He sympathized with the patriotic goals of Ulrich von Hutten, and enthusiastically adopted Erasmus' program of learning and religious reform. He also lent a hand in the composition of the famous Epistolae obscurorum virorum (1515). With his appointment as professor of poetry in July 1518, he came to occupy a secure and influential position in the university. When Luther passed through Erfurt in April 1521, Eobanus greeted him with a speech on behalf of the university and later also composed poetry in praise and support of Luther. His faithful adherence to the Lutheran movement did not, however, prevent the continuation of his sincere friendship and correspondence with Erasmus.In 1523 Eobanus took up the study of medicine, hoping to alleviate his increasing financial hardship. Although he did not gain a medical degree, his efforts produced a very successful and widely read didactic poem on dietetics, Bonae valetudinis conservandae praecepta (1524). Through the influence of Joachim Camerarius and Melanchthon, he obtained a post at Nuremberg in 1526. Together with Camerarius he taught until 1533 at the Gymnasium of St. Aegidius which had recently be founded by Melanchthon. But, finding a regular life distasteful, he again went back to Erfurt in 1533. He found the intellectual climate there deteriorated to such a degree, that he was glad to accept a position at the University of Marburg. Here he was elected rector in 1538 and completed his verse paraphrase of the Psalms, which was highly praised by Luther and reprinted more than fifty times. He also produced the only Latin version of the Iliad ever to be published (1540). When he died at Marburg in October 1540, Eobanus was considered the foremost Latin poet of his age (cf. I. Grässer Eberbach, Helius Eobanus Hessus: der Poet des Erfurter Humanistenkreises, Erfurt, 1993, passim).

authors.name: Goselini Giuliano
authors.biography: Giuliano Goselini (1525–1587) stands as one of the most compelling and multifaceted figures of sixteenth-century Italian political and literary culture. Operating at the turbulent intersection of Renaissance humanism, imperial statecraft, and Counter-Reformation diplomacy, Goselini embodied the ideal of the scholar-courtier who seamlessly combined high lyrical ambition with the demanding, pragmatic duties of chancery governance. As principal secretary to Don Ferrante Gonzaga (the Imperial Governor of the Duchy of Milan) and subsequently to successive Spanish governors under King Philip II, Goselini occupied a privileged vantage point from which to observe, record, and shape the geopolitics of the Italian Wars and the consolidation of Spanish hegemony in Northern Italy. His career represents a definitive bridge between the civic humanism of early modern Italy and the emerging bureaucratic apparatus of the early modern Absolutist state.Born in Rome in 1525 to a family of Milanese origins, Goselini spent his early formative years amidst the vibrant intellectual milieu of the Papal capital and Lombardy. His early education was steeped in classical philology, rhetoric, jurisprudence, and Latinity, cultivating a literary prose style marked by syntactic elegance and historical gravity. Returning to Milan during a decade of severe political instability following the death of Francesco II Sforza and the definitive absorption of the Duchy into the imperial sphere of Charles V, Goselini quickly attracted the notice of local aristocratic patrons and imperial officials through his eloquence and administrative aptitude. His formal entry into political life occurred in 1546, when he entered the service of Don Ferrante Gonzaga, Marquis of Castiglione and Newly appointed Governor of Milan. For nearly a decade, Goselini functioned as Gonzaga's right-hand confidant, drafting sensitive diplomatic dispatches, managing espionage networks, and composing state manifestos during the grueling conflicts against French forces in Piedmont and the complex negotiations surrounding the Council of Trent.The high-stakes political environment of Spanish Milan, however, rendered Goselini vulnerable to court intrigue and factional rivalries. Following Ferrante Gonzaga’s fall from imperial favor and subsequent recall in 1554—triggered by accusations of fiscal mismanagement and geopolitical miscalculations in Parma and Monferrato—Goselini became a target of Gonzaga's political enemies within the Milanese Senate and the Spanish crown. In 1555, Goselini was arrested on charges of high treason, financial corruption, and secret complicity in anti-Spanish conspiracies. Incarcerated within the formidable dungeons of the Castello Sforzesco in Milan for nearly two years, he faced severe interrogation and the threat of execution. Demonstrating extraordinary resilience and rhetorical skill, Goselini drafted an extensive series of legal defenses, analytical memorials, and formal apologiae that ultimately demonstrated his unwavering loyalty to the crown and exposed the malice of his accusers. Released and fully rehabilitated in 1557 under the governorship of Cristoforo Madruzzo, Prince-Bishop of Trent, Goselini was reinstated into the Milanese chancery, eventually attaining the prestigious office of Secretary of the Secret Council (Segretario del Consiglio Segreto), a position he held with immense authority under subsequent Spanish governors, including Gabriel de la Cueva, Duke of Alburquerque, and Antonio de Guzmán, Marquis of Ayamonte, until his death in 1587.Goselini’s literary production is broad, encompassing historical narrative, lyric poetry, political theory, and epistolary collections. His masterpiece is unquestionably the Vita del Principe Don Ferrando Gonzaga, marchese di Mantova, e duca di Ariano, first published in Venice in 1574 by the publisher Giovanni Battista Valvassori, and subsequently reissued in expanded editions by Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari and Barezzo Barezzi. Far more than a conventional panegyric, the Vita is a monumental work of military and political historiography. Writing with the analytical sharpness of Tacitus and the realistic political insight of Machiavelli—tempered by strict Counter-Reformation orthodoxy—Goselini provided an exhaustive chronicling of the Italian Wars, imperial strategy, siege warfare, and court politics. He meticulously defended Gonzaga’s controversial military decisions while offering an unprecedented primary account of the administration of Renaissance Milan under Habsburg rule. The work established Goselini as one of the premier historians of his generation, lauded across European courts for its stylistic vigor and wealth of archival detail.In addition to his historiographical endeavors, Goselini was a celebrated poet whose work reflected the refined Petrarchist revival of the late Cinquecento. His Rime, first issued in Venice by Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari in 1572 and subsequently enlarged in 1573 and 1588, achieved wide acclaim across the Italian Peninsula. Goselini’s lyrical verse ranges from sublime love poetry written in the polished vernacular tradition to gravitas-laden moral sonnets, heroic encomia dedicated to European princes, and poignant elegies reflecting upon his unjust imprisonment in the Castello Sforzesco. His literary networks were vast: he maintained close epistolary and intellectual exchanges with major literary figures of the era, including Torquato Tasso, Annibale Caro, Girolamo Ruscelli, Lodovico Domenichi, and Giovan Battista Pigna. Goselini was also an active member of prestigious literary academies, notably the Accademia dei Trasformati in Milan and the Accademia degli Affidati in Pavia, contributing significantly to the cultural cohesion of Lombard elite society.The material and typographical history of Goselini’s works illustrates the sophisticated commercial dynamics of sixteenth-century Italian publishing. Recognizing Venice as the undeniable printing capital of the Western world, Goselini systematically entrusted his manuscripts to elite Venetian printshops. His long-standing partnership with Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari ensured that his Rime and revised historical treatises were produced with superior typographical craftsmanship, featuring elegant italic fonts, intricate woodcut printer's devices (such as Giolito's famous Phoenix), and lavish ornamental initials. Following his death in Milan in 1587, his extensive epistolary correspondence was collected and published as De le lettere di M. Giuliano Goselini (Venice: Paolo Megietti, 1589; later reissued by the Giunti press in 1592). This epistolary corpus remains a cornerstone resource for historians, offering invaluable insights into the daily mechanics of chancery drafting, literary patronage, and secret diplomatic maneuvering in sixteenth-century Italy.The historical legacy of Giuliano Goselini is that of an indispensable architect of Lombard historical memory and administrative culture. While nineteenth-century historiography occasionally viewed him through the narrow lens of Spanish domination in Italy, modern scholarship—spearheaded by historians such as Federico Chabod, Claudio Mutini, and Maria Antonietta Visceglia—has fundamentally reassessed Goselini as a crucial figure in the development of early modern political rationality. His ability to synthesize high literary art with imperial governance allowed him to articulate a sophisticated defense of Italian political identity within the framework of the Spanish Empire. Today, Goselini is recognized not only as an exceptional biographer and poet, but as a central witness to the transformation of Renaissance Italy into the bureaucratic landscape of the early modern world.

publishers.name: Meietti Paolo
publishers.biography: Paolo Meietti was a printer, publisher, and bookseller active in Venice, Padua, Vicenza, and Bologna, and the son of Giovanni Battista. He worked both on his own and with his brother Antonio. In Padua, he had a shop at Porteghi Alti in the San Lorenzo district. As a publisher, he used Lorenzo Pasquato’s printing press in Padua, those of Giorgio Angelieri and Giovanni Alberti in Venice, Giorgio Greco’s in Vicenza, and Giovanni Rossi’s in Bologna. He continued to work as a publisher and bookseller at least until 1615.

academic_description: 8vo. [8], 215, [1] leaves. Collation: a8, A-Z8, Aa-Dd8. The leaves a7, a8 and Dd8 are blank. With the printer's device on the title-page. Entries of ownership on the title-page by Carolus de Bonfilijs and Blasius Parallius. Contemporary vellum, manuscript title on the spine. First edition published posthumously by Bartolomeo Ichino and dedicated by him to Don Luis de Castilla (Milano, January 1, 1592).“Recueil postume de 230 lettres, dans lequel se mêlent les lettres personelles de Goselini, 9 lettres qu'on lui addresse ou qui parlent de lui et des ses ouvrages, et 6 lettres au moins qu'il écrit au nom d'autrui. Les 2 lettres les plus anciennes sont de 1547 et de 1550, mais le plus grand nombre est postérieur à 1570; la plus tardive est du 24 décembre 1586. Le classement semble déterminé par des efforts faits dans des voies différentes: ordre chronologique, groups de lettres sur des sujets semblables ou sur une même affaire, séries de lettres à un même destinataire comme ces 21 lettres exceptionnellement intitulées XXII [sic] lettere all'Illustre Signor Annibal Guasco, ou ces dizaines de lettres à un reverend anonyme, parent et ami de Goselini; mais aucun n'aboutit vraiment. Le compilateur s'est peut-être contenté de mettre bout à bout les paquets de lettres dans l'ordre où ils lui parviennent” (J. Basso, Le genre épistolaire en langue italienne (1538-1662). Répertoire chronologique et analytique, Roma & Nancy, 1990, p. 326).“Eppure […] il primo volume, se non erro, che issi nel frontespizio la condizione di segretario del suo autore è quello delle Lettere scritte (a suo nome o a nome d'altri?) da Giuliano Goselini, edito nel 1592, ‘Secretario già di D. Ferrante Gonzaga in Milano: poi del Re Catholico, appresso gli altri Governatori, et Capitani Generali in quello stato, et in Italia': è privo della divisione per ‘capi' e conserva, in molte lettere, sia la data che il nome del destinatario e del luogo” (A. Milano, March 16, 1565 (l. 214v) The little we know about the early years and the education of Giuliano Goselini (or Gosellini) is told by his friend, the poet Francesco Melchiori in the Sommario della vita del signor Giuliano Goselini, which the latter had published at Venice in 1588, soon after his friend's death, together with the fifth edition of Goselini's Rime.Goselini was born in Rome in 1525 and at the age of two moved to Nizza Monferrato, his father's hometown. At fourteen he came back to Rome and was welcomed in the family of the cardinal Guido Ascanio Sforza di Santa Fiora, nephew of pope Paul III. In 1542 he is found as chancellor at the service of the prince of Molfetta and viceroy of Sicily, Ferrante Gonzaga. In 1546 Gonzaga was elected general governor of the Duchy of Milan and Goselini followed him as secretary and from 1550 on he was appointed secretary of the Secret Chancellery.In Milan he made the acquaintance of other literati connected to that court like Leone Leoni, Luca Contile, and Girolamo Muzio, and became a member of the local Accademia dei Fenici. When Gonzaga was removed from the government of Milan in 1554, Goselini could keep his office in the chancellery thanks to his reputation as a poet and his good relationships with Gonzaga's two main opponents, Diego de Vargas and Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, Bishop of Arras. But at the same time he was also able to remain in good terms with Gonzaga and his family (the sons Cesare and Ferrante, and the grandson Ferrante II) for the rest of his life.Between 1556 and 1557 Goselini visited Philipp II's court in Brussels to consolidate his position in Milan, but in 1558 he lost his office. Through the intervention of Cesare Gonzaga, he was soon after rehabilitated and won the favour of the new governor, Don Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, who in 1560 wanted him at his side during a long sojourn at the Spanish court.In August 1567 Goselini was involved in a dubious plot and imprisoned by order of governor Gabriel de la Cueva, Duke of Alburquerque. With the help of Cesare Gonzaga and Emanuele Filiberto, Duke of Savoy, in June 1568, he was finally released and acquitted of all accusation. In 1572 he published the first edition of his successful Rime, followed a year later by a volume with a commentary to them (Dichiaratione di alcuni componimenti del S. Giuliano Gosellini). In 1574 he issued his main historical work, Vita del principe don Ferrante Gonzaga, a tribute to his patron and benefactor. Goselini died in Milan in February 1587 (cf. F. Pagella, Un poligrafo alessandrino del Cinquecento: Giuliano Goselini, in: “Rivista di storia, arte, archeologia per la provincia di Alessandria”, XXXII, 1923, pp. 3-39).
