authors.name: Ariosto Ludovico
authors.biography: Ludovico Ariosto (8 September 1474–6 July 1533) was the supreme poet of the Italian Renaissance romance and one of the most influential writers in the formation of modern European literary culture. His Orlando furioso, first published at Ferrara in 1516 and definitively revised in 1532, transformed the inherited traditions of Carolingian and Arthurian chivalric romance into an extraordinarily sophisticated poetic architecture of interlaced narratives, shifting perspectives, irony, erotic desire, political allegory, and psychological instability. At once a continuation of Matteo Maria Boiardo's unfinished Orlando innamorato and a radical reinvention of the chivalric poem, the Furioso became one of the great commercial and cultural successes of sixteenth-century Europe.Ariosto's achievement, however, extends far beyond the Furioso. His Satire constitute an unusually intimate document of the intellectual's relationship with court, patronage, money, travel, and personal independence; his comedies helped establish the forms of learned Renaissance comedy in the vernacular; his Latin poetry belongs to the humanist culture of late fifteenth-century Ferrara; and his Rime and other shorter works reveal the continuing interaction between Latin, Petrarchan, courtly, and popular traditions. Above all, Ariosto occupies a crucial position in the history of Italian literary language. His progressive revision of the Furioso, culminating in the 1532 edition, represents one of the most consequential acts of linguistic self-revision in Renaissance literature, as he moved from the mixed northern Italian literary idiom of the first edition toward a more consistently Tuscan literary language under the decisive influence of Pietro Bembo.Early life, family, education, and humanist formationAriosto was born on 8 September 1474 at Reggio Emilia, where his father, Count Niccolò Ariosto, served the Este dynasty as commander of the citadel. His mother, Daria Malaguzzi Valeri, belonged to an established Reggio family. Ludovico was the eldest of ten children. In 1484 the family moved to Ferrara, the principal political and cultural centre of the Este court, where Ariosto would spend most of his life.His father initially directed him toward the study of law. Between approximately 1489 and 1494 Ariosto attended legal studies at the University of Ferrara, but he disliked the profession and eventually obtained permission to abandon it. His intellectual interests had already turned decisively toward literature. From the mid-1490s he devoted himself to the study of Latin authors under the humanist Gregorio da Spoleto, whose teaching played an important role in his formation. Ariosto began composing Latin poetry, demonstrating a familiarity with the classical literary tradition that would remain fundamental throughout his career.His early literary environment was the extraordinarily cultivated court of Ferrara. He encountered the Latin and vernacular traditions cultivated under the Este, and his intellectual circle included figures such as Ercole Strozzi and Pietro Bembo. Bembo's presence in Ferrara in 1502–1503 was particularly significant for the subsequent history of Ariosto's language, although the full extent and chronology of their intellectual exchange must not be reduced to a simple master-disciple relationship.The death of Niccolò Ariosto in 1500 transformed Ludovico's circumstances. As eldest son, he became responsible for a large family and could no longer devote himself exclusively to literary studies. In 1502 he was appointed captain of the fortress of Canossa; in 1503 he entered the service of Cardinal Ippolito d'Este. His subsequent career therefore developed within the structures of Este patronage, even though the Satire would repeatedly reveal his ambivalence toward courtly service.From 1503 to 1517 Ariosto served Cardinal Ippolito, undertaking various missions and diplomatic journeys. His service brought him into contact with the turbulent political world of the Italian Wars and repeatedly interrupted his literary work. In 1517, when Ippolito expected him to accompany him to Hungary, Ariosto refused and entered the service of Ippolito's brother, Duke Alfonso I d'Este. This change considerably improved the conditions under which he could pursue literature.Between 1522 and 1525 Ariosto served as governor of Garfagnana, a difficult frontier territory troubled by factional conflict and banditry. The experience supplied a striking counterpoint to the image of Ariosto as the detached court poet: his correspondence and Satire reveal the practical difficulties of administration, the pressures of political authority, and his persistent desire for intellectual and personal independence.After returning to Ferrara in 1525, Ariosto increasingly concentrated on literary activity and on the revision of his major works. He supervised theatrical productions at the Este court and continued revising the Orlando furioso until its definitive printing in 1532.Latin poetry and the transition to the vernacularAriosto's earliest literary production was predominantly Latin. His Latin poems include elegies, epigrams, epithalamia, epitaphs, odes, and other occasional compositions, demonstrating his integration into the humanist culture of late fifteenth- and early sixteenth-century Italy.His eventual predominance as a vernacular author did not represent a rejection of classical culture. On the contrary, the Furioso depends upon a profound assimilation of classical epic, elegiac, historiographical, and rhetorical models. Ariosto's relationship to antiquity is nevertheless fundamentally Renaissance rather than imitative: classical materials are incorporated into a heterogeneous literary world in which ancient mythology, medieval romance, contemporary politics, Petrarchan lyricism, and popular narrative coexist.The first collected edition of his Latin Carmina appeared posthumously in Venice in 1553, edited by Giovan Battista Pigna and printed by Vincenzo Valgrisi. This chronology is significant because, unlike the Furioso, much of Ariosto's Latin and minor poetic production reached print only after his death.The theatreAriosto was also a foundational figure in the development of Renaissance learned comedy (commedia erudita). His dramatic production emerged from the theatrical culture of the Este court and combined the structures of Plautine and Terentian comedy with contemporary Italian social observation.La Cassaria was first represented at Ferrara in 1508 and was originally written in prose. I Suppositi followed in 1509, likewise initially in prose. Ariosto subsequently transformed both plays into verse versions. Il Negromante underwent a particularly complex compositional history, existing in more than one version, while La Lena, first performed in 1528, represents the mature phase of his theatrical writing.The editorial history of the comedies is markedly different from that of the Furioso.The early circulation of La Cassaria and I Suppositi included unauthorized printed editions derived from theatrical scripts. The later plays circulated partly through manuscripts and posthumous printings. Il Negromante appeared in print after Ariosto's death, while La Lena was first printed in 1551. The first collected edition of Ariosto's theatre appeared only in 1562 in the Giolito press, edited by Girolamo Porcacchi. Thus the dramatic corpus was not established through a single authorially controlled edition comparable to the Furioso.The SatireBetween approximately 1517 and 1524 Ariosto composed the seven Satire, written in terza rima. They are among the most revealing documents of his intellectual personality. Their form deliberately recalls Horatian satire and epistle, but their subject matter is distinctly Renaissance: courtly service, patronage, money, ecclesiastical and political ambition, travel, family obligations, literary independence, and the practical conditions of intellectual life.The Satire do not constitute a systematic philosophical treatise, nor should their ethical position simply be labelled Stoic. Their recurring ideal is rather one of measured independence: Ariosto repeatedly contrasts the freedom of the private intellectual life with the dependence generated by patronage and office. The resulting voice is simultaneously ironic, conversational, self-conscious, and autobiographical.Their first circulation was partly clandestine. A first unauthorized edition appeared in 1534, shortly after Ariosto's death, while the important Giolito edition appeared at Venice in 1550. The history of the Satire therefore illustrates the general problem affecting Ariosto's minor works: unlike the Furioso, they were not stabilized by a final authorial edition.Orlando furioso: conception and literary architectureAriosto's masterpiece grew out of the unfinished Orlando innamorato of Matteo Maria Boiardo. Ariosto adopted Boiardo's characters and narrative world but radically expanded and reorganized them. The poem was probably begun around 1504–1506, with the earliest secure evidence dating from the first decade of the century.The Furioso is constructed in ottava rima, with the characteristic rhyme scheme ABABABCC. Its immense narrative structure is organized through entrelacement: Ariosto repeatedly interrupts one narrative line at moments of maximum tension and moves to another character, geographical location, or episode before eventually returning to the suspended action.Three broad narrative axes dominate the poem. The first is the war between Charlemagne's Christian forces and the Saracen armies of Agramante. The second is Orlando's love for Angelica and his descent into madness when he discovers her relationship with Medoro. The third is the romance of Ruggiero and Bradamante, whose eventual union establishes the legendary ancestry of the Este dynasty. These plots are not simply separate stories. Ariosto continually allows them to intersect, echo, contradict, and comment upon one another. The resulting narrative is simultaneously epic, romance, comedy, tragedy, satire, erotic poetry, and philosophical reflection.The episode of Astolfo's journey to the Moon provides the most famous emblem of Ariosto's narrative imagination. Astolfo travels to the lunar world to recover Orlando's lost reason, which is stored there among the innumerable things lost by humanity. The episode transforms an adventure-romance motif into an extraordinary meditation on human folly, desire, reputation, ambition, and the instability of rational consciousness.Ariosto's irony is equally important. The narrator frequently reminds the reader of the artificiality of storytelling, comments upon his own narrative procedures, addresses the audience directly, and shifts between comic distance and emotional involvement. The poem therefore does not merely tell stories: it continuously reflects upon the processes by which stories are invented, believed, interrupted, remembered, and transmitted.The first edition: Ferrara, 1516The first edition of the Orlando furioso was printed at Ferrara by Giovanni Mazzocco da Bondeno and appeared on 22 April 1516. It consisted of forty cantos and was dedicated to Cardinal Ippolito d'Este. The edition was an in-quarto volume and was produced under Ariosto's close supervision. The print run is often estimated at approximately 1,300 copies, although the exact figure remains uncertain.The linguistic character of this first Furioso is crucial. It is not yet the linguistically standardized poem familiar to modern readers. Ariosto's language combines Tuscan literary elements with the northern Italian literary koinè, Ferrarese and Po valley forms, Latinisms, and expressions of popular or regional origin. The first edition therefore documents an earlier stage in Ariosto's conception of literary Italian.Its immediate success was extraordinary. The poem quickly escaped the confines of the Este court and began circulating throughout Italy. Numerous reprints followed, often without the degree of authorial control that Ariosto desired.The second edition: Ferrara, 1521Ariosto responded to the rapid circulation of the Furioso by producing a second edition, printed at Ferrara by Giovan Battista Della Pigna on 13 February 1521. It retained the forty-canto structure but incorporated numerous textual corrections and linguistic modifications. The scale of revision is significant. The 1521 text does not constitute a wholly new poem, but Ariosto systematically corrected vocabulary, morphology, spelling, and individual verses. The surviving evidence indicates hundreds of substantive interventions, together with an errata that demonstrates his increasing concern with linguistic precision.The 1521 edition occupies a particularly important place in the history of Ariosto's textual development because it represents the intermediate stage between the mixed literary language of 1516 and the more systematic Tuscanization of 1532.The third edition: Ferrara, 1532The definitive edition appeared at Ferrara on 1 October 1532, printed by Francesco Rosso da Valenza. It expanded the poem from forty to forty-six cantos and substantially reorganized and enlarged the narrative.The new material includes major episodes such as the story of Olimpia, the adventures associated with Marganorre and Drusilla, the episode involving Ruggiero and Leone, and other additions that fundamentally alter the scale and balance of the poem. Ariosto did not merely append six cantos to the earlier text: he revised existing material, redistributed episodes, modified transitions, and transformed the poem's linguistic surface.The linguistic revision is perhaps the most consequential feature of the 1532 edition. Following the publication of Pietro Bembo's Prose della volgar lingua in 1525, Ariosto moved decisively toward the Tuscan literary model based principally on the great fourteenth-century authors. This process has often been described as a "conversion" to Bembo's linguistic programme, although the relationship was not mechanical. Ariosto adopted Bembo's norms selectively and poetically, retaining forms whenever rhythm, sound, meaning, or expressive force required them.The poem itself acknowledges Bembo in the final canto, where Ariosto praises him as the figure who has demonstrated what the "pure and sweet" vernacular should be. The 1532 Furioso consequently became one of the principal monuments of the emerging Italian literary language.The 1532 edition was Ariosto's last major authorial intervention. He died less than a year later, on 6 July 1533, at Ferrara.The Cinque cantiThe Cinque canti occupy a peculiar position in the textual history of the Furioso. They consist of five cantos, amounting to 548 ottave, which were not incorporated into the 1532 poem.They were first published posthumously in 1545 by the heirs of Aldo Manuzio at Venice, appended to an edition of the Furioso, and were printed separately in 1546 by Bernardo Giunti. Their intended relationship to the Furioso remains debated. Some scholars have interpreted them as material belonging to a projected continuation; others have proposed that they represent an earlier stage of Ariosto's work. They must therefore not simply be treated as "cantos 47–51" of the Orlando furioso.The posthumous explosion of the FuriosoAriosto's death did not interrupt the circulation of the poem; rather, it inaugurated an extraordinary phase of editorial expansion. More than 360 Italian editions of Ariosto appeared during the sixteenth century, including editions printed in France and numerous editions produced in Venice. The Venetian publishing industry—especially the presses associated with the Giolito family, Vincenzo Valgrisi, Zoppino, Valvassori, Bindoni and Pasini—played a decisive role in making Ariosto one of the most widely circulated Italian authors of the Renaissance.The first properly illustrated edition of the Furioso was printed by Nicolò Zoppino at Venice in 1530, with woodcuts at the beginning of the cantos. This inaugurated a major transformation in the way readers experienced the poem: the Furioso increasingly became not only a textual but also a visual object.The most important early Venetian edition was that produced by Gabriele Giolito de' Ferrari in 1542, edited by Lodovico Dolce. It was followed by numerous reprints and helped establish the editorial model through which Ariosto was presented to a mass reading public. The 1542 edition appeared between 31 May and 23 June, according to documentary evidence recently highlighted by the University of Bologna project on Ariosto's printers and publishers.An even more influential stage came with Vincenzo Valgrisi's Venetian edition of 1556, edited by Girolamo Ruscelli. Ruscelli supplied extensive annotationi, explanatory material, summaries, interpretative apparatus, and a glossary of difficult words. The edition also contained forty-six full-page woodcuts, one for each canto, transforming the complex narrative structure into a sequence of visual tableaux.The Valgrisi-Ruscelli edition thus represents a crucial moment in the "canonization" of Ariosto. The reader was no longer presented simply with Ariosto's poem: the text was surrounded by biography, annotations, summaries, allegorical interpretation, vocabulary, indexes, and images. The editorial apparatus actively taught readers how the poem should be navigated and interpreted.This tradition culminated in elaborate later sixteenth-century editions, including the Venetian edition of 1584, which in turn became an important source for Sir John Harington's English translation of 1591.Ariosto and the history of Italian literary languageThe editorial history of the Furioso is inseparable from the history of Italian. The 1516 edition represents a northern Italian literary idiom still characterized by substantial linguistic variation. The 1521 edition introduces systematic corrections, while the 1532 edition undertakes a much more extensive alignment with the Tuscan literary model associated with Petrarch and codified theoretically by Bembo. Ariosto's importance is therefore not simply that he "adopted Tuscan." His achievement lies in demonstrating that the Tuscan literary norm could sustain an enormous narrative poem whose origins lay in the northern Italian chivalric tradition. The Furioso helped elevate the romance tradition from a regional and courtly form into one of the central genres of Italian literary culture.At the same time, Ariosto did not become a mechanical follower of Bembo. His linguistic choices remain responsive to metre, rhyme, sound, narrative register, characterization, and expressive effect. The result is a literary language that is normative without being rigid and classical without ceasing to be dramatically flexible.Rime, Erbolato, and the minor worksAriosto's Rime circulated initially in manuscript and were not established in a definitive authorial collection during his lifetime. A major printed collection appeared at Venice in 1545, together with L'Erbolato, a short prose work attributed to Ariosto. L'Erbolato is a satirical mock discourse presented as the speech of a quack medicine seller. Its comic rhetoric and parody of learned and commercial language complement the more serious social observations of the Satire.The posthumous history of these works illustrates an important distinction in Ariostean textual scholarship: the Furioso is an authorially controlled printed text existing in three successive authorial states, whereas much of the rest of the corpus survived through manuscripts, copies, unauthorized editions, and posthumous editorial constructions. Modern Ariosto scholarship has consequently devoted substantial attention to reconstructing the textual history of individual works rather than relying on the later sixteenth-century collected editions.European receptionThe Furioso rapidly became an international phenomenon. In Spain, Jerónimo de Urrea's translation appeared in 1549 and was repeatedly reprinted. In France, Ariosto circulated in translation and adaptation throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. In England, Sir John Harington published the first complete English translation in 1591. Harington's version was not a neutral linguistic transfer: he added moral commentary, adapted the poem's rhetorical presentation, and participated in the broader process through which Ariosto was assimilated to English literary expectations.The English reception was particularly important. Edmund Spenser drew extensively upon Ariosto in The Faerie Queene (1590), although he transformed Ariosto's narrative techniques into a more explicitly allegorical and moralizing structure. Shakespeare also encountered Ariostean materials: the plot of Much Ado About Nothing is connected to the Ariostean story of Ariodante and Ginevra, while the Orlando furioso belongs more generally to the repertory of Italian narrative sources available to Elizabethan dramatists.Ariosto's influence subsequently extended through European poetry, opera, visual art, translation, parody, and adaptation. The poem was particularly important for the development of the European romance tradition and for the idea of the long narrative poem as an open structure capable of incorporating heterogeneous genres and tones.Critical controversy: Ariosto and TassoThe central theoretical controversy surrounding Ariosto in the later sixteenth century concerned the legitimacy of romance itself. Ariosto's Furioso does not conform to the Aristotelian ideal of a tightly unified epic action. Its narrative proliferates, interrupts itself, changes protagonists, crosses geographical and generic boundaries, and frequently shifts from the sublime to the comic.This structural freedom became a central issue in Renaissance literary criticism. Giovan Battista Pigna defended the romance tradition in I Romanzi (1554), while Giambattista Giraldi Cinzio also contributed to the theoretical defence of Ariostean narrative. The later rise of Torquato Tasso's Gerusalemme liberata provided a contrasting model of epic unity, moral seriousness, and Aristotelian organization.The opposition between "Ariosto" and "Tasso" subsequently became one of the defining conceptual binaries of Italian Renaissance poetics: romance versus epic, multiplicity versus unity, irony versus moral seriousness, narrative freedom versus formal discipline. Yet modern scholarship has increasingly shown that Ariosto's apparent freedom is supported by an extraordinarily sophisticated system of structural recurrence, thematic parallelism, and narrative control.Modern textual scholarship and the editorial reconstruction of AriostoModern Ariosto scholarship has progressively moved away from treating the 1532 Furioso as the only relevant textual state. The landmark critical edition prepared by Santorre Debenedetti and Cesare Segre, Orlando furioso secondo l'edizione del 1532 con le varianti delle edizioni del 1516 e del 1521, published in Bologna in 1960, established a fundamental scholarly framework by presenting the definitive text together with the variants of the two earlier authorial editions.The broader project Tutte le opere di Ludovico Ariosto, launched by Mondadori in the 1960s, produced important volumes for the Furioso, the comedies, and the Satire, Erbolato, and Lettere, although the projected complete series was never finished. Subsequent scholarship has greatly refined the picture. Modern editions of the 1516 Furioso, including those by Marco Dorigatti (2006) and Marco Praloran and Tina Matarrese (2016), have returned particular attention to the first authorial state. New editions of the theatre, La Cassaria, the Cinque canti, and the Satire, together with studies of Ariosto's autograph manuscripts, have likewise demonstrated the necessity of treating his corpus as a complex network of authorial, manuscript, and printed traditions.This development is fundamental to understanding Ariosto's achievement. The Orlando furioso is not a single immutable work that happened to receive three editions. It is a poem whose meaning is partly constituted by its successive authorial states: the forty-canto poem of 1516, the revised forty-canto poem of 1521, and the expanded and linguistically transformed forty-six-canto poem of 1532.Death and legacyAriosto died at Ferrara on 6 July 1533, only months after the publication of the definitive Orlando furioso. He left behind a body of work whose subsequent editorial history would become almost as important as its original composition. During the sixteenth century alone, Ariosto's works appeared in hundreds of editions, and the Furioso became a central object of illustration, commentary, translation, adaptation, and scholarly controversy. The poem's success was not simply a consequence of its narrative appeal. Printers, editors, commentators, illustrators, translators, and booksellers progressively transformed the Furioso into a European cultural object.Its history is therefore inseparable from the history of the Renaissance book. Ariosto himself understood the power of print sufficiently to revise the Furioso repeatedly and to supervise its successive editions. Later publishers expanded that process by adding illustrations, summaries, allegories, annotations, glossaries, biographies, indexes, and translations. Ariosto's lasting importance consequently rests on several achievements at once. He perfected the Italian chivalric romance; transformed ottava rima into a vehicle of extraordinary intellectual and tonal range; created a new model of narrative multiplicity; contributed decisively to the stabilization of Italian literary language; established Renaissance comedy in forms of lasting importance; and provided European literature with one of its most influential representations of desire, madness, illusion, heroism, and the instability of human reason.Above all, the Orlando furioso remains a monument to the paradoxical union of order and freedom. Its surface appears endlessly centrifugal—characters disappear and return, stories are interrupted, geographical horizons continually expand, and the narrator refuses to surrender entirely to any single moral or ideological perspective. Yet beneath this apparent proliferation lies one of the most carefully revised literary structures of the Renaissance. Ariosto's three authorial editions demonstrate that this structure was not accidental: it was the product of nearly three decades of continuous poetic, linguistic, and editorial labour.For this reason Ariosto occupies a unique position in European literary history. He was not merely the great poet of Ferrara or the author of the Orlando furioso. He was one of the principal architects of the Renaissance vernacular book, and the successive transformations of his works—from manuscript circulation to authorial printing, from illustrated Venetian editions to European translations and from Renaissance commentary to modern critical editions—form a history of literary transmission almost as remarkable as the poem itself.

academic_description: 4to (249x156 mm). 508, [44] pp. Collation: A-Z8 Aa-Ll8 Mm4. Printer's device on title page and ll. Ff1r, Kk1r, and Mm4r. Leaf Ii8 is a blank. Colophon on l. Ii7v. Text printed in two columns, italic and roman type. With a woodcut architectural title page, numerous decorated initials, and 52 woodcut vignettes printed at the beginning of every book of the poem and the final stanza. On l. Ff1r Gli Cinque canti opens with a separate title page; on l. Kk1r Le sposizione di tutti i vocaboli […] raccolte da M. Lodovico Dolce begins, likewise with a separate title page. Contemporary Lyonnaise binding in richly gilt-tooled light brown morocco, flat spine, panels with large gilt-stamped centre- and corner-pieces, gilt and gauffered edges (skillfully restored, lower joint slightly cracked). On l. A2r the ownership inscription “Juris Consulti D. Joseph Lishri [?]”; on the last back flyleaf the manuscript note “Respize”. Upper margin of l. Ff1 repaired, some staining, slightly and uniformly browned, small round wormhole to the lower margin in the first half of the volume, not affecting the text. A good copy ruled in red throughout. Preserved in a cloth box.The very rare first Italian-language edition printed in France of Ariosto's poem. In the same year Faure-Honorat also issued an 8vo edition and Rouillé an edition in 16mo. The Furioso had previously been printed in Paris and Lyons only in its French and Spanish translations.The significant production of Italian books that came out of French presses in the 1540s and 1550s were intended not only for Italians residing in France, but also the many French speakers who had learned Italian over the course of war, study, or business, including many impressive noblewomen (cf. J. Balsamo, L'italianisme lyonnais et l'illustration de la langue française, in: “Lyon et l'illustration de la langue française à la Renaissance”, Lyon, 2003, pp. 211-229).

authors.name: Rabelais François
authors.biography: François Rabelais (c. 1494 – 9 April 1553) stands as one of the towering intellectual giants of the Northern Renaissance, a quintessential polymath whose career fused Franciscan and Benedictine monasticism, pioneering Hellenic scholarship,Galenic and Hippocratic medicine, Erasmian evangelical theology, and unprecedented literary innovation in the vernacular French tongue. Operating at the tumultuous crossroads of European Humanism, the Protestant Reformation, and the explosion of print culture in sixteenth-century France, Rabelais authored a five-volume prose cycle—comprising Pantagruel (1532), Gargantua (1534), Le Tiers Livre (1546), Le Quart Livre (1548/1552), and the posthumously published Le Cinquième Livre (1564)—that reconfigured the parameters of European satire, narrative architecture, and philosophical comedy. Through his invention of 'Pantagruelism'—a stoic yet joyous philosophical disposition rooted in Christian faith, intellectual freedom, and a contempt for religious bigotry—Rabelais forged a literary universe wherein high scholarly erudition seamlessly coexists with exuberant folk humor, anatomical realism, and linguistic virtuosity.Early Life, Monastic Lineage, and Humanist EducationRabelais was born at La Devinière, a modest family estate situated near Seuilly in the vicinity of Chinon, Touraine. While the exact year of his birth remains a subject of archival debate among scholars—ranging from 1483 to 1494, with c. 1494 accepted by modern consensus—his lineage is securely tied to the legal bourgeoisie of Touraine; his father, Antoine Rabelais, was a prosperous lawyer (avocat) at the royal court of Chinon. Little is documented regarding Rabelais's earliest education, though early biographical tradition suggests initial schooling at the Benedictine Abbey of Seuilly, followed by study at the Franciscan friary of La Baumette near Angers. By the late 1510s, Rabelais had entered the Franciscan Order as a novice, taking holy orders at the convent of Puy-Saint-Martin at Fontenay-le-Comte in Poitou.It was within the austere walls of Fontenay-le-Comte that Rabelais transformed himself into an accomplished Hellenist. In close collaboration with his fellow friar Pierre Amy, Rabelais immersed himself in Classical Greek, a discipline viewed with intense suspicion by the traditionalist theological faculty of the Sorbonne and the conservative Franciscan leadership. During this formative Poitevin period, Rabelais established epistolary contact with the preeminent French humanist Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), the royal librarian and master of Greek scholarship. The correspondence reveals Rabelais as a brilliant young scholar deeply invested in the restoration of ancient texts, legal humanism (mos gallicus), and Erasmian biblical philology. However, the Franciscan superiors at Fontenay-le-Comte, reacting to the destabilizing spread of Lutheran doctrines, cracked down on Greek studies in late 1523, confiscating the Greek manuscripts and printed books belonging to Rabelais and Amy. Seeking intellectual asylum, Rabelais successfully petitioned Pope Clement VII for permission to transfer from the Order of Friars Minor to the more scholarly Order of Saint Benedict. Entering the Benedictine Abbey of Maillezais under the direct patronage and protection of its humanist bishop, Geoffroy d’Estissac, Rabelais spent several years serving as d'Estissac's secretary, traveling across Poitou and expanding his networks among lawyers, administrative officials, and literary figures.Medical Studies, Medical Humanism, and the Lyonnese CrucibleDespite his comfortable position within Benedictine patronage, Rabelais eventually cast off his monastic habit without formal authorization—becoming an apostate friar, though retaining his priestly status—to pursue the study of medicine. In September 1530, he matriculated at the prestigious Faculty of Medicine at the University of Montpellier, one of Europe's premier medical centers. Exhibiting remarkable academic speed, Rabelais obtained his bachelor's degree in medicine (baccalauréat en médecine) on 1 November 1530, delivering authoritative lectures on the Greek medical texts of Hippocrates and Galen directly from original Greek codices, rather than relying on corrupted Medieval Latin translations. His philological approach to medical science aligned him with the vanguard of Renaissance medical humanism.By late 1532, Rabelais had relocated to Lyon, the vibrant commercial, financial, and printing hub of southern France. Lyon offered a unique intellectual sanctuary: free from the immediate jurisdiction of a university faculty of theology like the Sorbonne, it possessed a thriving press culture fueled by master printers, intellectual sodalities, and international merchants. Rabelais secured an appointment as physician to the municipal hospital of Lyon, the Hôtel-Dieu de Notre-Dame de Pitié du Pont-du-Rhône, a post he held with distinction. Simultaneously, he entered into a fruitful collaboration with the eminent scholarly printer Sebastian Gryphius (c. 1492–1556). For Gryphius's press, Rabelais edited and published critical Latin editions of Hippocrates's Aphorisms, Galen's Ars medica, and the legal texts of the Roman jurist Lucius Volusius Maecianus, demonstrating his rigorous academic philology.The Genesis of the Pantagruelian Cycle: Genius under a PseudonymIt was during his initial months in Lyon, late in the autumn of 1532, that Rabelais published his first major vernacular work: Les grandes et inestimables Cronicques du grand et énorme géant Gargantua, followed rapidly by his own original creation, Pantagruel. Les horribles et espadvantables faictz & prouesses du tresrenommé Pantagruel Roy des Dipsodes, filz du grand géant Gargantua. Published under the cryptographic anagrammatic pseudonym Alcofribas Nasier ('Abstracteur de Quinte Essence'), Pantagruel appropriated the popular, lowbrow format of chivalric folk almanacs and giant-tales sold at fairs, elevating it into a masterpiece of satire and humanist philosophy. The narrative recounts the birth, education, and heroic exploits of the giant prince Pantagruel and his comic, rogue companion Panurge—a masterwork of linguistic invention featuring pseudo-scholastic debates, invented vocabularies, legal parodies, and the famous 'Library of Saint-Victor' catalogue, which mercilessly ridiculed Medieval scholastic theology.Recognizing the extraordinary commercial and intellectual impact of Pantagruel, Rabelais followed it in 1534 with Gargantua (titled La vie treshorrificque du grand Gargantua, pere de Pantagruel), which served chronologically as a prequel to the story of Pantagruel. Gargantua represents Rabelais's most sustained articulation of Erasmian humanist educational theory and political philosophy. Contrasting the archaic, mind-numbing scholastic pedagogy of Master Tubal Holofernes with the dynamic, encyclopedic, and holistic humanist curriculum overseen by the tutor Ponocrates, Rabelais laid out an ideal vision for the moral and physical cultivation of the Renaissance prince. The volume culminates in the famous Picrocholine War—a biting satire of unprovoked imperial aggression modeled on contemporary conflicts—and the establishment of the utopian Abbey of Thélème. Governed by the sole rule 'Fay ce que vouldras' ('Do what thou wilt'), Thélème reflected an optimistic Christian humanist anthropology, asserting that well-born, educated individuals possessed an innate moral instinct (honneur) that naturally inclined them toward virtue and civic harmony.Diplomatic Missions, Roman Journeys, and Papal AbsolutionThe publication of Gargantua coincided with a dramatic shift in French political and religious life. In October 1534, the Affair of the Placards—in which anti-Catholic broadsheets attacking the Mass were posted across Paris and even on the bedchamber door of King Francis I—provoked a severe royal crackdown on Protestant sympathizers and humanist evangelicals. The Sorbonne formally condemned both Pantagruel and Gargantua as obscene and heretical. In this perilous climate, Rabelais sought the protection of his powerful patron, Cardinal Jean du Bellay, Bishop of Paris and one of King Francis I's chief diplomats.Rabelais accompanied Cardinal du Bellay on several high-level diplomatic embassies to the Papal Court in Rome (in 1534, 1535–1536, and 1548–1550). During these Italian sojourns, Rabelais served as personal physician, botanist, and antiquarian researcher to the Cardinal. In Rome, Rabelais conducted archaeological excavations, studied classical topography, corresponded with Italian humanists, and collected rare botanical specimens to introduce to France. Utilizing his access to the papal court, Rabelais submitted a formal supplication to Pope Paul III requesting absolution for his unauthorized departure from the Benedictine order. In a papal bull issued in January 1536, Paul III granted Rabelais full absolution, permitting him to re-enter the Benedictine order and practice medicine without performing surgical operations. Shortly thereafter, Rabelais was secularized as a canon of the collegiate church of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris under Jean du Bellay's oversight.In May 1537, Rabelais formally received his Doctorate of Medicine from the University of Montpellier, solidifying his status as one of the most distinguished medical authorities in the realm. Over the following decade, he balanced his medical duties with diplomatic service, accompanying King Francis I and Emperor Charles V to their historical summit at Aigues-Mortes in 1538, and serving as royal physician to Guillaume du Bellay, Seigneur de Langey, during his governance of Piedmont in Turin (1540–1543).The Later Books: Philosophical Maturation and Theological PerilAfter a twelve-year literary hiatus caused by political turbulence and the deaths of his patrons, Rabelais published Le Tiers Livre des faictz et dictz heroiques du noble Pantagruel in Paris in 1546 under his real name, equipped with a royal privilege granted by Francis I. Moving away from giantism and physical slapstick, the Tiers Livre is a deeply cerebral, philosophical masterpiece structured around Panurge's existential dilemma: whether he should marry, and whether marriage will inevitably doom him to cuckoldry, spousal abuse, or robbery. Panurge consults a bewildering array of experts and divinatory methods—including a sibyl, a mute, a poet, a physician (Rondibilis), a philosopher (Trouillogan), a theologian (Hippothadée), and a court fool (Triboulet). The book serves as a profound interrogation of epistemological uncertainty, human self-deception (philautia), and the ongoing Renaissance debate over gender and marriage known as the Querelle des Femmes. The volume concludes with an extraordinary praise of the miraculous plant Pantagruelion (hemp), an allegory for human ingenuity, navigation, and civilizational progress.Despite royal protection, the Tiers Livre was immediately condemned by the Sorbonne as heretical. Following the death of Francis I in 1547 and the accession of Henry II, religious persecution intensified under the newly created Chambre Ardente. Rabelais fled to Metz, a free imperial city, where he worked as city physician, before returning to Rome with Cardinal du Bellay. A preliminary, partial edition of Le Quart Livre appeared in 1548, with the full, definitive edition published in Paris by Michel Fezandat in 1552.The Quart Livre presents an epic, voyage narrative modeled on the Odyssey, Lucian's true histories, and contemporary New World voyages of discovery (such as those of Jacques Cartier). Pantagruel, Panurge, and Brother Jean sail toward the Oracle of the Holy Bottle (L'Oracle de la Dive Bouteille). Along their journey, they encounter fantastical islands that allegorize the fanaticisms of early modern Europe: the Papimanes (blindly fanatical devotees of papal authority), the Papefigues (anti-papal rebels), the island of Ruach (whose inhabitants consume nothing but wind), and the terrifying sea-monster Physeter. The Quart Livre represents Rabelais's most mature aesthetic achievement, featuring the famous episode of the paroles gelées ('frozen words')—where sounds spoken in a northern sea freeze in the air and thaw into visible, audible language—and a stark, tragicomic defense of Erasmian evangelical moderation against both Catholic scholasticism and Calvinist dogmatism.The backlash against the 1552 Quart Livre was immediate and severe. The Parlement of Paris suspended the sale of the book at the instigation of the Sorbonne. However, Rabelais enjoyed high-level protection from powerful figures such as Odet de Coligny, Cardinal de Châtillon, to whom the Quart Livre was dedicated. In January 1551, Rabelais had been awarded the lucrative cures of Saint-Martin de Meudon and Saint-Christophe du Jambet by Cardinal du Bellay, though he resigned these benefices in early 1553 shortly before his death. Rabelais died in Paris in April 1553 and was buried at the Church of Saint-Paul.Typographical Context, Print Networks, and Censorship EvasionThe publishing history of Rabelais's works provides a crucial window into sixteenth-century print culture. Rabelais worked directly with the premier printers of Lyon and Paris. His earliest editions of Pantagruel were printed by Claude Nourry (known as Le Prince) in Lyon in 1532, utilizing Gothic typefaces suited for popular entertainment. As Rabelais's humanist stature grew, he transitioned to Roman typography and sophisticated layouts, entrusting editions to François Juste in Lyon and later to Chrestien Wechel and Michel Fezandat in Paris.Because his writings routinely provoked theological condemnation, Rabelais employed complex typographical and textual strategies to evade censorship. He repeatedly revised his texts across successive printings—most notably in the 1542 edition published by François Juste—expunging direct attacks on the Sorbonne and substituting terms such as 'theologians' for 'Sorbonnistes'. Moreover, unauthorized, pirated printings flooded the early modern book market, most famously those produced by his contemporary Étienne Dolet (1509–1546), the radical printer and humanist who was ultimately burned at the stake for heresy in Paris. Dolet printed unexpurgated editions of Gargantua and Pantagruel in 1542 without Rabelais's consent, leading to a bitter rift between the author and the printer.In 1564, eleven years after Rabelais's death, a fifth volume titled Le Cinquième et dernier livre des faicts et dicts heroiques du bon Pantagruel was published in Paris. While completing the voyage narrative to the Oracle of the Dive Bouteille (where the oracle gives the final word: Trinch!, or 'Drink!'), the authenticity of the Cinquième Livre remains one of the most fiercely contested questions in French literary scholarship, with consensus suggesting it represents a compilation of Rabelaisian drafts edited and heavily augmented by a Protestant compiler.Critical Reception, Philosophical Interpretations, and LegacyThe historical reception of François Rabelais reflects the changing paradigms of European intellectual history. In his own lifetime, Rabelais was attacked from both ends of the religious spectrum: condemned as a heretic and libertine by the Roman Catholic Sorbonne, he was simultaneously denounced by John Calvin in his 1550 treatise De Scandalis, which accused Rabelais of atheism and profane mockery of the Scriptures. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Enlightenment thinkers such as Voltaire viewed Rabelais ambivalently, praising his anti-clerical wit while dismissing his exuberant vulgarity as coarse medieval farce.The nineteenth century witnessed a profound scholarly and romantic re-evaluation of Rabelais. Scholars such as Abel Lefranc pioneered modern historical-critical Rabelaisian studies, founding the Société des études rabelaisiennes in 1903 and producing landmark critical editions of his complete works. Lefranc posited a controversial thesis that Rabelais was a secret rationalist and early atheist. This view was decisively challenged in 1942 by the great Annales historian Lucien Febvre in his epochal monograph Le Problème de l'incroyance au XVIe siècle: La religion de Rabelais. Febvre demonstrated that sixteenth-century mentalities lacked the conceptual and linguistic tools for modern atheism, establishing that Rabelais operated entirely within a framework of Erasmian Christian Humanism.In the mid-twentieth century, the Russian literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin revolutionized Rabelais studies with his seminal work Rabelais and His World (1965/1968). Bakhtin posited Rabelais as the supreme literary expression of 'folk carnival culture', identifying the concepts of grotesque realism, the bodily lower stratum, and carnivalesque laughter as subversive mechanisms that overturned medieval feudal and ecclesiastical hierarchies. Submitting the text to rigorous philological and theological scrutiny, late twentieth-century scholars such as M. A. Screech, Gérard Defaux, Terence Cave, and Mireille Huchon further elucidated Rabelais's deep mastery of evangelical theology, classical rhetoric, legal jurisprudence, and medical theory.Today, François Rabelais is recognized not only as the father of modern French prose, but as an indispensable architect of the European novelistic tradition. His influence echoes through the works of Laurence Sterne, Jonathan Swift, Miguel de Cervantes, James Joyce, and Milan Kundera. By weaving radical erudition with cosmic laughter, Rabelais demonstrated that comic fiction could serve as the ultimate vehicle for profound philosophical inquiry.

academic_description: Three parts in one volume. 12mo (134x74 mm), red morocco leather binding. The covers are adorned with a double gilt fillet, and the spine, featuring five raised bands, is richly embellished with gilt tooling and titling. The endpapers are of marbled paper, gilt edges (Masson-De Bonnelle). The pagination is as follows: pp. 347, [7] + pp. 469, [9] + pp. 166, [32]. Collation: A-Z12 Aa-Vv12, with the final blank leaf Vv12 absent. Notably, there is a woodcut depicting Dive Bouteille on leaf Tt3r. The verso of the title page bears a stamp with the intertwined initials "SG." A pencil annotation on the rear endpaper reads "Salle Drouot Giraud-Badin 11 juin 1957 Frs. 103,000." This copy is in excellent condition.Very rare edition that undoubtedly appeared after 1584, the year when the final appendices to Rabelais's work were annexed for the first time. The printing date might be a typographical error, suggesting it should be read as 1585. However, the edition could also be slightly later. Typographically, it presents itself as a sixteenth-century imprint.

authors.name: Rollenhagen Georg
authors.biography: Georg Rollenhagen (1542–1609) stands as one of the most significant and multifaceted figures of late German Protestant Humanism (Späthumanismus). Operating at the vital intersection of Lutheran theology, classical philology, pedagogical reform, and vernacular satire, Rollenhagen synthesized the intellectual legacy of Philipp Melanchthon with the vibrant print culture and municipal politics of late sixteenth-century Magdeburg. Best remembered for his colossal beast epic, the Froschmeuseler (1595), Rollenhagen bridged the stylistic gap between the civic didacticism of Sebastian Brant’s Narrenschiff and the emerging Baroque satirical narrative later perfected by Johann Jakob Christoffel von Grimmelshausen. As a long-standing rector of the Magdeburg Altstädtisches Gymnasium and a devoted Lutheran pastor, his literary production was inextricably linked to the institutional consolidation of the Protestant Reformation in northern Germany.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationBorn on April 22, 1542, in the Mark Brandenburg town of Bernau near Berlin, Georg Rollenhagen was raised in a prosperous and politically active burgher family. His father, George Rollenhagen, was a respected cloth merchant (Tuchmacher) and town mayor, providing young Georg with both financial stability and an early immersion in civic governance. Rollenhagen’s initial schooling took place in Bernau, followed by periods of study in Gardelegen and Magdeburg, where he attended the prestigious Altstädtische Schule under the guidance of early Lutheran humanists such as Friedrich Widebrand. In the summer of 1560, Rollenhagen matriculated at the University of Wittenberg, the supreme epicenter of Lutheran scholarship. Although Philipp Melanchthon passed away in April of that same year, his educational paradigm—rooted in the synthesis of Neo-Latin eloquence, Aristotelian dialectic, and evangelical theology—exerted an overwhelming influence on Rollenhagen’s intellectual formation. At Wittenberg, Rollenhagen studied under prominent Melanchthonian scholars, including the physician and humanist Caspar Peucer and the philologist Esrom Rüdinger. Rollenhagen achieved the academic degree of Magister Arts in 1567, having established himself as a talented poet in both Latin and the vernacular, deeply committed to the Lutheran ideal of the preceptorem patriae.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksIn 1567, Rollenhagen was called to Magdeburg to serve as Subrektor of the Altstädtisches Gymnasium, ascending to the position of Rektor in 1575—a office he retained with extraordinary distinction for over thirty years. Simultaneously, from 1573 onward, he served as a preacher at the church of St. Ulrich. Rollenhagen’s dramatic output emerged directly from his pedagogical obligations to write and stage school dramas (Schuldramen) designed to cultivate Latin fluency, moral rectitude, and civic virtue among his pupils. His major dramatic works include Abraham (1569), a biblically inspired play emphasizing divine obedience and patriarchal faith; Tobias (1576), a widely performed domestic drama depicting filial piety, marital morality, and providential protection; and Vom Reichen Mann und armen Lazarus (1590), a sharp social critique targeting economic avarice, uncharitableness, and the moral responsibilities of the merchant class.Rollenhagen’s undisputed masterpiece, however, is Der Froschmeuseler (Magdeburg, 1595), an immense vernacular beast epic written in rhyming couplets (Knittelvers). Formally structured as an expansive adaptation of the Pseudo-Homeric Batrachomyomachia (The Battle of the Frogs and Mice), the Froschmeuseler expands the ancient fable into a profound allegorical commentary on early modern European politics, religious discord, and socio-economic structures. Composed across three massive books, the poem uses the tragic collision between the kingdom of the frogs (allegorizing established political authority and land-owning aristocracy) and the mice (allegorizing rising merchant classes, religious dissidents, or foreign factions) to interrogate the causes of civil war, tyranny, and social disintegration. Rollenhagen interweaves extensive theological discourses, natural philosophy, Aesopic fables, and political theory into the narrative, explicitly addressing the horrors of the Schmalkaldic War, the siege of Magdeburg (1550–1551), and the devastating potential of sectarian conflict within the Holy Roman Empire. Through the voice of the wise mouse Elbendorff, Rollenhagen advocates for a Melanchthonian middle course: political moderation, respect for constitutional order, religious irenicism within Lutheran parameters, and a just war doctrine (bellum iustum).Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe print history of Rollenhagen’s works reflects the crucial role of Magdeburg as a dominant publishing hub in the late sixteenth century. Magdeburg’s print shops, which had gained international fame during the mid-century as the production house of the anti-Imperial Magdeburg Centuriators, possessed the technical sophistication required for large-scale vernacular editions. The princeps edition of the Froschmeuseler was printed in 1595 by the prominent Magdeburg publisher Paul Donat in association with Johann Francke. Printed in a handsome Fraktur typeface with elaborate woodcut illustrations depicting anthropomorphic rodents and amphibians engaged in council and battle, the volume was designed to appeal simultaneously to erudite scholars and broader literate burgher audiences.The immediate commercial success of the Froschmeuseler sparked a series of authorized and unauthorized printings across key German printing centers, including Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig, and Strasbourg. Printers quickly recognized the work's dual utility as a popular entertainment piece and an educational text for moral instruction. Rollenhagen’s meticulous oversight of typography and woodcut programs influenced the visual culture of late German Humanism, directly shaping the artistic development of his son, Gabriel Rollenhagen (1583–1619), who would achieve international renown as an emblem poet through his landmark publication Nucleus Emblematum (1611–1613).Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyDuring his lifetime, Georg Rollenhagen was revered throughout Protestant Germany as an exemplary educator and a bulwark of Lutheran orthodoxy, though his moderate, Melanchthonian sympathies occasionally placed him in subtle tension with the more rigid Gnesio-Lutheran theologians of Magdeburg. Upon his death on May 20, 1609, he was eulogized as a monumental figure in northern German civic and intellectual life.The critical reception of Rollenhagen’s work underwent dynamic shifts across subsequent centuries. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, his Froschmeuseler remained continuously in print, praised by Baroque literary theorists and Enlightenment intellectuals alike. Johann Christoph Gottsched and Gotthold Ephraim Lessing admired Rollenhagen’s masterly handling of the vernacular fable, citing his linguistic vigor and structural clarity as pivotal steps in the maturation of German national literature. In the nineteenth century, early Germanist philologists such as Karl Goedeke and Johannes Bolte institutionalized Rollenhagen’s position in the literary canon, highlighting his work as an invaluable historical document depicting the social, political, and linguistic realities of the late Reformation era. Modern scholarly debate continues to explore Rollenhagen’s sophisticated integration of classical mythology, Aesopic traditions, and Protestant political theory, affirming his status as a titan of early modern European didactic literature.

academic_description: 8vo (160x92 mm). [400] leaves. Collation: A-Ddd8. The final leaf is a blank. Title printed in red and black with a vignette in the center partly and 16 small woodcuts in the text (two repeated, one full page). Contemporary flexible vellum (slightly soiled and rubbed). Donation note on the front pastedown dated 13 June 1596, manuscript monogram on the title page. Slightly browned and foxed, more heavily at places, small corner tear to title page, all in all a good, genuine copy.Extremely rare first edition of this didactic-humoristic animal epic, a most singular and remarkable work of German literature between the sixteenth-century and the Baroque period. The work is dedicated to the learned Heinrich Rantzau (1526-1599), then the king of Denmark's representative in the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein. As Rollenhagen points to on several occasions, the work was written for the learned male youth: “Und ihr junge lustige Knaben / Die lust zu ehrbar kurtzweil haben.” (leaf C4v), and summarizes his intention: “Damit im schertz die gute Leer / Bey der Jugend schaff desto mehr ”(leaf C4v) (cf. O. Brunken, Georg Rollenhagens ‘Froschmeuseler' – ein späthumanistisches dikaktisches Tierepos für die Jugend des gebildeten ‘Mittelstandes', in: “Schiefertafel”, 5, 1982, pp. 46-73).In 1566, when Rollenhagen still was a student at Wittenberg, he had heard Veit Ortel's lecture on the pseudo-Homeric Batrachomyomachia and made a first attempt at a German version. Nearly thirty years later his magnum opus was accomplished and bore little resemblance to the Greek original (who has 305 lines, whereas the Froschmeuseler has over 20,000). The work is divided into three books, the first of which deal with the individual in the society, the second the ideal constitution of a state and the relationship between state and church (here is included a sharp polemic against popery), and the third deals with international relationships, especially war and peace (cf. R. Richter, Georg Rollenhagens Froschmeuseler: Ein rhetorisches Meisterstück, Bern, 1975, p. 61). Rollenhagen did not intend his work to be simply an allegorical polemic. He also conceived it to be an antidote to and a weapon against the Volksbücher as the “weytbrümbter Eulenspiegel / oder auch andere Schandbücher / der Pfaff von Kalenberg / Ratziporus, Rollwagen / etc.” (leaf A8r). He wanted to tell the truth to the world, laughingly, since the world did not seem to care for truth seriously written. The immense pile of fable, proverb, tale, and anecdote woven into the plot proper is shown by the sources he enumerated, which go from the Reinecke Fuchs and Fischart's Flöh Hatz to the Indian Panchatantra (Büch der bÿspel der alten wÿsen, Urach, ca. 1480).The Froschmeuseler was an immediate success, was reprinted many times (1596, 1600, 1608, 1615, 1616, 1618, 1621, 1627, 1637, and 1683) and knew several adaptations and abridged versions. It satisfied, seemingly, a yearning by the German-reading people for a long, comprehensive, poetic work which gave aesthetic pleasure and was also didactic. Rollenhagen was one of the first of the literati to employ the German Language in such a work and produced a true expression of the German national character, an ingenuous expression of the fatherland as is found in Johann Fischart, Burkhard Waldis, and a very few others in the sixteenth century. However, the historic contribution of the Froschmeuseler is that Rollenhagen related his comic poem to the world affairs and the political struggles of his time. The Froschmeuseler is not only an instructive work on morals, virtue, or religion, but also an anticipation of the political didacticism of the German Baroque in the seventeenth century.Georg Rollenhagen was born in Bernau near Berlin. Despite the adversities of a sickly youth and the early loss of his father, he was able to obtain a brilliant scholarly and literary career. He attended school at Prenzlau, Mansfeld, and Magdeburg. From 1560 to 1563 he studied at the University of Wittenberg, and then was appointed rector of the Johannisschule in Halberstadt. He returned to Wittenberg to earn a master's degree in philosophy in 1567, and in the same year became prorector of the ‘Gymnasium' in Madgeburg. There he spent the rest of his life. Under his direction the Magdeburg ‘Gymnasium' became the foremost ‘Gelehrtenschule' in Germany. Rollenhagen's literary production goes far beyond the Froschmeuseler, so he produced several dramas, Abraham (1569), Tobias (1576), and Vom reichen Manne und armen Lazaro (1590), German translations of some of Terence's comedies (1592), two short rhymed chronicles Der Hinckende Both (1589) and Der Post Reutter (1590), a collection of fables, Alte Newe Zeitung von der Welt Lauff (1592), and a sermon on the Ascesion (1592) (cf. E. Sobel, Georg Rollenhagen, Sixteenth Century Playwright, Pedagogue, and Pulicist, in: “Publications of the Modern Language Association of America”, 70, 1955, pp. 762-780).

authors.name: Rojas Fernando
authors.biography: Spanish writer (b. perhaps Montalbán c. 1470 - d. Talavera 1541), considered the author of La Celestina because the name of the bachelor Fernando de Rojas appears in some acrostic verses preceding the work as the author of the final twenty acts. These were supposedly composed as a continuation of the first act, which circulated in manuscript form and was attributed by some to Juan de Mena, and by others to Rodrigo de Cota.

publishers.name: Bindoni Bernardino
publishers.biography: Bernardino Bindoni (fl. 1532–1574) stands as a vital exemplar of the industrious artisan-publishers who defined the golden age of Venetian typography during the mid-sixteenth century. Operating at the vibrant intersection of commercial enterprise, vernacular humanism, and popular print culture, Bindoni contributed substantially to the democratization of reading materials in Renaissance Italy. While the Venetian book trade was dominated at its high intellectual tier by patrician-oriented houses such as the Aldine Press or the noble patrons of Greek and Latin philology, Bernardino Bindoni carved out an exceptionally successful niche by supplying the rapidly expanding market for vernacular literature (editoria volgare), chivalric epics, devotional treatises, theatrical comedies, and practical manuals. His workshop mirrored the dynamic economic reality of Venice as the typographic capital of Europe, where printing presses functioned not merely as intellectual sanctuaries but as highly competitive, capital-intensive manufacturing centers catering to readers across the Italian peninsula and the wider Mediterranean world.The lineage of the Bindoni family traces its roots to the northern lake regions of Lombardy, specifically the Lake Maggiore area (Isola Superiore and Stresa), from which numerous families of skilled craftsmen, engravers, and typographers migrated to the Venetian Republic during the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. In Venice, the Bindoni dynasty established a complex network of workshops. Bernardino was closely linked through kinship and trade to other prominent family members, most notably Francesco Bindoni and Pasquale Bindoni, who operated individual and collaborative presses near the commercial heartland of Rialto, the parish of San Zulian (San Giuliano), and along the bustling street of the Frezzaria. Bernardino Bindoni began his independent typographical career around 1532, establishing his own imprint while maintaining structural and logistical ties to his relatives. His early formative years were shaped by the rigorous apprenticeship system of the Venetian guild of printers and booksellers (Arte dei Stampatori e Librai), where he mastered the mechanics of typefounding, composition, presswork, and the intricate financial arrangements required to secure paper stock and commercial distribution.Throughout his active decades from 1532 through the mid-1570s, Bernardino Bindoni assembled a vast and diverse publishing program that captured the shifting literary tastes of mid-Cinquecento Italy. A cornerstone of his production was chivalric and narrative poetry, a genre that enjoyed immense commercial success. Bindoni issued widely sought-after editions of Matteo Maria Boiardo’s Orlando Innamorato, Luigi Pulci’s Morgante, and Andrea da Barberino’s popular prose romance Guarino detto il Meschino. In addition to chivalric literature, his press played a key role in disseminating canonical Italian poetry and prose, producing sturdy, accessible editions of Francesco Petrarca’s Canzoniere, Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron, and the works of contemporary authors such as Pietro Aretino, Niccolò Franco, and Ludovico Dolce. Bindoni's output was by no means limited to belles-lettres; he systematically printed vernacular translations of classical Latin authors (including Cicero, Ovid, and Virgil), practical medical and astrological handbooks, devotional guides for lay confraternities, and popular theatrical texts, including early Venetian commedie and dialogues that appealed to urban readers.From a typographical and bibliographical perspective, the workshop of Bernardino Bindoni offers a fascinating window into sixteenth-century print production techniques. His early imprints frequently employed a robust Venetian Gothic type (rotunda) suitable for devotional works and popular epics, but he rapidly adapted to the market demand for humanistic Roman types and elegant Italic fonts (corsivo), modeled after the groundbreaking designs of Francesco Griffo for Aldus Manutius. Bindoni’s editions are noteworthy for their expressive use of woodcut illustrations, ornamental title-page borders, and historiated initials, which added significant visual allure for middle-class readers. His printer’s marks (marche tipografiche) evolved over time, often featuring allegorical figures, religious motifs such as Tobias and the Angel, or Justice, alongside his initials B. B.. Financially, Bindoni operated both as an independent publisher financing his own editions and as a printer-for-hire working ad instantia (at the commission of) major bookseller-publishers, most notably the powerful house of Marchiò Sessa and his heirs, as well as trade partners across Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna.The later phase of Bernardino Bindoni's career coincided with profound ideological and regulatory transformations within the Venetian Republic and the Catholic World. The advent of the Roman Inquisition and the promulgation of the Pauline (1559) and Tridentine (1564) Index Librorum Prohibitorum severely restricted the printing of controversial vernacular works, satirical dialogues, and unapproved religious translations. Bindoni adapted to this climate of heightened censorship by shifting a larger portion of his catalogue toward strictly orthodox religious literature, hagiography, and approved educational manuals. Modern historical and bibliographical scholarship—spearheaded by analytical cataloging projects such as EDIT16 and the monumental research of Fernanda Ascarelli, Marco Menato, and Brian Richardson—has recognized Bernardino Bindoni not as a mere secondary artisan, but as a central figure in the infrastructure of the Venetian press. His enduring legacy resides in his extraordinary technical versatility and commercial stamina, which enabled the literature of the Italian Renaissance to reach an unprecedentedly broad and diverse reading public.

A very good copy.EARLY VENETIAN EDITION of one of the great works of Spanish literature in its Italian version by Alfonso Ordoñez who dedicates his translation to Madonna Feltria da Campofregoso. The Comedia de Calisto y Melibea of Fernando de Rojas, also known as Celestina, after the character of the same name, was first printed in Burgos in 1499. The first Italian edition was issued in Rome in 1506 and reprinted several times during the 16th century. The title woodcut, showing the main characters of the dialogues, had previously been used in the Stefano Nicolini da Sabio editions and derives from the first octavo edition (Seville [i.e. Venice], May 1523). 11 of the 16 illustrations are formed from the varying rearrangements of five small distinct blocks, each of which portrays either a human figure or a landscape feature.

authors.name: Lombroso Cesare
authors.biography: Cesare Lombroso (born Marco Ezechia Lombroso; November 6, 1835 – October 19, 1909) stands as one of the most provocative, influential, and hotly contested figures in the history of nineteenth-century medicine, psychiatry, and legal theory. Recognized globally as the founding father of modern criminal anthropology and the intellectual architect of the Italian Positivist School of Criminology (Scuola Positiva), Lombroso radically transformed the Western conception of crime from a moral or rational choice—as posited by Classical criminologists such as Cesare Beccaria and Jeremy Bentham—into a biological, pathological, and somatic phenomenon. Operating at the turbulent intersection of Risorgimento political consolidation, Darwinian evolutionary theory, phrenology, and alienism, Lombroso sought to construct an empirical science of human deviation, postulating that the criminal was not a free-willed agent of sin, but an evolutionary throwback, a biological anomaly burdened by hereditary stigmata and physical degeneration.Born into an affluent, observant Jewish family in Verona—then under the domain of the Austrian Empire—Lombroso was the son of Aronne Lombroso, a merchant, and Zefora Levi. His early intellectual formation took place within a vibrant, multi-lingual, and highly cultured Venetian-Jewish milieu, where he manifested a precocious aptitude for linguistics, ancient history, and natural philosophy. In 1852, he enrolled in the Faculty of Medicine and Surgery at the University of Pavia, later continuing his medical studies at the University of Padua and the University of Vienna. During his time in Vienna, Lombroso was profoundly influenced by the mechanistic materialism of German physiology and the emerging cellular pathology of Rudolf Virchow, as well as the radical scientific positivism of Jacob Moleschott. He was equally mentored in linguistic anthropology by Paolo Marzolo, whose comparative methodologies inspired Lombroso to search for anatomical and behavioral evolutionary parallels between prehistoric man, modern indigenous populations, and the institutionalized insane.Lombroso graduated from the University of Pavia in 1858 with a thesis on cretinism in Lombardy, establishing an early research pattern that linked regional pathology, nutrition, and environmental factors to mental degradation—a topic he would expand in his groundbreaking studies on pellagra and endemic malnutrition among the Northern Italian peasantry. Upon the outbreak of the Second War of Italian Independence in 1859, Lombroso volunteered as an army surgeon in the Piedmontese military forces. This military service proved foundational: stationed in Southern Italy during the post-unification counter-insurgency campaign against regional banditry (brigantaggio) in Calabria and Campania between 1861 and 1862, Lombroso performed extensive anthropometric examinations on hundreds of Italian soldiers and Southern peasant insurgents. He recorded measurements of crania, facial symmetry, skin pigmentation, and tattoos, laying the raw empirical foundation for his future theories on physical stigmata and racial geography.The decisive turning point in Lombroso’s scientific career occurred in December 1870 while serving as the director of the asylum in Pesaro and subsequently performing autopsies at the University of Pavia. While dissecting the cranium of a notorious Calabrian brigand named Giuseppe Villella, Lombroso discovered a distinct anatomical anomaly: a median occipital fossa (fossa occipitalis media) situated at the base of the skull, a structural trait characteristic of lower primates and rodents rather than modern Homo sapiens. Lombroso described this moment as an epiphany of scientific illumination, asserting that the crime of the bandit was not an act of free volition, but the unavoidable manifestation of an ancient, primitive organism resurfacing within modern society. This insight gave birth to his central doctrine of atavism (atavismo)—the concept that criminals were evolutionary throwbacks whose biological structure impelled them toward anti-social behavior.In 1876, Lombroso published the first edition of his monumental masterpiece, L'uomo delinquente (Criminal Man), a work that grew from a single modest volume of under 250 pages into an encyclopedic, five-volume treatise by its definitive fifth edition in 1896–1897. In this text, Lombroso codified the typology of the "born criminal" (delinquente nato), detailing an array of physical and anatomical stigmata: facial asymmetry, prominent jaws, excessive arm length, low forehead, abnormal ear shape, and insensibility to physical pain (analgesia). Over successive editions, Lombroso integrated complex psychological and behavioral markers, analyzing the prevalence of tattooing, prison slang (gergo), hyper-sexuality, emotional instability, and graphic jail-cell graffiti (il palimpsesto del carcere). As his theories expanded, Lombroso incorporated additional clinical categories alongside atavism, identifying moral insanity (follia morale) and, above all, epilepsy as co-equal etiology in criminal pathology, viewing crime as a neuro-pathological explosion linked to sub-cortical lesions.Lombroso’s career reached its zenith following his appointment in 1876 to the Chair of Forensic Medicine and Public Hygiene at the University of Turin, where he later held the chairs of Psychiatry (1896) and Criminal Anthropology (1905). In Turin, Lombroso created a powerhouse of positivist research, surrounding himself with brilliant younger scholars, most notably the legal philosopher Enrico Ferri and the magistrate Raffaele Garofalo. Together, they established the Italian School of Positivist Criminology, advocating a total revolution in penal jurisprudence. Rejecting retributive justice, they argued that penal law should serve solely as a mechanism of social defense (difesa sociale), replacing fixed prison sentences calibrated to the crime with indefinite institutional detention, asylum confinement, or biological neutralization tailored to the specific anatomical and psychological danger (pericolosità) of the offender.Beyond the study of criminal males, Lombroso extended his positivist taxonomy to encompass virtually all forms of social deviation and intellectual exceptionalism. In Genio e follia (Genius and Insanity, first published in 1864 and massively expanded in later editions), he posited that extraordinary creative genius was itself a form of hereditary neurosis, a degenerative epileptoid psychosis that shared identical neuro-biological roots with criminality. In 1893, co-authoring with his son-in-law, the historian Guglielmo Ferrero, Lombroso published La donna delinquente, la prostituta e la donna normale (The Female Offender, the Prostitute and the Normal Woman). This work argued that women were biologically less evolved than men but possessed lower rates of violent crime due to their inherent passivity and maternal instincts; when female criminality did erupt, Lombroso claimed, it manifested predominantly as prostitution, which he classified as the true female equivalent of male violent crime.The dissemination of Lombrosian thought was intrinsically linked to the printing culture of late nineteenth-century Turin, particularly his profound commercial and intellectual partnership with the prominent publishing house Fratelli Bocca Editori. Bocca established the prestigious monographic series Biblioteca Antropologico-Giuridica, which became the international flagship for positivist legal, psychiatric, and anthropological literature across Europe and Latin America. In 1880, Lombroso, Ferri, and Garofalo founded the influential journal Archivio di psichiatria, antropologia criminale e scienze penali per servire allo studio dell'uomo alienato e delinquente. Published continuously by Bocca, this periodical served as the global clearinghouse for scientific case studies, skull measurements, clinical photographs, and penal reform proposals, securing the international dominance of the Turin school.Lombroso's ideas rapidly crossed national borders, provoking fierce international debate at the International Congresses of Criminal Anthropology, beginning with the inaugural congress in Rome in 1885. While his theories found enthusiastic adoption in Latin America (especially Argentina and Brazil), Eastern Europe, and the United States, they met severe resistance from the French Sociological School of Criminology led by Alexandre Lacassagne, Gabriel Tarde, and René Worms. At the 1889 Paris Congress and the 1892 Brussels Congress, Lacassagne and Tarde vigorously dismantled Lombroso's biological determinism, arguing that the social environment (le milieu social) was the true incubator of crime, famously declaring that "societies have the criminals they deserve." Lombroso responded by gradually refining his model, incorporating environmental, economic, climatic, and social factors into his late masterwork, Le crime, causes et remèdes (Crime: Its Causes and Remedies, 1899).In his final decade, Lombroso’s intellectual trajectory took an unexpected and controversial turn toward mediumship, spiritism, and occult phenomena. Following his encounters in the early 1890s with the famed Neapolitan spiritualist medium Eusapia Palladino, Lombroso became convinced that psychic phenomena, telekinesis, and spirit apparitions were legitimate physical forces capable of scientific measurement. This shift dismayed many of his rationalist and materialist disciples, but Lombroso defended his spiritualist investigations—culminating in his posthumously published Ricerche sui fenomeni ipnotici e spiritici (1909)—as a natural extension of his lifelong quest to explore the hidden frontiers of human neuro-biology and abnormal psychology.Lombroso died suddenly of cardiac failure at his home in Turin on October 19, 1909. Demonstrating an absolute lifetime devotion to empirical materialism, his last will and testament directed that his body be subjected to autopsy by his colleague Mario Carrara, and that his brain and complete skeleton be preserved for scientific study. His private collection of crania, anatomical specimens, prison artwork, criminal artifacts, and weapons formed the core of the Cesare Lombroso Museum of Criminal Anthropology at the University of Turin, which remains one of the world's most astonishing repositories of nineteenth-century scientific material culture. While twentieth- and twenty-first-century historiography, legal scholars, and geneticists have thoroughly invalidated his biological determinism and exposed the underlying racial, class, and gender biases of his methodologies, Cesare Lombroso remains an unassailable titan of modern intellectual history—the man who fundamentally shifted the focus of modern justice from the abstract nature of the crime to the physical and psychological reality of the criminal.
