authors.name: Ferrero Guglielmo
authors.biography: Guglielmo Ferrero (July 21, 1871 – August 3, 1942) stands as one of the most singular, internationally celebrated, and multifaceted Italian intellectuals of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Operating at the intersections of legal criminology, positivist sociology, classical historiography, political philosophy, and anti-fascist public activism, Ferrero achieved global renown for his radical reinterpretation of Roman antiquity and his seminal theories on political legitimacy, the psychology of power, and the systemic crises of modern European civilization. Emerging from the vibrant intellectual crucible of late nineteenth-century Italian positivism under the tutelage of Cesare Lombroso, Ferrero evolved from an ardent youthful radical into a master historiographer whose multi-volume Grandezza e decadenza di Roma revolutionized ancient history by applying modern socio-economic, psychological, and institutional analyses. In his later years, forced into exile by Benito Mussolini’s dictatorial regime, Ferrero transitioned into a profound philosopher of political power, crafting a trilogy on the French Revolution, the Napoleonic era, and the Congress of Vienna that culminated in his masterpiece, Pouvoir: Les génies invisibles de la cité (1942). Across his prolific career, Ferrero remained an unrelenting champion of liberal-humanist values, offering a prophetic critique of mass democracy, Caesarism, militarism, and totalitarian coercion.Born in Portici, near Naples, to Piedmontese parents—Giuseppe Ferrero, a high-ranking magistrate, and Marie Delposte—young Guglielmo spent his formative years relocating across the Italian peninsula in tandem with his father’s judicial assignments. This peripatetic childhood cultivated an expansive, non-parochial outlook. He commenced his higher education at the University of Florence before transferring to the University of Pisa and ultimately the University of Bologna, where he completed his doctoral thesis in law in 1891 under the supervision of the renowned legal scholar Giovanni Bovio. However, the definitive catalyst of his early intellectual trajectory was his association with the founder of criminal anthropology, Cesare Lombroso, at the University of Turin. Lombroso recognized the brilliant young scholar’s analytical acumen and recruited him to co-author the monumental study La donna delinquente, la prostituta e la donna normale (1893). In this work, Ferrero synthesised positivist empiricism with psychological typology, though he increasingly introduced subtle sociological nuance that departed from Lombroso’s strict biological determinism. Ferrero’s familial and intellectual bonds with the Lombroso circle were solidified in 1901 when he married Gina Lombroso, Cesare's daughter—herself an accomplished physician, author, and translator who would become Guglielmo’s lifelong collaborator and biographer. During the mid-1890s, Ferrero traveled extensively across Northern Europe, an experience that yielded his first major independent sociological treatise, L'Europa giovane: Studi e impressioni su paesi nordici e germanici (1897). The book, which juxtaposed the vibrant industrial dynamism, civic discipline, and institutional vigor of Germany, England, and Scandinavia with the bureaucratic stagnation and economic underdevelopedness of the Latin South, created a sensation in Italian intellectual circles and established Ferrero as a leading public intellectual of the radical-liberal Left.At the turn of the twentieth century, Ferrero pivoted from contemporary sociological commentary to historical inquiry, embarking on the monumental enterprise that would guarantee his international fame: Grandezza e decadenza di Roma (published in five volumes between 1902 and 1907 by the Florentine publishing house Treves). Rejecting the traditional, romanticized, and purely political or military narratives of Roman history popularized by Theodor Mommsen and his predecessors, Ferrero interpreted the collapse of the Roman Republic and the rise of the Augustan Principate through the prism of modern economic, social, and moral transformations. He posited that Rome's expansion was driven not by a coherent imperial design, but by economic imperialism, consumerism, social luxury, the decay of agrarian civic virtues, and class conflict. Figures like Julius Caesar were stripped of their mythic hero status; Ferrero depicted Caesar as a brilliant but destructive demagogue whose actions unleashed anarchic forces he could not control, while Augustus was framed as a cautious, conservative administrator seeking to restore equilibrium amidst structural ruin. The historiographical impact of Grandezza e decadenza di Roma was immediate and global. Translated into French, English, German, Spanish, and Russian, the work catapulted Ferrero into international celebrity. In 1906, he was invited to deliver a prestigious series of lectures at the Collège de France; in 1907, he embarked on an extensive lecture tour of South America (Argentina and Brazil); and in 1908, upon the personal invitation of President Theodore Roosevelt, Ferrero visited the United States, delivering addresses at Harvard University, Columbia University, and the White House. Ferrero used his American observations to write Fra i due mondi (1913), a philosophical dialogue reflecting on the tension between quantitative American industrial progress and qualitative European cultural heritage.The outbreak of the First World War in 1914 marked a dramatic turning point in Ferrero’s political and philosophical thought. Initially an anti-militarist—as articulated in his 1898 treatise Militarismo—Ferrero came to view the conflict between the Triple Entente and the Central Powers as an apocalyptic struggle between democratic civilization and Germanic military autocracy. He ardently advocated for Italian intervention on the side of the Allies, publishing incendiary polemics such as La guerra europea (1915). However, the war's catastrophic aftermath, the collapse of the Romanov, Hohenzollern, and Habsburg empires, and the subsequent rise of totalitarian movements filled him with profound apprehension. When Benito Mussolini seized power in Italy in 1922, Ferrero emerged as an uncompromising defender of constitutional democracy and individual liberty. He refused to align with the Fascist regime, publicly signing Benedetto Croce’s Manifesto degli intellettuali antifascisti in 1925. Consequently, the Fascist government subjected Ferrero to unrelenting harassment, placing his Florentine residence under constant police surveillance, confiscating his personal papers, banning the republication of his books, and denying him an international passport. During this period of 'internal exile' (confino casalingo), Ferrero wrote La rovina della civiltà antica (1921), an evocative historical parallel between the third-century collapse of the Roman Empire and the contemporary disintegration of European order, arguing that the destruction of political authority without a legitimate successor leads inevitably to barbarism.In 1930, following intense diplomatic pressure from international academic institutions, the League of Nations, and prominent intellectual figures such as Albert Einstein and William Rappard, the Fascist government finally granted Ferrero permission to leave Italy. He accepted a permanent professorship in modern history at the prestigious Graduate Institute of International Studies (Institut universitaire de hautes études internationales) in Geneva, Switzerland, alongside a chair at the University of Geneva. This Swiss exile initiated the final, most intellectually brilliant chapter of his life. In Geneva, Ferrero developed his mature philosophy of history and political legitimacy, producing a monumental historical trilogy on the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Era: Aventure. Bonaparte en Italie (1796-1797) (1936), Reconstruction. Talleyrand à Vienne (1814-1815) (1940), and his supreme theoretical synthesis, Pouvoir: Les génies invisibles de la cité (1942). In these works, Ferrero conceptualized political power as being haunted by a fundamental human emotion: fear. Dictatorships and autocratic regimes, according to Ferrero, are born of fear and govern through terror because they lack organic legitimacy. True legitimacy—which he categorized into monarchical, aristocratic, democratic, and representative principles—functions as an invisible, consent-based shield that protects both the rulers and the ruled from mutual terror. He highlighted the Congress of Vienna and figures like Talleyrand and Tsar Alexander I as exemplars of constructive statesmanship because they established a legitimate, balanced European order that averted general warfare for a century. Ferrero died suddenly on August 3, 1942, at Mont Pèlerin, overlooking Lake Geneva, leaving behind a legacy that profoundly influenced post-WWII political science, constitutional thought, and European integration studies.

academic_description: 8vo (242x154 mm). XI, [1 blank], 640 pp. and 8 (4 folding) plates. The first leaf is a blank. With the engraved portrait of Messalina on the title page, and several diagrams, photographs and statistical tables in the text. Editor's printed wrappers (some foxing, spine fragile, occasional tears to the margins and to the back cover). On the front cover bookplate of the “Libreria Moderna-Milano”. An exceptional uncut copy preserved in a cardboard box.Rare first edition of this very influential work on criminal woman, considered as the first modern criminology text to exclusively focus on the subject.A first draft of the work, written in collaboration with Salvatore Ottolenghi, had appeared two years earlier in the “Giornale della R. Accademia di Medicina” (nos. 9-10). The final draft was written in collaboration with the author's son-in-law, the talented law student Guglielmo Ferrero.In Criminal Woman, Lombroso applies to women the same theories expressed in his Uomo delinquente (‘Criminal Man'), published in 1876, the work that marks the foundation of criminal anthropology. In the text, he outlines a comparative analysis of “normal women” opposed to “criminal women” such as “the prostitute”.Lombroso was convinced of the pathological nature of the born criminal (whom he distinguishes, medically and legally, from the casual offender who commits a crime driven by special circumstances or needs) and of the possibility of explaining and predicting moral degeneration from its physical abnormalities. According to Lombroso, there is a correlation between somatic and mental deformities with reference to specific factors as atavism, degeneration, and epilepsy. He believes that criminals are more often found to suffer from physical, nervous and mental abnormalities than non-criminals, and that these abnormalities are either inherited or the result of physical degeneration. Lombroso also deals with the legal implications of his theories, particularly in relation to the issue of “moral insanity”, understood as a serious disturbance of social behavior. He thus initiated a branch of psychiatric research which has cast new light on the complex problem of criminal responsibility (cf. M. Gibson, Born to Crime. Cesare Lombroso and the Italian origins of Biological Criminology, Westport, 2002, passim).Lombroso was born in Verona in 1835 to a wealthy Jewish family. He studied literature, linguistics, and archaeology at the universities of Padua, Vienna and Paris, before becoming an army surgeon in 1859. In 1866 he was appointed visiting lecturer at Pavia and in 1871 he took charge of the insane asylum at Pesaro. He became professor of forensic medicine and hygiene at Turin in 1878. Later he was appointed as professor of psychiatry (1896) and criminal anthropology (1906) at the same university. He died in Turin in 1909 (cf. M.E. authors.name: Homer
authors.biography: Homer (Greek: Ὅμηρος, Hómēros; fl. c. 8th century BCE) stands as the foundational, monumental figure of Western literature. Revered throughout classical antiquity as the Poet (ὁ Ποιητής) par excellence, his biographical reality, historical incarnation, and ultimate textual authorship have constituted one of the most vibrant, complex, and enduring debates in intellectual history—a complex known since the late eighteenth century as the Homeric Question. In the ancient imagination, Homer was conceived as an Ionian bard, born along the Aegean seaboard of Asia Minor—most frequently associated with the city of Smyrna or the island of Chios—who performed hexameter epics while afflicted with blindness. Yet modern classical scholarship, informed by historical linguistics, comparative oral tradition, archaeology, and textual criticism, views Homer either as the supreme master-singer who consolidated centuries of Mycenaean and Archaic oral tradition into the definitive structures of the Iliad and the Odyssey, or as the personified honorific eponym for a collaborative guild of oral bards, the Homeridai of Chios.The cultural significance of Homer to classical antiquity cannot be overstated. His epics served as the primary instrument of Panhellenic identity, an encyclopedic repository of mythological lore, moral exempla, theological structures, and military ethos. From the archaic rhapsodes performing at Panathenaic festivals to the philosophical discourses of Plato and Aristotle, Homer was the supreme pedagogical text of the Mediterranean world. In the early modern era, the rediscovery, printing, and philological reconstruction of the Homeric epics became a vital engine of Renaissance humanism, shaping early modern European literature, political theory, and editorial practices from the Italian Quattrocento through the Enlightenment.Biographical Legends, Lineage, and the Ancient 'Lives'Ancient biographical traditions regarding Homer are preserved in a corpus of pseudepigraphical texts known as the Vitae Homericae (Lives of Homer), the most prominent of which were historically attributed to Herodotus of Halicarnassus (the Vita Herodotea), Plutarch, and Proclus. These accounts, though recognized by modern scholarship as mythobiographical constructs rather than verified historical records, illuminate how the ancient world conceptualized the epic poet. According to these narratives, Homer was originally named Melesigenes, denoting his supposed birth near the river Meles in Smyrna, as the son of the nymph Cretheis. The name Hómēros was subsequently explained through folk etymologies: either derived from ὁ μὴ ὁρῶν ('he who does not see'), reflecting his legendary blindness, or from ὅμηρος ('hostage' or 'companion'), signifying his status during regional geopolitical conflicts in Ionia.The geography of Homer’s life in ancient tradition is inextricably tied to the East Greek world of the late eighth century BCE. Chios, where a hereditary guild of rhapsodes called the Homeridai ('descendants of Homer') operated well into the classical period, claimed the poet as its native son—a claim famously endorsed by the author of the Homeric Hymn to Delian Apollo, who self-identifies as 'a blind man who dwells in rocky Chios.' Other Ionian and Aeolian cities, including Colophon, Cyme, and Rhodes, similarly asserted claims to his nativity, giving rise to the famous epigram preserved in the Greek Anthology regarding the seven cities contending for Homer's origin. The legendary tradition culminates in his journey to the island of Ios, where, according to the pseudo-Herodotean life and the Certamen Homeri et Hesiodi ('Contest of Homer and Hesio d'), the poet died of frustration after failing to solve a riddle posed to him by young fishermen.The Homeric Poems: Narrative Architecture, Orality, and Poetic ArtistryThe two monumental works attributed to Homer—the Iliad (Ἰλιάς) and the Odyssey (Ὀδύσσεια)—represent the absolute zenith of ancient epic poetry. Composed in dactylic hexameter within a specialized, artificial poetic dialect combining Ionic, Aeolic, and archaizing Mycenaean linguistic elements, these poems transformed oral narrative tradition into monumental literary architecture. The Iliad, structured across twenty-four books comprising 15,693 lines, focuses upon a concentrated episode during the tenth year of the Trojan War: the catastrophic wrath (mênis) of Achilles, its devastating consequences for the Achaean army, and its resolution through the death of Hector and the tragic reconciliation between Achilles and King Priam. Rather than depicting the entirety of the Trojan conflict, Homeric technique concentrates cosmic human suffering, heroic honor (timê), and existential mortality into a span of roughly fifty-four days.The Odyssey, comprising 12,110 lines across twenty-four books, constructs a complex non-linear narrative detailing the ten-year return (nostos) of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, following the fall of Troy. Interweaving motifs of wanderings across mythic maritime geographies, domestic strife in Ithaca, divine retribution, and Telemachus’s maturation, the Odyssey explores themes of identity, cunning intelligence (mêtis), hospitality (xenia), and the restoration of social order. In addition to these two masterworks, antiquity attributed to Homer the Homeric Hymns—a collection of thirty-three hexameter poems praising various Olympian deities—as well as comedic or mock-heroic works such as the Batrachomyomachia ('Battle of the Frogs and Mice') and the lost comic epic Margites, though modern scholarship firmly assigns these to later archaic and classical authors.The groundbreaking research of American classicists Milman Parry and Albert Bates Lord in the 1930s revolutionized Homeric studies by demonstrating that the poems were products of an oral-formulaic traditional artistry. Drawing comparative evidence from South Slavic oral epic bards (guslars), Parry and Lord proved that the ubiquitous Homeric epithets (e.g., 'swift-footed Achilles,' 'rosy-fingered Dawn'), repeated half-lines, and recurrent narrative scenes ('type-scenes') were not stylistic adornments or memory aids for a single written text, but rather a sophisticated, fluid compositional system that allowed illiterate oral bards (aoidoi) to improvise massive hexameter narratives in real time. Homer is thus understood by modern 'Oralists' as the master singer who brought this ancient, evolving tradition to its monumental peak at the precise historical moment when the Greek alphabet was adopted in the eighth century BCE.Textual Transmission: From Athenian Recension to Alexandrian PhilologyThe journey of the Homeric text from oral performance to written monument represents one of the most vital chapters in the history of the book. According to classical historical sources, including Cicero and Diogenes Laërtius, the first official standardization and transcription of the Homeric poems occurred in Athens under the tyrant Peisistratus (or his son Hipparchus) in the sixth century BCE. This 'Peisistratid Recension' mandated that rhapsodes perform the Homeric epics in fixed sequence at the Quadrennial Panathenaic Games, establishing an authoritative Athenian exemplar that stabilized the fluidity of the oral tradition.The formal textual criticism of Homer was initiated during the Hellenistic period within the monumental setting of the Library of Alexandria. A succession of brilliant chief librarians—most notably Zenodotus of Ephesus (c. 325–260 BCE), Aristophanes of Byzantium (c. 257–180 BCE), and Aristarchus of Samothrace (c. 216–144 BCE)—devoted their scholarly lives to collecting, collating, and purifying the multi-variant manuscripts (ai kat' polēis and ai kat' andra editions) circulating throughout the Mediterranean. Aristarchus, considered the father of scientific textual philology, divided both the Iliad and the Odyssey into twenty-four books corresponding to the letters of the Greek alphabet. He established a rigorous system of critical signs (marginal symbols such as the obelos to mark suspected interpolations, the diple to highlight notable phrasing or interpretations, and the asteriskos) and composed extensive commentaries (hypomnemata). The scholarly labor of these Alexandrians, preserved and expanded through Byzantine marginal commentaries known as scholia (particularly the Scholia A preserved in the famous tenth-century manuscript Venetus A / Marcianus Graecus 454), formed the bedrock of the surviving Homeric textual tradition.In the medieval Byzantine Empire, Homer was obsessively studied, copied, and commented upon by Christian scholars. The most monumental Byzantine contribution came from Eustathius of Thessalonica, the twelfth-century archbishop and scholar, whose monumental commentaries (Pareckbolai) on the Iliad and Odyssey synthesized centuries of ancient scholia, historical geography, lexicography, and allegorical interpretation, preserving innumerable excerpts from lost classical texts.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Renaissance CirculationThe Renaissance recovery of Homer in the Latin West was a watershed moment in European intellectual history. While Homer had been virtually lost to Western Western Europe during the Middle Ages—known only through meager Latin synopses such as the Ilias Latina—the influx of Byzantine scholars following the Council of Florence (1439) and the Fall of Constantinople (1453) sparked an intense humanist effort to translate and print the original Greek text. Leontius Pilatus, encouraged by Petrarch and Giovanni Boccaccio, produced the first complete, albeit literal, Latin prose translation of Homer in Florence between 1360 and 1362. However, it was not until the late fifteenth century that Homer was committed to movable type.The milestone editio princeps of Homer's complete works was published in Florence in 1488 (dated December 9, 1488 / January 1489). This monumental two-volume folio, printed at the expense of the Florentine brothers Bernardo and Neri Nerli along with Giovanni Acciaiuoli, was edited by the eminent Greek émigré scholar Demetrius Chalcondyles (Demetrios Chalkokondyles), with technical typography directed by Demetrius Damilas. Set in an elegant, expansive Greek typeface derived from contemporary Byzantine manuscripts, the 1488 Florentine Homer represents one of the supreme masterpieces of early Greek typography and incunabula printing, establishing the baseline text for Western humanism.In the early sixteenth century, the locus of Homeric publishing shifted to Venice, dominated by the legendary press of Aldus Manutius. Aldus recognized the urgent need for portable, affordable scholarly editions of the classics. In 1504, the Aldine Press issued its first octavo edition of Homer, printed in Aldus's revolutionary, cursive Greek typeface designed by Francesco Griffo of Bologna. The Aldine Homer was reprinted and refined in 1517 and 1524, democratizing access to the original Greek text across the academies, universities, and private libraries of Renaissance Europe. Concurrently, in Florence, the press of Filippo Giunta issued important editions in 1519, contributing to a fierce typographical rivalry for the humanist market.Another monumental achievement in sixteenth-century Homeric printing occurred in Rome between 1542 and 1550, where the printer Antonio Blado published the editio princeps of Eustathius of Thessalonica’s vast commentaries on Homer. Edited by a circle of Greek scholars including Matthaeus Devarius and Majoranus under the patronage of Pope Paul III and Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, this four-volume folio set utilized the exquisite Greek type cut by Giovanni Honorato of Venice, based on the handwriting of the scribe Nikolaos Sophianos. Shortly thereafter, in Geneva, the master scholar-printer Henri Estienne II (Henricus Stephanus) published his monumental Poetae Graeci Principes Heroici Carminis (1566), featuring a brilliantly emended text of Homer accompanied by critical notes, setting a new standard for early modern philology.Vernacular translations rapidly expanded Homer's influence beyond classical scholars. In England, George Chapman published his famous translations of the Iliad (1611) and the Odyssey (1614–1616) in forceful fourteen-syllable rhyming couplets, immortalized centuries later by John Keats. In France, Anne Dacier published monumental prose translations of the Iliad (1699) and Odyssey (1708), which ignited the famous literary controversy known as the Querelle des Anciens et des Modernes (Quarrel of the Ancients and the Moderns). In the eighteenth century, Alexander Pope produced his heroic couplet translations of the Iliad (1715–1720) and Odyssey (1725–1726), published by Bernard Lintot in lavish subscriber folios that constituted both a literary masterpiece and a historic financial triumph for independent authorial publishing.Critical Reception, Philological Controversies, and Enduring LegacyThe modern scientific study of Homer was inaugurated in 1795 with the publication of the Prolegomena ad Homerum by the German philologist Friedrich August Wolf. Applying rigorous historical-critical methods to the transmission of the text, Wolf argued that the Iliad and Odyssey were not the unified creations of a single, conscious literary artist, but rather collections of shorter, independent oral songs composed by various bards over centuries, which were only compiled into unified long poems during the Peisistratid era. Wolf’s work polarized the academic world throughout the nineteenth century, dividing classical philology into two warring factions: the Analysts (such as Karl Lachmann, Gottfried Hermann, and Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff), who sought to dissect the epics to isolate the original 'authentic' kernels from later interpolations, and the Unitarians (such as Gregor Wilhelm Nitzsch and William Ewart Gladstone), who maintained the structural and artistic integrity of the poems as the creation of a single poetic mastermind.In the twentieth century, this dichotomy was fundamentally reshaped by the synthesis of archaeological discoveries and oral-formulaic theory. The excavations of Heinrich Schliemann at Hisarlik (Troy) and Mycenae in the 1870s proved that the Late Bronze Age civilization depicted in the epics had a tangible historical reality, even if Homer reflected a complex historical amalgam of Mycenaean memories, Dark Age social structures, and Archaic Ionian geography. Following Parry and Lord's oral-formulaic revolution, mid-twentieth-century scholars like Cedric Whitman, Geoffrey Kirk, and Albin Lesky demonstrated how monumental oral composition could exhibit intricate structural symmetry—such as the elaborate 'ring composition' analyzed throughout the Iliad.In late twentieth and early twenty-first-century scholarship, methodologies such as Neo-analysis (spearheaded by scholars like Wolfgang Kullmann) and historical-evolutionary models (such as Gregory Nagy’s model of five distinct stages of Homeric textualization from fluid performance to rigid canon) have further illuminated the dynamic evolution of the epics. Furthermore, comparative mythologists such as M. L. West have established deep structural and thematic linkages between Homeric epic and ancient Near Eastern literature, such as the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh and Ugaritic poetry.Homer’s influence upon Western culture remains immeasurable. From Virgil’s Aeneid, which directly repurposed the structural motifs of the Odyssey and Iliad, to Dante’s placement of Homer at the head of the non-Christian poets in Limbo (Inferno IV), down to James Joyce’s modern reinterpretation of the epic structure in Ulysses (1922) and Derek Walcott’s Caribbean epic Omeros (1990), Homeric epic remains the foundational blueprint for Western narrative art. As the ultimate archetype of the poet, Homer embodies the transformative power of language to conquer mortality, establishing an enduring poetic mirror in which humanity continues to contemplate heroism, suffering, fate, and redemption.

academic_description: Four parts bound in two folio volumes (315x195 mm). Ilias: pp. XI, [1 blank], 312; [4], 336. Odysseia: pp. [8], 297, [3 blanks]; [4], 336. Exquisite contemporary binding in full marbled leather, spine with five raised bands adorned with elaborate gilt tooling and dual labels with the title and volume number stamped in gold, boards framed within triple gilt fillet with corner decorations, marbled endpapers, gilt edges (hinges slightly weakened, minimal losses at the headcaps and corners, spine of the first volume slightly cracked, some scuffing, yet remarkably well preserved). Very slight uniform browning. An excellent copy with wide margins. This is the first edition magnificently printed by the brothers Robert and Andrew Foulis, the esteemed custodians of the Typographia Academiae Glasguensis, a veritable editorial masterpiece regarded as one of the finest editions ever published of the Iliade and the Odissea in Greek, both typographically and textually.The text was edited by the Glasgow scholars James Moor and George Muirhead (the former being the brother-in-law of Robert Foulis). The volumes were printed using the splendid Greek typeface designed and engraved by Alexander Wilson, a renowned type cutter from Glasgow. This edition earned the Foulis brothers the silver medal from the Select Society of Edinburgh.

authors.name: Maaler Josua
authors.biography: Josua Maaler (also recorded in Latinized forms as Joshua Maler or Pictorius; 15 June 1529 – 5 June 1599) stands as one of the most pivotal figures in the history of Germanic philology and early modern lexicography. Operating within the vibrant intellectual epicenter of post-Reformation Zurich, Maaler executed a monumental linguistic paradigm shift by compiling Die Teütsch spraach (1561), recognized by modern historical linguists as the very first comprehensive dictionary devoted to the German language in which German served as the primary, headword-entry language rather than a subordinate target rendering for Latin. Embedded within the scholarly circle of the Zwinglian Reformer Heinrich Bullinger and the polymathic naturalist and bibliographer Conrad Gessner, Maaler transformed vernacular lexicography from an auxiliary pedagogical instrument for Latin comprehension into an autonomous, noble philological discipline. His work served as a cornerstone for the consolidation of the High Alemannic written standard (Gemeines Teütsch) and fundamentally altered the trajectory of European bilingual lexicography during the Northern Renaissance.Born in Zurich into a prominent family of civic functionaries and artisans, Maaler was the son of Balthasar Maaler, an official civic bookbinder, printer’s associate, and administrator who provided his son with early exposure to the physical mechanisms of print culture and book production. Maaler’s formative education unfolded at the prestigious Schola Tigurina (the Grossmünster academy in Zurich), an institution reorganized under the ideological guidance of Huldrych Zwingli and led by Heinrich Bullinger. There, Maaler received rigorous training in classical Latin, Greek, and Hebrew under the tutelage of illustrious humanist scholars including Theodor Bibliander, Peter Martyr Vermigli, and Conrad Gessner. Recognizing the young scholar’s exceptional aptitude for linguistic analysis, the Zurich church authorities sponsored his academic peregrinatio academica. In 1547, Maaler traveled to French-speaking Switzerland to study at the Academy of Lausanne under Pierre Viret and Theodore Beza, perfecting his mastery of French. His scholarly travels subsequently extended to England during the reign of Edward VI—where he spent time at Oxford and Cambridge in the circle of continental Protestant refugees—and to the University of Paris, exposing him to French Renaissance humanism before he returned to Zurich in 1551 to take up holy orders in the Reformed Church.Maaler’s primary contribution to Western scholarship, Die Teütsch spraach: Alle wörter, namen vnd rëden arten der Teütschen spraach, in eyn vnvergleichlich artlich vnd vollkommne ordnung gebracht, was conceived as an explicit reversal and expansion of the Dictionarium Latinogermanicum compiled by the Zurich humanist Johannes Fries (Frisius) in 1556. While Fries had provided a dictionary intended to assist German students in writing Latin prose by listing Latin headwords with German translations, Maaler recognized that the dignity of the vernacular demanded an inverted architecture. Working meticulously over several years, Maaler reorganized and radically expanded Fries’s corpus, establishing an alphabetized, lemmatized inventory of over 11,000 German entry words translated into classical Latin. In doing so, he created a monumental structural matrix for Early New High German. Maaler did not merely list words; he categorized complex idiomatic expressions, syntactic turns of phrase, legal terminology, and botanical nomenclature, relying heavily on the High Alemannic dialect of Zurich while incorporating regional expressions from across the Holy Roman Empire. The work was introduced by a legendary prefatory letter (Epistola nuncupatoria) penned by Conrad Gessner, who elevated Maaler’s dictionary to a statement of national and linguistic pride, arguing that the German language possessed a structural purity, antiquity, and expressiveness equal to Greek, Latin, and Hebrew.The material production and typographical presentation of Die Teütsch spraach reflect the apex of sixteenth-century Swiss printing technology. Published in 1561 in a magnificent folio edition by the legendary Zurich printer Christoph Froschauer the Elder (and completed under the direction of his nephew, Christoph Froschauer the Younger), the volume was a masterpiece of typographic layout. Froschauer utilized contrasting typefaces to visually segregate and privilege the two languages: crisp, dynamic German Schwabacher and Fraktur types were deployed for the main German headwords and vernacular idioms, while elegant Roman Antiqua and Italic types were employed for the corresponding Latin translations and grammatical definitions. This visual distinction established a standardized typographical convention for multilingual dictionaries throughout Northern Europe. The print run was distributed extensively across European trade routes, finding its way into university libraries, monastic collections, civic chancelleries, and the private studies of humanists from London to Strasbourg, Nuremberg, and Basel, cementing Zurich’s reputation as a world capital of evangelical press culture.Following the publication of his masterwork, Maaler dedicated the remainder of his life to his pastoral duties while maintaining an active engagement with civic and historical writing. He served as pastor in the parish of Elgg from 1552 to 1571, before being called to the pastorate of Glattfelden, where he ministered until his death in 1599. During these decades, he compiled an extensive, meticulously detailed autobiographical diary and chronicle—his Lebensbeschreibung or Tagebuch—which preserved crucial historical details regarding daily life, ecclesiastical politics, economic conditions, and public health crises in sixteenth-century Switzerland. Maaler’s lexicographical legacy echoed through the centuries: his dictionary served as the primary source text for Justus Georg Schottelius in his foundational 17th-century treatises on the German language, inspired the lexicographical works of Kaspar Stieler, and provided indispensable historical citation material for Jakob and Wilhelm Grimm in the compilation of their monumental Deutsches Wörterbuch. Modern philologists recognize Josua Maaler as a pivotal visionary who liberated the German language from classical subordination and established the structural blueprint for modern vernacular lexicography.

publishers.name: Christoph Froschauer
publishers.biography: Christoph Froschauer (c. 1490 – 1 April 1564) stands as one of the most transformative figures in the annals of early modern European printing, humanism, and the Protestant Reformation. As the founder and guiding genius of the Officina Froschoveriana in Zurich, Froschauer elevated the Limmat city from a modest Swiss urban enclave into a premier capital of European scholarly publication and theological debate. His press, famously emblazoned with the typographic printer's mark depicting frogs under a tree—a playful canting visual pun on his surname—became the chief material engine of the Swiss Reformation. Working in intimate intellectual tandem with the reformer Huldrych Zwingli, his successor Heinrich Bullinger, the encyclopedic naturalist Conrad Gessner, and the chronicler Johannes Stumpf, Froschauer pioneered crucial developments in vernacular Bible translation, Protestant dogmatics, natural science, cartography, and humanist bibliography. His career encapsulates the dynamic convergence of print technology, evangelical theology, civic republicanism, and international scholarly networks during the sixteenth century.Born around 1490 in the Bavarian town of Kastl in the Upper Palatinate (Oberpfalz), Froschauer’s early life and precise parental lineage remain veiled in historical obscurity, though his later familial connections and extraordinary technical proficiency suggest a rigorous early apprenticeship in the vibrant printing hubs of Southwestern Germany, most notably Strasbourg and Augsburg. Seeking new commercial horizons, Froschauer migrated southwards across the Rhine, arriving in Zurich around 1517 or early 1518. He initially entered the printing workshop of Hans Rüegger, an established local printer. Following Rüegger’s death in 1519, Froschauer made a decisive strategic and personal move by marrying Rüegger’s widow, Resli (Theresia) Pfister. This union provided Froschauer with ownership of the established printing shop and enabled him to obtain full citizenship (Bürgerrecht) of Zurich on 9 November 1519. Free from the restrictive guild systems that governed other European cities, Zurich offered Froschauer an ideal environment to expand his enterprise, purchase modern press machinery, and forge key alliances with the city's civic and ecclesiastical leaders.Froschauer’s press attained momentous historical celebrity in the spring of 1522 through the iconic event known as the Wurstessen (the "Affair of the Sausages"), which served as the dramatic catalyst for the Zurich Reformation. On the evening of 9 March 1522, during the solemn observance of Lent, Froschauer hosted a gathering at his workshop home near the Zurich town wall for his press workforce, who were exhausted from the grueling physical labor of printing Zwingli’s Latin treatises and biblical commentaries. Among the assembled guests were the humanists Leo Jud, Klaus Hottinger, and Huldrych Zwingli himself, who had been appointed People's Priest (Leutpriester) at the Grossmünster in 1519. In direct defiance of Roman Catholic canon law regarding Lenten abstinence, Froschauer served sliced, cured sausages (Rauchwürste) to his workers. While Zwingli abstained from eating the meat himself, his presence and immediate public defense of the act transformed the private supper into a major public confrontation. Zwingli promptly delivered and published through Froschauer's press his landmark sermon Von Erkiesen und Freiheit der Speisen ("Concerning Choice and Liberty Regarding Foods"), arguing that ecclesiastical laws absent from Holy Scripture possessed no binding spiritual authority over Christian consciences. Froschauer's bold defense before the Zurich City Council—arguing that physical labor demanded sustenance—solidified the intimate alliance between his printing house and the nascent Zurich Reform movement.Throughout the 1520s and 1530s, the Officina Froschoveriana functioned as the central publication house for the Swiss Reformation. Froschauer worked tirelessly to publish Zwingli’s prolific output, including his theological defenses, anti-Anabaptist tracts, and liturgical reforms. The ultimate monument of this biblical-typographical partnership was the complete Zurich Bible (Zürcher Bibel), often designated the Froschauer Bible, published in 1531. Predating Martin Luther’s complete translation of the Bible (1534), the Zurich Bible was translated by Zwingli, Leo Jud, Theodor Bibliander, and their circle of scholars at the Zurich Prophei (the precursor to the Zurich Academy). Printed in a magnificent folio format, Froschauer’s 1531 Bible was lauded across Northern Europe for its linguistic clarity, elegant typography, and striking series of decorative woodcuts designed by prominent artists associated with the school of Hans Holbein the Younger and Hans Asper. Froschauer’s press produced dozens of editions of the Bible in various sizes—ranging from magnificent display folios to portable octavo and duodecimo volumes—ensuring that the Zurich vernacular Scripture reached lay readers, scholars, and clergy across German-speaking territories, the Swiss Confederation, and international evangelical communities.Following Zwingli’s tragic death at the Battle of Kappel in October 1531, Froschauer maintained an equally productive relationship with Zwingli’s successor as Antistes of the Zurich Church, Heinrich Bullinger. Over three decades, Froschauer issued hundreds of Bullinger’s works, including his monumental Decades (Sermones Decades quinque), a comprehensive compendium of Reformed theology that became required reading for clergy throughout England, Scotland, the Netherlands, and Germany. Froschauer’s shop became an essential hub for international Protestant humanism. During the reign of Mary I in England (1553–1558), when Protestant scholars faced persecution, Zurich served as a primary sanctuary for Marian exiles such as John Jewel, Miles Coverdale, and Alexander Nowell. Froschauer welcomed these exiles into his home and press network, printing English theological treatises and maintaining correspondence that fundamentally shaped the Elizabethan Religious Settlement. His international scholarly connections extended to Italy, France, and Poland, printing the Latin theological, philosophical, and exegetical masterworks of Italian evangelical exiles like Peter Martyr Vermigli and Girolamo Zanchi.Beyond theology, Froschauer made monumental contributions to early modern natural science, geography, and bibliography through his collaborative relationship with the legendary Zurich polymath Conrad Gessner. Recognizing Gessner’s genius, Froschauer financed, printed, and distributed Gessner’s most ambitious scholarly projects, which redefined Renaissance humanism. In 1545, Froschauer published Gessner’s Bibliotheca Universalis, a groundbreaking universal bibliography that cataloged all known Latin, Greek, and Hebrew printed books and manuscripts. Between 1551 and 1558, Froschauer issued Gessner’s epic four-volume Historia Animalium, widely considered the founding masterpiece of modern zoology. This monumental publication featured hundreds of meticulous woodcut illustrations of quadrupeds, birds, fish, and aquatic creatures, requiring extraordinary technical coordination in woodblock carving, ink mixing, layout design, and paper sourcing. Similarly, Froschauer printed Johannes Stumpf’s grand illustrated Swiss chronicle, Gemeiner löblicher Eydgnoſchafft Stetten, Landen und Völckern Chronick (1547/1548), decorated with over 1,300 woodcuts, maps, heraldic coats of arms, and topographical views, establishing a high watermark for early modern Swiss book design and historical cartography.To support his immense production schedule—which generated over one thousand distinct titles during his lifetime—Froschauer established a highly sophisticated commercial and manufacturing infrastructure. He acquired paper mills, including the paper mill at the Enge near Zurich, guaranteeing a steady supply of high-grade, watermark-certified paper suitable for complex multi-language printing featuring Greek, Hebrew, and Latin typesets. Froschauer was a regular and influential figure at the Frankfurt Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse), where he established distribution channels extending across the Holy Roman Empire, France, England, and Italy. Following the death of his first wife in 1550, Froschauer married Dorothea Locher, further solidifying his elite social standing within the Zurich patriciate. In recognition of his immense services to the city, the Zurich City Council elevated Froschauer to civic distinction, granting him prestigious municipal privileges.Christoph Froschauer died on 1 April 1564, falling victim to a devastating outbreak of the bubonic plague that swept through Zurich, claiming the lives of many prominent scholars and citizens that year. His death marked the end of a golden era in Swiss printing, but his legacy endured through his nephew and adopted apprentice, Christoph Froschauer the Younger (c. 1532–1585), who assumed leadership of the press and maintained its high standards of scholarship and typography. The Officina Froschoveriana continued to operate under successive generations until its eventual historical evolution into the famous Zurich publishing firm Orell Füssli. Froschauer’s life stands as a testament to the power of the printed page in transforming religious doctrine, disseminating scientific empiricism, and establishing the structural foundations of early modern European intellectual culture.

related_names.name: Gessner Conrad
related_names.biography: Conrad Gessner (also rendered as Konrad Gesner, Conradus Gesnerus, and under the pseudonym Euonymus Philiatrus; born March 26, 1516, Zurich – died December 13, 1565, Zurich) stands as one of the most monumental figures of Northern Renaissance humanism. Often venerated as the father of modern universal bibliography and the founder of early modern zoology and botany, Gessner embodied the ideal of the polymathic scholar (homo universalis). Operating at the vital crossroads of classical philology, empirical natural philosophy, bibliographical systematization, and early modern print culture, Gessner transformed the organization of human knowledge during a period of intense religious upheaval and intellectual expansion. His monumental compilations—most notably the Bibliotheca Universalis (1545–1549) and the multi-volume Historia Animalium (1551–1558)—established unprecedented standards for empirical observation, cross-referencing, and information management, laying the structural groundwork upon which Enlightenment taxonomy and modern scientific cataloguing were subsequently built.Early Life, Tragic Bereavement, and Humanist Formation (1516–1541)Conrad Gessner was born into modest circumstances in Zurich in March 1516, the son of Urs Gessner, a local furrier, and Agathe Frick. Recognizing the boy's extraordinary intellectual aptitude, his father entrusted his early education to his great-uncle, Johannes Frick, a chaplain who cultivated young Conrad's initial interest in botany through the cultivation of medicinal herbs. The course of Gessner's early life was fundamentally shattered by the Second War of Kappel in October 1531, in which his father was killed alongside the Swiss Protestant Reformer Huldrych Zwingli. Orphaned, impoverished, and destitute, the fifteen-year-old scholar found salvation within Zurich's evangelical humanist network. The reformer Heinrich Bullinger, Zwingli’s successor, together with the scholar Konrad Pellikan and the canon Oswald Myconius, intervened to secure financial patronage for Gessner's continued studies.Under their aegis, Gessner embarked upon an itinerary across the leading humanist academies of Europe. He studied Hebrew, Greek, and Latin at the Grossmünster school in Zurich before travelling to Strassburg in 1532 to study under the renowned humanist and reformer Wolfgang Capito. In 1533, Gessner moved to France, enrolling at the University of Bourges and later in Paris, where he deepened his command of classical philology, natural philosophy, and medicine. Political and religious instability forced his return to Switzerland, where he temporarily accepted a teaching position in Zurich. In 1537, at the age of twenty-one, Gessner was appointed Professor of Greek at the newly established Academy of Lausanne. This academic position provided him with the financial stability to publish his early philological works, including a revised edition of the Greek-Latin dictionary of Hesychius. Driven by an insatiable ambition to master the healing arts, Gessner resigned his professorship at Lausanne in 1540 to complete his medical studies at the University of Basel. In 1541, he defended his doctoral dissertation on medical theory and was awarded the degree of Doctor of Medicine, subsequently establishing his medical practice in his native city of Zurich.The Monumental Bibliographical Project: Bibliotheca Universalis and Information ManagementGessner's scholarly reputation was permanently cemented with the publication of the Bibliotheca Universalis (Zurich: Christoph Froschauer, 1545), a massive folio volume that represented the first comprehensive universal bibliography of printed and manuscript literature in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew ever attempted. Prompted by the loss of classical texts and the cataclysmic destruction of European libraries—such as the sack of the Bibliotheca Corviniana in Buda—Gessner sought to construct an imperishable "virtual library" that would preserve the total sum of human knowledge against time, fire, and political chaos. The initial 1545 volume catalogued over 12,000 titles by roughly 3,000 authors, arranged alphabetically according to the author's given name, complete with biographical notices, critical assessments, and incipits.Recognizing that an alphabetical catalog served primarily for reference rather than thematic inquiry, Gessner published the second part of his bibliographical architecture, the Pandectarum sive Partitionum universalium libri XXI, in 1548. In the Pandectae, Gessner devised an astonishing conceptual taxonomy, classifying the entirety of human knowledge into twenty-one distinct faculties and disciplines—ranging from Grammar, Dialectic, and Rhetoric to Mathematics, Astronomy, Geography, Philosophy, Medicine, and Theology. Gessner introduced innovative mechanisms of information management: he pioneered the use of movable paper slips (early index cards) to organize entries and implemented sophisticated cross-referencing systems. The Bibliotheca Universalis provided the methodological template for all subsequent bibliographical control, directly influencing Gabriel Naudé, Antoine du Verdier, and the development of modern library science.The Empire of Nature: Historia Animalium, Botanical Researches, and Philological ScienceHaving mapped the realm of written texts, Gessner turned his encyclopedic intellect toward the book of nature. Between 1551 and 1558, he published his masterwork of natural history, the Historia Animalium, printed in four massive folio volumes by Christoph Froschauer (with a fifth volume on serpents published posthumously in 1587). Spanning over 4,500 pages, the work was divided systematically: Volume I on viviparous quadrupeds (1551), Volume II on oviparous quadrupeds (1554), Volume III on birds (1555), and Volume IV on aquatic animals (1558). In this colossal work, Gessner combined exhaustive philological erudition—drawing upon Aristotle, Pliny, Aelian, and medieval bestiaries—with empirical, autopsy-based observation and anatomical dissection.For each animal, Gessner structured the narrative using a rigorous eight-part entry system: name in ancient and modern languages, geographical distribution, anatomy and physical description, habits and natural physiology, utility to man, moral or symbolic associations, culinary applications, and medical remedies derived from the creature. A defining feature of the Historia Animalium was its lavish use of over 1,200 woodcut illustrations. Gessner realized that visual accuracy was essential for scientific identification; he commissioned artists, gathered original drawings from correspondents across Europe—including Albert Dürer's famous rendering of the rhinoceros—and personally sketched specimens. Furthermore, Gessner maintained an extensive correspondence network (a res publica litteraria) with leading European naturalists, including John Caius in England, Guillaume Rondelet and Pierre Belon in France, and Pietro Andrea Mattioli in Italy, who provided him with exotic specimens, field observations, and anatomical descriptions.Parallel to his zoological work, Gessner was a pioneering botanist and mountain climber. He conducted extensive botanical field studies throughout the Swiss Alps, recognizing long before his contemporaries that distinct plant zones corresponded to alpine altitudes. In his Libellus de lacte et operibus lactariis (1541), which included the famous essay Descriptio Montis Fracti (an account of Mount Pilatus), Gessner expressed a distinctly modern appreciation for the aesthetic and scientific majesty of mountains. Over his lifetime, Gessner assembled hundreds of original plant illustrations and detailed dissections of floral structures, identifying the importance of the flower and fruit in plant classification. Although his planned monumental Historia Plantarum remained unpublished at his death—its visual materials scattered until their 18th-century rediscovery by Casimir Christoph Schmiedel—his botanical observations directly foreshadowed the taxonomic principles of Carl Linnaeus.In addition to natural history, Gessner made groundbreaking contributions to comparative linguistics with his treatise Mithridates. De differentiis linguarum (1555). In this work, he catalogued 130 known languages and presented the Lord's Prayer rendered in twenty-two different tongues, laying one of the earliest foundations for comparative European philology.Typographical Architecture, Epistolary Networks, and the Froschauer PressThe extraordinary productivity of Conrad Gessner cannot be detached from the intellectual and typographical ecosystem of Renaissance Zurich, specifically his intimate collaboration with the master printer Christoph Froschauer. The Froschauer press served as the physical site where Gessner's structural vision was realized. Producing works of such immense complexity required specialized typographical strategies. Froschauer utilized clean Roman and Italic fonts, elaborate Greek types, and multi-column grid layouts capable of accommodating dense Latin prose alongside Greek commentary, Hebrew roots, and complex marginalia.Gessner worked in close proximity to the print shop, acting as proofreader, editor, and visual supervisor. The integration of high-quality woodcuts into the textual grid of the Historia Animalium required unprecedented technical coordination between printers, woodcutters, and scholars. Gessner's published letters reveal an individual deeply immersed in the materiality of the book: he selected paper stocks, negotiated print runs, managed distribution logistics, and actively curated his scholarly image within the republic of letters. His domestic residence in Zurich became a dynamic center of scholarly pilgrimage, housing a private botanical garden, a natural history museum of specimens, and an immense library of rare manuscripts.Medical Service, Later Years, and Posthumous LegacyIn 1554, Gessner was appointed official Town Physician (Stadtphysikus) of Zurich, a post he held until his death. In this capacity, he actively combated regional epidemics, treated patients across all social strata, and conducted public health inspections. Despite his demanding medical duties and declining physical health, he continued his publishing endeavors. Under the pseudonym Euonymus Philiatrus, he published De remediis secretis (1552), a highly influential work on chemical medicine, distillation, and pharmacopeia that bridged traditional Galenic medicine with early Paracelsian chemical therapies.In 1564, the bubonic plague struck Zurich with devastating force. Gessner devoted himself unsparingly to the care of the afflicted while systematically recording the epidemiological progression of the disease. In late 1565, Gessner contracted the plague himself. Realizing his death was imminent, he requested to be carried into his beloved museum and library at the Grossmünster, surrounded by his books, plant specimens, and scientific instruments. He died on December 13, 1565, at the age of forty-nine.Conrad Gessner’s legacy is colossal. In natural history, he bridged the gap between ancient authority and modern empirical investigation. In bibliography, he created the architectural framework of modern information retrieval. His taxonomic insights were explicitly acknowledged by Carl Linnaeus, who named the plant genus Gesneria and the family Gesneriaceae in his honor. Gessner's life remains an enduring testament to the Renaissance ideal of total erudition, where philology, nature, and the printed page united in the service of universal knowledge.

academic_description: 4to (237x143 mm). [8], 536 leaves. With errors in leaf numbering. Collation: *8 a-z8 A-Z8 Aa-Xx8. Original blind-stamped pigskin over wooden boards, spine with four raised bands, metal clasps preserved, manuscript initials (?) inked at the bottom edge (slightly soiled and rubbed). Wax stamp with the initials “WJ” on the front pastedown. Some pale occasional foxing and browning. Wide margins. A superb copy. Rare first and only edition. In his preface to his Deutsches Wörterbuch (Leipzig, 1854, col. XXI), Jacob Grimm, who regretted that Die teütsch Spraach was never reprinted, writes: “The palpable need for such a German dictionary prompted Josua Maaler, also known as Pictorius, to follow Gessner’s advice and adapt Fries’ Dictionarium Latinogermanicum, composing it in German […] it is a richly endowed treasure trove of words and idioms drawn from the living Swiss language - in fact, the first true German dictionary. It was unfortunate that no further editions were published”.“[Maaler] eventually settled in Switzerland as a clergyman, and there in 1561 he produced his major work, Die Teütsch spraach, which Jacob Grimm was later to acclaim as the first true German dictionary. Conrad Gessner, author of the celebrated Mithridates (1555), contributes a preface to the work in which he looks back respectfully to Dasypodius as ‘vir pius et eruditus, praeceptor olim meus’. The retarded state of German lexicography, as compared with English, French and Italian, is for Gessner all the more lamentable, given the greater antiquity and purity of German” (W. J. Jones, Lingua teutonum victrix? Landmarks in German Lexicography, 1500-1700, in: “Histoire, Epistémologie, Langage”, 1991, p. 135).Contad Gessner’s preface is a notable addition to Maaler’s dictionary, as it builds upon and expands his significant work on comparative linguistics, Mithridates, published in 1555. Gessner briefly touches on the circumstances surrounding the dictionary’s creation before offering a comprehensive defence of the study of Germanic languages and their lexicography. Though not always free from speculation and hardly immune to unreliable sources, he presents his readers with the state of the art in linguistics at the time in an eloquent and precise manner (cf. M.H. Graf, Vergleichende germanische Philologie im 16. Jahrhundert ‘Aus Conrad Gessners Vorrede zum Wörterbuch von Josua Maaler, 1581’, in: “Turicensia Latina”, 2003, pp. 176-177).Maaler’s dictionary was part of the Zurich humanists’ efforts to promote the German language as a national language and raise its status. It is the first comprehensive German dictionary to contain long definitions, example phrases and proverbs in German as well as Latin, thus extensively documenting German vocabulary and its semantic, syntactic and pragmatic usage (cf. (O. Reichmann & K.-P. Wegera, eds., Frühneuhochdeutsches Lesebuch, Tübingen, 1988, p. 67).“Der nächste Schritt, der in der ersten Hälfte des 16. Jahrhunderts gemacht wurde, hat es nämlich gleichfalls noch nicht auf ein Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache abgesehen. Es soll vielmehr nur an die Stelle des barbarischen Lateins der bisherigen Vocabularien echtes antik klassisches Latein gesetzt werden, so dass der Benutzer mit Hülfe des lateinisch-deutschen Wörterbuches die alten Klassiker verstehen, mit Hülfe des deutsch-lateinischen sich selbst einen guten lateinischen Ausdruck aneignen kann. In diese Klasse von Büchern gehört das Dictionarium Latinogermanicum und das dazu gehörige Dictionarium Germanicolatinum, welches der im J. 1559 verstorbene Lahrer des Griechischen zu Strassburg Petrus Dasypodius im J. 1536 herausgab […] Dagegen macht den entscheidenden Fortschritt zu einem wirklichen Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache der Zürcher Josua Maaler (Pictorius) in seinem Werk: Die Teütsch spraach […] Der Verfasser, Pfarrer zu Elgau, im Züricher Gebiet, wurde von Conrad Gesner veranlasst, das 1556 zu Zürich erschienene lateinisch-deutsche Dictionarium des Joh. Frisius zu einem alphabetisch geordneten deutschen Sprachschatz umzuarbeiten. Das beigefügte Latein sollte freilich auch hier zugleich dem Lateinschreibeden eine gute Übersetzung der deutschen Redeweisen an die Hand geben; die eigentliche Absicht aber gieng auf eine Sammlung des deutschen Wortschatzes. In der gehaltreichen Vorrede, die Conrad Gesner dem Werke hinzufügte, sagt er, in einem Gespräch zwischem ihm und Frisius, dem auch Pictorius beiwohnte, sei die Rede auf die lebenden Sprachen Europaìs gekommen, und da hätten die Unterredenden bemerkt, wie viel die den Deutschen benachbarten Völker: die Franzosen, Italiener und Engländer, für Verschönerung und Bereicherung ihrer Sprachen thäten, und dass sie reichhaltige Wörterbücher derselben besässen, in denen wohl geordnet die einzelnen Ausdrücke, ihre Anwendung und Bedeutung, und ebenso die Redensarten erklärt würden. ‘Da empfanden wir es schmerzlich’, fährt Gesner fort, ‘dass unserem Deutschland ein Mann fehle, der dasselbe für unsere Sprache leistete’. So veranlassten sie den Pictorius, sich dieser Arbeit zu unterziehen. Wie sehr dabei das Deutsche im Vordergrund stand, sieht man unter Anderem auch daraus, dass der Verfasser nicht bloss der einheimischen Jugend, sondern auch den Fremden: Franzosen, Italienern und Engländern, zur Erlernung der deutschen Sprache behülflich sein wollte. Um sich zu überzeugen, dass Maaler’s Unternehmen wirklich ein neues war, ‘dergleichen bisher nie gesehen’, braucht man es nur mit dem vorangehenden deutsch-lateinischen Wörterbuch des Dasypodius zu vergleichen” (R. von Raumer, Geschichte der germanischen Philologie: vorzugsweise in Deutschland, Munich, 1870, pp. 84-86).Many details about Maaler’s life can be found in his autobiography, which he wrote between 1593 and 1596. The original manuscript has been lost. A copy from 1784 held at the Zurich Central Library is incomplete, but it is the most comprehensive one that has survived. It was published as the autobiography of a Zurich pastor from the second half of the 16th century in the “Zürcher Taschenbuch” (new series 8, 1885, pp. 123-214; 9, 1886, pp. 125-203, from now SZ).Josua Maaler (Maler, Mahler, Pictorius) was born in Villigen (Black Forest). His father, Balthasar, was initially a monk; after the Reformation, he moved to Zurich (1524), where he was granted citizenship, worked as a bookbinder, and married - in his third marriage - the widow of Eustachius Froschauer the Elder, making Josua the stepbrother of Christoph Froschauer the Younger. The young Maaler attended Latin school in Zurich and received a scholarship from the city council to fund his education. This enabled him to study under Pierre Viret at the Academy of Lausanne in 1549 and subsequently to undertake a study trip to England (cf. W.D. Robson-Scott, Josua Maler’s Visit to England in 1551, in: “The Modern Language Review”, 45/3, 1950, pp. 346-351).On his way there, he attended Petrus Ramus’s lectures in Paris (SZ, p. 133), studied under Petrus Martyr in Oxford (SZ, p. 153), and under Immanuel Tremellius in Cambridge (SZ, p. 156). On his return journey, he was a guest of Johannes Froschauer the Elder in Frankfurt for ten days and attended the lectures of Heinrich Glareanus in Freiburg im Breisgau (SZ, p. 184). After his return, he married Margaretha Ochsner and, following his successful examination, served as a pastor or dean in five parishes in eastern Switzerland beginning in 1552: Witikon (1552–1553), Elgg (1553–1571), Bischofzell (1571–1582), Winterthur (1582–1598). In 1598, he was called to Glattfelden, where he died on June 5, 1599 (cf. J. Bächtold, Josua Maler (Pictorius), Zurich, 1884, pp. 5-30; see also P.O. Müller, Maaler, Josua, in: “Frühe Neuzeit in Deutschland 1520-1620. Literaturwissenschaftliches Verfasserlexikon”, W. Kühlmann & al., eds., Berlin, 2015, vol. 4, cols. 233-238).

title: Palazzi di Roma de più celebri architetti disegnati da Pietro Ferrerio pittore et architetto. Libro primo [-secondo]

authors.name: Ferrerio Pietro
authors.biography: Pietro Ferrerio (c. 1600 – 1654) stands as a pivotal figure in mid-seventeenth-century Roman print culture, architectural draftsmanship, and copperplate etching. Active in Rome during the artistic height of the High Baroque pontificates of Urban VIII Barberini and Innocent X Pamphilj, Ferrerio's primary historical significance resides in his conception, drawing, and initial execution of the monumental architectural treatise Palazzi di Roma de' più celebri architetti. Published in collaboration with the dominant Roman print establishment of Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi at the sign of the Paris clock near Santa Maria della Pace, Ferrerio's suite of etched plates established an unprecedented empirical standard for the graphic documentation of secular architecture in the Papal Capital. By bridging the gap between the theoretical, woodcut-illustrated Renaissance architectural treatises of Sebastiano Serlio, Andrea Palladio, and Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, and the expansive, empirical copperplate pattern books of the later Baroque and Enlightenment eras, Ferrerio transformed architectural drawing into an internationally circulating print medium that defined the reception of Roman architecture across early modern Europe.Virtually nothing is preserved regarding Ferrerio's early origins prior to his documented maturity in Rome during the 1630s and 1640s, though contemporary title pages consistently designate him as pittore et architetto ("painter and architect"). Trained in both the fine arts and the technical disciplines of architectural survey, Ferrerio operated within the vibrant artistic crucible of Barberinian Rome, where artists were expected to navigate effortlessly between design, orthographic projection, and graphic printmaking. His artistic formation coincided with a period of intense transformation in Roman architectural practice, characterized by the audacious structural inventions of Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Francesco Borromini, and Pietro da Cortona, alongside the ongoing consolidation of Renaissance monuments built by Bramante, Raphael, Baldassarre Peruzzi, Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, and Michelangelo. Ferrerio mastered the technique of copperplate etching, utilizing fine lines and precise hatching to capture both the subtle textural variations of travertine rustication and the crisp, geometric shadows cast by complex classical entablatures and pediments.The core of Ferrerio's intellectual and artistic production is embodied in his project for Palazzi di Roma de' più celebri architetti. Unlike earlier architectural topographers who favored pictorial, perspective-driven city views (vedute) framed by ruinous landscapes, Ferrerio approached his subjects with strict orthographic rigor. Each plate presents measured façade elevations, ground plans, and structural details drawn to scale, recorded using the standard palmo romano. Ferrerio systematically documented the grandest aristocratic residences of Rome, including the Palazzo Farnese, the Palazzo della Cancelleria, the Palazzo Barberini at the Quattro Fontane, the Palazzo Pamphilj in Piazza Navona, and the Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne. His plates provided precise line drawings of piano nobile windows, portals, loggias, and cornices, creating an objective visual encyclopedia of Roman palace design. Through this meticulous methodology, Ferrerio's work aligned closely with the antiquarian ethos of contemporary Roman circles, most notably the scientific and artistic network surrounding Cassiano dal Pozzo and his Museo Cartaceo ("Paper Museum"), which sought to catalog the physical world through exhaustive visual documentation.The printing and publication history of Ferrerio's work reflects the sophisticated commercial infrastructure of seventeenth-century Roman printmaking. Ferrerio aligned himself with Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi (1627–1691), the head of the famed De Rossi publishing dynasty based at Santa Maria della Pace. The De Rossi press was instrumental in centralizing the production and distribution of architectural etchings, transforming Rome into the European capital of graphic art publishing. Ferrerio etched approximately 44 plates for the first volume of the Palazzi di Roma before his sudden death in Rome in 1654. Recognizing the immense commercial and artistic value of the project, Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi retained Ferrerio's etched copperplates and preserved his name on the original title page. To complete and expand the monumental series, De Rossi recruited the brilliant young draftsman and engraver Giovanni Battista Falda (1643–1678). Falda contributed a second book, titled Nuovi disegni dell'architetture e piante de' palazzi di Roma, which added dozens of new plates, ground plans, and updated elevations of contemporary Baroque additions. The combined two-volume collection was reissued in multiple editions throughout the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries by Domenico de Rossi and his successors.The critical reception of Ferrerio's etchings was immediate and far-reaching, exerting a profound impact on European architectural theory, pattern book design, and Grand Tour connoisseurship. Bound copies of Palazzi di Roma were acquired by foreign ambassadors, scholars, and visiting architects, providing European readers with exact visual renderings of Roman Baroque masterworks that had previously been accessible only through direct travel or hand-drawn sketches. Ferrerio's publication set the standard for subsequent national architectural surveys throughout the continent. In France, it served as a primary model for Jean Marot's celebrated architectural prints, known as the Grand Marot (Recueil des plans, profils et élévations de plusieurs palais et maisons de Paris). In the Holy Roman Empire, master builders such as Paul Decker (Fürstlicher Baumeister) and Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach derived structural motifs directly from Ferrerio's copperplates. Furthermore, in eighteenth-century Britain, Ferrerio's clear orthographic methodology directly inspired Colen Campbell's groundbreaking Vitruvius Britannicus (1715), which laid the foundation for British Neo-Palladianism. Today, Ferrerio is recognized by architectural historians as a master draftsman who transformed architectural printmaking from an auxiliary trade into a central pillar of early modern architectural discourse.
