authors.name: Falda Giovanni Battista
authors.biography: Giovanni Battista Falda (1643–1678) stands as one of the most seminal topographers, engravers, and visual chroniclers of seventeenth-century Rome. Working at the vibrant apex of the Roman High Baroque under the aegis of the premier print publisher Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi, Falda created a visual lexicon of the Holy City that defined the European perception of urban grandeur, architectural innovation, and papal triumph for over a century. Operating during an era dominated by the transformative urban planning of Popes Alexander VII Chigi, Clement IX Rospigliosi, and Clement X Altieri, Falda rendered the monuments, fountains, palaces, villas, and civic rituals of Rome with an unprecedented synthesis of analytical clarity, mathematical perspective, and atmospheric vitality. His celebrated print suites—most notably Il Nuovo Teatro delle Fabriche, et Edificii, in Prospettiva di Roma Moderna, Le Fontane di Roma, Li Giardini di Roma, and his colossal 1676 twelve-sheet plan of Rome—transcended mere documentation; they served as sophisticated instruments of papal propaganda, topographical handbooks for early Grand Tourists, and foundational models for subsequent generations of vedutisti, extending from Lievin Cruyl and Gaspar van Wittel to Giuseppe Vasi and Giovanni Battista Piranesi.Born in the northern Italian town of Valduggia, in the Valsesia region of Piedmont, in November 1643, Falda demonstrated an exceptional precocity for draughtsmanship during his early childhood. Recognizing his talent, his family arranged for his initial artistic instruction locally before sending him to Rome around 1655–1657, when the young artist was scarcely fourteen years old. Upon his arrival in the papal capital, Falda was placed under the guardianship of a relative who introduced him to the workshop of the painter and engraver Ercole Ferrata, as well as the broader artistic milieu of the Accademia di San Luca. Crucially, his extraordinary talent for architectural drawing and spatial perspective quickly attracted the eye of the master sculptor and architect Gian Lorenzo Bernini, who reportedly mentored the youth and commended his ability to translate complex stone structures into graphic form. However, the definitive turning point in Falda's life occurred when he entered into an exclusive commercial and artistic relationship with Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi (1627–1691), proprietor of the famous printshop Stamperia alla Pace located near the church of Santa Maria della Pace.De Rossi recognized in Falda the ideal craftsman to execute his ambitious vision of systematically documenting the modern architectural renaissance of Rome. Under De Rossi's direct patronage and intellectual guidance, Falda was retained not merely as an etcher, but as an on-site surveyor and designer. Between 1665 and his untimely death in 1678, Falda produced hundreds of copperplate etchings that mapped the ideological and physical reconfiguration of the city. His first monumental project was Il Nuovo Teatro delle Fabriche, et Edificii, in Prospettiva di Roma Moderna, launched in 1665 with subsequent volumes appearing in 1665 and 1669 (and a posthumous fourth book executed by Alessandro Specchi in 1699). Breakaway from the stylized or fantastical Renaissance views of early printmakers, Falda’s plates for the Nuovo Teatro presented orthographic precision combined with dynamic three-quarter bird’s-eye perspectives. He meticulously recorded the newly completed facades of Bernini, Francesco Borromini, Pietro da Cortona, and Carlo Rainaldi, portraying buildings such as the Palazzo Chigi-Odescalchi, the church of Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, the Propaganda Fide, and the twin churches of Piazza del Popolo with absolute fidelity to line, scale, and decorative detail.In addition to monumental civic and ecclesiastical architecture, Falda directed his etching needle toward the hydraulic and landscape marvels of the city. In 1675, De Rossi published the first two books of Falda's seminal work on urban hydraulics, Le Fontane di Roma nelle piazze, e luoghi publici della città, con li loro prospetti, come sono al presente. This suite recorded the magnificent fountains constructed by the popes, from the monumental Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi in Piazza Navona to the modest neighborhood spouts and monastic fountains. Falda captured the kinetic motion of cascading water alongside the surrounding urban fabric, establishing a harmonious dialogue between stone, water, light, and public space. This was complemented by Li Giardini di Roma con le loro piante ed alzate e prospettive (published around 1670–1683), in which Falda documented the aristocratic villas and manicured gardens of the Roman elite, such as the Villa Borghese, Villa Ludovisi, and Villa Pamphili. In these plates, he combined ground plans (*piante*) with elevated perspective views (*alzate e prospettive*), providing architectural historians with invaluable records of historical garden design, parterres, grottoes, and antiquarian sculpture displays that have since been altered or destroyed.Falda’s absolute cartographic masterpiece arrived in 1676 with the publication of his monumental twelve-sheet bird's-eye map of Rome, titled Nuova Pianta et Alzata della Città di Roma con tutte le strade, piazze, et edificii fabricati et publici.... Measuring roughly 1.5 by 1.5 meters when assembled, this plan represents one of the greatest achievements of early modern cartography. Building upon the sixteenth-century cartographic tradition of Antonio Tempesta and Leonardo Bufalini, Falda achieved an unparalleled synthesis of mathematical planimetry and pictorial elevation. Every individual street, alley, courtyard, garden plot, church, and palace is etched with astonishing micro-graphic clarity. The map served as a brilliant instrument of Counter-Reformation and Baroque urban identity, highlighting the grand avenues cut through the medieval fabric by Pope Sixtus V and Alexander VII to connect the major pilgrimage basilicas. The borders of the map were embellished with heraldic shields, allegorical figures, and dedication cartouches that celebrated the reign of Clement X and the administrative efficiency of the Roman curia.Beyond permanent urban structures, Falda was deeply involved in capturing the ephemeral pageantry and political theater of Baroque Rome. He etched elaborate series depicting papal catafalques, imperial ambassadorial entries, canonization ceremonies, and carnival floats. His prints documented the elaborate temporary structures designed by Bernini and Cortona for religious feast days and dynastic celebrations, such as the *Macchina della Chinea* erected annually by the Kingdom of Naples in front of the Palazzo Farnese. In these works, as well as in the staffage (*macchiette*) that populates his architectural views, Falda showcased his keen observational skills regarding Roman social life. Carriages of cardinals, water-carriers, street vendors, foreign tourists, beggars, and aristocratic retinues animate his plazas, providing a lively sociological backdrop to the timeless stone monuments.Technically, Falda was a master of the etching technique, often combining soft etching with delicate engraving burnishing to achieve dramatic chiaroscuro contrasts and crisp spatial depth. Working on high-quality copper plates supplied by De Rossi, Falda utilized fine parallel hatching and cross-hatching to create gradations of shadow, capturing the blinding sunlight of the Roman summer against dark, deeply recessed porticoes and cornices. The paper stock used at the Stamperia alla Pace—frequently bearing the famous *Fleur-de-lis in a Circle* watermark—ensured that impressions were crisp, rich, and durable, allowing De Rossi to distribute them in vast quantities across Europe. These print albums were bound in calfskin or vellum and purchased eagerly by northern European aristocrats on the Grand Tour, diplomatic envoys, and foreign architects who sought to bring the stylistic innovations of the Roman Baroque back to Paris, London, Vienna, and Madrid.Tragically, Giovanni Battista Falda’s brilliant career was cut short when he died in Rome on August 22, 1678, at the young age of thirty-four. He was interred with honors in his parish church of Santa Maria della Pace, directly adjacent to the printshop where his entire professional life had unfolded. Despite his brief life, Falda’s graphic output was immense, comprising hundreds of meticulously engraved plates. Following his death, Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi retained the copperplates, continuing to print new editions throughout the late seventeenth century. The business was later inherited by Domenico de Rossi and Lorenzo Filippo de Rossi, before the plates were eventually acquired by the Papacy in 1738 to form the core of the Calcografia Camerale (now the Istituto Centrale per la Grafica in Rome), where Falda's original copperplates remain preserved to this day.The critical legacy of Falda’s work is profound. He transformed architectural topography from stiff technical draughtsmanship into a dynamic narrative art form. By fusing rigorous perspective with atmospheric warmth and human activity, he established the definitive visual archetype of Rome as the majestic capital of Western Christendom and classical antiquity. His prints provided the direct structural and compositional template for Giuseppe Vasi’s Delle Magnificenze di Roma Antica e Moderna (1747–1761) and inspired the breathtaking scale and dramatic intensity of Giovanni Battista Piranesi's Vedute di Roma. In the history of graphic art and urban cartography, Giovanni Battista Falda remains an towering figure whose etchings continue to serve as an indispensable gateway into the spatial, architectural, and visual imagination of the Roman Baroque.

publishers.name: De Rossi Giovanni Giacomo
publishers.biography: Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi (1627–1691) stands as the central colossus of Baroque print publishing, a visionary entrepreneur, cartographic coordinator, and cultural impresario who single-handedly transformed Rome into the international epicenter of early modern copperplate print production. Operating from his famous workshop at the sign of 'Parione' near the church of Santa Maria della Pace, De Rossi elevated the commercial print trade from a fragmented craft into a sophisticated, highly organized, and transnational publishing industry. His career spanned five decades of tumultuous intellectual and artistic fervor in Papal Rome, coinciding with the pontificates of Urban VIII Barberini, Innocent X Pamphili, Alexander VII Chigi, Clement IX Rospigliosi, Clement X Altieri, and Innocent XI Odescalchi. Through strategic alliances with the foremost architects, painters, antiquarians, and engravers of the era—including Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Pietro da Cortona, Giovanni Pietro Bellori, Pietro Santi Bartoli, and Giovanni Battista Falda—De Rossi systematized the visual recording of Roman antiquity, contemporary Baroque architecture, urban topography, and European cartography, codifying a visual rhetoric of power and elegance that dominated European visual culture throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.Born in Rome in 1627, Giovanni Giacomo was the son of Giuseppe de Rossi the Elder (c. 1570–1639), a printmaker and dealer originally from Milan who had established a modest print shop in Rome during the early decades of the seventeenth century. The De Rossi lineage became a sprawling, highly competitive dynasty of printmakers, divided into separate branches across the city. Upon the death of Giuseppe the Elder in 1639, the business was initially managed by his widow and subsequently divided among his sons. Giovanni Giacomo, endowed with extraordinary commercial foresight and artistic judgment, assumed full control of the primary family workshop near Santa Maria della Pace around 1660, after purchasing the shares and copperplates of his brothers, including Giovan Battista de Rossi and Matteo Gregorio de Rossi. Unlike his competitors, who often relied on reprinting worn, low-quality plates inherited from Renaissance masters, Giovanni Giacomo instituted a rigorous program of acquiring, refurbishing, and systematically commissioning new copperplates executed by the most talented engravers in Europe. His formative years were spent mastering the intricate mechanics of plate etching, ink formulation, paper sourcing from Umbria and the Fabriano mills, and navigating the complex legal frameworks of papal privileges (privilegia) and copyright protections.De Rossi’s intellectual and artistic network was unprecedented in its breadth and sophistication. Recognizing that architectural and topographical prints met an insatiable demand among foreign diplomats, Grand Tourists, and European monarchs, he commissioned the northern Italian draughtsman and engraver Giovanni Battista Falda to execute sweeping topographical surveys of the Eternal City. This collaboration yielded landmark publications such as Il Nuovo Teatro delle Fabriche, et Edificii, in Prospettiva di Roma Moderna (published in multiple books starting in 1665) and Le Fontane di Roma, which provided the European elite with precise, theatrical, and orthographically ambitious views of Baroque urbanism. Simultaneously, De Rossi aligned his press with the intellectual circle of Giovanni Pietro Bellori, the premier art theorist and antiquary of Counter-Reformation Rome. In tandem with the artist-engraver Pietro Santi Bartoli, De Rossi published monumental antiquarian treatises, including Colonna Traiana (1672) and Gli antichi sepolcri, overo Mausolei romani et etruschi (1690). These works combined exacting archaeological illustration with Bellori's classical art theory, serving as foundational texts for European Neoclassicism. In the domain of cartography, De Rossi revolutionized Italian mapmaking through his publication of the monumental atlas Mercurio Geografico overo Guida alla Geografia Universale (1690–1692), featuring plates engraved by Giacomo Cantelli da Vignola and revised according to the latest scientific and astronomical measurements.The operational scale of the Stamperia alla Pace set new benchmarks for early modern publishing. De Rossi established an international distribution network that extended from Rome to Venice, Paris, Nuremberg, Antwerp, Madrid, and London. To maintain total control over his catalog, he was among the first Italian publishers to issue periodic printed trade catalogs—his famed Indice delle stampe intagliate in rame a bulino, e in acqua forte possedute da Gio. Giacomo de Rossi (published in 1677, 1686, and 1689). These catalogs provided prospective buyers across Europe with detailed descriptions, plate sizes, series counts, and prices for thousands of individual prints, architectural suites, cartographic sheets, and devotional images. De Rossi maintained extraordinary quality control: he employed master engravers such as Cornelis Bloemaert, François Spierre, Robert van Audenaerd, and Etienne Baudet, ensuring that etching and engraving techniques achieved unprecedented tonal depth, clarity, and durability. By securing strict papal privileges from successive pontiffs, he protected his vast capital investments against pirated copies, effectively monopolizing the Roman print market.Upon his death in Rome in 1691, Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi left an astonishing inheritance: a pristine inventory of over three thousand engraved copperplates, an extensive international client list, and the most lucrative print shop in Southern Europe. Having no direct male heirs, he bequeathed the business to his adopted son, Domenico de Rossi (born Domenico Fedeli, 1659–1730), who continued the firm's expansion into the eighteenth century by publishing landmark architectural suites such as the Studio d'architettura civile. The historical legacy of Giovanni Giacomo's press achieved its ultimate consolidation in 1738, when Pope Clement XII Corsini purchased the entire De Rossi inventory of copperplates for the Papal State to prevent its dispersal. This acquisition formed the founding core of the Calcografia Camerale (later the Regia Calcografia and today the Istituto Centrale per la Grafica in Rome), preserving De Rossi’s massive plate archive intact. Today, Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi is recognized not merely as a merchant, but as a central architect of Baroque visual culture whose publications dictated European architectural taste, cartographic knowledge, and antiquarian scholarship for over two centuries.

publisher_data: [Rome], Si vendeno per Gio. Giacomo Rossi all'insegna di Parigi alla Pace, [1655-1691]
academic_description: Two parts bound in a single oblong folio volume (mm. 370×475). This volume comprises a total of 106 engraved plates accompanied by captions in Italian. Of these, 101 plates (including one folding plate composed of two separate sheets), along with the two engraved title pages, originate from the series I Palazzi di Roma. Five plates, conventionally considered part of the series (the map of the Collegio Romano, the map of Villa Borghese, the palace of Prince Chigi, Palazzo Bolognetti, and one of the two Corsini palaces), are absent and have been replaced by five unrelated folding plates, yet still from the presses of Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi (Colonna Traiana, Colonna Antonina, Obelisco Vaticano, Obelisco Lateranense, and Obelisco di Santa Maria Maggiore). The first part is dedicated to Cardinal Antonio Barberini, while the second part is dedicated to Cardinal Camillo Massimo. The title of the second part reads: Nuovi disegni dell'architettura e piante dei palazzi di Roma dei più celebri architetti, disegnate e intagliate da Gio. Battista Falda. The binding is modern, in hazelnut morocco with gilt decorations on the boards and spine, with ancient speckled edges, preserved in a marbled cardboard slipcase. There are some minor stains and occasional foxing, with the right margin of the last leaf trimmed by approximately 10 mm, yet it remains a beautiful copy, very fresh, with the plates excellently impressed.Despite the recent binding, the replacement folding plates have been part of this volume from the outset, as evidenced by the ancient edges and the old handwritten numbering of the plates. The plates of I Palazzi di Roma are in the first state before numbering. The first state is also recognizable by the captions on the plates that still attribute the ownership of the palace located in Piazza S. Marco in the Rione della Pigna to the d'Aste family, a palace that would later be acquired by the Marquis Rinuccini; or on the plate of Palazzo Caffarelli, subsequently acquired by G.A. Coltrolini; or again on the plate of Palazzo Mattei, acquired in 1682 by G.F. Negroni. Two of the plates not included in the volume, the map of the Collegio Romano and the map of Villa Borghese (engraved by Antonio Barbey after a drawing by Carlo Quadri), were added to the series by Domenico de Rossi, heir of Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi, only after 1691.“This is the first publication to provide systematic, measured, and uniformly scaled illustrations of Roman palaces built in the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth centuries. By focusing exclusively on the palace, this book becomes a compendium of exempla, not only illustrating the great houses of a very special city, but also establishing the typology of the residential palace. Thus the book is of great documentary value, even though the illustrations do not aspire to high aesthetic achievement […] This trendsetting book on Roman palaces is divided into two parts. Ferrerio was the author of most of the illustrations in the first part, except for one sheet engraved by Giovanni Battista Falda, who was also responsible for forty of the sixty sheets of the second part. While Falda's work and successful career as an engraver associated with the Roman publisher Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi have been amply documented, much less is known about Ferrerio, who seems to have practiced as an architect and engraver, and whose principal claim to recognition is this album of palace illustrations. He was a member of the Accademia di San Luca, where he was a registered member in 1634 […] The illustrations in this collection demonstrate that Ferrerio was closely focused upon his work. He uses an unadorned style of representation, showing the chosen palaces in line drawings in plan, section, and elevation. Cross-hatching in the elevations is reserved for window and door openings, while in the sections cross-hatching is used to represent depth of space. An engraved line tightly frames the engraved illustrations, and the regularity and consistency of the representational style is as remarkable as the uniformity with which it presents the palace facades, which are especially striking in the austerity of their disciplined composition. The symmetry and regularity of the facades is not matched by the plans, however; these show mostly the piani nobili, which illustrate less ideal conditions. The irregularities that emerge in the plans show that in many cases the palace had originated as a collection of multiple buildings, rather than newly planned and consistently realized construction. Ferrerio's plans are not always accurate, although the individual cases are difficult to prove with certainty given the constant work and alterations that these buildings were subject to over time. Each of the two parts is dedicated to a high-ranking prelate: part 1 to Cardinal Antonio Barberini and part 2 to Cardinal Gamillo Massimi. The dedication to Cardinal Antonio contains significant references to festival settings and theatrical events. The dedication claims that Roman buildings form a theater of glory that resounds with applause at the happy return of the cardinal. The cardinal had gone into voluntary exile in France after the death of his uncle and protector, Pope Urban VIII Barberini, in 1644 and returned to Rome in 1655, the year of publication of the first part of Palazzi di Roma […] Though all the chosen palaces are represented in elevation, full treatment in section and plan is provided only for a select few. In the first part, Palazzi Farnese, Madama, Medici, Cesi, Alessandrino, Spada, Colonna, and the Collegio Romano are shown in plan. Many of the sheets are endowed with a scale, but the buildings are shown isolated, without any urbanistic context. In the second part, while all palaces are shown in elevation, Palazzo Farnese in Caprarola, the extension of Palazzo Quirinale, Palazzi Nerli, Crescenzi, d'Este, Borghese, d'Aste, Falconieri, Silvestri, Giustiniani, Sacchetti, Lancellotti, Mellini, and Santo Spirito are also illustrated with a plan. In addition, Palazzi Farnese, Quirinale, and Santo Spirito are shown in section, thus illustrated in the three academically correct representational modes. This album is the result of the unprecedentedly ambitious publication policy of the print dealer Giovanni Giacomo de Rossi. The engravings in the second part of the book, by Falda, are part of the younger artist's apprenticeship work for de' Rossi […] A celebratory historical approach, Ferrerio's book effortlessly shows off the copiousness of Roman residential architecture. The work of Renaissance architects receives slightly more attention than that of contemporary designers: there are eleven architects in the first part and seven in the second part with a total of twenty-five buildings; there are eleven mannerist and proto-baroque masters with twenty buildings, and nine baroque masters with thirteen buildings. Nine masters are represented in both parts of the work: Michelangelo, Gian Lorenzo Bernini, Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, Domenico Fontana, Giacomo della Porta, Francesco Borromini, Baldassare Peruzzi, Carlo Maderno, and Girolamo Rainaldi. The illustration of these palaces would seem to fulfill several interests of architects and patrons of architecture. With its accurate elevations and plans, the book documents the individual palace and suggests models for palace construction. By providing a compendium of Roman palaces, the book illustrates the wealth of the city's patrician families, implicitly lauding the investment practiced by their predecessors” (The Mark J. Millard Architectural Collection, Volume IV: Italian and Spanish Books, Fifteenth through Nineteenth Centuries, Washington DC-New York, 2000, pp. 136-140).Little is known of the life of Pietro Ferrerio. Active in Rome during the first half of the seventeenth century, between 1634 and 1653, he was listed among the painters and architects of the Accademia di San Luca. Ferrerio is particularly remembered for the first book of the print collection “Palazzi di Roma dei più famosi architetti”. The work was commenced by Ferrerio around 1638. While Falda designed and engraved the second book, the engraver of the first book remains unknown: Ferrerio signed the plates only as a draftsman. He died in Rome on 10 March 1654 (cf. E.M. Stella, Ferrerio, Pietro, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 46, Rome, 1996, s.v.).Giovanni Battista Falda was born near Vercelli in 1643. At the age of 14, he was sent to Rome and placed under the care of an uncle who recommended him to G.L. Bernini. However, it was his encounter with the printer G.G. De Rossi, who had a workshop in Piazza della Pace, that marked a turning point in Falda's artistic career. De Rossi directed his talent towards the art of engraving and completed Falda's cultural education by introducing him to many emerging artistic personalities, such as F. Borromini and Pietro da Cortona, from whom Falda learned the rules of perspective and architecture. In De Rossi's workshop, he could also appreciate the work of great engravers like J. Callot, S. Della Bella, and I. Silvestre. At about the age of twenty, after completing his apprenticeship, Falda was warmly received at the papal court, so much so that Alexander VII entrusted him with the task of designing the residence of Castel Gandolfo. In 1665, he published the first book of the Nuovo Teatro delle fabbriche, et edificii, in prospettiva di Roma moderna for the publisher De Rossi, followed by the second and third books between 1665 and 1669. The work aimed to disseminate the new image of Rome, with its palaces, churches, and gardens, according to a planned urban expansion project, in line with the cultured and refined Fabio Chigi's criteria: the pope, in fact, decided to open new roads and embellish the city with fountains and monuments, also as a demonstration of his family's financial and cultural power. Prior to this, engravings of Rome had mainly focused on the ancient city. Only after the completion of the urban renovations and architectural achievements of the popes in the seventeenth century did collections dedicated to the modern city begin to appear. With the Nuovo Teatro and his other collections dedicated to fountains and palaces, Falda became the disseminator of modern Rome. More generally, Falda's work reveals the intention to celebrate papal policy. The specifically informative and commercial aspect of the engraved views was skillfully exploited by the publisher De Rossi, who established an indissoluble and highly profitable partnership with Falda, to whom we owe much of the printed vedutistic production of the century in Rome, with a fortune comparable only to that of G.B. Piranesi's work in the following century. In those years, De Rossi at the Pace, in collaboration with Falda, became the principal publisher in Rome, eclipsing both his relatives De Rossi who worked in Piazza Navona and other actors in the sector. A testament to the effectiveness of the collaboration between Falda and De Rossi is the famous map of Rome from 1676, which enjoyed great success and can be considered a representation of the city at the height of its Baroque period. Even in the posthumous collection I giardini di Roma, which describes the most famous Roman gardens, Falda combines the accuracy of representation with a skilful use of perspective. Falda died of cancer at the age of only thirty-five in Rome in 1678. He worked tirelessly despite the brevity of his career. By the end of his life, he had engraved approximately three hundred works: many of these are preserved in Rome at the Calcografia Nazionale and relate to the complete series of the palaces of Rome, the Nuovo Teatro, the fountains of Rome, Tivoli, and Frascati, and the gardens. Falda achieved great success, and his works were imitated in Italy and Europe until the end of the eighteenth century (cf. A. Margiotta-Simonetta Tozzi, Falda, Giovanni Battista, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 44, Rome, 1994, s.v.).

authors.name: Cassini Samuele
authors.biography: Samuele da Cassini (also recorded in contemporary Latinity as Samuel de Cassinis, Samuel Cassinensis, or Samuele da Casale; fl. c. 1470–1510) stands as one of the most enigmatic yet intellectually fierce polemicists of the Italian Renaissance. A friar of the Order of Friars Minor Observant (Ordo Fratrum Minorum de Observantia), Cassini operated at the volatile intersection of late medieval Scotist scholasticism, Franciscan Observant piety, and early modern demonological debate. Writing during the transitional decades between the dawn of Italian incunabular printing and the onset of the Protestant Reformation, Cassini achieved enduring historical significance primarily through his courageous, early sixteenth-century attack on the emerging witch-hunting orthodoxy promulgated by Dominican inquisitors. His seminal vernacular treatise, the Questione de le strie (printed in Pavia in 1505), directly challenged the physical reality of the witches' sabbat, the nocturnal flight of sorceresses, and the judicial validity of confessions extracted under inquisitorial torture. Beyond his pioneering role in the history of skeptical demonology, Cassini was a prolific controversialist who engaged in high-stakes theological battles over Eucharistic transubstantiation, the Immaculate Conception, and the hierarchical boundaries between theology, medicine, and judicial astrology in the academic centers of Milan, Pavia, Genoa, and Venice.Born in the mid-fifteenth century in the Piedmontese town of Cassine (near Alessandria and Casale Monferrato), Cassini entered the Observant branch of the Franciscan Order during a period of intense institutional vigor and spiritual reform. The Observant movement, which emphasized strict adherence to the Rule of St. Francis, poverty, and itinerant preaching, provided Cassini with a rigorous education in Scotist metaphysics and Lombard intellectual traditions. Details regarding his early schooling remain inextricably bound to the conventual studia of the Franciscan province of Genoa and Milan. By the late 1470s, Cassini had established himself as a formidable lector in theology and logic, thoroughly steeped in the works of John Duns Scotus, William of Ockham, and Bonaventure. His formative years were marked by an acute sensitivity to the rivalries separating the Franciscan Order from the Order of Preachers (Dominicans), a factional divide that was not merely institutional but deeply doctrinal, pitting Scotist voluntarism and Mariological devotion against Thomist intellectualism and maculist theology. This intellectual environment fostered Cassini's uncompromising dialectical style, characterized by an unyielding reliance on canon law, textual authority, and a sharp, often caustic vernacular prose intended to reach beyond the cloistered walls of the university faculty to influence civic magistrates and educated laymen.Cassini's scholarly output spans several crucial theological and philosophical controversies that defined Northern Italian intellectual life at the turn of the sixteenth century. In the 1490s, operating within the vibrant orbit of Sforza Milan, he published works defending Franciscan Eucharistic theology, notably his Liber de compendio veritatis de realitate corporis Christi in eucharistia (Milan, 1490), in which he deployed intricate Scotist distinctions to analyze the nature of the real presence and transubstantiation against contemporary philosophical misreadings. Simultaneously, Cassini immersed himself in the fiercely contested debate over the Immaculate Conception. Aligning with the traditional Franciscan defense of Mary's freedom from original sin, he launched aggressive literary attacks against prominent Dominican theologians, including Vincenzo Bandello (later Master General of the Dominican Order), whose maculist treatise had ignited widespread outrage among Observant friars. Cassini's polemical range expanded further when he intervened in the faculty disputes at the University of Pavia and Wittenberg, engaging in a celebrated paper war with the German humanist physician Martin Pollich von Mellerstadt regarding the epistemic supremacy of theology over medical science and astrological prognostication. In these exchanges, Cassini defended the traditional medieval hierarchy of the sciences, insisting that divine revelation and scholastic theology must retain ultimate supervisory authority over natural philosophy and empirical medicine.The zenith of Cassini's intellectual legacy arrived in April 1505 with the publication of the Questione de le strie (Question of the Witches), printed in Pavia by Jacobus de Paucis Drapis. This work represents one of the earliest published systematic critiques of the new demonology codified in the infamous Malleus Maleficarum (1486) by Heinrich Kramer and Jakob Sprenger. Writing in a direct, accessible Italian vernacular, Cassini mounted a devastating legal and theological assault on the claims made by Dominican inquisitors—most notably Bernardo Rategno da Como (Bernardo da Como) and Isidoro de Isolanis—who asserted that witches physically flew through the night to assemble at sabbats, renounced Christ in bodily presence, and performed harmful sorcery (maleficium). Grounding his argument in the authoritative ninth-century canon law decree Canon Episcopi (incorporated into Gratian's Decretum), Cassini insisted that the illusion of nocturnal flight and metamorphosis was a demonic deception played upon the imagination of foolish, melancholic women, rather than an objective physical reality. He argued that to believe that human beings could be corporeally transported through the air by demonic agency was itself an heretical aberration that ascribed to the Devil powers reserved exclusively to God Almighty. Consequently, Cassini condemned the widespread execution of alleged witches by inquisitorial tribunals as judicial murder, asserting that confessions obtained through torture were illusions built upon illusions.The printing and material transmission of Cassini's works offer a vivid window into the publishing climate of Renaissance Lombardy. His major Eucharistic and polemical tracts were issued from the workshops of premier Milanese printers, including Uldericus Scinzenzeler and Philippus de Mantegatiis, who catered to the academic and monastic markets of the Sforza duchy. The Questione de le strie, issued in Pavia—a city renowned both for its venerable university and its proximity to active inquisitorial tribunals in Como and Bergamo—was deliberately crafted as a modest octavo format, facilitating its rapid dissemination among urban judges, municipal councilors, and secular lawyers who were increasingly called upon to confirm inquisitorial death sentences. The typographical execution of Cassini's Italian text, replete with scholastic distinctions translated into the vernacular, underscored his intention to democratize theological critique. However, his radical anti-inquisitorial stance provoked immediate and fierce retaliation from the Dominican order. Inquisitor Bernardo Rategno da Como authored a prompt refutation, embedding a defense of the physical sabbat and inquisitorial jurisdiction into his influential manual Lucerna Inquisitorum (1511). Meanwhile, Dominican inquisitor Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (Prierias) also targeted Cassini's thesis in his demonological writings, seeking to marginalize the Franciscan friar as a dangerous theological deviant who undermined the Church's battle against Satanic heresy.Despite the bitter resistance of Dominican inquisitors, Samuele da Cassini's writings left an indelible imprint on the history of legal skeptical humanism and demonological theory. Though his physical life fades from the archival record around 1510–1516, his Questione de le strie was seized upon by subsequent generations of skeptics, natural philosophers, and legal reformers. In the mid-sixteenth century, the pioneering German physician Johann Weyer cited the arguments of early Italian critics of witch-hunting, acknowledging the crucial wedge that scholars like Cassini had driven into the edifice of inquisitorial demonology. In modern historiography, pioneer scholars of witch trials such as Joseph Hansen, Henry Charles Lea, and Lynn Thorndike identified Cassini as a vital, transitional voice who deployed medieval canon law to resist the early modern witch craze. Contemporary historians, including Cesare Vasoli, Marina Montesano, and Matteo Duni, have further illuminated Cassini's complex legacy, framing his work not merely as an isolated act of humanitarian skepticism, but as a sophisticated manifestation of Franciscan Scotist theology and Observant institutional opposition to Dominican judicial overreach. Today, Cassini is recognized as a monumental figure in the intellectual prehistory of the European Enlightenment's critique of religious superstition and judicial tyranny.

publishers.name: Bevilacqua Simone
publishers.biography: Simone Bevilacqua (also recorded in typographical colophons as Symon de Bevilaqua Papiensis, Simone di Niccolò Bevilacqua, or Simone da Pavia; ca. 1450 – ca. 1518) stands as one of the most dynamic, technically proficient, and geographically mobile figures in the annals of early European print culture. Active during the transitional threshold between the incunabula era and the dawn of the sixteenth-century printing revolution, Bevilacqua’s career exemplifies the complex socio-economic, technological, and intellectual networks that defined Northern Italian humanism. Originating from Pavia, his typographic trajectory traversed key urban nodes of early modern intellectual life, including Vicenza, Venice, Pavia, Capodistria (modern Koper in Slovenia), and ultimately the Duchy of Savoy and Lyons. Through his prolific production of classical Latin texts, vernacular poetry, astronomical treatises, and legal monographs, Bevilacqua contributed decisively to the standardization of typographical layouts, the dissemination of humanist commentary, and the cross-regional transfer of print technology across the Alps.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education in Lombardy and the VenetoBorn in Pavia around the middle of the fifteenth century, Simone Bevilacqua belonged to a regional context defined by the intellectual influence of the University of Pavia and the burgeoning print trade of the Duchy of Milan. His self-designation in colophons as Papiensis explicitly links his identity to Lombardy, though no definitive archival record reveals his precise familial background or initial apprenticeship. It is highly probable that he acquired his foundational knowledge of punch-cutting, type casting, matrix assembly, and press mechanics within the active typographic shops of Pavia or Milan during the late 1470s or early 1480s, a period when printers in Northern Italy were refining the transition from heavy Gothic characters to elegant Humanistic Roman founts.By the late 1480s, Bevilacqua had migrated into the Venetian terraferma, establishing his first independent press in Vicenza around 1487. Vicenza at this juncture was an intellectual outpost deeply connected to Venetian commerce and humanist scholarship, home to rigorous educational circles and pioneering printers like Giovanni da Reno and Rigo di Ca Zeno. In Vicenza, Bevilacqua published several modest humanist works, demonstrating his early mastery of Roman type design and establishing ties with regional scholars. His stay in Vicenza served as a crucial proving ground where he established operational relationships with paper suppliers from the Riviera del Garda (notably Toscolano-Maderno) and local financial backers, preparing him for entry into the competitive epicenter of international printing: Venice.The Venetian Golden Age (1492–1506): Classical Humanism, Dante, and Scientific PrintingIn 1492, Bevilacqua relocated his operations to Venice, setting up his workshop in the vibrant neighborhood of San Lio, near the Rialto—the commercial and literary heart of the Republic. Venice was then the undisputed printing capital of the Western world, home to master typographers such as Erhard Ratdolt, Nicolas Jenson, and the emerging Aldus Manutius. Bevilacqua rapidly distinguished himself through his remarkable productivity, aesthetic precision, and astute selection of texts. Over a fourteen-year period in Venice (1492–1506), his press issued over one hundred distinct editions, spanning classical philosophy, legal doctrine, Christian theology, science, and Italian vernacular literature.One of the supreme achievements of Bevilacqua’s Venetian output was his grand illustrated folio edition of Dante Alighieri’s La Commedia, published on November 29, 1493. Featuring the famous narrative commentary of the Florentine humanist Cristoforo Landino, Bevilacqua’s Dante was adorned with expressive woodcut illustrations framed by elaborate architectural borders. This edition not only catered to the high demand for vernacular literary masterpieces among patrician and merchant audiences but also showcased Bevilacqua’s sophisticated integration of woodcuts with complex text-and-commentary typographical grids. His press relied on distinct founts of Roman type (notably a clear 112mm Roman) alongside fine Gothic types reserved for liturgical and legal texts.Beyond vernacular poetry, Bevilacqua established himself as a primary publisher of classical Latin texts accompanied by contemporary humanist scholarship. He printed major editions of Lucan’s Pharsalia (1493 and 1498), featuring the commentary of Omnibonus Leonicenus and Joannes Sulpitius Verulanus, as well as the complete works of Lactantius (1493), the legal and rhetorical writings of Cicero, Quintilian, Ovid, and Persius. He worked closely with eminent humanists of the era, including Antonio Mancinelli, Filippo Beroaldo, and Lorenzo Valla, frequently printing their revised textual corrections and introductory epistles. Furthermore, Bevilacqua made significant contributions to the dissemination of early modern scientific and astronomical literature; his 1499 and 1501 editions of Johannes de Sacrobosco’s Sphaera Mundi, decorated with intricate woodcut diagrams of the heavens and planetary motions, were widely adopted in university curricula across Europe.Itinerancy, Technical Innovations, and Expansion: Pavia, Capodistria, and the Savoyard FootprintDespite his commercial success in Venice, Bevilacqua belonged to the highly mobile class of Renaissance artisan-entrepreneurs who adapted to shifting political, economic, and epidemiological landscapes. Around 1502–1503, he temporarily returned to his native Pavia, where he established a brief partnership to print legal monographs for the academic community of the University of Pavia, before returning to Venice to resume operations. However, rising production costs and intense competition in the Venetian market led him to explore untapped regional markets on the periphery of the Venetian Republic.In 1506, Bevilacqua transferred his press to Capodistria (Koper, in modern Slovenia), on the Istrian peninsula. This move was of immense historical and typographical significance, as Bevilacqua introduced the art of printing with moveable type to Istria. In Capodistria, under the patronage of local municipal authorities and ecclesiastical figures, he printed humanistic and devotional works aimed at regional clerics and administrators, effectively extending the typographic reach of the Venetian Renaissance across the Adriatic Sea.By 1511, Bevilacqua had embarked on the final, extraordinary phase of his career, migrating across the Alps into the Duchy of Savoy and the surrounding regions of Western Europe. Documented in locations such as Chéry, Chambéry, and Lyons between 1511 and 1518, Bevilacqua operated under the protection of Duke Charles III of Savoy and prominent local patrons. In Lyons and Savoy, he printed legal works, local synodal decrees, and religious texts, adapting his typographic repertoire to French legal and liturgical sensibilities while maintaining the refined Italianate aesthetic he had perfected in Venice. His mobility demonstrates the remarkable portability of early printing equipment—punches, matrices, and presses—and highlights how master printers functioned as vectors of intellectual and technological exchange between Northern Italy and Western Europe.Critical Reception, Bibliographical Legacy, and Historiographical AssessmentSimone Bevilacqua’s death is believed to have occurred around 1518, likely in Savoy or Lyons, as no subsequent colophons bearing his signature appear after this date. In the centuries following his death, his vast output became the subject of extensive study by pioneering bibliographers and descriptive catalogers of incunabula. Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century scholars such as Georg Wolfgang Panzer, Ludwig Hain, and Konrad Haebler systematically cataloged Bevilacqua’s editions, praising the exceptional clarity of his Roman founts and his meticulous presswork.In modern scholarship, particularly within the monumental work of the Catalogue of Books Printed in the XVth Century Now in the British Museum (BMC) and studies by Italian book historians such as Alfredo Cioni and Paolo Veneziani, Bevilacqua is recognized not merely as a commercial printer, but as a pivotal figure who linked humanist editorial practices with large-scale commercial publishing. His 1493 Dante remains an icon of early Italian print illustration, featured prominently in Victor Masséna, Prince d'Essling's definitive study of Venetian illustrated books. Today, copies of Bevilacqua’s imprints are preserved in the world's major rare book depositories, including the British Library, the Bibliothèque nationale de France, the Vatican Library, and the Huntington Library, standing as monumental witnesses to the typographical mastery and geographical expansiveness of the High Renaissance print trade.

academic_description: 4to (187x132 mm). [56] leaves. Collation: a-o4. The last leaf is a blank. 33-35 lines. Gothic type. The name of the author appears in the colophon (l. o3v): “perfectus est iste tractatulus per me fratrem Samuelem de Casinis die 26 octobris 1510”. Woodcut initial on l. a2v. Later cardboards. Label removed from title-page verso, some occasional minor staining, a good copy.First edition of one of the very first printed treatises dedicated to the Waldensians. On 5 December 1510, a group of dissident cardinals who were opposed to Pope Julius II, led by the Castilian Bernardino López de Carvajal, entered Milan triumphantly under the protection of Louis XII of France. Among them was Samuele da Cassine, a Observant Franciscan friar who had previously taken an unwelcome stance against Savonarola. He dedicated to Carvajal his work against the Waldensians, defending suffrage for the dead and purging of souls. The work or part of it had been published in Italian a few month earlier under the title Victoria triumphale contra li errori de valdeisi (Cuneo, 1510).A marginal but noteworthy chapter in the context of these considerations on Carvajal's role in the fight against heresy, as well as with regard to the events of the Council of Pisa-Milan, is the dedication addressed to him by the Observant friar Samuele da Cassine in his refutation of Waldensian beliefs. The date of dedication and printing of what is nothing more than the Latin translation (De statu ecclesie. De purgatorio. De suffragijs defunctorum. De corpore Christi. Libellus feliciter incipit contra valdenses qui hec omnia negant) of a work in the vernacular published two months earlier (Victoria triumphale contra li errori de Valdesi, already addressed to the Duke of Savoy), appears to be 5 December 1510, the same day on which the dissident cardinals, led by Carvajal, entered Milan. The coincidence should not be accidental […] The place of publication was Cuneo, but the printer was Simone Bevilacqua from Pavia. The author, who had resided in the convent of Sant'Angelo in Milan but had been absent from the Lombard capital for more than six months due to the capitular congregation of the Genoese province held in April 1510, and was perhaps about to return, seems to have identified Cardinal Carvajal as the leading figure in the group of dissident prelates who had fled Rome. Moreover, Samuele da Cassine must have had more compelling reasons to try to ingratiate himself with the Spaniard because his texts against Savonarola first, and then against Savonarola's ‘living saints', may have irritated the cardinal, who, as already mentioned, also had a close relationship with the Savonarolans. The formulation, translation and dissemination of this text demonstrates how acute the problems associated with the presence of the Waldensians in the Piedmont valleys were, with an echo that may have been amplified in Milan by the presence among the royal senators of Alberto Cattaneo, canon of San Nazzaro in Brolio, brother of Giulio, secretary of justice, […] who was also a leading figure in the crusade against the Waldensians in 1487-1488. Above all, Carvajal was identified by the friar as a reference point to whom the pamphlet should be addressed, probably because, despite his conspicuous disobedience to the incumbent pontiff, his strenuous fight against any kind of heresy, deviation or diversity of belief from orthodoxy was so well known that he was considered sympathetic to further persecution of the Waldensian community (cf. E. Rossetti, Visioni di riforma. Il cardinale spagnolo Bernardino López de Carvajal e le élite milanesi nella crisi religiosa di primo Cinquecento (1492-1521), PhD thesis, University Ca' Foscari of Venice, 2017, pp. 166-168).The Waldensians originated with the merchant Valdo of Lyon, who in 1173 decided to live as Jesus had asked the apostles to. From the 13th to the 16th century, the movement spread throughout much of Western and Central Europe. However, due to persecution, it survived only in Southern Europe. In 1532, the remaining Waldensians joined the Protestant Reformation, forming an independent Reformed Church in 1559. From 1562 onwards, their presence was limited to the Cottian Alps, where they were partly French and partly subjects of the House of Savoy. At the end of the 17th century, French Waldensians who were being persecuted by Louis XIV took refuge in Germany. During the 19th century, many Waldensians left their impoverished homeland in Piedmont to settle in America. Since the Emancipation of 1848, the Waldensian Church has spread throughout Italy and has become one of the most prominent voices of Italian Protestantism. The Waldensian Church is unique in being the only Protestant church that can be traced directly back to a “heretical”movement of the early Middle Ages.Samuele da Cassine or Cassini or De Cassinis (lat. Samuel Cassinensis) was probably born in Cassine near Alessandria around the middle of the 15th century. Little is known about his life, and even his baptismal name is unknown, as he abandoned it when he joined the Observant Friars Minor of the Province of Genoa. As far as his studies are concerned, we know that, after acquiring a good education in the literary disciplines in Italy, he was sent to Paris to improve his knowledge of philosophy and theology at the university there. He was a professor in France and Italy, probably in the schools of his Order, and in his mature years and period of greatest intellectual activity, he mostly lived in Piedmont and Milan. He was renowned as a profound connoisseur of Aristotelian philosophy. Around 1493, he returned from France to Italy, and the following year, he published in Milan a manual of philosophy and theology, which gained some notoriety and enjoyed a certain favour among the students for whom it was intended (Liber ysagogicus in apices Scoti theologorum principis, necnon ad investiganda Aristotelis profunda logicalia, Milan, 1494). In 1495 Cassine was still in Milan, preparing the edition of Burlifer's Formalitates, which he would publish the following year, accompanied by his own commentary. In the years that followed, he expressed his aversion to Girolamo Savonarola's prophecies, publishing the Invectiva in prophetiam fratris Hieronymi in 1497, a work that also aimed to support the anti-Florentine and anti-Savonarola policy of Ludovico il Moro, Duke of Milan, to which Giovan Francesco Pico della Mirandola responded shortly afterwards with a Defensio Hieronymi Savonarolae Ferranensis (Florence, undated). Cassine replied to Pico by publishing Reseratio atque clarificatio falsarum solutionum ad argumenta Samuelis Cassinensis que facta júerunt in falsam prophetiam Hieronymi Ferrariensis (Milan, 1498), dedicated to Alexander VI. Also in 1498, he published a philosophical pamphlet dedicated to Duke Ludovico il Moro (Quaestio de immortalitate animae, Milan, 1498). A few years later, in 1505, he published, possibly in Pavia, a work on witches (Questione de le strie. Questiones lamearum). Finally, in 1510, he published the Expositio triplex librorum octo phisicorum Aristotelis in Cuneo, dedicating the work to the University of Paris, and his treatise against the Waldensians. He presumably died soon after 1510 (cf. R. Ristori, Cassini, Samuele, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, Rome, 1978, vol. 21, pp. 487-490).

authors.name: Hofmann Ludwig
authors.biography: Ludwig von Hofmann (1861–1945) stands as one of the most singular and transformative figures in modern German art, occupying a vital intellectual and stylistic bridge between nineteenth-century Classical Idealism, the decorative linearity of Jugendstil (Art Nouveau), European Symbolism, and the nascent currents of early twentieth-century Expressionism. Born in Darmstadt on March 14, 1861, into an eminent Hessian bureaucratic and aristocratic lineage, Hofmann synthesized the formal discipline of European academic traditions with an ardent utopian vision of idyllic harmony, physical liberation, and sun-drenched Arcadian landscapes. His father, Karl Hofmann (1827–1910), was a distinguished statesman who served as Prime Minister of the Grand Duchy of Hesse (Großherzogtum Hessen) and later as Secretary of State in the Imperial Home Office in Berlin under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Raised within the highest echelons of the Wilhelmine political and cultural elite, young Ludwig was afforded an exceptionally cultured upbringing, which fostered both his deep appreciation for classical antiquity and his lifelong immersion in music, literature, and visual design.Hofmann’s formal artistic training began in 1883 at the prestigious Großherzoglich Badische Kunstschule in Karlsruhe, where he studied under the prominent landscape painter Theodor Hagen and the historicist master Ferdinand Keller. Hagen’s emphasis on plein-air observation and realistic tonal values provided Hofmann with a rigorous technical foundation in painterly light and atmosphere. In 1886, seeking to expand his creative horizons, Hofmann moved to Munich—then the vibrant artistic capital of the German lands—to enroll at the Königliche Akademie der Bildenden Künste. There he studied in the master class of Wilhelm von Lindenschmit the Younger, absorbing the dramatic chiaroscuro and psychological depth characteristic of the Munich School. However, the decisive turning point in Hofmann’s early intellectual development occurred in the autumn of 1889, when he relocated to Paris to attend the famed Académie Julian. In Paris, exposed to the academic masterworks of Jules-Joseph Lefebvre and Tony Robert-Fleury, Hofmann simultaneously encountered the groundbreaking innovations of French Post-Impressionism and Symbolism. He was profoundly moved by the monumental, serene decorative mural schemes of Pierre Puvis de Chavannes, the enigmatic color harmonies of Paul Gauguin, and the synthesize methods of the Nabis (Paul Sérusier, Maurice Denis, and Édouard Vuillard). This Parisian encounter catalyzed Hofmann’s departure from academic realism toward a stylized, decorative, and evocative visual language centered on the human form integrated into timeless natural environments.Upon settling in Berlin in 1890, Hofmann rapidly established himself as a prominent figure within the progressive avant-garde of the imperial capital. Dissatisfied with the conservative, state-sanctioned exhibition policies of the Verein Berliner Künstler and the reactionary historicism favored by Kaiser Wilhelm II, Hofmann joined forces with a group of visionary young artists. In 1892, alongside figures such as Max Liebermann, Walter Leistikow, Franz Skarbina, and Konrad Böse, he co-founded the Gruppe der Elf (Group of Eleven). This radical exhibition association directly challenged the official art establishment, staging independent, highly publicized exhibitions that introduced impressionist and symbolist tendencies to the Berlin public and effectively paved the way for the formation of the Berlin Secession (Berliner Secession) in 1898. During this Berlin period, Hofmann’s stylistic signature matured: he rejected narrative historical painting in favor of poetic compositions featuring graceful, often nude figures—ephebes, maidens, and dancers—moving rhythmically through sunlit coastal landscapes, pristine meadows, and ethereal forests. These works reflected not merely an aesthetic choice, but an ideological alignment with the contemporary Lebensreform (Life Reform) movement, which advocated a return to nature, physical culture, sunbathing (Lichtgebet), and spiritual renewal as antidotes to the industrial alienation of modern urban life.Hofmann’s intellectual network expanded dramatically in 1895 with the founding of the groundbreaking art and literary periodical PAN, established by a consortium of elite intellectuals including the art critic Julius Meier-Graefe, the poet Otto Julius Bierbaum, Count Harry Kessler, and Eberhard von Bodenhausen. Hofmann was not only a co-founder and major financial subscriber but also served as the artistic director responsible for shaping the visual identity of the journal. PAN became the premier vehicle for international Jugendstil and Symbolism, publishing original graphic prints by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Auguste Rodin, Friedrich Nietzsche, Paul Verlaine, and Stéphane Mallarmé. Hofmann contributed numerous original color lithographs, decorative vignettes, headpieces, and ornamental cover designs to PAN, establishing himself as a master of graphic illustration and fine book design. His fluid, serpentine line work and exquisite spatial arrangement directly influenced a generation of European illustrators and typographers.In 1903, Hofmann was appointed professor at the Großherzoglich-Sächsische Kunstschule in Weimar by Grand Duke Wilhelm Ernst, an appointment brokered by the influential patron of modernism Count Harry Kessler. Hofmann’s arrival in Weimar initiated a golden era of cultural revival known as Neuweimar (New Weimar). Working alongside colleagues such as the Belgian architect and designer Henry van de Velde and the painter Count Leopold von Kalckreuth, Hofmann sought to forge a synthesis of all the arts (Gesamtkunstwerk). His studio in Weimar became a vibrant salon frequented by the global intellectual elite, including writers Hugo von Hofmannsthal, Rainer Maria Rilke, André Gide, and Gerhart Hauptmann, as well as the sculptor Auguste Rodin. Hofmann’s deep artistic friendship with Count Harry Kessler proved particularly fruitful; together they traveled to Greece and Italy in 1907, an expedition that deeply reinforced Hofmann’s commitment to Mediterranean classical idealism. During his Weimar years, Hofmann executed major monumental mural decorative projects, including the cycle for the vestibule of the Weimar Court Theater (1905) and monumental panels for the University of Jena (1911) and Henry van de Velde’s iconic Villa Esche in Chemnitz.Hofmann’s engagement with graphic arts and typography reached its zenith through his collaboration with Count Harry Kessler’s private press, the Cranach-Presse, founded in Weimar in 1913. Working with hand-press methods, custom-designed typefaces, and handmade paper, Hofmann illustrated monumental limited editions that are now regarded as masterpieces of twentieth-century book arts. His magnificent woodcut and lithographic illustrations for Virgil’s Eclogues (Bucolica) and Georgics, as well as works by Thomas Mann, Stefan George, and Leopold von Andrian, set new standards for typographical balance, printmaking execution, and page layout. Hofmann treated the printed book not merely as a container for text, but as a harmonious sculptural and visual object wherein typography, paper texture, margin proportion, and graphic illustration existed in perfect equilibrium.In 1916, during the mid-point of the First World War, Hofmann accepted a prestigious call to succeed Carl Bantzer as professor of monumental painting at the Kunstakademie Dresden (Dresden Academy of Fine Arts), a position he held with great distinction until his retirement in 1931. In Dresden, Hofmann educated multiple generations of German artists, instilling in them a rigorous understanding of architectural space, compositional rhythm, and color theory. Although the post-war rise of Expressionism, New Objectivity (Neue Sachlichkeit), and the Bauhaus shifted critical attention toward more radical political and structural avant-gardes, Hofmann remained dedicated to his singular vision of idyllic classical harmony, producing late works characterized by broad, expressive brushwork, heightened color intensity, and monumental simplification of form.The final decade of Hofmann’s life was darkened by the rise of National Socialism in Germany. Despite his aristocratic heritage and international renown, his artistic ideology—centered on spiritual freedom, peaceful Arcadian sensualism, and cosmopolitan humanist values—was fundamentally antithetical to Nazi racial aesthetic dogma. In 1937, as part of the regime’s systematic campaign against modern art, 337 of Ludwig von Hofmann’s works were forcibly confiscated from German public museums and galleries by the Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. Several of his graphic prints and paintings were included in the infamous defamatory exhibition Entartete Kunst (Degenerate Art) in Munich and subsequent touring locations. Stripped of his institutional honors and public standing, Hofmann retired to his home and studio in Pillnitz, near Dresden. He survived the catastrophic Allied bombing of Dresden in February 1945, but his health declined rapidly in the aftermath of the war. Ludwig von Hofmann died in Pillnitz on August 23, 1945, leaving behind a monumental legacy that spans the transition from nineteenth-century Academic Idealism to the foundations of twentieth-century visual modernism and fine book production.

academic_description: (478x390 mm). Loose sheets housed within the publisher's portfolio, crafted from blind-stamped and black-printed cardboard. The title page and ten lithographic plates are printed on handmade paper, with this copy retaining the often missing typographic text sheet. This is copy number 56 of a total edition of 100, with the plates numbered and signed in pencil by the Artist. An excellent copy, with only some imperfections to the publisher's portfolio."With his second portfolio, 'Rhythmen' (Rhythms), Ludwig von Hofmann returns to the theme of the body in motion—already central to his 'Tänze' (Dances) portfolio published fourteen years earlier—to explore it further through the expressive means he had developed in the meantime. Across the ten sheets, Hofmann unfolds figurative compositions that, in their overarching structures, transcend the individual body, even while being sustained by it. Against the backdrop of Eurythmy, the body here does not serve as an instrument for a dance of subjective expression, but emerges—in keeping with the portfolio's title—as the medium of a higher rhythm that governs existence; in this way, the human body in motion is endowed with a symbolic dimension, tied to the mysterious meaning of existence. Consequently, in Hofmann's work, the human body is neither decentered nor dissolved into fragments—as is typical of Expressionism—but remains intact, comparable to the art of Hans von Marées, and is activated precisely in its anthropomorphic nature by virtue of a new metaphysical conception of the human being. This makes Hofmann, who operates as a solitary figure amidst the current of Modernism, a classical artist." (Saur, AKL - Allgemeines Künstlerlexikon. Vol. 74. Berlin, 2012, p. 144 ff.)

authors.name: Champier Symphorien
authors.biography: Symphorien Champier (ca. 1474–1539) stands as one of the most prolific, enigmatic, and quintessential figures of the early French Renaissance. Operating at the dynamic intersection of late medieval scholastic encyclopedism and the emergent humanist movement, Champier was a practicing physician, a civic magistrate, a royal historiographer, and an insatiable polymath. Based primarily in Lyon—the supreme commercial and typographical crossroads of Western Europe during the early sixteenth century—he acted as a primary conduit through which Italian Renaissance Neoplatonism, medical humanism, and Hermetic philosophy were translated, adapted, and disseminated into the French intellectual vernacular. Far from being a mere passive compiler, Champier utilized his vast literary output to construct an ambitious, syncretic worldview that sought to reconcile ancient Greek medicine with Christian theology, Aristotelian physics with Platonic metaphysics, and chivalric French historiography with classical erudition.Born around 1474 in Saint-Symphorien-le-Château, in the Lyonnais region, Champier belonged to a family of modest local prominence. His early intellectual formation took place at the University of Paris, where he was exposed to the vibrant circle of Christian humanists centered around Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples. This Parisian experience proved seminal: Lefèvre’s pious Aristotelianism and his enthusiasm for the newly translated corpus of Marsilio Ficino and Hermes Trismegistus profoundly shaped Champier’s lifelong intellectual trajectory. Seeking a professional vocation, Champier subsequently migrated south to the renowned Faculty of Medicine at the University of Montpellier, the historical citadel of Western medical pedagogy. There, he absorbed both the traditional Arabo-Galenic medical curriculum and the emerging critical philology of the early medical humanists, culminating in the attainment of his doctorate in medicine around 1503.Upon completing his medical studies, Champier established himself in Lyon, where he rapidly integrated into the city’s ruling patriciate and intellectual elite. His professional prestige earned him appointment as personal physician to Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, whom Champier accompanied on military campaigns during the Italian Wars, most notably participating in the expedition that culminated in the Battle of Marignano in 1515. For his valiant service on the battlefield, Champier was knighted by the Duke. Returning to Lyon with elevated social status, he served multiple terms as a city consul (échevin) and was instrumental in founding the Collège des Médecins of Lyon in 1536, an institution designed to regulate medical practice, combat empiricism and charlatanry, and elevate the scholarly standing of the medical profession against the encroachment of uneducated apothecaries and barbers.Champier’s published oeuvre is astonishing in its thematic range and volume, reflecting an unyielding commitment to intellectual synthesis. Among his most influential philosophical works is the Symphonia Platonis cum Aristotele et Galeni cum Hippocrate, published in Lyon in 1516 by Jean Marion. In this monumental treatise, Champier applied the concordist methodology pioneered by Pico della Mirandola and Marsilio Ficino, seeking to demonstrate the fundamental harmony underlying Platonic philosophy, Aristotelian logic, Hippocratic etiology, and Galenic physiology. For Champier, natural science and medicine were not autonomous empirical disciplines but integral components of a universal Christian theology. His medical treatises, such as the Rosa gallica (1514) and the Cribratio medicamentorum (1515), participated vigorously in the fierce contemporary debates over the authority of medieval Islamic authorities like Avicenna and Rhazes. Championing a form of French medical nationalism, Champier advocated a return to the pristine Greek and Roman sources, attempting to purge pharmacology of Arabist accretions while defending traditional Galenic humoral theory against radical innovation.Simultaneously, Champier was a pioneering pioneer in the realm of medical historiography and bio-bibliography. His De medicinae Claris Scriptoribus (1506) represents one of the earliest systematic histories of medical literature ever printed, offering critical notices and bio-bibliographical sketches of ancient, medieval, and contemporary medical authors. Beyond medicine and philosophy, Champier authored numerous vernacular treatises aimed at aristocratic patronage and moral edification, including La Grant Nef des folz du monde (1503), an adaptation of Sebastian Brant’s famous satire, and La Nef des dames vertueuses (1503), a major contribution to the querelle des femmes in which he defended the moral and intellectual dignity of women using Neoplatonic arguments concerning spiritual beauty. His historical works, such as Les Grandes Chroniques des gestes et vertueux faictz des tresexcellens ducz et princes des royaumes de Hierusalem, de Cypre, de Sicile et de Calabre (1516), served to legitimize the territorial and dynastic ambitions of his patron, the Duke of Lorraine.The physical production of Champier’s works offers a vivid window into the gold age of Lyonnese and Parisian printing. Champier maintained intricate, highly strategic relationships with the foremost printer-publishers of his day, including Josse Bade (Jodocus Badius Ascensius) in Paris, as well as Jacques Sacon, Guillaume Balsarin, and Jean Marion in Lyon. Champier was extraordinarily attentive to the visual and typographic presentation of his books, frequently supervising the inclusion of intricate woodcut illustrations, elaborate architectural title borders, and complex marginal annotations. His texts were designed not merely for academic consumption but as luxurious physical artifacts meant to appeal to noble patrons, wealthy merchants, and international scholars. The print runs of his works circulated extensively across France, the Italian peninsula, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Low Countries, cementing Lyon’s reputation as an international hub of humanist book trade.Despite his immense popularity and social prominence, Champier was a controversial figure during his lifetime and in subsequent historiography. His complex position—standing firmly with one foot in medieval scholastic syncretism and the other in Renaissance humanism—made him a target for younger, more radical humanist reformers. Most famously, François Rabelais, a contemporary physician at the Hôtel-Dieu of Lyon, parodied Champier’s dense, eclectic, and often verbose style in Pantagruel, mocking his pedantic citations and conservative medical positions. Furthermore, Champier’s aggressive stance against radical astrology and magic, set forth in his Dialogus in magicarum artium destructionem (ca. 1500), drew criticism from traditional astrologers, even as his own reliance on Hermetic and Neoplatonic occult sympathies left him open to charges of inconsistency.Symphorien Champier died in Lyon around 1539, leaving behind a monumental bibliographical legacy that bridges two cultural epochs. Modern historiography, led by scholars such as Paul Allut and Brian P. Copenhaver, has re-evaluated Champier no longer as a mere pedantic compiler, but as a crucial historical agent who facilitated the naturalization of Italian Renaissance philosophy within Northern Europe. His life and works remain indispensable for understanding the transmission of Neoplatonism, the evolution of early modern medical humanism, and the vital role of the printing press in shaping the intellectual contours of sixteenth-century Europe.

publisher_data: [Lyon], Jean Phiroben & Jean Divineur for Jacques François Giunta, 1519
academic_description: 8vo (157x105 mm). [96] leaves. Collation: a-m8. Title printed in red and black and a full-page woodcut at the end showing the author with his patron and his wife kneeling in prayer. 20th-century gilt calf, marbled endleaves. Skilfully repaired worm track to the outer margin of several leaves not affecting the text, small repaired hole to l. e8 with loss of some text (the missing text has been supplied by hand), uniformly browned, still a good copy.Rare first edition of Champier's most interesting work, a significant document for the development of cultural nationalism among Renaissance intellectuals. Champier was in Italy three times: in 1506, in 1509 and in 1515. During his last travel he spent some time at Pavia, where he was admitted to the ‘collegium artistarum et medicorum'. The speech by Pietro Antonio Rustico, lecturer on logic and medicine, held on that occasion and printed toward the end of the volume, shows how proud Champier was about this honor. Rustico also alludes to Champier's family ties in Italy, which he sees in the Campeggi families of Bologna and Pavia. At the end of the speech Rustico enumerates and praises the hitherto books published by Champier, important as an early bibliography. The main part of the volume though consists of a ‘epistolary duel' with Girolamo da Pavia, an Augustinian monk from Asti, with whom Champier had for five years an intensive correspondence through the Lyonese publisher Balthazar de Gabiano (cf. P. Jodogne, La correspondence de Symphorien Champier avec Jérôme de Pavie dans le ‘Duellum epistolare', in: “The Late Middle Ages and the Dawn of Humanism Outside of Italy”, G. Verneke & J. Ijsewijn, eds., Den Haag, 1972, pp. 44-56).In the Duellum Champier defends the French culture against the pretended superiority of the Italian claimed by some scholars, namely Sabellico, Foresti and Battista Mantovano. He also sees in many Italian writers detractors moved only by jealousy and malice and mentions Valla, Merula, Poggio, Pico and Girolamo Balbo. Fierce of his Lyonnais origins he praises the antique origins of his native city on the authority of Berosus, which however was rightly questioned by Girolamo da Pavia and Raphael Maffei of Volterra. Even though Champier was not familiar with Annius of Viterbo's Antiquities (1498), in which the Berosus tradition made its first appearance, Champier contributed to the Gallican, anti-Italian Italia mendax narrative based on Berosus' assertions about the origin of the names “Gallia” and “Lugdunum” (cf. R. Cooper, Symphorien Champier et l'Italie, in: “L'Aube de la Renaissance”, Genève, 1991, pp. 233-246; see also W. Stephens, Giants in Those Days, Lincoln, 1989, pp. 171-174).The volume contains furthermore various letters by Champier to others, e.g. a letter to Erasmus (Ep. 680a), in which Champier intervenes in his favor in the latter's dispute with Lefèvre d'Etaples over Psalm 8; a letter to Lefèvre d'Etaples followed by Champier's commentary on the Definitiones Asclepii (first published with Lazzarelli's translation in 1507), expressing his attitude to the Hermetic writings. But the book also contains letters addressed to Champier, mainly from other scholars and physicians, among them Alessandro Benedetti and Robert Cockburn, bishop of Ross (cf. A. Broadie, James Liddell on Concepts and Signs, in: “The Renaissance in Scotland: studies in literature, religion, history and culture”, A.A. MacDonald, et al. eds., Leiden, 1994, p. 82; see also J. Durkan, Robert Cockburn, bishop of Ross and French humanism, in: “Innes Review”, IV, 1953, pp. 121-2.).The volume closes with Catalogus preceptorum, patronorum, familarium et auditorum, in which Champier lists his teachers, patrons, friends and students.Though some scholars believe the work to be printed either at Basel or at Venice, it was in fact printed at Lyon, where the two printers Johann Froben and Jean Divineur were active for several Lyonese publishers such as Luxembourg de Gabiano, Jacques Giunta and François Fradin.Symphorien Champier, was born into a bourgeois family at Saint-Symphorien-sur-Croise, near Lyon and studied at the University of Paris before 1495, when he matriculated at the medical school of Montpellier, which granted him his doctorate in 1504. He taught liberal arts in Grenoble and took a doctorate in theology in 1502. In 1509 he was appointed physician to Antoine Duke of Lorraine, who brought him to Nancy. Champier followed the duke several time to Italy, where he was involved in the battles of Agnadello (1509) and Marignano (1515). During his stays in Italy he won recognition as an academic teacher from the University of Pavia. In 1519 he became an alderman in Lyon, and for the last twenty years of his life he was at the center of the cultural Renaissance of that city, while simultaneously promoting the study of medicine by helping to found the College of the Holy Trinity and sponsoring translations of, and writing commentaries on, the works of Hippocrates and Galen. In the 1530s he was involved in a controversy on the merits of Greek and Arab medicine with the German physician Lorenz Fries and also with the botanist Leonhard Fuchs. Michael Servetus, who was his student, wrote a defense of Champier against Fuchs, In Leonardum Fuchsium Apologia. Defensio pro Symphoriano Campeggio (1536). Champier became more and more hostile to Arabic medicine and in Clysteriorum campi contra Arabum (this work was ironically put by Rabelais in his library of Saint-Victor), he even goes so far to advise his readers to refrain from reading the Arabs. With over fifty titles to his credit, Champier was a very prolific author, editor and compiler. His most important writings were in medicine, pharmacy, philosophy, and occultism, but he also worked in theology, history, biography, genealogy, poetry, patristics, and many other fields. The famous scholar printer Etienne Dolet remarked in his Commentariorum linguae latinae (Lyon, 1536): ‘From the schools of the physicians these rushed to the battle: Symphorien Champier, Jacques Dubois, Jean Ruelle, Jean Cop, François Rabelais, Charles Paludan. From all sides this serried band of doctors made such inroads into the camp of the barbarian that, wherever they stood, no place was left to the enemy' (cf. B.P. Copenhaver, Symphorien Champier and the Reception of the Occultist Tradition in Renaissance France, The Hague, 1978, pp. 45-86; see also R. Cooper, Les derniers année de Symphorien Champier, in: “Réforme, Humanisme, Renaissance”, 47, 1998, pp. 25-50).
