academic_description: 4to (218x157 mm). [12], 9-118, [4], 119-614, [2] pp. Collation: a6 B-O4 P4+2 Q-Z4 Aa-Zz4 Aaa-Zzz4 Aaaa-Hhhh4. Printer's device on title page. Woodcut head- and tailpieces. Contemporary limp vellum with inked title on spine (sightly soiled and stained, traces of ties). On the front pastedown bookplate of Count Giacomo Manzoni (1816-1889, cf. Catalogue de la Bibliothèque du feu M. Le Comte Jacques Manzoni, première partie, Città di Castello, 1892, p. 10, no. 94), on title page old manuscript ownership's entry “Monasterii Astinesis”. Light browning and staining, a few gathering more heavily browned, a very good, genuine copy.First edition of Baldi's collected literary works dedicated to Francesco Maria II della Rovere, Duke of Urbino. The volume opens with a long didactic poem, La Nautica, which is dedicated to Ferrando Gonzaga, Prince of Molfetta. It has some preliminary verses addressed to Baldi and with his answers (e.g., by Torquato Tasso, Giuliano Goselini, Muzio Manfredi, Stefano Guazzo, and many others). The work, in four books (pp. 23-1159), condenses most of the knowledge about the art of navigation of the time, including ship building, astronomical, meteorological and geographical notions (cf. G. Zaccagnini, Le fonti della ‘Nautica' di Bernardino Baldi, in; “Giornale storico della letteratura italiana, 40, 1902, pp. 366-396; see also C. Spalanca, ‘La nautica' di Bernardino Baldi fra scienza e letteratura, in: “Letteratura e scienza nella storia della cultura italiana”, V. Branca, ed., Palermo, 1978, pp. 452-464).There follow his eclogues (14, pp. 120-266), dedicated to Ranuccio Farnese, Prince of Parma (cf. F. Venturi, Bernardino Baldi e la tradizione dell'egloga nel Cinquecento, in “Giornale storico della letteratura italiana”, 622, 2011, pp. 249-58), and an epitalamium on the marriage of Beatrice degli Obizzi.The Sonetti romani (pp. 275-304, on pp. 305-306 is a list of the monuments described), dedicated to Francesco Maria della Rovere, were written during Baldi's sojourn in Rome in the years 1586-1587. They may be linked to those composed by Joachim Du Bellay (Antiquitez de Rome, 1558). The fifty-two sonnets describe buildings and works of art of antique Rome. The order of the sonnets follows the usual touristic itinerary from Porta del Popolo to Porta San Paolo (cf. G. Röllenbleck, Das Ende des Humanismus im 16. Jahrhundert: Bernardino Baldis ‘Sonetti Romani', in: “Studia Humanitatis, Ernesto Grassi zum 70. Geburtstag”, München, 1973, pp. 149-160; see also I. Filograsso, I ‘Sonetti Romani', di Bernardino Baldi, in: “Bernardino Baldi (1553-1616), studioso rinascimentale: poesia, storia, linguistica, meccanica, architettura”, E. Nenci, ed., Milano, 2005, pp. 55-79).The Rime varie (pp. 309-360) contain “quarantacinque testi comparsi nella raccolta veneziana di Versi e prose del 1590, dedicati all'urbinate Vittoria Galli in data novembre 1588: ma la composizione – in quanto avvenuta, come dice proprio Baldi ‘in tempi diversi' prima dell'ordinazione – dovrebbe così risalire alla prima metà degli anni '80 circa. Si tratta per lo più di sonetti encomiastici (alla stessa Galli e al figlio Narciso, a Ferrante Gonzaga, a Girolamo Pallantieri e alla moglie, al poeta Muzio Manfredi autore della tragedia Semiramide, eccetera), imbastiti con un linguaggio sostenuto e un robusto apparato classico e mitologico. Di un qualche interesse è un piccolo nucleo di componimenti sulle arti figurative, in particolare due ampie canzoni […] l'una cioè alla pittura e l'altra alla scoltura” (M. Volpi, Bernardino Baldi lirico, in: “Bernardino Baldi (1553-1616), studioso rinascimentale: poesia, storia, linguistica, meccanica, architettura”, E. Nenci, ed., Milano, 2005, p. 26).To Baldi's lyric compositions follow his prose dialogues (cf. V. Caputo, ‘Leggendo Platone': Bernardino Baldi tra scritti dialogici e scritti biografici, in: “Studi Rinascimentali”, 18, 2020, pp. 129-140). In the first work, written in 1587 and entitled Della Dignità (pp. 361-398), dedicated to Vespasiano Gonzaga, Duke of Sabbioneta, a dialogue between Fronimo and Nemesio, Baldi es­ta­bli­shes a strong link between the concept of dignity and that of happiness. There is a cor­res­pon­dence between this dialogue and the following, L'Arciero ovvero della felicità del principe (pp. 399-502, ‘The Archer or on the happiness of the Prince'). The two dialogues assume the features of two complementary paragraphs of a common reflection, directly linked to the figure of the prince. There is an explicit relationship between ‘dignity', belonging to the private sphere, and ‘happiness', belonging to the public sphere, since the first must have as its end the achievement of the second. A similar argument can be found in the homonymous dialogue written by Torquato Tasso in 1581, which greatly influenced Baldi (cf. V. Caputo, ‘Dignità' e ‘felicità'. Note su Bernardino Baldi e Torquato Tasso, in: “L'Io felice. Tra filosofia e letteratura”, Milano, 2017, pp. 77-94; see also Id., Il principe ‘come‘ arciere. La felicità pubblica secondo Bernardini Baldi, in: “Il ‘Barlume che vacilla'. La felicità nella letteratura italiana dal Quattro al Novecento”, Milano, 2016, pp. 37-56). “Nel dialogo morale, Arciero, la denominazione architettonica travalica l'accezione tecnica, acquisendo un significato filosofico e morale di ‘eccellente virtuoso, capace di congiungere e servirsi di varie arti per realizzare un fine'. La virtù ‘architettonica' è quindi attribuita ai nobili e ai capi militari (‘l'Arciero', ‘il Capitano'), ‘poiché sotto il fine di quella si raccolgono, et uniscono insieme tutti i fini di altre arti minori'. La virtù ‘architettonichissima' è sinonimo della ‘civile' o ‘politica', qualità essenziale del Principe, il quale affina le arti di governo così come l'artista perfeziona le proprie opere” (A. Siekiera, L'ingegno e la maniera di Bernardino Baldi, in: “Saggi di letteratura architettonica da Vitruvio a Winckelmann”, F.P. Di Teodoro, ed., 2009, p. 305).Of great importance for the history of architecture and art is the following Descrittione del palazzo ducale di Urbino (pp. 503-573). The work was written during Baldi's stay in Rome in 1587. “Il testo sul Palazzo ducale fu scritto, come s'è detto, a Roma, per esplicita richiesta del ‘cardinal d'Aragona', che quasi sicuramente è da identificarsi con Innico d'Avalos, figlio del marchese del Vasto e di Maria d'Aragona, dal 1561 l'abate commendatario di Procida […] Mentre compone la Descrittione lontano da Urbino, il Baldi si serve soltanto della sua memoria per ‘ricostruire' l'intero edificio attraverso l'analisi del progetto e della messa in opera di elementi principali, come le strutture portanti e la disposizione degli ambienti, accentuando, con vividezza illustrativa, tutte le componenti di significativo linguaggio architettonico, come il cortile d'onore, la sala delle udienze, le soprallogge, lo scalone d'onore, la facciata ad ali e quella dei torricini. La misura costante del valore artistico è per lui l'architettura classica, studiata nei suoi principi nel trattato di Vitruvio e nei testi dei suoi interpreti, Alberti e Barbaro, e così pure indagata nelle opere edificate sia da antichi che da moderni” (A. Siekiera, Introduzione, in: Bernardino Baldi, “Descrittione del Palazzo Ducale di Urbino”, Alessandria, 2010, p. 12).There follows a very original work, the Cento apologi, which is dedicated to the physician and man of letters at the court of Mantova, Giovanni Battista Cavallara. It is modelled on Leon Battista Alberti's Aesopian Apologi centum (1437), and Baldi substitutes in it talking animals with tools and machines which dialogue on the principles of the ars mechanica (cf. A.Siekiera, La défence des ‘artes mechanicae' et la poésie de Bernardino Baldi, in: “Colloque de Peyresq: La poésie scientifique de Lucrèce à nos jours”, Juin 2008, online: https://unimol.academia.edu/SiekieraAnna, and D. Marsh, Renaissance Fables: Leon Battista Alberti; Leonardo da Vinci; Bartolomeo Scala; Bernardino Baldi, Tempe, AZ, 2004, pp. 318ff).The volume ends with La favola di Museo de gli amori di Leandro, et d'Ero tradotta dal greco (pp. 591-614). This is the first Italian translation of Musaeus's poem, written in 1585 and dedicated to Lavinia Feltria della Rovere (cf. M. Cerutti, Bernardino Baldi volgarizzatore di Museo, in: “Bernardino Baldi (1553-1616), studioso rinascimentale: poesia, storia, linguistica, meccanica, architettura”, E. Nenci, ed., Milano, 2005, pp. 81-93).Bernardino Baldi was born at Urbino from a noble family originally from Perugia. He first studied medicine and later philosophy at Padua. In Urbino he devoted himself to mathematics under Federico Commandino and Guidobaldo del Monte. In 1580 he was invited to the court of Mantua by Ferrante Gonzaga, who in 1585 secured him the post of abbot of Guastalla. Baldi then took the orders, and thereafter gave much attention to ecclesiastical scholarship. He visited Rome and was made ‘Protonotarius Apostolicus'. In 1609 he resigned his abbacy to enter the service of the Duke of Urbino, Francesco Maria della Rovere, as historian and biographer, a post he held until his death. Baldi was also responsible for several public works in the duchy of Ferrara, including the Baccanello Bridge at Guastalla, and the Church of Santa Chiara at Urbino. Besides that, he was a poet and prose stylist of remarkable ability, a historian of architecture, an orientalist, and an expert in twelve languages, including Persian and Arabic. However, his most significant achievements were made in the field of mathematics and physics: his commentary on the Mechanica of Aristotle was the most important work of its kind to appear up to that time, and his Vite dei Matematici stands as the first large scale history of mathematics (cf. G. Zaccagnini, Bernardino Baldi nella vita e nelle opere, Pistoia, 1908, passim; see also P.L. Rose, The Italian Renaissance Mathematics, Genève, 1975, pp. 243-279; and A. Serrai, Bernardino Baldi. La vita, le opere, la biblioteca, Milano, 2002, pp. 17-158).

title: Lettera di messer Bartolomeo Ammannati architetto, e scultor fiorentino. A gli honoratissimi Accademici del disegno

authors.name: Ammannati Bartolomeo
authors.biography: Bartolomeo Ammannati (1511–1592) stands as one of the most complex, formidable, and transformative figures of the Italian High Renaissance and Mannerist periods. Operating at the dynamic intersection of sculpture, monumental civic architecture, and Counter-Reformation urban planning, Ammannati served as a principal architect to Duke Cosimo I de' Medici and Pope Julius III. His career encapsulates the stylistic shift from the heroic, classicizing muscularity of Michelangelo Buonarroti and Jacopo Sansovino toward the dramatic rustication, spatial tension, and intellectual rigor of late sixteenth-century Tuscan Mannerism. Beyond his structural and figurative achievements, Ammannati occupied a unique place within the literary and religious networks of early modern Italy. His marriage to the renowned poet Laura Battiferri connected him to the highest elite of Renaissance humanism, while his late-life spiritual crisis—influenced profoundly by the Society of Jesus—led him to formulate one of the earliest explicit Counter-Reformation manifestos on the moral responsibilities of visual artists, directly addressing the aesthetic and theological dilemmas surrounding the representation of the nude figure.Born in Florence on June 18, 1511, into a family of modest background, Ammannati received his initial artistic training in the turbulent atmosphere of early sixteenth-century Tuscany. He entered the workshop of the fiery and contentious sculptor Baccio Bandinelli, from whom he absorbed a mastery of monumental marble carving, anatomical muscularity, and the intense rivalry that characterized Florentine workshop culture. Seeking to refine his technique and distance himself from Bandinelli's tempestuous circle, Ammannati moved to Venice, where he joined the bottega of Jacopo Sansovino. Under Sansovino’s tutelage at the Library of San Marco and the Marciana precinct, Ammannati mastered the integration of classical architectural ornament with sculptural relief, absorbing the Venetian synthesis of light, tactile surface texture, and pictorial elegance. This dual training—Florentine anatomical disegno paired with Venetian sculptural harmony—formed the foundation of his distinctive artistic identity. In the early 1540s, Ammannati established his independence in Padua, earning the patronal backing of the humanist jurist and scholar Marco Mantova Benavides. For Benavides, Ammannati executed the magnificent Benavides Monument in the church of the Eremitani and carved a colossal statue of Hercules, works that signaled his complete command of classicizing iconography and architectural framing.The 1550s marked Ammannati’s ascension to the premier rank of Italian court artists. Moving to Rome under the pontificate of Pope Julius III (Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte), Ammannati collaborated with Giorgio Vasari and Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola on the design and execution of the Villa Giulia. Here, Ammannati was responsible for the dramatic nymphaeum and subterranean loggia, creating an immersive, multi-layered architectural experience that synthesized natural rock formations, caryatids, and refined classical orders. In 1550, Ammannati married Laura Battiferri, an intellectual alliance that elevated his social standing and introduced him to key figures of Italian humanism, including Agnolo Bronzino, Annibale Caro, and Benedetto Varchi. Following the death of Julius III in 1555, Ammannati returned to Florence to enter the service of Cosimo I de' Medici. His Florentine period yielded his supreme architectural and sculptural masterpieces. Between 1560 and 1577, he directed the dramatic expansion of the Palazzo Pitti, creating the iconic rear courtyard whose heavy, cyclopean rustication seamlessly bridged the urban palace with the terraced landscapes of the Boboli Gardens. Simultaneously, Ammannati won the hotly contested commission for the Fontana del Nettuno (popularly known as Il Biancone) in the Piazza della Signoria, prevailing over rivals such as Benvenuto Cellini and Giambologna. In civil engineering, his masterpiece remains the Ponte Santa Trinita (1567–1569), featuring graceful, catenary elliptical arches that scholars suspect were designed in consultation with Michelangelo, providing unprecedented structural elegance across the Arno River.Ammannati's publishing and typographical footprint is intimately tied to both his architectural theory and his profound Counter-Reformation conversion. While his extensive unexecuted manuscript treatise on the ideal city—known as La Città—circulated in architectural circles and remained preserved within Florentine humanist libraries, his most famous published text emerged from his late-life crisis of faith. In 1582, through the prestigious press of Bartolomeo Sermartelli in Florence, Ammannati published his seminal Lettera del Sig. Bartolomeo Ammannati Architetto, et Scultor Fiorentino. A gli Honoratissimi Accademici del Disegno. Printed in a slim, elegant octavo format characteristic of Sermartelli's religious and academic publications, the letter served as an open retraction of his earlier artistic output. Deeply affected by the decrees of the Council of Trent and his close friendship with the Jesuits, Ammannati publicly repented for having carved provocative nude figures—most notably the sea nymphs of the Neptune Fountain—and implored his fellow artists at the Accademia del Disegno to restrict their talents exclusively to sacred and morally edifying subjects. This publication, alongside the editions of Laura Battiferri's poetry issued by the Giunti and Giolito presses in Venice and Florence, positions the Ammannati household at the center of late sixteenth-century Italian print culture, bridging classical Renaissance humanism and Counter-Reformation piety.In his final years, Ammannati devoted his wealth and artistic energy almost entirely to religious architecture, most notably directing the design and construction of the Church of San Giovannino dei Gesuiti in Florence. Dying on April 13, 1592, Ammannati left a complex historiographical legacy. While early modern critics like Benvenuto Cellini mocked the monumental scale of his Neptune sculpture—coining the famous Florentine street rhyme, "Ammannato, Ammannato, quanto marmo hai rovinato!"—later historians recognized his genius in spatial orchestration and structural engineering. From Filippo Baldinucci’s seventeenth-century biographies to modern reassessments by Nikolaus Pevsner, Manfredo Tafuri, and Michael Kiene, Ammannati is recognized as a master who articulated the transition from High Renaissance harmony to the tension, theatricality, and spiritual austerity of late Mannerism and the early Baroque.

publishers.name: Sermartelli Bartolomeo
publishers.biography: Bartolomeo Sermartelli (1532–1604) stands as one of the most prominent, prolific, and culturally influential typographers, booksellers, and publishers active in Florence during the golden age of the Medici Grand Duchy. Operating across a crucial historical period defined by the political consolidation of Duke (later Grand Duke) Cosimo I de' Medici, the artistic and intellectual patronage of Francesco I, and the pragmatic statecraft of Ferdinando I, Sermartelli transformed his printing house into a vital epicenter for vernacular humanism, linguistic standardization, and counter-reformation erudition. While early sixteenth-century Florentine typography had been dominated by the monumental output of the Giunti press and mid-century state patronized printing had centered on the official printer Lorenzo Torrentino, Bartolomeo Sermartelli carved out a unique and expansive publishing empire. Over a printing career spanning more than five decades—from his earliest documented imprints in the mid-1550s until his death in 1604—Sermartelli issued over six hundred distinct titles. His production range encompassed foundational Italian vernacular literature, scholarly treatises commissioned by the Accademia Fiorentina and the nascent Accademia della Crusca, historical and genealogical monuments, legal codices, and official liturgical texts for the Archdiocese of Florence. Through his close collaborations with leading intellectuals of the Tuscan Renaissance, including Vincenzo Borghini, Benedetto Varchi, Pier Vettori, Scipione Ammirato, Giovan Battista Gelli, and Torquato Tasso, Sermartelli played an indispensable role in shaping the textual transmission and typographical presentation of late Renaissance Italian culture.Born in Florence in 1532 into a family of modest local standing, Bartolomeo Sermartelli received a solid foundational education in grammar, Latin, and vernacular rhetoric, which enabled him to navigate both the scholarly demands of the Florentine intelligentsia and the mercantile realities of the book trade. In the early 1550s, he entered the print trade as an apprentice, acquiring technical mastery in composition, ink formulation, press mechanics, and font selection. By 1553, Sermartelli had established his independent workshop and formal matriculation within the Arte dei Medici e Speziali, the powerful Florentine guild that traditionally governed stationers, booksellers, and printers alongside physicians and apothecaries.Positioning his initial workshop in the vibrant urban heart of Florence—near the Piazza San Firenze, the Via della Condotta, and later expanding operations along the Via del Cocomero—Sermartelli established strategic proximity to both the civic administrative hubs of the Palazzo Vecchio and the scholarly circles of the Studio Fiorentino. In his early years of independence, Sermartelli successfully navigated a competitive landscape dominated by the widow and heirs of Bernardo Giunti and the privileged enterprise of Lorenzo Torrentino, the Flemish printer brought to Florence by Cosimo I in 1547. Rather than directly challenging Torrentino's monopoly over official ducal statutes and grand classicizing Latin folios, Sermartelli strategically prioritized vernacular literature, contemporary Italian poetry, localized historical monographs, and academic dissertations, thereby securing a loyal customer base among Tuscan nobles, academicians, and wealthy patrician collectors.The defining dimension of Bartolomeo Sermartelli’s publishing program was his intimate alignment with the intellectual agenda of the Florentine Academies. As Cosimo I sought to establish Tuscan Italian as the preeminent cultural and diplomatic language of Europe, Sermartelli emerged as an unofficial printer to the Accademia Fiorentina and later maintained vital links with the scholars who founded the Accademia della Crusca in 1583. His press became the primary engine for the philological and historical scholarship of Don Vincenzo Borghini, the learned Benedictine prior of the Ospedale degli Innocenti and chief cultural advisor to the Medici court. Sermartelli printed Borghini’s monumental Discorsi (1584–1585), a masterwork of Tuscan antiquarianism, epigraphy, and historical geography that set new standards for critical methodology in historical research. Furthermore, Sermartelli worked closely with Benedetto Varchi, printing key editions of his linguistic masterwork L'Ercolano (1570), a dialogue that established the theoretical foundations for the superiority of the Florentine spoken tongue, as well as Varchi's academic lectures, funeral orations, and historical writings. Beyond philology and linguistics, Sermartelli’s catalogue reflected the broader literary canon of the Italian Renaissance. He printed key editions of Dante Alighieri (including commentaries and textual defenses), Giovanni Boccaccio, Francesco Petrarca, Ludovico Ariosto, and modern poetry by Agnolo Bronzino and Laura Battiferri. Notably, Sermartelli was also instrumental in the dissemination of contemporary epic poetry; he produced early Florentine printings of Torquato Tasso’s Gerusalemme Liberata and Aminta, navigating complex intellectual disputes regarding epic form and linguistic purity. In the realm of history and political thought, Sermartelli published Scipione Ammirato’s monumental Storie fiorentine, providing the Grand Duchy with its definitive patrician narrative of Florentine history.From a typographical and material perspective, Bartolomeo Sermartelli’s output represents a high point of late sixteenth-century Tuscan book production. His shop maintained multiple rolling and platen presses, utilizing high-quality rag paper sourced primarily from the historic paper mills of Pescia, Collodi, and the Villa Basilica in the Lucchese and Tuscan hills. Material analysis of his imprints reveals a sophisticated aesthetic sensitivity: Sermartelli frequently deployed clear, elegant Roman types (tondo) modeled on classical proportions for main body texts, alongside fluid, highly legible Italic fonts (corsivo) inspired by Venetian and Roman calligraphic traditions (such as those of Ludovico Vicentino degli Arrighi and Aldus Manutius). For title pages and decorative capitals, his workshop employed an extensive inventory of woodcuts, including ornate inhabited initials featuring mythological motifs, grotesque strapwork, architectural borders (cornici silografiche), and tailpieces. Central to Sermartelli's brand identity were his distinctive printer's devices (marche tipografiche). His most famous mark featured a slow-moving tortoise bearing a billowing sail upon its shell—an explicit visual rendering of the classical adage Festina Lente ("Make haste slowly"), which was also the personal emblem (impresa) adopted by Grand Duke Cosimo I de' Medici. Variations of this mark depicted the tortoise anchored near a stormy sea or set within an elaborate cartouche featuring female allegories of Prudence and Fortitude. Alternatively, Sermartelli frequently used devices depicting the heraldic Lily of Florence (Giglio fiorentino), held aloft by cherubs or flanked by mottoes emphasizing purity, civic pride, and academic excellence, such as Maturitate or In Domino Confido.The latter half of Sermartelli's career coincided with the intensification of Counter-Reformation policies following the closing decrees of the Council of Trent (1563) and the publication of the Roman Index Librorum Prohibitorum. Sermartelli demonstrated remarkable political and ideological adaptability, preserving his commercial viability while strictly adhering to ecclesiastical censorship. He secured lucrative official commissions from the Archdiocese of Florence, printing diocesan synodal decrees, catechisms, missals, breviaries, and devotional manuals approved by Archbishop Alessandro de' Medici (later Pope Leo XI). Concurrently, when printing works by authors whose political or religious standing was controversial—such as Niccolò Machiavelli or certain Protestant-leaning humanists—Sermartelli employed subtle publishing strategies, including anonymous or pseudonymous imprints, sanitized texts revised by inquisitorial correctors, or carefully framed commentaries that neutralised potential heterodoxy. As Bartolomeo advanced in years during the late 1590s, he gradually integrated his son, Michelangelo Sermartelli, into the management of the firm. Following Bartolomeo’s death in Florence in 1604, Michelangelo took full control of the workshop, continuing to print under the name Eredi di Bartolomeo Sermartelli and maintaining the family’s high typographical standards well into the seventeenth century. Today, Bartolomeo Sermartelli is recognized by bibliographers and historian of the book not merely as an efficient craftsman, but as a central architect of Grand Ducal Florence's intellectual infrastructure, whose imprints remain indispensable primary sources for the study of Renaissance literature, philology, and print culture.

academic_description: 4to (208x154 mm). [8] leaves. Collation: A-B4. Italic type. Woodcut printer's device on title page, woodcut initial. Modern carta rustica. Small stain around a repaired tiny hole going through each leaf. Bookplate of Giannalisa Feltrinelli (see sale Christie's London, 2 June 1998, lot 1091).Rare first edition (it was reprinted in Florence in 1687) of Ammanati's famous letter to the Accademia del Disegno, the artist's guild at Florence, in which he denounced the display of nude sculpture, including his own colossal figure of Hercules in Padua and the Neptune fountain in the Piazza della Signoria in Florence.One of the leading Mannerist sculptors and architects in Florence, Ammannati worked for Cosimo de' Medici on his programme of public works, remodelling Palazzo Pitti and the Boboli gardens, and building the Ponte Santa Trinita and the Neptune fountain in the Piazza della Signoria. Under the influence of the Counter-Reformation, however, at the end of his life Ammannati reconsidered his artistic expression and his art became more religious in tone. The present letter expressed his remorse at depicting nude bodies in his previous art, despite the importance of the shape of the body in his earlier work. As an example of virtuous sculpture from his last period, Ammannati cites in the letter the tomb of Giovanni Boncompagni, commissioned by Gregory XIII in 1572 for the cemetery of Pisa, which depicts Christ between Peace and Justice.Although Ammannati doesn't mention it directly in the letter, this radical change may have been due to his advancing age and his new collaboration as patron and architect for the Jesuits, for whom he designed and financed the renovation of the church and college of San Giovannino. It was probably around 1572, thanks to the influence of his wife Laura Battiferri, that Ammannati began to be more involved in the activities of the Society of Jesus in Florence (cf. V. Kirkham, Creative Partners: The Marriage of Laura Battiferra and Bartolomeo Ammannati, in “Renaissance Quarterly”, LV, 2, 2002, pp. 498-558).“When the first Jesuits arrived in Florence in 1551, they hoped to set up a community for twelve members of their order with the support of the Duchess Eleonora di Toledo. During the first few years, the Florentine Jesuits experienced many setbacks, and finding a permanent residence was one of their main concerns. For several years, they were forced to occupy a number of unsuitable, rented houses. They probably expressed their troubles to Eleonora, because in 1554 her husband, Duke Cosimo I de'Medici, donated the medieval church and the rectory of San Giovannino to them. The location was almost perfect: a central position, easily reached by students from all over town. However, the medieval building was too small and in a state of disrepair […] In Florence, due to the absence of a devoted and wealthy patron, no improvement of the accommodation of the Jesuit community was forthcoming. Almost fifteen years after establishing their foundation in Florence, the Jesuits still faced an insecure future. In 1566 a committee of supportive and prominent citizens was founded to find a solution, and it is likely that Ammannati soon became involved with their work […] Indeed, Ammannati's assistance proved to be of great value. His close involvement with the construction of the new complex was exceptional; Ammannati not only proposed to make the designs, he and his wife also offered to take care of a substantial part of the expenses. The couple had agreed to pay for the construction of the college as early as 1577, although Ammannati hoped to persuade Giacomo Salviati, the cousin of Francesco de' Medici, to be the main patron of the church. It seems that Salviati pulled back, making Ammannati responsible for bearing the cost of both the church and school. The best proof of Ammannati's and Battiferri's generosity was the decision of the childless couple in 1581 to make the Jesuit community in Florence their heir. His sympathy with the Jesuits was in keeping with his religious awakening at the end of his life. In 1582, when Ammannati was seventy-one, he wrote a well-known letter to all the artists in Florence expressing remorse for the character of his artistic oeuvre and warning his colleagues to refrain from making unchaste images. He repented for creating the sensual ignudi for the Neptune fountain on Piazza della Signoria in Florence, saying that it was improper to erect these kinds of images in a public place, where the statues could evoke impure thoughts. This change in thinking might have sprung from the prospect of his death, for Ammannati was old and probably in bad health, but it seems that his contact with the Jesuits was in part responsible […] Following the decision to enlarge the existing site, Bartolomeo Ammannati planned a new building. In 1579 the construction of the new nave of the church began, and already in 1581 the church was consecrated after the first three bays were built. However, after this successful start, the acquisition of new land largely failed, compelling Ammannati to adjust his design. In 1590 he produced a carefully made plan, which is now preserved in the Archivio di Stato in Rome (ASR) […] The complex of San Giovannino is adapted to its specific situation. Ammannati had to create a design that complied with the new ideological and functional demands of the Jesuits while taking into account the grave spatial and financial limitations. The final design of 1590 demonstrated his flexibility and acute observation, which were architectural skills championed in Antonio Possevino's encyclopedia, the Bibliotheca selecta (1593). Possevino consulted Valeriano and Ammannati for his chapter on architecture, which is wellknown for its dismissal of blind adherence to Vitruvius's De architectura […] The Florentine Jesuits were particularly proud of overcoming the problems they encountered in building their church. In 1581, when San Giovannino was consecrated, the annual report remarked with enthusiasm that the people considered it almost a miracle that, in spite of many setbacks, the church was built so swiftly that it seemed to have appeared suddenly. The admiration of San Giovannino is apparent in its influence on seventeenth- and eighteenth-century churches in Florence and Tuscany. Several churches were inspired by Ammannati's system of alternating chapels and confessionals in niches […] But although Ammannati did not have the stature of a Farnese or a Borromeo, and although his support for the Jesuits did not spring from political aspirations, he had one thing in common with those grander patrons. He, too, wanted to demonstrate his stature, and the prospect of burial in the church is likely to have pleased him. Ammannati and Laura Battiferri were granted this unusual privilege in recognition of their zeal for the Jesuit cause, because without their ongoing efforts the new complex would never have been accomplished. The couple were even permitted to decorate the chapel of Saint Bartholomew with an altarpiece. The altarpiece that Ammannati commissioned from Alessandro Allori is still visible in the second chapel on the left, and it is said that the couple are depicted on the lower right. Clearly, Ammannati could not have wished for a better expression of his prestige, to be buried in front of the chapel of Saint Bartholomew in a church he designed and financed. He was highly satisfied with his achievement, as he wrote to the Accademia del Disegno in 1582, boasting that, through his contribution, the very beautiful San Giovannino (la bellissima Chiesa di S. Giovannino) was being erected. Even though their sepulcher must have originally been no more than a humble stone with an inscription, it drew prestige from the lack of other private tombs. In that sense Ammannati's intentions were not so far removed from those of Farnese at Il Gesù. San Giovannino would be his mortuary monument” (M. Hurx, Bartolomeo Ammannati and the College of San Giovannino in Florence: Adapting Architecture to Jesuit Needs, in: “Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians”, vol. 68, no. 3, September 2009, pp. 339-341 and 351-354).“Lo stesso Bartolomeo Ammannati, accademico della prima ora, amico di Vasari e Borghini, considerò la scomparsa degli amici il momento opportuno di scrivere, nel 1582, una ‘lettera agli Accademici del Disegno'. In quello scritto, dato alle stampe, rivendicava a sé un metodo didattico, diretta espressione di una discussione accademica, capace di far comprendere ai giovani artisti il vero metodo di fare l'arte. L'obiettivo dell'Ammannati era però un altro. Sempre più vicino alle pratiche della pietà della Compagnia di Gesù, da poco instaurata anche a Firenze, l'architetto esprimeva il suo pubblico confiteor pregando tutti i membri dell'Accademia affinché non raffigurassero nudità ‘coprendo quelle parti che si deono ricoprire e che vedere non si possono se non con vergogna, e che ragione et arte ricoprir c'insegna, è grandissimo e gravissimo errore'. Il messaggio, rivolto proprio a quegli allievi del disegno, era tra le più insidiose mistificazioni scritte nel periodo. L'Ammannati, infatti, nel testo loda spesso il magistero michelangiolesco, al quale è perfino dedicato l'epitaffio finale, ma al contempo, con un'abile espediente retorico, sublima le pulsioni estetiche ed artistiche del Buonarroti in un'aurea di eterea castità e vergogna: ‘i buoni cristiani sempre facevano le buone e belle figure'. Ecco che, ribaltando le prospettive, persino una presunta frase attribuita al divino artista diveniva, nelle mani di sapienti pedagoghi, strumento di potere e di pressione sull'animo delle giovani generazioni. Del resto lo stesso Ammannati, il 28 aprile del 1583, fece dono all'Accademia di un torso michelangiolesco non finito, un modello ricevuto dallo stesso Granduca e identificato oggi con l'eponimo di Dio Fluviale, previsto da Michelangelo come ornamento di una tomba dei duchi di casa Medici ai lati dei sarcofagi di San Lorenzo. L'episodio, apparentemente in contraddizione, rappresentando il modello una divinità nuda - ma non evidentemente sessuata - si può inquadrare perfettamente nella concezione accademica dell'Ammannati per cui occorreva studiare, copiare, ispirarsi (anche secondo le indicazioni del De pictura di Leon Battista Alberti), ma con discernimento. Nella piccola collezione dell'Accademia si aggiungeva così, alla copia in gesso del Cristo della Minerva di Michelangelo di cui, oltre che per la didattica, si disponeva largamente per l'uso liturgico interno all'accolita, il ‘modello di terra cruda grande in sur una basa di lengio' che rimarrà preziosa reliquia, per almeno due secoli, di un padre a cui mai fu permesso di fare da padrone” (E. Sartoni, Arte e potere. Il mito di Michelangelo padre e “fondatore” dell'Accademia del Disegno, in: “L'immortalità di un mito. L'eredità di Michelangelo nelle arti e negli insegnamenti accademici a Firenze dal Cinquecento alla contemporaneità”, S. Bellesi & F. Petrucci, eds, Florence, 2014, pp. 47-48).Bartolomeo Ammannati was a prominent sculptor and architect of the Italian Mannerist period. He began as a pupil of Baccio Bandinelli before working under Jacopo Sansovino and Giovanni Angelo Montorsoli. In the 1530s and 1540s, Ammannati collaborated on Sansovino's project for the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice and Montorsoli's tomb for the poet Jacopo Sannazaro in Naples. Between 1544 and 1548, he worked as a sculptor and architect in Padua for the humanist and antiquarian Marco Mantua Benavides. Ammannati's tomb for Benavides in the Church of the Eremitani illustrates his take on Michelangelo's unfinished wall tombs in the Medici Chapel. In 1550, Ammannati married Laura Battiferra, an accomplished poet and a prominent figure in the devotional culture of Counter-Reformation Italy. He traveled to Rome where he undertook important commissions related to the papal family, including tombs for the Del Monte in S. Pietro in Montorio and portions of Julius III's Villa Giulia, on which he collaborated with Giorgio Vasari and Jacopo Vignola. In 1555, Ammannati returned to Florence to serve under Duke Cosimo I de' Medici. His works during this period exemplify Mannerism at its height, from the bronzes of the Neptune Fountain to the courtyard of the Palazzo Pitti. As architect and engineer, he was also responsible for the Ponte Santa Trinità and the Column of Justice. In his later years, Ammannati took on architectural projects outside of Florence and he grew increasingly dedicated to the Jesuit order. He and Laura left their possessions to the Jesuits and helped with the reconstruction of the church of S. Giovannino in Florence, funding a chapel where they were buried (cf. Ch. Avery, Ammanati [Ammannati], Bartolomeo [Bartolommeo], in: “Grove Art Online” J. Rodenbeck, ed., New York, 2003).

authors.name: Velthuysen Lambert
authors.biography: Lambert van Velthuysen (1622–1685) stands as one of the most formidable, complex, and multifaceted intellectual figures of the Dutch Golden Age. Operating at the turbulent intersection of Cartesian rationalism, Hobbesian natural law theory, Calvinist theology, and Erastian political theory, Velthuysen occupied a preeminent position in the mid-seventeenth-century Republic of Letters. As a physician, city regent of Utrecht, and prolific polemicist, he played a decisive role in mediating the philosophical revolution wrought by René Descartes and Thomas Hobbes within the context of the Dutch Reformed Church and the political structures of the United Provinces. Far from being a mere popularizer or passive eclectic, Velthuysen deployed an original synthesis of mechanical philosophy, biblical hermeneutics, and state supremacy over ecclesiastical authorities (jus circa sacra) to defend freedom of philosophical inquiry and civil toleration against the rising tide of Voetian scholastic orthodoxy. His extensive writings—spanning natural law, Biblical accommodation, medical theory, and anti-clerical political philosophy—exerted a profound influence on European intellectual developments, casting a long shadow over the early Enlightenment debates surrounding Spinozism, deism, and the secularization of political ethics.Born into an influential patrician family in Utrecht and baptized on October 18, 1622, Velthuysen was the son of Henrick van Velthuysen, a prosperous merchant and respected municipal official, and Sophia van Werckhoven. His high social standing granted him access to the elite educational networks of the young Dutch Republic. Velthuysen matriculated at the University of Utrecht shortly after its elevation to university status in 1636. During his formative academic years, the university was a battlefield between two diametrically opposed intellectual camps: the traditionalist Aristotelian-scholastic establishment led by the formidable theologian Gisbertus Voetius, and the avant-garde mechanical movement spearheaded by Henricus Regius, a devoted disciple of René Descartes. Velthuysen immersed himself in both faculties, reading deeply in Reformed theology, Classical humanities, mathematics, and medicine. He pursued advanced medical and philosophical studies not only at Utrecht but also at the University of Leyden and the University of Franeker, ultimately securing doctorates in both philosophy and medicine. This rigorous dual training endowed him with a refined understanding of scholastic disputation alongside an acute appreciation for observational science and Cartesian physics, shaping the methodical, analytical rigor that characterized his lifelong literary output.Velthuysen’s intellectual career gained momentum in the 1650s through his bold intervention in the raging controversies over Cartesian philosophy. When Voetius and his orthodox allies condemned Cartesianism as a gateway to atheism, skepticism, and the subversion of scriptural authority, Velthuysen authored landmark treatises defending the compatibility of the new philosophy with Christian revelation. In his celebrated 1655 Dutch treatise, Bewys dat de stellinghen van Des Cartes geen exempelen van haeresie en sijn ('Proof that the Propositions of Descartes are Not Examples of Heresy'), expanded into Latin as Demonstratio quod veritates quae in Scriptura Sacra proponuntur non contradicant veritatibus veris inventis a Cartesio (1655), Velthuysen formulated an influential theory of biblical accommodation. He argued that Sacred Scripture was revealed to instruct humanity in moral salvation rather than technical natural science; consequently, scriptural references to astronomical or physical phenomena were written according to common human perception rather than absolute physical reality. By separating the domain of natural philosophy—governed by clear and distinct rational evidence—from the realm of divine revelation, Velthuysen established a hermeneutical shield that shielded Cartesian physics and Copernican heliocentrism from charges of theological heresy.Concurrently, Velthuysen established himself as one of the earliest and most sophisticated Continental readers of Thomas Hobbes. In his groundbreaking 1651 monograph, Epistolica dissertatio de principiis justi et decori, vindicata a sublestis castigationibus Johannis Vedelii ('Epistolary Dissertation on the Principles of Justice and Decency'), he systematically engaged Hobbes’s De Cive (1642). Velthuysen adopted the Hobbesian premise that the primary law of nature is rooted in self-preservation (conservatio sui) and the rational calculation of utility. However, unlike Hobbes, Velthuysen rejected absolute political Leviathanism and moral skepticism. He integrated self-preservation into a divine moral framework, contending that God endowed human beings with natural instincts and rational faculties that naturally incline them toward sociability, justice, and natural rights. This revolutionary harmonization of Hobbesian naturalism with Reformed moral theology provoked fierce condemnation from orthodox theologians, notably Johannes Vedelius and Voetius, who accused Velthuysen of undermining divine law and introducing pagan epicureanism into the Christian commonwealth.Velthuysen’s commitment to political theory was deeply entwined with his civic role as a member of the Utrecht city council (Vroedschap) and governor of the local Latin School. In the arena of church-state relations, he emerged as a fierce champion of Erastianism—the doctrine asserting the supreme authority of the civil magistrate over ecclesiastical affairs. In works such as Het gebruyck van de rede in 't beleyd van de godtsdienst ('The Use of Reason in the Management of Religion', 1656) and Tractatus de idololatria et superstitione (1669), Velthuysen combated the theological encroachments of the 'Further Reformation' (Nadere Reformatie). He argued that the public enforcement of religion, the licensing of preachers, and the management of church property belonged exclusively to the sovereign civil magistrate (the Staten and municipal regents). To prevent clerical tyranny, Velthuysen advocated for a broad civil toleration: while the magistrate should maintain a public Reformed church for civic cohesion, freedom of conscience must be protected, allowing dissenting Protestant sects and even Catholics to practice their faith privately without civil persecution.Among the most famous intellectual encounters of Velthuysen’s career was his engagement with Baruch Spinoza. Following the anonymous publication of Spinoza’s Tractatus Theologico-Politicus in 1670, Jacob Ostens forwarded a copy to Velthuysen seeking his judgment. Velthuysen responded with a lengthy, blistering critique, published as an open letter in 1671 (subsequently incorporated into Spinoza’s correspondence as Letter 42). While recognizing Spinoza’s extraordinary analytical acuity, Velthuysen condemned the work as a insidious attack on religion. He accused Spinoza of subverting divine providence, reducing God to blind natural necessity, discarding miracles, and annihilating moral accountability by equating divine law with physical determinism. Spinoza reacted with profound irritation in Letter 43, defending his piety and accusing Velthuysen of misrepresenting his system. Despite this fierce initial exchange, the two philosophers later met in person in Utrecht and maintained a respectful, if fundamentally irreconcilable, dialogue, underscoring Velthuysen’s role as the foremost Cartesian-Christian critic of radical Spinozism.The publishing history of Velthuysen’s works provides a vivid window into the vibrant print culture of the seventeenth-century Dutch Republic. His treatises were initially produced by prominent printing houses in Utrecht, such as Theodorus van Ackersdijck and Gisbertus van Zijll, who catered to the academic and political controversies of the university city. As his international reputation expanded, his Latin opera were distributed throughout Europe via the sophisticated publishing networks of Amsterdam and Rotterdam. In 1680, the eminent Rotterdam publisher Reinier Leers issued Velthuysen’s monumental collected works, Opera Omnia, in two handsome quarto volumes. Beautifully set in clear Roman and Italic types with elegant engraved frontispieces, this definitive edition compiled his philosophical, theological, and political treatises, ensuring their wide dissemination across the scholarly academies, noble libraries, and universities of Germany, France, Great Britain, and Switzerland.Lambert van Velthuysen died in Utrecht on April 9, 1685, leaving behind an enduring legacy as a courageous defender of intellectual freedom, rational theology, and secularized natural law. In the generations following his death, his ideas deeply informed the political and philosophical synthesis of Samuel von Pufendorf, Christian Thomasius, Pierre Bayle, and John Locke. Modern historiography—led by scholars such as C. Louise Thijssen-Schoute, Jonathan Israel, Theo Verbeek, and Wiep van Bunge—reassesses Velthuysen not merely as a transitional figure between Descartes and Spinoza, but as a primary architect of modern European liberalism. His visionary integration of Cartesian epistemological clarity, Hobbesian natural law, Erastian state responsibility, and religious toleration remains a cornerstone in the intellectual history of the Western Enlightenment.
