related_names.name: Hobbes Thomas
related_names.biography: Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury (5 April 1588 – 4 December 1679) was one of the most consequential philosophers of early modern Europe and one of the principal architects of modern political philosophy. His writings transformed the conceptual vocabulary of sovereignty, political obligation, natural right, social contract, representation, law, liberty, necessity, and the relationship between civil and ecclesiastical authority. At the same time, Hobbes developed an ambitious materialist and mechanistic philosophy of nature, mind, language, and human action, attempting to construct a unified system of knowledge founded upon bodies, motion, nominal definition, and demonstrative reasoning.His intellectual career unfolded against the extraordinary political and scientific transformations of seventeenth-century Europe: the final decades of the Tudor monarchy, the Jacobean and Caroline periods, the English Civil Wars, the Commonwealth and Protectorate, the Restoration of Charles II, and the emergence of the new experimental science associated with figures such as Galileo, Mersenne, Gassendi, Descartes, Boyle, and the Royal Society. Hobbes's political philosophy was shaped by this world of instability, but his response was radically different from the classical and medieval traditions against which he reacted. Political order, for Hobbes, was not grounded in an Aristotelian conception of the naturally political human being or in a teleological hierarchy of natural ends. It arose from the rational necessity of securing peace among fundamentally vulnerable and competitive individuals.His most famous works—The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic, De Cive, Leviathan, De Corpore, De Homine, Behemoth, and the writings on liberty and necessity—form a body of work whose importance extends far beyond political theory. Hobbes was simultaneously a philosopher, political theorist, translator, classicist, historian, rhetorician, mathematician, optical theorist, theologian, and polemicist. His complete philosophical system was conceived as a tripartite science of Body, Man, and Citizen, although the order of composition and publication ultimately differed radically from the original plan.Birth, Family, and EducationHobbes was born on 5 April 1588 at Westport, then a separate settlement immediately outside Malmesbury in Wiltshire. The traditional story, preserved in Hobbes's own autobiographical verse, connected his premature birth with the panic caused by the expected arrival of the Spanish Armada. He famously wrote that his mother gave birth to “twins at once, myself and fear.”His father, Thomas Hobbes senior, was vicar of Charlton and Westport. He was not a major intellectual or ecclesiastical figure, and his career ended disastrously after a quarrel and physical altercation with another clergyman. He subsequently disappeared from the family's life. Hobbes and his siblings were therefore largely supported by his uncle Francis Hobbes, a prosperous Malmesbury glover and alderman.Hobbes showed exceptional intellectual ability from childhood. He attended the school attached to the church at Westport, where he learned Latin and Greek at an unusually early age. The tradition that he translated Euripides' Medea into Latin verse during his adolescence is consistent with the extraordinary classical education that prepared him for Oxford.In 1603 Hobbes entered Magdalen Hall, Oxford, where he studied within the scholastic curriculum then dominant in English universities. He graduated B.A. in 1608. The Aristotelian natural philosophy and scholastic logic taught at Oxford left a lasting negative impression upon him. Hobbes subsequently attacked the scholastic use of obscure terminology and abstract entities, arguing that philosophy should proceed through precise definitions and demonstrative reasoning rather than through verbal disputes concerning entities that could not be clearly conceived.The Cavendish ConnectionThe decisive event of Hobbes's early adult life was his appointment in 1608 as tutor to William Cavendish, later second Earl of Devonshire. The Cavendish family became the central institutional and financial support of Hobbes's entire career.His relationship with the Cavendishes lasted for more than seventy years. Hobbes served successively as tutor, secretary, intellectual adviser, and family associate. The connection gave him access to private libraries, aristocratic patrons, political networks, and the financial independence necessary for a life devoted primarily to scholarship.His association with the Cavendish family also enabled repeated journeys to the Continent. These travels were crucial to the development of his philosophy because they brought him into direct contact with intellectual cultures considerably more dynamic than the scholastic environment he had known at Oxford.The First Continental Tour and Humanist ScholarshipIn 1610, Hobbes accompanied William Cavendish on his first major European tour, visiting France and Italy. The journey exposed him to continental humanism, classical scholarship, and the changing intellectual landscape of early seventeenth-century Europe.During his early career Hobbes was not yet primarily a philosopher. He was deeply engaged with classical literature, rhetoric, and history. His intellectual interests included Thucydides, Tacitus, and other historians whose writings he interpreted in relation to questions of political order and civil conflict.He also became associated with Francis Bacon. Hobbes worked within Bacon's intellectual circle and is traditionally described as having served as Bacon's amanuensis and translated some of Bacon's essays into Latin. Their relationship is important, but Hobbes should not simply be regarded as a disciple of Bacon. His mature philosophy departed sharply from Baconian empiricism by emphasizing deductive demonstration, nominal definition, and mechanical causation.The Translation of ThucydidesHobbes's first major printed publication was not a philosophical treatise but a translation of Thucydides.The first edition appeared in London in 1629 under the title Eight Bookes of the Peloponnesian Warre written by Thucydides the sonne of Olorus. Interpreted with faith and diligence immediately out of the Greeke by Thomas Hobbes secretary to the late Earle of Deuonshire. It was printed for Henry Seile at the Eliot's Court Press.The translation was reissued in 1634, and later during Hobbes's lifetime in further editions, including 1648 and 1676. The work is fundamental for understanding Hobbes's early political thought. His Thucydides is not merely a linguistic exercise. The Greek historian provided Hobbes with a powerful historical demonstration of the destructive effects of faction, ambition, popular demagogy, and political instability. Thucydides consequently became an important intellectual precursor to Hobbes's later theory of civil conflict.The translation also reveals a characteristic feature of Hobbes's intellectual method: classical texts were not merely objects of antiquarian scholarship but instruments through which the political problems of his own age could be examined.The Discovery of Geometry and the New ScienceHobbes's intellectual transformation accelerated during his continental travels of the late 1620s and 1630s. A famous anecdote, recorded by John Aubrey, relates that Hobbes encountered a copy of Euclid's Elements and was struck by the demonstrative structure of geometry. According to the story, he initially encountered the Pythagorean theorem and, finding its conclusion apparently impossible, worked backward through the propositions until he understood the demonstration. The anecdote became central to the later mythology of Hobbes as a philosopher who attempted to reconstruct knowledge according to geometrical method.The exact historical details of the story should nevertheless be treated with caution. What is beyond doubt is that geometry and the idea of demonstrative science became central to Hobbes's mature philosophy.During his continental travels he encountered the intellectual circles associated with Marin Mersenne, Galileo Galilei, Pierre Gassendi, René Descartes, and other figures of the emerging scientific culture.His encounter with Galileo was especially significant. Hobbes developed a mechanical conception of nature in which physical reality consists fundamentally of bodies in motion. Human perception, imagination, appetite, aversion, and action were subsequently interpreted within the same general framework.Hobbes's mature philosophy therefore attempted to eliminate the sharp separation between physics, psychology, and political theory. Human beings are bodies; their mental operations are motions within those bodies; their passions produce actions; and political institutions are artificial constructions created by human beings to control the consequences of these passions.The Philosophical System: Elementa PhilosophiaeHobbes conceived his philosophy as a systematic science divided into three principal sections:De Corpore — BodyDe Homine — ManDe Cive — CitizenThis structure was intended to proceed from the most general principles of body and motion, through human nature, to the artificial body of the commonwealth.The intended logical sequence was therefore:Body → Man → Citizen.The actual publication sequence was radically different. Because of the English political crisis, Hobbes published the political section first:De Cive — 1642Leviathan — 1651De Corpore — 1655De Homine — 1658.This reversal is one of the most important facts in the history of Hobbes's works. The political philosophy for which he became famous was, in his own conception, only the final part of a much larger natural-philosophical system.The Elements of Law, Natural and PoliticHobbes's first systematic statement of his mature political philosophy was The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic, composed in 1640. The work circulated in manuscript among politically interested readers and was not originally published as a single book. Hobbes's manuscript tradition is particularly important: several manuscript copies survive, including copies preserved in the Cavendish collection at Chatsworth and in the British Library. In 1650, without Hobbes's authorization, the work was printed in two separate parts:Human Nature, or the Fundamental Elements of Policy and De Corpore Politico, or the Elements of Law, Moral and Politic.Thus the familiar title The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic refers primarily to the manuscript work of 1640 rather than to a contemporary authorized printed edition. A complete scholarly edition based on the manuscripts was eventually produced by Ferdinand Tönnies in 1889, an event of major importance in Hobbesian textual scholarship. The work already contains many of the principles later developed in De Cive and Leviathan: human equality, competition, fear, the state of nature, the laws of nature, covenant, sovereignty, and the necessity of an undivided political authority.Exile and De CiveThe political crisis of 1640 profoundly altered Hobbes's circumstances. Fearing that his writings and royalist associations might expose him to danger, he left England for France in late 1640.In Paris he entered the intellectual world surrounding Mersenne and came into direct contact with leading continental philosophers and mathematicians. The first edition of ** De Cive ** appeared in Paris in 1642 under the title Elementorum Philosophiae Sectio Tertia De Cive. It was a comparatively small edition. A substantially revised second edition appeared at Amsterdam in 1647, printed by the Elzevir press, and this became the principal early Latin form of the work.The importance of De Cive is enormous. It represents Hobbes's first published systematic exposition of his political philosophy and anticipates much of the argument later developed in Leviathan.The central problem is the relationship between natural liberty and political obligation. Human beings possess by nature the right to do whatever they judge necessary for their preservation. Yet universal liberty in the absence of a common power generates insecurity. Rational individuals therefore have reasons to seek peace and establish a sovereign authority capable of enforcing covenants.An English version appeared in 1651 as Philosophicall Rudiments Concerning Government and Society, making the argument available to the English political world just as Leviathan was being published.Hobbes and DescartesHobbes participated in the intellectual controversies surrounding René Descartes's Meditationes de prima philosophia. At Mersenne's request, Hobbes contributed objections to Descartes's Meditations, published in 1641 among the Objectiones and Responsiones. These became known as the Third Objections. Hobbes objected particularly to Cartesian dualism and to the conception of an immaterial thinking substance. His insistence that thought must be understood in relation to corporeal processes was consistent with his broader materialist programme.The disagreement was therefore not merely personal or terminological. It concerned the fundamental ontology of early modern philosophy: whether thought required an immaterial substance or could be explained through the motions of bodies.Leviathan: Composition, Publication, and StructureHobbes's masterpiece, Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Commonwealth Ecclesiasticall and Civil, appeared in London in 1651, printed for Andrew Crooke. The first edition is one of the most famous books in the history of political thought and in the history of European printing. Its engraved frontispiece depicts the sovereign as a gigantic human figure whose body is composed of hundreds of individual human beings. In his right hand he holds the sword of civil authority; in his left, the staff of ecclesiastical authority.The image is not merely decorative. It visualizes Hobbes's conception of the commonwealth as an artificial person constituted by the multitude but represented by the sovereign. The first edition is known as the “Head” edition, because of the distinctive ornament on its title page. A second, unauthorized edition, traditionally called the “Bear” edition, appeared with a different title-page ornament and was probably printed in the Netherlands. The two editions are textually significant: they are not simply typographical reproductions, and the first edition itself contains variations because Hobbes was in Paris while the book was being printed in London and corrected proof sheets were exchanged imperfectly. Large-paper copies of the first edition preserve some of Hobbes's later corrections.The textual history of Leviathan is therefore unusually complex. The 1651 English text cannot simply be treated as a single mechanically uniform state of the book.The Four Parts of LeviathanLeviathan consists of four parts:Of ManHobbes begins with an analysis of human nature. Sensation, imagination, memory, language, reason, passion, appetite, aversion, and voluntary motion are treated within a broadly mechanical framework.Reason is famously defined as a form of reckoning or computation, particularly the addition and subtraction of consequences.Human beings are fundamentally moved by appetites and aversions. There is no Aristotelian natural final cause directing human beings toward an objectively defined good. Instead, what individuals call good and evil depends upon their appetites and aversions.The famous proposition that human beings possess a “perpetuall and restlesse desire of Power after power” is therefore inseparable from Hobbes's anthropology.Of CommonwealthThe second part develops the theory of political sovereignty.In the state of nature, individuals possess extensive natural liberty but lack an effective common authority. Because individuals are sufficiently equal in vulnerability and capacity to threaten one another, insecurity becomes pervasive.The resulting condition is the famous state of war, in which there is no assured peace and no common power capable of enforcing agreements. Hobbes's solution is the creation of the artificial person of the commonwealth. An important conceptual correction is necessary here: the sovereign is not simply one of the parties to the social contract. The fundamental covenant is made among individuals, who authorize the sovereign to act in their name. Sovereignty is therefore not merely delegated government but the constitutive principle that creates the political person.The sovereign must possess sufficiently undivided authority to make peace possible. Yet Hobbes also recognizes a limit that becomes fundamental to later interpretations: an individual cannot be understood as obliged to abandon the most basic right of self-preservation.Of a Christian CommonwealthThe third part is one of the most controversial and important sections of Leviathan.Hobbes subjects Scripture, prophecy, miracles, revelation, ecclesiastical authority, and Christian political organization to his theory of sovereignty. He rejects the existence of an independent ecclesiastical jurisdiction capable of competing with civil sovereignty. In his account, the authority to determine publicly recognized doctrine belongs to the sovereign commonwealth.This is not simply conventional Erastianism. Hobbes's treatment of Christianity is considerably more radical because it is embedded within his materialist philosophy of language, revelation, prophecy, and political representation.Of the Kingdome of DarknesseThe fourth part attacks the intellectual and institutional forces that Hobbes believes have obscured rational understanding and weakened civil sovereignty. He attacks Scholastic philosophy, ecclesiastical power, papal authority, the doctrine of incorporeal substances, and various forms of theological superstition.The section is polemical, satirical, and deliberately provocative. It is also central to understanding why Leviathan generated such intense hostility among both religious and political opponents.The Latin Leviathan of 1668One of the most important facts in the editorial history of Hobbes is that the Latin Leviathan of 1668 is not simply a translation of the English edition of 1651. It appeared in Amsterdam in the collection Thomae Hobbes Malmesburiensis Opera Philosophica quae Latine Scripsit Omnia, printed by Joannes Blaeu. The Latin text contains substantial revisions, omissions, additions, and reformulations. Particularly important are the changes concerning theological questions, the Trinity, the interpretation of Scripture, and the relation between philosophy and theology.Consequently, the two versions must be studied as distinct textual witnesses to Hobbes's thought rather than as identical English and Latin editions. The 1668 Latin text is indispensable for reconstructing the final development of Hobbes's political and theological philosophy.Return to England and De CorporeHobbes returned to England in 1651 and continued to develop the philosophical system of which Leviathan represented the political culmination. The first section of the planned Elementa Philosophiae, ** De Corpore **, appeared in London in 1655 as Elementorum Philosophiae Sectio Prima De Corpore.The work contains Hobbes's systematic treatment of:logic and method;language and names;first philosophy;geometry;motion;matter;magnitude;mechanics;natural philosophy.For Hobbes, philosophy concerns bodies and their properties, and explanation proceeds through the generation and effects of bodies in motion.The work therefore provides the metaphysical and methodological foundation that Leviathan presupposes.De HomineThe second section of the philosophical system, ** De Homine **, appeared in 1658. It deals with human beings after the general analysis of body undertaken in De Corpore. Particular attention is given to perception, imagination, passions, human action, and optics. With De Homine, Hobbes formally completed the tripartite structure of the Elementa Philosophiae, although the political component, De Cive, had of course appeared sixteen years earlier.The resulting trilogy was therefore:De Corpore — natural philosophy and methodDe Homine — anthropology and psychologyDe Cive — political philosophy.Liberty, Necessity, and the Bramhall ControversyOne of Hobbes's most important non-political controversies concerned free will and necessity.His debate with John Bramhall, Bishop of Derry, began in the 1640s and continued through several exchanges. Hobbes's position was deterministic but not simply equivalent to the modern claim that human beings are passive machines. He argued that voluntary actions can be free in the relevant sense while still being causally determined. Liberty concerns the absence of external impediments, whereas necessity concerns the causal order through which actions arise.The principal exchange was eventually published in: Of Libertie and Necessitie (1654) and The Questions Concerning Liberty, Necessity, and Chance (1656). These writings are indispensable for understanding Hobbes's philosophy of action and the conceptual foundations of later compatibilist theories.Hobbes versus Wallis and the Royal SocietyAfter the publication of De Corpore, Hobbes became embroiled in increasingly bitter mathematical controversies, particularly with John Wallis, Savilian Professor of Geometry at Oxford. Hobbes claimed to have solved problems that mathematicians considered insoluble or extraordinarily difficult, including problems connected with the quadrature of the circle and duplication of the cube.Wallis responded with sustained and often devastating mathematical criticism. The dispute became personal as well as technical and continued for years.Hobbes's mathematical arguments were ultimately unsuccessful, but the controversy is historically important because it reveals the tension between his philosophical conception of demonstrative science and the rapidly developing mathematical practices of the seventeenth century.Hobbes and Robert Boyle: Vacuum and Experimental ScienceHobbes also became an opponent of the experimental programme associated with Robert Boyle and the newly founded Royal Society. In 1661, Hobbes published Dialogus Physicus de Natura Aeris, attacking aspects of Boyle's experimental investigation of air and the vacuum.Hobbes rejected the existence of a true vacuum and objected to the epistemological status of experimental demonstrations that did not, in his view, establish universal causal necessity. The controversy became one of the classic confrontations between two models of early modern science:Hobbes's deductive, mechanical, geometrical ideal of demonstration;Boyle's experimental, observational, and corpuscular methodology.The dispute later became historically important in the work of historians of science such as Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer.The Political and Religious Problems of the RestorationThe Restoration of Charles II in 1660 placed Hobbes in a complicated position. Charles II had known Hobbes during his exile in France, where Hobbes had served as mathematical tutor to the future king. The Restoration therefore did not simply destroy Hobbes's position at court. Nevertheless, Leviathan had alienated almost every major political and religious constituency: royalists regarded it as insufficiently royalist and dangerously supportive of obedience to whoever possessed effective power; Anglicans objected to its subordination of ecclesiastical authority to the sovereign; Catholics and Presbyterians alike rejected its attack on independent ecclesiastical jurisdiction.Hobbes consequently became increasingly vulnerable to accusations of atheism and irreligion. The controversy reached Parliament in 1666, when legislation concerning atheism and profaneness specifically raised Leviathan as a problematic book. Hobbes was not formally convicted of atheism, but the political climate made further publication of controversial works in England increasingly difficult.Behemoth and the History of the Civil WarsHobbes's history of the English Civil Wars, ** Behemoth, or The Long Parliament **, was written in the late 1660s, traditionally dated around 1668. The work takes the form of a dialogue concerning the causes and development of the English Civil Wars from 1640 onward.It is particularly valuable because Hobbes interprets the Civil Wars through the conceptual categories developed in his political philosophy: faction, religious division, competing claims to authority, popular rhetoric, institutional conflict, and the breakdown of sovereign power. Charles II refused to authorize publication. Hobbes's manuscript nevertheless circulated, and unauthorized European editions appeared.The first genuine edition was published posthumously, in 1681/1682, by William Crooke, Hobbes's publisher and literary agent. The surviving evidence shows that Crooke attempted to present a more reliable text than the unauthorized editions and that Hobbes himself had regretted the appearance of unlicensed versions.Behemoth therefore occupies a peculiar position in Hobbes's bibliography: composed during his lifetime, suppressed from authorized publication, circulated in unauthorized forms, and only properly published after his death.The Later WorksHobbes remained extraordinarily productive during his eighties.Among his later works were writings on geometry and mathematics, polemical responses to Wallis, philosophical problems, natural philosophy, theology, and history.His ** Dialogus Physicus de Natura Aeris ** appeared in 1661.His ** Seven Philosophical Problems ** appeared in the early 1670s.His ** Decameron Physiologicum ** was published in 1678, representing a late statement of his natural-philosophical interests.He also composed the ** Historia Ecclesiastica Carmine Elegiaco Concinnata **, an extensive Latin verse history of the Church, which was published only after his death.These late works demonstrate that Hobbes never abandoned the ambition to produce a comprehensive philosophy extending beyond political theory.Homer and the Return to Classical LiteratureIn his final years Hobbes returned conspicuously to the classical literature that had formed his youth.He translated Homer's Iliad and Odyssey into English verse. The Iliad appeared in 1675 and the Odyssey in 1675–1676, in successive publications. These translations are important for more than biographical reasons. Hobbes's entire intellectual career had been marked by an engagement with classical texts, from his early study of Greek and Latin to his translation of Thucydides and his later Homeric work. The translations also demonstrate that the elderly Hobbes remained engaged with questions of literary form, rhetoric, political history, and the relationship between ancient and modern culture.DeathHobbes spent his final years under the protection of the Cavendish family. He died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick Hall, Derbyshire, at the age of ninety-one. He was buried at St John the Baptist's Church, Ault Hucknall, near Hardwick. His death did not terminate the publication of his works. On the contrary, the decades following his death witnessed a continuing stream of editions, translations, polemics, biographies, and collected works.The Early Posthumous TraditionAn important early source for Hobbes's biography is the collection ** T. Hobbes Malmesburiensis Vita **, published at Charleville in 1681. It brought together several biographical materials, including Hobbes's own autobiographical writings, the biographical material associated with John Aubrey, and Hobbes's Latin verse autobiography. These sources established many of the anecdotes that subsequently shaped the traditional image of Hobbes: his premature birth during the Armada crisis, his precocious education, his discovery of Euclidean geometry, his continental travels, his intellectual controversies, and his extraordinary longevity. Because these biographies were composed within or close to Hobbes's own lifetime, they remain indispensable, but they must be treated critically. Later scholarship has demonstrated that some of the anecdotes were shaped by retrospective self-fashioning and by the conventions of seventeenth-century philosophical biography.The Eighteenth-Century ReceptionHobbes's reputation in the eighteenth century was deeply controversial. The term “Hobbism” was frequently used polemically to associate his philosophy with atheism, materialism, moral relativism, and political absolutism. Yet Hobbes's influence extended across precisely the intellectual traditions that opposed him. His theory of natural right, his analysis of the state of nature, and his account of political obligation profoundly affected the development of modern natural-law theory.Spinoza, Pufendorf, Locke, and Rousseau all developed political philosophies in intellectual environments in which Hobbes's arguments could not simply be ignored. Locke rejected Hobbes's absolutism but retained important elements of the contractual framework. Rousseau radically transformed the concept of sovereignty by relocating it in the collective people rather than in an individual sovereign. Spinoza adapted Hobbesian ideas of natural power and right to a different theory of political association and religious authority. Hobbes's influence therefore cannot be measured simply by identifying philosophers who agreed with him. His opponents were often among his most important intellectual heirs.The History of Hobbes's Printed WorksThe editorial history of Hobbes's works is unusually complex because several of his most important texts existed in different manuscript, English, and Latin forms. His bibliography can be divided into several major phases.The early humanist phaseThe first printed phase is represented principally by the 1629 Thucydides, followed by its reissues and by shorter literary and classical works.The political manuscripts of the 1640sThe Elements of Law circulated primarily in manuscript before being printed without authorization in 1650.The Latin political phaseDe Cive was first printed in 1642 and substantially revised in 1647.The English Leviathan phaseThe 1651 Leviathan became Hobbes's most famous English publication and generated an unusually complicated textual and typographical tradition.The systematic philosophical phaseDe Corpore (1655) and De Homine (1658) completed the planned Elementa Philosophiae.The Latin collected phaseThe 1668 Opera Philosophica brought together Hobbes's Latin philosophical works and included the substantially revised Latin Leviathan.The late English and posthumous phaseHobbes's later English works—including Behemoth, the mathematical controversies, and his translations of Homer—were published in circumstances ranging from royal censorship to unauthorized circulation and posthumous publication.The Major Collected EditionsThe first important large-scale collection was ** The Moral and Political Works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury **, published in London in 1750. It gathered a substantial selection of Hobbes's moral and political writings and included a biography.The decisive nineteenth-century achievement was Sir William Molesworth's collected edition.Molesworth published:The English Works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, 11 volumes, London, 1839–1845; and Thomae Hobbes Malmesburiensis Opera Philosophica quae Latine Scripsit Omnia, 5 volumes, London, 1839–1845.The English collection includes De Corpore, De Cive, Leviathan, Behemoth, the writings on liberty and necessity, the mathematical controversies, the Dialogue, Hobbes's Thucydides, and his Homer translations. Molesworth's edition remained the fundamental collected edition of Hobbes for more than a century. It is still indispensable bibliographically, but it is not a modern critical edition and does not incorporate the full manuscript and correspondence tradition.The Molesworth volumes were repeatedly reprinted, including the important twentieth-century reprint by Scientia Verlag, Aalen, 1962.The Modern Critical Edition: The Clarendon EditionThe twentieth and twenty-first centuries witnessed a fundamental transformation in Hobbesian textual scholarship. Oxford University Press's Clarendon Edition of the Works of Thomas Hobbes was conceived as a critical edition designed to replace the nineteenth-century Molesworth collection as the scholarly standard. Among its most important achievements is the edition of De Cive by Howard Warrender, which presents both the Latin and English versions.The Correspondence of Thomas Hobbes, edited by Noel Malcolm, appeared in two volumes in 1994 and dramatically expanded the documentary basis for understanding Hobbes's intellectual networks, publication history, and relations with other scholars. The most monumental achievement to date is Noel Malcolm's three-volume edition of Leviathan, published in 2012 as volumes III–V of the Clarendon Edition of the Works of Thomas Hobbes.Malcolm's edition presents the English and Latin texts in parallel and reconstructs the development of the text from manuscript through the English edition of 1651 and the Latin version of 1668. Its apparatus records textual variants and its introductory volume provides an extensive reconstruction of the composition, transmission, printing, and revision of Leviathan. It is now the indispensable scholarly edition of the work. Other important modern editions include:Ferdinand Tönnies, The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic (1889), which reconstructed the work from manuscript evidence;Howard Warrender, De Cive: The Latin Version and De Cive: The English Version (Oxford, 1983);Richard Tuck, Leviathan (Cambridge, 1991);Edwin Curley, Leviathan, with Selected Variants from the Latin Edition of 1668 (Indianapolis, 1994);J. C. A. Gaskin, The Elements of Law (Oxford, 1994);Bernard Gert, On the Citizen (Cambridge, 1998);and Paul Seaward's modern edition of Behemoth for the Clarendon tradition.The scholarly situation has therefore changed fundamentally since Molesworth. The modern study of Hobbes requires attention not merely to the text as traditionally printed but to manuscript witnesses, unauthorized editions, alternative English and Latin versions, authorial revisions, correspondence, and the material history of individual books.Hobbes's Philosophical LegacyHobbes's philosophical importance rests on the extraordinary unity of his system.His nominalism led him to emphasize the role of names and definitions in philosophical reasoning. His materialism restricted philosophy to bodies and their properties. His mechanics explained natural phenomena through motion. His psychology interpreted perception and passion through bodily processes. His theory of action linked desire and aversion to voluntary motion. His political philosophy then constructed the commonwealth as an artificial body created to secure peace. The result was one of the first genuinely comprehensive attempts to construct a modern philosophy without relying upon Aristotelian teleology.His conception of the state of nature became one of the most influential thought experiments in political philosophy.His theory of sovereignty transformed the vocabulary of political authority.His conception of the artificial person anticipated later theories of corporate personality and representation.His analysis of covenant and authorization became fundamental to modern contractarian thought.His theory of liberty and necessity remains central to debates concerning determinism and free will.His analysis of language, definition, and reasoning as computation contributed to the emergence of modern theories of semantics and rational calculation.And his materialist account of human beings anticipated, in important respects, later naturalistic approaches to psychology and philosophy of mind.Twentieth-Century ReinterpretationHobbes's modern revival began in large part with the work of Ferdinand Tönnies, whose Thomas Hobbes: Leben und Lehre (1896) helped establish systematic modern Hobbes scholarship.The twentieth century subsequently produced radically different interpretations.Leo Strauss emphasized Hobbes's break with classical natural law and interpreted him as a foundational figure in the transformation of modern political philosophy.C. B. Macpherson famously interpreted Hobbes through the concept of possessive individualism, relating his anthropology to the emerging structures of competitive market society.Howard Warrender emphasized the moral and normative foundations of Hobbes's theory of obligation.Richard Tuck situated Hobbes within the history of natural rights, international law, and early modern political thought.Quentin Skinner and the Cambridge School placed Hobbes within the precise rhetorical, political, and intellectual contexts of seventeenth-century England and challenged interpretations that detached his texts from their historical languages.Noel Malcolm subsequently transformed the field through his work on Hobbes's biography, correspondence, manuscripts, textual history, and the material history of Leviathan.Thomas Hobbes occupies a singular position in the history of European thought because he combined a radical theory of political sovereignty with a radical theory of matter, motion, language, and human nature. His political philosophy cannot be isolated from his natural philosophy. The commonwealth is an artificial body; human beings are natural bodies; passions are motions; reason is calculation; political authority is an artificial power created to regulate the consequences of natural human vulnerability.At the centre of the system stands a stark anthropological insight: human beings are sufficiently equal in their capacity to harm one another that peaceful coexistence cannot be taken for granted. Political order therefore requires an artificial power capable of making covenants effective. The originality of Hobbes lies not simply in his advocacy of strong government. His deeper achievement was to reconstruct political philosophy from the foundations upward. Instead of beginning with the traditional question of the best regime, he began with bodies, motion, desire, vulnerability, language, conflict, and the problem of collective security.The publication history of his works mirrors this intellectual revolution. The manuscript Elements of Law, the successive editions of De Cive, the typographically extraordinary Leviathan of 1651, the revised Latin Leviathan of 1668, the systematic De Corpore and De Homine, the controversial Behemoth, and the enormous nineteenth- and twentieth-century editorial enterprises all testify to the unusual textual life of his philosophy.Hobbes therefore belongs simultaneously to the history of political philosophy, metaphysics, materialism, early modern science, classical scholarship, theology, rhetoric, mathematics, and the history of the book. His works have never ceased to provoke disagreement because the problems they formulate remain unresolved: How much liberty can coexist with security? What makes political authority legitimate? Can rational individuals create binding obligations? Is human action compatible with causal necessity? What is the relationship between religion and sovereign power? Can political order exist without a common authority?Few philosophers have formulated these questions with greater systematic force. And few have left behind a textual tradition in which the history of the ideas is so inseparable from the history of their manuscripts, editions, printers, revisions, translations, censorship, and reception.

related_names.name: Descartes René
related_names.biography: René Descartes (1596–1650), known across the early modern Latinate Respublica Literaria by his Latinized name Renatus Cartesius, stands as the pivotal architect of Western modern philosophy and a foundational figure of the Scientific Revolution. Operating at the turbulent intersection of late Renaissance Scholasticism, early modern natural philosophy, and modern mathematical synthesis, Descartes systematically dismantled the teleological Aristotelian worldview that dominated European universities. In its place, he erected an unapologetically rationalist, mechanistic, and dualist philosophical paradigm. His philosophical project—characterized by the methodological deployment of radical doubt, the foundational formulation of the cogito, ergo sum, the defense of innate ideas, and the division of reality into thinking substance (res cogitans) and extended substance (res extensa)—reconstructed the parameters of epistemology, metaphysics, optics, and physiology. Simultaneously, his invention of analytic geometry synthesized algebra and geometry, providing the indispensable mathematical framework for early modern physics.Born on March 31, 1596, at La Haye en Touraine (a town subsequently renamed Descartes in his honor), he was the son of Joachim Descartes, a magistrate and councillor in the Parlement of Brittany at Rennes, and Jeanne Brochard, who died shortly after his birth. Raised by his maternal grandmother and a nurse, young René belonged to the noblesse de robe, an elite social stratum of legal administrators and royal bureaucrats. In 1607, at the age of eleven, he was sent to the newly founded Jesuit college of La Flèche in Anjou, established by King Henri IV and directed by Father Étienne Charlet. For eight years, Descartes underwent a rigorous humanistic and philosophical education. The curriculum at La Flèche combined classical grammar, rhetoric, and literature with a deep immersion in the Scholastic-Aristotelian curriculum, studying logic, natural philosophy, mathematics, and metaphysics via the commentaries of the School of Coimbra (Conimbricenses), Francisco Toledo, Pedro da Fonseca, and Francisco Suárez. While Descartes praised the institution for its intellectual rigor, he subsequently reflected in his Discours de la méthode that book-learning had saddled him with doubt and uncertainty rather than clear, demonstrable truth. Leaving La Flèche in 1614, he matriculated at the University of Poitiers, where he earned a baccalaureate and licentiate in civil and canon law in 1616, satisfying his family's judicial ambitions before embarking on an independent intellectual quest.Driven by a desire to study "the great book of the world," Descartes traveled to the Netherlands in 1618 to join the Protestant army of Prince Maurice of Nassau as a gentleman volunteer (soldat à la suite). This period marked a crucial intellectual catalyst through his friendship with the Dutch physician and natural philosopher Isaac Beeckman. Beeckman introduced Descartes to a brand of physical-mathematics that sought to explain physical phenomena through micro-mechanical models of matter and motion, sparking Descartes's early work on hydrostatics, acoustics, and falling bodies (the Compendium Musicae, dedicated to Beeckman in 1618). Following the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War, Descartes traveled to Bavaria in 1619, serving under Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria. It was during the winter of 1619, while stove-heated in a room near Neuburg an der Donau, that Descartes experienced a series of intense intellectual epiphanies and three vivid dreams on the night of November 10–11. He interpreted these visions as a divine mandate to unify all human knowledge under a singular, universal mathematical method (the mirabilis scientiae fundamenta). This methodological vision culminated in his unfinished treatise Regulae ad directionem ingenii (Rules for the Direction of the Mind), written between 1619 and 1628, which laid the groundwork for his intuitive-deductive method.During the 1620s, Descartes traversed Europe, visiting Italy and residing periodically in Paris. In the French capital, he entered the vibrant intellectual circle surrounding the Minim friar Marin Mersenne, who served as the central clearinghouse for European scientific and philosophical correspondence. Mersenne's network exposed Descartes to the debates surrounding libertinism, Pyrrhonian skepticism (popularized by Michel de Montaigne and Pierre Charron), and the emerging new physics of Galileo Galilei and Pierre Gassendi. Seeking total solitude and liberation from social obligations to systematically construct his system, Descartes relocated permanently to the Dutch Republic in late 1628. Over the next twenty years, he moved frequently between various Dutch towns and country estates—including Franeker, Leiden, Amsterdam, Deventer, Utrecht, and Endegeest—benefiting from the religious tolerance and intellectual dynamism of the Dutch Golden Age.Descartes's first major publication project was the ambitious natural-philosophical treatise Le Monde (The World) or Traité de la lumière, accompanied by L'Homme (Man). In these works, he constructed a fully mechanistic universe composed of a continuous fluid matter divided into three element types, operating solely via motion, impact, and spatial rearrangement under God's conserved laws of nature, completely eschewing Aristotelian substantial forms and occult qualities. However, upon learning in 1633 of the condemnation of Galileo by the Roman Inquisition for defending Copernican heliocentrism, Descartes prudently withdrew Le Monde from publication, as his own physics relied upon a moving Earth. Instead, he presented his natural philosophy implicitly in 1637 through a French masterwork published anonymously at Leyden by the printer Jan Maire: Discours de la méthode pour bien conduire sa raison, et chercher la vérité dans les sciences. This work served as a preface to three scientific essays demonstrating his method: La Dioptrique (explaining the law of refraction/Snell's law and eye anatomy), Les Météores (a mechanical account of weather phenomena and the rainbow), and La Géométrie. In La Géométrie, Descartes introduced the method of representing geometric curves through algebraic equations using a coordinate system, thereby inventing analytic geometry and revolutionizing early modern mathematics.The publishing history of Descartes's works reflects the burgeoning international book trade centered in the Low Countries and Paris. Jan Maire's 1637 quarto edition of the Discours was printed in the vernacular French rather than Latin to reach an educated lay audience beyond the university faculties, featuring elegant typography and woodcut diagrams personally supervised by Descartes. Moving to secure his philosophical foundation, Descartes authored his metaphysical masterpiece in Latin: Meditationes de prima philosophia (Meditations on First Philosophy). First published in Paris in 1641 by the publisher Michel Soly, the work featured six set objections gathered by Mersenne from leading intellectuals—including the theologian Johan de Kater (Caterus), Thomas Hobbes, Antoine Arnauld, and Pierre Gassendi—alongside Descartes's exhaustive replies. A second, revised edition was published in Amsterdam in 1642 by the famed printing house of Louis Elzevir (Elsevier), incorporating a seventh set of objections by the Jesuit Pierre Bourdin and Descartes's letter to Father Dinet. The Elzevir press became Descartes's primary publisher, producing elegant, widely circulated octavo and duodecimo editions that reached university professors, theologians, and scholars across Europe.In 1644, Elzevir published Descartes's Principia philosophiae (Principles of Philosophy), dedicated to Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia. Designed to replace traditional Scholastic textbooks in university curricula, the Principia synthesized Cartesian metaphysics, mechanistic vortex physics (explaining planetary motion through rotating celestial matter), and physical cosmology into a rigorous four-part system.Descartes's intellectual life in the 1640s was deeply shaped by his intensive correspondence with Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia (1618–1680), daughter of Frederick V, Elector Palatine. Elisabeth posed penetrating critiques regarding Cartesian dualism, specifically questioning how an unextended, immaterial soul could causally act upon a material, extended physical body (the mind-body interaction problem).Their dialogue pushed Descartes to refine his psychological and ethical theories, culminating in his final published treatise, Les Passions de l'âme (The Passions of the Soul), printed concurrently in Paris by Henry Le Gras and in Amsterdam by Louis Elzevir in 1649. In this work, Descartes analyzed human emotions as physiological processes mediated by the movement of animal spirits flowing through the nervous system, identifying the pineal gland (conarium) as the principal seat of the soul where mind and body interact.The dissemination of Cartesianism triggered fierce theological and academic battles. In the Dutch Republic, Descartes became embroiled in the "Utrecht Crisis" (1639–1643), where Gisbertus Voetius, rector of the University of Utrecht and a staunch Calvinist theologian, accused Descartes of atheist tendencies and subversive skepticism. A similar theological assault erupted at the University of Leiden led by Martinus Schoock and Reinerus Regius. Seeking refuge from these polemics, Descartes accepted an invitation from Queen Christina of Sweden in 1649 to join her court in Stockholm as a royal tutor and philosopher-in-residence. The harsh Scandinavian winter, combined with the Queen's demanding schedule requiring tutorials at five o'clock in the morning in an unheated library, severely compromised Descartes's frail health. In early February 1650, he contracted severe pneumonia and died in Stockholm on February 11, 1650, at the age of fifty-three.Following his death, Descartes's remains underwent a complex journey; his body was buried in Sweden, exhumed in 1666, and transported to France, where it was eventually reinterred in the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris. In 1663, despite the efforts of French Cartesian scholars like Claude Clerselier (who published Descartes's voluminous posthumous correspondence between 1657 and 1667), the Roman Catholic Church placed Descartes's works on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum donec corrigantur (until corrected), perceiving his mechanistic physics as incompatible with the Eucharistic doctrine of transubstantiation. Nevertheless, Cartesianism swept through European intellectual life, fundamentally reshaping European philosophy. His dualist framework directly inspired the rationalist metaphysics of Baruch Spinoza, Nicolas Malebranche, and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, while provoking the empirical critiques of John Locke, George Berkeley, and David Hume. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Descartes was elevated as the foundational symbol of the Enlightenment and the modern philosophical subject, securing his legacy as the indispensable initiator of modern epistemological inquiry.

academic_description: Two works in one volume, 12mo (132x75 mm). [16], 269, [3] pp. Collation: *8 A-L12 M4; [8], 80 pp. Collation: *4 A-C12 D4. Printer's device on the title pages. 18th-century calf gilt, lettering piece on spine, marbled edges and flyleaves (slightly stained and rubbed, joints repaired). Tiny stamp on the first title page (an initial L inscribed in a triangle). Very light occasional foxing. A very good, genuine copy.Rare first edition of these two works by the Dutch philosopher and theologian Lambert van Velthuysen, which were published separately but are often found together, not only because they were printed by the same printer in the same year, but also because they complement each other in bringing together the ideas of Hobbes and Descartes and helping to disseminate them in the Netherlands. Both works were included in Van Velthuysen's Opera omnia, published in 1680, but with substantially revised texts. The Epistolica dissertatio was also published in 1706 in an anonymous English translation.“[…] philosophy penetrated more deeply into Dutch society than probably anywhere else in Europe, and the new philosophies were often developed and transformed in ways of which their authors would never have conceived. Thus, even if the two most important and influential philosophers in the Netherlands were Descartes and Hobbes, one cannot ignore the many Dutch philosophers who to a great extent created the context in which these men were read. One of the most important, and the most prolific, of these men was Lambert van Velthuysen, and the Letter [on the principles of justness and decency, containing a Defence of the Treatise De cive of the learned Mr. Hobbes] is his most original and interesting contribution. Indeed, the interest of the Letter extends far beyond the purely philosophical, the text being to a considerable extent autobiographical in nature. It tells us much about the preocupations of a member of Utrecht's ruling class, and Van Velthuysen's desire to rationalize the minutest parts of his life provides us with insights into his most private feelings, making this as valuable a text for the study of Dutch seventeenth-century culture as it is for philosophy. A central preocupation of the Letter is the justness for a Christian of inflicting punishments, a question to which Van Velthuysen repeatedly returned. His main justification for it is the maintenance of social order, another central theme of the Letter along with that of maintaining one's place within the social order and the dignity and respect that go with it, all governed by the classical notion of decorum. But he seems to have discovered a basic foundation for such arguments in the Hobbesian principle of self-preservation, and like Hobbes he uses it to reformulate classical and medieval natural law theories […] For Van Velthuysen, as for Hobbes, man was primarily driven by the instinct for self-preservation, and he formed socities not for mutual benefit but for his own well-being. From this principle, it was claimed, it was possible to derive all of natural law and thus the basis of morality. Unlike Hobbes, however, Van Velthuysen derives the entire foundation of natural law from first principles. The social order is superimposed upon a world order instituted by God that is directed towards the particular end that God had in mind when creating the universe, what is nowadays usually referred to as Intelligent Design and which was used to justify so much of the new philosophy and science of the seventeenth century. In the present case, it is the source of a natural revelation that shows us how we ought to behave, and the lesson it teaches us is that we have such a strong desire for self-preservation that it is God's will that we do everything in our power to maintain our well-being. Self-preservation is thus transformed from a basic right, which we are free to exercise, into the fundamental law of nature that is, in a sense, God's commandment. This is the unifying principle of the work by means of which Van Velthuysen works out his entire moral philosophy. On the way, we are given insights into his views on sex and drugs, marriage and divorce, his duties as a physician, and general deportment that are frequently somewhat naïve in their candour […][T]he Epistolica dissertatio exists in two different versions: the first edition of 1651, published anonymously as an individual treatise, and the second, amended edition produced for Van Velthuysen's Opera omnia of 1680 […] The 1680 edition, for obvious reasons, can be viewed as the definitive version of the work, the changes that were made reflecting the development of Van Velthuysen's thought during the intervening thirty years […] Conversely, the 1651 edition has the merit of being the original version of the work, written in answer to questions that were pressing at the time rather than to fit into a volume of collected works. In addition, as has already been stated, much of the interest of the text stems from the fact that it not only presents Van Velthuysen's ideas but is also an important landmark in the Dutch reception of Hobbes, and specifically of De Cive, a process that was at its height in the late 164os and early 165os. The first edition fully belongs to this process and presents an undiluted response to Hobbes's political thought, for the most part favourable. The reception of Hobbes in the Netherlands was in turn conditioned by the reaction to new philosophies in general and to Descartes in particular, and the 1651 edition of the Epistolica dissertatio represents one of the first publications by a philosopher who was favourably inclined towards Cartesianism, even if the work can only be called Cartesian in a very limited sense. On balance, therefore, the 1651 edition appears altogether more interesting from an historical perspective. Furthermore, the 1651 edition also contains the lengthy Probatio ex scriptura sacra [pp. 213-269], representing about one fifth of the entire text, that was totally suppressed in 1680, presumably because it would have had to have been entirely rewritten” (M. de Mowbray, Translator's preface, in: L. Velthuysen, “A Letter on the principles of justness and decency, containing a Defence of the Treatise De cive of the learned Mr. Hobbes”, Leiden, 2013, pp. XI-XIII and XVI-XVII).“Lambert van Velthuysen's Epistolica dissertatio de principis Justi et Decori, continens apologiam pro tractatu clarissimi Hobbaei, De Cive, published anonymously in 1651, marked a decisive moment in the English philosopher's influence in the Netherlands: for the first time, the text recommended adopting an openly favourable position with regard to Hobbes's thought […] Van Velthuysen nevertheless had a genuine interest in De Cive and Cartesian philosophy, which meant that his commitment was destined to open up a new philosophical perspective: one that brought Cartesianism and politics closer together by applying the theory of passions to the definition of the best government. Spinoza, a major figure, also joined that trend, as did republican authors such as the brothers Johan and Pieter de la Court […] The ‘Dissertation in the form of a letter', written in support of De Cive, was among the first titles that Van Velthuysen published. In this he announced his intention to defend Hobbes's ‘principles' and stated that he fully subscribed to his ‘moral doctrine'. Such an undertaking was not lacking in boldness, as Van Velthuysen was well aware, taking the opportunity to praise intellectual courage at the same time: ‘Who ever attempted a great and memorable deed without risk?' (p. 66). Above all, he seems to have been one of those best placed -on account of his education, his position and his friendships- to provide a Dutch perspective on certain aspects of Hobbesian philosophy. His ties with Spinoza, even though they subsequently loosened, linked him with the enlightened milieu of Spinoza's ‘circle': in addition, whereas the Aristotelian tradition, in the academic world, still retained an idea of politics that was far removed from the actual situation in the Netherlands at the time, Van Velthuysen -in his functions as an alderman, a representative of civil power to consistories, and a doctor- found himself directly confronted with the pratical, specific problems of civilian life. The Epistolica dissertatio, therefore, is an instance of a reception that was determined by several factors. At the same time, it qualifies as reception in the form of active appropriation. Rather than just faithfully transmitting an idea or presenting a system, Van Velthuysen's ‘apology' goes much further. In particular, it directly applies a principle borrowed from Hobbes -that of self-preservation- to current events. To use some of the terms used in a letter from Etienne de Courcelles to Van Velthuysen shortly before the Epistolica dissertatio was published, Van Velthuysen's work does not merely consist in ‘following in the footsteps' of the author he defends, but ‘in building on the foundations laid by Hobbes and successfully completing those that remain unfinished' […] The fact that Van Velthuysen was born in Utrecht placed him at the crossroads of the newest philosophical questions and the most radical Reformed orthodoxy. Utrecht university was the first, in the Netherlands as elsewhere, to teach Cartesian ideas […] Van Velthuysen belonged to the second generation of Descartes' disciples. He was the one who deliberately spread the discussion of Cartesianism beyond the university. In the first instance, he addressed a learned audience with his Latin treatise ‘A Disputation on the finite and the infinite', published in 1651 and written in defence of the Cartesian theories of movement, space and bodies. In his own way, he distinguished the physical and mathematical infinite from the divine infinite and, like Descartes, reached the conclusion that the theological and philosophical spheres were separate. In 1655, however, he published a series of pamphlets in Dutch in defence of Copernicanism […] [in which when] comes the question of the movement of the Earth, […] Van Velthuysen reaffirms the principal rules for interpreting Scripture that he had already presented in 1651 in the Epistolica dissertatio. In order to show that the new physics did not contradict the teaching of Scripture, he gives a few simple, precise rules for interpreting sacred texts. While the Bible's authority is absolute, it is the meaning and not the letter that is authoritative. When interpreting it, all the circumstances in which it was written (historical, stylistic, linguistic, etc.) must be taken into account. In the long ‘Proof from Holy Scripture' published as an annexe to the first edition of the Epistolica dissertatio [pp. 213-269], Van Velthuysen provides several examples in which this method is applied […] Van Velthuysen's conception of the interpretation of Holy Scripture placed him within the trend of Protestant rational exegesis, which tends to see the Bible as an historical text to which one should apply a philological approach comparable to that used by humanists on ancient texts […] Van Velthuysen's commitment to Cartesianism was, therefore, concurrent with his interest in Hobbes's thought. That remarkable concurrence reflected a movement that brought these two philosophies together under the same thought system, whether to criticize them or adhere to them. On the one hand, the Hobbesian ‘danger' could be compared with the danger that Cartesian philosophy represented, while, on the other hand, the first disciples of Hobbes found they were also the staunchest Cartesians -for example, the De la Court brothers and Spinoza. From his very first works, Van Velthuysen, a pioneer of ‘political Cartesianism', launched himself wholeheartedly into two of the major philosophical battles of the century -those around Descartes and Hobbes- and, in doing so, demonstrated those very qualities he had advocated at the beginning of the Epistolica dissertatio […] Despite being well aware that he would be subjected to violent criticism, he was nevertheless undaunted by the manner in which his text might be received […] It is true that he submitted his manuscript to Etienne de Courcelles at the same time as that of the Disputatio de Finito et Infinito; de Courcelles approved of his analysis of Hobbes and encouraged him not to allow his critics to distract him, which was certainly a source of strength for him. Nevertheless, the enterprise carried a certain amount of risk, yet Van Velthuysen did not shy away from that […]The Epistolica dissertatio is presented as a letter addressed to an anonymous correspondent, whom Van Velthuysen describes as an ‘uncommonly learned philosopher, a man to whom I was most eager to recommend myself', but with whom -hence the reason for the letter- he is in disagreement: he ‘disagreed with me on certain points' (p. 57). Who might this correspondent be? […] one possibility is that it could be Descartes […] However, there is no concrete evidence to support this theory […] In terms of political ideas, the author of the Epistolica dissertatio was not an unreserved supporter of Hobbes. He was a long way from espousing all the ideas of Hobbes, whom he had nevertheless recommended, and seems somewhat caught between two worlds: the world of the traditional system of the monarchomachs, and the world of modern absolutism. Although the Epistolica dissertatio devotes a great deal of space to the question of magistrates -which seems to be the main objective of this discourse- it only deals with it from a particular angle: the right to punish. From Hobbes to Van Velthuysen, the perspectives remain very different. First of all, while the idea of a state of war is not absent from the Epistolica dissertatio, it is not the result of an anthropological definition of man, as was the case with Hobbes, but rather stems from a theological conception in which the nature of man is determined by the Fall. For Van Velthuysen, human history begins with the sin of Adam and Eve, and not with a war of all against all. Consequently, it is the very idea of an original sin that justifies the political institution, and it is the principle of self-preservation that stands as a basis […] The political state is part of the divine plan and belongs to the reordering of nature after original sin. It then derives from the principle of self-preservation […] He categorically excludes the need for a complete transfer of the rights of individuals to the sovereign, and supports the existence of a contract between the people and the sovereign in order to safeguard the subjects' right to resistance in the event of tyranny […] The Epistolica dissertatio takes great care to define the rules of a free society by setting out two opposing influences: that of Calvinist thought, with Beza and Junius Brutus -the theorization of a subject's to resist the monarch to its highest level-, and that of Hobbes, who entrusted political omnipotence with the task of guaranteeing civil piece. Although this attept does not achieve the systematic character of a true theory, it nevertheless has the great merit of introducing what is known as Cartesian politics […]” (C. Secretan, Introduction, in: L. Velthuysen, op. cit., pp. 1-3, 8-13, 17, and 31-36).First discussed mainly at the University of Utrecht in the 1640s, Dutch Cartesianism took the form of an academic philosophy only in the 1650s at the University of Leiden, where Cartesian ideas were first introduced by A. Heereboord (1614-1659) and where they soon collided or mixed with Hobbes's philosophy, which was also rapidly gaining ground. The Cartesian philosopher Johannes “De Raey may also have been reacting to Van Velthuysen, who published a defence of Hobbes's De cive and provided a combination of Descartes's and Hobbes's philosophy in the disputation De finito et infinito as well as ‘political' Hobbesians such as the De la Court brothers and Abraham van Berkel (the translator of Leviathan into Dutch), as he would note, in his Cogitata [de interpretatione, 1692], the ‘replacement' of meaning in words such as good or bad, such that what is good by nature is replaced with a conventional good, as it is defined in Hobbes Leviathan and De cive. The dissemination of Hobbes's thought may explain, in part, the development of foundationalism by De Raey, as he would counter the erosion of Descartes's metaphysics - and the application of philosophy to politics” (A. Strazzoni, Dutch Cartesianism and the birth of philosophy of science: from Regius to ‘s Gravesande, Berlin-Boston, 2019, pp. 109-110).Little is known about Van Velthuysen's life. Born into a patrician family in Utrecht in 1622, he studied theology in Geneva and Utrecht and graduated in philosophy from the University of Utrecht in 1644. In 1647 he enrolled as a medical student at the University of Leiden. After graduating in 1650, he settled permanently in Utrecht as a doctor. Like other Cartesians from Utrecht (F. Burman, J.G. Graevius, L. Wolzogen), he was a member of the “College der Savanten”, a kind of academy that met weekly to discuss new books and ideas. In 1665 Van Velthuysen became governor of the West India Company and in 1667 alderman of Utrecht. From 1669 he had the role of ‘political commissioner' to the consistory of the Church of Utrecht. He died in Utrecht in 1685 (cf. Secretan, op. cit., pp. 6-8).“During the 1650s and 60s, Lambert van Velthuysen (1622-85) was regarded by his contemporaries as a radical author, ready to embrace the two major new philosophies, namely those of Descartes and Hobbes, and in the view of Voetians. What made him a particularly dangerous representative of the novatores was his willingness to present these novelties not only in Latin, but also in Dutch. The fact is, however, that by the end of the 1660s Van Velthuysen, instead of representing the most radical wing of Dutch Cartesianism, decided to attack both Lodewijk Meyer and Spinoza, since he felt these authors were indeed subversive in the way in which they turned Cartesianism into an essentially atheist and materialist philosophy that threatened to undermine the very basis of Christian society. But after having accused Spinoza, in a brief but exciting exchange of letters that took place in 1671, of teaching sheer atheism , the two seem to have become quite friendly” (W. Van Bunge, H. Krop, B. Leeuwenburgh, and P. Schuurman, eds., Dictionary of Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century Dutch Philosophers, Bristol, 2003, s.v.).

authors.name: Giraldi Cinzio Giovanni Battista
authors.biography: Giovanni Battista Giraldi Cinzio (born late November 1504 in Ferrara; died December 30, 1573 in Ferrara), also frequently styled in Latinized and European vernacular variants as Cinthio, Cyntio, or Cinthius, stands as one of the most prominent humanists, dramatists, literary theorists, and prose writers of the Italian High and Late Renaissance (Cinquecento). Operating at the intellectual crossroads of the Este court in Ferrara, the Studio Ferrarese, and the flourishing print networks of Venice and Piedmont, Giraldi Cinzio decisively reshaped early modern European literature. His polymathic career bridged medical philosophy and courtly diplomacy, while his creative output laid the theoretical and formal foundations for Senecan vernacular tragedy, the pastoral satyr play, and the Counter-Reformation novella. Beyond the Italian peninsula, his narrative creations served as primary source material for Elizabethan and Jacobean playwrights, most notably William Shakespeare, who adapted Giraldi’s prose tales into the dramatic masterworks Othello and Measure for Measure.Born into a respected citizen family of Ferrara during the reign of Duke Alfonso I d'Este, Giraldi received a rigorous humanist and scientific education at the University of Ferrara (the Studio Ferrarese). His formative years were marked by close contact with leading intellectual figures of the northern Italian Renaissance, most notably the distinguished humanist polymath Celio Calcagnini and the eminent philologist Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, a relative whose scholarly circles exposed young Giovanni Battista to classical philology, rhetoric, and Greek literature. Concurrently, Giraldi pursued higher studies in natural philosophy and Galenic medicine under the guidance of Ludovico Bonaccioli, earning his doctorate in philosophy and medicine in 1531. Immediately following his graduation, Giraldi was appointed to the faculty of philosophy at the University of Ferrara, where for over a decade he delivered lectures on Aristotle’s Physics and Nicomachean Ethics. This deep grounding in Aristotelian philosophy and natural medicine profoundly shaped his later literary theory, imparting a systematic, empirical, and psychological rigor to his analysis of human passions, moral agency, and dramatic catharsis.Giraldi’s formal entry into the political and cultural life of the Ferrarese court occurred under Duke Ercole II d'Este. Following the death of Celio Calcagnini in 1541, Giraldi succeeded his master as the principal professor of rhetoric at the university and was increasingly entrusted with diplomatic and administrative responsibilities by the ducal house. In 1547, Ercole II appointed Giraldi as official Ducal Secretary (segretario ducale), a prestigious post he held until the Duke’s death in 1559. During these decades, Giraldi was at the center of court spectacle, theatrical production, and ideological debates. It was within this vibrant courtly setting that Giraldi executed his historic dramaturgical breakthrough with the tragedy Orbecche, written in 1541 and performed with sensational success in Giraldi’s private residence in Ferrara before Duke Ercole II, Cardinals, and foreign dignitaries. Featuring original stage music composed by Alfonso della Viola and stage designs by Girolamo da Carpi, Orbecche was the first regular vernacular tragedy constructed on the Senecan model to be brought to the physical stage in early modern Europe. Rejecting the restraint of classical Greek tragedy in favor of Seneca’s chilling atmosphere of horror, ghost apparitions, psychological cruelty, and graphic violence, Giraldi inaugurated a genre of dramatic moral shock that would echo across European theatre for over a century.Giraldi’s dramatic experiments expanded throughout the 1540s and 1550s to encompass a broad tragic corpus—including Didone, Altile, Cleopatra, Gli Antivalomeni, Epitia, Euphimia, Arrenopia, and Selene. Crucially, Giraldi formulated the dramatic genre of the tragedia a lieto fine (tragedy with a happy ending), a structural hybrid that avoided ultimate catastrophe for virtuous characters while preserving tragic tension, thereby anticipating the development of modern tragicomedy. In 1545, Giraldi further demonstrated his genre-defining ambitions with Egle, designated as a favola satirica (satyric fable). Drawing upon fragments of Euripides' Cyclops and ancient descriptions of satyr plays, Egle represented an explicit attempt to revive the third canonical dramatic genre of antiquity, positioning itself as a direct predecessor to Torquato Tasso’s Aminta and Battista Guarini’s Il pastor fido in the evolution of the pastoral drama.Giraldi’s theoretical treatise, the Discorsi intorno al comporre de i romanzi, delle comedie, e delle tragedie (published in Venice by Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari in 1554), established him as one of the most original literary critics of the Cinquecento. Writing in response to strict Neo-Aristotelian commentators who condemned Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso for failing to adhere to classical unities and epic structures, Giraldi forcefully defended the legitimacy of modern genres. He argued that modern vernacular authors were not rigidly bound by Aristotle's Poetics—which had been written without knowledge of modern romance—and that genre conventions naturally evolve across history according to language, custom, and audience pleasure. This historicist defense of the romanzo ignited a fierce priority controversy with his former student and rival courtier Giovan Battista Pigna, who claimed ownership of the theoretical principles published in Giraldi’s treatise. The bitter quarrel with Pigna alienated Giraldi from Duke Alfonso II d'Este (who had succeeded Ercole II in 1559 and favored Pigna), ultimately forcing Giraldi to leave Ferrara in 1562.The subsequent decade of Giraldi’s life was defined by intellectual exile and mobility across northern Italy. He moved first to Mondovì in Piedmont under the patronage of Duke Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy, where he taught humanities at the newly established ducal academy. It was during his residence in Piedmont that Giraldi published his monumental prose collection, Gli Hecatommithi (or Ecatommithi, meaning "The Hundred Tales"), printed in two monumental octavo volumes in Monte Regale (Mondovì) by Lorenzo Torrentino in 1565. Framed around a group of Ferrarese noblemen and women fleeing the horrific sack of Rome in 1527 by sea toward Marseilles, the Hecatommithi comprises ten decades of moralizing novellas exploring themes of martial fidelity, tyrannical abuse of power, treacherous friendship, illicit passion, and ultimate divine retribution. Written under the shadow of the Council of Trent, the work explicitly rejected the perceived licentiousness of Boccaccio’s Decameron, adopting a grave Counter-Reformation moral purpose while supplying vivid narrative plots that achieved immense transnational success.Giraldi’s typographical history reflects his prominent status within the early modern Italian book trade. His long-standing collaboration with the eminent Venetian printer-publisher Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari ensured that works such as Orbecche (1543), Egle (1545), and the Discorsi (1554) were distributed throughout Europe in elegant, highly readable italic fonts decorated with Giolito's iconic phoenix woodcut emblem. When Giraldi migrated to Piedmont, he established a strategic partnership with the heirs of the ducal printer Lorenzo Torrentino in Mondovì for the princeps of Gli Hecatommithi (1565), before subsequent Venetian publishers (including Domenico Farri, Girolamo Scotto, and Cesare Arrivabene) reissued multiple editions across the late sixteenth century. In 1568, following an invitation from the Venetian Senate, Giraldi accepted the prestigious Chair of Rhetoric at the University of Pavia, where he taught with great acclaim until failing health compelled him to return to his native Ferrara shortly before his death in December 1573.The critical reception and legacy of Giraldi Cinzio are vast and multifaceted. Although nineteenth-century Italian romantic criticism (notably Francesco De Sanctis) occasionally criticized Giraldi’s style as theatrical and melodramatic, modern scholarship has re-evaluated him as a central figure in the transition from High Renaissance humanism to Mannerist and Baroque sensibilities. His theatrical innovations established the Senecan aesthetic of horror and psychological excess that directly influenced European drama, while his novellas provided the primary plot structures for major works of world literature. Gabriel Chappuys’s French translation of the Hecatommithi (Paris, 1583) and various English adaptations disseminated Giraldi’s narratives across northern Europe, providing William Shakespeare with the plot for Othello (derived from Decica III, Novella 7, telling the tragedy of Disdemona and the Moorish Captain) and Measure for Measure (derived from Decica VIII, Novella 5, recounting the story of Epitia and Juriste). Today, Giraldi Cinzio is recognized as a master architect of early modern dramatic theory, narrative fiction, and theatrical practice whose works continue to define the intellectual landscape of the Italian sixteenth century.
