publishers.name: Gadaldino Cornelio
publishers.biography: Gadaldino Cornelio (also frequently recorded in archival records as Cornelio Gadaldini or Cornelio Gadaldino; active fl. 1555–1560) stands as one of the most enigmatic yet pivotal figures in the mid-sixteenth-century Italian book trade. Operating at the turbulent intersection of the Venetian Republic’s flourishing printing industry and the clandestine evangelical circles of the Duchy of Este, Gadaldino exemplified the dual identity of the early modern publisher-merchant: an astute commercial agent on the one hand, and a covert vector for heterodox religious ideas on the other. During his documented period of peak activity between 1555 and 1560—a decade marked by the radicalization of the Roman Inquisition under Pope Paul IV (Gian Pietro Carafa)—Gadaldino facilitated the transit, printing, and sale of humanistic, reformist, and suspect theological texts across Northern Italy. His career highlights the porous boundaries between mainstream typography and underground book circulation during the decisive phase of the Italian Counter-Reformation.Born into the renowned Gadaldini typographical family originating from Modena, Cornelio inherited a heritage deeply steeped in both classical erudition and mechanical craftsmanship. The family line had already established a substantial reputation through Agostino Gadaldini, a distinguished printer-humanist active in Venice who collaborated with leading medical scholars and philologists to produce authoritative Latin translations of Galen and Hippocrates. Formed within this family milieu, Cornelio acquired a sophisticated understanding of typography, paper procurement, type founding, and, above all, the complex web of distribution routes that linked Venice—the undisputed capital of European typography—to the urban centers of the Po Valley, including Ferrara, Bologna, and Modena. His early education in the Venetian officinae around the Rialto and the parish of San Giuliano exposed him not only to the technical mechanics of the press, but also to the vibrant, international community of scholars, proofreaders (correttori), and itinerant merchants who frequented the lagoons.Gadaldino’s intellectual orientation was profoundly shaped by his intimate connections to the Accademia Modenese (the literary circle of Modena), an intellectual hub gathering prominent figures such as Ludovico Castelvetro, Giovanni Grillenzoni, Filippo Valentino, and Antonio Gadaldini. This academy became notorious in the eyes of ecclesiastical authorities for its intense engagement with evangelical theology, Erasmian humanism, and Northern European Protestantism. Within this environment, Gadaldino functioned as an indispensable cultural broker. Rather than limiting his activities to standard devotional or legal compendia, he mobilized his commercial infrastructure to circulate clandestine literature, including the works of Juan de Valdés (such as the Alfabeto christiano and the Ciento i diez consideraciones), Bernardino Ochino, Marcantonio Flaminio, and the foundational text of the Italian Reformation, the Trattato utilissimo del Beneficio di Giesù Christo crocefisso. Gadaldino’s press strategy favored small formats—most notably the portable octavo (in-ottavo) and duodecimo—which could be easily concealed within merchant bales of grain or textiles for transport past municipal customs officers and episcopal censors.The typographical landscape of the 1550s presented unprecedented hazards for independent booksellers like Gadaldino. Following the promulgation of the first Roman Index Librorum Prohibitorum by Paul IV in 1559, the Holy Office initiated a systematic crackdown on printers who omitted their names or utilized fictitious locations (nomen typographi). Gadaldino’s publishing practices during the years 1555–1560 demonstrate extraordinary tactical adaptability. To evade inquisitorial scrutiny, his press frequently resorted to anonymous imprints, neutral woodcut devices, or false attributions to foreign printing centers such as Basel, Strasbourg, or Geneva. Despite these precautions, the river trade routes along the Po River—where Gadaldino shipped crates of books disguised as general merchandise—came under increasing surveillance by the inquisitorial tribunals of Modena and Venice. Archival documents from the Sant'Uffizio indicate that Gadaldino was repeatedly implicated in the testimony of arrested reform sympathizers, who named his shop as a primary source for unauthorized vernacular translations of the Holy Scriptures and Protestant commentaries by Philip Melanchthon and Jean Calvin.The legacy of Gadaldino Cornelio remains central to modern historiographical debates regarding the survival and suppression of heterodox print culture in Renaissance Italy. Scholars of early modern book history, led by figures such as Delio Cantimori, Silvana Seidel Menchi, and Massimo Firpo, have identified Gadaldino as a key representative of the reforma clandestina—a network of printers and booksellers whose daring commercial enterprises maintained the flow of radical ideas across Europe long after official institutional channels had been closed. Though the intensification of inquisitorial prosecutions in the late 1560s ultimately dismantled the Gadaldini family’s distribution networks in Modena and Venice, Cornelio’s activity between 1555 and 1560 stands as a powerful testament to the resilience of typographical humanism and the vital role played by early modern book artisans in the defense of intellectual liberty.

related_names.name: Imperiali Giuseppe Renato
related_names.biography: Giuseppe Renato Imperiali (29 April 1651 – 15 January 1737) stands as one of the most formidable figures of the Roman Curia during the transitional epoch bridging the late Baroque Counter-Reformation with the early Italian Enlightenment (Illuminismo). Elevated to the Sacred College of Cardinals in 1690, Imperiali exerted an extraordinary influence over the temporal administration, diplomatic posture, and intellectual life of the Papal States for nearly half a century. As Prefect of the Sacra Congregazione del Buon Governo for over four decades, he oversaw the municipal finances, public works, and fiscal administration of the entire pontifical territory, operating at the very center of Roman administrative statecraft. Simultaneously, Cardinal Imperiali achieved international renown within the European Republic of Letters (Res publica literaria) as an unexcelled bibliophile and cultural patron. His private library, housed in the Palazzo Imperiali at Piazza Santi Apostoli in Rome and cataloged by the eminent scholar Giusto Fontanini in 1711, served as a vital institutional nexus for European humanists, antiquarians, theologians, and natural philosophers, embodying the ideal of the open, public-facing aristocratic library.Born in the Apulian fiefdom of Francavilla Fontana in the Kingdom of Naples on 29 April 1651, Giuseppe Renato was the eldest son of Michele II Imperiali, Prince of Francavilla and Marquis of Oria, and Brigida Grimaldi, daughter of the Prince of Gerace. The Imperiali family, belonging to the ancient Genoese patriciate (the Albergo Imperiali), had successfully expanded its economic and feudal influence into Southern Italy during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries while maintaining crucial ties to the Holy See. Young Giuseppe Renato was earmarked early for an ecclesiastical career in Rome under the direct mentorship and protection of his paternal uncle, Cardinal Lorenzo Imperiali (1612–1673), himself a prominent Curial prelate and Governor of Rome. Sent to the Papal capital at a young age, Giuseppe Renato received a rigorous education in canon and civil law (utroque jure) under private tutors, complemented by studies in classical humanities, theology, and diplomatic history. Following his uncle’s death in 1673, the young nobleman inherited substantial wealth and political connections, which facilitated his rapid integration into the prelatial ranks during the pontificates of Clement X (Altieri) and Innocent XI (Odescalchi). He entered the Curial hierarchy as a Referendary of the Supreme Tribunals of the Apostolic Signatura of Justice and Grace in 1679, subsequently obtaining the lucrative office of Cleric of the Apostolic Camera in 1683.Imperiali’s administrative capabilities came to full fruition under Pope Alexander VIII (Ottoboni), who appointed him General Treasurer of the Apostolic Camera (Tesoriere Generale) in 1689. In this role, Imperiali demonstrated remarkable financial acumen in reorganizing the Papal treasury, managing debt obligations (luoghi di monte), and reforming tax collection procedures across the Papal provinces. Impressed by his administrative efficiency and aristocratic pedigree, Alexander VIII elevated him to the cardinalate in the consistory of 13 February 1690, assigning him the deaconry of San Giorgio in Velabro (which he later exchanged for the title of Santa Pudenziana, and ultimately the presbyterial title of San Lorenzo in Lucina). Immediately following his elevation, Imperiali was appointed Papal Legate to Ferrara (1690–1696). His legation in Ferrara proved to be a masterclass in territorial governance: he actively mediated territorial and hydraulic disputes concerning the diversion of the Po River, implemented agricultural stabilization measures, modernised local grain reserves (annona), and checked the territorial encroachments of the neighboring Duchy of Modena and the House of Habsburg.Upon his return to Rome in 1696, Pope Innocent XII (Pignatelli) appointed Cardinal Imperiali to the presidency of the Sacra Congregazione del Buon Governo, a position he retained continuously under five successive popes (Innocent XII, Clement XI, Innocent XIII, Benedict XIII, and Clement XII) until his death in 1737. In this capacity, Imperiali became the de facto minister of internal affairs for the Papal States. He conducted extensive investigations into municipal corruption, restructured local taxation, enforced rigorous auditing standards for communal budgets, and promoted public works, such as the drainage of marshlands and the construction of roads and granaries. His long tenure was marked by an uncompromising defence of central Papal authority against local feudal oligarchies and municipal privileges, earning him both widespread respect for his impartiality and bitter enmity from regional aristocracies. Within the Sacred College, Imperiali aligned himself with the zelanti—the faction of independent cardinals committed to defending the spiritual liberty and administrative integrity of the Church against the interference of the European dynastic monarchies (Spain, France, and Austria).Imperiali’s political prestige reached its absolute zenith during the dramatic Conclave of 1730, convened following the death of Pope Benedict XIII. Supported by the zelanti and the imperial faction aligned with the Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI, Imperiali emerged as the leading candidate for the Papal throne. He secured a formidable consensus, coming within a mere two votes of the required two-thirds majority necessary for election. However, his uncompromising stance on Papal sovereignty and his past political disputes with the House of Bourbon led King Philip V of Spain to exercise the royal right of veto (exclusive), delivered formally by Cardinal Cornelio Bentivoglio. This diplomatic intervention blocked Imperiali’s accession, leading ultimately to the election of Cardinal Lorenzo Corsini as Pope Clement XII. Despite this bitter political reversal, Imperiali maintained his immense influence in Curial affairs, serving as a trusted senior advisor to Clement XII and continuing his oversight of internal Papal administration.Beyond his political and curial duties, Giuseppe Renato Imperiali achieved enduring historical distinction as one of the preeminent literary patrons and bibliophiles of early eighteenth-century Europe. In his residence at the Palazzo Imperiali at Piazza Santi Apostoli, he assembled the Bibliotheca Imperialis, a legendary collection comprising over 25,000 printed volumes and thousands of rare manuscripts spanning theology, canon law, patristics, classical literature, civil history, and natural philosophy. Unlike many contemporary aristocratic collections, Imperiali transformed his library into an active research institution open to scholars, foreign visitors, and young academics regardless of their social standing or political affiliation. To manage this vast repository, Imperiali employed the friar and scholar Giusto Fontanini as his domestic chaplain and chief librarian. In 1711, Fontanini published the celebrated catalog Bibliothecae Josephi Renati Imperialis Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae Diaconi Cardinalis Sancti Georgii Catalogus secundum auctorum cognomina ordine alphabetico dispositus (Rome: Typis Francisci Gonzagae), a monumental folio volume that became an indispensable reference work for librarians, book collectors, and bibliographers across Enlightenment Europe due to its innovative cross-referencing system and meticulous typographical descriptions.Imperiali’s salon at Piazza Santi Apostoli functioned as a primary gathering place for the intellectual elite of Rome and a key node in the international Republic of Letters. He was a generous protector of the Accademia degli Arcadi (in which he was enrolled under the Arcadian pseudonym Cleante Focide), sponsoring poetry recitals, antiquarian debates, and historical studies. He maintained an extensive correspondence with international scholars, including the Maurist monk Jean Mabillon, the historian Ludovico Antonio Muratori, the bibliographer Domenico Silvio Passionei, and the antiquarian Bernard de Montfaucon. Imperiali was also a major patron of the visual arts, commissioning works from prominent Baroque and Rococo masters such as Francesco Trevisani, Sebastiano Conca, and Tommaso Chiari, and expanding his family’s collection of ancient Greco-Roman sculpture. In matters of ecclesiastical scholarship, he leaned toward learned Augustinian and Dominican erudition, providing protection to scholars accused of rigorism or Jansenist sympathies, such as Gian Lorenzo Berti, while maintaining a strict orthodoxy in his public acts.Cardinal Giuseppe Renato Imperiali died in Rome on 15 January 1737 at the advanced age of eighty-five. His death was mourned across Europe as the passing of a statesman of majestic stature and an incomparable champion of learning. In accordance with his testament, he was buried in the Basilica of Sant'Agostino in Rome, where his executors erected a monumental funerary monument designed by the architect Paolo Posi and sculpted in polychrome marbles by Pietro Bracci, featuring an allegorical representation of Fame and Charity. Imperiali bequeathed his magnificent library in trust (fideicommissum) for public utility, ensuring that it remained open to the citizens of Rome. Although the collection suffered partial dispersal during the political upheavals of the late eighteenth century and the French occupation of 1798, the legacy of the Bibliotheca Imperialis and Imperiali's administrative reforms enduringly influenced the institutional and cultural history of the Papal State throughout the Enlightenment.

related_names.name: Von Hübner Alexander
related_names.biography: Joseph Alexander, Graf von Hübner (born November 26, 1811, in Vienna; died July 30, 1892, in Vienna) stands as one of the most enigmatic, versatile, and influential diplomatic figures of the nineteenth-century Habsburg Monarchy. Operating at the high-stakes intersection of Metternichian conservatism, Neo-Absolutist imperial administration, and late-nineteenth-century global travel literature, Hübner embodied the transitional statecraft of an empire striving to maintain its European hegemony amid the explosive growth of romantic nationalism, constitutional liberalism, and imperialist expansion. Best remembered in international diplomatic history for his high-strung ten-year tenure as Austrian Plenipotentiary and Ambassador to the court of Napoleon III in Paris—where he found himself at the epicenter of the diplomatic maneuvering surrounding the Crimean War and the outbreak of the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859—Hübner was simultaneously a acute political observer, an archivist-historian of the Papacy, and a pioneer of imperial travel literature whose accounts of North America, Japan, the British Empire, and East Asia provided late-Victorian and Bismarckian Europe with a sophisticated socio-political diagnosis of global modernization.The circumstances of Hübner’s birth and lineage were shrouded in an open secret that fundamentally shaped his social mobility and psychological outlook. Born in Vienna during the twilight of the Napoleonic Wars, he was formally recognized as the son of Josef Hübner, an imperial official; however, contemporary diplomatic circles and subsequent historical scholarship confirmed that he was the illegitimate son of the Imperial Chancellor, Prince Klemens Wenzel von Metternich, and Maria Antonia von Leykam (later Countess Beust). This patrician lineage, though legally unacknowledged, opened the gilded doors of the Ballhausplatz—the Austrian Foreign Ministry—to the young Hübner. Educated at the University of Vienna, where he completed rigorous studies in jurisprudence, state sciences, and classical humanities, Hübner was thoroughly steeped in the Restoration political philosophy of Metternich and Friedrich von Gentz. In 1833, under the direct protection and tutelage of Metternich, Hübner entered the Austrian diplomatic service, embarking on an apprenticeship that took him to key European capitals: as an attaché in Paris (1837), secretary of the legation in Lisbon (1841), and eventually Consul General in Leipzig (1844). In Leipzig, a vital node of the German Confederation’s publishing industry and liberal intellectual life, Hübner observed the rising tide of Pan-German nationalism and economic integration under the Zollverein, refining his analytical capabilities and political instincts.The revolutionary storm of 1848 represented the crucible of Hübner’s early career. Sent on a delicate special assignment to Lombardy-Venetia to assist Field Marshal Josef Graf Radetzky von Radetz, Hübner was caught in Milan during the violent insurrection known as the Cinque Giornate (Five Days of Milan, March 18–22, 1848). Taken hostage by the provisional Italian revolutionary government under Gabrio Casati, Hübner spent three grueling months in captivity, witnessing at firsthand the fervor of the Italian Risorgimento and the structural vulnerabilities of the Habsburg military apparatus in northern Italy. Following his diplomatic exchange and release, he rejoined the imperial court, which had fled the revolutionary violence of Vienna for the safety of Olmütz (Olomouc). Recognizing Hübner's formidable pen and strategic acumen, the newly appointed Prime Minister, Prince Felix von Schwarzenberg, placed him in charge of the imperial press department (Presseleitung). In this role, Hübner became the chief architect of the state’s counter-revolutionary propaganda, shaping the political rhetoric of the young Emperor Franz Joseph I and establishing the ideological foundation for the era of Neo-Absolutism.In 1849, Schwarzenberg dispatched Hübner to Paris as Envoy Extraordinary, elevating him to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the French Republic and subsequently to the Second Empire of Napoleon III—a post he held with distinction until 1859. Ennobled as a Baron (Freiherr) in 1854 for his diplomatic services, Hübner’s decade in Paris marked the zenith of his geopolitical impact. Navigating the treacherous waters of French imperial ambitions, Hübner played a decisive role in preserving Austrian neutrality and interest alignment during the Crimean War (1853–1856), culminating in his participation at the Congress of Paris in 1856. However, the rising tension between Austria and the allied forces of France and the Kingdom of Sardinia (led by Count Cavour) culminated in the dramatic New Year’s Day reception at the Tuileries Palace on January 1, 1859. In a deliberate diplomatic confrontation that reverberated across Europe, Napoleon III publicly addressed Hübner with the famous words: "Je regrette que nos relations avec votre gouvernement ne soient pas aussi bonnes que par le passé..." This public rebuke signaled the imminent French military intervention in Italy, which erupted months later in the devastating Franco-Austrian War. Upon his recall to Vienna following the Austrian defeat at Solferino, Hübner was briefly appointed Imperial Minister of Police in the short-lived Cabinet of Count Agenor Gołuchowski (1859); however, finding himself at odds with the emerging constitutional concessions and federalist schemes, he quickly resigned from active domestic administration.Hübner returned to international statecraft in 1865 when he was appointed Austrian Ambassador to the Holy See in Rome, serving until 1867. Operating in the shadow of the Papal States’ declining temporal authority and the imminent Italian annexation of Rome, Hübner formed close ties with Pope Pius IX and Cardinal Secretary of State Giacomo Antonelli, defending Habsburg ecclesiastical interests during the volatile renegotiation of the Austrian Concordat. Following his retirement from full-time diplomatic post, Hübner was elevated to the hereditary rank of Count (Graf) in 1888 and appointed a lifelong member of the Austrian House of Lords (Herrenhaus) in 1879, where he aligned himself with the High Conservative faction. During the final two decades of his life, Hübner transformed himself into an internationally acclaimed author and globe-trotting observer. His monumental archival study Sixte-Quint (1870)—a deeply researched, multi-volume biography of Pope Sixtus V based on unexamined state papers in Rome, Simancas, and Paris—established his reputation as a serious historian of early modern statecraft. Concurrently, his world travels resulted in widely translated masterpieces of travel literature, including Ein Spaziergang um die Welt ("A Ramble Round the World," 1871) and Durch das Britische Reich ("Through the British Empire," 1886), which provided granular, aristocratic diagnoses of American democracy, Meiji-era Japan, colonial India, and British imperial governance. His posthumously published memoirs, Ein Jahr meines Lebens 1848–1849 (1891), remain an indispensable primary source for the administrative and psychological history of the Habsburg Monarchy during its greatest existential crisis.

Full-page woodcut portrait of the author on title-page verso. Woodcut historiated initials. Text printed in two columns. Roman and italic types. Colophon and register at l. †3v. Errata at ll. †1v-4r. Late 17th-/early 18th-century stiff vellum, inked title on spine, sprinkled edges (slightly stained). Title page slightly soiled, outer blank margin of title-page verso reinforced with a slip of paper, occasional light staining and foxing, a good, genuine copy with a few old annotations in the index at the end.Provenance. Front pastedown with the armorial bookplate of Alexander von Hübner (1811-1892), Austrian diplomat, born as Josef Hafenbredl and an illegitimate child of the chancellor K. von Metternich (1773-1859) with the niece of the Viennese glass merchant Rohrweck. From the year 1833 he assumed the name Alexander von Hübner and served on several missions in Italy. During the 1848 Revolution he was taken hostage in Milano and later in the 1860s served as Austrian ambassador in Rome. On the title page stamp of Cardinal Giuseppe Renato Imperiali (1651-1737). Elevated to the Sacred College of Cardinals in 1690, Imperiali exerted a great influence over the temporal administration, diplomatic posture, and intellectual life of the Papal States for nearly half a century. As Prefect of the Sacra Congregazione del Buon Governo for over four decades, he oversaw the municipal finances, public works, and fiscal administration of the entire pontifical territory, operating at the very center of Roman administrative statecraft. Simultaneously, Cardinal Imperiali achieved international renown within the European Republic of Letters (Res publica literaria) as a bibliophile and cultural patron. His private library, housed in the Palazzo Imperiali at Piazza Santi Apostoli in Rome and cataloged by the eminent scholar Giusto Fontanini in 1711, served as a vital institutional nexus for European humanists, antiquarians, theologians, and natural philosophers, embodying the ideal of the open, public-facing aristocratic library. Imperiali’s library was sold in 1793.Rare first and only edition. This verse novel, which Giraldi had extensively discussed theoretically in his Discorsi (1554), was intended to be the practical realization of his ideas. Conceived in fifty cantos, it was published incomplete in Modena in 1557, with only twenty-six cantos, and was never republished. The Ercole is dedicated to the Duke of Ferrara and Giraldi's patron, Ercole II d'Este, who passed away in 1559 and was succeeded by his son Alfonso II, often mentioned as a child in the poem, indicating a complex, layered compositional process.Ercole is a poem overtly pro-French and pro-papal (in line with the Este foreign policy) and is closely linked to the tumultuous events of contemporary history. With this poem, Giraldi seeks to offer an alternative model to Ariosto's Orlando Furioso: moving from the substantial unity of action with a myriad of characters to the unity of the protagonist with a multiplicity of actions. In this sense, Giraldi's novel is an objectively experimental work compared to the codified grammar of the verse poem in the 16th century. Classical mythology, also criticized by Tasso in both practical realizations and theoretical pronouncements in the Discorsi dell’arte poetica (1564), becomes an alternative option not only to the chivalric material of Carolingian descent but also to the historical material that guided another significant mid-16th-century epic experiment, Giovan Giorgio Trissino's Italia liberata dai Goti. The centrality of classical mythology in Ercole allows for a coherent discussion of an "Ovidian antecedent," identifying in the Metamorphoses the only narrative poem that presents, due to the choice of mythological material and the "gratuitousness" of many episodes, structural and thematic analogies with Giraldi's poem. This work is constructed additively, without a criterion in the selection of episodes (beyond their plausibility) and without a true focal point, apart from the protagonist's figure.Giraldi, like all those who wrote narrative poems in the 16th century after Ariosto's masterpiece, intended to propose with Ercole an integral alternative model to the Furioso: this is demonstrated by his use of topical modules of "war poems" (the reviews and catalogues: some incredibly extensive) and moral allegories, typical of the modern poem (above all, Hercules at the crossroads, of probable Ariostean and Trissinian ancestry). Thus, alongside the overall experimentalism of the project, there are also explicit structural homages to tradition, indicative of an ambition, inevitably destined to be frustrated, to rewrite the coordinates of the genre in which his work is placed. Perhaps the most significant aspect of Ercole is the use of the prophecy module (already used by Ariosto and earlier by Virgil), which, in a poem with fluid material and essentially paratactic development, serves to construct a semblance of framework, creating overlaps of temporal registers and thus compensating for the sequential structure of the work. It is curious to note that when Giraldi makes historical prophecies, he is almost systematically contradicted by the actual development of the events to which he alludes. Consider the inevitable prophecy of a new anti-Muslim crusade, with Pope Paul IV invoked as the natural political and military leader: historical fate had it that Pope Carafa died in 1559, unable to materially pursue any such political and religious project. Another element of interest (also linked to a consolidated epic tradition) is the description of the exploits of a specific character (with a clear distinction between war exploits and amorous exploits). Those of Hercules, in the poem, are expanded and amplified to excess. On the other hand, it is only on a level of eloquent elaboration that one can express the creative freedom of an author who deliberately renounces, from the outset, to create an original poem in terms of inventio: almost all the episodes of the work are in fact codified by a robust literary and mythological tradition (with some significant exceptions, such as the Argonautic expedition, in which not Jason, but, understandably, from the encomiastic perspective that partly accompanies Giraldi's work, Hercules himself is the captain of the expedition).Beyond its objective limitations, Giraldi's poem represents an important chapter in the development, far from linear, of chivalric and narrative poetry of the 16th century (especially in Ferrara) and testifies, well beyond the intentions of its author, to the crisis and unrest in which the Este duchy found itself around the mid-century, on the historical plane. To unravel these knots (but not entirely, perhaps, and not without an acute personal crisis), we must await a non-Ferrarese poet, Torquato Tasso, who, by recovering the Ariostean model, but bent to his own needs and intentions, and certainly also keeping in mind the nearby Giraldian Ercole, will propose a new, formidable declination of the verse novel with the Gerusalemme Liberata (cf. D. Rasi, Tra epica classica e tradizione romanzesca: introduzione all’«Ercole» di G. B. Giraldi Cinzio, in: “Schifanoia”, 4, 1987, pp. 73-83; also R. Bruscagli, Vita d’eroe: l’Ercole, in: “Schifanoia”, 11, 1991, pp. 9-19).In the Biblioteca Ariostea, there is an autograph manuscript by Giraldi Cinzio (Classe I 406), containing three unpublished cantos of Ercole, along with numerous corrections and revisions (cf. C. Molinari, 'Correctio et rescritto in forma grande': note sul codice Classe I 406 della Biblioteca Comunale Ariostea (I Canti Undici dell’ “Ercole” di G.B. Giraldi Cinzio), in: “Studi italiani”, 2005, nr. 2, July-December, pp. 139-198). In it, the author states that the tenth canto was composed at the home of Ludovico Castelvetro (on the relationship between Giraldi and Castelvetro, see S. Jossa, Rappresentazione e scrittura. La crisi delle forme poetiche rinascimentali (1540-1560), Naples, 1996, pp. 139-252).G.B. Cinzio initially studied medicine and philosophy, then human letters, succeeding his master C. Calcagnini in the chair in 1541. During the duchy of Ercole II d'Este and in the years of Renata of France's circle, he was the undisputed protagonist of the Ferrarese cultural scene. In 1561, following a conflict with the dukes of his city, he went into voluntary exile first to Mondovì, then to Turin, and finally to Pavia. Among his students, we particularly remember G.B. Pigna, with whom Giraldi had a violent clash regarding the discourse on novels that Pigna published in 1554, arousing the ire and accusations of plagiarism from the old master (cf. G.B. Giraldi Cinzio, Discorso dei romanzi, edited by L. Benedetti, G. Monorchio, and E. Musacchio, Bologna, 1999, passim).The fame and influence of Giraldi were not limited to the Ferrarese environment but had a European resonance. He is credited with the European revival of Senecan theatre with its dark tones and cruelties, in open opposition to the Trissinian formula. The Orbecche, in particular, performed at the author's home in the presence of the duke in 1541, enjoyed considerable public success and constitutes one of the most successful Italian examples of Senecan tragedy (cf. P.R. Horne, The Tragedies of Giambattista Cinthio Giraldi, London, 1962, passim). In 1563, Giraldi published a collection of novellas, the Hecatommithi, which were widely disseminated throughout Europe and provided Shakespeare with material for Othello and Measure for Measure (cf. P. Cherchi, M. Rinaldi, and M. Tempera, eds., Giovan Battista Giraldi Cinzio gentiluomo ferrarese, Florence, 2008, passim).

authors.name: Weigel Christoph
authors.biography: Christoph Weigel the Elder (9 November 1654 – 5 February 1726) stands as one of the most prolific, erudite, and aesthetically influential copperplate engravers, art publishers, cartographers, and art dealers of the German High Baroque. Operating at the vibrant intersection of visual art, craft technology, and early Enlightenment encyclopedism, Weigel transformed the traditional print workshop into an expansive publishing empire centered in the Imperial Free City of Nuremberg. His monumental visual documentation of early modern society—most notably his seminal 1698 publication Abbildung der Gemein-Nützlichen Haupt-Stände (commonly known as the Ständebuch)—represents an unparalleled zenith in the historical cataloging of human labor, mechanical arts, and social hierarchy. Beyond his contribution to the representation of trades, Weigel produced massive illustrative cycles for sacred Scripture, heraldic compendia, architectural treatises, and cartographic atlases. In doing so, he synthesized the refined craftsmanship of the Augsburg printmaking school, the opulent courtly aesthetic of Imperial Vienna, and the sophisticated commercial distribution networks of Nuremberg and Frankfurt am Main. His career embodies the transition of the early modern printmaker from an anonymous artisan to an authoritative intellectual entrepreneur whose visual inventories shaped the empirical worldview of early eighteenth-century Europe.Born in Redwitz (now Marktredwitz in Upper Franconia), Weigel was raised in an environment shaped by Lutheran piety and regional craft traditions. Recognizing his innate talent for precise draughtsmanship and mechanical arts, his family arranged for his early apprenticeship in goldsmithing and copperplate engraving. To refine his technical mastery, the young Weigel traveled to Augsburg, which was then the premier capital of German line engraving, print manufacture, and goldsmithing. In Augsburg, Weigel immersed himself in the rigorous techniques of burin engraving, etching, and the newly developing medium of mezzotint (Schabkunst), learning to manipulate tonal values, light, and texture with exceptional delicacy. Seeking further professional advancement, Weigel traveled to Vienna, the imperial seat of the Habsburg Monarchy. There he gained direct exposure to imperial court art, worked alongside prestigious court goldsmiths and engravers, and absorbed the dramatic visual rhetoric of the Counter-Reformation and Habsburg triumph. Subsequent residences in Frankfurt am Main and Regensburg—the seat of the Perpetual Imperial Diet (Immerwährender Reichstag)—expanded his contact with foreign diplomats, scholars, humanists, and publishing houses. This period of itinerant training not only perfected his skills as an engraver (sculptor) and draftsman (delineator) but also embedded him within an extraordinary network of European intellectuals, political patrons, and book-trade agents.The pivotal epoch of Weigel’s artistic maturity began in 1698 when he gained citizenship (Bürgerrecht) in the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, establishing his independent workshop, print shop, and art commerce store (Kunst- und Buchhandlung). That same year witnessed the publication of his masterpiece, the Abbildung der Gemein-Nützlichen Haupt-Stände. Spanning over two hundred meticulously detailed copperplate engravings accompanied by moralizing poetic verses and prose descriptions—many composed in collaboration with the famed Augustinian preacher Abraham a Sancta Clara—the Ständebuch reorganized the medieval genre of the "Dance of Death" or "Estate Book" into a progressive, secularized encyclopedia of early modern professions. Weigel visually cataloged every stratum of contemporary society, from sovereign princes, scholars, and theologians down to paper-makers, type-founders, bookbinders, lens-grinders, compass-makers, and street vendors. What set Weigel’s work apart from earlier predecessors like Jost Amman was his obsessive technological accuracy: each plate depicted the exact tools, machinery, spatial layouts, and physical gestures intrinsic to the craft. His depiction of the printing arts, in particular, remains one of the primary historical visual sources for early modern typographic mechanics, press construction, and ink application. In addition to this socio-technical survey, Weigel achieved international renown for his devotional and biblical works, such as the Biblia Ectypa (1695) and the Passio Domini Nostri Jesu Christi (1693), which utilized intricate copper engravings to render biblical narratives with theatrical Baroque chiaroscuro, serving both as private devotional aids and artistic exemplar books.The operational scale of Weigel’s establishment in Nuremberg reflected the highest sophistication of early eighteenth-century print enterprise. Functioning simultaneously as engraver, editor, printer, and international distributor, Weigel constructed an integrated publishing house capable of handling large-scale visual production. He invested heavily in rolling presses (Kupferdruckpressen), imported high-grade paper from European mills, and employed a team of journeymen engravers, colorists (Illuministen), and letterpress typographers. His firm pioneered the commercialization of pocket atlases and cartographic collections, most notably the Atlas Portatilis (published in collaboration with his brother Johann Christoph Weigel and cartographers such as Johann David Köhler), which democratized geographical knowledge for the merchant class and grand tourists. Weigel actively competed and collaborated with Nuremberg’s cartographic titan, Johann Baptist Homann, securing imperial printing privileges (Privilegia Impressoria) from the Holy Roman Emperor to protect his copperplates from unauthorized pirating across imperial territories. His publishing catalog expanded to encompass architectural treatises by scholars like Leonhard Christoph Sturm and Paul Decker, heraldic compendia (Weigelsches Wappenbuch), and vast historical line-engraving series illustrating European wars, coronation ceremonies, and city views. Through his sophisticated commercial agents at the Frankfurt and Leipzig book fairs, Weigel’s engraved plates circulated throughout the Holy Roman Empire, the Dutch Republic, France, Britain, and the Italian peninsula.Upon his death on 5 February 1726 in Nuremberg, Christoph Weigel left behind an enduring intellectual and artistic legacy that fundamentally shaped the visual culture of the Enlightenment. His widow, Elisabeth Cecilia Weigel, along with his heirs and descendants, continued the operations of the Weigel publishing house for decades, republishing his famous copperplates and expanding his cartographic catalog under the family name. In the history of art and typography, Weigel is recognized as a master strategist who elevated copperplate engraving from a decorative secondary art into a primary engine of scientific, technical, and religious communication. His visual encyclopedism laid the conceptual groundwork for the mid-eighteenth-century projects of Diderot and D'Alembert, while his extraordinary technical precision provided an invaluable visual archive for modern historians of technology, material culture, and social history. Today, Weigel’s prints, emblematic volumes, and atlases are preserved as prized treasures in major national libraries, print cabinets, and antiquarian collections worldwide, standing as monumental testimonies to the intellectual brilliance and mechanical mastery of the German Baroque book arts.

academic_description: 4to (218x173 mm). Engraved title page and C numbered leaves printed on recto only with emblem illustration and Latin text in verse. The printed leaves are interfoliated with blank leaves presumably to allow annotations. 19th-century marbled boards (rebacked, slighlty worn and rubbed). Ownership entry on the title page “T.B. De Wassenaer, 1762”. A good, clean copy. Rare first edition, first issue (a second issues was printed much later in Nuremberg in 1766), of this series of 100 educational emblematic illustrations by Christoph Weigel, engraved by Jan Luiken (1649-1712) (41) and Casper Luiken (1672-1708) (59). The engravings, which are accompanied by a 10-line Latin verse in letterpress and were meant for the instruction of the yougth, illustrates natural phenomena and situations in human life, including: the sun, moon, and stars; the elements; the weather; geological formations; agriculture and horticulture; shipping and harbors; mining; times of day and seasons; various mammals, birds, and fish (including scenes of fishing and whaling); stages of life; health and illness; wealth and poverty; war and natural disasters.Christoph Weigel the Elder was a prolific and influential copperplate engraver, art publisher, cartographer, and art dealer. Operating at the intersection of visual art, craft technology, and early Enlightenment encyclopedism, Weigel transformed the traditional print workshop into an expansive publishing empire centered in the Imperial Free City of Nuremberg. His monumental visual documentation of early modern society - most notably his seminal 1698 publication Abbildung der Gemein-Nützlichen Haupt-Stände (commonly known as the Ständebuch) - represents an important stage in the historical cataloging of human labor, mechanical arts, and social hierarchy. Beyond his contribution to the representation of trades, Weigel produced massive illustrative cycles for sacred Scripture, heraldic compendia, architectural treatises, and cartographic atlases. In doing so, he synthesized the refined craftsmanship of the Augsburg printmaking school, the opulent courtly aesthetic of Imperial Vienna, and the sophisticated commercial distribution networks of Nuremberg and Frankfurt am Main. His career embodies the transition of the early modern printmaker from an anonymous artisan to an authoritative intellectual entrepreneur whose visual inventories shaped the empirical worldview of early eighteenth-century Europe.Born in Redwitz (now Marktredwitz in Upper Franconia), Weigel was raised in an environment shaped by Lutheran piety and regional craft traditions. Recognizing his innate talent for precise draughtsmanship and mechanical arts, his family arranged for his early apprenticeship in goldsmithing and copperplate engraving. To refine his technical mastery, the young Weigel traveled to Augsburg, which was then the premier capital of German line engraving, print manufacture, and goldsmithing. In Augsburg, Weigel immersed himself in the rigorous techniques of burin engraving, etching, and the newly developing medium of mezzotint (Schabkunst), learning to manipulate tonal values, light, and texture with exceptional delicacy. Seeking further professional advancement, Weigel traveled to Vienna, where he gained direct exposure to imperial court art, worked alongside prestigious court goldsmiths and engravers, and absorbed the dramatic visual rhetoric of the Counter-Reformation and Habsburg triumph. Subsequent residences in Frankfurt am Main and Regensburg expanded his contact with foreign diplomats, scholars, humanists, and publishing houses. This period of itinerant training not only perfected his skills as an engraver (sculptor) and draftsman (delineator) but also embedded him within an extraordinary network of European intellectuals, political patrons, and book-trade agents.The pivotal epoch of Weigel’s artistic maturity began in 1698 when he gained citizenship (Bürgerrecht) in the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, establishing his independent workshop, print shop, and art commerce store (Kunst- und Buchhandlung). That same year witnessed the publication of his masterpiece, the Abbildung der Gemein-Nützlichen Haupt-Stände. What set Weigel’s work apart from earlier predecessors like Jost Amman was his obsessive technological accuracy: each plate depicted the exact tools, machinery, spatial layouts, and physical gestures intrinsic to the craft. His depiction of the printing arts, in particular, remains one of the primary historical visual sources for early modern typographic mechanics, press construction, and ink application. In addition to this socio-technical survey, Weigel achieved international renown for his devotional and biblical works, such as the Biblia Ectypa (1695) and the Passio Domini Nostri Jesu Christi (1693), which utilized intricate copper engravings to render biblical narratives with theatrical Baroque chiaroscuro, serving both as private devotional aids and artistic exemplar books.The operational scale of Weigel’s establishment in Nuremberg reflected the highest sophistication of early eighteenth-century print enterprise. Functioning simultaneously as engraver, editor, printer, and international distributor, Weigel constructed an integrated publishing house capable of handling large-scale visual production. He invested heavily in rolling presses (Kupferdruckpressen), imported high-grade paper from European mills, and employed a team of journeymen engravers, colorists (Illuministen), and letterpress typographers. His firm pioneered the commercialization of pocket atlases and cartographic collections, most notably the Atlas Portatilis (published in collaboration with his brother Johann Christoph Weigel and cartographers such as Johann David Köhler), which democratized geographical knowledge for the merchant class and grand tourists. Weigel actively competed and collaborated with Nuremberg’s cartographic publisher, Johann Baptist Homann, securing imperial printing privileges (Privilegia Impressoria) from the Holy Roman Emperor to protect his copperplates from unauthorized pirating across imperial territories. His publishing catalog expanded to encompass architectural treatises by scholars like Leonhard Christoph Sturm and Paul Decker, heraldic compendia (Weigelsches Wappenbuch), and vast historical line-engraving series illustrating European wars, coronation ceremonies, and city views. Through his sophisticated commercial agents at the Frankfurt and Leipzig book fairs, Weigel’s engraved plates circulated throughout the Holy Roman Empire, the Dutch Republic, France, Britain, and the Italian peninsula.Upon his death on 5 February 1726 in Nuremberg, his widow, Elisabeth Cecilia Weigel, along with his heirs and descendants, continued the operations of the Weigel publishing house for decades, republishing his famous copperplates and expanding his cartographic catalog under the family name. In the history of art and typography, Weigel is recognized as a master strategist who elevated copperplate engraving from a decorative secondary art into a primary engine of scientific, technical, and religious communication. His visual encyclopedism laid the conceptual groundwork for the mid-eighteenth-century projects of Diderot and D’Alembert, while his extraordinary technical precision provided an invaluable visual archive for modern historians of technology, material culture, and social history (cf. J.E. Wessely, Weigel, Christoph, in: “Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie”, vol. 41, Leipzig, 1896, pp. 464-465; see also M. Bauer, Christoph Weigel (1654-1726), Kupferstecher und Kunsthändler in Nürnberg: Leben und Werk eines barocken Verlegers, in: “Archiv für Geschichte des Buchwesens”, 24, 1983, pp. 1-116; and K. Stopp, Die Graphikwerkstatt Weigel in Nürnberg: Bibliographie der durch Christoph Weigel und seine Erben verlegten Kupferstichwerke und Atlanten, Stuttgart, 2007, pp. 15-210).

publishers.name: Groulleau Estienne
publishers.biography: Estienne Groulleau (also documented in Latinized forms as Stephanus Groulleau or Stephanus Gruleau, c. 1501 – c. 1563/1564) stands as one of the most vital, prolific, and culturally influential Parisian booksellers and printers (libraires-imprimeurs) of the mid-sixteenth century. Operating during the vibrant yet politically turbulent reigns of Francis I, Henri II, Francis II, and the early regency of Catherine de' Medici for Charles IX, Groulleau occupied a central position within the intellectual and typographical epicenter of Renaissance Paris—the famed Rue Saint-Jacques. While he was active primarily between 1540 and 1563, Groulleau’s career encapsulates the Golden Age of the French Renaissance book trade, a transformative era characterized by the rapid expansion of vernacular humanism, the courtly popularization of chivalric romances, the translation of Italian classicism and architectural treatises, and the emergence of the Pléiade poets. Far from being a mere commercial merchant, Groulleau acted as a crucial cultural mediator who shaped the literary taste, aesthetic sensibilities, and reading habits of the French aristocracy and the rising urban bourgeoisie.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationLittle is known regarding Estienne Groulleau’s earliest years or precise regional birth, though bibliographical consensus places his birth in the opening decade of the sixteenth century (c. 1501–1510) within the Duchy of Île-de-France. His formal entrance into the guild system of Parisian booksellers occurred during the late 1530s, a period marked by strict regulation under the watchful eye of the Parlement de Paris and the Sorbonne’s Faculty of Theology. Groulleau’s definitive ascension into the elite echelon of the Parisian print market was cemented through a highly strategic dynastic marriage: he married Marie Janot, the daughter of the celebrated Royal Printer (Imprimeur du Roi pour the françoys) Denis Janot and his formidable wife, Jeanne de Marnef, who hailed from the illustrious De Marnef printing dynasty. This matrimonial alliance integrated Groulleau into an unparalleled network of Parisian typographers, woodcut illustrators, and privileged booksellers.Following the untimely death of Denis Janot in December 1544, Jeanne de Marnef briefly assumed control of the family workshop before marrying the royal bookbinder Étienne Roffet. Through his marriage to Marie Janot, Groulleau inherited a substantial share of the vast typographic stock, decorative woodcut blocks, criblé initials, and publishing privileges previously accumulated by the Janot-Marnef workshop. Establishing his primary shop at the sign of Saint John the Baptist (« à l'enseigne Saint-Jean-Baptiste ») on the Rue Saint-Jacques—directly across from the Collège de Cambrai—Groulleau inherited not only Denis Janot’s structural physical assets but also his prestigious aesthetic tradition, which synthesized French Gothic heritage with the refined, Italianate ornamentation pioneered by Geofroy Tory.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksGroulleau’s publishing catalog represents an extraordinary cross-section of sixteenth-century French intellectual and literary life. Primary among his achievements was his central involvement in the production and dissemination of the French translation of Amadis de Gaule. Translated from Spanish into elegant French prose by Nicolas de Herberay des Essarts, Amadis de Gaule became the quintessential literary sensation of the Valois court under Francis I and Henri II. Groulleau, inheriting the royal privilege to print subsequent books of the cycle from Denis Janot, issued numerous folio and quarto editions of the romance throughout the 1540s and 1550s. Through these editions, Groulleau helped construct the visual and linguistic vocabulary of French courtly chivalry, influencing everything from noble etiquette and military romanticism to decorative arts and courtly festivals.Beyond chivalric fiction, Groulleau was a monumental proponent of Italianate vernacular humanism in France. He produced landmark editions of Italian masterpieces translated into the French vernacular, most notably Antoine Le Maçon's monumental translation of Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron (Le Décaméron de Jean Boccace), Jacques Colin's translation of Baldassare Castiglione’s Il Libro del Cortegiano (Le Courtisan), and French renderings of Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso (Roland Furieux). Groulleau’s press was also deeply aligned with contemporary French poetic innovation; he published key editions for members of La Pléiade and associated poets, including Pierre de Ronsard, Joachim Du Bellay, Jacques Peletier du Mans, and Guillaume Guéroult, as well as emblem literature composed by the humanist polymath Gilles Corrozet.Furthermore, Groulleau played an indispensable role in the dissemination of High Renaissance architectural theory and scientific knowledge in France. Working alongside the brilliant humanist scholar and translator Jean Martin, Groulleau published fundamental French translations of Classical and Italian architectural canons, including Vitruvius’s De Architectura (Architecture, ou Art de bien bastir), Leon Battista Alberti’s De re aedificatoria, and Sebastiano Serlio’s architectural treatises. Illustrated with splendid, full-page woodcuts depicting classical orders, geometrical proportions, and perspective studies, these volumes served as foundational textbooks for French Renaissance architects, stonecutters, and patrons, directly influencing the architectural design of the Louvre, the Château de Fontainebleau, and the Château d'Anet.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationFrom a typographical and bibliographical standpoint, Estienne Groulleau was an innovator in commercial publishing strategy. Recognizing the immense financial capital required to publish lavishly illustrated folios—such as multi-volume chivalric romances and architectural manuals—Groulleau formed a famous, highly effective publishing association or syndicate (a early modern form of publishing cartel) alongside three other major Parisian booksellers: Vincent Sertenas, Jean Longis, and Gilles Corrozet. Under this collective arrangement, the four associate publishers pooled their financial resources to fund massive print runs. The resulting sheets were shared among the syndicate members, each issuing the final bound copies under their own individual imprint, title page cartouche, and publisher’s device (such as Groulleau’s sign of Saint John the Baptist or his mottoes).Typographically, Groulleau’s workshop reflected the crowning stylistic transition of mid-sixteenth-century French printing. Moving decisively away from the older Gothic types (lettres bâtardes) that had dominated early French printing, Groulleau adopted the elegant Roman (Antiqua) typefaces designed by the legendary punchcutter Claude Garamont (Garamond), paired with the fluid Cursive/Italic fonts created by Robert Granjon. His books are renowned for their impeccable presswork, balanced margins, and extravagant visual decoration. His pages frequently feature exquisite Renaissance woodcut frames, strapwork cartouches, grotesques, foliage, and historiated initials—many originating from the original woodblocks designed for Denis Janot and Geofroy Tory, alongside new woodcuts commissioned from top Parisian engravers working in the School of Fontainebleau style.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyOperating during an era of mounting religious radicalization in France—marked by the escalation of Lutheran and Calvinist heresy trials, the execution of printer Etienne Dolet in 1546, and the eventual outbreak of the French Wars of Religion in 1562—Groulleau maintained a carefully calculated professional trajectory. By focusing heavily on royal privileges, secular vernacular literature, classical architecture, courtly romance, and non-controversial humanist poetry, he successfully navigated the treacherous censorship regimes imposed by the Faculty of Theology at the Sorbonne and the royal edicts of Châteaubriant (1551) and Compiègne (1557).Following Estienne Groulleau’s death around late 1563 or early 1564, his workshop and vast accumulation of typographic materials were managed briefly by his widow, Marie Janot, and subsequently absorbed or redistributed within the wider network of Parisian booksellers, including Lucas Breyer and later generations of the De Marnef family. In modern analytical bibliography and book history—pioneered by foundational scholars such as Philippe Renouard, Annie Parent, Henri-Jean Martin, Jeanne Veyrin-Forrer, and Stephen Rawles—Groulleau is recognized as a cornerstone figure of the French Renaissance book trade. His preserved editions, highly sought after by institutional archives and rare book collectors worldwide, remain enduring monuments to the aesthetic brilliance, typographical mastery, and cultural dynamism of mid-sixteenth-century Paris.

publisher_data: Paris, Estienne Groulleau [for Jean Longis and Vincent Sertenas booksellers], 1555
academic_description: 8vo (169x104 mm). [11], 245, [1] leaves. Collation: ã8 ē4 A-Hh8. Lacking the blank leaves ē4, Hh7 and Hh8. Groulleau’s device on title page. Woodcut initials. Colophon on l. Hh5r, Privilège du Roi on ll. Hh5v-6v. Roman and italic types. 19th-century gilt hazelnut calf, spine in compartments with lettering piece, gilt edges, marbled endleaves, blue silk bookmark (part of the spine and hinges skillfully repaired). On the front flyleaf bookplate with the monogram “AMB”, on the title page barely readable ownership entry “Le marquis De P[…]” and library stamp “Ex bibliotheca J. Richard M.D.” (repeated on l. A1r). Contemporary manuscript notes on ll. Q2r and Q6r in a French hand. Worm tracks repaired on the lower blank margin of most of the volume only occasionally minimally affecting the text, title page slightly soiled, some occasional light browning, all in all a good copy. Extremely rare first edition of this collection of fifty-four moralizing stories, often rather coarse and spicy, nevertheless dedicated “Aux sages et vertueuses Dames de France”. The work is traditionally attributed to Antoine de Saint-Denis, a priest from the diocese of Mans, who seems to have been in close relationship with Marguerite de Navarre. “Par ses tendances come par sa forme littéraire, ce recueil appartient bien au petit cercle des contes de la reine de Navarre, et la personalité d’Antoine de Saint-Denis [curé de Champfleury] s’y encadre sans difficulté […] Il faut reconnaître que, en effet, si Marguerite d’Angoulême étendit largement sa protection sur le monde entier des lettres et des arts, elle se fit tout près d’elle un cenacle choisi de poëtes et de conteurs, et que sa personalité fut, pour ceux-ci, una cause vivante démulation autant qu’un centre d’attraction […] Par ces points de contact fréquents entre le livre de la reine de Navarre et le recueil de Comptes du monde adventureux se trouve corroborée l’opinion que j’ai déjà émise au sujet de la priorité des ces Comptes, priorité d’allieurs publiquement affirmée par les amis de l’auteur au moment de l’impression du recueil in 1555, et qui ne souleva de la part des contemporaines aucune réclamation” (F. Frank, Notice, in: “Les comptes du monde adventureux”, Paris, 1878, pp. XIV, XXIV and CXXVII; see also V.-L. Saulnier, Martin Pontus et Marguerite de Navarre, la Réforme lyonaise et les sources de l’Héptameron, in: “Bibliothèque d’Humanisme et Renaissance”, XXI, 1959, pp. 577-594). At the beginning of each story the author gives his short general moral lesson and at the end he addresses specifically to women to tell them what lesson they have to draw from the story. As in Boccaccio’s Decameron, the stories are told within a narrative frame, which is in itself a short story. The author is traveling from Provence to Savoy through the Dauphiné. Along the way he meets a gentleman who is accompanying his recovering wife to a thermal center. He joins them and their group, and during the journey - on horseback, during and after meals - they tell each others short stories to entertain themselves. Investigations about the sources of the stories were made by G.-A. Pérouse in his Nouvelles françaises du 16me siècle (Genève, 1977, pp. 139-155). Thus the main source of the stories is Masuccio Salernitano (c. 1410-1475), as at least thirty stories are drawn from him. Some single stories are adaptations from the Pecorone of Giovanni Fiorentino (fl. mid 14th cent.), from Heinrich Bebel (1472-1518), from Matteo Bandello (1485-1561) (cf. V.-L. Saulnier, Sur une nouvelle de Bandello et l’un des Comptes du Monde adventureux, in: “Bibliothèque d’Humanisme et Renaissance”, XXIII, 1961, pp. 347-350), from Le petit Jehan de Saintré by Antoine de La Sale (c. 1388-1461) (cf. G.-A. Pérouse, Les Comptes du Monde adventureux et le roman de Jehan de Saintré, in: “Bibliothèque d’Humanisme et Renaissance”, XXX, 1968, pp. 457-469), and from the Cent Nouvelles nouvelles (c. 1450s). The remaining stories, however, are original and “constituent un ensemble de récits inspirés par des anecdotes françaises et contamporaines, dont la note est très distincte de celle que rend le reste du recueil; ce sont des nouvelles, au sens propre du terme” (Pérouse, op. cit., p. 144). “[…] A.D.S.D. est écrivain et, de plus d’une manière, y fait preuve d’originalité. Tout d’abord, ses ‘histoires’ sont loin d’être tout “traduites”; et, lorsque traduction il y a, celle-ci est rarement simple traduction. Mais notre auteur se distingue encore par son recours à un récit liminaire (alors que les collections commerciales en sont depourvues, on l’a constaté), ou par le fait que ses emprunts s’addressent à la ‘deuxième génération’ des modèles italiens, enfin et surtout par sa constante volonté d’enseigner […] Tout cela étant, les Comptes du Monde adventureux ont bien une place entre Taillemont et Tahureau. Mais ils sont aussi liés de près à l’Heptameron […] Malgré la date tardive de leur publication, au bord des années de crise, les Comptes du Monde adventureux se rattachent assurément, pour une part, à la grande époque du genre. Les quinze récits realists qui s’y détachent ont leur place à côté des Nouvelles Récreations et surtout de l’Heptaméron: narrations ‘ancrées’ dans la réalité sociale quotidienne de ce côté-ci des Alpes, et exprimant ces réalités françaises dans des intrigues souvent fort reussies, ce sont proprement des ‘nouvelles’ au sens que nous avons voulu dégager au début de cette étude – éléments épars d’un authentique ‘Decameron françois’ ”(Pèrouse, op. cit., pp. 140 and 154). “La répartition des délits et du personnel criminel entre histoires comiques et histoires tragiques dans l’Heptaméron et Les Comptes du monde adventureux délivre un premier enseignement: les crimes les plus graves sont associés aux histoires tragiques tandis que les crimes bénins sont majoritaires dans les histoires comiques – ce qui n’exclut néanmoins pas la présence de délits majeurs. Dans ces deux recueils, les histoires tragiques accordent une place prépondérante aux crimes les plus graves tels que le meurtre, le viol ou encore l’adultère – ce dernier délit étant lui-même considéré comme le plus criminogène de tous, dans la mesure où il entraîne dans son sillage une multiplication des crimes les plus graves, de l’homicide au crime de lèse-majesté […] [D]ans la trente-quatrième histoire des Comptes du monde adventureux, l’adultère monnayé d’une dame avec un étudiant mène le mari trompé à assassiner son épouse et dans la cinquantième histoire, l’adultère d’une dame avec un écuyer la conduit à commettre un homicide, celui d’un enfant innocent. De manière générale, les pulsions sexuelles et les malheurs liés à l’amour et au désir sont au cœur des histoires tragiques où désir et violence sont étroitement associés […] (dans Les Comptes du monde adventureux, sur onze histoires criminelles trois tragiques, un mariage clandestin, cinq relations sexuelles illicites et quatre adultères peuvent être comptabilisés): l’amour est mortifère et malheureux dans la peinture tragique […] Cependant, contrairement à ce qui se passe dans l’Heptaméron, les histoires comiques réservent dans Les Comptes du monde adventureux une place importante aux délits mineurs, vols, duperies et autres bons tours, dont les victimes provoquent le rire, et non la compassion. Ce personnel criminel professionnel est représentatif de la perspective facétieuse et satirique, tandis qu’il est le plus souvent absent des histoires tragiques ou y apparaît au second plan. La satire des milieux marchands et artisans, dans la tradition des fabliaux, est présente dans la onzième histoire où un couturier voleur se fait meunier et apprend à être un peu larron pour éviter d’être réduit à la mendicité ; les moines malhonnêtes sont mis en scène dans la dixneuvième histoire et dans la vingt-deuxième, alors que les membres du clergé apparaissent au contraire comme des proies faciles pour les voleurs du fait même de leur cupidité et de leur soif d’argent dans les trente-troisième et quarante-sixième histoires. Ces figures criminelles sont héritières de la tradition satirique et se caractérisent par la ruse, la finesse, la duplicité dont elles font preuve pour mystifier leurs victimes. La vingt-quatrième histoire est très représentative, puisque le menu larcin accompli par les protagonistes est assimilé à une plaisanterie, une raillerie permettant de rire aux dépens d’un personnage respecté, un docteur ès lois de la ville de Boulogne: l’identité de la victime, un notable, représentant de la justice ou membre du clergé, contribue beaucoup à faire ressortir le sel des bons tours accomplis par des personnages mi-voleurs mi-plaisantins” (E. Ziercher, Représentations du sujet criminel, entre facétie et pathétique, in: “Juges et criminels dans la narration brève du XVIe siècle, J.-C. Arnould, ed., 2010, pp. 2-3 and 8; see also W.K. Pietrzak, Le Tragique dans les nouvelles exemplaires en France au XVIe siècle, Lódź, 2006, ad indicem; and L. Dion, Histoires de mariage. Le mariage dans la fiction narrative française (1515-1559), Paris, 2017, ad indicem). The present edition was shared between four Parisian publishers: Estienne Groulleau, Jean Longis, Robert Le Mangnier and Vincent Sertenas, and is extant with three variant title pages bearing the name of one or the other publishers. The work was very successful and was reprinted seven times until the end of the century. The 1582 edition contains an addition of five “discours modernes et facetieux”, that do not appear in the latest known 16th-century edition printed in 1595. The first modern edition is the one edited and commented by F. Frank cited above, that was reprinted at Geneva in 1969 (cf. Pérouse, op. cit., p. 502).

authors.name: Iona Giovanni Battista
authors.biography: Giovanni Battista Iona (also recorded as Giovanni Battista Jona, born Judah Jona; c. 1588 – 1668) was an Eastern European Jewish scholar, Christian Hebraist, and lecturer who served the Roman Curia and the Papal See during the seventeenth century. Originating from Lemberg (Lviv) in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Iona converted from Judaism to Roman Catholicism, subsequently becoming a prominent figure in the institutionalization of Hebraic studies within the Catholic Counter-Reformation apparatus. His intellectual career illustrates the intersection of early modern Jewish rabbinic erudition and Catholic polemical philology in post-Tridentine Rome.Born into a Jewish family in the late sixteenth century, Iona received a traditional Talmudic and rabbinic education in Poland. He subsequently traveled through the Ottoman Empire, spending time in Palestine and Constantinople. During his travels in the Italian peninsula during the early seventeenth century, he established contact with Catholic ecclesiastical authorities. He formally converted to Catholicism in Tuscany around 1625, adopting the baptismal name Giovanni Battista Iona. His knowledge of Hebrew, Aramaic, and rabbinic literature facilitated his integration into Roman academic and missionary institutions.Following his conversion, Iona relocated to Rome under papal patronage. He was appointed reader and professor of Hebrew at the Archiginnasio della Sapienza (the University of Rome) and taught language courses at the Collegio Urbano de Propaganda Fide. In this institutional role, Iona produced pedagogical and polemical works designed for missionary activities targeting Jewish communities. His scholarship focused on comparative biblical analysis, emphasizing messianic prophecies in the Old Testament and rabbinic commentaries that Catholic exegesis interpreted as prefigurations of Christian theology.The central work associated with Iona's career was a translation of the Four Gospels into Hebrew, titled Evangelia quadrupla Hebraice, printed at Rome in 1668 by the press of the Sacra Congregatio de Propaganda Fide. The typographical execution relied on specialized Hebrew metal type fonts maintained by the Polyglot Press of Propaganda Fide, conforming to seventeenth-century ecclesiastical standards for oriental typography. Prior to this, Iona authored the polemical treatise Discorso sopra la venuta del Messia (Rome, 1663), printed by the press of the Camera Apostolica. He also served as a scriptor and cataloger of Hebrew manuscripts for the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana.Iona's output was integrated into the broader framework of seventeenth-century Catholic missionary strategy and Hebraic philology. While contemporary papal authorities utilized his translations and teaching as functional tools for conversionary strategies, modern historical scholarship evaluates his work within the context of Jewish-Christian intellectual transmission, scriptural translation methodologies, and state-sponsored Oriental typography in early modern Rome.

publishers.name: Propaganda Fide
publishers.biography: Propaganda Fide—officially designated as the Sacra Congregatio de Propaganda Fide (the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith)—stands as one of the most transformative bureaucratic, intellectual, and typographic institutions of early modern Europe and the globalizing Catholic Church. Established on January 22, 1622, by Pope Gregory XV through the papal bull Inscrutabili Divinae Providentiae, the Congregation was conceived as the central executive organ for the coordination, administration, and ideological standardization of Roman Catholic missionary enterprise across non-Christian territories and areas dominated by Protestantism. Operating at the intersection of Counter-Reformation diplomacy, global ethnography, and linguistic humanism, Propaganda Fide fundamentally reshaped the geopolitical landscape of global Catholicism by seeking to dismantle the monopolistic ecclesiastical patronage systems (*Patronato Real* and *Padroado*) previously exerted by the Spanish and Portuguese crowns. Through its vast archival infrastructure, international educational network, and pioneering polyglot printing operations, the Congregation turned early modern Rome into a premier nerve center for global information collection, linguistic codification, and transcultural communication.The institutional genesis of Propaganda Fide emerged from decades of reformist impulse within the Roman Curia following the Council of Trent (1545–1563). Preceded by provisional papal commissions under Pope Gregory XIII in 1568 and a short-lived congregation initiated by Pope Clement VIII in 1599, the definitive establishment in 1622 was propelled by a coalition of high-ranking curial prelates and visionary reformers, notably Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi (nephew of Gregory XV), the Capuchin preacher Girolamo da Narni, and the Spanish prelate Juan Bautista Vives. Realizing that the rapid expansion of global trade routes required a unified theological and administrative strategy, the founders designed Propaganda Fide as an autonomous, centralized body capable of bypassing secular imperial rivalries. The structural capacity of the Congregation expanded dramatically under Pope Urban VIII (Maffeo Barberini, reigned 1623–1644), who in 1627 promulgated the bull Immortalis Dei Filius, establishing the Collegio Urbano de Propaganda Fide in Rome. Designed as an elite international seminary, the Collegio Urbano brought young men from across the Levant, Asia, Africa, Eastern Europe, and the Americas to the Holy City, instructing them in Scholastic theology, Latin rhetoric, canon law, and their native languages, thereby forging a highly disciplined, indigenous, and Rome-loyal clerical elite capable of returning to their homelands as Apostolic Vicars and missionaries.Intellectually, Propaganda Fide became one of the seventeenth century’s most vital hubs for Oriental philology, comparative linguistics, and ethnographic scholarship. The Congregation actively solicited detailed field reports (*relazioni*), travel itineraries, cultural treatises, and handwritten manuscripts from thousands of Franciscan, Dominican, Augustinian, and Jesuit missionaries stationed across the globe. To process and publish this unprecedented volume of non-European linguistic material, Propaganda Fide cultivated intimate intellectual networks with renowned humanists, linguists, and Eastern Christian scholars residing in Rome. Prominent among these were Maronite intellectuals from Mount Lebanon—such as Abraham Ecchellensis (Ibrāhīm al-Ḥāqilānī), Gabriel Sionita, and Victor Scialac—who provided essential expertise in Arabic, Syriac, Chaldean, and Samaritan texts. The Congregation also maintained close scholarly dialogues with polymaths such as the Jesuit Athanasius Kircher, utilizing his investigations into Coptic and Sinology to refine their understanding of non-Western written traditions. Through these collaborative networks, Propaganda Fide systematically reduced unwritten or vernacular languages into Latinized grammars and compiled groundbreaking bilingual and trilingual dictionaries, bridging the intellectual divide between Tridentine Catholicism and global cultures.Central to Propaganda Fide's monumental global agenda was its proprietary publishing house, the Typographia Polyglotta Vaticana (or Typographia de Propaganda Fide), founded in Rome in 1626 under the direct aegis of Urban VIII. Recognizing that printed text was the most effective vehicle for uniform religious instruction and linguistic standardization, the Congregation constructed an extraordinary punch-cutting and typefounding shop equipped to print in dozens of distinct non-Latin scripts. Under the typographical direction of master printers and punch-cutters such as Stefano Paolini, Francesco Maggi, and drawing upon the historic matrices cut by Robert Granjon during the late sixteenth century, the Polyglotta produced exquisite fonts for Arabic, Syriac, Ge'ez (Ethiopic), Armenian, Coptic, Georgian, Persian, Turkish, Cyrillic, Glagolitic, Tamil, and Devanagari. Among the press's most famous, bibliographically celebrated outputs was the iconic Alphabetum series—individual typographical and grammatical manuals published throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (including the Alphabetum Arabicum, Alphabetum Armenum, Alphabetum Tibetanum, and Alphabetum Grandonico-Malabaricum). These volumes not only functioned as pedagogical tools for foreign missionaries but also represented landmark monuments in the history of European typography and comparative script analysis.Despite its formidable administrative and cultural successes, Propaganda Fide operated amidst fierce geopolitical controversies and ideological resistance. Throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the Congregation engaged in a prolonged struggle against the Iberian monarchs, who viewed the papal appointment of Vicars Apostolic in the East Indies, China, and the Americas as a direct violation of their royal patronage rights. Simultaneously, Propaganda Fide found itself deeply embroiled in intense theological disputes concerning missionary methodology, most dramatically exemplified by the Chinese Rites Controversy (*Controversia dei Riti Cinesi*). The Congregation served as the primary administrative battleground where Dominican and Franciscan critics clashed with Jesuit missionaries regarding the accommodation of Confucian funerary rites and ancestral veneration among Chinese converts. Following decades of rigorous investigation, translation of classical Chinese texts, and heated debates within Propaganda Fide's commissions, Popes Clement XI (bull *Cum Deus optimus*, 1704) and Benedict XIV (bull *Ex quo singulari*, 1742) issued definitive condemnations of the Chinese Rites, profoundly altering the trajectory of Christian missions in East Asia.The institutional flexibility of Propaganda Fide enabled it to survive major European political upheavals, including the French Invasion of Rome in 1798 and the Napoleonic Occupation. During the Napoleonic era, the contents of the Congregation's rich historical archives and its irreplaceable polyglot matrices were forcibly confiscated and transported to Paris to enrich the imperial press; however, following the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the vast majority of these treasures were restored to Rome. Over the course of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the institution adapted to the collapse of European colonial empires and the modern emergence of autonomous local churches across the Global South. In 1967, Pope Paul VI renamed the institution the *Congregatio pro Gentium Evangelisatione* (Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples), preserving its historical mandate within a modernized curial structure. This legacy was further reaffirmed in 2022 by Pope Francis through the apostolic constitution *Praedicate Evangelium*, which merged the institution into the newly created Dicastery for Evangelization. Today, the historical archives of Propaganda Fide, preserved in the historical palace at Piazza di Spagna in Rome, remain one of the world's premier research repositories for early modern global history, historical linguistics, typography, and transcultural religious encounters.
