academic_description: Folio (350x235 mm). [28], 395, [1 blank] pp. Collation: [π]4 ++-+++4 ++++2 A-Bbb4 Ccc6. Parallel text in Hebrew and Latin arranged in two columns. Half title, title within a typographic frame with the woodcut device of the Congretatio de Propaganda fide in the center. With four large woodcut vignettes at the beginning of each Gospel showing the Evangelists with their symbols, taken from the Arabic Gospels printed in Rome in 1590-‘91 by the Typographia Medicea. Woodcut initials and ornaments. Contemporary grey cardboards, inked title on spine (endleaves renewed). Some marginal worm tracks partly skillfully repaired, lower inner corner of the first quire repaired not affecting the text, some scattered browning due to the paper, all in all a very good, genuine copy. Uncut with deckle edges.First edition of the Gospels in the Hebrew translation from the Vulgate by the converted Jew Giovanni Battista Iona, who completed his version before 1639. The preliminary matter includes a dedication to Pope Clement IX, a twenty-two-page introduction printed in parallel columns in Latin and Hebrew, and the approbations. Jehudas Jona was born in a Jewish Sephardic family in Safed in 1588 and renamed Giovanni Battista in Warsaw in 1625. After travelling around various cultural centres in Europe, he settled in Rome, where he lectured at La Sapienza University from 1649 to 1664, and subsequently at the Collegio dei Neofiti until his death in 1668. Among his students was Giulio Bartolocci. Like other teachers of the discipline, he was also a Hebrew scriptor in the Vatican and an interpreter of other Eastern languages. In addition to teaching, he was intensely involved in apologetics. We know of his Hebrew and Latin sermons on the true Messiah and the descent of the Holy Spirit, as well as his translations of Bellarmine’s catechism, the Gospels and St Thomas’s Summa contra Gentiles. He died before completing the Hebrew version of the Acts of the Apostles, as well as various dialogues and polemical pamphlets against the Jews, which he left as manuscripts (cf. G. Rita, Le discipline umanistiche da Sisto V a Clemente XII (1587-1740), in: “Storia della Facoltà di Lettere e Filosofia de ‘La Sapienza’”, L. Capo-M.R. Di Simone, eds., Rome, 2000, p. 280).“Three main points may be adduced from [the introduction]. First, one particular reason for which Iona wished to read the Gospels in Hebrew was his belief – a widespread one – that the Gospel of Matthew was originally written in Hebrew. Iona was therefore hoping to find this original version of Matthew or, at least, an approximation to it. Second, the Hebrew versions of the Gospel of Matthew that Iona actually found – the translation included in Shem-Tov ibn Shaprut’s fourteenthcentury polemical treatise ʾEben Bōḥan (The Touch Stone) and the translation published in Paris in 1555 by Jean du Tillet and Jean Mercier – disappointed him greatly, since he deemed that they were written in poor Hebrew, or in what he calls ‘stammered language’ […] Iona believed that the rendering of the Gospel into ‘bad’ Hebrew was a polemical technique used by the authors of these translations in order to make the Gospel ‘despicable’ to Jews […] Third, Iona hoped that his own translation was written in such ‘pure’ Hebrew that may enable it to be perceived as being ‘like the rest of the Holy Scriptures’, that is, as being similar to the books of the Hebrew Bible […] Iona hopes that the reading of his translation will be convincing to some Jews and therefore bring about their conversion. It may be noted that Iona’s translation is one of the earliest Hebrew translations of the New Testament in which such a missionary aim is mentioned. Only in the eighteenth and nineteenth century did the mission to the Jews become a main motivation for producing Hebrew translations of the New Testament […] Regarding the Hebrew used by Iona in the translation, it may first be observed that it has some clear ‘biblicizing’ features […] Last but not least, it is not rare to find in Iona’s translation renderings of undeniable quality, that is, cases in which Iona manages to find a translation that both faithfully renders the meaning of the Latin expression or phrase and is idiomatic in Hebrew and resonates with Jewish culture” (E. Shuali, Giovanni Battista Iona’s Hebrew translation of the four Gospels, in: “Journal of Jewish Studies”, 2023, 74.2, pp. 408-428). In 1626, Urban VIII established the Polyglot Printing House of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith with the aim of producing publications for missionary work. The press soon amassed a considerable amount of typographical material (23 alphabets), which was augmented by oriental characters donated by the Vatican and Medici printing houses. The creation of new typefaces was entrusted to the punchcutter S. Paolini. The press mainly printed religious books, grammars and lexicons.

authors.name: Descartes René
authors.biography: René Descartes (1596–1650), known across the early modern Latinate Respublica Literaria by his Latinized name Renatus Cartesius, stands as the pivotal architect of Western modern philosophy and a foundational figure of the Scientific Revolution. Operating at the turbulent intersection of late Renaissance Scholasticism, early modern natural philosophy, and modern mathematical synthesis, Descartes systematically dismantled the teleological Aristotelian worldview that dominated European universities. In its place, he erected an unapologetically rationalist, mechanistic, and dualist philosophical paradigm. His philosophical project—characterized by the methodological deployment of radical doubt, the foundational formulation of the cogito, ergo sum, the defense of innate ideas, and the division of reality into thinking substance (res cogitans) and extended substance (res extensa)—reconstructed the parameters of epistemology, metaphysics, optics, and physiology. Simultaneously, his invention of analytic geometry synthesized algebra and geometry, providing the indispensable mathematical framework for early modern physics.Born on March 31, 1596, at La Haye en Touraine (a town subsequently renamed Descartes in his honor), he was the son of Joachim Descartes, a magistrate and councillor in the Parlement of Brittany at Rennes, and Jeanne Brochard, who died shortly after his birth. Raised by his maternal grandmother and a nurse, young René belonged to the noblesse de robe, an elite social stratum of legal administrators and royal bureaucrats. In 1607, at the age of eleven, he was sent to the newly founded Jesuit college of La Flèche in Anjou, established by King Henri IV and directed by Father Étienne Charlet. For eight years, Descartes underwent a rigorous humanistic and philosophical education. The curriculum at La Flèche combined classical grammar, rhetoric, and literature with a deep immersion in the Scholastic-Aristotelian curriculum, studying logic, natural philosophy, mathematics, and metaphysics via the commentaries of the School of Coimbra (Conimbricenses), Francisco Toledo, Pedro da Fonseca, and Francisco Suárez. While Descartes praised the institution for its intellectual rigor, he subsequently reflected in his Discours de la méthode that book-learning had saddled him with doubt and uncertainty rather than clear, demonstrable truth. Leaving La Flèche in 1614, he matriculated at the University of Poitiers, where he earned a baccalaureate and licentiate in civil and canon law in 1616, satisfying his family's judicial ambitions before embarking on an independent intellectual quest.Driven by a desire to study "the great book of the world," Descartes traveled to the Netherlands in 1618 to join the Protestant army of Prince Maurice of Nassau as a gentleman volunteer (soldat à la suite). This period marked a crucial intellectual catalyst through his friendship with the Dutch physician and natural philosopher Isaac Beeckman. Beeckman introduced Descartes to a brand of physical-mathematics that sought to explain physical phenomena through micro-mechanical models of matter and motion, sparking Descartes's early work on hydrostatics, acoustics, and falling bodies (the Compendium Musicae, dedicated to Beeckman in 1618). Following the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War, Descartes traveled to Bavaria in 1619, serving under Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria. It was during the winter of 1619, while stove-heated in a room near Neuburg an der Donau, that Descartes experienced a series of intense intellectual epiphanies and three vivid dreams on the night of November 10–11. He interpreted these visions as a divine mandate to unify all human knowledge under a singular, universal mathematical method (the mirabilis scientiae fundamenta). This methodological vision culminated in his unfinished treatise Regulae ad directionem ingenii (Rules for the Direction of the Mind), written between 1619 and 1628, which laid the groundwork for his intuitive-deductive method.During the 1620s, Descartes traversed Europe, visiting Italy and residing periodically in Paris. In the French capital, he entered the vibrant intellectual circle surrounding the Minim friar Marin Mersenne, who served as the central clearinghouse for European scientific and philosophical correspondence. Mersenne's network exposed Descartes to the debates surrounding libertinism, Pyrrhonian skepticism (popularized by Michel de Montaigne and Pierre Charron), and the emerging new physics of Galileo Galilei and Pierre Gassendi. Seeking total solitude and liberation from social obligations to systematically construct his system, Descartes relocated permanently to the Dutch Republic in late 1628. Over the next twenty years, he moved frequently between various Dutch towns and country estates—including Franeker, Leiden, Amsterdam, Deventer, Utrecht, and Endegeest—benefiting from the religious tolerance and intellectual dynamism of the Dutch Golden Age.Descartes's first major publication project was the ambitious natural-philosophical treatise Le Monde (The World) or Traité de la lumière, accompanied by L'Homme (Man). In these works, he constructed a fully mechanistic universe composed of a continuous fluid matter divided into three element types, operating solely via motion, impact, and spatial rearrangement under God's conserved laws of nature, completely eschewing Aristotelian substantial forms and occult qualities. However, upon learning in 1633 of the condemnation of Galileo by the Roman Inquisition for defending Copernican heliocentrism, Descartes prudently withdrew Le Monde from publication, as his own physics relied upon a moving Earth. Instead, he presented his natural philosophy implicitly in 1637 through a French masterwork published anonymously at Leyden by the printer Jan Maire: Discours de la méthode pour bien conduire sa raison, et chercher la vérité dans les sciences. This work served as a preface to three scientific essays demonstrating his method: La Dioptrique (explaining the law of refraction/Snell's law and eye anatomy), Les Météores (a mechanical account of weather phenomena and the rainbow), and La Géométrie. In La Géométrie, Descartes introduced the method of representing geometric curves through algebraic equations using a coordinate system, thereby inventing analytic geometry and revolutionizing early modern mathematics.The publishing history of Descartes's works reflects the burgeoning international book trade centered in the Low Countries and Paris. Jan Maire's 1637 quarto edition of the Discours was printed in the vernacular French rather than Latin to reach an educated lay audience beyond the university faculties, featuring elegant typography and woodcut diagrams personally supervised by Descartes. Moving to secure his philosophical foundation, Descartes authored his metaphysical masterpiece in Latin: Meditationes de prima philosophia (Meditations on First Philosophy). First published in Paris in 1641 by the publisher Michel Soly, the work featured six set objections gathered by Mersenne from leading intellectuals—including the theologian Johan de Kater (Caterus), Thomas Hobbes, Antoine Arnauld, and Pierre Gassendi—alongside Descartes's exhaustive replies. A second, revised edition was published in Amsterdam in 1642 by the famed printing house of Louis Elzevir (Elsevier), incorporating a seventh set of objections by the Jesuit Pierre Bourdin and Descartes's letter to Father Dinet. The Elzevir press became Descartes's primary publisher, producing elegant, widely circulated octavo and duodecimo editions that reached university professors, theologians, and scholars across Europe.In 1644, Elzevir published Descartes's Principia philosophiae (Principles of Philosophy), dedicated to Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia. Designed to replace traditional Scholastic textbooks in university curricula, the Principia synthesized Cartesian metaphysics, mechanistic vortex physics (explaining planetary motion through rotating celestial matter), and physical cosmology into a rigorous four-part system.Descartes's intellectual life in the 1640s was deeply shaped by his intensive correspondence with Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia (1618–1680), daughter of Frederick V, Elector Palatine. Elisabeth posed penetrating critiques regarding Cartesian dualism, specifically questioning how an unextended, immaterial soul could causally act upon a material, extended physical body (the mind-body interaction problem).Their dialogue pushed Descartes to refine his psychological and ethical theories, culminating in his final published treatise, Les Passions de l'âme (The Passions of the Soul), printed concurrently in Paris by Henry Le Gras and in Amsterdam by Louis Elzevir in 1649. In this work, Descartes analyzed human emotions as physiological processes mediated by the movement of animal spirits flowing through the nervous system, identifying the pineal gland (conarium) as the principal seat of the soul where mind and body interact.The dissemination of Cartesianism triggered fierce theological and academic battles. In the Dutch Republic, Descartes became embroiled in the "Utrecht Crisis" (1639–1643), where Gisbertus Voetius, rector of the University of Utrecht and a staunch Calvinist theologian, accused Descartes of atheist tendencies and subversive skepticism. A similar theological assault erupted at the University of Leiden led by Martinus Schoock and Reinerus Regius. Seeking refuge from these polemics, Descartes accepted an invitation from Queen Christina of Sweden in 1649 to join her court in Stockholm as a royal tutor and philosopher-in-residence. The harsh Scandinavian winter, combined with the Queen's demanding schedule requiring tutorials at five o'clock in the morning in an unheated library, severely compromised Descartes's frail health. In early February 1650, he contracted severe pneumonia and died in Stockholm on February 11, 1650, at the age of fifty-three.Following his death, Descartes's remains underwent a complex journey; his body was buried in Sweden, exhumed in 1666, and transported to France, where it was eventually reinterred in the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris. In 1663, despite the efforts of French Cartesian scholars like Claude Clerselier (who published Descartes's voluminous posthumous correspondence between 1657 and 1667), the Roman Catholic Church placed Descartes's works on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum donec corrigantur (until corrected), perceiving his mechanistic physics as incompatible with the Eucharistic doctrine of transubstantiation. Nevertheless, Cartesianism swept through European intellectual life, fundamentally reshaping European philosophy. His dualist framework directly inspired the rationalist metaphysics of Baruch Spinoza, Nicolas Malebranche, and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, while provoking the empirical critiques of John Locke, George Berkeley, and David Hume. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Descartes was elevated as the foundational symbol of the Enlightenment and the modern philosophical subject, securing his legacy as the indispensable initiator of modern epistemological inquiry.

authors.name: Barbapiccola Giuseppa Eleonora
authors.biography: Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola (c. 1700 – c. 1740) was an important figure in early 18th century Naples and a groundbreaking champion for the inclusion of women in natural philosophy and the physical sciences, achieved international scholarly renown through her 1722 translation into Italian of René Descartes’ Principia Philosophiae, which was prefaced by an original feminist manifesto “A’ Lettori” (‘To the Readers’). In this prefatory discourse, Barbapiccola articulated a harsh critique of contemporary educational disparities, arguing that women’s intellectual perceived inferiority was not a consequence of biological or ontological deficiency, but rather the artificial product of systemic educational deprivation. By deploying Cartesian epistemology itself - specifically the doctrine of clear and distinct ideas and the radical dualism of mind and body - Barbapiccola demonstrated that the faculty of reason is fundamentally ungendered, thereby establishing a philosophical foundation for female intellectual emancipation.Born in Salerno around the turn of the eighteenth century, Barbapiccola belonged to an educated, socially prominent family with deep clerical, legal, and intellectual ties across the Kingdom of Naples. Her upbringing was profoundly shaped by her uncle, Agostino Barbapiccola, a learned ecclesiastic, canonist, and active participant in Neapolitan literary circles. Recognizing his niece’s exceptional aptitude, Agostino facilitated her rigorous domestic education, exposing her to classical Latin, modern French, geometry, natural history, and metaphysics. Unlike many of her female contemporaries whose education was confined to devotional literature and domestic arts within convent walls or noble households, Barbapiccola gained direct access to the private libraries and private academies of Naples. During this era, Naples was experiencing a dramatic philosophical shift: the traditional Aristotelian-Scholastic paradigm, long enforced by ecclesiastical authorities, was being vigorously challenged by the jusnaturalism, atomism, and mechanical philosophy promoted by the Accademia degli Investiganti - a vanguard institution founded by Tommaso Cornelio, Leonardo Di Capua, and Lucantonio Porzio. It was within this intellectually charged atmosphere of Neapolitan Cartesianism that Barbapiccola acquired her deep mastery of modern physics and mechanical philosophy.Barbapiccola’s magnum opus, her Italian translation of Descartes’ Principia, was a masterpiece of philosophical translation and linguistic adaptation. Translating Descartes’ original Latin text (first published in Amsterdam in 1644) alongside Claude Clerselier’s authoritative French version (1647), Barbapiccola aimed to make modern mechanical philosophy accessible to an Italian readership, particularly to women who were routinely denied instruction in academic Latin. In her self-assured preface, she boldly situated her work within the long history of female intellectual achievement, evoking classical and modern precedents such as Hypatia of Alexandria, Diotima, Veronica Gambara, Vittoria Colonna, Cassandra Fedele, Anna Maria van Schurmann and Anne Dacier among others. Barbapiccola explicitly challenged the misogynistic assertions of philosophers such as Claude Fleury, who argued in his Traité du choix et de la méthode des études (1686) that female physiology was too delicate or soft to comprehend abstract scientific principles. Barbapiccola contended that if female nerves were indeed more delicate, women were uniquely endowed with superior perceptual sensitivity and cognitive agility, making them exceptionally suited for scientific inquiry. Her translation was not merely a passive linguistic exercise, but an active intervention in European philosophical discourse, seeking to dismantle the gendered barriers surrounding the res publica literaria.Barbapiccola was an active member of the prestigious Accademia degli Arcadi (the Arcadian Academy), adopting the pastoral pseudonym Mirista, under which she composed erudite poetry and exchanged philosophical verses with leading scholars of the realm. Chief among her allies and admirers were the eminent philosopher and historian Giambattista Vico (who is quoted in the preface) and Gherardo degli Angeli. Gherardo was so profoundly impressed by Barbapiccola’s erudition and translation project that he composed an encomiastic sonnet, titled In lode della signora Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola, che ha tradotto da’ francesi ne’ nostri favellari i Principi della Filosofia di Renato Des-Cartes (Rime Scelte, Florence, 1730, vol. 3, p. 104). In this poem, Gherardo celebrated her as a shining beacon of Neapolitan genius who had surpassed the achievements of foreign scholars. Barbapiccola was very close to Vico’s favourite daughter Luisa, also a highly educated woman and a poetress (the two exchanged poems), and cultivated close ties with prominent Neapolitan natural philosophers, including Pietro Antonio de Martino, Bernardo De Dominici, and the literary patron Antonio Niccolini.The publishing history of Barbapiccola’s I Principi della Filosofia di Renato Des-Cartes reflects the complex geopolitical and censorial realities of early eighteenth-century Naples. Printed in 1722, the title page bears the false or strategic imprint of Turin, a common typographical maneuver utilized by Neapolitan publishers to bypass local ecclesiastical censorship and political scrutiny regarding Cartesian mechanical philosophy, which remained controversial due to its implications for Eucharistic theology and scholastic physics. The edition included comprehensive diagrams of Cartesian vortices, planetary orbits, and atomic structures, meticulously reproduced to ensure that Italian readers could fully grasp Descartes’ physical cosmology.

related_names.name: Coscia Niccolò
related_names.biography: Niccolò Coscia (1682–1755) stands as one of the most enigmatic, controversial, and deeply polarizing figures within the annals of the eighteenth-century Roman Curia. Rising from obscure provincial poverty in the Kingdom of Naples to the highest echelons of temporal and ecclesiastical governance in the Papal States, Coscia embodied both the apex and the ultimate collapse of early modern papal favoritism (*cardinal-nipote* surrogacy). As the undisputed chief minister and favorite of Pope Benedict XIII (Vincenzo Maria Orsini), Coscia wielded near-absolute administrative, financial, and political authority over Rome and the Papal States for six years (1724–1730). His rapacious accumulation of wealth, systemic sale of public and sacred offices, and ruthless monopolization of curial channels ignited unprecedented hostility among the Sacred College of Cardinals. Following Benedict XIII’s death, Coscia became the subject of one of the most celebrated criminal trials in papal history, resulting in his conviction for extortion, fraud, and forgery, his imprisonment in Castel Sant'Angelo, and his dramatic eventual rehabilitation under Pope Benedict XIV. In the broader landscape of Enlightenment-era legal and political history, Coscia's rise and fall illustrate the intense structural friction between traditional dynastic patronage networks and emerging bureaucratic accountability within the early modern Italian states.Born on 25 January 1682 in Pietradefusi (historically known as Petrafusa), a modest rural commune situated within the Principato Ultra of the Kingdom of Naples and under the spiritual jurisdiction of the Archdiocese of Benevento, Niccolò Coscia belonged to an impoverished and socially obscure family. His early prospects were fundamentally reshaped by a fateful encounter with Cardinal Vincenzo Maria Orsini, O.P., then serving as Archbishop of Benevento. Recognized by Orsini during a routine pastoral visitation to Pietradefusi for his precocious intellect and administrative potential, the young Coscia was brought under the direct patronage of the cardinal-archbishop. In May 1696, Orsini conferred upon him the first clerical tonsure, initiating his career within the archiepiscopal curia of Benevento. Under Orsini’s paternal guidance, Coscia acquired practical training in diocesan administration, canonical procedure, and fiscal management. Recognizing the need for formal legal credentials, Orsini facilitated Coscia’s matriculation at the prestigious Archiginnasio of Rome, La Sapienza, where he pursued rigorous studies in jurisprudence, culminating in the award of the doctorate in utroque iure (both civil and canon law) on 30 March 1715.Coscia’s early advancement through the regional ecclesiastical hierarchy was rapid and closely tethered to Orsini’s personal favor. In October 1703, Orsini granted him a canonry in the collegiate church of San Bartolomeo in Benevento, which Coscia strategically exchanged in April 1708 for a more lucrative canonry within the metropolitan cathedral chapter, simultaneously receiving appointment as chancellor of the archiepiscopal curia. Ordained to the presbyterate on 28 March 1705, Coscia assumed the influential role of private secretary to Cardinal Orsini. Over the next fifteen years, he consolidated his hold over the archdiocese of Benevento, accumulating prestigious benefices and administrative titles including master of the chamber (*maestro di camera*), archiepiscopal treasurer, apostolic visitor, archpriest, and mitred abbot of the ancient abbey of San Lorenzo d'Aprice. Coscia’s unwavering devotion to Orsini secured his position as the cardinal's primary political confidant, accompanying him as official *conclavista* to the papal conclaves of 1721 (which elected Innocent XIII) and 1724.The elevation of Cardinal Orsini to the Chair of Saint Peter as Pope Benedict XIII on 29 May 1724 precipitated Coscia’s meteoric ascendance in Rome. The newly elected pontiff, a deeply ascetic Dominican friar who disdained political statecraft and administrative routine, effectively surrendered the temporal governance of the Papal States and the direction of the Roman Curia to Coscia. On 7 June 1724, Coscia was named Secretary of Memorials (*Segretario dei Memoriali*), gaining direct control over all petitions, favors, and administrative requests presented to the sovereign pontiff. Nineteen days later, on 26 June 1724, he was consecrated Titular Archbishop of Traianopolis. Benedict XIII’s insistence on elevating his provincial favorite to the Sacred College met with ferocious resistance from established Roman curial factions; in the consistory of 11 June 1725, twenty of the twenty-six cardinals present openly opposed Coscia’s promotion. Unmoved by the Sacred College’s unprecedented protest, Benedict XIII forced through Coscia’s creation as Cardinal-Priest of Santa Maria in Ara Coeli (later opting for San Prassede).Armed with cardinalitial rank, Coscia established a virtual dictatorship over the papal administration. On 5 September 1725, he was appointed Archbishop Coadjutor of Benevento with the right of succession, assuming full operational control of the wealthy southern archdiocese, which Benedict XIII retained *in commendam* until his death. Coscia further expanded his institutional authority by acquiring the roles of Protector of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, Protector of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual (1725), Protector of the City of Avignon, and Prefect of the Congregation of Avignon (1726). Operating through a tight network of Neapolitan and Beneventan henchmen—famously dubbed the *Beneventani* by resentment-filled Roman courtiers—Coscia transformed curial patronage into a lucrative commercial enterprise. Offices, benefices, judicial reprieves, tax exemptions, and diplomatic concessions were systematically sold to the highest bidder. Coscia diverted vast sums from the papal treasury (*Camera Apostolica*) and the grain supply administration (*Annona*), accumulating a colossal private fortune while leaving the public finances of the Papal States severely degraded.The typographical and documentary record of Coscia’s administration is intimately tied to the output of the *Stamperia della Reverenda Camera Apostolica* and private Roman printing houses. During his tenure as Secretary of Memorials and Coadjutor of Benevento, hundreds of official edicts, papal decrees, judicial ordinances, and financial concessions were issued under his direct signature. Conversely, Coscia’s absolute dominance sparked a clandestine explosion of satirical literature and *pasquinades* across Italy. Libels, handwritten lampoons, and anonymously printed pamphlets printed in Venice, Naples, and secret Roman workshops denounced the cardinal’s extortionate practices, portraying him as a rapacious parasite exploiting the holy simplicity of Pope Benedict XIII.The death of Benedict XIII on 21 February 1730 shattered Coscia’s political empire. As the pope lay dying, violent anti-Coscia riots erupted throughout Rome; the residences of the *Beneventani* were sacked by angry crowds, and members of Coscia’s faction were hunted through the streets. Terrified for his life, Cardinal Coscia fled the capital in disguise, seeking asylum in Cisterna under the protection of Prince Michelangelo Gaetani, Duke of Caserta. From his refuge, Coscia issued defiant legal declarations to the Sacred College, warning that any conclave assembled without his vote would be canonically invalid. After forty days of tense diplomatic negotiations, guaranteed safe passage by Duke Gaetani’s armed retinue, Coscia returned to Rome under heavy escort and securely entered the conclave of 1730, which ultimately elected Cardinal Lorenzo Corsini as Pope Clement XII.The pontificate of Clement XII marked the definitive judicial reckoning for Coscia. Driven by popular outrage and the financial ruin of the papal treasury, Clement XII established an extraordinary judicial commission, the *Congregazione Particolare di Cardinali*, specifically tasked with investigating Coscia’s administrative crimes. Forced to resign his coadjutorship of Benevento on 8 January 1731, Coscia fled to Naples in March 1731, prompting the immediate confiscation of all his Roman real estate, financial assets, and personal chattels. Facing the threat of total canonical degradation, Coscia surrendered to papal authorities in March 1732, taking up enforced residence at the monastery of Santa Prassede while his formal trial proceeded. The prosecution compiled a massive dossier of legal briefs, financial ledgers, and witness testimonies printed in official trial volumes by the *Stamperia Vaticana*.On 9 May 1733, the *Congregazione Particolare* pronounced its historical verdict. Cardinal Niccolò Coscia was found guilty of grand extortion (*estorsione*), systemic forgery (*falsificazione*), embezzlement, and gross breach of public trust (*abuso di fiducia*). He was sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment in the fortress of Castel Sant'Angelo, ordered to pay an astronomical indemnity of 100,000 scudi, stripped of his active and passive voice in future papal elections, and hit with the sentence of major excommunication (*excommunicatio major*). Coscia was incarcerated in comfortable quarters within Castel Sant'Angelo, where his health rapidly deteriorated due to severe gout. Recognizing his fragile physical state and canonical submission, Pope Clement XII lifted the major excommunication on 23 February 1734 and restored his voting rights for future conclaves in July 1738. From 1735 onward, Coscia was granted temporary leaves of absence from prison to seek therapeutic treatment at thermal baths in Tuscany and Lazio.Following the death of Clement XII in February 1740, Coscia was released from Castel Sant'Angelo to participate in the marathon conclave of 1740, which resulted in the election of Cardinal Prospero Lambertini as Pope Benedict XIV. Seeking to heal deep political rifts within the Sacred College and displaying his characteristic judicial clemency, Benedict XIV ordered a full review of Coscia’s criminal trial. On 8 January 1742, Benedict XIV issued a papal decree granting Coscia a complete pardon for the remainder of his ten-year sentence, restoring his cardinalitial privileges, and absolving him of all remaining legal liabilities. Retiring from public life, Coscia spent his final thirteen years in quiet, comfortable obscurity in Naples, where he died on 8 February 1755 at the age of seventy-three. In modern scholarship, Coscia’s trial remains a landmark case study in early modern canon law, judicial accountability, and the institutional evolution of the Roman Curia away from unrestricted favorite-driven governance.

related_names.name: Vico Giambattista
related_names.biography: Giambattista Vico (born June 23, 1668, Naples, Kingdom of Naples—died January 23, 1744, Naples) stands as one of the most original, radical, and far-reaching thinkers in the history of European philosophy. Writing at the crossroads of the late Baroque and the early Enlightenment, Vico constructed an monumental philosophical system that challenged the dominant Cartesian rationalism of his era. By pioneering a philosophical science of human history, culture, and mind, he anticipated fundamental tenets of modern historical consciousness, cultural anthropology, hermeneutics, philosophy of language, and sociology. While his intellectual contemporaries in France and England sought to ground all valid knowledge in the mathematical paradigms of mechanical physics, Vico insisted that human historical existence—the domain of the factum—is uniquely accessible to human understanding precisely because it is the creation of human activity. His masterpiece, Principii di una scienza nuova intorno alla natura delle nazioni (commonly known as the Scienza Nuova), reoriented European thought by establishing that human cognition is intrinsically historical and that myth, poetry, and law represent the primary imaginative structures through which humanity first articulated its reality.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationGiambattista Vico was born in the bustling heart of Naples, above the modest bookstore owned by his father, Antonio Vico, on the Via San Biagio dei Librai—the renowned street of booksellers and binderies that served as an intellectual artery of the Neapolitan Kingdom. His mother, Candida Masullo, was the daughter of a carriage maker. In his celebrated autobiography, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo (composed between 1725 and 1731), Vico recounts a pivotal childhood trauma: at the age of seven, he suffered a severe fall from a ladder, fracturing his skull so badly that the attending physician predicted either death or permanent brain impairment. After a grueling three-year convalescence, Vico emerged with a melancholy, introspective temperament and an insatiable hunger for self-directed study, earning him the reputation of an extraordinary autodidact.His formal education began at the Jesuit college (the Collegio Massimo at the Gesù Vecchio in Naples), where he was exposed to Scholastic grammar, logic, and Aristotelian philosophy under the guidance of Antonio del Balzo. Impatient with the rigid dogmatism of formal scholastic pedagogy, Vico frequently withdrew from classes to master scholastic metaphysics and canonical law on his own. He subsequently enrolled at the University of Naples to study civil and canon law, receiving his doctorate in 1694. However, the turning point of his intellectual development occurred between 1686 and 1695, when he accepted a position as tutor to the children of the noble Rocca family at their castle in Vatolla, located in the rugged Cilento region south of Naples. This nine-year period of rural seclusion provided Vico with an idyllic sanctuary and access to the extensive library of the Rocca family. There, isolated from the prevailing Cartesian trends of Naples, he undertook an immersive reading of Classical literature, Renaissance humanism, patristic theology, and modern legal philosophy, laying the groundwork for his future intellectual system.Philosophical Trajectory: The Four Authors and Anti-CartesianismDuring his years at Vatolla and his subsequent return to Naples, Vico formulated his distinctive philosophical canon, centering on four intellectual anchors whom he explicitly designated as his primary inspirations: Plato, who taught him the contemplation of the ideal man and universal truth; Cornelius Tacitus, who revealed man as he actually exists in historical reality; Francis Bacon, who demonstrated how empirical observation and methodological rigor could be applied to advance human knowledge; and Hugo Grotius, who attempted to construct a universal system of jurisprudence combining natural law, history, and philology. To these, Vico added deep engagements with Renaissance humanists such as Lorenzo Valla and Pico della Mirandola, as well as classical rhetoricians like Cicero and Quintilian.In 1699, Vico secured the modest chair of Rhetoric at the University of Naples, a position he would hold for over four decades. His primary duty was to deliver the annual Latin inaugural address (*oratio inauguralis*) at the opening of the academic term. Between 1699 and 1707, Vico delivered six inaugurals exploring the moral, civic, and pedagogical functions of education. However, it was his seventh inaugural address, delivered in 1708 and published in 1709 under the title De nostri temporis studiorum ratione (*On the Study Methods of Our Time*), that signaled his definitive break with contemporary Enlightenment epistemology. In this profound treatise, Vico criticized René Descartes's method of radical doubt and exclusive reliance on clear and distinct mathematical ideas. Vico argued that Cartesian rationalism, by prioritizing abstract geometry over rhetoric, history, and civic prudence (*prudentia*), crippled the human imagination (*ingenium*) and destroyed the common sense (*sensus communis*) required for moral and political life.Vico developed his metaphysical counter-attack against Cartesianism in his 1710 Latin treatise, De antiquissima Italorum sapientia ex linguae Latinae originibus eruenda (*On the Most Ancient Wisdom of the Italians Unearthed from the Origins of the Latin Language*). Here, Vico introduced his foundational epistemological principle: the convertible principle of the true and the made—verum et factum reciprocantur seu convertuntur (the true and the made are interchangeable). According to Vico, complete and perfect knowledge (*scientia*) of a thing can only be possessed by the creator of that thing. Consequently, God alone possesses true knowledge of the natural universe, because God created it. Human beings, by contrast, cannot truly 'know' nature in an ultimate metaphysical sense; they can only know that which human beings themselves construct—namely, mathematics, language, law, social institutions, and history itself.The Genesis and Structure of the *Scienza Nuova*Vico's realization that human beings can possess authentic knowledge of the historical world culminated in his legal studies of the early 1720s, titled collectively as the Diritto Universale (*Universal Law*, 1720–1722), comprising De universi iuris uno principio et fine uno and De constantia iurisprudentis. In these works, Vico sought to harmonize natural law theory with concrete historical jurisprudence, identifying law as the structural glue of human civilization.This research provided the direct catalyst for his masterpiece, the Scienza Nuova. The evolution of this work represents one of the most intense authorial journeys in early modern thought, resulting in three distinct principal editions:1. Scienza Nuova Prima (1725): Published under the title Principii di una scienza nuova intorno alla natura delle nazioni per la quale si ritruovano i principii di altro sistema del diritto naturale delle genti. In this edition, Vico outlined his core discovery: that the origin of human civilization lies not in rational political social contracts formulated by enlightened philosophers, but in the primitive, terrifying, and imaginative experiences of early humanity.2. Scienza Nuova Seconda (1730): Drastically restructured and rewritten, this edition introduced the famous frontispiece (*dipintura*)—a complex emblematic engraving illustrating the allegorical architecture of the work—and organized the treatise into five comprehensive books: Establishment of Principles, Poetic Wisdom, Discovery of the True Homer, The Course the Nations Run, and The Recourse of Human Affairs.3. Scienza Nuova Terza (1744): Published posthumously shortly after Vico's death, this definitive edition refined the prose and perfected his theory of the storia ideale eterna (ideal eternal history) and the divine providence (*provvidenza*) governing human development.At the center of Vico's Scienza Nuova is the concept of Sapienza Poetica (Poetic Wisdom). Vico asserted that early human beings (*the giants* or *bioni*) were not rational philosophers but creatures dominated by overwhelming senses and vivid imaginations. Faced with terrifying natural phenomena such as thunder and lightning, primitive humans did not formulate abstract physical theories; instead, through a spontaneous act of imaginative metaphor (*metafora fantastica*), they personified the sky as the divine giant Jove. From this original poetic myth sprang religion, marriage, burial rites, and the foundational institutions of human society. Human history, according to Vico, progresses through three distinct ages, each characterized by its own language, law, authority, and nature:The Age of the Gods (*Età degli Dei*): Primitive humanity lives under divine rule, governed by terrifying omens, oracles, and mythic poetry. Religion and family structures are established.The Age of the Heroes (*Età degli Eroi*): Aristocratic, warlike societies emerge, dominated by heroic figures like Achilles and Hercules. Law is harsh, poetic, and grounded in class domination by the patricians over the plebeians.The Age of Men (*Età degli Uomini*): Fully human, rational, and egalitarian societies develop, characterized by civil equality, prose language, abstract law, and philosophical reflection.However, Vico's view of history was neither linear nor naively progressive. He observed that rational civilization, when it reaches an extreme state of intellectual hyper-abstraction, skepticism, and moral decadence—what Vico famously termed the barbarie della riflessione (barbarism of reflection)—collapses back into chaos. Society undergoes a ricorso (a historical recourse or re-cycle), forcing humanity to return to a primitive condition from which the cycle of civilization must begin anew under divine providence.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Neapolitan PublishingThe physical production of Vico's works offers a fascinating window into the economic and logistical realities of the early modern Neapolitan publishing trade. In 18th-century Naples, publishing was heavily constrained by ecclesiastical censorship, royal licensing, and chronic financial scarcity. When Vico prepared the first edition of the Scienza Nuova in 1725, he had originally secured a promise of financial patronage from Cardinal Lorenzo Corsini (later Pope Clement XII), to whom the work was dedicated. However, at the last moment, Corsini withdrew his financial backing, citing sudden personal expenses. Devastated and lacking funds, Vico was forced to sell a cherished family ring and drastically abbreviate his manuscript to cut printing costs.The 1725 edition was printed in Naples by Felice Mosca, one of the premier printers of the city, located in the immediate vicinity of Via San Biagio dei Librai. Mosca's press was renowned for its solid typography, utilizing classic Roman and Italic types, yet the constrained budget forced a compact octavo format with minimal ornamentation. For the 1730 edition, Vico personally oversaw the engraving of the celebrated allegorical frontispiece (*la dipintura*), designed by Domenico Antonio Vaccaro and engraved by Antonio Baldi. This emblem served as a visual mnemonic device summarizing Vico's entire philosophical system for the reader. The final edition of 1744, also produced by the press of Felice Mosca, was finalized on Vico's deathbed; he corrected the final proofs in late December 1743, just weeks before his death on January 23, 1744. He was buried in the church of San Filippo Neri (Girolamini) in Naples, where his personal library and archival remnants are preserved to this day.Historiographical Reception, Controversy, and Enduring LegacyDuring his lifetime, Vico remained a relatively obscure provincial scholar. His complex, dense Italian prose, filled with archaisms, neologisms, and intricate structural digressions, alienated contemporary French and Anglo-Saxon philosophes who favored clear, rationalist diction. A prominent exception was the Swiss scholar Jean Le Clerc, who published a brief, respectful notice of Vico's *De antiquissima* in his prestigious journal Bibliothèque Choisie in 1711, establishing a tenuous intellectual link with northern Europe.The true international discovery of Vico occurred in the 19th century, largely through the French historian Jules Michelet. In 1827, Michelet published an abridged French translation of the Scienza Nuova (*Oeuvres choisies de Vico*), which ignited a European re-evaluation of Vico's genius. Michelet declared Vico to be the true founder of the philosophy of history, inspiring romantic thinkers like Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Auguste Comte, and Thomas Carlyle. Karl Marx subsequently cited Vico in Das Kapital, praising Vico's insight that human history differs from natural history because humans have made the former but not the latter. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Wilhelm Dilthey integrated Vico into the foundations of the *Geisteswissenschaften* (human sciences), highlighting Vico as the precursor to modern hermeneutics.In Italy, the Vico revival reached its zenith through the monumental scholarship of Benedetto Croce and Giovanni Gentile. Croce's landmark monograph, La filosofia di Giambattista Vico (1911), alongside the meticulous textual critical editions prepared by Fausto Nicolini, established Vico as the supreme peak of Italian philosophical culture. In the second half of the 20th century, scholars such as Isaiah Berlin (Vico and Herder, 1976), Giorgio Tagliacozzo, and Donald Phillip Verene spearheaded an international Anglo-American resurgence in Vico studies. Today, Vico is recognized as an indispensable visionary whose critiques of technological rationalism, insistence on the imaginative origins of human thought, and profound structural analysis of myth and culture continue to vitalize philosophy, comparative literature, post-colonial theory, and the social sciences worldwide.

academic_description: 4to (220x155 mm). [40], 350, [18] pp. and the portrait of Giuseppa Barbapiccola engraved by Francesco de Grado. Collation: [†]-†††4 **-***4 A-Zz4. With several woodcut illustrations and diagrams in text (some full page). Lavishly bound in contemporary stiff vellum gilt, on the panels gilt coat-of-arms of Cardinal Niccolò Coscia (1682-1755, a much discussed cardinal who during his life time lived also in Naples and may have personally met Barbapiccola, see below), marbled pastedowns, red marbled edges (slightly soiled and worn). Small hole to l. K4 slightly affecting the text, small tear to the lower blank margin of l. S4, some occasional pale staining, a very good, genuine copy with wide margins. Rare first edition. “In 1722 Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola (ca. 1700-ca. 1740) translated René Descartes’s Principles of Philosophy (1644), working primarily from the 1647 French edition rather than the Latin original. Allegedly published in Turin by Giovan Francesco Mairesse, it was in all likelihood one of many books published in Naples under false imprimatur in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The fact that a Neapolitan artist, F. De Grado, engraved Barbapiccola’s portrait for the translation makes it even more probable that it was both written and published there. Like many philosophical works published in Naples, including a number of books that Barbapiccola cited in her preface, it may have been part of the semiclandestine circulation of books in the capital city of the Kingdom of Naples […] More than simply a translation of Descartes’s important work, Barbapiccola’s Italian edition was also a manifesto of women’s right to learn. In her preface, entitled ‘The Translator to the Reader’, she presented Descartes as the creator of a philosophy that celebrated the female mind […] Barbapiccola demonstrated that one did not need to be of royal blood to understand Descartes or, more generally, to reflect on important philosophical questions. But she did far more than this, since her preface was simultaneously a history of women’s learning, a history of philosophy, and an autobiography. She self-consciously presented herself as an heir to the seventeenth-century tradition of Cartesian women and celebrated its arrival in the city of Naples, where she was one of several women known for their philosophical crudition by the early eighteenth century. Another leading female Cartesian, the duchess of Limatola, Aurelia d’Este (1683-1719), had recently died , making it possible for a younger, less noble woman to claim the place that d’Este had occupied as the preeminent Cartesian woman in the city. Barbapiccola offered her own tribute to d’Este when she praised Paolo Mattia Doria for writing his Dialogues in Which It Is Demonstrated That Woman, in Almost All the Important Virtues, Is Not Inferior to Man (1716), a work he addressed to his famous aristocratic pupil, Aurelia d’Este, while he was still enamored with Cartesian philosophy […] Barbapiccola’s preface brought together several different strands of intellectual debate then preoccupying scholars in Naples. On the one hand, it responded to the growing anti-Cartesianism of important philosophers such as Vico and Doria, who increasingly felt that a modern metaphysics that emphasized the mathematical certainty of reason limited the possibilities for other kinds of discussions about the nature of knowledge. On the other hand, it sought to integrate some of the new philosophical insights of Neapolitan scholars into a fresh reading of Descartes. Her preface, for example, invoked Vico’s On the Most Ancient Wisdom of the Italians (1710), a controversial book dedicated to Doria that presented his new historical consciousness about the origins of knowledge as an implicit alternative to Cartesian epistemology. Within a decade, both philosophers would tum away from Descartes, leaving others to defend his philosophy: Barbapiccola, for example, would argue that these different approaches to knowledge were not incompatible […] So much of Barbapiccola’s text is concerned with these philosophical issues that it is easy to forget that she also intended her work as a defense of women’s right to philosophize. History gave her inspiration for her pursuit of learning with its numerous examples of learned women. Knowledge of languages such as Latin gave her the tools for reading and understanding the kind of learning that lay beyond the traditional scope of women’s studies. But it was Cartesian philosophy that gave her the tools to think critically about knowledge […] Through the early 1730s, Neapolitan scholars continued to celebrate Barbapiccola as the woman who had made Descartes glorious in Italy, even as the fascination with Descartes was eclipsed by a new passion for the writings of English philosophers such as John Locke and Isaac Newton.The printer-bookseller Bernardino Gessari advertised Barbapiccola’s translation in 1734 as one of the books to be purchased at his shop on Via San Biagio del Libra. Her book also circulated in other parts of the italian peninsula. In 1740 , for example, when the Sienese cleric Giovan Nicolò Bandiera published his important and controversial treatise on women’s education, he knew enough about Barbapiccola’s work to include her name in his list of contemporary women engaged in philosophical and scientific pursuits in Naples” (P. Findlen, Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola, in: “The Contest for Knowledge: Debates over Women’s Education in Eighteenth-Century Venice”, R. Messbarger and P. Findlen, eds., Chicago, 2005, pp. 37-45).Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola, an important figure in early 18th century Naples cultural circles and a groundbreaking champion for the inclusion of women in natural philosophy and the physical sciences, achieved international scholarly renown through her 1722 translation into Italian of René Descartes’ Principia Philosophiae, which was prefaced by an original feminist manifesto “A’ Lettori” (‘To the Readers’). In this prefatory discourse, Barbapiccola articulated a harsh critique of contemporary educational disparities, arguing that women’s intellectual perceived inferiority was not a consequence of biological or ontological deficiency, but rather the artificial product of systemic educational deprivation. By deploying Cartesian epistemology itself - specifically the doctrine of clear and distinct ideas and the radical dualism of mind and body - Barbapiccola demonstrated that the faculty of reason is fundamentally ungendered, thereby establishing a philosophical foundation for female intellectual emancipation.Born in Salerno around the turn of the eighteenth century, Barbapiccola belonged to an educated, socially prominent family with deep clerical, legal, and intellectual ties across the Kingdom of Naples. Her upbringing was profoundly shaped by her uncle, Agostino Barbapiccola, a learned ecclesiastic, canonist, and active participant in Neapolitan literary circles. Recognizing his niece’s exceptional aptitude, Agostino facilitated her rigorous domestic education, exposing her to classical Latin, modern French, geometry, natural history, and metaphysics. Unlike many of her female contemporaries whose education was confined to devotional literature and domestic arts within convent walls or noble households, Barbapiccola gained direct access to the private libraries and private academies of Naples. During this era, Naples was experiencing a dramatic philosophical shift: the traditional Aristotelian-Scholastic paradigm, long enforced by ecclesiastical authorities, was being vigorously challenged by the jusnaturalism, atomism, and mechanical philosophy promoted by the Accademia degli Investiganti - a vanguard institution founded by Tommaso Cornelio, Leonardo Di Capua, and Lucantonio Porzio. It was within this intellectually charged atmosphere of Neapolitan Cartesianism that Barbapiccola acquired her deep mastery of modern physics and mechanical philosophy.Barbapiccola’s magnum opus was a masterpiece of philosophical translation and linguistic adaptation. Translating Descartes’ original Latin text (first published in Amsterdam in 1644) alongside Claude Clerselier’s authoritative French version (1647), Barbapiccola aimed to make modern mechanical philosophy accessible to an Italian readership, particularly to women who were routinely denied instruction in academic Latin. In her self-assured preface, she boldly situated her work within the long history of female intellectual achievement, evoking classical and modern precedents such as Hypatia of Alexandria, Diotima, Veronica Gambara, Vittoria Colonna, Cassandra Fedele, Anna Maria van Schurmann and Anne Dacier among others. Barbapiccola explicitly challenged the misogynistic assertions of philosophers such as Claude Fleury, who argued in his Traité du choix et de la méthode des études (1686) that female physiology was too delicate or soft to comprehend abstract scientific principles. Barbapiccola contended that if female nerves were indeed more delicate, women were uniquely endowed with superior perceptual sensitivity and cognitive agility, making them exceptionally suited for scientific inquiry.Her translation was not merely a passive linguistic exercise, but an active intervention in European philosophical discourse, seeking to dismantle the gendered barriers surrounding the res publica literaria. Barbapiccola was an active member of the prestigious Accademia degli Arcadi (the Arcadian Academy), adopting the pastoral pseudonym Mirista, under which she composed erudite poetry and exchanged philosophical verses with leading scholars of the realm. Chief among her allies and admirers were the eminent philosopher and historian Giambattista Vico (who is quoted in the preface) and Gherardo degli Angeli. Gherardo was so profoundly impressed by Barbapiccola’s erudition and translation project that he composed an encomiastic sonnet, titled In lode della signora Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola, che ha tradotto da’ francesi ne’ nostri favellari i Principi della Filosofia di Renato Des-Cartes (Rime Scelte, Florence, 1730, vol. 3, p. 104).In this poem, Gherardo celebrated her as a shining beacon of Neapolitan genius who had surpassed the achievements of foreign scholars. Barbapiccola was very close not only to Vico, but also to Vico’s favourite daughter, Luisa, a highly educated woman and a poetress (the two women exchanged poems), and cultivated close ties with prominent Neapolitan natural philosophers, including Pietro Antonio de Martino, Bernardo De Dominici, and the literary patron Antonio Niccolini.The publishing history of Barbapiccola’s I Principi della Filosofia di Renato Des-Cartes, which had been put on the Index of prohibed books as early as 1683, reflects the complex geopolitical and censorial realities of early eighteenth-century Naples. Printed in 1722, the title page bears the false or strategic imprint of Turin, a common typographical maneuver utilized by Neapolitan publishers to bypass local ecclesiastical censorship and political scrutiny regarding Cartesian mechanical philosophy, which remained controversial due to its implications for Eucharistic theology and scholastic physics. The edition included comprehensive diagrams of Cartesian vortices, planetary orbits, and atomic structures, meticulously reproduced to ensure that Italian readers could fully grasp Descartes’ physical cosmology.The owner of the present volume, Niccolò Coscia, was born on 25 January 1682 in Pietradefusi (also known as Petrafusa) in the Archdiocese of Benevento, into a poor and obscure family. He studied at La Sapienza University in Rome, obtaining a doctorate in utroque iure (both canon and civil law) on 30 March 1715. He met Cardinal Vincenzo Maria Orsini, the Archbishop of Benevento and future Pope Benedict XIII, while still young. During one of the cardinal's pastoral visits, he encouraged Coscia to enter the ecclesiastical state and conferred the first tonsure in May 1696. Niccolò studied under the cardinal’s auspices and learned about the affairs of the archiepiscopal curia. In October 1703, the cardinal granted him a canonry in the collegiate church of San Bartolomeo in Benevento. In April 1708, he exchanged this for another in the chapter of the metropolitan cathedral, at the same time being named chancellor of the curia. He was ordained on 28 March 1705 and was appointed secretary to Cardinal Orsini, Archbishop of Benevento. In the archdiocese of Benevento, he served as master of the chamber, treasurer, apostolic visitor, archpriest, and abbot mitered of S. Lorenzo d'Aprice.He accompanied Cardinal Orsini to the conclaves of 1721 and 1724 as conclavist. When Cardinal Orsini was elected pope, Coscia followed him to Rome. On 7 June 1724, he was appointed secretary of Memorials. On 26 June 1724, Coscia was elected titular archbishop of Traianopoli and was created cardinal in the consistory of 11 June 1725. Twenty of the twenty-six cardinals present at the consistory opposed his promotion. The Pope remained unmoved, however, and promoted Archbishop Coscia to the cardinalate. On 5 September 1725, he was appointed archbishop coadjutor of Benevento with the right of succession and was put in charge of governing the archdiocese, a responsibility that was retained by Pope Benedict XIII until his death. Coscia was also appointed Protector of the Sovereign Order of Malta and the Order of the Friars Minor Conventual in 1725, and Protector of the city of Avignon and Prefect of the Congregation of Avignon in 1726.Cardinal Coscia’s conduct had created a great deal of animosity among the other members of the Sacred College of Cardinals. When Pope Benedict XIII died, Cardinal Coscia hid in Rome before fleeing to Cisterna in the fiefdom of Prince Michelangelo Gaetani, Duke of Caserta. Despite the cardinal’s behaviour, the duke gave him refuge and protection. Cardinal Coscia warned the Sacred College that the election of the new pontiff would be invalid without his vote, and he was given assurances that he would be allowed to participate in the conclave. It took him forty days to arrive in Rome with the Duke of Caserta, who accompanied him into the city until the Cardinal had securely entered the conclave. Coscia thus participated in the 1730 conclave, which elected Pope Clement XII. He resigned from the government of the archdiocese on 8 January 1731, not without protest, and sought refuge in Naples the following March, which resulted in the confiscation of all his possessions. In March 1732, he returned to Rome to face the charges against him, residing in S. Prassede while the trial was ongoing. On 9 May 1733, he was charged with extortion, forgery, and breach of trust. He was sentenced to ten years’ imprisonment and excommunication, and was ordered to pay a substantial indemnity. He was imprisoned in Castel SantìAngelo, but was treated fairly.On 23 February 1734, the same pope lifted the major excommunication penalty and restored his active voice in the July 1738 conclave.From 1735 onwards, he was permitted to visit various thermal baths to treat his gout. Following the death of Pope Clement XII, he was released and permitted to participate in the 1740 conclave, which elected Pope Benedict XIV. He retired to private life in Naples in 1741. The new pope ordered a review of the case, and on 8 January 1742 he pardoned the remaining time of his ten-year sentence, reinstated his cardinalate, and absolved him of all charges. Coscia died in Naples on 8 February 1755 (cf. F. Petrucci, Coscia, Niccolò, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 30, Rome, 1984, s.v.).

authors.name: Giovio Paolo
authors.biography: Paolo Giovio (1483–1552)—physician, prelate, historian, biographer, and consummate humanist collector—stands as one of the most brilliant, complex, and pivotal intellectual figures of the High and Late Italian Renaissance. Operating at the very epicenter of European geopolitics during the tumultuous decades of the Italian Wars, the Protestant Reformation, and the expansion of the Ottoman Empire, Giovio fashioned a new mode of contemporary history and biographical portraiture that profoundly reshaped early modern historiography. As the Bishop of Nocera de' Pagani, a trusted advisor to Medici popes, and the creator of the world's first modern portrait museum at his villa in Como, Giovio transcended the classical revival of the Quattrocento to construct an expansive, globalized vision of XVI-century history. His massive Latin chronicle, the Historiarum sui temporis libri XLV, alongside his biographical Elogia and his foundational emblem book, Dialogo dell'imprese militari et amorose, served as indispensible reference points for contemporary statesmen, scholars, and artists throughout early modern Europe.Born in Como on 19 April 1483 into a respected local patrician family, Paolo was the younger son of Luigi Zio (or Giovio), a notary who died around the turn of the century. Left an orphan at a formative age, Paolo was raised and educated under the direct mentorship of his elder brother, Benedetto Giovio, a distinguished humanist scholar, poet, and collector of local antiquities. Benedetto provided his younger brother with a rigorous grounding in Latin poetry, classical rhetoric, and epigraphy. However, seeking a practical profession capable of securing advancement in the fractured political landscape of Lombardy, Paolo pursued medical studies. He matriculated first at the University of Pavia, where he studied philosophy and medicine under prominent figures such as Agostino Nifo and the Pietro Torrigiano tradition, and subsequently transferred to the University of Padua, then the supreme center of Aristotelian natural philosophy and empirical medical instruction in Europe. Under the tutelage of Pietro Pomponazzi and Marcantonio Della Torre, Giovio earned his doctorate in medicine around 1506. His early medical training left an indelible mark on his intellectual methodology: throughout his later career as a historian and biographer, he retained an empirical, diagnostic gaze, treating political actions, human character, and historical catastrophes with the clinical acuity of a seasoned physician.After practicing medicine briefly in Como and Milan—where he witnessed firsthand the volatile shifting alliances between the Sforza, the French crown, and the Swiss cantons—Giovio relocated to Rome around 1512–1513, attracted by the brilliant literary court of Pope Leo X (Giovanni de' Medici). Embraced by the Medici circle for his sharp wit, effortless Latinity, and social grace, Giovio was appointed professor of philosophy at the Archiginnasio della Sapienza. It was during these initial Roman years that Giovio abandoned clinical medicine to devote himself entirely to historical writing and courtly diplomacy. He commenced work on his magnum opus, the Historiarum sui temporis libri XLV, conceiving a grand narrative that would trace European political affairs from the epochal invasion of Italy by Charles VIII of France in 1494 down to his own era. His fortunes became inextricably linked to the Medici dynasty; following the brief and austere pontificate of Adrian VI (whose biography Giovio would later write with biting psychological acuity), Giovio attained high favor under Pope Clement VII (Giulio de' Medici). Clement granted him apartments in the Vatican, loaded him with benefices, and in 1528 appointed him Bishop of Nocera de' Pagani in the Kingdom of Naples—a position that provided Giovio with both ecclesiastical status and an income, though he rarely resided in his diocese.Giovio's middle years were defined by catastrophe, resilience, and intense literary production. During the devastating Sack of Rome in 1527, Giovio was trapped inside Castel Sant'Angelo alongside Clement VII, witnessing the pillage of the Holy City by the imperial troops of Charles V. The tragedy hit Giovio personally and professionally: the draft manuscript of the first decade of his Historiarum was looted from its hiding place in the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. While portions of the lost manuscript were miraculously recovered years later in Spanish hands, the trauma of 1527 deepened Giovio's disillusionment with political idealism and confirmed his commitment to a realistic, Tacitean analysis of power. Following the Sack, Giovio served as an influential diplomatic agent and cultural impresario. He accompanied Clement VII to the imperial coronation of Charles V in Bologna in 1530 and maintained close relations with Cardinal Ippolito de' Medici, Cardinal Alessandro Farnese (later Pope Paul III), and the Imperial chancellor Granvelle. Giovio expanded his diplomatic horizon far beyond Italy, cultivating correspondents across Europe and gathering reports on the Ottoman court of Suleiman the Magnificent, which culminated in his widely translated tract on Turkish military power and organization, the Commentario delle cose de' Turchi (1531).Central to Giovio's enduring legacy was his revolutionary creation of the Musaeum at his villa in Borgo Vico on the shores of Lake Como. Constructed between 1537 and 1543 on the ruins of a villa formerly owned by Pliny the Younger, Giovio's villa was specifically engineered to house his vast collection of portraits of illustrious historical and contemporary figures—a collection that grew to over four hundred paintings. Giovio was the first to use the term Museum in its modern structural and organizational sense. To accompany these portraits, which included European monarchs, Ottoman sultans, popes, military commanders, humanists, poets, and artists, Giovio drafted two series of literary biographical sketches: the Elogia veris clarorum virorum imaginibus subposita (1546) and the Elogia virorum bellica virtute illustrium (1551). In these works, Giovio synthesized classical biographical technique (derived from Suetonius and Plutarch) with vivid eyewitness anecdotes, art historical observations, and psychological portraiture. His active patronage and consultation directly inspired Giorgio Vasari to compose his Vite de' più eccellenti pittori, scultori, e architettori (1550), a monumental enterprise originally conceived during a famous dinner conversation at Cardinal Farnese's palace in which Giovio urged Vasari to write a history of Italian art.The publishing history of Giovio's oeuvre represents a masterclass in early modern print culture and typographical distribution. Recognized across the Continent as a stylist of fluid, majestic Latin prose, Giovio carefully navigated the elite printing houses of Italy, France, and Switzerland. The first monumental folio edition of his Historiarum sui temporis was printed in Florence by Lorenzo Torrentino in two volumes between 1550 and 1552, utilizing exquisite Roman types that epitomized the ducal printing policy of Cosimo I de' Medici. Concurrently, in Paris, the supreme royal printer Robert Estienne published Giovio's Vitae duodecim Vicecomitum Mediolani Principum (1549), a masterful edition adorned with woodcut portraits attributed to Geoffroy Tory's workshop and set in the famous Grecs du Roi and magnificent Roman types carved by Claude Garamont. Venetian presses, particularly those of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari and Vincenzo Valgrisi, proliferated Italian translations of Giovio's works (translated by Lodovico Domenichi and Girolamo Ruscelli), ensuring his accessibility to a vernacular readership. In Basel, the Protestant publisher Heinrich Petri issued monumental folio editions of Giovio's complete historical works, accompanied by detailed woodcut portraits carved by Tobias Stimmer, which preserved the visual record of Giovio's lost Lake Como portrait collection for future generations.Despite his immense literary success and international stature, Giovio's final years were shadowed by political friction and moral controversy. Falling out of favor with Pope Paul III and failing to secure the coveted Archbishopric of Como, Giovio retired to Florence in 1549 under the generous protection of Duke Cosimo I de' Medici. He spent his remaining years polishing his historical narratives and writing his famous Dialogo dell'imprese militari et amorose (published posthumously in 1555), a seminal work that codified the early modern Renaissance theory of personal heraldic emblems and devices. Giovio died in Florence on 11 December 1552 and was buried in the church of San Lorenzo, where a monumental statue by Francesco da Sangallo was later erected in his honor.In the centuries following his death, Giovio's reputation suffered under the attacks of Protestant polemicists and strict Counter-Reformation critics who condemned his candid, pragmatic, and sometimes partisan historiography. The famous accusation that he possessed two pens—a calamo d'oro (golden pen) for his patrons and a calamo di ferro (iron pen) for his enemies—dominated 18th- and 19th-century evaluations of his work. However, modern 20th- and 21st-century scholarship, spearheaded by T. C. Price Zimmermann, Eric Cochrane, and Franco Minonzio, has thoroughly rehabilitated Paolo Giovio. He is now recognized not as a venal mercenary of the pen, but as a brilliant pioneer of global micro-history, a master of diplomatic psychology, and a foundational figure in the history of art criticism, museum studies, and early modern European intellectual networks.

publishers.name: Calvo Francesco Minicio
publishers.biography: Francesco Minicio Calvo (also documented in Renaissance Latinity as Franciscus Minitius Calvus and in modern Italian scholarship as Francesco Minizio Calvo; fl. 1521–1548; died c. 1548/1549) stands as one of the most intellectually compelling and commercially versatile figures in the annals of High Renaissance typography and humanist bookselling. Operating across a crucial transalpine axis that linked the vibrant publishing houses of Basel with the papal court in Rome and the ducal capital of Milan, Calvo embodied the early modern ideal of the bibliopola eruditus—a book merchant who was not merely a mechanical entrepreneur, but an active scholar, editor, and cultural diplomat. At a time when European print culture was undergoing a dramatic shift toward typographic standardization, international trade networks, and specialized editorial scholarship, Calvo carved out a distinct niche by forging intimate ties with Northern European humanists, curial prelates, medical reformers, legal innovators, and court historians. His career spans three turbulent decades marked by the intellectual zenith of the Clementine pontificate, the cataclysmic destruction of the Sack of Rome in 1527, and the subsequent reconfiguration of northern Italian publishing under Spanish-Imperial influence in Milan.Early Life, Transalpine Journeys, and Humanist FormationOriginating from the town of Menaggio on the western shore of Lake Como in Lombardy, Calvo was born into an environment deeply attuned to the trade routes connecting northern Italy with the Swiss Cantons and the Holy Roman Empire. Little is recorded regarding his precise birthdate or early family lineage, but his mastery of Latin, his deep familiarity with classical literature, and his exceptional diplomatic tact indicate a rigorous humanist education, likely pursued in Milan or Pavia. By the late 1510s, Calvo had emerged not as a stationary artisan, but as an itinerant merchant of rare manuscripts and early printed books. It was during this formative period that Calvo established a legendary partnership with the great Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam and the renowned Basel printer Johann Froben. Recognizing Calvo’s scholarly acuity and reliability, Erasmus entrusted the young Lombard with the physical transport of precious codices, authorial proofs, and personal correspondence across the Alps. In the critical edition of Erasmus’s letters (Opus Epistolarum), the great scholar repeatedly commends Calvo for his extraordinary diligence, characterizing him as a vital bridge between the transalpine Northern Renaissance and the intellectual academies of the Italian peninsula.The Roman Enterprise (c. 1521–1527) and the Curial Humanist CircleBy 1521, drawn by the political and financial patronages of the papal court under Leo X and later Clement VII, Calvo established a permanent press and bookselling establishment in Rome, situated in the bustling district of Parione near the Piazza Navona and the papal chancery. Operating under the imprint In Aedibus F. Minitii Calvi, Calvo transformed his workshop into a vibrant literary salon frequented by the premier minds of the Roman Renaissance. His Roman production was distinguished by its elevated editorial standards and its pioneering contribution to medical, topographical, and legal humanism. In 1525, Calvo issued a landmark monument of Renaissance scholarship: the first complete Latin translation of the Hippocratic Corpus (Hippocratis Coi Medicorum Omnium Facile Principis Octoginta Volumina), executed by his associate, the scholar-physician Marco Fabio Calvo of Ravenna. This monumental folio transformed European medical education by rendering the primary Greek medical texts accessible to Latinate scholars prior to the print publication of the original Greek text by Aldus Manutius's successors. Furthermore, in early 1527, Calvo published Marco Fabio Calvo’s groundbreaking Antiquae Urbis Romae cum Regionibus Simulachrum, a revolutionary topographical atlas featuring intricate architectural woodcuts that visually reconstructed ancient Rome district by district. Beyond medical and antiquarian texts, Calvo’s press served as the primary printing venue for early legal treatises by the legal humanist Andrea Alciato and court biographies authored by the historian Paolo Giovio, solidifying Calvo's position at the absolute epicenter of Clementine intellectual life.The Cataclysm of 1527, Escape, and the Milanese Resurgence (1528–1548)The golden age of Calvo’s Roman establishment came to a brutal and devastating end in May 1527, when the unpaid imperial armies of Emperor Charles V breached the walls of Rome. During the infamous Sack of Rome, Calvo’s printing shop, manuscript collection, paper stock, and physical presses were thoroughly plundered and destroyed. Calvo himself was captured, subjected to extortion, and briefly imprisoned by imperial soldiery before managing to escape the devastated city. Bankrupt but resilient, Calvo retreated north to his native Lombardy. By 1528–1530, he successfully re-established his publishing business in Milan, obtaining legal protection, printing monopolies, and commercial privileges from Duke Francesco II Sforza and, later, from the Spanish gubernatorial administration. In Milan, Calvo adapted his enterprise to the changing economic and spiritual climate of northern Italy. He resumed his fruitful publishing partnership with Paolo Giovio, printing authoritative editions of Giovio’s historical works, biographies of the Sforza and Visconti dynasties, and political tracts. Additionally, Calvo expanded into publishing refined italic editions of contemporary Italian poetry, classical Latin texts for university instruction, and theological-devotional treatises that anticipated the early currents of Catholic reform. His Milanese imprints were instantly recognizable by his distinctive printer's mark—often depicting the allegorical figure of Calpurnia or a veiled female emblem of Chastity and Knowledge—and by his exquisite use of sharp Roman typefaces and delicate woodcut initials.Typographical Mastery, Bibliographical Legacy, and Critical HistoriographyFrancesco Minicio Calvo’s legacy extends far beyond his individual press runs; he represents a crucial transitional archetype in the history of the European book trade. Unlike traditional printer-craftsmen who remained confined to their printshops, Calvo operated as an international publishing strategist, integrating manuscript discovery, editorial supervision, typography, and Pan-European distribution. Modern bibliographical scholarship—pioneered by eminent historians such as Dennis E. Rhodes, Angela Nuovo, Frank Hieronymus, and Luigi Balsamo—has demonstrated that Calvo’s network was pivotal in introducing Erasmian humanism to central Italy while simultaneously exporting Italian legal and historical scholarship to Northern Europe. His surviving imprints are held in the world’s most prestigious rare book repositories, including the British Library, the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and the Bodleian Library. Scholars of print culture continue to examine Calvo’s output as a testament to how humanistic erudition, artistic innovation, and commercial adaptability managed to survive and flourish amid the catastrophic political upheavals of 16th-century Italy.
