academic_description: 4to (208x145 mm). [20] leaves. Collation: A-E4. Title page within an elaborate woodcut border featuring the printer’s device at the bottom. Colophon on l. E3v. Roman and italic types. Contemporary cardboards “alla rustica” with parchment reinforcements on the spine (worn, losses to spine, slightly soiled). Some light marginal staining and foxing, overall a good, genuine copy with wide margins. Provenance. On the title page ownership entry “Aureliae Gabiae”. Aurelia Gabbia Abbagara (1546-1609), a female scholar and printer renowned in early seventeenth century Rome for her extraordinary linguistic and mathematical skills, was related to the Armenian Abgar family. In 1593 Aurelia appears in the recordings of the notary Giovanni Prisco Giovenali on the occasion of the sale of a typography in her possession to Giovanni Stefano Scorza, for the sum of 500 scudi. According to the document, Aurelia worked as a “stampatrix” in via del Crocifisso and she was the widow of the “quondam March’Antonio Abbagaro”. A tombstone with a portrait and a commemorative Latin inscription dedicated to her is located inside the church of Santa Maria Egiziaca (the Temple of Portunus) in Rome (cf. C. Santus, New Documents on the Armenian Presence and Printing Activity in Early Modern Rome: Marco Antonio Abagaro (Sult‘anšah), Bartolomeo Abagaro and the “Typographia Gabiana”, in: “Revue des Études Arméniennes”, 2022, pp. 195-223). Her father was Giovan Battista Gabia (d. 1590). Born in Verona in the early 16th century, he was professor of Greek at the University of Rome from around 1553 until 1582. Alongside teaching, he was also active as a translator and editor of Greek and Hebrew texts (cf. E. Del Gallo, Gabia, Giovan Battista, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 51, 1998, s.v.).Rare first edition, dedicated by the author to the Archbishop of Cosenza, Giovanni Ruffo de Theodoli (d. 1527), of the first Western account of Russia. The work was reprinted by Froben in Basel in 1527. It was then translated twice into Italian: the first translation was printed by Imperatore in Venice in 1545, the second appeared in the second volume of Giovanni Battista Ramusio’s Navigationi e Viaggi (1559). It was also included in the collection Novus orbis regionum (1532) and Rerum moscovitarum auctores varii published in 1600. On title-page verso are three poems by Girolamo Delio degli Alessandri, Giano Vitale, and Pietro Corsi. On l. E3r is a poem by Benedetto Lampridio (1478-1540).In Vitale’s poem and on l. A2v there are references to a map of Moschovia, that is today known in only two copies. “The first printed map carrying name ‘Moschovia’ in its title was compiled in Rome in 1525 by Paolo Giovio (1483-1552). He announced it in Libellus de legatione Basilii magni (Rome, 1525), a book he published based on his conversations with Dimitri Gerasimov, an envoy to Pope Clement VII from Grand Duke Vassily III of Moscow. The map’s importance transcends Muscovy, extending to the other medieval Rusian states: the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Novgorod Republic, the lands of the sedentary and nomadic successors of the Mongol Empire (Tartaria), as well as the modern states of Ukraine, Lithuania, Poland, Belarus, and the Russian Federation. For a long time, only several manuscript renditions of the 1525 map were known issued in 1550s by the Venetian mapmaker Battista Agnese, while the printed version was presumed lost. An article in Imago Mundi Vol.72:1 (2020) reported the discovery of an original imprint of the 1525 map back in 2006 at Biblioteca Marciana in Venice. In fact, this was the second known imprint of the map.The first one was sold on December 7, 1993, by Sotheby’s in London and subsequently made its way to the Russian State Archive of Ancient Acts (RGADA) in Moscow (D.A. Khotimsky, The two surviving copies of the 1525 Moscovia map by Paolo Giovio: A comparative study, in: “Conflict & Cartography. The 29th International Conference on the History of Cartography”, Bucharest, 2022). Dmitry Gerasimov, ambassador of Grand Duke Vasily III Ivanovich, arrived in Rome in June 1525. During his two-month stay, he was entertained and interviewed by Paolo Giovio on behalf of Clement VII. The Libellus is therefore the result of those conversations and was published for the occasion as a true “instant book.”In the history of relations between the Russian world and Western Europe, the years in which this mission took place represent a joint effort to bring the Principality of Muscovy and the Holy See closer together - no longer merely from an anti-Turkish perspective, but now also from an anti-Protestant standpoint, in line with the policy pursued since 1518 by Emperor Maximilian I, who sponsored the dispatch of ambassadors Sigmund von Herberstein (1516) and Francesco Da Collo (1518-1519) and supported the peace agreement between the Prince of Muscovy and the King of Poland.These were situations and events that had been unfolding for over a decade and had already aroused Giovio’s interest as early as 1514, when he devoted a section of the first book he wrote for the Historiae to the Russo-Polish War, a topic he later briefly revisited in the historical-political conclusion of the Libellus, dedicated to the major political and military events of the reign of Basil III. It can therefore be said that the reason for the Muscovite ambassador’s visit to Rome was, in essence and primarily, linked to current political events. The Libellus, which originated as a diplomatic account, subsequently gained popularity as a geographical text thanks to its inclusion, as mentioned above, in famous travel anthologies of the time (I. Melani, “Venire a unirsi con esso noi nelle cose della fede”. Un vescovo, un papa, un ambasciatore e “un re di nome non finto”. La Moscovia di Paolo Giovio e la sua tradizione ramusiana, in: “Paradigmi dello sguardo. Percezioni, descrizioni, costruzioni e ricostruzioni della Moscovia tra Medioevo ed Età moderna (Uomini, Merci, Culture)”, Viterbo, 2011, pp. 109-130). Paolo Giovio was born in Como.Because of his father’s early death, Paolo was brought up by his brother, Benedetto, himself a writer of distinction, of whom he speaks with admiration and affectionate gratitude. He took his degree in medicine at Pavia and at first yielded to his brother's kindly insistence that he should justify the expense of his training by practicing that profession, although he was already secretly bent on a literary career. Benedetto’s historical works on Como and the Swiss had excited his rivalry and such scholars as Pomponazzi, whom he heard at Padua, and Lodovico Celio and Giasone Maino at Pavia and Milan had increased his enthusiasm for letters. When, therefore, an outbreak of the plague drove him to Rome (probably about 1516), he found himself free to follow his inclination and he devoted himself to the writing of history.His ready tongue and pen quickly won the favor of Leo X, who thought (or at least said) that his History of His Own Times was second only to Livy. Leo gave him the rank of cavaliere with a pension. Hadrian VI made him canon of the cathedral of Como, remarking that it was a point in his favor that he was no poet. All the Medici were his friends, “by far the surest and strongest safeguards of my life and studies”. He was the constant companion of Clement VII with rooms in the Vatican and when that unhappy pontiff fled for his life during the sack of Rome, it was Giovio who flung his own purple cloak over the Pope’s too conspicuous white robes. His devotion was rewarded the next year by the bishopric of Nocera. Later, in 1530, we find him accompanying Cardinal Ippolito de’ Medici to Bologna for the coronation of Charles V and in 1533 to Marseilles for the marriage of Catherine de’ Medici. The Roman Academy had welcomed him with enthusiasm and scholars had honored him with the dedications of their works.Until the fall of Rome his fortunes had prospered. In that catastrophe he lost many of his possessions including some of his manuscripts and retired for a time to the island of Ischia to bewail his calamities. His reputation, too, had begun to wane. The acclaim with which his writings had been received was gradually tempered by the suspicion that his talents were at the service of the highest bidder. Some of the talk was probably, as he would have us believe, the result of ignorance and envy, but his extravagant eulogy of the infamous Alessandro de’ Medici and his careless frankness as to his own attitude toward the subjects of his biographies certainly support the charges. Still he continued to find supporters. For twenty years he enjoyed the favor of Pompeo Colonna and among others to whom he owed benefits and encouragement were the Marquis of Pescara and his wife Vittoria Colonna, Ippolito d’Este, Isabella d’Este, the Marquis of Vasto, Giberti, and Ottavio Farnese. With the accession of Paul III, however, he fell out of favor at the Vatican. Unsuccessful in his efforts to induce the Pope to make him bishop of Como and disappointed in his hopes of a cardinal’s hat, he finally retired to Como and then to Florence, where he died on December 11, 1552.He was buried in San Lorenzo and his statue still guards the stairs that lead to the Laurentian library. Probably the occupation that gave Giovio most pleasure in his later years was the building and furnishing of the villa on Lake Como, where he collected the portraits of famous men, princes, soldiers, prelates, and scholars. Some of the portraits were originals, some were copied from statues, busts, or paintings. They are now scattered and only a few remain in the possession of his family. The copies made by order of Cosimo I may be seen in the Uffizi. Though Giovio left instructions in his will that not so much as a nail should be removed, Boldoni in his Larius (1617) laments the almost complete ruin of the villa. Whatever may be thought of his sincerity, as a writer Giovio commands our interest. If he is far from being Livy's equal, he shares with his greater countryman the “pictured page”. His work and letters are full of vivid descriptions, many of them those of an eye-witness, e.g. the horrors of the sack of Rome, the passionate scenes on the election of Hadrian VI, the plundering of his native Como by the troops of Pescara (cf. T.C. Price Zimmermann, Paolo Giovio, Princeton, 1995, passim; and B. Agosti, Paolo Giovio. Uno storico lombardo nella cultura artistica del Cinquecento, Florence, 2008, passim).

authors.name: Ernest Augustus, Duke of York and Albany
authors.biography: Ernest Augustus, Duke of York and Albany (17 September 1674 – 14 August 1728), Prince-Bishop of Osnabrück and younger brother of King George I of Great Britain, was an important member of the Hanoverian dynasty during the transition from the late seventeenth-century European order to the Hanoverian accession of 1714. His career combined the roles of a German territorial prince, an Imperial military officer, a Protestant ruler of the constitutionally exceptional Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück, and a senior member of the dynasty that came to occupy the British throne. Although he never exercised sovereign authority in Britain, his position within the Hanoverian family made him an important intermediary between the dynasty's German territories and the new British monarchy.Early Life, Family, and EducationErnest Augustus was born at Osnabrück on 17 September 1674, the youngest of the seven surviving children of Ernest Augustus, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg and later Elector of Hanover, and Sophia of the Palatinate. He was therefore the younger brother of George Louis, the future King George I of Great Britain. Through his mother, he was a grandson of Frederick V, Elector Palatine and the so-called “Winter King” of Bohemia, and of Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of King James I of England and VI of Scotland.His father was at that time Prince-Bishop of Osnabrück, and Ernest Augustus spent his earliest years within the Osnabrück and Hanoverian court environment. After the family established itself more firmly at Hanover, he was educated within the sophisticated intellectual and political milieu associated with his mother Sophia and with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, whose presence at the Hanoverian court contributed greatly to its European cultural reputation. His education also included the customary princely training in languages, diplomacy, courtly conduct, and military affairs. As a young prince he undertook travels that included visits to France and Italy, acquiring the international experience expected of a member of a major German dynasty.Unlike his elder brother George Louis, whose position as heir to the Hanoverian territories became increasingly secure after the establishment of primogeniture, Ernest Augustus had no prospect of inheriting the family's principal territories. His career consequently developed along the traditional paths open to younger German princes: military service, diplomacy, and, ultimately, territorial rule in Osnabrück.Military CareerErnest Augustus entered Imperial military service and participated in the wars fought by the Holy Roman Emperor against France and the Ottoman Empire. During the Nine Years' War he served with Hanoverian and Imperial forces and was present at the Battle of Neerwinden in 1693. His military career continued during the War of the Spanish Succession, when the interests of the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg were closely aligned with the Imperial and Allied cause against France.He was particularly associated with the Allied operations in the Low Countries and took part in the Siege of Lille in 1708. His military service was significant less for the independent command of large formations than for the experience it gave him as a dynastic prince operating within the military and political structures of the Empire. The surviving evidence does not justify attributing to him a prominent independent role at the Battle of Malplaquet in 1709, as the original account does; the more securely documented episode is his participation in the siege of Lille.His military career also strengthened his connections with the Imperial political world at a time when the Hanoverian family was becoming increasingly important within the Empire. The elevation of his father to the electoral dignity in 1692 and the family's subsequent political alignment with the Imperial cause placed Ernest Augustus within a wider network of dynastic and military interests extending from Hanover to Vienna.The Hanoverian Succession and His Dynastic PositionThe death of Queen Anne in August 1714 transformed Ernest Augustus's position. His elder brother George Louis succeeded to the British throne as George I, while retaining his electoral territories in the Holy Roman Empire. The resulting personal union between Great Britain and Hanover created a new political configuration in which members of the Hanoverian family acquired important functions on the Continent.Ernest Augustus became one of the most senior members of the family remaining in Germany. He was closely associated with the court at Herrenhausen, received diplomatic visitors, and participated in the political and cultural affairs of the Hanoverian dynasty. His position became particularly important after George I moved his principal residence to London. Ernest Augustus consequently functioned as an important representative of Hanoverian interests in Germany, although describing him simply as a formal “Regent of Hanover” would be misleading: his authority derived primarily from his position within the dynasty and from the confidence placed in him by his brother.He was also involved in the upbringing and supervision of the young Frederick Louis, George I's grandson and the future Prince of Wales. Keeping Frederick in Germany served a broader dynastic purpose, demonstrating that the new British royal family remained closely connected to its German territories.Prince-Bishop of OsnabrückThe decisive stage of Ernest Augustus's career began with the death of the Catholic Prince-Bishop Karl Joseph of Lorraine in 1715. The constitutional structure of Osnabrück was exceptional within the Holy Roman Empire. Under the arrangements established by the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 and the associated perpetual capitulation of the see, the principality alternated between a Catholic bishop and a Protestant ruler belonging to the House of Brunswick-Lüneburg. During Protestant periods, the ruler was not a Catholic ecclesiastical bishop in the conventional sense but a Lutheran territorial prince exercising the secular government of the principality.The succession nevertheless generated considerable controversy. Ernest Augustus's elder brother Maximilian William had converted to Catholicism and, with support from Catholic interests including the papal side, sought the see himself. The cathedral chapter ultimately rejected this claim and adhered to the confessional provisions governing the principality. Ernest Augustus was unanimously postulated by the cathedral chapter as Protestant Prince-Bishop on 2 March 1716. He arrived in Osnabrück on 9 June of the same year and thereafter took an active role in the government of the territory.His administration was substantially more interventionist than that of his immediate predecessor. Ernest Augustus sought to restore what he regarded as the constitutional and confessional balance established by the Peace of Westphalia and to strengthen the territorial authority of the prince-bishop. His policies brought him into repeated conflict with the Catholic cathedral chapter, whose members defended their traditional ecclesiastical and political privileges.Among the contentious issues were the position of the Jesuits, the number and privileges of religious houses, the jurisdiction of ecclesiastical courts, and financial questions involving the territorial treasury. Ernest Augustus attempted to restrict the jurisdiction of the archdeacons to genuinely ecclesiastical matters and to assert greater control over areas that had developed under the previous Catholic administration. These efforts generated litigation and appeals to the Imperial courts and remained an important feature of his government throughout his reign.Economic and Administrative PoliciesErnest Augustus was nevertheless more than a dynastic figurehead. He took a direct interest in the economic development and material administration of the principality. His government promoted mining and manufacturing and supported several industrial enterprises. Contemporary and later accounts associate his administration with the reopening of abandoned iron mines at the Hüggel, the development of coal production, the salt works at Rothenfelde, and the establishment or encouragement of manufacturing enterprises including glass, wax-processing, and porcelain production.He also sponsored infrastructural works, including bridges and public buildings, and supported charitable and ecclesiastical institutions. His economic policies reflected the broader early eighteenth-century tendency toward cameralist and mercantilist government, in which territorial rulers sought to increase production, employment, and fiscal resources within their lands.His efforts were not always successful. In particular, attempts to reform woodland administration and restrict traditional communal rights encountered resistance from the territorial estates. The government therefore had to negotiate continuously between the prince's conception of territorial improvement and the established corporate privileges of the estates and the cathedral chapter.Duke of York and AlbanyErnest Augustus's position within the British monarchy was formally enhanced during a visit to England in 1716. On 29 June he was created Duke of York and Albany in the Peerage of Great Britain and Earl of Ulster in the Peerage of Ireland. The titles deliberately associated him with the British royal family and had previously been borne by members of the Stuart dynasty.His elevation was primarily dynastic rather than territorial. Ernest Augustus never exercised authority over York, Albany, or Ulster; the titles were honorary peerages attached to his position as the king's brother. They also strengthened the public visibility of a Hanoverian prince within the British political hierarchy at a time when the new dynasty was still establishing itself.He was subsequently appointed a Knight of the Order of the Garter. Contrary to the traditional chronology sometimes given in biographical summaries, the Garter appointment did not take place in 1716: it was completed in 1718, together with that of his grand-nephew Frederick Louis, later Prince of Wales.Court, Culture, and Personal LifeErnest Augustus maintained close connections with the cultural life of the Hanoverian court. His interests extended beyond administration and military affairs to music and court culture, and his influence at Herrenhausen may have contributed to the establishment of George Frideric Handel's position at the Hanoverian court. His role should nevertheless be understood primarily as that of a senior dynastic patron and political figure rather than as the head of an independent artistic establishment comparable to the major princely courts of the period.He never married and left no legitimate descendants. His unmarried status was consistent with the position of a younger dynastic prince whose career had been directed toward military, ecclesiastical, and political service rather than dynastic marriage. Later historians have also discussed evidence concerning his intimate relationships with men, particularly in connection with his correspondence and association with Johann Franz von Wendt. Such evidence has led some modern writers to describe Ernest Augustus as homosexual, but the surviving documentation does not warrant presenting every alleged relationship as an established fact. It is safer to state that his sexuality has been the subject of historical interpretation and that he maintained unusually close relationships with male members of his household and circle.Death and LegacyErnest Augustus died at Schloss Osnabrück on 14 August 1728, aged fifty-three, after continuing to divide his time between Osnabrück and the Hanoverian court. His death marked the end of the second Protestant phase of the early modern Osnabrück succession. In accordance with the constitutional arrangements of the principality, the see passed again to a Catholic ruler. On 4 November 1728 the cathedral chapter elected Clemens August of Bavaria, already Prince-Bishop of several other territories and Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. The succession demonstrated the continuing vitality of the confessional alternation established by the Peace of Westphalia.Ernest Augustus was buried in the princely vault of the Leineschloss in Hanover. His British peerages became extinct upon his death, since he left no legitimate issue. His historical importance, however, lies less in the British titles he briefly held than in the unusual combination of roles he embodied. He was simultaneously a member of the Hanoverian dynasty, an Imperial prince, a Protestant ruler of a constitutionally exceptional Westphalian territory, and a close relative of the first Hanoverian king of Great Britain.His career illustrates the complex political world of the early eighteenth-century Holy Roman Empire, in which dynastic interests, confessional law, territorial sovereignty, Imperial institutions, and the emerging British-Hanoverian connection overlapped. As Prince-Bishop of Osnabrück, he also represents an important episode in the long history of the principality's bi-confessional constitution and in the consolidation of Hanoverian influence in north-western Germany.

academic_description: 4to (185x148 mm). Pp. [8]. Unbound. Uniformly browned. Exteremly rare original edition of the ordinances, promulgated by Ernest Augustus of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1674-1728), concerning the administration of justice, policing and private law, with particular reference to Gypsies, foreign beggars, Jewish beggars and other vagabonds. More specifically, the decree prohibits gypsies, beggars and begging Jews (“Bettel-Juden”) to enter territories under the rule of Ernstest Augustus II, Prince-Bishop of Osnabrück. Inhabitants of his territories are forbidden to accommodate any of these vagrant groups, violations will be punished and denunciations rewarded. Children of such groups under ten year of age will be removed from their families and raised by Christian foster parents. Male gypsies will be branded with a hot iron and driven out of the country, re-entry will be punished by hanging. Other beggars (including Jews) found inside the country will be expelled and threatened with corporal punishment should they return. Prince Ernest Augustus was the youngest son of Elector Ernest Augustus and Sophia of Hanover, and the younger brother of King George I of Great Britain. He served as a military commander and later as the Protestant Prince-Bishop of Osnabrück from 1715 until his death, receiving the British title Duke of York and Albany in 1716.

title: Tarih-i Enderun

authors.name: Hafiz Hizir Ilyas
authors.biography: Tayyarzâde Hâfız Hızır İlyas Ağa (ca. 1801–1864) stands as one of the most remarkable chroniclers, court musicians, and institutional eyewitnesses of the late Ottoman classical period and the dawn of the Tanzimat era. Writing from the vantage point of an insider embedded within the secluded quarters of the Imperial Palace (Enderûn-ı Hümâyûn), Hızır İlyas produced the Târîh-i Enderûn (frequently styled as Letâif-i Enderûn), a monumental record that bridges traditional Ottoman court historiography and early modern personal memoir. Operating under the reign of Sultan Mahmud II (r. 1808–1839)—a period marked by violent centralizing reforms, the annihilation of the Janissary Corps, and the systemic Westernization of state administrative structures—Hızır İlyas provided an unmatchable prosopographical and cultural portrait of top-level palace life during a era of transformative political upheaval.Born in Istanbul around the turn of the nineteenth century into a family associated with Ottoman officialdom—as indicated by his patronymic designation Tayyarzâde (son of Tayyar)—Hızır İlyas received an elite education designed for elite palace service. In 1227 AH (1812 CE), during the early years of Mahmud II's reign, he was inducted into the Enderûn-ı Hümâyûn, the prestigious palace academy situated in the Inner Court of Topkapı Palace. He was initially placed in the Seferli Odayı (Page Brigade of the Campaign), an imperial chamber that had evolved into an academy for music, recitation, pageantry, and personal service to the sovereign. Recognizing his exceptional vocal talents and flawless memorization of the Quran, palace preceptors trained him rigorously in Islamic theology, Arabic and Persian literature, calligraphy, and classical Ottoman music (Makâm theory and performance). Upon completing the memorization of the Quran, he earned the title Hâfız, an accolade that granted him direct access to sacred and ceremonial recitations within the imperial apartments.Hızır İlyas's extraordinary talent as a vocalist (hânende) brought him to the personal attention of Sultan Mahmud II, himself a passionate patron of the arts, an accomplished composer, and an avid performer. Elevated to the Kiler-i Hümâyûn (Imperial Pantry Department) and subsequently to the coveted Hass Oda (Privy Chamber), Hızır İlyas participated regularly in the Sultan's private musical assemblies (fasıl). His proximity to Mahmud II allowed him to observe the intimate workings of the imperial household, the informal networks of court patronage, and the deeply personal anxieties of a monarch determined to dismantle the old order. Hızır İlyas witnessed firsthand the catastrophic events of the Vaka-i Hayriye (the "Auspicious Incident" of 1826), which saw the bloody suppression and destruction of the Janissary Corps, the abolition of the Bektashi dervish order, and the rapid introduction of Western military drills, clothing regulations, and musical institutions supervised by figures such as Giuseppe Donizetti Pasha. Hızır İlyas recorded these tectonic shifts not merely as abstract political developments, but as felt experiences within the physical and social landscape of Topkapı Palace.Following his graduation (çıkma) from palace service into the imperial civil administration (kalemiyye), Hızır İlyas held numerous mid- and senior-level administrative posts throughout the Ottoman bureaucratic network. He served within the Evkâf-ı Hümâyûn Nezâreti (Ministry of Imperial Pious Endowments), held directorships within the state tobacco and customs monopolies (Duhân Mukâtaası), and took up regional administrative roles in provincial councils across the Balkans and Western Anatolia. It was during his mature post-palace years that he authored his magnum opus, the Târîh-i Enderûn. Spanning the years between 1812 and 1859, the text functions as a hybrid work: simultaneously a formal chronicle, a personal diary, an anecdotal anthology (letâif), and an institutional treatise on palace etiquette, architectural spaces, eunuch hierarchies, and musical repertoires. Hızır İlyas provided meticulous accounts of imperial circumcisions, royal weddings, public executions, military reviews, and court banquets, preserving details regarding forgotten musical compositions and the everyday jargon of the page corps that would otherwise have been lost to history.The printing history of Hızır İlyas's work represents a vital milestone in nineteenth-century Ottoman print culture. In 1276 AH (1859–1860 CE), the manuscript was published in Istanbul at the Matbaa-i Âmire (the official Imperial Printing House) under the title Letâif-i Enderûn. Issued as a massive single volume printed in elegant Ottoman Turkish moveable type, the printed edition represented a departure from traditional restricted-circulation palace manuscripts, making intimate imperial history accessible to the expanding literate public of the early Tanzimat era. The publication sparked considerable interest among Ottoman intellectuals and early European Turcologists, who viewed it as an authoritative, unfiltered account of Mahmud II's court and the internal mechanics of Ottoman royal absolutism. Hızır İlyas spent his final years in Istanbul, continuing his administrative obligations while serving as a venerated elder statesman of classical Ottoman musical and literary culture until his death in 1864 (1281 AH).In modern historiography, the work of Hızır İlyas is celebrated as an irreplaceable primary source for Ottoman social history, musicology, and political transition. Scholars of Ottoman court life emphasize that while official court chroniclers (vakanüvis) like Sahaflarşeyhizâde Esad Efendi presented highly sanitized, state-sanctioned accounts of Mahmud II's reign, Hızır İlyas provided a nuanced, humanized narrative that captured the anxieties, cultural ambivalences, and domestic realities of the imperial court. His detailed musical references remain foundational for historical musicologists researching early nineteenth-century Ottoman makâm practice and the institutional transition from classical palace ensembles to Westernized imperial bands. Through his vivid prose, Hızır İlyas immortalized the final twilight of classical Topkapı Palace culture, establishing himself as a key historical voice bridging the early modern Islamic empire and the modern Ottoman state.

publishers.name: Matbaa-i Amire
publishers.biography: The Matbaa-i Amire (Ottoman Turkish: مطبعة عامره, 'The Imperial Printing House'), also historically designated as the Darüttıbaat-ı Amire or the Matbaa-i Hümayun, represents the monumental, state-sponsored institutionalization of typographic print culture within the Ottoman Empire. Established in its permanent imperial administrative form in 1211 AH (1796/1797 AD) under the reforming initiative of Sultan Selim III (r. 1789–1807), the institution transformed the production of text, the dissemination of legal-bureaucratic decrees, and the intellectual landscape of the Near East. Positioned at the structural intersection of imperial governance, military technology, and graphic communication, the Matbaa-i Amire bridged the centuries-old manuscript tradition of Islamic calligraphic art with the mechanical realities of early modern and nineteenth-century print capitalism. Its creation marked a decisive departure from early sporadic printing ventures, establishing a continuous, state-monopolized printing press that laid the bureaucratic and pedagogical foundations for the Tanzimat reforms and the modern Turkish nation-state.To understand the historical necessity and organizational architecture of the Matbaa-i Amire, one must situate it within the broader trajectory of printing technology in the Ottoman lands. Non-Muslim communities within the empire had operated printing presses using typography as early as the late fifteenth century—notably the Jewish press established in Constantinople by David and Samuel ibn Nahmias in 1493, followed by Armenian presses in 1567 and Greek presses in 1627. However, the production of texts in the Arabic script for the Muslim majority remained bound to the manuscript medium for centuries, sustained by a powerful guild of scribes (müstensihler), calligraphers (hattâtîn), and an intellectual framework that prioritized the oral-mnemonic transmission of sacred knowledge under the oversight of the ulema (religious scholars). The pivotal breakthrough for Islamic-script printing occurred in 1727, when Sultan Ahmed III issued an imperial decree (ferman) backed by a legal ruling (fatwa) from Sheikh al-Islam Abdullah Efendi, granting Ibrahim Müteferrika and Mehmed Said Efendi permission to establish a printing press for non-religious works, such as dictionaries, histories, geographies, and tactical military manuals. Although the Müteferrika press produced seventeen seminal titles across twenty-three volumes between 1729 and 1742, its operations ceased shortly after Müteferrika’s death in 1745. The presses fell into disuse despite brief attempted revivals by Qadi Zade Sulaiman Efendi in 1784, demonstrating that private or semi-private print enterprises lacked the systemic administrative infrastructure required for long-term viability.The true institutional foundation of a permanent state-run printing organ emerged during the reign of Sultan Selim III, whose overarching military and administrative reform program—the Nizam-ı Cedid ('New Order')—demanded rapid, standardized dissemination of technical literature, artillery instruction manuals, fortification treatises, and organizational regulations. In 1795, a printing shop was initially set up within the framework of the Mühendishane-i Berrî-i Hümayun (Imperial School of Military Engineering) at Hasköy under the leadership of the school’s chief instructor and engineer, Abdurrahman Efendi. Recognizing the necessity of a centralized, dedicated facility, Selim III authorized the construction of a custom-built imperial printing complex across the Bosphorus in Üsküdar in 1796/1797. This press, formally named the Matbaa-i Amire, integrated the original typographical equipment purchased from the heirs of Ibrahim Müteferrika with newly imported European presses, matrixes, and lead fonts acquired primarily from France and Italy. The Üsküdar facility functioned as a high-capacity state enterprise, publishing technical works such as Mahmud Raif Efendi's famous French-language survey Tableau des nouveaux règlemens de l'Empire Ottoman (1798), alongside classical Arabic-Ottoman lexicons like the Vankulu Lughati and tactical military handbooks designed for the newly trained Nizam-ı Cedid troops.The institutional evolution of the Matbaa-i Amire accelerated dramatically during the reign of Sultan Mahmud II (r. 1808–1839), a monarch whose radical centralizing policies reshaped the Ottoman state apparatus. Following the bloody suppression and abolition of the Janissary Corps in 1826 (the Vaka-i Hayriye or 'Auspicious Incident'), Mahmud II recognized that total administrative control required a unified imperial voice. In 1831, the physical operations of the press were relocated from Üsküdar to the historic peninsula of Istanbul, established near the Bâb-ı Âli (Sublime Porte) and the Beyazıt district, directly adjacent to the center of government. That same year marked the inaugural publication of Takvim-i Vekayi ('Calendar of Events'), the first official state gazette published in Ottoman Turkish, with parallel editions appearing in French, Armenian, Greek, Arabic, and Persian. The mandatory publication of imperial decrees, legislative codes, diplomatic announcements, and official appointments within Takvim-i Vekayi transformed the Matbaa-i Amire from a specialized publisher of military and lexical texts into the primary engine of imperial governance and ideological communication.Typographically and technologically, the Matbaa-i Amire stood at the forefront of Eastern press innovation throughout the nineteenth century. Printing in the Arabic script presented formidable typographic challenges due to the fluid, cursive nature of the letterforms, which vary in shape based on their position within a word (initial, medial, final, or isolated) and require complex ligatures and diacritical marks. Early lead type designed in Western Europe often distorted traditional calligraphic aesthetics, creating friction with traditional readers and scribal elites. To mitigate this, master typefounders at the Matbaa-i Amire painstakingly cut steel punches and cast copper matrices that replicated the elegant proportions of Naskh (Nesih) and Nastaliq (Ta'liq) hands perfected by Ottoman calligraphers. A major technological revolution occurred in 1831 with the introduction of chemical lithography (taş basması) to Istanbul by the French military officer and lithographer Henri Cayol. The Matbaa-i Amire rapidly adopted lithographic presses, as lithography allowed calligraphers to write directly onto treated paper or stone with grease pencils, preserving the precise aesthetic nuance, kerning, and ligatures of sacred calligraphic art. This process dramatically lowered production costs, allowed for the mass reproduction of religious commentaries, Quranic texts, and popular poetry, and effectively reconciled traditional scribal aesthetics with high-volume mechanical reproduction.As the nineteenth century progressed into the Tanzimat era (1839–1876), the administrative control and intellectual scope of the Matbaa-i Amire expanded exponentially. Administratively placed under the purview of the Meclis-i Vâlâ-yı Ahkâm-ı Adliye (Supreme Council of Judicial Ordinances) and later the Maarif Nezareti (Ministry of Public Instruction), the Imperial Press functioned as the primary publishing organ for the burgeoning Ottoman bureaucracy and modernizing educational system. It produced the formal legal codes of the empire, including the Dustur (the official collection of Ottoman statutes) and the civil code, the Mecelle-i Ahkâm-ı Adliyye, formulated under Ahmed Cevdet Pasha. Simultaneously, the press produced hundreds of thousands of standardized textbooks for the newly founded network of primary (Sıbyan), middle (Rüşdiye), and secondary (İdadi) schools, ranging from arithmetic and geography to natural sciences and Ottoman grammar. To meet this immense demand, the Ottoman government invested heavily in modern European machinery, replacing manual wooden and iron screw presses with advanced steam-powered cylinder presses supplied by manufacturers such as König & Bauer and Marinoni, while sourcing industrial-grade paper from the state-owned Beykoz paper factory and specialized European mills.The broader cultural and structural impact of the Matbaa-i Amire on Ottoman society cannot be overstated. By standardizing language, terminology, and legal syntax across its vast output, the Imperial Press played a fundamental role in simplifying written Ottoman Turkish, steering it away from over-ornate, hyper-Persianized chancery styles toward a clearer, more functional prose style suitable for public administration and journalism. Furthermore, while the Matbaa-i Amire retained a state monopoly over official gazettes and educational textbooks, its success catalyzed the rise of commercial private printing houses across Istanbul, Izmir, Cairo, and Beirut. Key figures of the Young Ottoman movement, such as İbrahim Şinasi, Namık Kemal, and Ali Suavi, built upon the print infrastructure and public reading habits cultivated by the Imperial Press to launch private newspapers (such as Tercüman-ı Ahvâl and Tasvîr-i Efkâr), thereby forging a modern Ottoman public sphere.During the reign of Sultan Abdülhamid II (r. 1876–1909), the Matbaa-i Amire was subjected to rigorous bureaucratic oversight and centralized censorship protocols managed by the Encümen-i Teftiş ve Muayene (Inspection and Examination Commission). Nevertheless, its physical infrastructure continued to modernize, incorporating stereotyping, photo-engraving, and automatic linotype casting machines by the turn of the twentieth century. Following the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 and during the tumultuous years of the First World War, the press maintained its critical role in military mobilization, publishing field maps, propaganda pamphlets, and official war dispatches. Following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and the establishment of the Republic of Turkey under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923, the historical institution was reorganized and renamed the Devlet Matbaası (State Printing House). Following the radical Alphabet Reform (Harf Devrimi) of November 1928, which replaced the Arabic-based Ottoman alphabet with the Latin-based modern Turkish alphabet, the physical presses and veteran typographical craftsmen of the former Matbaa-i Amire executed the massive task of re-printing the republic's entire legal, educational, and bureaucratic literature, thus ensuring institutional continuity between the imperial past and the modern Turkish state.

academic_description: 8vo (239x158 mm). 34 (index) pp., [1 blank] leaf, 503 pp. Ink stamp of Matbaa-i Amire on p. [1]. Title on table of contents: Vakayi-yi letaif-i enderun. Title from colophon: Letaif-i vakayi-yi enderuniye. Ottoman Turkish in Arabic script. Contemporary Turkish wallet-style leather binding, gilt tughra (Ottoman sultan’s calligraphic monogram) within a double gilt frame on the panels, gilt ornaments and frame on the overlapping extension, marbled endleaves (slightly worn and rubbed, spine repaired in the middle). Few leaves slightly loosened, some occasional marginal staining, a few leaves slightly browned, marginal tear to a leaf, overall a very good, genuine copy in a gift binding.First edition. Vekâyi-i Letâ’if-i Enderûniyye, commonly referred to as Târîh-i Enderûn, is the only known work of Hafız Hızır İlyas. It is a primary source on Ottoman palace life, detailing events, honours and ceremonies from the time at the Enderun, the imperial Ottoman palace school and court, with a particular focus on the reign of Mahmud II. The text vividly describes court ceremonies and social gatherings, as well as the complex relationships among palace officials. It also contains personal reflections on family dynamics, rivalries, and the ambitions of individuals within the Ottoman court. As a rare literary and historical bridge to the late period of Ottoman divan literature, the work offers insights into the lives and works of notable poets and scholars of the time.

authors.name: Frischlin Nicodemus
authors.biography: Nicodemus Frischlin (22 September 1547 – 29 November 1590) stands as one of the most brilliant, mercurial, and tragic luminaries of late Northern Humanism (Späthumanismus) in the Holy Roman Empire. A polymathic classicist, crowned imperial poet laureate (Poeta Laureatus), playwright, satirst, and philologist, Frischlin’s career represents both the aesthetic zenith and the violent socio-political friction of post-Reformation German academic life. Writing during the confessionally charged decades following the Peace of Augsburg (1555), Frischlin elevated Neo-Latin drama (Dramatica Latina) to unprecedented heights, fusing the comic elegance of Terence and Plautus with the moral urgency of Philippist Lutheranism and contemporary social critique. His explosive intellectual trajectory—marked by fiery disputes with university faculties, biting satires aimed at the territorial nobility, imperial elevations, imprisonment, and a fatal escape attempt from a mountain fortress—reflects the precarious status of the early modern scholar within the entrenched feudal and courtly structures of late sixteenth-century Germany.Born in the Swabian town of Balingen within the Duchy of Württemberg, Frischlin belonged to a staunchly evangelical lineage that embodied the emerging Lutheran pastoral intelligentsia. His father, Jakob Frischlin, served as a Protestant pastor, instilling in young Nicodemus an early mastery of biblical scholarship and classical tongues. In 1563, at the age of sixteen, Frischlin matriculated at the famed Tübinger Stift, the elite Protestant seminary established within the former Augustinian monastery at the University of Tübingen under the administrative reforms of Duke Ulrich and Duke Christoph of Württemberg. At Tübingen, Frischlin studied under some of the most formidable intellects of the Lutheran Reformation, including the classicist and historian Martin Crusius (Martin Kraus, 1526–1607), the theologian Jakob Heerbrand (1521–1600), and Dietrich Schnepf. Exhibiting extraordinary precocity, Frischlin attained his Bachelor of Arts in 1563 and his Master of Arts in 1565. His phenomenal memory, effortless command of Latin and Greek verse, and sharp philological acumen led to his appointment as Extraordinary Professor of Poetry and History at the University of Tübingen in 1568, when he was merely twenty-one years of age. His early marriage to Cherubin Cornicula in 1568 further anchored him to the academic community, though his fiery temperament soon alienated colleagues who viewed his rapid rise with envy.Frischlin’s literary oeuvre spans sacred drama, historical tragedy, philological commentary, epic poetry, and scathing social satire. His dramatic output revolutionized the school drama (Schuldrama) by transforming pedagogical exercises into sophisticated, politically charged masterpieces. Among his earliest dramatic triumphs was Rebecca (1576), a biblical comedy based on the Old Testament narrative of Genesis, which combined classical iambic trimeter with Protestant marital ethics. This was rapidly followed by Susanna (1577), a sacred tragedy exploring judicial corruption, female piety, and state justice, which gained widespread acclaim across German-speaking lands. In 1578, Frischlin published his celebrated satirical drama Priscianus Vapulans ("Priscian Scourged"), an ingenious allegorical comedy in which the classical Roman grammarian Priscian is physically beaten and tormented by medieval scholastic theologians—personified by figures corrupting Latin syntax—until he is rescued by humanistic philology. In Julius Redivivus (written in 1585), widely considered his masterpiece, Frischlin staged a brilliant Renaissance fantasy: Julius Caesar and Marcus Tullius Cicero return from the Underworld to traverse sixteenth-century Germany, marvelling at the modern inventions of printing, artillery, and German humanistic scholarship, while simultaneously decrying the moral laxity and alcoholism of the nobility. His theological satire Phasma (1580) directly waded into the bitter inter-confessional polemics of the era, allegorizing the disputes between Lutherans, Zwinglians, Calvinists, and Roman Catholics over the Eucharist.Beyond his dramatic compositions, Frischlin was an indefatigable philologist and commentator. He produced comprehensive grammatical manuals, including the Nomenclator Trilinguis (Latin, Greek, and German), alongside authoritative commentaries on Virgil’s Bucolics and Georgics, the comedies of Terence, the satires of Persius, and the works of Horace. His intellectual network spanned the highest echelons of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1576, after delivering a dazzling panegyric oration at the Imperial Diet of Ratisbon (Regensburg), Emperor Rudolf II bestowed upon him the prestigious title of Poeta Laureatus and raised him to the rank of Imperial Count Palatine (Comes Palatinus). However, this imperial favor amplified Frischlin’s arrogance and escalated his feuds with the Swabian territorial aristocracy and his university peers. The crisis erupted in 1578 with his famous address, Oratio de vita rustica ("Oration on Rustic Life"). In this text, Frischlin praised the labor, moral purity, and economic indispensability of the peasantry while delivering an uncompromising, caustic indictment of the uneducated, decadent, and parasitic lives of the Swabian knights (Ritter). The outraged nobility demanded his punishment, triggering a decades-long cycle of lawsuits, physical assaults, and political persecution.The print production and dissemination of Frischlin’s works form a crucial chapter in early modern German typography and publishing history. His early dramas and academic lectures were initially issued by the dominant university presses of Tübingen, notably Alexander Hock and Georg Gruppenbach. These imprint editions were meticulous typographical productions, typically rendered in elegant Roman types (Antiqua) for Latin verse and classical quotations, interspersed with italic (Cursiva) for dramatic stage directions and high-quality Woodcut ornaments. As conflict rendered Tübingen inhospitable, Frischlin sought publishing channels in major imperial printing hubs. His works were eagerly printed in Frankfurt am Main by prominent entrepreneurial publishers such as Johann Spies and Sigmund Feyerabend, as well as in Strasbourg by the houses of Bernhard Jobin and the Rihel family. The Frankfurt editions, often printed in compact octavo and quarto formats, featured elaborate woodcut title borders and vignettes. Following his death, Frischlin’s scattered manuscripts and extensive literary remainders were compiled and published through the devoted editorial labor of his brother, Jakob Frischlin (1557–1621), a schoolmaster and author in his own right. The posthumous publication of Frischlin’s collected works, including the monumental Operum Poeticorum (Strasbourg, 1598) and his Comoediae et Tragoediae, guaranteed his texts a permanent place in the European Republic of Letters, circulating widely across Scandinavian, Dutch, and English humanist circles.Frischlin’s final years were defined by peripatetic exile and profound personal tragedy. Forced to resign his professorship at Tübingen in 1582 under pressure from Duke Ludwig of Württemberg and the hostile faculty led by Martin Crusius, Frischlin accepted a position as rector of the Protestant Latin School in Laibach (now Ljubljana, Slovenia) from 1582 to 1584. Yet his combative nature prevented long-term stability. Returning to Germany, he lived as an itinerant scholar in Frankfurt, Mainz, Wittenberg, Braunschweig, and Kassel, vainly seeking a permanent academic chair or princely patronage. Unable to silence his pen, Frischlin authored increasingly unsparing vindications and libelous pamphlets—such as his Declaratio and Expostulatio—attacking the Württemberg privy councillors and noble court officials. In March 1590, while residing in Mainz, he was arrested by local authorities acting on an extradition request from Duke Ludwig of Württemberg. He was secretly transported to the formidable fortress of Hohenurach (Burg Hohenurach), situated high above the valley of Bad Urach in the Swabian Jura, where he was subjected to strict solitary confinement and rigorous interrogation.Desperate to regain his freedom and convinced that he would face lifelong imprisonment or execution, Frischlin planned a daring escape. On the night of 29 November 1590, using improvised ropes constructed from twisted bedsheets and clothes, he attempted to descend the sheer, icy cliff face beneath his prison window. Mid-descent, the rope snapped, and Frischlin fell into the rocky abyss below, dying instantly at the age of forty-three. His violent death shocked the early modern scholarly community, transforming him into an immediate martyr for academic freedom and poetic expression. While his contemporary detractors condemned his polemical violence and vanity, subsequent generations recognized Frischlin as the greatest German Neo-Latin dramatist of the sixteenth century. His works profoundly influenced early modern German theatre, bridging the gap between medieval carnival plays and the Baroque tragedy of Martin Opitz and Andreas Gryphius, leaving behind an indelible legacy of linguistic brilliance, fearless social criticism, and tragic artistic heroism.

publishers.name: Jobin Bernhardt
publishers.biography: Jobin Bernhardt (also rendered in contemporary German typographical registers as Bernhard Jobin, Bernhart Jobin, or in Latinized colophons as Bernhardus Jobinus; fl. 1570–1593/1594) stands as one of the most versatile, intellectually vibrant, and commercially influential printmakers, engravers, and typographers of the Northern Renaissance. Active in the Imperial Free City of Strasbourg during the crucial decades of the late sixteenth century, Jobin inhabited the dynamic intersection where Protestant humanism, vernacular satirical literature, fine art engraving, and musical publication converged. Operating in an era characterized by intense confessionalization, rapid expansion of the book market, and profound artistic cross-pollination between the Swiss Confederation and the Holy Roman Empire, Jobin elevated the Strasbourg press from a localized engine of evangelical pamphlet production into an international center for illustrated literature, instrumental music books, and sophisticated woodcut iconography.The precise origins and early formative years of Jobin Bernhardt remain partially shrouded in the archival record of the Upper Rhine, though early genealogical registers suggest roots in Belfort (Beffert) or the surrounding Alsatian hinterlands before his permanent establishment in Strasbourg. Trained initially in the meticulous craft of the Formschneider (woodblock cutter and engraver), Jobin mastered the mechanical and artistic techniques required to translate complex painterly designs onto high-relief wooden matrixes. His decisive integration into the intellectual and cultural elite of Strasbourg was formalized around 1566 through his marriage to Anna Fischart, the sister of the renowned humanist polymath, satirist, and legal scholar Johann Fischart (c. 1546–1590). This matrimonial alliance forged an extraordinary creative partnership between printer and author that would define the landscape of late sixteenth-century German vernacular literature. Settling in Strasbourg, Jobin acquired citizenship, matriculated into the local guild of painters and printers, and established an independent printing house equipped with multiple presses, casting matrices, and specialized woodcut workshops.The editorial program of Jobin Bernhardt was distinguished by his close, symbiotic relationship with Johann Fischart, whose sprawling, polyphonic, and linguistic-experimental works Jobin printed, illustrated, and distributed across the Holy Roman Empire. Jobin was the exclusive publisher responsible for issuing Fischart's most radical literary achievements, including the celebrated Geschichtklitterung (1575, expanded in 1582 and 1590)—an extraordinary, highly creative adaptation and radical transformation of François Rabelais's Gargantua. Through Jobin’s meticulous typography and typographic design, Fischart’s complex linguistic puns, neologisms, and layered marginal commentaries were organized into readable, visually dynamic printed pages. Jobin also manufactured and published Fischart’s biting anti-papal and anti-Jesuit satires, such as Nachtrab oder Nebelkräh (1570), Das Podagrammisch Trostbüchlein (1577), and Ehezucht (1578), alongside moralizing domestic treatises and translated histories. These publications established the Jobin press as the preeminent mouthpiece of vibrant, combative Lutheran and Reformed vernacular culture in Southwestern Germany.Parallel to his literary publications, Jobin Bernhardt achieved international renown through his collaborative artistic ventures with the master Swiss painter and illustrator Tobias Stimmer (1539–1584). Recognizing Stimmer’s genius in Mannerist block design, Jobin engaged Stimmer to produce monumental series of woodcuts that Jobin himself cut into wood or oversaw through his studio assistants. Among their most celebrated achievements was the magnificent Neue Künstliche Figuren Biblischer Historien (printed by Jobin in 1576), an emblem-like pictorial Bible featuring intricate architectural borders, expressive figural groupings, and accompanying poetic verses in German and Latin written by Fischart. Jobin was also instrumental in printing and publishing Stimmer's famous portrait series, including the Icones sive Imagines Vivae Literis Claris Virorum (1589), which provided iconic, authoritative visual likenesses of Protestant Reformers, contemporary European scholars, legal minds, and political rulers. Jobin’s precise cutting technique—preserving the delicate cross-hatching, calligraphic fluidity, and dramatic chiaroscuro of Stimmer’s drawings—set a new standard for Northern European book illustration, challenging the dominance of Nuremberg and Frankfurt presses.Beyond vernacular satire and visual arts, Jobin Bernhardt holds a monumental position in the history of Renaissance music printing and instrumental pedagogy. A skilled lutenist himself, Jobin recognized the growing demand among urban patricians, university students, and noble amateurs for printed instrumental music in German lute tablature (Deutsche Lautentabulatur). In 1572, Jobin printed and published his landmark anthology Das erste Buch der Lauten, followed swiftly in 1573 by Das ander Buch der Lauten. These monumental volumes featured intricate woodcut music types and contained elaborate arrangements of vocal chansons, motets, madrigals, and German lieds by European masters such as Orlando di Lasso, Clemens non Papa, and Jacques Arcadelt, alongside original dances (passamezzi, gagliarde, padovane) composed by leading lutenists including Sixt Kargel, Melchior Neusidler, and Valentin Bakfark. Jobin designed a clear, highly legible system for printing the complex numeric and alphabetical grids of lute tablature alongside elaborate woodcut initial letters and ornamental headpieces, making his music books highly prized across the Continent.The operational infrastructure of Jobin's printing office reflected the sophisticated business strategies required by late sixteenth-century print capitalism. Situated in Strasbourg—a key trade node connecting the Rhineland, Switzerland, France, and the Low Countries—Jobin actively sought Imperial Privileges (Privilegia Caesarea) from Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolf II to protect his costly music books and illustrated editions from piracy by rival printers in Basel, Nuremberg, and Frankfurt. Jobin maintained an active presence at the biannual Frankfurt Book Fair (Frankfurter Buchmesse), where he distributed his catalogues, bartered unbound sheets with international booksellers, and acquired paper stock. His pressmarks frequently featured symbolic allegories of industry, faith, and artistic truth, including motifs of the anvil, celestial globes, and personifications of Veritas and Fides, signaling the intellectual integrity and technical precision of his shop.Following Jobin Bernhardt’s death in Strasbourg around late 1593 or early 1594, his extensive printing establishment, inventory of copperplates and woodblocks, and editorial privileges were inherited and carried on by his son, Tobias Jobin, who continued publishing under the family name into the early seventeenth century. The legacy of Jobin Bernhardt remains an essential pillar of early modern bibliographical study. His presses preserved the seminal literary output of Johann Fischart, defined the visual landscape of late Renaissance German art through the woodcuts of Tobias Stimmer, and revolutionized the dissemination of lute repertoire across Western Europe. Scholars of typography, musicology, and art history continue to regard Jobin as an exemplar of the early modern master craftsman—a publisher who seamlessly synthesized artistic mastery, mechanical innovation, and humanist erudition.

publisher_data: Impressum in Iazygi- / bus-Metanastis, Anno Chri- / ti-nati [sic] 1592. Antichristi verò / revelati 75. [Strassburg, Bernhard Jobin], 1592
academic_description: 8vo (141x90 mm). [64] leaves. Collation: A-H8. Text in Latin, but summaries, two final choirs and epilogue in German verse. Woodcut ornament on the title page. Modern boards. Bookplate Martin Schupp on the title page. Some ancient underlining and annotations. Slightly uniformly browned, margins cut short occasionally affecting the printed marginalia. Apparently unrecorded variant of the first edition (?) with the misprint “Chriti” instead of “Christi” at the bottom of the title page. The edition was printed in Strassburg by Bernhard Jobin. Several variant issues of this 1592 edition are known, and establishing a chronological order for them is basically impossible. Jobin and his heirs reprinted the work in 1593, 1595 (in Frischlin’s collected works) and 1598. It remained popular throughout the 17th century and was also translated into Italian (Augsburg, 1611) and German (Augsburg, 1671).This comedy, which appeared two years after Frischlin’s tragic death while attempting to escape from the Hohenurach fortress, is a seminal work on the religious conflicts of the late 16th century. In it, Frischlin presents various religious movements and sects of his time on stage in a satirical and allegorical manner from a decidedly Lutheran perspective. The work was written amid the bitter confessional conflicts of the late Reformation, particularly the dispute between Lutheran orthodoxy and emerging Calvinism (so-called “crypto-Calvinism”) as well as the Catholic Counter-Reformation.A ghost (‘phasma’) appears in a town, causing turmoil among the citizens. This ghost serves as an allegory for religious aberrations and heresies, as well as the hypocrisy of the various religious factions. Frischlin, a combative Lutheran, attacks everyone. He criticises the Jesuits (Catholicism), the Calvinists (Zwinglians) and the Anabaptists equally. Following the model of ancient comedy (Terence in particular), Frischlin uses satire to ridicule his theological opponents; laughter becomes a weapon in the denominational dispute, while drama becomes a medium for religious propaganda. Controversial theological dogmas (such as the doctrines of the Lord's Supper and predestination) are brought to the stage and presented in a polemical and exaggerated manner to an educated audience of scholars and students. Although Lutheran authorities were often sceptical of theatre due to its potential immorality, Phasma demonstrated how Neo-Latin school drama could be deliberately employed to strengthen confessional identity (cf. D.F. Strauss, Leben und Schriften des Dichters und Philologen Nicodemus Frischlin, Frankfurt a.M., 1856, pp. 125-130; and R.E. Schade, Komödie und Konfession. Eine Dokumentation zu Frischlins ‘Phasma’ (1592), in: “Euphorion”, vol. 86.3, 1992, pp. 284-318).After receiving his early education in Balingen, Königsbronn and Bebenhausen, Nicodemus Frischlin matriculated at Tübingen in 1562. In 1568, he was appointed professor of poetics and history at the university. Following difficulties with his colleagues at the university, he took up the position of head of the Landeschule in Laibach. However, the quarrels resumed when he returned to Tübingen. In 1577, he was crowned ‘poeta laureatus’ by Emperor Rudolph II. He then led a nomadic life, travelling to Prague, Wittenberg, Kassel, Marburg, Braunschweig and Frankfurt. Ultimately, he was arrested in Mainz and imprisoned in the Hohenurach fortress. He died while attempting to escape (cf. S.M. Wheels, Publish and perish: on the martyrdom of Philipp Nicodemus Frischlin, in: “Neophilologus”, LVIII, 1974, pp. 41-51; and R.E. Schade, Philipp Nicodemus Frischlin, in: “Deutsche Dichter der frühen Neuzeit (1450-1600)”, S. Füssel, ed., Berlin, 1993, pp. 613-625).

publishers.name: Dalla Volpe Lelio
publishers.biography: Lelio Dalla Volpe (1685–1749) stands as one of the most transformative figures in eighteenth-century Italian typography, book design, and intellectual culture. Operating from the vibrant university city of Bologna during the height of the Enlightenment (Illuminismo), Dalla Volpe elevated Bolognese printing from a period of late Baroque provincial stagnation to an internationally recognized standard of aesthetic elegance and scholarly rigor. Working under his iconic press mark, All'Insegna della Volpe ('At the Sign of the Fox'), he established a printing house that became the central nexus for the Republic of Letters in Emilia-Romagna. His shop served not merely as a commercial enterprise, but as an intellectual salon where scientific empiricism, artistic theory, and humanist scholarship converged. As the official printer to both the prestigious Accademia delle Scienze dell'Istituto di Bologna and the artistic Accademia Clementina, Dalla Volpe played an indispensable role in disseminating modern Newtonian and Galilean science, art historical theory, and contemporary literature across Europe.Born in Bologna in 1685, Dalla Volpe was raised in an urban milieu steeped in academic traditions yet undergoing profound institutional transformation. His early formative years coincided with the intellectual campaigns led by General Count Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, who sought to liberate Bolognese intellectual life from scholastic conservatism by founding the Istituto delle Scienze in 1711. Dalla Volpe received a rigorous apprenticeship in both typography and calcography (copperplate engraving). Unlike many contemporary printers who relied solely on movable letterpress type, Dalla Volpe recognized early in his career that the future of academic and artistic publishing lay in the seamless integration of typography with fine calcographic illustration. Establishing his independent workshop in the heart of Bologna near the Piazza Maggiore, he rapidly acquired an exceptional inventory of founts, modeled after the finest Roman and Venetian cuts, as well as heavy-duty rolling presses capable of rendering delicate copperplate engravings with unprecedented precision.The cornerstone of Dalla Volpe's intellectual influence was his close, symbiotic relationship with the leading luminaries of the Bolognese Enlightenment. Chief among these was the polymath and philosopher Francesco Maria Zanotti, long-time secretary of the Accademia delle Scienze, whose influential treatises on moral philosophy, optics, and Newtonian mechanics were published with extraordinary typographic care by Dalla Volpe. Equally critical was his collaboration with Francesco Maria's brother, the painter, poet, and art theorist Giampietro Zanotti. In 1739, Dalla Volpe published Giampietro Zanotti's monumental two-volume Storia dell'Accademia Clementina di Bologna, a masterwork of eighteenth-century book production. This magnificent folio publication, lavishly illustrated with portraits, historiated initials, vignettes, and tailpieces designed and engraved by leading Emilian artists such as Domenico Maria Fratta, Ercole Lelli, and Donato Creti, demonstrated Dalla Volpe's unmatched ability to harmonize visual art with crisp, perfectly balanced letterpress typography.Dalla Volpe's press became the primary engine for the dissemination of cutting-edge scientific research. He was entrusted with printing the official transactions of the Accademia delle Scienze, including the Commentarii of the Institute, which circulated throughout the scientific academies of London, Paris, Berlin, and St. Petersburg. He printed the astronomical ephemerides and mathematical papers of Eustachio Manfredi, the pioneer of modern Italian astronomy, as well as the landmark medical and chemical studies of Jacopo Bartolomeo Beccari. Furthermore, Dalla Volpe's press was instrumental in supporting the academic career of Laura Bassi, the world's first woman to be appointed a university chair in physics; Dalla Volpe printed her public philosophical theses and academic dissertations, signaling his press's participation in the vanguard of progressive gender and scientific discourse in Papal Europe. In the realm of belles-lettres, Dalla Volpe published the dramatic works and poetic treatises of Pier Jacopo Martello, the lyric poetry of Eustachio Manfredi, and refined editions of Italian classics, equipping them with erudite apparatuses and critical commentaries.From a technological and material perspective, Dalla Volpe revolutionized the typographic standards of the Emilian publishing trade. He rejected the cheap, highly acidic papers and worn founts common in provincial Papal presses, instead sourcing premium rag paper from the renowned mills of Fabriano and the foothills of the Apennines. His typographic compositions featured generous margins, wide leading, and pristine presswork using deep black, oil-rich inks. Operating under the watchful gaze of the Papal Legate and the Master of the Sacred Palace in Bologna, Dalla Volpe navigated the delicate political dynamics of Church censorship with remarkable diplomacy. He secured lucrative civic and ecclesiastical privileges (con licenza de' Superiori) while simultaneously publishing scientific texts that championed Cartesian and Newtonian natural philosophy. His distribution network extended far beyond the Papal States, establishing direct commercial channels with major bookselling centers in Venice, Florence, Milan, Rome, Lyons, and Leipzig.Upon his death in Bologna in 1749, Lelio Dalla Volpe left behind a flourishing business and a towering typographic legacy. The press was inherited and expanded by his son, Petronio Dalla Volpe (1718–1798), who maintained the house's rigorous aesthetic and intellectual standards well into the late eighteenth century, continuing to serve as printer to the University and the city's academies. Contemporaries from Scipione Maffei to Ludovico Antonio Muratori praised Lelio Dalla Volpe as the restorer of Bolognese printing prestige. In modern historiography, bibliographers and book historians such as Albano Sorbelli, Luigi Balsamo, and Maria Gioia Tavoni have recognized Dalla Volpe not merely as an artisan or tradesman, but as an indispensable cultural broker of the Enlightenment—a master typographer whose aesthetic vision and scholarly commitments gave physical form to the intellectual rebirth of eighteenth-century Italy.

related_names.name: Leonardis Giacomo
related_names.biography: Giacomo Leonardis (1723–1794) stands as one of the most prolific and technically versatile figures in the late eighteenth-century Venetian printmaking ecosystem. Born in Palmanova in the Friuli region—then a garrison town under the firm dominion of the Most Serene Republic of Venice—Leonardis migrated early in his formative development to the lagoon capital. His career unfolded during a brilliant twilight period of Venetian art, an era characterized by the luminous painterly innovations of Giambattista Tiepolo, Sebastiano Ricci, and Pietro Longhi, matched concurrently by an unprecedented boom in commercial printmaking and international book publishing. Within this dynamic artistic network, Leonardis established himself as a master of reproductive etching and burin engraving, bridging the gap between painterly invention and widespread graphic dissemination across Enlightenment Europe.The early education of Leonardis in Friuli remains sparse in archival documentation, yet his rapid integration into the artistic institutions of Venice underscores a rigorous grounding in draftsmanship and copperplate technique. Upon establishing his residence in Venice, he aligned himself with the institutional apparatus of the Accademia di Pittura e Scultura di Venezia, founded in 1750 under the presidency of Giambattista Tiepolo and Giovanni Battista Pittoni. Leonardis's extraordinary command of anatomical drawing and chiaroscuro tonal gradation earned him prestigious institutional recognition; most notably, in 1765 he was awarded the first prize in printmaking by the Accademia, a distinction that solidified his reputation among the patrician patrons and leading publishers of the Serenissima. His academic training exposed him to the sophisticated etching strategies of Joseph Wagner, whose Venetian workshop had revolutionized reproductive printmaking by combining light etching (acquaforte) with crisp, disciplined burin retouching (bulino).Throughout his mature career, Leonardis devoted much of his artistic energy to the transcription of major painted masterpieces into the graphic medium. His reproductive portfolio reflects a deep affinity for Venetian Rococo and Baroque masters, including Giambattista Tiepolo, Domenico Tiepolo, Sebastiano Ricci, Giulio Carpioni, Jacopo Bassano, Paolo Veronese, and Jacopo Tintoretto. In translating these monumental oil paintings and frescoes onto copperplates, Leonardis developed a distinct stylistic signature: he utilized a soft, fluid etched line to capture the shimmering atmospheric light and loose brushwork (pennellata) characteristic of Venetian painting, subsequently employing fine burin cross-hatching to build dense shadows, tactile textures, and sculptural form. His prints after Carpioni's bacchic friezes and Sebastiano Ricci's mythological compositions were widely sought after by European connoisseurs, serving to canonicalize Venetian visual culture within the private print cabinets of Paris, Leipzig, and London.In addition to his standalone reproductive sheets and print series, Leonardis was a central protagonist in the flourishing Venetian book trade, collaborating with prominent publishers such as Antonio Zatta, Giambattista Pasquali, and Simone Occhi. His most ambitious typographical contribution arrived with the monumental four-volume edition of Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, issued by Antonio Zatta between 1772 and 1773. For this celebrated publishing venture, Leonardis etched and engraved dozens of elaborate full-page illustrations, decorative headpieces (testate), tailpieces (finalini), and architectural borders, frequently working from preparatory designs supplied by Bernardo Novelli and Charles-Nicolas Cochin. His contributions to architectural treatises, liturgical folios, and illustrated editions of Torquato Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata and Dante Alighieri's La Divina Commedia further highlight his ability to harmonize graphic design with complex literary iconographies.The logistical and commercial operations of Leonardis's workshop in Venice were intimately intertwined with the regional paper manufacturing mills of Bassano and the international distribution channels managed by the Remondini firm. Printing on high-grade rag paper bearing historical Venetian watermarks, Leonardis managed multiple state revisions of his copperplates, ensuring both high impression quality for elite collectors and broader commercial runs for the book market. His dual role as an academic printmaker and a commercial illustrator positioned him at the center of the Venetian Enlightenment, maintaining close intellectual contacts with patrician collectors such as the Manin and Pisani families. Upon his death in Venice in 1794, on the eve of the Venetian Republic's political dissolution, Leonardis left behind an expansive graphic archive that remains a definitive document of eighteenth-century Venetian taste, print technology, and reproductive aesthetics.

publisher_data: Bologna, Lelio dalla Volpe impressore dell'Instituto delle Scienze, 1762
academic_description: Folio (384x256 mm). XVI, XXIV, 75, [1 blank] pp. including an allegorical frontispiece (depicting Juno presenting the coats of arms of the bride and groom's families to Zeus, seated on his throne; at the bottom are Diana and Hecate, along with a view of the city of Bologna), a full-page portrait of the bride and groom, as well as 10 head- and tail-pieces, all engraved by Giacomo Leonardis after Vittorio Bigheri, Flaminio Minozzi, and others. Engraved historiated initials. Contemporary cardboards (rebacked). Some occasional foxing, pale stain towards the end of the volume, a very good, genuine copy with wide margins.A lavish publication printed by Lelio della Volpe to commemorate the wedding of Giovanni Lambertini and Lucrezia Savorgnan. The text comprises ten chapters on the wedding rites observed by the Romans, as well as a letter and an essay by Floriano Malvezzi (Diomede Egeriaco). Malvezzi was a scholar of natural history and antiquities, highly regarded for his erudition and frequently consulted on matters concerning art galleries and museums.Giacomo Leonardis, a native of Palmanova, studied under Giambattista Tiepolo and likely in Wagner's Venetian workshop. He was the engraver of some of the finest Venetian editions of the 18th century, including Il Goffredo, ovvero Gerusalemme liberata di Torquato Tasso (Venice, Antonio Groppo, 1760-1761), La Divina Commedia di Dante Alighieri (Venice, Antonio Zatta, 1757-1758), and Ariosto's Orlando furioso (Venice, Antonio Zatta, 1772-1773).“Splendida edizione con allusioni in rame, e tenuta in pregio per le opere che vi si contengono in prosa e in verso […] La parte poetica presenta dieci capitoli in terzine su i particolari riti osservati dai Romani precedenti le loro nozze. Vi si prestarono valorosi rimatori bolognesi ed esteri citati in fronte. Stimatissima è pur la prosa che sta avanti le poesie, ove di questa parte di storia romana ragiona, per il fino criterio e l'erudizione con cui è scritta appoggiata all'autorità de' classici autori citati a piè di pagina: siccome commendevoli sono le annotazioni che hanno relazione a detta prosa. L'autore di essa e delle annotazioni è Mons. Floriano Malvezzi velato col nome accademico di Diomede Egeriaco […] La sola storica narrazione venne riprodotta in simile occasione colle stampe di Perugia nel 1791, ed in Bologna nel 1823. Del medesimo è pur la descrizione in tutti gl'intagli sparsi pel libro, tratti da frammenti antichi, da cammei, e da medaglie alludenti all'accennato soggetto. Opportune si presentano anche le annotazioni alle poetiche composizioni delle quali ne ha merito l'altro egregio cimeliarca Giacomo Tazio Biancani, colle quali mette fine alla presente pregevolissima Raccolta acconcia a porgere diletto insieme ad utilità; il che di raro avviene a siffatti libri le più volte tributati al solo fasto, spessissimo alla menzogna” (G. Canterzani, Catalogo dei libri pubblicati da Lelio e Petronio dalla Volpe, Bologna, 1979, p. 223).
