publishers.name: Ibarra Joaquín
publishers.biography: Joaquín Ibarra y Marín (Zaragoza, 19 or 20 July 1725 – Madrid, 13 November 1785) was the foremost Spanish printer of the second half of the eighteenth century and one of the principal representatives of the European typographical renewal associated with the Enlightenment. His importance lies not in the invention of a single revolutionary printing device, but in the exceptional integration of typography, type design, paper manufacture and finishing, presswork, illustration, editorial scholarship, and workshop organization achieved under his direction.His Madrid establishment produced books for the Crown, the Royal Academy of Spain, learned institutions, ecclesiastical authorities, booksellers, and private patrons. Among its most celebrated productions were the 1772 edition of Sallust's La conjuración de Catilina y la guerra de Jugurta, translated by the Infante Don Gabriel de Borbón and revised by Francisco Pérez Bayer, and the four-volume 1780 edition of Cervantes's Don Quixote, commissioned by the Real Academia Española. The latter employed types cut expressly for the project by Jerónimo Antonio Gil and a large programme of copperplate illustration by leading Spanish artists and engravers. The Biblioteca Nacional de España regards the 1780 Don Quixote as a landmark in the editorial history of Cervantes and in the history of Spanish manual printing.Ibarra's career coincided with the Bourbon reform of Spanish cultural institutions under Ferdinand VI and, above all, Charles III. His workshop became one of the principal material infrastructures through which the Spanish Enlightenment was given physical form. The books issued from his press demonstrate the close relationship between scholarship, royal patronage, the learned academies, the book trade, and the technical crafts of eighteenth-century Madrid.Family, Birth, and Early FormationIbarra was born in Zaragoza in July 1725. The exact day is given as 19 or 20 July in different modern records; the Biblioteca Virtual de Aragón gives 20 July, while the BNE authority record gives 19 July. His father, Juan Ibarra, was a manufacturer of silk taffeta, while his mother, Mariana Marín, was the sister of the printer Antonio Marín. Ibarra was also the younger brother of Manuel Ibarra, who became printer of the Pontifical and Royal University of Cervera.His professional education took place within this family network. He learned the printing trade in Cervera in association with his brother Manuel and subsequently continued his formation in Madrid, where he was connected with the workshop of his uncle Antonio Marín. The Universidad de Valladolid and the Biblioteca Histórica de la Universidad de Valladolid place his Cervera period before his move to Madrid in 1742, followed by the establishment of his own business in 1753.This apprenticeship was decisive. Unlike a printer who merely operated an inherited press, Ibarra acquired familiarity with the entire organization of the printing establishment: composition, correction, presswork, paper, type, workshop discipline, and the commercial relationship between printer, bookseller, patron, and author.Establishment in MadridIbarra established his own printing business in Madrid in 1753. His first establishment was in the Calle de las Urosas. In 1766 he transferred his workshop to the Calle de la Gorguera, a location situated in one of the principal commercial areas of eighteenth-century Madrid and close to the city's major booksellers and cultural institutions. Contemporary and bibliographical evidence confirms Ibarra's imprint from the Calle de la Gorguera from 1766 onward.The workshop grew rapidly. Ibarra participated in the organization of the Madrid printing and bookselling trade and was involved in the Real Compañía de Impresores y Libreros del Reino. The scale of his establishment eventually enabled him to execute very large scholarly and illustrated commissions requiring several presses, numerous compositors and pressmen, correctors, apprentices, engravers, and other specialized craftsmen.The workshop was therefore not simply a place where texts were mechanically reproduced. It was an integrated production centre in which the physical form of a book was planned in close relation to its intellectual and editorial purpose.Royal and Academic PatronageIbarra's reputation grew together with his relationship with the Bourbon court and the principal learned institutions of Madrid. He eventually received the title of Impresor de Cámara de Su Majestad, becoming one of the official printers associated with the royal establishment.His relationship with the Real Academia Española was particularly important. The Academy's own records show that Ibarra formally received the title of Impresor de la Real Academia on 3 June 1779, although he had already been printing for the institution for several years. The Academy recorded his death in November 1785 and immediately arranged for the continuation of its printing work by his widow and heirs.His workshop consequently became one of the principal typographical instruments of the Spanish Enlightenment.Among the Academy's earlier productions issued by Ibarra was the Gramática de la lengua castellana of 1771, an important example of the close relationship between the printer and the institutional codification of Spanish language and literature.Typographical TechniqueIbarra's fame rested above all on the extraordinary consistency of his production. He paid close attention to the quality and preparation of paper, the composition and density of ink, the regularity of type, the pressure and registration of the press, and the relationship between type, page, illustration, and margins. Accounts of his workshop have particularly emphasized the process known as satinado, by which paper was given a smoother and more uniform surface.His technical achievement should nevertheless not be reduced to a single “invention.” The distinctive quality of Ibarra's books resulted from the systematic coordination of established techniques and from his unusually exacting standards of production. He also worked within the broader movement toward improved Spanish type design. Important specialists associated with this typographical environment included Antonio Espinosa de los Monteros and Jerónimo Antonio Gil. The latter produced types specifically for the 1780 Don Quixote.The so-called “Ibarra” typeface became associated retrospectively with the visual qualities of his books and was subsequently revived in modern type design. The twentieth-century recovery of the Ibarra typeface was itself the subject of a major Zaragoza project devoted to the history and digitization of his typography.The 1772 SallustThe supreme typographical achievement of Ibarra's career before the Don Quixote was the 1772 edition of Sallust: Cayo Salustio Crispo, La conjuración de Catilina y la guerra de Jugurta, Madrid, por Joachin Ibarra, Impresor de Cámara del Rey Nuestro Señor, 1772.The translation was prepared by the Infante Don Gabriel de Borbón and revised under the supervision of Francisco Pérez Bayer. The BNE describes the volume as one of the peaks of Ibarra's activity and, more broadly, of the entire period of manual printing in Spain. The typographical design deliberately differentiated the Spanish translation from the Latin original. The Spanish was printed in italic type in a continuous line, while the Latin was set in roman type in two columns. The edition was printed on exceptionally fine paper and contained engraved illustrations associated with Mariano Salvador Maella and other artists.The book was produced in a very limited edition—120 copies—and functioned partly as a presentation volume. Its rarity, technical refinement, and close integration of typography and illustration helped make it one of the canonical examples of eighteenth-century Spanish book production.The 1772 Sallust also demonstrated the extent to which Ibarra's reputation had become international. His work was increasingly regarded not merely as competent Spanish printing but as a form of book production capable of competing with the most sophisticated European presses.The 1780 Don QuixoteIbarra's most famous production was the four-volume El ingenioso hidalgo Don Quixote de la Mancha, published in Madrid in 1780 for the Real Academia Española. The project was conceived as an authoritative Academy edition of Cervantes. Its scholarly apparatus included the Vida de Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra and an analysis of the Quixote by Vicente de los Ríos. The BNE records the edition as four folio volumes and identifies Ibarra as printer of the King and the Royal Academy.The physical production was exceptionally ambitious. Jerónimo Antonio Gil designed and cut types expressly for the project. The illustration programme involved major painters and engravers, including Antonio Carnicero, José del Castillo, Bernardo Barranco, Gregorio Ferro, José Brunete, Pedro Arnal, Juan Barcelón, Fernando Selma, Francisco Muntaner, and Manuel Salvador Carmona.The edition also included a map of the route of Don Quixote prepared by the geographer Tomás López on the basis of geographical observations associated with José de Hermosilla. The illustrations were consequently part of the intellectual programme of the edition rather than merely decorative embellishments. The Academy was presenting Cervantes as one of the foundational authors of Spanish national literary culture, while Ibarra's workshop provided the material form in which that cultural programme could be realized.The 1780 Don Quixote became one of the supreme achievements of eighteenth-century Spanish printing and remains one of the most important monuments of the European illustrated book.Major Scholarly and Literary ProductionsThe importance of Ibarra's workshop cannot be reduced to the two famous masterpieces.Among the important works printed under his imprint were editions of classical, historical, literary, linguistic, scientific, theological, and administrative texts. His production included works by or associated with Juan de Mariana, Antonio de Solís, Nicolás Antonio, Benito Jerónimo Feijoo, Benito Bails, Antonio Ponz, Antonio de Nebrija, Saint Augustine, and Buffon.Among the notable productions are:Dictionarium Aelii Antonii Nebrissensis, Madrid, 1771. The BNE records Ibarra as printer of this major Latin-Spanish lexicographical work.Gramática de la lengua castellana, composed by the Real Academia Española, Madrid, 1771.La conjuración de Catilina y la guerra de Jugurta, translated by the Infante Don Gabriel de Borbón, Madrid, 1772.Principios de matemática, by Benito Bails, Madrid, 1776, a three-volume mathematical treatise extensively illustrated with engraved plates.Viage de España, by Antonio Ponz, issued in numerous volumes beginning in 1776 and continuing beyond Ibarra's death; the BNE records volumes published under Ibarra's imprint from 1776 to 1788.Teatro crítico universal, by Benito Jerónimo Feijoo, eight volumes, 1778–1779, printed by Ibarra on behalf of the Real Compañía de Impresores y Libreros.El ingenioso hidalgo Don Quixote de la Mancha, four volumes, 1780.Historia natural, general y particular, translated from Buffon by José Clavijo y Fajardo, with the first volume appearing under Ibarra's imprint in 1785.These works demonstrate the breadth of his workshop's production: Ibarra was not merely the printer of luxury books but an important participant in the dissemination of the scientific, linguistic, historical, literary, and pedagogical culture of late eighteenth-century Spain.Bibliographical EnterprisesIbarra's workshop was also deeply involved in major bibliographical projects. The most important was the continuation of Nicolás Antonio's Bibliotheca Hispana. The Bibliotheca Hispana Nova appeared in 1783–1788, while the Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus followed in 1788. These publications extended beyond Ibarra's death and therefore properly belong to the history of his printing establishment rather than to his personal lifetime production alone.Their importance lies in the conjunction of bibliography, historical scholarship, and printing. The Ibarra establishment had become sufficiently large and institutionally important to participate in projects that were themselves part of the infrastructure of Spanish scholarship.Binding and the Material BookIbarra's activities were not confined strictly to printing. Recent research into the archives of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando has demonstrated that he also undertook bookbinding, although on a relatively modest scale. His workshop produced bindings in parchment, half-binding, and other ordinary formats, while luxury bindings were often entrusted to specialist workshops such as that of Antonio Sancha. This distinction is important. Ibarra should not be portrayed as one of the principal luxury bookbinders of eighteenth-century Madrid; rather, he combined printing with a limited amount of binding activity within the broader organization of his establishment.Workshop Organization and ScaleThe scale of the Ibarra establishment was exceptional for eighteenth-century Madrid. Large commissions such as the Don Quixote required the coordinated labour of compositors, correctors, pressmen, apprentices, engravers, type specialists, paper suppliers, illustrators, and booksellers. The workshop therefore anticipated in certain respects the increasingly rationalized organization of graphic production that would become characteristic of nineteenth-century printing. It nevertheless remained fundamentally a hand-printing establishment, dependent upon human labour, hand presses, skilled craftsmanship, and the physical preparation of individual sheets. Its achievement was thus one of organization and refinement rather than industrial mechanization.Death and Continuation of the PressJoaquín Ibarra died in Madrid on 13 November 1785. The Real Academia Española recorded his death in its proceedings and, recognizing his exceptional service, authorized the continuation of its printing work by his widow and heirs. The subsequent firm operated under the imprint Viuda de Ibarra, Hijos y Compañía, which remained active into the nineteenth century.The survival of the Ibarra imprint after 1785 illustrates the extraordinary prestige acquired by the workshop. The name “Ibarra” became not merely the surname of an individual printer but a mark of typographical authority.Historical SignificanceIbarra's importance in the history of European printing rests on the synthesis he achieved.He did not invent printing, paper finishing, copperplate illustration, or typefounding. His achievement was to integrate these techniques with exceptional consistency and to place them at the service of major intellectual projects. His books embodied several central characteristics of the Spanish Enlightenment:collaboration between printers and scholars;increasing institutionalization of learned publishing;royal and academic patronage;renewed attention to Spanish literary heritage;improvement of type design and typographical regularity;integration of text, illustration, and cartography;growing concern with the material quality of the book;and the transformation of the printed volume into an object of both scholarship and cultural prestige.The 1772 Sallust and 1780 Don Quixote are therefore not isolated luxury productions. They represent the culmination of a broader transformation of Spanish book culture during the reign of Charles III.Joaquín Ibarra remains consequently one of the central figures in the history of eighteenth-century Spanish typography and one of the clearest examples of how the material culture of the book participated in the intellectual ambitions of the European Enlightenment.Recent research has expanded the study of Ibarra beyond the traditional celebration of his typography. Particular attention has been given to his workshop organization, type design, binding activity, relations with academies, and the material production of eighteenth-century books. The study of the archives of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando has shown that Ibarra combined printing with limited bookbinding activity and that the workshop's binding production was generally modest rather than devoted to luxury bindings.The 1993 monograph directed by José Luis Acín Fanlo and Pablo Murillo López remains the fundamental modern monographic study of Ibarra. The volume contains 227 pages and extensive illustrations and includes studies of the history of the workshop, Ibarra's typography, and the modern recovery of the Ibarra typeface.The University of Navarra's virtual exhibition Joaquín Ibarra y Marín, impresor de su Magestad provides an important bibliographical framework for the study of Ibarra and situates him within the network of eighteenth-century Spanish printers, engravers, typefounders, and scholars.The commemoration of the tercentenary of Ibarra's birth in 2025 also generated renewed institutional interest in his biography and typography. The Universidad de Valladolid and the Universidad Complutense de Madrid both emphasized his central role in Spanish eighteenth-century printing and the continuing importance of his workshop for the history of the book.

academic_description: 4to (251x174 mm). [4], 121, [1 blank] pp. and 2 folding engraved plates: one showing a genealogical tree (Arbol cronologico de Estudios) and one with a large map of the province of Granada (Provincia de N. Padre S. Francisco de Granada), both signed “Vazq.z fc.” and the map dated 1783. Contemporary Spanish mottled calf, gilt spine, marbled edges, green silk bookmark (slightly worn and rubbed). Some marginal tears to the plates, a good, genuine copy.Rare first edition. Father Manuel María Trujillo was one of the most important Franciscan reformers of the Enlightenment era. He was personally committed to raising the cultural standards of both his Order and the Spanish Church. The precursor to his Exhortación Pastoral (Madrid, 1786) can be found in the Plan de Estudios de la Provincia de los Observantes de Nuestro Padre San Francisco de Granada (‘Study Plan of the Province of the Observants of Our Father St. Francis of Granada') published during his tenure as provincial of that province.The motives for his reform were primarily related to a climate of widespread decline within the Franciscan Order: an excessive proliferation of study houses, privileges and corruption in the conduct of the lecturers, and deficiencies in the student education. In his Plan de Estudios, Trujillo (which was closer to the University of Granada's stady plan than to those developed within the Order) designed the career path of the enlightened Franciscan: philosopher, theologian, moralist, and preacher. The work consisted of two parts: an analysis of the “ruin of literature” -that is, the cultural decline of the Province- and an exposition of the means to overcome it. Upon being appointed General Commissioner, Trujillo adopted this curriculum for the provinces and apostolic colleges of the Americas and the Philippines (cf. G. Areta Marigó, Propaganda Fide: memoria de la muerte, in: “La portentosa Vida de la Muerte Joachín Bolaños”, Madrid, 2016, p. 264; see also El Reino de Granada y el Nuevo Mundo, Granada, 1994, II, p. 215).
